rooms.desc: Flickering flames in clear glass globes strung from the railings of rooftop terraces illuminate the eastern end of the Street of Metalsmiths.  The sweet smell of blossoms perfumes the warm night air.  Blue doors give ingress to the shops of bladesmiths and weaponsmiths who offer their wares in the graceful white buildings gleaming softly in the moonlight.  From the southeast can be heard the gentle splashing of a fountain, nearly drowned out by the sound of clanging metal from the west.

The resonant clang of metal being hammered into shape rings through the air through the open doors of nearby shops.  Blasts of heat from the forges roll out of the flat-roofed white buildings and rise in transparent shimmers to meet the night sky.  Arranged in an extended geometric pattern, contrasting blocks of dark and light stone pave the ground.

Strung on silken cords between upright awning poles, clear blown glass globes hold twinkling flames that illuminate the patterned pavement.  In the wavering shadows, potted plants form a fresh, green border outside ivory buildings ornamented with raised arabesque designs.  Colorful mosaic tiles set in kaleidoscopic grids frame doors painted in various shades of blue that lead into the various buildings that line the street.

A tall poplar forms a natural bridge across the swiftly moving river, its roots still entangled in a great mass of deadwood on the western riverbank. A kingfisher perched on one of the silvered branches of the felled tree calmly watches the rushing waters for the glimmer of its next meal.

Curving away from the North Wall Road, a narrow byway slinks between crowds of shuttered buildings.  Overhead, a dingy awning stretched over keyhole arches straddling the alley provides escape from the harsh sun.  Holes poked through the fabric allow shafts of sunlight to pierce the gloom at irregular intervals.  Despite the shade, the air is hot and oppressive, each sweltering breeze tainted with the mingled odors of exotic spices, rotting garbage and decay.

As the street climbs up the great hill, so the packed stone buildings housing many city residents climb also.  The wall, on the other hand, built to avoid the hill, stays at the same height, contributing to the greater amount of eye-stinging sand at this level.

Several twisting passages meet in a labyrinthine tangle at the crest of the hill, where a steep cliff prohibits further progress to the south.  Mournful gusts of wind sweep showers of fine sand across the crumbling remains of buildings left to bake in the merciless sun.  One ancient stone construct, alone maintaining some semblance of its former glory, stands apart at the edge of the precipice.

Hot, dry wind blows over the rocky promontory, spraying endless clouds of abrasive sand over eroded hovels that lean away from the edge of the precipice in a miserable cluster.  To the north, west and south, the cliff drops away sharply.  Below, the vast, faceless expanse of the shimmering desert stretches to the horizon.

Perched high on the rocky hillside, windowless houses huddle together as if seeking protection from the elements, while far below, the city spreads out like a pool of glittering gems spilled onto the desert.  A tattered fabric awning, ripped from its moorings by the relentless winds, flaps uselessly against the sun-bleached wall of one house.  Wind-sculpted drifts of sand spill across the twisted alleyway, their forms endlessly changing at the whim of the breeze.

One winding alley tunnels under another, creating a squalid, enclosed thoroughfare between the North Wall Road and the maze of passages wending into the bowels of Golden Heights.  A sour stench, redolent of unwashed bodies and decomposing refuse, hangs in the suffocating air.  Despite the pitiful efforts of a soot-encrusted lantern, gloom overspreads the corridor.  In the dim light, shadowed doorways blend almost seamlessly with the filthy walls in which they stand.

Along the side of the road, a small guardhouse clings to the scant portion of the wall reaching these heights on the hill.  Red and black uniformed guards slow the flow of traffic here, barring most of the city's poor from proceeding to the lower, wealthier depths of the city.

The road, flanked by the ever-present guardian that is the wall, steadily climbs up a large hill in the city's northwest sector.  The higher the street ascends, the more sand one can find tossed about.  Bland and nondescript buildings occupy the entire stretch.

Drab, stone buildings huddle tightly about the street like frightened children around a midnight campfire.  The prodigious people of the city, wasting little time, rush to and fro the buildings and down the packed street.

The roadway, winding through a tight corridor consisting of packed buildings and the soaring wall, begins a slight elevation to the west, while the ground further east is still flat and level.  The dust and sand along the street is of a somewhat heavy concentration here.

Plain, stone buildings crowd the narrow and sand splattered street.  The thick wall of the desert city casts its weight upon the road, while the denizens scurry about their tasks under the watchful eye of a giant.

Sounds of clicking and rustling emerge from the city's outskirts as the infinite sands of the desert batter against the massive wall looming above.  The thin, snakelike trail is heavily occupied by homes and buildings pressed closely together.

Above the thickly packed residential buildings wound along the street, the impressive heights of the two temples and the palace can be discerned by a watchful eye.  Far-off sights on the other side of the street are obscured by the looming bulk of the wall.

The entrance to Sh'kial's Square is marked by a tall wrought-iron gate.  Fountaining up to either side are a pair of leafy potted plants, shaded from the full advance of the sun by a pair of unassuming stone overhangs projecting from the gate supports.

A low, rippling wall surrounds the great Dragon Temple, rising and falling in coils etched with rambling geometric patterns.  Here and there an elegant eth'ral'khh glyph marks the stone -- the carver's signature, cleverly hidden amongst the coils.

Cowled monks and hooded priests stride purposefully through the intersection, traveling between the temples and the guildhall to the north.  From somewhere nearby can be heard the soft chorus of reverent voices intoning hymns.  A tall building, its stucco aged to the color of ivory by long exposure to the desert sun, stands looming over the crossroads.  The center of attention upon the cobbled street is reserved for an exquisite fountain in the middle of the way.

Irregular grey slate blocks pave the empty square, forming a dull counterpoint to the grand majesty of the temple that rises suddenly from the ground.  A stone wall surrounds the temple grounds, sharply dividing the bare stone of the square from the sacred gardens within.  The destination of many a pilgrim, well-worn marble steps lead up into the famed Temple of Hav'roth.

The firm stone wall that surrounds the temple in the middle of the square runs unbroken around the grounds.  No buildings open onto the square from the south, forming a uniformly blank wall at ground level, with only a few windows above.  A long shallow arcade fronts a quiet building on the west side of the empty square, with no apparent entry to the interior.

Potted plants surround the entrance to a quaint shop tucked beneath a silken green and gold awning propped up by a pair of cedar poles.  Priests debate the finer point of theology in low but audible tones as they pass and young acolytes run along the road to their lessons for the day.  A fragrance of incense drifts through the way, carried along by the warm air.

Only a few ochre-painted doors open from the whitewashed walls into the quiet avenue, and they look little used.  A heavy bronze censer stands in the center of the intersection, incense lingering about the dull metal in twisting smoky trails.  The dull industrial clank of metal on metal sounds from somewhere to the southwest, anchoring the Street of Priests into the material world.

A crisp and dry nightly breeze seems almost perpetual to the tiny hill lifted up from the surrounding city here.  Across Muspar'i, save for the occasional pocket of unceasing activity where flickering torches split the night below, all rests in contemplative slumber.

Darkness hangs heavily in the stillness that drapes this sector of the Street of Stoneworkers, muffling what small nighttime sounds might otherwise be heard.  The daytime bustle has retreated to the residential districts of the city, and all is quiet.

Several tables in this small shop contain a wide array of bones, some quite crude in their craftsmanship and clearly made of actual bones, while others exhibit a fine make and appear to be created of more coveted materials.  A painting on the far wall, displaying a touch of elegance in the banal bustle of the merchant streets, illustrates a harsh western steppe.

Throngs of well-dressed shoppers promenade the exclusive district where North King's Passage, connecting Shorka's Square with the rest of the city, intersects the Street of Metalsmiths.  Arranged in a geometric pattern that continues to the east and west, contrasting dark and light paving stones cover the ground.  Crescent arches trimmed with narrow, inset bands of semi-precious stone open into creamy white buildings hung with white silk awnings that offer relief from the harshest rays of the sun.

Encircling an oval reflecting pool that sparkles in the sunlight, elegant shops with columned arches line the cul-de-sac at the western end of the Street of Metalsmiths.  The fragrance of roses perfumes the warm air, wafting from climbing rosebushes that ascend to second story balconies and bedeck the ornate railings with a profusion of glorious pink blooms.

The southern stretch of the red-tile North King's Passage connects the Street of Metalworkers with S'zella's Square, one of Muspar'i's main gathering places.  In olden days, the royal family would use this route to reach the square and address the populace.

To the west lies the blood red North King's Passage, which runs from S'zella's Square directly to Shorka's Square and the palace, allowing the king to make his ceremonial trips to this gathering place.  A large statue of S'zella looks out over the square from a bronze perch, and rows of benches huddle around the famed poet.

Whitewashed walls stretch eastward along the avenue, spotted by bright blue doors at irregular intervals along the way.  A large inn occupies much of the southern side of the street, abutting a tall open arch leading further west to S'zella Square.  The occasional caravan rattles through the arch and down the cobbled road, seeking an end to its long journey.

The wide, greyish-blue limestone arches of the city's caravansary line the north side of the street, its shady interiors sheltering the city's visiting merchants from the bustle and heat of the city.  In the street, caravans jostle against one another in a near constant snarl of traffic.  Traders and caravan drivers shout over the tops of animals in vain attempts to argue over rates or issue orders.

The gentle sound of splashing water drifts in from the southwest, a melodic counterpoint to the soft sounds of people drifting along the street.  Whitewashed buildings and small shops rise up on either side, each decorated with mosaics of glazed tile in soothing sea colors of green and blue.  Small torches repose in earthenware holders against the coming of night.

The low wall continues around a sharp corner, its golden coils lifting and angling away to the east.  It glitters faintly in the light of the sun, unlit torches placed at even spans along its length.  The Street of Potters can be seen stretching away to the south, though the Square has no access to it.

Two great golden dragons, one with a foreleg raised as if in judgement over a petitioner, the other rearing up in protection over those who stand before it, mark the break in the long golden-coiled fence surrounding the Dragon Temple.  Beyond the tall wrought-iron fence between them, glimpses of the temple itself can just barely be seen.

The tall sandstone mass of the Cleric's Guildhall peeks over the tops of the buildings to the east, but no path appears to lead to it from here.  The gleaming gold sheathed domes of the temple lifts up, standing out from its dreary surroundings.  Apparently by some unspoken law, no building has a door opening onto the grey flagstone square, lending it a sense of strange loneliness.

Opposite the splendor of the Great Temple of Hav'roth is a less than glamorous view of the hill known as Golden Heights.  In an unwelcome accompaniment to the view is the horrid odor that the breeze will bring when the wind comes down off of the infamous bluff.  Birds land upon the grey flagstone of the square to forage for whatever tidbits they can find, but seldom stay long on the barren surface.

The street slopes down to the heavy sandstone pile of the Cleric Guildhall at the end of the way, with its doors and tiled roofs the same pale red color as the dull stucco walls of the buildings on either side of the road.  A bizarre variety of statues and colorful icons reside within a plethora of niches carved from between the pillars at the front of the guildhall.  Out of the way of passing strollers, an old S'Kra priest sits upon a bench, napping the day away.

Crimson tiles pave the street that connects the palace and other government buildings in Shorka's Square to the northwest with the center of public life, S'zella's Square, to the southeast.  The tiles are worn to a paler rose color around the edges by time and weather, and by the feet of travelers making their way through the city.

Shorka's statue presides over the comings and goings in this square, the city's bureaucrats beneath her gaze as they cross the mosaicked stretches between various government offices, as if in her service still.  To the southeast, the North King's Passage meanders through the twisting curves of the city, leading away from the square.

The city's monumental statue of Shorka dominates the entirety of this square, her back to the palace named in her honor as her head turns to the spiraling bulks of the two temples.  All around the queen's commemoration, government offices go about their work.
The back of Shorka's statue is visible from this quieter and more secluded corner of the square.  The Queen's hand stretches high into the heavens, as if clutching at the whole of the firmament.

Stern yet matronly, Shorka's statue watches over her children and the other denizens of the sun's egg.  Buildings, distinguished by the waveringly graceful banner of the city, stand welcoming and open to the people traversing the roads.

Rows and rows of metal benches, crafted in the city's own forges, fill this square.  As much a public gathering place as the boisterous Street of Performers, S'zella's Square is packed with eager food vendors and their exotic delicacies.

Benches fill the square named after famed poet and musician S'zella, who likely would be pleased that his square so closely borders the Street of Instrument Makers.  The melodic sounds of that road add a pleasing touch to the gatherings held here.

Bearing southeast from S'zella's Square, the Street of Instrument Makers bears an air of quiet dignity.  Occasional music, rising faintly in brief experimental riffs, filters onto the streets from nearby shops.

Pale blue tile, the color of the gentle waves of a southern lagoon, pave the road that flows from the Street of Nobles, past the Street of Instrument Makers and on to the entertainments in Heketha Square.  The South King's Passage allows the well-off to avoid the bustling crowds of the mercantile streets.

A long veranda, curtained with weighty crimson silk embroidered heavily along its length with racing geometric designs, extends along the length of one luxurious manor here.  A chiseled rail of white stone parallels it, as if trying to ward off the property it guards from the surrounding city.

A tiny pond set into the cobbles of one yard and surrounded by reeds gives off the unmistakable scent of standing water.  Minute fish swim languidly just beneath the surface, their larger cousins no doubt deigning to remain in the cooler depths below.

Layer upon layer of shelving fills this cramped shop, each wooden plank hosting a multitude of stone eggs in a variety of divergent shapes and sizes.  The eggs, clearly the central focus of the store, are popular items in Muspar'i as it is believed they bring good fortune.

Bright glissandos emanate occasionally from the well-traveled door of the string shop nestled here in the center of the Instrument Makers.  From further back in the shop, one can periodically catch the twang of a less healthy sound as an aspiring sitarist takes lessons from Dhralduum Lohogi'hhskapo, Muspar'i's premiere instrumental Bard.

The blue tile of South King's Passage connects the Street of Instrument Makers here with the Heketha Square.  The street is mostly ceremonial, used by the king and other nobles when they wish to awe the less fortunate before a night of celebration in the theater.

Stacks of paper wobble upon wooden desks, the desert heat belying the Zolurenesque quality of the room -- bustling clerks prove that bureaucracy is universal, even in the sweltering, eternally-summer sands of Velaka.  S'Kra guards, armed with wicked dirks and belts bearing vials of brownish liquid, watch over the office's lockboxes.

Sarhali's studio carries a scent of newness, as if the walls have been recently painted and the floor laid with fresh sawdust.  The tiny shop has an air of quiet pride and accomplishment, from the curtained archway leading outside to the baked tile floor of the gallery to the east.  A S'Kra mannequin with its hands upraised as if in a dance stands gracefully in the center of the room.

The line of stalls drops away here to make way for a set of tiny shops, none of which save one -- a snugly placed two-story building with whitewashed walls and a slanting tile roof -- display any outstanding signature.  Sparing greenery, carefully pruned, nestles between the shops, bringing an occasional flare of color to the demure, sophisticated storefronts.

The gallery is simple, its white walls unadorned but clean and the floor tiles likewise scrupulously swept but bearing no carving.  The simplicity of the room leaves the onlooker unburdened by detail, the better to appreciate the quality of Sarhali's merchandise.

Stalls continue down the busy street, but those offering the occasional ribbon or trinket afoot have greatly decreased in number.  The stalls themselves, occasionally curtained with a more expensive cloth, carry more pride in their demeanor.  Proprietors bow more deeply, and if their gestures lack the polish of nobility, they make a brave and often effective attempt at mimicking it.

Nestled deep into the Street of Cloth Weavers is the Naarti'hhs'naartin -- the jewel of jewels, the renowned dwelling place and mastercraft shop of Malkhhan t'nar'Daarni.  Set a fashionable distance away from the bustle of the street, this cul de sac holds the three-storied, triple-winged building snugly beneath the shade of rare and carefully tended uuryvhh trees.

A series of low buildings squat close to the road, huddled like hens before a feed tray.  The Street of Cloth Weavers extends to the west, where bright colors flash from the displays of silk and other finery, but this street is deceptively drab in comparison.

Fanciful silk curtains offset a rainbow colored door in shockingly dissonant bright hues.  Elaborately crafted instruments are creatively strewn about a likewise silk bedecked table in this shop's center, the wares seeming more like some jeweler's gewgaws than mouthpieces of a bard's musical talent.

Small, thick carpets intricately patterned across their length layer the sanded stone floor, their only common feature being their lush, velvety softness.  In the middle of it all stands Srenhaar, who watches over his merchandise with a lordly air, planted opposite a curtained archway to the south leading to his workroom.

Tall piles of stacked stone line the street, narrowing it considerably.  Although space is at a premium, several storefronts manage to crowd their way toward the narrow path, looming high overhead.  A fine, powdery dust, the byproduct of the stonemasons working here, hangs perpetually in the air.

The close clay buildings seem to crowd in upon themselves in this southern corner of the Street of Stoneworkers.  Here the soft stone shows its age, with hairline cracks running across the occasional wall or storefront, some extending from the ground below to the crest of the structure several stories overhead.

The looming gate of the city watches over this square from the southeast, while less-bustling and quieter streets packed with merchant shops run to the north.  From the northwest the constant, dull roar of the crowds filling Tuul Yamshuk Staho, the primary road for all visitors, can be heard, an ever-present heartbeat for this section of the city.

Rows of fine sandpits line the walls of Srenhaar's workroom, filled with luxurious sand in every imaginable color, from deep greens to the palest of whites.  A rough table with three chairs arranged around it sits in the center of the area, a motley collection of expensive wood fragments scattered across its surface.

A curtain of multi-colored beads hangs in front of a closed screen that divides the purchasing room from Shoiya's shop.  Sitting behind a counter of dark rosewood, an elderly Elothean woman polishes a jeweler's loupe hanging from her neck.  Several boxes on the counter hold various gems nestled in black velvet cloth.

Each performer that passes reaches up to touch the outstretched carved hand of a magnificent statue that dominates the street.  Having paid homage to the noble S'Kra depicted, they continue on their way, returning their attentions to the crowds that gather to watch the never-ending sideshows.  A display of paintings are sheltered under the awning of a nearby building.  The budding artist hovers protectively in front of the oils as he hawks his greatest works.

Joyous sounds, like those of a lively carnival, parade into the Heketha Square from the north, where the Street of Performers merges with the square.  Singers, storytellers, and dancers of all ilk keep the masses entertained there, while a more sophisticated crowd finds its enjoyment from the theater dominating the square.

As a stark contrast to the ever-present sounds of celebration coming from the northern parts of the square, where it intersects with the Street of Performers, a more sedate sound flits through this corner.  The Street of Instrument Makers angles off to the west, stretching into the distance.

The rambling music fluting continuously from a nearby shop could not quite be called a cacophony, but comes perilously close.  The nasal tones of a double-reeded yarghul combine with the elegant rise and fall of the shaku, and, surprising amidst the more sophisticated instruments, the simple shepherd's minjayrah.

The arching entryway to the Heketha Theater stands at this part of the square, where it serves the wealthier citizens of the city with its high-class entertainment.  The building rises above the blue-tile street like the cresting wave that gives it its name.

The Bard's Guild takes up a large portion of Heketha Square's corner here, facing off with the theater on the other side of the square.  An endless promenade of performers traverses the short route between the guildhall and the rambunctious Street of Performers eastward.

Colorful woven tablecloths cover several round tables of a small street side cafe.  An elaborate scrolled ironwork railing sets off the tables and chairs from the onslaught of traffic that continually presses down the street.  Various patrons sip their drinks, huddled in private conversations oblivious to the pace of life around them, while others watch the unending parade of performers that frequent this spot.

A great silver spire representing the solitary civilization here shoots up from the mosaic ground of the Great Gate Square like an isolated plant struggling to survive in the scorching desert.  The statuary monument appears to be a silver spike protruding straight upward while a serpent-like shape coils and curls around it.

This small square serves as an intersection between the various streets of the city.  Gentle tunes from the Street of Instrument Makers to the west serve as a harmonic backdrop to the laughter and singing from the Street of Performers.  All that clashes with the raucous, chaotic sounds of the Great Gate Square to the northeast.

The southmost end of the Street of Instrument Makers, leading further southeast to the Street of Alchemists and east to Gate Square, sharply contrasts the two adjacent atmospheres with its air of constant musical movement.  A rhythmic beat that pulses with the heart keeps a constant undertone to travelers' shifting feet.

The smooth-sanded walks and elegant statuary nestled into this cozy turn of the street make it clear that the denizens of this district enjoy the finer things in life.  While a certain amount of noise filters down from the nearby Street of Instrument Makers, the tasteful gardens and spacious architecture contend that this remains one of the most sophisticated places in the city.

A tasteful jumble of color sets this section of the Street of Nobles apart from its neighbors.  While most of the manors keep their gardens behind discreet whitewashed walls, the front gates of one stately edifice along this row teem with climbing greenery.

The street narrows to little more than an alley with ramshackle buildings stacking up in a crazed pattern of construction.  Stone fronts rise next to stucco and wood, with no regard to aesthetics whatsoever, built instead on whatever was the least expensive and most readily available material.  Equally odd scents drift up and down the street to irritate the nose and eyes, an unavoidable side effect of the alchemical profession.

Old wooden beams reach across the street overhead, giving the impression the buildings on either side are holding each other up.  The poles are liberally strung with herbs and less identifiable items drying in the open air, making their true purpose apparent.  Most of the figures passing along the way take no notice of the strange gaudy sight of the poles, their own robes carrying the odd stains that mark them as practicing alchemists.

The Great Gate Square stretches northward, allowing access to the gate and many of the mercantile streets, as well as the massive boulevard known as the Tuul Yamshuk Staho.  To the south, odd smells and sounds float on the desert winds from the quirky Street of Alchemists.

The draconic hulk known as the Great Gate of Muspar'i dominates the square named after it, towering over the mosaic path underfoot.  Serving as the near-singular point of travel between the merchant city and the Velaka Desert, the gate is at once both intimidating and awe-inspiring.

rooms.desc: The narrow street pulls back ever so slightly to allow enough room for the traffic to flow around a statue that has been given the place of honor in the middle of intersection.  Robed figures stride purposefully through the street, intent on their tasks for the day.  Unusual and occasionally caustic odors linger in the air, drifting out of the workshops and storefronts of the many practitioners that call this street home.

The narrow street snakes along between the buildings that lean far in over the way, lending a feeling of claustrophobia to the lane.  Small bundles of both familiar and exotic herbs sit behind glass windows in the many storefronts, next to cryptically labeled ceramic pots.  Strange aromas that tickle and tingle the senses waft out from doorways and linger throughout the street.

The way ends in a small dim square that the buildings overshadow so far as to give the impression of a man-made cave and the sky is little more than a patch of daylight high above.  With no breeze, the still air of the dead end seems to diminish the distinct odors of the street to a dull mustiness.  Lacking through traffic the end of the street is rather quiet, with only the occasional pedestrian moving directly towards their destination.

Pale buildings line the street, reflecting the glow of the sunlight.  On the ground, bits of confetti swirl against the paving stones, occasionally lofting high into the air to perform a sprightly dance with an errant breeze.  The wind is fickle, however, quickly casting its partner aside to fall in colorful puddles of paper upon the ground, scuffed by passing feet until a streetsweeper's broom gathers it into oblivion.

Always a festival of artwork and music, the Street of Performers is one of the liveliest streets in the city.  Peals of laughter and bursts of applause fill the air as wandering performers of all kinds amuse, entertain and delight the people who crowd the area at all hours.  Colorful silken awnings on poles help to keep off the hot sun and add splashes of bright decoration to the celebration.

Sounds of clicking and rustling emerge from the city's outskirts as the infinite sands of the desert batter against the massive wall looming above.  The thin, snakelike trail is heavily occupied by homes and buildings pressed closely together.

Narrow alleyways spike through the crowded street like the quills of a dyrachis.  The road, filled with high stone buildings and tiny homes, clings desperately to the hillside, vainly clawing toward the wall for protection.  The wall, however, failing to reach these heights, offers no safety from the buffeting sands of the Golden Heights.

Along the side of the road, a small guardhouse clings to the scant portion of the wall reaching these heights on the hill.  Red and black uniformed guards slow the flow of traffic here, barring most of the city's poor from proceeding to the lower, wealthier depths of the city.

Curving away from the North Wall Road, a narrow byway slinks between crowds of shuttered buildings.  Overhead, a dingy awning stretched over keyhole arches straddling the alley provides escape from the harsh sun.  Holes poked through the fabric allow shafts of sunlight to pierce the gloom at irregular intervals.  Despite the shade, the air is hot and oppressive, each sweltering breeze tainted with the mingled odors of exotic spices, rotting garbage and decay.

A few benches and enthusiastic food vendors fill this square, which often serves as a gathering spot for the people of the city.  To the east, the great boulevard of the Tuul Yamshuk Staho provides for every need of the city's newcomers and visitors.

Whitewashed walls reflect the light from windows, giving them a strange ghostly hue in the night.  Occasional sounds of revelry carry on the air from somewhere to the west.  A wall topped with slate blue tiles separates the Carousel Square from the staho, but no gate blocks the wide archway leading through the wall to the square.

A thin channel of water divides the sandstone cobbles of the square, lending a sense of calm movement to the residential area.  Night winds stir the towering palm trees, spreading their shadowy fronds back and forth over the rooftops.  Each palatial house has been angled to face the central masterpiece -- a fountain of the namesake goddess -- as if in permanent homage.

Large windows ring the room, allowing a breeze to enter and cool Shh'yris as he labors at his forge.  The building, unlike most on Surlaenis, is made entirely of stone.  A large rack upon one wall is filled with tools of the smith's art.

The street broadens slightly at a terminus of variegated sandstone structures accented with pieces of glazed tile and fronted by smoothly curving clay jugs spilling over with hardy green vines.  Doors and arches punctuate the linked facades at intervals, giving passage into the various shops open for business in this quiet, drowsy part of the city.

The buildings arch out over the street from both sides, obscuring the sky and blocking most of the ambient light.  Barely visible within the darkness is a narrow doorway, set flush with the sandstone walls.

Tawny sandstone structures line the street, their rounded corners and irregular outlines vaguely resembling great cats huddled sleepily together against the chill desert night.  Set into the facade of one small shop is a hexagonal window, giving glimpses of the wares within.

Every now and then, a passerby flips a coin into the fountain and whispers requests for peace and luck to the limestone goddess rising from the watery depths.  The soft splashes mimic the water burbling through the dark furrow splitting the cobbled street.  Rows of dark palm trees shelter the houses at this point of the square, reinforcing the neighborhood's angled symmetry.

The road winds among low, rounded hills barely deserving of the name.  Clumps of trees around the base of the hills thin out rapidly as bare rock rises out of the good earth.  The ragged summits are worn and weathered with age.

Great piles of coal fill the corner of the room.  The forge fire burns with white-hot flames, fueled by the coal and the efforts of Shh'yris's apprentices who labor at the bellows.  Sweat pours from their bodies, only to sizzle as it strikes the hot stone floor.

The courtyard is planted with low growing herbs that form a pleasing pattern of mounds set against small white pebbles.  The focal point of the garden is a small white statue of a unicorn, her head bowed and horn resting humbly upon the ground.  A bench rests beneath the shelter of the overhanging roof, and despite the traffic in and out of the healers' quarters, it is a peaceful spot, as the interior light filters softly through the paper screens.

Light blue and green cushions cover the floor, placed there for guests waiting with friends and family to see the empath.  White paper walls glow in the light from several lanterns hanging from the ceiling.  An archway of white birch is set in the northern wall, leading to the empath.

Plump cushions, and the patients lying on top of them, litter the floor.  A section of the paper screen wall has been removed to allow a breeze to enter.  Bloody bandages fill a basket in the corner of the room.  A young Elothean woman tends the patients lying on the floor.

Water splashes down a slick rock chute built into the hillside on the far side of the pond, tumbling into the dark green water to send ripples shimmering across the surface.  A weathered grey pier juts out into the pond, giving residents a launching point from which to dive.  At night, the sound of crickets mingles with the hoarse croaks of frogs serenading the moons.

Several sections of the paper walls have been removed, creating windows to let the cool breeze enter.  Beyond the windows lie the multicolored rock gardens that surround the government buildings, as well as the crushed shell path ringing the lake.  A clerk sits behind a white birch counter, waiting for those who need to pay their debts to the Tribunal.

Tiered marble benches occupy a large portion of the square here, arranged in a half circle around an open expanse of darkened sandstone tiles.  Nearby, the central statue gives off a soft glow, bathing the area in a bluish light.

Wrapped in the tranquil embrace of night, an overwhelming quiet has descended upon the square.  Light emanates from the central statue, casting a soft, bluish glow over the now darkened sandstone tiles that encircle its base.

The sound of fabric flapping in the night breezes comes down to the street from somewhere overhead, beyond the range of sight.  An inn to one side has seen better days, but still looks well off with what customers it manages to attract.  The crowds of the day have dissipated, leaving only the occasional patron stepping into the inn for the night.

Discordant sounds roll out of an upper level window down to the street, shattering the quiet of night.  Hand blown lanterns, now the only source of light, cast their kaleidoscope of colors on the faces of passersby.  The flickering lights highlight an older S'Kra leaning drunkenly against an ironwork railing as he reels from the effects of his late visit to a local pub.

Soft light from the central statue casts a bluish glow over this portion of the square, illuminating the darkened sandstone tiles.  Chiseled granite steps lead up towards the ornately carved doors of the Royal Library, beckoning all to enter within.

Light from the central statue casts its soft bluish glow over this portion of the square where sandstone tiles have been arranged in an intricate mosaic.  Several elegantly carved marble benches rest nearby, sitting solemnly beneath the canopy of some palm trees.

The Street of Scribes ends in a small cul-de-sac, where a wooden bench, the perfect comfort for errant readers, is set beside a stunning golden monument in the center of the circle.  Beyond the street's buildings, all huddled close together, the massive temples of the city blot out the northern horizon.

In the midst of the narrow Street of Scribes stands a large silver obelisk, serving as an island that the crowd, bustling from shop to shop, must flow around.  Signs of scrolls, inkpots, and tomes hang in the windows of the shops bundled along the street.

A narrow street branches off here from the expansive Square of Sanyrsen.  The elegant arches of the royal academy and the imposing towers of the Warrior Mage Guildhall, the square's major landmarks, are easily visible here, looming over the small buildings crowded in along this street.  The stores here are all well kept and decked in fineries not often seen on the poorer merchant streets, suggesting that the shopkeeps here cater to a wealthier clientele.

Several twisting passages meet in a labyrinthine tangle at the crest of the hill, where a steep cliff drops away into empty darkness, prohibiting further progress to the south.  Mournful gusts of wind sweep showers of fine sand across the crumbling remains of buildings lying shrouded in shadows.  One ancient stone construct, alone maintaining some semblance of its former glory, stands apart at the edge of the precipice.

Hot, dry wind blows over the rocky promontory, spraying endless clouds of abrasive sand over eroded hovels that lean away from the edge of the precipice in a miserable cluster.  To the north, west and south, the cliff drops away sharply into a vast sea of darkness.

Perched high on the rocky hillside, windowless houses huddle together as if seeking protection from the elements, while far below, the lights of the city sparkle like a pool of starlight spilled onto the desert.  A tattered fabric awning, ripped from its moorings by the relentless winds, flaps listlessly in the sultry night breeze.  Shadows spill across the twisted alleyway, concealing its secrets within a shifting cloak of darkness.

Curving away from the North Wall Road, a dark, narrow byway slinks between crowds of shuttered buildings.  A guttering lantern casts strange, shifting patterns of light and shadow onto the surrounding walls and the dingy awning stretched overhead.  Even at night the air is hot and oppressive, each sweltering breeze tainted with the mingled odors of exotic spices, rotting garbage and decay.

A few residents meander through the square, though most of the neighborhood's tourists are absent due to night's darkness enshrouding the communal fountain.  A small manmade stream parts the sandstone street, and the water moves swiftly along its route like blood through a vein.  The houses and palm trees, all facing toward the square's middle, enclose the area and feature the dim city skyline as their backdrop.

A wide arc of gold-veined white marble columns supports one of the many domes of the temple and marks the boundary between the portico and the greenery of the sacred gardens beyond.  Birds roost for the night near the roof, finding perches among the ornately scrolled stonework.  An artfully carved archway in the temple wall reveals a stairway leading down below the main level of the temple.

Columns of purple quartz rise stoically toward the vaulted ceiling high above, supporting the rough-hewn obsidian walls of the Temple.  Embroidered gold carpeting marks a clear path beneath them, receding deeper into the shadowy confines of the structure.  Wooden torches rest within iron sconces set high upon the columns, casting a dim, flickering light upon the area.

The courtyard is barren of ornament, and black gritty sand is raked in a stark pattern over the enclosed yard.  The roof of the building overhangs to provide little shelter from wind and rain -- a most unpleasant place to be waiting in bad weather.  A sturdy metal door at the far end of the courtyard is the only entrance into the windowless building.

Torches spaced along the length of the glittering golden wall cast a ruddy light along the temple path.  Dancing fitfully in the night air, they drape playful, ever-moving shadows across the intricate patterns of the dragon's-coil wall.

Gurgles from the central fountain follow the water as it flows into a narrow channel spanning the length of the street.  Lights from the windows of Shorka's Palace squeeze through the tall palm trees overhead to stripe both the houses and cobblestone.  Since all of the residences in the quiet neighborhood face inward, illumination dots the night from every angle of the square.

Inside the hollow trunk of a huge sequoia, nearly as old as Sana'ati Dyaus, is the Grand Hall of Izma Ru'ef University.  Along the curved, arching walls are carved bas reliefs in the native wood, scenes of the glory of the Elven Empires of Elanthia.  Busts sculpted of precious hardwoods stand on pedestals in a semi-circle along the hall, likenesses of eminent lorethews, Elven and non-Elven, who have taught at the University.

Darkness muffles this normally bustling avenue in a cloak of subdued neutrality.  While the occasional hopeful crier still plies his wares by torchlight, most have retreated to their pallets, wherever those meager dwellings might be.

A single lamp burns brightly in the gloom of the tiny office, creating a claustrophobic feeling of eternal twilight.  A battered pine chair, a steel manacle dangling from one of its slats, sits next to a desk covered by stacks of dusty parchment.  Squeezed into a corner, a barrel has been set up as a makeshift table and holds the remains of the guards' last card game.

A passing breeze occasionally stirs the heavy curtains bordering a long veranda here, bravely lifting and parting the hem of the heavy silk.  A soft glow from beyond the curtain, escaping in shards of light when the fabric is disturbed, indicates that its owners have not yet retired to sleep, but no sounds further betray their activities.

Faint light shimmers off of the tiny pond set here, its surface dyed an inky black by night, and reflects upward to throw flickering patterns on the surrounding stone.  Small, expensively fragranced oil lamps, their wicks sheltered from nightly breezes by tiny panes of glass, strategically illuminate the languid water garden.

The trees thin slightly here, opening up around the ruins of a cabin.  The vine-choked structure struggles to stand under the weight of a fallen tree, with the occasional foreboding creak emanating from its boards.  Off to one side, a pile of rocks marks the location of a crumbling well.

A strong odor of rotting vegetation fills this small cabin, despite planks missing at varying intervals leaving the area open to the outside.  Dead branches reach through the broken ceiling above like long, bony fingers, in contrast to the tender seedlings pushing up through the floorboards.  A small, rotting area rug is pulled back in one corner, revealing a trapdoor.

A rusted lantern hanging from above shines a gentle glow over this space, which is little more than a cave carved in the vague shape of a room.  Makeshift tables and shelves line the walls, covered with an assortment of gears and metal scraps.  Heavy wooden supports stand at the north and south ends of the area, framing parts of the cavern that were left in their natural states.

Water bubbles up from a crystal clear spring before overflowing into a smooth rock chute in the hillside.  The chute twists and turns as it runs down the slope until it finally ends a few feet above the deep green waters of Willow Pond.

The path curves sharply to the southwest and southeast, hugging a cluster of stalactites and stalagmites.  A gear is deeply embedded in the rock, almost appearing as though it was naturally formed along with the stone.

Deep gouges are cut in the walls, like scars in the stone, forming clean furrows as though the tool used was slicing through clay instead of hard rock.  A ruddy stain, vaguely resembling a handprint, mars the surface alongside the gash.

Curving gently, the tunnel is shaped in such a way that it makes it difficult to tell which directions various skittering noises are coming from.  Overhead, roots squeeze through cracks, further dampening sounds.

The coolness of the air is heightened by the addition of moisture and creating a scent similar to dust after the rain.  Droplets of water cling to the stone walls, making them look as though they're perspiring.

Cracks spread across the stone walls in an intricate cobweb pattern, as if something with massive strength punched the rock.  A small clump of lichen clings to one of the fractures, following the jagged line like a tiny, greenish lightning bolt.

Streaks from foot traffic cut through the grime to reveal cracked tiles composing the once majestic image of a dragon grasping Elanthia between massive jaws.  From the walls to the ceiling, the entire room is in a complete state of disrepair, ravaged by the onslaught of time and unwelcome looters, squatters and miscreants.

Nearly splintered in two, what used to be an ironwood desk clutters the room's western side.  Crumpled papers and broken quills litter the floor, evidence that the broken furniture likely housed some of the complex's files.  The layers of shredded documents upon the ground resemble the covering of ripped parchments still clinging to the walls like flaky sheets of bark to a birch tree.

With a table stationed between two couches, the room was likely a lounge area for residents while the building was in operation.  Now, however, the dilapidated furniture serves no more purpose than to exist as a perpetual eyesore in the collage of destruction.

Overflowing bags of refuse border a broken door, the garbage left forever just footsteps from the dump neighboring the lot outside.  It makes no difference, since the rest of the halls and rooms harbor the same grunge and filth.  The rotting odor is also omnipresent, as if it oozes from all of the stained sandstone walls like an invisible slime.

Looking more like trash flung haphazardly across the ground than an intentional embellishment, the shredded remains of a runner extend from the landing all the way to the end of the split-level hall.  Insect carcasses congregate along the edges, with the occasional rodent skeleton joining the morbid death party.  Wax drippings along the smoke-stained walls point to where candles used to light the area.

The ratty carpet bunches unevenly in places, making travel inconvenient and precarious.  Massive chunks are missing from the ceiling, revealing patches of the sky not obscured by neighboring buildings.  The city's constant companion, sand, certainly does not shy away from imposing its presence here either.

Notes of urban life trickle into the hallway from several holes in the roof.  Every little noise echoes off the sandstone walls and travels in and out of the opened apartments.  The splotched, threadbare runner fails to buffer the sound, creating the false impression that the complex is alive with residential commotion once again.

The room is completely empty, which proves slightly unnerving compared to the rest of the building's chaos.  No decorations line the walls, and no carpet softens the floor.  A single piece of paper adhered to the decimated door frame exists as the lone accoutrement.

Faint pastel paint coats the rough walls in spots.  A mangled crib with several splintered rods rests in one corner, as if prepared to cradle an undead infant due to the furniture's condition -- one of intense disrepair and overwhelming neglect.  Tastelessly completing the scene, a mobile crafted from sharp glass shards, limp cigarillo butts and rusty razor blades dangles over the petite bed.

Surprisingly intact, an end table leaning against the wall supports a small cactus in a clay pot.  Though the vessel is chipped, the glazed facade still reflects the color of the drab runner flowing down the floor of the long hallway.  Salt stains along the ceiling indicate where the desert rain, infrequent as it may be, leaks through the building's decaying roof.

Pointy pieces of glass jut from the edges of the traumatized window pane, painting a contorted, almost dreamlike panorama of the Musparan skyline.  A bed rests against the wall at an unnatural angle, while a chair dangles from a sconce close to the ceiling.  Perhaps a squatter happened by and sculpted the furniture into artwork with the few bits that remained in the room after the building's abandonment.

Dozens of feathers litter the ground from the ripped mattress lumped into one corner.  The room is completely disheveled, with furniture upended and drawers unceremoniously uprooted from their stations.  One may deduce that someone conducted a thorough, albeit destructive, search of the premises in the past.

A faded runner travels the length of the split-level hallway.  The rug's moth-bitten edges and multiple burn marks insinuate a lack of care for the fabric, much like the rest of the fixtures in the condemned building.  Uneven holes in the roof provide limited illumination, fulfilling the job once held by the candle-less sconces affixed to the walls near the crumbling ceiling.

Crude graffiti sprawls across the dingy walls, probably tagged by transients with no regard for preventing further damage in the ramshackle building.  A pair of empty door frames, one on each side of the hall, exposes the abandoned flats beyond.  Sand fills in the ragged gaps of the floor's faded runner, causing it to almost look whole.

Missing doors, either stolen or destroyed, permit unrestricted access to the uninhabited flats on both sides of the hall.  A curious metal rack hangs from the middle of the ceiling here.  At first glance, the gnarled coils appear to be a piece of art, alien amongst the decidedly uncultured environment.  However, it proves to be no more than a chandelier with all of its valuable crystals removed, placing it much more in line with the theme of devastation dominating the complex.

Broken bottles on the floor mix with the glass from the room's shattered window.  Tattered curtains patterned with abstract dust images still grip a bent rod above the square hole, the edges of the fabric frayed from flapping unabated in the brutal desert winds.  No furniture outfits the living space, the pieces assumedly removed by looters looking for some quick coin.

Bursts of soot cover nearly every surface, alluding to a fire that fortunately seems to have been contained to this one room.  The charred corpses of furnishings rest in peace upon the floor, their dismembered remains strewn at odd angles.  Light patches on the walls contrast with the blackness, exposing where framed pictures and other mementos hung in the apartment while occupied by a full-time tenant.

Dark stains mar the walls at the hallway's end and match the ominous puddle soaked into the sandstone floor.  Slight breezes filter in from the flats on either side of the corridor, their windows completely wrecked and their doors mysteriously absent.  Empty sconces dangle from the walls as if they attempted to flee the dire situation around them but gave up out of sheer hopelessness.

Indubitably the deserted residence of a chronic hoarder, the room is cluttered with an eclectic variety of worthless junk.  A repugnant stench with unknown origins inherently worsens the already depressing situation.  The only light entering the area comes from the hallway, as the apartment's window is completely blocked from view due to the fortress of garbage.

A few lopsided stools are situated around an overturned crate in the center of the sticky floor.  The scene implies the attendance of squatters who use the space for illicit activities, especially judging by the empty alcohol bottles piled nearly to the ceiling in one corner.  Unfortunately, one visitor seems to have emptied the contents of his stomach next to the busted door frame, forcing all who enter the apartment to pass by the stinking mess.

No trace of greenery, no whiskers of grass and no clusters of color break the monotony in the seemingly never-ending darkness.  Instead, the sand covers anything and everything in a relentless attempt to assimilate any foreign objects into the monochromatic scenery.  There are no diamonds in the rough here, merely stones turned to dust before even having the chance to shine.

Tongues of chilled air flick the loose grains of sand from their temporary resting places to shower the neighboring dunes with new sediment.  Because of the shifting surroundings, many travelers prefer to avoid venturing here, knowing exploration carries a huge risk of getting lost or injured, especially at night.  As fickle and unpredictable as fate, the blustering sand recreates the shadows time and time again.

Cruel winds chill and maim the dunes, dispersing the sand carelessly and sloppily.  Any footprints are immediately erased by the constant churning of particle-filled wind, though the tracks would be nearly impossible to see in the dark anyway.  It is no wonder the S'Kra Mur refer to this place as the 'Lands of Evil,' for the terrain is truly inhospitable indeed.

Indistinguishable from one another at night, windswept dunes characterize the land from every possible viewpoint.  Only the whooshing sound of sand journeying from one spot to another fills the quiet air.  Despite the lack of life, there is never a dull moment, for the dust swirls in a tumultuous dance forever under the black sky.

Whorls of sand tumble over the shadowed dunes like trained acrobats.  Meanwhile, the night carries on, oblivious to the dusty mess kicked up in ribbons and sheets by the forceful winds that threaten to obscure the heavens.  Sudden blasts of cold air are more common than not in the dreary, treacherous expanse, the disruptions often strong enough to send one falling head over heels into the darkness.

Cold replaces the usual desert clime as if night sucked all the warmth from the air and sand.  The landscape stands as a testament to the heat -- submissive to its punishment while staying barren and withered under the brutal temperatures and fierce winds.  No living thing stands a chance of survival for very long in the grueling environment.

The absence of even the slightest hint of flora and fauna alludes to the environment's unfriendly and unwelcoming nature.  Animals wander in unknowingly at night after suffering the sun all day, only to die and have their remains swept into the shadows.  S'Kra Mur storytellers speak of a great curse upon the land, causing it to remain bereft of life until the end of days.

Funnels of sand barrel into each other and create translucent curtains that shroud the black horizon.  Every direction mimics the next in the hazy darkness.  Travel becomes increasingly difficult not only due to poor visibility, but also because one's feet are continuously swallowed by the voracious desert.

Wisps of sand swerve over the ground like mist hovering above a darkened bog.  The grains writhe and twitch to reconstruct the plane in ghost-like movements.  Thankfully, the lack of moisture anywhere in the vicinity limits the danger of potential fields of quicksand.

Black and impenetrable, the desert night claims many victims foolish enough to wander into its grasp unprepared.  The grey heights of the towering dunes are matched equally in breadth and scope by the shadowy depths of the sunken depressions.  Cold wind molds the landscape with invisible fingers just as a potter shapes a vase, though the sand, while yielding, refuses to maintain any recognizable profile.

A repetitive barrage of granules ricochets around the mounds like invisible crossbow fire in the night, the ceaseless torrent enough to make even the most steadfast traveler check his footing.  The swells of sand rise and fall like the chests of a slumbering army.  They face the chilling winds' assault with resigned dignity, accepting the inevitable truth that life is fleeting, especially for the likes of a desert dune.

Cold winds pummel the area, making breathing difficult and labored.  The horizon appears depressingly far away, and the blackness feels almost constrictive.  One must keep his wits about him at all times, lest he succumb to the desert's deadly deception.

Giant dunes perspire fine lines of sand down their sloping sides as if in fear of the desert's nighttime chill.  The real culprit, however, is likely a simple combination of gravity and wind.  Regardless, the mounds slowly fade into the blackness, diminished by their own dusty sweat, only to be rebuilt by the next heavy, replenishing gust.

Blotches of night sky occasionally emerge from their hiding places in the sandy clouds blanketing the land.  Bulimic dunes hack and cough themselves up into the air with the aid of the unforgiving wind, regurgitating particles that float noiselessly amid the darkness before rejoining their siblings on the ground.  The effect is disorienting but not without a hint of natural aesthetics only the desert can supply.

Like the ebb and flow of the ocean tide, so moves the sand in waves upon itself in the desolate desert.  The stinging wind flip-flops its course as if trying to shake some nocturnal predator, resulting in varied patterns across the dunes.  Yet the currents of cold air never exhaust themselves and tirelessly trek across the hilly terrain, leaving only soft whispers in their wake.

Darkness casts a deathly pallor across the rolling dunes to either side of the trade road.  Swirling sand, caught up by the ever-present wind, plays games with the shadowed recesses in the sand, changing the form of the hulking dunes grain by grain.

Here the sand dunes rise again, pitching the travelers of the trade road back into a world of sand and sky.  The surfaces of the great sand hills are smooth and supple, their elegant curves as deceptively gentle as a veiled maiden's.

The stars are obscured in the distance, where a far-away range of mountains cuts a jagged swath across the horizon.  Between here and there lies only sand, which sparkles with a subtle, quiet beauty under the hushed veil of night.

The dunes level out here into a brief stretch of even terrain, marked only by a single dusty purple cactus that squats stubbornly near a small collection of flat, rounded rocks.  Rounded dunes rise again in every direction, obscuring the winding path of the trade road to the north and south.

A great blot of shadow engulfs an expansive stretch to one side of the trade road, tracing the edges of a massive rock.  Darker tufts of shadow mark out the presence of several tiny patches of sparse desert grass.

A small path branches off from the trade road, obviously less frequently used, with the highway's steady line of paved blocks slowly dying away here.  Canyon walls begin to form on the sides of the path, and the road's elevation begins to gradually slope downward.

The last paving-stone vestiges of the Velakan Trade Road have vanished from this narrow sand path, and it opens up to a rocky canyon further below.  Large, unnatural webs cling to the rocks of the canyon walls.

A huge, rounded shape rises to one side of the trade road, crosshatched with lighter and darker patches of shadow.  The available starlight plays dancing games across the pale sand to either side of the dune.

The land here flattens out slightly in a low stretch between two massive dunes.  The ground is parched and cracked, creating a mosaic of small cakes of dried mud, the only remnant of a long since departed desert storm.
Sparse, parched grasses line the edges of the paved trade road, their roots finding purchase beneath the sand-worn stones.  Sand continually attempts to envelop them, but they stubbornly persist.
This arm of the trade road, truthfully little more than a sandy path packed down by continuous travel, winds between two rows of small dunes as it stretches out toward the palace gate of Muspar'i.

The pale sand surrounding the trade road glitters by night, minute grains catching what starlight filters down from the open bowl of the dark sky overhead.  The dunes are marked by long, spidering fissures, their edges softened by harsh desert winds and their depths hiding tiny unknown inhabitants.

The oppressive heat of the day lingers by night only in the lower layers of sand to either side of the path.  A great stillness keeps its grip on the shifting dunes that drift ever closer to engulf the trade road.  The air carries a biting chill, for the desert is a harsh mistress -- by day or by night.

Ever changing, the landscape of Velaka stretches out to the south and east beyond the border of the main trade road.  To the north stands the high wall of the city, beyond which can be seen the dome of the palace roof.  The dunes to the west, though small, are close enough to block further view in that direction.

An acrid, briny scent drifts over the dunes to the west on an unrefreshing breeze, carrying with it grains of salt and sand.  The creeping dunes of the Velaka surround the road almost entirely, blocking passage north.

As if molded by Hav'roth himself, the dunes to the north part wide, leaving a sloping valley for travelers to approach the palace gate of Muspar'i.  Over the gate, the palace roof glitters in the darkness, just beyond the ominous silhouette of a tall tree.

rooms.t: [Velakan Trade Road, Before the Palace Gate]
rooms.desc: Great iron-banded gates stand tall within the otherwise unbroken barrier of limestone blocks that is the wall around Shorka's Palace.  Deep carving in the stone depicts a fearsome cobra, though much of the detail has been worn away by the harsh Velakan environment.
Skirting along beside the tall stone walls of the palace courtyard, a barely passable trail is created by the bordering sand dunes that perpetually loom just outside of the city.
A low point between two dunes affords a passing glimpse of the salt lake to the west, and the briny scent carries more freely from it on the wind.

The dunes seem to shy away from the mighty wall as it curves outward, reaching father into the harsh desert landscape.  Far beyond the dunes, the southwestern arm of the Gemfire Mountains stands in the distance.

Sloping away from the high wall, the mighty sand dunes recede into the ground, leveling out as they approach the shores of Lake Ratamipak.  The massive body of murky water stands motionless amidsts the shifting sands, hardly a ripple disturbing its surface.
The imposing wall that surrounds the palace grounds slopes gently to the north and southwest, curving like the body of some great serpent.  A small sand dune collects near the crook of the path.

To the west, the great expanse of black water that is Lake Ratamipak stretches toward the horizon, the vast salt flat that borders its northern shore emitting a ghostly glow in the darkness.  A sinuous river, appropriate for its namesake, passes beneath the sandstone bridge on its way westward to feed the salty lake.  The water trickles by quietly underfoot.
The nearly nonexistent trail to the northeast grows to a respectable path as it progresses to the south.  Stray pieces of crumbled sandstone mingle amongst the fine grains of sand underfoot.

As it follows the curve of the palace wall, the lightly packed sand of the path suggests its purpose as a scenic byway.  Unlike the more heavily traveled trade roads that cross the desert, this trail allows for a leisurely pace while partially sheltered from the sand-laden winds by the wall of Shorka's Palace itself.

A broad patch of ground beside the wall offers travelers a place to rest, away from the traffic of the main road.  Chunks of discarded limestone, possibly left here since the building of the city, serve as makeshift seats.

Even in the dark, the waters of Lake Ratamipak are visible from this promontory, although it has the illusionary appearance of a flat dark desert plain that is spoiled only by a slight movement of its surface.  Making its way to the lake, the road begins descending to the northwest away from the city's plateau and towards the murky waters.

Despite its well-traveled and productive nature, any sign of civic maintenance upon the road abruptly ends, with little more than a rocky path continuing to the west.  Several large stones have been pushed or dragged off the path, but were never carted away.  Some idle soul has skillfully carved a stylized representation of a dragon onto the side of the largest stone.

The hardy scrub pines that have managed to survive and spread on this rocky slope are nearly invisible by night, but their dark shapes soften the hard edges of the sharp rocks and the unmistakable scent of pine fills the air.  The area has proven attractive to the local wildlife as well -- rustling noises can be heard as small animals move about, and intermittent calls of night birds also break the silence.

Just above the shoreline, an irregular patchwork pattern of saltern ponds spread out along the shore of the lake in spots of dull pewter, reflective blue, dun yellow, and bright white dependent on which stage the particular pond is in.  Surrounding the road are innumerable rocks covered with a fine edging of salt encrustation from water blown off the lake and deposited here.

The road ends here where the salt flats begin, between the poorest of the salterns.  Low walls of clay-rich soil divide the irregularly shaped pools of water, fed by a system of tiny canals and moveable wooden chutes that carry salt water from the nearby Lake Ratamipak.  The ponds around the end of the road here are furthest from the lake, giving them the least access to water and going through fewer production cycles, making them marginal investments.

At the northern end of the shore, only the most meager of ponds are present.  Ill-supplied by the complicated network of waterways, these salterns are among the poorest to be found here, some little more than troughs.  Even the crews on the ponds seem less professional, showing an edge of desperation or despair in their sluggish activity.

A cluster of salterns is at the stage of moving its cargo back to the city.  Laborers occasionally approach the pathway next to stacks of heavy sacks stained a dusty white, awaiting their loads for the long trudge back to town.  In a pool next to the abrupt rise of hills to the east, workers shovel out a layer of sand that has cascaded down into the pond, ruining the current production cycle.

A strange contraption squats in the middle of the intersection -- a sort of tall round hut on stilts with a maze of wooden waterways radiating outward.  With three spouts along its sides, a large bronze pipe delivers water to the channels.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Life seems rare even here, despite being the only large body of open water in the entire Velaka, no doubt repelled by the intense saltiness of the lake water.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Smooth and level, the lakebed forms an even plane that leads deeper into the nearly stagnant tarn.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Here away from shore, the bottom drops off rapidly, making it difficult to move further out into the lake.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Here away from shore, the bottom drops off rapidly, making it difficult to move further out into the lake.

Darkly colored flagstones pave the courtyard, swept clean of any desert sands that may have blown in.  The featureless stones leave no cover for any intruder that might have breached the gate of the old fort, giving the arrow slits high up on the walls an ominous character.  A wide set of stone stairs leads up to the main entrance of the old keep.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  The lakebed dips lower, forcing the hardly moving water to form a small eddy that ebbs and flows into itself.
In the shadow of the sandstone bridge, the waters of the Heke'mhhg seem tenebrous and oily.  A cluster of dead weeds sways restlessly at the river's edge, the dried husks persisting despite all odds.

The tall main doors of the keep have been left open to allow the easy traffic of bank patrons to the wide stairs that lead down to the courtyard.  Equally lofty windows flank the door with their aged iron shutters propped open, permitting a view of the flagstone courtyard and the passage of breezes rather than footsteps.  Passageways lead both ways around the immutable stone core, drawing the visitor further into the old keep.

The curved stone walls of the passageway are blank, save for a few strategically placed wall sconces bearing torches to light the way.  Old rugs have been stretched across the floor to absorb the noise of passage, but seem to do a better job capturing the dust of the desert tracked in by bank patrons.

The cloudy water of the Heke'mhhg River pours into the dark and murky Lake Ratamipak, churning up silt and salt in the process.  The process causes a long, serpentine trail to form in the water, reaching toward the center of the lake like a narrow, forked tongue.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Life seems rare even here, despite being the only large body of open water in the entire Velaka, no doubt repelled by the intense saltiness of the lake water.

A patchwork pattern of settling ponds blankets the area.  Dull and uninteresting to the average eye, they are nonetheless a continuing source of riches and wealth.  From these humble beginnings, the extracted salt travels to every corner of Kermoria, putting coin into the pockets of traders along the way.

A stumpy windmill stands at the shore, its diminutive scale not preventing it from being the tallest object in the vicinity of the irregular geometry of settling ponds.  With a slow and quiet "thump, thump, thump," the pumps the windmill drives feed the complicated system of tiny canals and sluices that keep the ponds going.

One of the most successful clusters of ponds is located here at the south end of the flat.  Workers carrying torches move quickly and efficiently between tasks, giving the scene an almost mechanical quality.  Seated on a raised platform in the center of it all, a plump foreman smiles benignly over his tiny kingdom.

Strangely organized and tightly packed ponds of various sizes force traffic into narrow, regulated pathways that twist and turn with sudden odd angles.  Nevertheless, the paths are often busy with the coming and going of gleaners and laborers carrying torches who walk unperturbed beneath the water channels and walkways suspended overhead.

The hills end abruptly before the edge of Lake Ratamipak, leaving a narrow pocket of flatland that has been completely covered with ponds to recover salt from the waters of the grand lake.  Workers carrying torches routinely tend the salterns, filling them with water, removing debris from the ponds or harvesting the precious salt.

As it intersects with the Heke'mhhg river on its journey through the Velaka, the road rises here slightly to accommodate a great brass pipe that passes beneath it.  The cylinder allows the water to flow by unimpeded, passing out of sight under the path and palace wall alike.

After years of service, a large pond has been pulled out of the regular rotation for maintenance.  Workers repack the soil at the bottom of the pond to reduce leaking, while others laboriously scrape away at the yellow buildup of salt encrustations on the walls.  Bypassing the pool for now, water gurgles overhead in a wooden canal suspended on piles of rocks and the odd wooden pole.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Life seems rare even here, despite being the only large body of open water in the entire Velaka, no doubt repelled by the intense saltiness of the lake water.

Briny water rushes by, sweeping through its narrow desert path like an oily snake.  The banks of the river bear telltale saline stains, collected over many years from the murky river that has left them thoroughly encrusted with salt.
