rooms.desc: The narrow path here is bounded on the south by mats of decomposing water plants and swamp grasses.  The stench of marsh gas and the thrashing of slimy, watery things in the rotting reeds keep you from exploring in that direction.

A small, thin path meanders through an otherwise daunting thicket of brambles here.  Directly to the north is a dark, slate outcropping, while east lies a tall, attenuated tower.  The exterior of the tower is covered with carvings of fantastic and legendary beings and creatures, whose awesome and powerful visages you can discern even from this distance.  Through the foliage, you see the town gate to the west.

Rich farmland surrounds the road on both sides.  The fresh scent of the tilled soil rises all about you.  Southward, the walls of a fair-sized city rise near the banks of a glistening river.  A faint haze of smoke hovers over the town, blurring the outlines slightly.  To the north, distant hills rear up against the grey-blue horizon.

The scent of freshly-tilled earth rises from the farms on both sides of the road.  Heavily-loaded wagons and carts brimming with produce wend their way southward towards the walls of a city set near a glimmering river.  You note an amazing variety of races and types that are driving their goods into the town.

Neatly planted rows of grain mingle with tidy plots of vegetables covering the rich earth of well-tended farms along the wide road as it wanders across the land.  A farmer waves at you as he toils along behind a yoke of sturdy oxen that pull a heavy iron plow through the fertile soil.

Open grassland mingles with small farmsteads as the wide road passes through a cut where a low hill rises.  The road is edged with tall hedges, apparently to keep cattle from wandering into the orchards and vegetable plots you see beyond the heavy, guarding branches.  Some distance to the south, you see the smoke and haze of a city of some size.  Northwards, low hills rise against the sky.

Cattle wander aimlessly across the road as they crop at the rich grass growing in the rolling fields.  You spy a lone cow-herd nodding under a shade tree off to one side as his charges amble into your path in large numbers, enormous brown eyes gazing soulfully at you as they pass.

Open grassland mingles with a thinning forest from the north.  Here and there among the trees cattle wander.  They casually dine on the lush grass and occasionally reach up to consume the delicate leaves on the lower branches of the trees.  To the north, low hills rise up gently from the plains.  Southward, a heavy haze or smoke can be made out.

Trees to both sides of the road thin out southward where the land changes to open grassland.  Large grey squirrels leap across the road overhead from branch to branch and chitter down at you as they regard you with curious eyes.

Widely scattered trees stand aloof, like strangers at a party, barely noticing one another's presence.  Northwards, the open land nearby changes into a few low, rolling hills.  Like a bare head rising above thinning hair, the hills stand out from a fringe of trees about their base.

Growing in the shade of towering oak and fir trees, azalea bushes add bright splashes of color to the brown-green gloom of the forest.  Tangles of ivy creep alongside the trail and cloak the trees in jade filigree.

Longleaf pine and spruce outnumbering the hardwoods in the area drip a sticky sap that sugars the underbrush, and litter the trail with needles that crunch underfoot.  Spanning the branches of a stunted sourwood tree, an orbweaver's web twitches slightly with the struggles of a small fly.

Thin pine saplings, field laurel and shrub grass form a narrow border on the edge of the forest.  The darkness of the close-set trees to the northwest rustles with unseen movement, while the open grasslands stretching out to the west breathe quietly the open air.

Swift breezes ruffle the tall grasses beneath the wind-scoured sky that stretches far above like a pale awning.  Sprays of orange and purple wildflowers attract the attention of a few butterflies, who flutter across the trail.
To the northwest, a copse of birch trees stand thin and stark against the sky, the swift breezes animating their skeletal forms in a gentle dance.

Trees grow tall here, but they are scattered enough to allow moonlight and a good view of the sky.  Northwards, the land rises into low hills that disappear against the black sky of the night.  To the south, a gentle plain opens outward.  A soft breeze rustles the leaves in the boughs overhead in a pleasant susurration.

Rumbling carts from the North Turnpike lend a low bass to the sweet aria of field wrens, whose small choirs spot the meadow on either side of the trail.  Far to the north, a thick plume of grey smoke billows from the tall chimneys of a monastery.

The road crests the highest of the low hills, wandering among the cracked and worn rocks scattered across it.  Removed from the road and set gently upon a hill, like a princess on her ivory pedestal, stands a rough circle of tall stones arranged in two concentric rings.  Rising unsteadily from the crown of the hill, many of the stones lean against one another or are completely toppled.  Perhaps a place of worship in ancient times, not even legend recalls who came here or what gods they served.

Winding north and south over the brow of a low hill, the road is partly blocked by several roughly shaped stones that appear to have tumbled down from the hill crest above.  Small curls of a deep green vine have begun to wind the fallen stones into their embrace, and the tiny white flowers scattered among the leaves brighten the dull blue-grey of the stone.

A series of low hills, barely worthy of note, rise to the south while northwards, wide open grasslands run unhindered into the distance.  Far off to the north, at the edge of the horizon, the faint shape of distant mountains can just be made out.

Low hills to the south rise up from marshy land to the north.  Clouds of insects and tiny birds feeding upon them dart here and there.  The whine of millions of quivering wings combines with the thin rustle of the darting birds to form an annoying, discordant noise.

The ground underfoot squishes with each movement, and moisture oozes into the traces left.  Low rocks set in ragged rows appear to mark a path along the swampy ground.  Gnats and midges clog your nostrils and fly into your eyes and ears in an endless cloud.  The air is thick with rotting vegetable matter and less identifiable odors.

You travel in the midst of a boggy meadow.  The air is thick with a chill mist that blurs the outlines of anything not close by.  Pale rocks set along the path show the safest way to go among the almost trackless wastes.

A peaceful valley, sheltered by the surrounding hills, is laid out before you like a patchwork quilt of flowery meadows and neatly arranged farmland.  Centered in this multicolored vista is a small village.  You pause on the hilltop to enjoy this delightful view.  A meadowlark circles overhead for a moment, warbling its song to you, before swooping down toward the village, following the line of a well-traveled road.

A gentle breeze, carrying the sweet earthy scent of fresh herbs and flowers, rustles through the grass in the valley below you, making it flow like waves on an ocean.  A well-traveled road winds like a ribbon from a small village up to the top of the hill.

A large gate stands here, usually open to welcome travelers -- but wisely capable of closing to defend the residents within.  Traders, adventurers and farmers from the surrounding valley mingle here, moving in or out of the village at a leisurely pace, many of them Halflings.  A wooden wagon, carrying racks of freshly-baked meat pies, trundles into the gates, followed by several yapping dogs.  A neatly painted wooden sign is displayed in a prominent place.

The ground beneath you is boggy and soft.  Swarms of flies close about you, and some land to drill into your flesh for a morsel of blood and to leave a stinging welt as a souvenir of your visit to their lands.  Northwards, the ground rises from the bog into open lands, while southward a mist obscures the view.

Southward, the road dips into a boggy lowland, while to the north, open grasslands stretch.  No sign of habitation breaks the rippling waves of grass that grow shoulder-high to a tall Elf.  The air is alternately fresh with the smell of growing things and thick with the stench of the bog, as the wind veers aimlessly across the open land.

Thick grass grows up to the edge of the road.  Despite the isolation and empty land, the road itself is in surprisingly good shape.  Large paving stones rest on a level bed, each one tightly fitted to its neighbor so that nary a weed or seedling can force a way between them.  Perhaps some vanished town lay near here that knew the value of good roads.

The road runs straight as an arrow through the endless sea of tall grasses.  An occasional ripple among the stalks moving counter the wind shows there is life hidden beneath the green and gold surface.  The desperate flight of a covey of birds, as they break cover and scatter, shows that peace here is a shallow illusion.  For always the hunter awaits the careless and the weak.
A ruined building sits alongside the tidy stone road.  The remains perhaps of an ancient tollhouse or inn, it lies at the edge of a forest that rises up from a wide swathe of grassland.

The trees grow about you in abundance, their tops brushing the sky, their leaves shimmering with the breeze.  The chirping of birds flows on the wind and there seems to be an almost sentient life to the wood, as if someone or something smiles beneficently on all the denizens and events that occur within the forest's boundaries.

Low-lying taffelberry bushes grow about the tall deobar trees of the forest.  The scent of loam hangs thick and sweet in an almost tangible cloud.  The floor is carpeted with fallen leaves in the process of returning to the elements from whence they came, and some of the trees show evidence of having had their branches chopped off.

The trees cluster close, weaving a dark green canopy through which light slants cautiously, making tiny pools that flaunt dancing motes of dust.  The air is heavy and still, thick with silence without even a birdsong to break the enclosing stillness.

This is the heart of the wood, where the trees are the thickest and the outside world of skies and unforested land is the farthest away.  The trees grow close to each other, their leaves whispering back and forth, their crowns bowed in quiet conversation.  The silence is broken only by the sounds of a squirrel or similar creature's movements and the rush of a river coming from somewhere in the distance.

Deobar trees tower over you, their leaves rustling in time with the sounds of the river to the north.  Quiet and serene, this part of the forest has a rich scent to it, the overlapping canopy making pools of gloom that collect beneath the trees.

The forest to the south is thick and dark, a stark comparison to the open meadow around you.  Short, springy grass grows in soft mounds over hillocks and hollows.  Tiny white wildflowers peek out amongst the greenery, their petals open to accept the sunlight.

The land here is open and welcome, the grass thinning on the western horizon as it makes way for a farmstead.  Nearby you can hear the babble of a river, and the vegetation shows signs that something, probably cattle, has been here recently to grab a quick snack.  The air is clean and sweet, inviting you to take deeper breaths.

Vast, empty fields lie fallow about you.  The remains of an abandoned farmhouse dominates your view to the northeast, its doorways gaping, its windows wide open like empty eye sockets.  Nearby, a plow lies rusting, its blade sunk a good two feet into dirt whose only future crop will be grass.  To the south the land is gradually returning to the meadow it originally was, the edge of creeping green vivid against the bare brown of exposed earth.

The darker colors of the serrated wirgars grasses that grow in this particular part of the plains stand out against their lighter cousins.  You catch the scent of sirese on the wind, the fragrance of the tiny wildflower wrapping around you.  To the south the land turns a rough brown, shifting abruptly from plains to farming land.

Blue sky and sweet winds mingle with vibrant greens and yellows to create a place that seems blessed by Hodierna herself.  Restless clouds chase each other through the sky, and the blithely cheerful songs of birds create a natural, if chaotic, symphony to be enjoyed by all.

The grasslands shimmer slightly, the gentle hand of the wind running its fingers through the plant life.  Here and there colorful wildflowers dare to peep their heads up through the endless browns and greens of the plains.  Dominating the gentle sighing of the grass can be heard the bustling sounds of the tiny village of Kaerna, surrounded by a wooden town wall which masks the village's graceless sprawl against the northern horizon.

Under the shadow of eastern section of The Crossing's stone town wall, this footpath serves as a shortcut.  Barely wide enough for one person, thick brambles and brush allow passage in single file.   A few crevices in the wall make adequate handholds as you squeeze your way along the uneven ground and past thorny branches.

The remains of a mudwren nest sits overhead in a rough section of the town's stone wall.  A newer nest is under construction just below it tucked within a chink of the wall.  Small birds dart through the tall brush, bustling as much as the citizens along the streets inside the gates.

A gully eroded across the narrow way forces passage just next to the wall of the town.  Stagnant insect-infested water pools in muddy sections of the gully and a fetid odor of garbage saturates the air.

The path turns from the city ramparts and forks south and west.  Toward the north it runs along the town's outer wall, the stone structure within reach.  Sheltered from wind and sun, little vegetation except for stray weeds manages to thrive.
Crumbling mud bricks and loose rock lay in a pile near the sturdy stone town wall.  A small field mouse nibbles at a crust of bread, perhaps discarded from the wall workers' lunch portion.
The path winds in and out of a thick patch of stunted bushes near the exterior wall.  It emerges into an area of chipped rock where workers have dumped debris from the town wall's construction.

Thin-leafed sedges and weeds grow densely enough to hide partially buried stones that can jarringly catch the toe of a boot.  The hiss of wind across the field creates a background for the music of a small cloud of midges buzzing at head height.
rooms.loc: East Gate and Moon Mage Observatory

rooms.desc: A smooth, flat slate-grey outcropping abuts the stone rampart, the same slates that compose the hills and terrain to the west.  Bits of the slab have cracked and chipped, but for a few yards the path is wide enough to be called a path.

Barely more than an animal track, this footpath can just be discerned through a field of sedge.  The weeds dull the sounds along the nearby road and city, leaving only the whisper of the wind all about.
rooms.loc: East Gate and Moon Mage Observatory

rooms.desc: A cool wind twists through the air, carrying the crisp scent of pine.   A generous carpet of needles and loam lines the ground, churning up dust that offsets the sharper smells with a sweet mustiness.  In the distance, a sparrow whistles, calling out an ancient melody that only others of its kind can recall the words to.

Solitary and overbearing, the trees of the forest loom over all they behold.  Caught in a game of one-upsmanship, the trees clump in groups that attempt to outgrow the other.  One particular tree, a massive blackwood, overtowers them all, its boughs extending outward in an embrace that gathers up the forest with arms of shadow and leaf.

A scattering of trees marks the edge of the forest as it fades away into a wide field to the north and thickens to the south.  Clumps of grass and wildflowers grow in smooth rolling hollows and hillocks of green, and a pleasant breeze cools the air to an amiable degree.

Tawny grasses wave in a breeze rendered vocal by the whisper of the stalks rubbing together.  Here and there the field has been tramped down by the passage of careless feet, making paths that wind through the grasses in mazed patterns.  To the south a forest edges up against the horizon, clamoring for attention from the sky they would swallow whole.

Weathered beams of wood poke up through the grass like children peering cautiously around for signs of a malevolent bully.  Bits of cloth and paper still cling to the greyed and splintered wood, remnants of a happier time now long gone.

A sea of multi-hued grasses rises and falls all around.  From the deep greens of serrated seregrass to the tawny spun gold of common stalks, the panorama of color is incredible to consider, the palette of a crazed and yet highly imaginative painter.

Soft-scented air fills the glade where patches of blooming tulips splash color against velvety grass tailor-made for bare feet.  A lattice arch, covered with the pink blooms of jasmine honeysuckle, embraces and frames a small altar created from a living plant.  Benches of polished wood invite couples to stop and bask in the beauty of the area and the warmth of heart's devotion.

The soft, subtle fragrance of pine and roses mingles in an intoxicating cloud that perfumes the air and lingers in hair and clothing.  A luxurious carpet of dark green unrolls within a circle of trees, the glowing reds, golds, and butter-yellow of dayroses adding color to the sea of emerald.  A small path winds away from the glade and back toward a small well that seems as far away as a dream.

Couched amidst a bed of shrubbery is an old stone and mortar well.  A rusted winch assures that the bucket that last descended down into the construction's depths remains a permanent resident.  Grasses grow up to spill down in streams around it, gathering in a thick crescent.  A small pool of water is cupped by the lush growth that collects at the foot of the well, the gossiping grounds of housewives long since gone.

Slender aesaigo trees link their limbs and leaves together to form a loose screen of shade against the light.  The grass fades from amber to emerald as it sweeps west to east, its changing surface dotted with starflowers and buttercups.

Leaves dance in the swirl of a cool breeze as tall oaks and slim pines crowd against one another in a race for light and space.  Fallen pine needles and grass form a luxurious carpet, muffling footsteps and releasing sharp, clean scents into the air.
Vines curl around the trunks of the trees, displaying glossy green leaves with powdery grey underbellies.  The branches of the aesaigos shirk against one another, a mysterious sound.

The grass stirs in slow patterns as a breeze -- the only permanent resident of the empty hinterland -- swirls over it.  Like a wave searching for a shore, the wind pushes back and forth over the changing shades and hues of the growth, hunting for a haven it will never find.

Tiny, annoying gnats and flies whirr through the field, flying into faces and darting quickly away before they can meet their doom.  From time to time you catch a flash of movement as one of the local avians zooms in to snatch any particularly attractive or plump-looking bugs, but the sense of poetic justice is quickly erased as another buzzes in to take the place of the one that was consumed.

An ocean of grass edges around the beaten-down path that curls precariously through the field's vastness.  With the wind steadily running its fingers through the grasses, the stalks rise and fall in a continual show of motion as inexorable and reflexive as a heartbeat.

The soft chirr of insects hidden in the tall grasses mingles with the trilling of the nesting field larks that make their homes in the protective shade of the narrow-bladed but profuse growth.  You can catch glances of the tiny dun-colored creatures, their soft brown eyes peering up from between the criss-crossing stalks and their voices twittering questions that remain forever unanswered.

Great, rolling fields swallow up the world from one end of the sky to the next.  The natural perfection of the pristine grass is only marred by the paths that have been grudgingly trodden through them by the heavy feet of adventurers and their prey.

The subtle scent of hay and butter-yellow blossoms infuses the air with a fragrance that brings to mind summer breezes.  Crushed and tattered grasses form a ragged path through the growth, and the constant hum and buzz of insects lends a sense of drowsy solitude to the empty lands.

A picturesque village extends north from the town gate.  Quaint buildings, built specifically for those of short stature, border the lanes.  A kaleidoscopic array of color is displayed in every direction ... in the clothing of the Halflings, the painted buildings, and the lushly-hued blossoms covering the neatly tended beds and flowering trees.  A house, constructed to accommodate the hired Human guard, is situated next to the gate.  He stands at ease, casually perusing the incoming traffic.

Taffelberry Path, named after the favorite food of the Arthe Dale residents, is a straight, well-kept lane that heads further into the village to the north and back to the village gate to the south.  A group of rollicking Halfling lads passes you, laughing and elbowing each other, as they move eagerly toward an attractive red building to the east.

This is the courtyard of an old-fashioned country inn, stoutly constructed of red brick.  Beds of cheery marigolds border the building, while a colorful signboard hangs from a sunflower-yellow awning above the door.  Sounds of laughter and happy conversation drift from an open window.  A little dirt path curves around toward the rear of the inn.

Open areas flank both sides of the path at this point.  A charming little park extends to the west, and an open-air marketplace is situated to the east.  A Halfling pushing a wheelbarrow filled with fresh vegetables heads toward one of the market's wooden stands.

This charming park is alive with a medley of brilliant colors and sachet scents coming from the beds of primrose, hollyhock, larkspur and delphinium.  An iridescent green hummingbird darts from flower to flower, trying to avoid a group of giggling Halfling children who are rolling and somersaulting in the grass.  The carved garden bench looks like a pleasant spot to sit and enjoy the scene.  You can see a small shrine to the west, while a thumping sound comes from beyond the bushes to the north.

A simple shrine has been erected in the niche of a large stony outcrop.  Moonflower vines climb the column, twining their way around the opening, their brilliant white blossoms providing a festive border.  A carved figure of Glythtide has been set inside the niche.

A giant oak tree stands erect here, its massive branches reaching out to form a canopy over the local swimming hole.  Some sort of wooden structure is nestled in the foliage high up in the tree.  The grassy area surrounding the swimming hole appears to be a perfect spot for picnicking or lounging.

The Arthe Dale market is bustling with activity day and night.  Early morning travelers often stop in to chat with other adventurers, as they look over the local farmers' bountiful displays of fresh produce and home-baked treats, while late night visitors to the adjacent inn's common room usually come by for a sobering cup of hot coffee before heading home.  Plain wooden tables and benches offer a place for snacking, rest or conversation.

The path continues north and south, lined with a row of colorful sicle trees to the east and low bushes to the west.  A small meadow mouse, alarmed by your approach, scurries through an opening in the bushes.

This section of the park is an unadorned grassy strip, edged with low bushes.  At the far end a painted target has been set up.  A large number of rocks lay discarded at its base.  A Halfling man whirls his sling and sends a stone hurtling toward the target, hitting it dead center with a loud thunk.

The village's three main paths meet at this intersection.  Attractive shops with brightly colored awnings line Glaysker Lane to the east.  The quiet, shrub-bordered Tanglefoot Row heads north to the residential section, and you can see the village gate at the end of Taffelberry Path to the south.

The path circles around a bed of dark green ivy that has grown up over a white statue standing in the center.  A bright yellow building with blue shutters and colorful flowerboxes faces you.  There is a painted sign mounted next to the open doorway.  A Halfling female, her nose stuck in a notebook, wanders by, almost bumping into you as she heads toward the building.  She absentmindedly knocks on the sign (for luck?), as she enters the doorway, still concentrating on her notes.

The pale lavender-pink glaysker flowers that have been planted along the length of this cobblestone street breathe a subtle sweet fragrance into the air.  Your eye is caught by an attractive display in the window of a simple white cottage with a thatched roof and a light purple awning.

Tall, neatly-pruned hedgerows line the street, providing some privacy for the homes beyond, where Halfling residents move about, absorbed in domestic chores.  On one side a small woman hangs freshly washed pink and yellow sheets from a line, and on the other a man works at whitewashing a fence.  A small dragonfly whirs past you, alighting on one of the hedges briefly before continuing on its journey.

A small dwelling has been built into the side of a hill here.  White curtains flutter in the windows that open out from the sod-covered walls.  Several small carving tools have been left on a wooden bench, and bits of wood shavings lay discarded below it.

The lane ends to the north at the eccentric home of Arthe Dale's oldest, largest and wealthiest family, the Tanglefoots.  A freshly-painted white picket fence surrounds the property, and you can see a large well-tended yard beyond it.

A curious arrangement of objects has been grouped on either side of the doorway of a building, which is almost completely obscured by the entangled maiden's tress vines that grow up the sides and over the roof.  Stuffed animals, stone statues, pieces of furniture, a sundial, and assorted carved walking staves form a bizarre tableau.  A statue next to the door holds a plaque.

Small shops line the lane that bends from the northeast to the west.  A shamrock green awning tops the doorway to a yellow building with a matching green sign mounted on the wall.  A single pure note from a melancholy flute floats out from the doorway.

As you pause for a moment on the cobblestoned lane, your eye is caught by the entrance to a squat stone building with a blue awning.  A dazzling silver sword has been securely mounted to the arched entryway above a small engraved plaque.

The festive glaysker blossoms that edge the lane provide a striking contrast to a homely wooden shack that sits unadorned and colorless at the side of the path.  A plain wooden signpost stands at the shack's entrance.

Large oak trees line this well-traveled trail as it winds its way towards a secluded community nestled among the surrounding low-lying hills.  Wind-borne glaysker seeds have found a cozy home at the base of some of the trees, growing in an array of lavender and pink blooms.  Clay pots of carefully tended taffelberry bushes sit at measured intervals along the path.

A rounded building with a turf and flower-covered roof sits here at a sharp bend in the lane.  The round white door almost seems to provide entry into a small flowery hill.  Large beds of purple glaysker and bright yellow oralana flowers border the building.

The hills encircle diminutive knolls clustered about a small village green within the valley.  The hardened earth of the trail forks to meander its way past humble homes constructed within each knoll.  The scent of ripened berries wafts on the breeze.

Simple white arbors stand at the entrance of each path to the knolls.  Plump purple loganberries dangle amongst the deep green leaves of the bushes.  A copse of oak trees lines the back of the lots, creating pools of ever-changing shadows upon the ground.

Thick groves of oak trees lightly forest the surrounding hills of the valley.  Neatly trimmed blueberry hedges line this quiet lane that runs along the west side of the village green.  A thick carpet of lush green grass encases the cozy knoll homes that sit off the lane up stone-lined walkways.

An immense oak tree shelters a clear, sparkling pond beneath its leafy branches that canopy the village green from the weather.  The thick roots of the tree have broken through the compacted earth in several places, lending themselves as places of rest to the local citizens.  Stone-lined dirt pathways, like spokes of a wheel, venture toward the surrounding knolls.

The lane rises slightly to the northeast as is continues to circle around the edge of the valley.  A small circle of simple wooden chairs shelters beneath the boughs of a nearby oak, offering a place to sit at the day's end.  Trimmed mounds of blueberry bushes, laden with their deep blue pearls of sweetness, border the green to the southeast.

The stone-lined road continues from the northeast to the west, separating the grass-covered knolls to the south from an enormous tree at the center of the community.  Yellow and orange mums circle around the base of a a smaller oak at the side of the path, bobbing their bright, flowery heads in the breeze as if dancing in a merry child's game.

A strawberry patch has found its way from a nearby home to a white picket fence that borders the east side of the village green.  Weaving their way around each wooden picket, the strawberry vines create a tapestry of bright red teardrop fruits nestled among deep green leaves.

The scent of sweet strawberries fills the air surrounding the stone-lined path.  A cord of wood sits neatly stacked by one of the colorful round doors that decorate the surrounding knolls.  Near the woodpile, a hatchet sits partially buried in a stump, awaiting its next call to duty.

Skirting along the southwest base of a large hill, the road curves its way easterly past peaceful dwellings as it continues to wrap the edge of the village green.  Small tended gardens of herbs and flowers snuggle up to the walkways of the homes within the knolls.

Brightly painted round doors mark the entrances to the grassy knolls that border the northwest side of the road.  A single boysenberry plant in the corner of one yard has been trained to grow as a tree, its tangled branches reaching down to sweep along the ground.

A large, round hill separates this exclusive part of the community from the daily hustle and bustle nearby.  The deep green grass on this side of the hill is carefully manicured to the perfect height, nary a blade poking above the heads of its neighbors.  An olallieberry bush with its large, ruby-red fruits weaves itself through a picket fence that borders the brick path.

Ornately carved round doors mark the entrances to the affluent homes set in perfectly manicured knolls of dark, grass-covered earth.  Well-tended gardens filled with an abundance of flowers hug closely to each doorway, showing a year-round display of bright colors and pleasant scents.

A paved brick road circles around the large hillside to meander through this affluent portion of the village.  Trained to grow over a pristine white wood arbor, a nearby olallieberry bush tempts passersby with its brightly colored fruits dangling amidst bright, green leaves.

An old-fashioned country lane wends its way east beneath the sheltering overhang of flowering cherry trees.  Tiny thatched-roof cottages and other homes line the lane, surrounded by picket fences and neatly tended flower gardens.  The faint sound of children's laughter can be heard from some of the homes.

Apple blossoms drift in the wind, fallen from the flower-laden branches of the gnarled trees which shade the narrow lane.  Neat cottages stand side by side, some of brick, others of weathered cedar shingles, others with whitewashed wooden clapboards.  A covered well, gathering place for local housewives, stands beside the road.

The road runs alongside a sparkling brook that splashes as the water tumbles over smooth rocks lining the streambed.  Several homes nestle in the low-lying land around the brook, surrounded by neatly tended gardens.  A bench swing hangs from a tree branch beside the road, swaying gently in a passing breeze.

A stunted apple tree stands beside the lane, blackened and broken by a lightning strike.  The splintered branches have been carefully trimmed and stacked, drying for use in the winter's fires.  Several cottages stand nearby, their neatly cropped lawns and tended gardens evidence of industry on the part of their owners.

The lane ends at a shallow pond surrounded by weeping willow trees.  A weathered pier juts out over the water, where residents from nearby homes may relax near the cool water in the summertime or catch a fish or two for the evening's meal.

A tangled thicket of gooseberry bushes lines the road to the south.  Nearby, several small homes are scattered about, some near the road, others set back a ways to offer a modicum of privacy.  Cheerful windowboxes filled with pansies and geraniums add a splash of color to the tiny houses.

Pale white jasmine blossoms dangle amidst deep green waxy leaves on a whitewashed trellis, their fragrant nectar attracting a flock of brightly colored hummingbirds.  A low-pitched drone fills the air as chubby bumblebees float amidst the blossoms, their legs covered with a profusion of yellow pollen.  A local homeowner has taken advantage of the nearby flowers, erecting a beehive on the lawn to produce his winter's supply of honey.
The road rises to the crest of a low hill, giving a view of the nearby town.  Farmland spreads out around the village, while neatly thatched cottages and brick homes line the streets.

Several homes nestle in a hollow at the base of a hill, sheltered from the elements by tall poplars and fir trees.  A brook runs nearby, surrounded by mossy rocks and deep green ferns which thrive in the shady setting.  Lush patches of wild lady's slippers bob their pink and purple petals as a breeze gently brushes across the orchids.

A well-worn road winds its way through the valley, between a small town and the adjoining farmlands.  A proliferation of berry bushes crowds the edges as if trying to reclaim the portion of land heavily rutted by wagon and cart wheels.  To the north a village gate beckons weary travelers.

Berry bushes and green shrubs grow between the trunks of elm and birch trees.  Sparrows flutter out of the high branches to light gracefully on a twig, grab a ripe berry, and wing back to their perches.  In the distant northwest a small village can be seen.

Tracks left by wagons laden with heavy cargo mar the road with deep ruts.  A multitude of blackberry bushes, full of plump berries, mingle with a few scattered trees that line each side of this wide byway.

The road crests a small hill covered with ripe blackberry bushes.  Dozens of squashed berries have been imbedded into the packed earth by the wheels of overloaded wagons.  Occasionally a bird swoops down to greedily grab a tiny black treasure from a mature bush.
Small shrubs growing in tight clumps line the road on both sides.  Nestled in the brush are dense clusters of briarberry bushes with tiny berries hanging from woody stems.

Meandering gently through a dense meadow, the road is evenly covered in tiny stones laid to smooth the rough terrain.  Endless rows of briarberry bushes, cultivated and harvested for their woody roots, border each side of the wide road.

The road continues its trek through the lush meadow.  Flowers of all kinds grow haphazardly among dense groupings of briarberry bushes filled with bright red berries.  Irrigation ditches filled with rainwater line both sides of the road.

A wooden cart filled with freshly dug briarberry bushes is parked on the side of the roadway.  Coveted for their woody roots in the making of tobacco pipes, briarberry bushes are carefully harvested annually by the local Olvi families of the area.  Deep in the meadow, you can see a small group of Olvi thinning the denser clumps.

The road narrows a little here, as briarberry bushes laden with heavy plump berries mingle with wild cinnamon shrubs that fight to reclaim this well traveled byway.  Scattered amidst the dense brush are a few birch and elm trees, with occasional clumps of pink clover peeking through the heavy brambles.

Hardy, wild cinnamon shrubs grace both sides of the road as the path widens.  Their leathery leaves offer an open invitation to a mass influx of butterflies that migrate to this area in the spring.  Occasionally, the sound of small wildlife can be heard scurrying beneath the compact bushes.

The road crests a small hill flanked by dense clumps of wild cinnamon shrubs.  A multitude of migrating butterflies can be seen fluttering amidst the bushes, their beautifully colored wings complimenting the deep green of the leathery leafed shrubs.
A shallow gully runs across the road at the bottom of a small hill.  Thick walls of bushes grow wildly like untamed hedgerows bordering the road.
The road here snakes through some of the thickest bushes and brambles.  Fragrant cinnamon mixes with sweet raspberry in a panoply of earthy, spiced scents.
Bushes and vines grow wildly, high enough to block out most of the sky.  The road dips and weaves through high bushes and snarls of vicious brambles.
The narrow road rises up to the peak of a small hill, rife with tangled bushes.  A broken, berry-stained wooden pail lies shattered on the side of the road.
The path glides gently down a low rise toward the open ocean.  A small step ladder stands to one side of the road, overcome by creeping vines of bramble and raspberry.

A soft breeze carries the faint scent of the sea from the east.  The road begins to widen as if to hasten travelers towards the shore.  Interspersed with bramble and berry bushes are wild sirese flowers, their bright blooms swaying gently in the wind.

Dozens of wild raspberry bushes intermingled with clumps of sweet woodruff attempt to encroach upon the widening road.  Small woodland critters scamper beneath the brush, knocking ripe berries to the ground.

Atop a small hill, the road crests just high enough to see a bay to the east.  The fresh smell from the sea is strong and mingles with the scent of ripe raspberries that hang from the many bushes attempting to trespass upon the widening road.

A small harbor with several brightly painted docks cheerfully greets seafaring visitors to the small community of Arthe Dale.  A few seagulls can be seen greedily pecking at ripe berries pilfered from the many bushes that flank a road leading westward.

A cobblestone walk lined with lush taffelberry bushes points the way to a large greenhouse nestled amid colorful thornberry shrubs and maiden tress vines.  Brightly painted wooden benches are scattered around a small pond that rests at the base of a large mound dotted with fiddlehead ferns.  The greenhouse's glass door has been cheerfully painted with colorful flowers of all shapes and sizes.

A copse of brown, dried trees blocks all view of the community to the north.  The pot-holed path continues to the east, past abandoned knolls covered with patches of dried grass and the occasional tall, green weed.  Torn curtains flutter in the breeze through a nearby broken window.

Dry, matted grass and tall weeds cover the nearby abandoned knolls.  A gooseberry bush near the edge of the path has turned feral from neglect, becoming a wild tangle of thorny branches with nary a single berry in evidence among its browning leaves.

Islands of undaunted weeds appear in a sea of bare, parched earth along the path.  Broken pieces of furniture lie scattered across the yard of one home, some of them burned, others merely torn apart as if for sport.

Row upon row of cabbages, carrots, potatoes and turnips have been planted in this garden plot.  The industrious Halflings of Arthe Dale have maintained it well.  The rows are neatly arranged, and there is not a weed in sight.  A tiny ladybug flutters from plant to plant, sometimes thrown off her course by the gentle breeze.

A large section of the garden plot has been set aside for the small shrubs of deep green glossy leaves that bear the village's beloved taffelberries.  The branches of the low-growing bushes are laden with juicy black berries.
A modwyn vine arbor stands on the eastern edge of the garden.  Heavy clusters of grape-like modwyn fruit hang temptingly, waiting to be picked.  A large, low vat sits off to the side of the arbor.

Heavy stone walls lean drunkenly on each other, like tipsy soldiers staggering into the night.  Somehow, the roof has remained mostly intact, providing a modicum of shelter and warmth.  The remains of a fire, now cold and lifeless, show that others have sought refuge here as well.  A broken stone table is the only furnishing yet left to this abandoned station.  In all, a sad reminder of busier times on this ancient road, when traffic and trade must have been much heavier.
Not much is left of this building except mice and a few ratty blankets.  It seems well and truly abandoned, of no significant notice whatsoever.

The Northern Trade road runs like an arrow through the small town of Kaerna.  Composed mostly of ramshackle daub and wattle houses, the most distinguishing feature of Kaerna is its inn, which looms protectively over the other, smaller establishments.  Less a town and more a waystation than anything else, the tiny wooden-walled village hugs the road with a tenacious determination.

Even in the cool of the night the village remains active.  A soft, cheery glow shines from the windows and open doorway of the Gilded Unicorn Inn, and a few traders are yet about; checking their camels, inspecting their wagons, or preparing for the morning's excursions to come.  The stars overhead seem to stretch on forever, the moons smiling benevolently down on the sleeping village.

The grasslands lap like waves at the edge of Kaerna Village to the east.  The small, dun-colored houses of the town endure silently, islands in a sea of green.  To the west the land begins to take on a more rolling form, an abrupt and unusual change from the endless plains that stretch to the north and south.

The grasslands here are caught between the presence of rolling hills to the west and the small village of Kaerna to the east.  To the north and south is nothing but empty plains, wind-twisted and long ignored by humanity.

A few residences huddle here, alternately shouldered up against the back of the Gilded Unicorn Inn and the sides of the general store.  The store is squat but neat, its exterior newly whitewashed and a small garden carefully cultivated outside it.

The well has been craftily made of smooth interlocking stones.  A closer look reveals that no mortar was used in its construction despite its circular shape.  A wooden roof protects it from dirt and debris, and a fruitless modwyn vine twines all around.  Dappled shadows created by the moonlight give this place a sense of mystery and wonder.

Meandering eastward from the village well, a grassy footpath follows a gentle decline away from the bustle of the Northern Trade road and through a small copse of oak and aspen trees.  Wildflowers grow in abundant banks on either side of the path, their delicate blossoms evolving with the seasons in an endless, ever-changing cycle of color and fragrance.

A chattering brook traverses the footpath in a stony bed, its crystal waters dancing and sparkling over smooth grey rocks and the deep brown remnants of long-fallen logs.  Embedded in the soft earth either side of the stream, a broad ironwood plank forms a narrow bridge, allowing visitors to balance across the brook and continue eastward toward the village gate.

A low sandstone wall runs around Lower Kaerna, the modest proportions of the perimeter suggesting the villagers have few enemies other than the occasional adventurous bovine.  The village gate struggles with the attentions of a voracious ivy that pokes its brazen fingers into every nook and cranny of the surrounding stone and clings determinedly to the pristine paintwork.  An ironwood plank leads west across a nearby stream.

The gate opens onto a charming village green surrounded by quaint cottages and tranquil rural lanes.  In remarkable contrast with the fervent activity of Kaerna's west end, the rustic simplicity of Lower Kaerna envelopes the senses and blots out any memory of life on the trade routes.  No matter what activity might be taking place on or around the green, nothing here is done at any pace greater than an amble.

Running along the south side of the green, a narrow path leads past a group of tiny cabins that almost disappear into a thick copse of aspen and sweet chestnut trees.  Despite their modesty, each humble dwelling appears spotlessly clean and diligently maintained, their secluded location in the village's only uncombed spot is clearly a careful choice made by fastidious and discerning people.

The village pond occupies the best part of the northwest green, its brown waters rippling with the fussy antics of ducks and the occasional splash of a jumping fish.  Around the edge of the pond, tall bulrushes sway gently in the breeze, parting just enough to grant a glimpse of moorhens and a pair of haughty swans nesting silently in the shallows.

An old wagon wheel idles in one corner of the Green, as if to remind visitors to leave their work behind them and succumb to a more placid way of life.  Between its spokes, the green-keepers have planted a variety of low shrubs, the contrasting hues of their foliage creating a fascinating monument to indolence resplendent with different textures and colors.

Overlooking the carefully-tended lawns of the village green, a row of smart stone and thatch cottages enjoys a pleasing, scenic location.  Four vast oak trees stand aside the narrow road at the edge of the green, their thick trunks and spreading boughs dark with age.  Rooks' nests form a rambling roost along many of the branches, sending forth the occasional raucous squawk as one feathered resident disputes territory with another.

Between a pair of whitewashed lodges, the rustic beginnings of Blythe Lane lead off from the green to bring a pleasing impression of the surrounding countryside into the village.  The lane itself is actually a narrow, stony path bordered by vigorous cowslips and flowering nettles which flourish in cool, verdant banks outside snug homesteads and at the feet of overhanging sycamores.

By Lower Kaerna standards, Fourways is a throbbing thoroughfare, given that the only two roads of any size meet here.  Even so, the pace of life is relaxing to say the least, and those few folk who do choose to pass a moment here do little more than watch the world go by.  A small bronze statue on a stone pedestal occupies the central point of the crossroads.

A row of neat homes runs across the northern side of the green, the grandly-named High Street more of a country lane than the major artery its nomenclature might suggest.  Each dwelling here seems to take great pride in its prime location, presenting to the public a meticulously maintained facade complete with colorful curtains and window-boxes brimming with seasonal blooms.

Overlooking the lilies and willows growing in and around the village pond, the homes here have a sleepy look about them, their light curtains blowing softly from the wide-open windows which typify this safe and peaceful hamlet.  There is little activity to disturb the tranquil silence, save for the intermittent chirp of a bird or a soft splash of fin or feather in the quiet waters.

High Street continues its gentle progress to the east, its smooth sandstone paving diligently swept free of any dust and debris which might settle for half a moment.  The homes which claim this part of town are slightly larger than the average Lower Kaerna cottage, and each owner clearly takes great pride in preserving the superiority of the neighborhood.

Just north of the comparative bustle of Fourways, Lady Alice Drive begins its easy dawdle around the upper end of the village.  Countless rows of neat cobbles run the length of the lane as it curves past immaculate cottages and snug lodges, each home a picture-perfect tribute to the houseproud families who populate this tiny town.

Carefully planted in evenly spaced rows of fat wooden buckets, miniature fir and poplar trees line the drive with splashes of deep green.  Complementing the neat display, oaken planters bursting with seasonal blooms adorn the windowsills of many of the homes, combining the beauty of the wild with the modest gentility of the village.

The tantalizing aroma of fresh-baked bread and cakes wafts about on a light breeze regardless of the time of day, as if many of the locals spend most of their time steadfastly producing confections in industrious and cozy kitchens.  A trestle table standing in the garden of one cottage bears a tempting selection of the day's culinary produce, proudly offered to passers-by for the sampling.

A constant, fresh breeze slips around the crescent, its long journey down from the mountains and moorland beyond Kaerna drawing to a close in the sleepy hamlet.  From time to time, the sharp fragrance of pine and the peaty smell of damp earth wends its way into the village, giving a gentle reminder that there is indeed a wider, wilder world outside the encircling walls.

The drive narrows to little more than a carriage width here, squeezing between two matching whitewashed cottages that stand aside the passageway as if expecting to take tolls from passers-by.  A lush modwyn vine climbs recklessly up the side of each building, attracting a wide variety of dazzling butterflies and tiny birds to the deep tangle of its foliage and slender branches.

A narrow, cobbled lane leads off from the quiet end of High Street and forms a gently arcing crescent from one side of the tiny village to the other.  Lined with quaint thatched cottages and charming sandstone dwellings, Lady Alice Drive meanders through the serene village like a lazy smile, encouraging travelers along its sedate curve to adopt a pleasureable, unhurried gait.

Many of the homes here have matching curtains and gardens displaying identical selections of shrubs and blossoms, suggesting the sense of community in Lower Kaerna is particularly strong.  Large, wrought-iron flower baskets hang from tall blackwood poles at intervals along High Street, their lively displays of trailing ivy and seasonal wildflowers adding a simple yet elegant adornment to the street.

High Street draws to a close in a crescent following the curve of the village wall.  A half-circle of homes occupies the spacious turnaround, their sparkling windows and glossy paintwork a gleaming reflection of their owners' pride.  A box privet hedge borders the walkway around the crescent, intermittently giving way to numerous white gravel paths that lead to the front door of each dwelling.

Enclosing the path, a tall hawthorn and beech hedge thins out periodically to allow passage through to the cottages and cabins which nestle peacefully in their woodsy lots.  Thin plumes of blue-grey smoke drift from squat chimneys and waft across the lane in a faintly shifting haze, bringing to mind reassuring memories of hearth and home.

Blythe Lane draws to a drowsy close inside the village wall, where a bank of aromatic thyme and lavender grows strong and robust beneath the vine-clad grey and yellow sandstone.  Several of the homes in this area boast a similar display of scented herbs in their front gardens, infusing the air with a memorably pungent perfume reminiscent of a warm, dewy morning in the countryside.

The wooden wall surrounding the tiny waystop of Kaerna is a visible line drawn between the plains and hamlet.  Thick grasses and shrubs growing against the protective barrier seem intent upon reclaiming the village's side-by-side buildings for the prairie.  Off to one side stands an abandoned militia shack, a silent casualty to the ongoing war between civilization and nature.

The wind rushes through the grass, making a soft shirring sound.  Occasionally you catch the crackle of movement or the twitterings of birds, but any sounds of civilization generated by something other than yourself seem like the sort of thing you would think up in a dream.

Miles upon miles of uncivilized land lie before you, devoid of any sign of humanity.  A shifting sea of brown, green, and tan grasses rises about you, rustling with the movement of the occasional bird or butterfly that dares to plunge down into the vegetation.  A line of dark mountains rises to the north, shadowed and gloomy, they climb abruptly from the grasslands.

The road rises along the curve of a low hill that slopes down to the south into open grasslands.  The rocky crest of the hill rises sharply above you as you toil along the well-kept roadway.  Local stones from the hillside have been smoothed and shaped to form the roadbed and the footing is good.  Northwards though, the hills shift quickly into steep mountains.

You crest a low hill that gives a far-reaching view.  To the north a line of mountains rises steeply from the surrounding hills, while southward the hills fade out to forest and plain.  Far to the south, a heavy haze obscures the view, but you glimpse the occasional flash of open water.

You travel through a small dell that rises northwards into a narrow pass.  You follow the path with your eyes until it fades from view among the steeply rising mountains.  Southward a low hill rises, bearing the roadway along its shoulders.  A Trader's Guild outpost sits alongside the stony trail.

The roadway is made from cracked stone that seems to have fallen from the steep rocky shoulders of a mountain whose flank forms a boundary along your path.  Rising steeply to the north and falling away to low hills to the south, the road cuts a narrow path among the mountains.

You edge along a steep drop as the road narrows sharply in order to work its way along a narrow ridge of rock.  Snow-capped peaks tower overhead and an occasional eagle or hawk can be seen soaring on the high-road of the sky far overhead.  You envy them their direct routes as you gaze over the lip of the road and note the crumbling stone along its rim.

The road passes onto an almost level area as you work your way through a narrow gap in the mountains.  Huge boulders that have tumbled loose from the escarpments above you cause you to keep a wary eye out for more such unwelcome fellow-travellers.  A tiny roadside shrine has been erected here, perhaps by someone who made a lucky escape from such an avalanche of stone.

A huge boulder blocks much of the road, but room remains to squeeze by between it and the mountain wall.  One broken and shattered bone shows you that someone or something was far less fortunate in times past.  You look nervously up at the rock-strewn slopes above you and mutter a short prayer that the boulders rest easily these days.

The road rises sharply to the west as it wends among the steep mountains.  Eastward, it falls away into a narrow, heavily-wooded valley.  Evidence of frequent landslides shows in the piles of rock and small boulders that make passage here uneven and slightly risky.

Thick woods grow heavily along the shoulders of the roadway, blocking both sky and sight after a short distance.  Several sets of wolf tracks are evident in the heavy leaf mould under some of the trees.  Troublesome travelers' tales describing the forest's dangers come to mind as the journey continues through the close-set trees.

You come upon a small clearing in the heavy woods that allows a view of the sky.  A faint path can be made out that wanders into the trees, but it fades off before you can wonder about where it might lead.  There is an unnerving quiet here, even the wind seems to have died.  You feel a stranger in this wild place, perhaps an unwelcome stranger.

Tall trees grow close along both sides of the road.  Small animals skitter among the branches overhead and dart among low-growing shrubs that eke out an existence in the deep shade of the forest.  Something taller than you has clawed the bark off a tree trunk several feet overhead and you wonder just where the beast that wore such claws is currently.

Tall trees grow thickly to the south as the road climbs into a narrow valley.  Northwards, the land opens out into rolling hills that fade off into the looming shadow of several sharp mountain peaks, each distinct from the other.

Heavily wooded hills rise on both sides as the roadway winds among them.  The air is dead and stale, any breeze is blocked by the trees and hills.  Clouds of gnats and worse seem to follow you, getting in your mouth and hair.  There is a faint smell of damp earth and rotting vegetation.

Massive flocks of small black birds wheel and dive among the low hills on either side.  They seem to be feeding on the dense swarms of midges and other insects that lurk in the heavy air.  A miasma of musty smells and unknown odors roils in your nostrils.  The ground to the north descends into a faint mist or cloud in the air.

A cloud of flint-dry dust rises on every breeze, making you sneeze.  For the most part, you see the grasslands about you in a state of decay and near death.  Mountains rising sharply in the south form a counterpoint to others, sharper yet, that loom northwards.  Saw-edged peaks and broken crowns indicate their origins as volcanoes in the not-so-distant past.

Eroded wagon ruts cause you to notice that this road was once travelled with a greater frequency than it is now.  While safe from becoming overgrown by the dying grasses of the plains, this part of the trail is crumbling from disuse and the encroaching dust.

The winds veer around you, catching the grasses and your clothing in their grip and tugging like beggars vying for attention.   Flowers, closed for the evening, bob along in time with the lonely music the breezes create with the plains.  You can hear the babble of rushing water coming from the north.

A narrow river rushes past you on its way southwest, its turbulent grey waters creating a deafening roar.  To the north the land changes dramatically from plains to the darker, more verdant green of meadows.  To the south stretches a narrow strip of grassland.  A sturdy wood and stone bridge spans the river, allowing safe passage.

Smooth rounded pebbles, bleached by the sun to a pearly white, line the rocky bed of a sparkling stream.  Not much wider than a strong leap could carry you, the brook flows gently over clean stones, occassionally parting for a large rock thrust from its center.  Green clumps of reeds prospering along the grassy bank offer a safe haven to the shy water creatures which make their home here.

Cool tendrils of water slip down the rough surface of the mammoth stone outcropping, cascading to the rock's base with a sibilant whisper.  Water dances and leaps jubilantly beneath the waterfall, before rippling away in great waves, to finally die away and lie still at the pool's farthest reaches.  Along the banks, tall vilt reeds provide privacy for modest swimmers.

Taking the opportunity to examine the distant countryside, large green forests in the southwest, flatlands to the south and the large ocean expanse to the southeast all catch the eye.  All seem more attractive than the forbidding set of cliffs up ahead.
Placed in the wall of the sheer cliff that stands before you is a large stone door, currently blasted open.  Two large lifelike sentinels, one on either side of the door, have been scorched black.

Loose rocks from recent landslides cover the trail making progress slightly more precarious and slower.  A strong creeper seems to have won a battle with the steep cliff face and secured holds in the rock as far up as you can see.
