rooms.desc: Northwest of the road, a burnt-out farmhouse stands, or perhaps lies is a better word, since all that time or war has left is a stone chimney, cold among the meadow grasses.  Bright splashes of color -- wild red roses, orange butterfly weed, yellow day-lilies -- surround the ruins, like nature's funeral wreath.

As the road winds by the farmhouse, piles of grey stones, nearly swallowed by grass, trace the foundation of the farmhouse.  Some abandoned farming equipment sits rusting near the edge of an overgrown field.  A dull red stack of splintered planking set between the ruins and field marks the site of what was once a barn.

Fields stretch away from the road, some fallow, others filled with sun-colored wheat and strong green stalks of corn.  Beyond the fields to the west, the monastery's buildings and stone-enclosed walls parallel the road.  To the southwest lie the scattered ruins of an old farmstead.

Stone gives way to ruddy brick where the field-fencing wall adjoins the high walls enclosing the monastery complex.  A reddish patch on the monastery wall resolves into a bricked-up doorway.  At just about human eye-level, one of the bricks protrudes noticeably from the rest.

The road wends close to the monastery, where ivy leaves soften the gray walls, dappling the stone with their color and shadow.  To the other side of the turnpike, fields ascend and descend gently rolling hills, their furrows lending an odd texture to the contours of the land.

To the southwest the stone wall curves around the building complex, stretching in an unbroken expanse westward.  A tower at the corner of the monastery looms high into the air, overlooking the turning road, its travelers, and the fields beyond with a stony impartiality.

The grey bulk of a monastery rises to the south, an obvious landmark on the route. Cultivated fields surround it to both sides of the road, the checkered browns, yellows, and soft greens of the fields arranged in this landscape with a natural grace that any artist would envy.

A rotted wooden bridge partially spans a drying stream bed. The bridge footings descend into a mix of lush cattails and creekbroom -- a hint that some water remains.  Towards the center of the bridge, the planking has broken, leaving the bridge nearly impassable.

The small copse of birch trees provides a welcome oasis of shade in the open grassland.  The trees stand thin and tall, their pale trunks catching the sunlight and glowing softly in the shade of their rustling canopy.  Oddly set amidst the birches is a curiously bent black willow tree.

The cobblestone road curves gently here, the round stones smooth and freshly-swept by the ever vigilant groundskeepers.  A broad expanse of thick brambles stretches to the northwest, obscuring any vision of what may lie beyond them.

A thorny thicket of brambles obscures direct vision to the northeast, although the top half of the temple's massive orb is still visible.  Its lustrous black ironwood surface gleams in the sunlight, accented by polished silverwood window frames and sconces.  A bizarre contrast with the errant foliage, indeed.
Towering above the shorter birch, the twisted limbs of the willow tree offer a breathtaking view of the landscape.  The leafless branches clatter and scrape against each other in the wind.

Burnt shards of wood and bone are strewn outward from the ridge of a vast crater torn into the landscape.  The ragged pit gapes widely at the sky like a giant maw screaming in rage and sorrow.  An uneven trail littered with gravel and blasted rock weaves down the steep walls through thick layers of soil, sand and stone to the bottom of the great hole.

Stones charred and cracked from a great explosion jut from the jagged walls of the crater and alter the trail's course.  The sharp edges of silver-flecked stone glisten from the dark soil like the sword blades of a legion raised in battle.

Devoid of vegetation, the dark topsoil yields to a coarse grey loam.  Sand fused by fire crackles under foot, and the slippery grit sends shards of stone and unwary travelers alike hurtling down the slope.  A broken broadsword protrudes from a large sandstone, its blackened blade twisted like a coiled adder.

Fist-sized black stones carpet the narrow pass between two large shards of rock that rise from the base of the crater.  The stones glimmer with the dull iridescence of onyx and swallow the surrounding light.  As the carpet thickens nearer the bottom, the wall seems to fall off into darkness.

Tall slopes tower overhead in every direction, casting long shadows across the stony floor and chasing sunlight from the great crater.  Small avalanches of stone and gravel rain down from above, startling small flocks of birds that flap off into the pale sky.

The wind howls against the stony walls like braying hounds in the winter and whips up small whirlwinds of sand and skree.  Gossamer veils of shadow hover far above, casting a barren vista of monochrome greys and blacks.

The jagged base of the crater is run through with cracks in the black stone like open wounds in ebon flesh.  A buzzard perched atop mineral-flecked stone pecks at the stringy remains of a small meal.  It glances up occasionally to survey the vast pit littered with debris, and glare at the interlopers in its domain.

Whitewash and dark oak beams mix on the tiny half-timbered cottages which line the cobblestoned lane.  Granite-topped brick walls surround the houses, their hard outlines softened by deep green moss which clings to the mortar.  Kitchen gardens grow within the shelter of the walls -- herbs, fruit trees and vegetables all within easy reach of the door.

The tile roofs of the cottages along the lane are carefully laid out to channel rainwater away from the plaster walls and into barrels, where it may be collected for use in cooking and laundry.  A tangled mass of ivy sends winding tendrils out to wrap around the brick chimneys and walls of one cottage, leaving little to see but the diamond-shaped panes of glass in its windows.

A rishyarla bush grows close to the wall surrounding a nearby home, its pale yellow blossoms filling the air with an intense, sweet fragrance.  Like the other cottages which line the street, the half-timbered structure shows signs of careful upkeep.  The shrubs surrounding the house are carefully pruned, and cheesecloth netting protects the fruit trees from the ravages of the local birds.

At the center of the close, a grassy square provides an open area where cattle graze during the day.  The hoarse bray of a mule mingles with the sharp noise of a chisel as a stonemason works on the other side of the square, shaping the stones for a new fence.  A gravel-lined path leads to a small rose-covered gazebo.

The dark oak beams of the cottages have been carved with fanciful figures of gargoyles and fae, or with intricate knotwork patterns which run along the front of the homes.  Other homes have stark white plaster walls broken by a decorative arrangement of the exposed oak beams.

Diamond-shaped panes of thick, wavy glass attest to the age of the homes which line the cobblestoned streets.  Impurities in the glass have resulted in a faint violet tint to the glazing, an attractive contrast to the blackened solder which holds the windows together.

Housewives gather to gossip over the brick walls which divide the half-timbered cottages around the square.  Their sharp glances measure the probable worth of passersby, or take in the poorly mended sleeve of a neighbor's gown, all of which is discussed in low tones as they fold laundry or work in their tiny garden plots.

Nestled amidst the homes of the close, a tiny shop displays an assortment of carpets and other floor coverings hanging from its wall.  Imported from distant lands like Aesry Surlaenis'a and Mer'Kresh, the rugs feature wool dyed in vibrant shades of scarlet, blue and golden, and woven into intricate floral or geometric designs.

Painted wooden planters filled with herbs or colorful flowers grow outside the windows of cottages lining the street.  Within the brick walls surrounding each house, tiny gardens grow in the limited space.  At one home, a row of pies cools on the window ledge sending a tantalizing aroma wafting across the cobblestone street.

Dense brambles press in on all sides, giving this place a claustrophobic feel.  The few narrow gaps in the bushes are barely navigable, and from each branch and twig long, sharp spines threaten scratches and punctures.

Tiny grey-green leaves grow in dense spirals around the branches of the brambles which surround the trail.  In actuality it's hardly a trail -- more a gap in the foliage, beyond which is another gap, and perhaps another.  The gaps are narrow, and look like they were made by animals rather than people.  This place belongs to its four-footed inhabitants, and the clinging, snagging thorns are a warning to all others who come here.

The bushes on either side of the track loom high, dense enough to obscure whatever lies beyond.  Every now and again they rustle, sometimes on one side, sometimes on the other.  Something is moving about within the depths of the bramble patch.  And considering the long, wicked thorns sticking out from the brambles in every direction, anything that would casually rustle its way through them must have an incredibly tough hide.

A huge, spreading oak tree dominates the center of the clearing, lifting its great branches up into the sky.  The thorn bushes stop just outside the rounded perimeter, allowing grass and some flowers to grow beneath the great tree.

Gaps of bare dirt in the grass around the oak tree have been smoothed over and patted down.  In one of the larger ones, someone drew a smiling face with a beard and a little round hat, using a stick or perhaps a small finger.  Buttercups grow here and there in the grass, along with a few other flowers.  The brambles form a nearly solid wall about the clearing, but haven't penetrated into it.

Mounds of spiny bushes press in from all sides, thorn-laden branches reaching in like skeletal fingers.  Dusty sunbeams pierce through the branches overhead, illuminating drifting motes and falling leaves, throwing twisted shadows upon the ground.

The sound of calling birds blends with the rustles and crackles coming from all around the bramble thicket.  Thorny branches tremble in the breeze, dense living walls forming painful barriers in all but a very few directions.  Some scuffled tracks in the moist ground lead away to the north.

Birds chirp and call back and forth to each other, up in the leafy canopy spreading between several trees on either side of the narrow track.  There's an edge of urgency to the bird calls, as though there were a predator about, or some other lurking danger.

The brambles converge on a small stand of trees to form a dead-end in the trail.  The greenery grows dense here, with the swagged branches of the trees competing for light and air with the tough little thorn bushes.  The leaf litter on the ground is thick and spongy, covering the dirt and all but a few of the larger rocks.

rooms.desc: The brambles grow particularly dense here, leaving only a tiny pocket barely large enough to stand in.  In the leaves covering the ground are signs that some animal has made its nest here recently, leaving only scuffed ground and litter.

Small round leaves, grey-green with a white streak down the middle, cover the branches of the brambles which form this thicket.  Although the leaves grow in dense masses, they're unable to hide the sharp thorns which protect the bushes.  A pleasant, spicy scent emanates from the leaves, and when the breeze dies down and the air is still, the smell is sharp enough to sting one's sinuses.

The narrow track winds in and out among the brambles.  Its narrowness, along with its meandering path, suggest that it's a game trail, rather than anything built by or meant for people.  There certainly seem to be animals in here somewhere, if the hissing and honking noises coming from beyond the thicket walls are any clue.

The ground has been churned up by something.  It's dug and scored and turned over as though some one or some thing were searching for buried treasure.  The dug-up dirt is still dark and moist, so whatever was digging here left not too long ago.  Nearly hidden beneath a bush, the trampled remnant of something whitish is barely visible.
Something that hasn't bathed in far too long was here just a short time ago.  The pungent odor covers even the spicy scent of the bramble bushes, instilling in one a strong desire to be elsewhere.

The land rises to the north and east, and the brambles grow thicker.  Some kind of vine with striped green and white leaves spiraling up its length winds its way among the bushes, weaving them into a dense wall.  A squirrel would have a hard time finding a path in that direction, but the tangle of thorns is somewhat less dense in a couple of other places.

The ground pitches upward to the northeast, and dense, brambly foliage covers the hillside.  The rise is neither steep nor high, but the thickly spined vegetation makes it impossible to climb.  Mounds of thorny bushes grow in lush and painful profusion along the base of the hill as well, except for a narrow game trail which winds along its base.

A brisk breeze blowing up from the center of the bramble thicket to the southwest brings with it a number of strange sounds -- low hisses are occasionally pierced by outraged honks.  Something is in there, and it's probably not a group of picnickers.  The bushes shiver and rustle, marking the movements of whatever's back there.

A half-rotted corpse lies on -- and partially in -- the muddy, uneven ground.  One withered arm is stretched out in the direction of the low hill, its bony fingers clutching for a handhold that wasn't there.  Whatever killed it apparently gored it into immobility and then began to feast, beginning with the legs and working its way up.  The spicy scent of the brambles is overpowered by the foul stink of the decaying body, and even the cool breeze blowing up the hill isn't enough to disperse the stench.

A flowering vine winds its way among the thorny brambles, uncaring of the sharp spines.  Using the bushes as a living trellis, the vine sends its spiraling tendrils twining through the branches and twigs, decorating them with big trumpet-shaped flowers.  Arrowhead-shaped leaves provide a fresh green background for the pink and white striped blossoms.

In the bend of the trail there are signs that an animal has passed by here recently, but the bushes are thick and make it difficult to distinguish.  The thorns press in close on every side, even meeting overhead where they block out the blue of the sky and cast a gloomy shade over the thicket.  Only a couple of gaps in the bushes suggest a way out.

Something has passed this way recently, leaving tracks in the dark, loamy dirt.  Other spoor lie scattered about in the leaf litter covering the ground, and broken branches and shredded leaves indicate that whatever it was wasn't feeling terribly peaceful.

The bramble bushes aren't quite as dense in this spot, and there are a number of gaps big enough to slide through without doing too much damage to one's person.  This seems to be the intersection of a number of small trails, and judging by how churned and dug up the ground is, it sees a lot of use.

The trail curves through the bramble thicket, past some bushes of a different variety.  Foliage presses close all around, spreading both out and up in the competition for resources.  Birds rustle in the bushes, hunting for berries and small insects.  Something else that sounds much larger than a bird rustles through the brambles somewhere close by.

A stand of berry bushes holds its own on the western side of the track against the press of brambles.  The berries are greenish yellow with light brown veins, about the size of a large grape.  They don't look terribly appetizing, but judging by the stripped branches at the lower levels, something that lives in this thicket finds them yummy.

Mounds of thorny bushes press in on the narrow trail, leaving barely enough room to pass without getting stuck or scratched.  Rustling sounds occasionally drift by with the breeze, but it's hard to tell where the noises are coming from.  There's something moving around in here, though, just out of sight, behind the greenery.

A few stray sunbeams shine through the branches of the trees scattered about the thicket, illuminating the grey-green leaves of the brambles, and gleaming on the needle-sharp points of their thorns.  Here and there a clump of tough grass manages to grow around the base of the bushes, but most of the dirt is trampled and dug up, making it impossible for less hardy plants to survive.

Tracks about the size of a large palm show clearly in the firmly packed dirt.  Grey-green leaves, liberally spiked with long, sharp thorns, spread out from either side.  The foliage casts deep shadows across the tracks, emphasizing their size and depth.

Something large tore a gap in the brambles to the northwest.  Broken branches and oozing sap define the edges of a hole nearly an armlength across.  Broken and missing thorns testify to the toughness of whatever came crashing through -- the long, sharp spines weren't much of a deterrent.

Signs of a scuffle are everywhere.  The dirt underfoot is streaked and spotted with dried blood.  Patches of hide and broken spines lie scattered about, and there's a huge hole in the brambles to the southeast where something large went crashing through in a hurry.  The bark of a large tree is scarred by deep grooves the width of a finger or better, and drying sap streaks the wood in long, viscous dribbles.

Crackles and rustles betray the presence of... something... moving in the brambles up the slope to the northwest.  The thorny bushes are so dense in that direction, however, that not even a Halfling child could manage to penetrate them.  Interspersed among the brambles are a few trees, spotted here and there, spreading their green canopies over the harsher undergrowth.

Palm-sized tracks pressed deeply into the ground stand out against the lighter colored leaf litter.  Broken branches and bruised foliage up to the height of a large Human's shoulder tell a tale of violence, as do the darkened spots and streaks of blood spattered about.

Spiderwebs festoon the branches of the trees up overhead, draped and swagged like festival bunting.  The brambles below the trees are bare of webbing, although well-trimmed with long, sharp thorns.  Grey-green leaves spiral up the branches, large and round closer to the roots, small and oval at the tips.

There must be something good in the soil of the low rise to the northwest, because the brambles and other plants growing up there are lush and thick, forming an impenetrable barrier.  The thorn bushes spread across the slope in grey-green mounds, having penetrated into every available span of ground until they stand silhouetted against the sky at the top of the rise.

Signs of a mighty conflagration are everywhere.  Scarred furrows in the ground make footing uncertain.  Blackened thorn branches wave like spiny skeletons, stripped of leaves and hardened by fire.  Heat-fused lumps of something unidentifiable lie scattered about -- driven into the ground, entangled in the brambles, flattened across the backs of raw wounds in the bark of trees.  Something unimaginably hot has burned a huge gap in the undergrowth to the south, like a white-hot poker sizzling through flesh.

Dense brambles grow on the slope to the northwest, protecting the low rise with a wall of finger-length thorns.  The track underfoot has been churned up by passing feet, the leaf litter thrown about to reveal the rich dirt beneath.

A huge burned clearing, half a dozen long strides across, lies bare and blackened.  Even the tough brambles gave way before the heat of whatever came into this place, incinerated by the fire and now doubtless lying unidentifiable among the charred rubble and blackened dust crunching underfoot.  In the center of the consumed circle is a pit, a dark hole burrowed deep into the ground at a steep angle.  An acrid smell fills the air, sharp and sour, penetrating everything.

Dense, thorny bushes press in from all sides, grabbing at hair and clothing and dangling straps.  A single tree spreads its branches overhead, filtering out the sunlight and casting dancing shadows on the foliage below.

A huge oak tree stands sentinel in the center of a large clearing.  The bramble bushes stop suddenly around the edges, as though someone had drawn a wavering line across which they're forbidden to pass.  Short green grass grows here, although it's torn up in places, and a few flowers manage to bloom in spots and crannies.

The narrow trail winds through the bramble patch, and around a number of trees.  Thorn bushes press hard up against the tree trunks, but the trees are taller and rise up above the underbrush with uncaring dignity.

Thick leaf litter covers the ground, making it both spongy and crunchy.  Shriveled berries and little round leaves from the brambles combine with long pointed leaves from the trees to form a dense insulating mulch.  Here and there in the mulch a few mushrooms show their pale heads, thriving in the moist decay.

Dense bushes grow in irregular mounds, throwing grotesque shapes across what little bare ground there is.  Bright orange berries nestle in the shadows among thorns as long as a finger.  Picking them would probably be painful, and would likely result in a certain amount of bloodletting, but they're not edible anyway, so it doesn't really matter.

A few tall trees grow in the midst of the thorny brambles, rising high above the bushes.  Long, pointed leaves filter out much of the sun, but the tough thorn bushes do fine all the same.  The soil is rich and loamy, and there's plenty of water, so the bushes and the trees manage to coexist quite well.

A huge boulder rests in a crease between two gentle rises.  The slopes are covered with thick thornbushes, but nothing grows on the boulder except the occasional lichen.  Tall and steep, it looks like a giant's egg resting in a thorny basket.  Deep shadows obscure the niche beneath the lower curve of the boulder, which in any case is too low to put more than a hand into.

The soft sighing of the breeze blends with the chirrup of birds and the humm-buzz of insects to create some rather pleasant background noise.  The game trail curves from the east to the southwest, paralleling the base of the slope, through a dense thicket of brambles.  Tall purple grass grows in sprays here and there in the bushes, poking its narrow spears through the open lattice of the woody branches.

The oak tree in the center of the clearing casts a large patch of shade here on its north side.  A few ferns grow at the base of the trunk, providing a feathery border to the expanse of green grass that covers the ground between the tree and the brambles.  Off on the eastern side of the clearing the brambles give way to dense, mounding berry bushes.

Bright green berry bushes grow in rounded piles to the east of the oak tree, only gradually giving way to the brambles on the southern curve of the clearing.  Patches of bare dirt show dark against the lighter green of the grass, places where the ground has been torn up and smoothed over.  A few grey-green sprouts grow here and there in the grass, but none more than a couple of inches tall.

A rough platform perches at the intersection of three great branches.  Of different types of wood, and cut to different lengths and thicknesses, this obviously wasn't any kind of a professional job.  It's quite sturdy, though.  An old crate is nailed to one end, and a scrap of rug is similarly fastened to the middle.  You're high enough in the air to get a decent view of the bramble patch and the land surrounding it.

Fresh green tendrils carry a twisting vine through the thorny brambles and up into the swaying trees, cloaking the harsh thorns and tiny leaves in bright greenery.  Leaves shaped like arrowheads nod in the breeze, flanking trumpet-shaped flowers striped in pink and white.  Bees buzz and hum as they go about their work, collecting pollen from the gaudy blossoms.

A rutted animal track runs between and around a number of thorny brambles.  Little round leaves, dried to resemble nothing so much as oversized rolled oats, cover the ground, while their living green counterparts spiral their way up the branches of the bushes.

Several narrow tracks intersect here, in a spot that seems to get a lot of trampling.  A sickly-looking thorn bush grows in the middle of the intersection, trying to spread out and block passage, but bruises and scars and broken branches have prevented it from making much headway.  Some deep tracks in the dirt show that a large, heavy animal frequents this place, likely the cause of the bramble's misfortunes.

A crooked trail winds its way around a huge boulder.  Half buried in the soil, the great rock is rounded and smoothed, nearly polished in places.  Plush, green moss grows up the lower surfaces, and the top is carpeted in dead leaves and wind-blown dirt.  Enough of the rock itself shows that you can see it's made of a black and white flecked granite.

A low spot in the ground has collected water, creating a breeding ground for wriggling water bugs and spreading green growths.  Tracks in the mud indicate that a number of animals come here regularly to drink, although the slimy, bug-infested mud puddle looks anything but inviting to someone with fewer than four legs.

A few puffy yellow flowers have managed to force their way through the dense brambles in search of sunlight.  In among the tiny grey-green leaves of the bushes are a number of larger curled leaves, poking out here and there.  Only filtered light makes it through the leafy tree cover, but it's enough to support the scattering of flowers.

The game trail dead-ends here, surrounded by dense thorn bushes an all sides, with only a narrow gap in the foliage to the west.  Rustlings coming from the leafy shadows and the brambles sway back and forth, now here, now there.  Something is lurking in amongst the undergrowth.

The trail makes a sharp corner to avoid a particularly dense stand of brambles.  There's hardly enough space for a gnat to crawl through, or so it seems.  Something in the soil must be encouraging the unusually luxuriant growth.

The trail widens into a small clearing, surrounded by mature thorn bushes and carpeted with grass and a number of wildflowers.  Half a dozen thick stumps are spotted about the area, indicating that this used to be as thickly overgrown as any other part of the area, and indeed there are several hundred baby brambles, from tiny sprouts to couple of fat little bushes a foot or more tall.  Within a few years, this area will be impassable once more.

A large oak tree grows a short way south of the track, forcing its way up from among the thorny bushes pressing in all around it.  One of the thorn branches grew so close that the oak's bark has grown over it, trapping it forever against the gnarled trunk.

The narrow game trail runs from the northwest to the southeast, winding round and about the bramble bushes.  A smaller track pushes into the undergrowth to the northeast.  Cracked and splintered branches and scarred ground make it look like the northeastern track is of recent creation.  Broken thorns suggest that whatever made the new trail probably didn't have a good time doing it.

A flowering vine twines through the tangle of brambles, winding its tendrils around the woody branches, uncaring of their sharp thorns.  Large green leaves shaped like arrowheads decorate the vines, swaying in the breeze.  Here and there a flower lifts its head, trumpet shaped, striped in pink and white.  The blossoms show a delicate contrast to the tough bramble bushes with their small leathery leaves.

Something made its hurried way along this winding track, traveling northward as though driven by anger or fear.  The track has been forced through the brambles, and is none too wide.  Damaged bushes and blobs of hardened sap mark the passage of whatever did this.

Young oak trees fill what little space there is in between the thorn bushes, rising above the spiny undergrowth like giants striding through a cornfield.  Many years' accumulation of curled brown leaves blend on the ground with the crackly little grey leaves from the brambles, forming a thick, spongy loam.

Some small animal got itself caught on the long thorns of the bramble bushes.  Attempts to free itself only caught it more firmly, and it died pinned into that spiny prison.  Small scavengers have made of its body a hollow shell.  The skeleton is clean and white, doubtless picked over and polished by ants and beetles.

The thorn bushes in this area are half-naked and sick-looking.  Branches bare of leaves wave in the breeze, showing their thorns without the usual cover of little round leaves.  A number of leaves look half eaten, and here and there are tiny black worms, chewing and chewing, gorging themselves on the greenery, tough and leathery though it may be.

Tall brambles loom high on either side of the narrow track, their thorny limbs fluttering with little green leaves that spiral up the branches.  The breeze stirs the bushes, sending a soft rustle through the thicket, but every now and again a louder, harsher crackle and honk is heard, sounds made by no wind.  Something moves back in the thicket, in the densest parts where none, not even a Dwarf or Halfling, may venture.

The brambles are a bit thinner to the south, neither very high nor very dense.  Other types of plants grow intermixed with the thorn bushes, softening the appearance of the area into something approaching a gentle woodland.  A couple of tree ferns spread their feathery fronds over the thorns, while a stand of callas pushes its way in amongst them.  Here and there, tiny violets peek out from under larger leaves, hiding from the sun.

Most of the surrounding foliage is thornless, with only a few brambles mixed in.  The conglomerate of greenery is just as dense as the bramble thicket, but less painful when one brushes against it.  Tall, green bushes with leaves shaped like spearheads dominate, intermixed with leggy cane-like plants, huge grasses taller than a Tog's head, and a fibrous vine with straggly orange flowers.  A short clover covers the ground in fragrant patches, making this a pleasant little spot.

A deep gouge in the tough bark of a tree, about four feet above the ground, marks the place where the track makes an abrupt change in direction.  The gouge, a furrow the length of a Human's hand marked with a deep hole the length and width of a finger, is on the south side of the tree, indicating that whatever hit it was traveling north at some speed when it hit.  It seems to have wrenched itself free and then thundered on to the northeast.

The trail, already narrow, comes to a stop here.  The bramble bushes grow more densely to the north, and although they show signs of splintering in places, they stand stout and firm.  There is little else here but a few bones, large enough to have survived the ministrations of temperature and weather and ants.  The ground has been churned up recently, so much so that no tracks are evident.

A stone the size of two fists together has been disturbed, kicked out of its home in the loamy soil, leaving behind a shallow hole filled with half rotten acorns.  Some squirrel must have chosen this stone to guard his winter cache, but someone else -- or something else -- came along and kicked the rock aside.

A huge fallen tree trunk lies cradled in the embrace of a pair of relatively smaller trees, wedged tightly between them.  Soil has packed close about the lower curve of the trunk, burying it firmly -- it must have been resting here for a long time.  The game trail stops at the enormous trunk, which prevents movement to the east as the dense brambles block all other ways save the northwest.

The bramble thicket is not very dense here, and its tangled, matted shrubs seem to shrink back from the north side of the clearing, almost as if shunning it.  Just beyond the clearing rises a massive gate.  Sere vines and dead vermin are scattered about its base, but nothing, not even moss, mars its surface.

The ground beneath your feet is black and dead, as though it had once been engulfed in a great inferno.  Oddly enough, the Lich Gate before you appears pristine and intact, unscathed by the apparent waste and desolation that surround or perhaps radiate from it.

A cold breeze blows through the area changing its direction when you turn, as if guided by some unseen force.  Several paths lead off to the north into the trees.  Along the perimeter, a low wrought-iron fence serves as a token boundary for the cemetery.

The path begins to weave its way through dense trees, snaking around small burial sites that contain several old stone grave markers.  The grounds have been kept clear and the grass is cut low around each tombstone.  Someone must visit this place regularly.

Each of the graves in this part of the cemetery is marked with a simple wax candle.  Despite the constant breeze, the flames of every candle continue to burn and flicker, lighting the ground with an eerie orange glow.

Just beyond the iron fence that runs along the path to the southeast, you hear something moving about in the underbrush.  Faint pinpoints of light fade in and out of the trees and you would swear the temperature just dropped.  The outline of a square structure lies to the south, while a faint trail heads northwest through low-hanging trees.

Branches reach out towards you, groping at your clothing.  Just beyond the path, misty vapors weave their way between the trees, seeking unknown prey.  A worn path bends around from the southwest to southeast.  To the northwest, you spot some sort of clearing.

You are standing on the edge of a deep sinkhole, about eighty feet wide and perfectly round.  Peering into the deep hole, you find that it's filled with water, the surface about thirty feet below you.  Judging from the smoothness of the walls and a skeleton still clinging to the rocks below, you surmise that jumping into this cenote might be a bad idea.
The trees hang low over the path along the westward curve, forming an eerie tunnel of foliage.  From somewhere in the darkness, the hoot of an owl echoes through the woods.

The tunnel of trees opens up into a round clearing where eight gravestones have been placed in a circle.  The stone markers face inward, towards a small stone altar resting in the center.  There are ash marks across its surface, leading you to believe something was once set aflame upon it.
The trees have given way to a mausoleum crafted from white marble.  The entrance is marked by two smooth columns and perched just above, a solemn-looking stone gargoyle surveys the surroundings.

A low stone altar heaped with dried flowers, old rotted offerings of food and streaked with ancient pools of melted wax, stands opposite the heavy iron gateway which leads out of the crypt.  The walls are lined with closed graves, sealed with heavy marble facings, each bearing a polished bronze plaque with the name of one of the departed.  A lone flickering candle standing atop the stone fights a precarious battle against the heavy oppressive darkness of the crypt.

The ceiling and walls are mostly dirt aside from one bright patch of cracked marble overhead.  Two burning torches fixed to the ceiling in heavy iron brackets light up the tunnel with a deep reddish glow, glinting off bits of ivory bone and old wood in the walls.  The tunnel slopes downwards and to the east, fading into inky blackness beyond the light.
Massive silvery roots weave in and out, forming the walls of this cavern-like area under the foot of a huge tree.  Slightly above and to the west, there is a fissure in the wall of the root cave.

Nestled at the base of a terraced hillside, a small stone farmhouse seems caught in a struggle with the tendrils of ivy which seek to pull it down.  Though the farmhouse survives, the outcome of the battle is really not in doubt.  The ivy has already pulled over half the chimney, now a pile of rust-colored bricks lying in an untidy heap on the west side of the house.  To the north, a path leads to a small building behind the house, while a trail to the south leads back into the forest.

Wooden crushing vats clutter the ground, crusted with the remains of long evaporated grapes.  Dark stains discolor the wood, while unidentifiable lumps cling to the bottom.  Great aging barrels lie tumbled to one side, waiting for the vintner and his assistants to fill them before rolling them to the aging caves for storage.

Narrow oak planks are stacked outside a small wooden shed, the door of which stands open invitingly.  Wooden mallets, planes, copper strips, odd looking clamps and other worn tools lie on the ground within easy reach of a rough bench.  A half-finished barrel lies on the ground, its staves warped by the time and the elements, while completed barrels have been stacked neatly against the side of the shed.

Just beyond a small wooden shed lies a sturdy fence which separates the farm from the garden.  A simple affair of wood, the fence nevertheless serves to keep livestock within the farmyard, and away from the garden on the other side.  A stile crosses the fence, allowing men to pass, but frustrating any animal seeking an unoffered meal.

Green grass and tufts of wildflowers blanket the southern exposure of the steep hill.  Terraces cut into the hillside allow the grape vines to flourish on their trellises without risking the health of the workers who tend them.  A path to the east wends its way through the lowest level of the terrace, while a steep climb downhill leads to the farmyard below.

A warm breeze wafts along the terrace, rustling the leaves around you, and carrying with it the scent of grapes and growing things.  Footprints leave faint scuff marks on the smooth green of the grass as you pass through the lush rows of grapevines which border the terrace.

The smooth green turf has been torn up here, as though a struggle has taken place.  Tracks in the soil lead in all directions, and several vines have been pulled loose from their supporting trellises to be crushed underfoot.  The sharp, tangy scent of crushed grapes fills the air.

Wooden trellises line the walkway, one on each side of the terrace.  The wind or an animal has knocked down a section of the northern trellis, leaving an awkward tangle of wood and grape vines to be trampled by careless feet.  Proving the adage about an ill wind that blows no good, the break in the trellis provides a convenient place to climb up the hill to the next higher terrace.

A tangle of dried grapevines, evidently from the last time the vines were pruned, has been piled high at the east end of the walkway, blocking further travel in this direction.  Dried vines such as these would be burned at harvest time, their smoke seasoning the oaken barrels in which the wine will age.

A gap in the trellis on the outer edge of the terrace gives a view of the farmyard below.  Shadows seem to skitter about the yard, shifting like smoke before they can quite be seen.  A broken trellis on the terrace below provides a convenient place to scramble down the hill.

The air is filled with a low drone as bees fly to and fro.  A swarm has built their hive on a trellis here, black and yellow insects working steadfastly to gather nectar from nearby flowers and return to the hive to transform it into honey.  The sweet scent from the hive permeates the air.

Wispy patches of wildflowers and herbs grow with careless abandon, carpeting the floor of the terrace.  Honeybees float lazily from flower to flower, gathering their nectar with a single-minded intensity.  The drone of the bees is relaxing, as is the delicate fragrance of crushed thyme and flowers.

A rock lies half buried in the middle of the path, requiring passers-by to walk close to the edge of the terrace.  Deep green grape vines shiver with each passing footstep, the motion revealing the bleached silvery wood of the trellis to which they cling.

A crude stone firepit has been constructed at this end of the middle terrace, providing workers with a convenient place to stop and eat a meal during the day.  Sun-bleached poultry bones have been snapped, and half buried beneath the outer trellis.  A steep climb up the hill leads to the topmost level of the terraces.

Tendrils of grape vines caress the skin with every movement through this walkway.  About four feet apart, the vines which grow on the trellises to each side reach out as if to clutch at those who pass by.  A lop-eared brown rabbit peers out from under the inner trellis, its tiny pink nose twitching curiously.

A broken rake leans against a trellis, grape vines curling about its length.  Flecks of rust fall from the weathered tines at each touch of a gentle breeze, while splinters catch at the clothing of unwary passers-by.  The philosophical might murmur platitudes about the return to the earth of an implement used to wrest a living from it.

A cat lies beneath a trellis, unconcernedly washing her paw as she basks in the cool breeze.  Dark green leaves provide a sharp contrast with her orange and white fur, and her eyes gleam softly in the shadows as she glances about with half shut eyes.

Wrens warble musically as they call out to each other from their perch in the vines.  Hidden from predators, they hop about, the leaves swaying with their movements.  A cluster of tail feathers littering the ground indicates that such safety is, at best, fleeting.

The view from the upper terrace is breathtaking.  A small farmhouse nestles at the base of the hill, the red tile of its roof warm in the light.  A fence surrounds the farmyard, and a small stile allows workers to cross the fence to a field of grain which lies beyond.  The path leads east, and a steep climb leads down the hill to the middle terrace.

Morning glories compete with grape vines for space on the trellis, twining about each other as they grow.  The deep purple grapes provide a startling contrast to the pale blue of the morning glories as each climbs ever higher toward the sunlight.

A ladybug crawls along the trellis, her red carapace spotted with black.  Her progress from leaf to leaf is slow and steady, as she seeks out the tiny aphids which form a staple of her diet.  The vines which grow along the hillside thrive as a result of her patient hunting.

Grape leaves shiver in the wind, turning from deep green to a paler, greyish green as they move.  The shifting colors are dizzying, especially when combined with soft whistle of the wind past your ears, and the glimpses of the valley floor through the moving leaves, far, far below.  A dried leaf from last year's growth flutters past to drift over the terrace and off into oblivion.

A mole peers about myopically from the protection of a shady trellis, his velvety grey skin blending with the shadows.  A passing motion has him diving beneath the ground to disappear without a trace, though a hint of raised earth visible beneath the grass indicates the path of his underground burrow.

The sun warms this sheltered bower, caressing it with light.  Crimson roses climb in a perfumed tangle up a wooden arbor, filling the air with their heavy fragrance.  At the center of the arbor, years of careful trimming have created a tiny topiary donkey, which contentedly crops the grass.  A low boulder, worn smooth by years of wind and rain, provides a convenient place to sit and relax in this peaceful setting.

A thin top layer of sifted black and russet brown soil covers the earth, sterile and void of life.  Withered remains of what once were plants litter the ground, and browned stalks of lifeless weeds protrude from the wasted earth, casting long, harsh shadows.

A shadowy black lump of a hill broods on the horizon, like coal waiting in a child's Midwinter Day stocking.  A sere and scorching wind entangles itself with the air, parching your lungs and reminding you just how thirsty you are.

Scattered ashes and mounds of unidentifiable burnt paraphernalia lie scattered around the path which, oddly, appears to be swept clean.  Heat comes up in waves off the ground, causing the air to shimmer.

A looming hill rises to the north, its shadow falling heavily over you.  Covered in ashes that look as fine and thick as a new layer of snow, a deep channel of lava carves its way down one side of the hill, finally vanishing behind a steep embankment.

A hill rises to the east, covered in ash and casting a long shadow over everything.  Blasted skeletal structures are all that remain of a handful of small homes that crouch against the hill and beside the road as if they were waiting in ambush.  Broken bones lie scattered within the empty homes, silently relaying the unspeakable.

The path gradually rises to the northeast, sloping upward as it winds around an ash-coated flat-topped hill.  Smooth waves of hardened lava lash out amongst the ruins of what once were buildings, the basalt glittering coarsely in the sunlight.

A warm breeze blows dust off the blasted path that skirts the hill, tingling the flesh and parching the lungs.  Silence pervades all around, and here and there the trail is marked by runnels of frozen black that can only be old lava flows that hardened into basalt.

The path slopes upward to the southeast and winds gradually downward as it heads around a bend to the west.  Slick rivers of glassy black stripe the hill, darkening the path in a glittering runoff of cooled lava.  A sulfrous tang spikes the air, tracing the inside of your mouth with a metallic flavor.

The path steepens sharply as it climbs the hill, eventually vanishing from sight as it dips over the flat summit.  Slick smears of obsidian basalt make walking difficult, causing the path to become as treacherous as any ice-bound slope.

The path is almost totally consumed by black basalt, making climbing it a horrendous task.  Waves of frozen lava slip over the sharp lip of the flattened hilltop, creating waterfall structures that give little purchase and would be much more dangerous to clamber over if the slope were any steeper.

A desolate scape of shattered ruins scorched and covered in a thick layer of ashes rolls out all around you.  Flattened by forces at present unseen, a pale ruddy glow flows up through cracks in the hilltop, filling the air with a demonic light.  Wrecks of houses rest in peace amongst pools of frozen lava, skeletons of the former village of Crook.

The blasted remains of homes and their denizens lie scattered about you.  Composed of cinder and ash, the path of the lava can be clearly followed as it swept over the helpless villagers, incinerating them instantly and capturing what remained in rigid black glass.

The hard black glass that covers the surface of the earth is cracked in several places, releasing a faint red glow that spills out and up, creating a hazy veil of blood-colored mist.  A black hill rises to the east, a cancerous lump waiting to be excised.

The hill slopes down toward the southwest, too treacherous and glassy-slick to dare without risking breaking a few bones.  Fine clouds of ashes rise up around you when you walk, filling your nostrils with grit and the stench of death.  A steep channel of lava pushes its way down off the side of the hill, dusted with just enough grit to afford some moderate purchase.

Rising in a snubbed tower, the collapsed hill that broods in the center of Skeleton's Crook hilltop is covered in black basalt.  A strong ruddy light seeps from the arterial cracks breaking the mound's surface, each line connecting to one or the other until they form an arch-like pattern reminiscent of a doorway on the hill's north-facing side.

The flat ground is covered in a thick layer of glass that would be hard to maneuver over were it not for the ashes that cover it, supplying purchase to an otherwise frictionless surface.  A vast view of the lands to the east spreads out before you, unfurled like a map.

A hazy red nimbus lights the horizon in a pale glow.  Emanating from a small black hill that flows up to the northwest, the light is steady and slightly evil looking.  A slick lava channel carves its way down the hillside to the southwest, looking just coarse enough to make it difficult but not necessarily dangerous climbing.

A small circle of skeletal buildings are all that remains of the tiny village of Crook.  Blackened wooden beams now dig their foundations into a thick layer of cooled basalt and scorched earth, and the eyesockets of the skulls of those who did not escape the agony of the lava eruption stare blindly up at you.  Toward the west rises a second hill, gleaming dully with the everpresent ruddy glow of the shattered landscape.

Roughly halfway between the top and bottom of Skeleton's Crook hill, this steep channel is made even more treacherous by the thick coating of hardened black glass that covers the ground and walls.  Large bubbles of cooled lava have burst up to the surface in places, and a few are shattered, revealing fragments of razor sharp basalt.

Roughly halfway between the top and bottom of Skeleton's Crook hill, this steep channel is made even more treacherous by the thick coating of hardened black glass that covers the ground and walls.  Large bubbles of cooled lava burst up to the surface in places, and a few are shattered, revealing fragments of razor sharp basalt.

Walls and floors of solid, glittering basalt rise and fall around you, creating the sense that one is walking on a completely still lake of pure liquid black.  The sides sweep up to the northeast and northwest in treacherous channels that look as if they would be harder to climb were it not for the fact that they were dusted in a fine layer of grit that lends friction to their surface.

Dried lava lines the roadside, the ground beneath your feet speckled with iridescent flakes of the cooled molten rock.  The dusky stone winds northwest to a distant volcano, and eastward back to the main road.
Rocks are pushed to one side of the road to make a slender path through debris.  It looks scarcely traveled, the way lined by sparse vegetation.
Patterns of leaves and paw prints are barely visible in the walls of stone nearby.  The fossilized remains are an eerie reminder of the life trapped forever within the ash.
A withering flower rests to one side of the road.  Its dusk-colored leaves flail in the slight breeze, their color the brown of age and decay.
Splintered wagon wheels lie alongside a corroding iron frame.  It appears as if a Trader ran into some difficulty -- difficulty he was unable to recover from.
A dried watering hole stands forlorn amidst the skeletons of animals large and small.  All scraps of flesh have been worn or torn away leaving only the dusty ivory bone beneath.
The silhouette of the Greater Fist looms in the far distant horizon.  The Lesser Fist lingers closer, its shadow rising almost haughtily before you.
Coarse gravel lines the earth, a bed of sharp stones, like jagged teeth peering out of the earth.  Ready to pierce the foot of the unwary traveler, they stand sparkling against the spartan dirt.
Fronds of wilting palm trees scatter on the ground, the wind blowing them across the loose dirt.  Trunks and stalks lie half-buried by ash and crumbling stone.
Tall stones rise in small circular patterns, their forms eroded by wind and water both.  The designs they held have long since faded into invisibility, their meaning now undecipherable.
Pieces of once-tall pillars lie skewed and broken.  Debris from past volcanic eruptions blanket stone and statue, hearth and fallen home.
The ancient frieze of a tall arch is slowly crumbling to dust, paint and tile flaking off.  Burn marks streak the mural, obscuring what images were once there.
Dried and cracking brambles wrapped around a wrought iron fence line the road.  Flanking the dusky earth, the brackish thorns peek out from withering branches, daring to jab and stab at passers by.
A heart-shaped wrought iron sculpture is overgrown, writhing vines coiled around it.  The thick spike-like thorns appear to pierce the center, the sharp points gleaming with moisture.

A tangled mass of thorny bushes guard the roadside, making passage beyond the slender path impossible.  Small birds find ways to hide unscathed amidst the brambles, tiny forms huddled inside small cathedrals of withering vines.

The masses of thorny growths thin to the north.  Wrought iron sculptures where vines of roses once grew stand bare, metal corroding and long untended.  The eerie shapes stand like hollow souls over the dead ash-covered earth below.

Flecks of shattered jade lie strewn amidst the rough gravel of the road.  Images etched into the flat panels of rock that were once a busy street are now worn to nothingness, their patterns long forgotten.
Slender jade obelisks mottled with dust and ash stand guard over the narrow road.  The way is clear, footprints from recent travel constantly being worn over one another in the soft earth below.
An ornate jade plant rests amidst a circle of pale white stones.  Each leaf is delicately carved from the blushing green stone.  Despite being covered in filth, it remains a beautiful work of art.

An elaborate golden stand is firmly bolted to the stone of the road.  Remnants of a jade-green glass sphere lie in sharp slivers on the surrounding grass.  Bits of coarse vegetation grow between the pieces of glass.
Prickly, spine-covered bushes grow close to the ground.  Ripe red fruit tauntingly dangles from behind long, sharp thorns.
A tall barrier lines each side of the road, bladed edges topping the polished wooden beams that compose the wall.

Wooden panels in the fence are carved into the jagged images of swords and weapons from lands far and near.  The barbed metal partitions holding them together make touching the wall a most unpleasant thought.

Dust drifts through the archway over the cooled lava floor and piles in the corners of the stone building.  A bored Human attendant relaxes on a stool near a leather curtain that closes off the rest of the forge.
The volcano of the Lesser Fist looms over the barricade.  It ominously shadows all below it.  A glimpse of something reflective glints from near the maw of the fortress.

Ashes and dust coat the stone wall, covering the rock with a granulated layer of grey that abates only near an inset bronze plaque.  A sparkling crystal hand is attached over the polished metal, also clear of the choking dust.

The signs of ancient battle mark the area.  A tall statue, at least thirty feet in height, towers far above the parched landscape.  Eyes of faceted blue crystal sparkle brightly from the ash-streaked marble face.

A red-veined marble fountain proudly shimmers with droplets of clear, cool water.  Small flameroses grow up its sides, their tender green tendrils bearing small jade-green leaves that perfume the air with a heady scent.
Once a lovely garden, little remains of its original beauty.  Recent plantings line the roadside, clippings and trees freshly cultivated in an attempt to renew the land.

A delicate moonflower bush, petals closed as the flowers sleep during the day, stands encircled by an almost fragile iron trellis.  The clean area and well-tended soil betray an unseen caretaker overseeing the beautiful plant.

The long shadow of the Lesser Fist of Heaven dominates the small garden.  The formidable fortress to the west rises high above the ground below, with the silhouette of the Greater Fist behind it towering yet farther into the reaches of the sky.

A volcano lies to the west.  Fortified and well-guarded, it serves as the Fortress of the Crystal Hand.  The dark path, made from hardened lava, is streaked with veins of polished obsidian that glisten with a dull satin sheen.

A large stone staircase winds its way down the front of the volcano, carved into the face of the rock.  A glimmering crystal formation to the west seems to catch the scarce light, glowing with a scintillating aura.

The door to the volcanic fortress is comprised of two enormous obsidian panels, both ornately carved.  The slender path, chiseled from the lava, leads to a large stone staircase descending to the ground below.  Embedded in the dense rock above the entrance rests a crystal hand encircled by angular runes.

Light floods in from above, the only outlet to the distant skies being the gaping mouth of the volcano.  The slender outline of a catwalk is thrown against the canvas of the sky, a barely noticeable line.

A statue carved from a pale grey rock rests inside a circular path of dark stones at the center of the atrium.  Offerings of flowers and incense are left before it, testament to the monks' ever-enduring memories.  A rough obsidian path leads west toward the Guild library.

Small iridescent grey rocks carpet the rough lava floor.  They are meticulously raked into ornate spiraling patterns.  A slender obsidian walkway winds geometrically through the garden, dividing the crushed stone into abstract triangular shapes.
A dark walkway of obsidian frames the field of grey crushed stone at the center of the room.  Monks wander along the path, heads bowed in quiet contemplation.

Racks upon racks of weapons line the walls, most staves or keen-edged spears.  Some blades, well-polished and edged, gleam from among their wooden, practice counterparts.  The floor is clean and well-kept, the signs of monks recently training lingering about.

A tall stairway carved into the rock of the volcano winds its way precariously upwards, leading to a slender catwalk far above.  It appears impossibly steep, but several monks ascend the way with no problem.

The walls and ceiling are featureless grey rock with a smooth polished surface.  Dark linen pillows, flat and hard to the touch, are placed around the area.  A small censer lets the potent scent of sweet incense drift lazily about.
The skies open above, visible through a crystal dome capping the volcano.  Daylight makes the slender catwalk seem extremely treacherous as it stretches most precariously over the vast expanse below.
The thin platform extends further west, the expansive sky above seeming close indeed.  The crystal dome capping the volcano exposes the vast horizon, hiding nothing.
A large circular stone platform rests suspended in mid-air over the center of the volcano.  The precarious catwalk extends to its edge.

Monks kneel and sit on the charcoal gunny pillows scattered about the room.  In hushed whispers, they read and debate combative and mystical theory alike.  Glowing orbs of polished crystal illuminate the room, providing a gentle light for study and the gaining of wisdom.

The silence of the archives is broken only by the soft sound of scratching pens as monks work copying ancient texts that have begun to decay.  Files, treatises and endless scrolls of parchment line the bookcases to aid visitors in their researches.

The foyer to the Guild museum is sparsely decorated.  Featureless walls of polished lava rise up to the crystal dome, the edge of the catwalk barely in sight.  A winding spiral staircase descends into the stronghold below.
An elegant staircase made from polished stone spirals upwards to the main level.  A passage north leads to a series of catacombs carved into the base of the volcano.

The chambers of the museum appear to be carved from the basalt rock of the volcano.  A dark indigo silk runner lines the cold stone of the floor.  Silver sconces embracing small orbs of glowing tzgaa line the walls.
A large glass panel flanks the wall, parchment pages held securely in place behind the protective display.  A small brass plaque is tacked to the wall beneath it.
A large contraption, composed of many gears and glassine parts, focuses one thick crystal lens over an almost invisible specimen.  A sliver of something almost imperceptably small glitters beneath.

This room is plain and spartan, containing only an enclosed glass case bearing a treasure from ancient days.  Even the obsidian walls are featureless, the black rock smooth and polished.  A silverwillow sign hangs from delicate chains over the display.
Three panels of cloth hang from the walls depicting various scenes from the Guild's past.  One notable portrayal is that of Katzel's execution.
A bold bright blue banner hangs above this exhibit.  Older monks pass by, nodding and winking at each other, the occasional one bowing reverently towards the large painting on display.
Tapestries and paintings from various provinces of Elanthia cover the walls in this area.  Sculptures and other remnants from past civilizations attest to their age.

Swaths of velvet lie draped over this exhibit, one curtain drawn back to reveal a cracked oval mirror.  Ropes cordon off the display.  Most people lower their eyes as they pass, not daring to look, nervously shuffling onward.

An ancient ash tree crowns the top of a nearby hillside, spreading its branches outwards like long embracing arms.  A brilliant yellow spray of blooming mustard flowers grows beneath, shining like the early sun against the shaded green backdrop.

The trees seem to hold an aura of fragility about them, as if the burden of the moss that drips from their boughs weighs them down to the point of snapping.  Odd carvings have been hung from the branches of the trees, their stone and wooden visages stirring on the wind and clattering against one another.

Signs of sickening cling to the trees and the whisper of unseen creatures moving about alerts you to the fact that you are not alone.  The ground is a blasted, black color, and dry stalks of grass that hold no promise of life poke up from the barren earth.  To the northwest clamber a set of mountains that look less than a mile away, if that.

The trees that grow here just barely comprise a forest, their tortured, claw-like branches scraping the sky and rendering them so malformed it is impossible to tell what type of tree they are.  A matted layer of thick, molding leaves cover the floor, filling the air with a miasma-like stench that makes your stomach cringe.

The trees grow unsteadily along this rocky patch of ground, and in many places they have fallen.  The lapping of water greets your ears to the west, and glancing in that direction you can see a small lake the color of dull lead, its shores reaching all the way to the edge of a mountain range that makes an ugly black slash across the horizon.

The trees cling to a tedious life along the path that winds around the shore of the Silverwater Lake.  The ground is firmly packed, and ruts dig deeply into the earth on either side, remnants of a once thriving community.  The dead slap of water against water brings an eerie echo up from the lake shore.
A slight breeze mingles fresh, damp air from the outside with the musty dryness of this ancient cave.  The ground rises slightly as it heads north into the center of the lair.

The trees and undergrowth stop abruptly at the edge of this small clearing, the hard, cracked soil underfoot showing no sign of vegetation.  A broken cart lies near a cold fire pit in the center of the clearing, several pieces of unused firewood poking their heads over its splintered sides.  A small cave leads into the rocky hillside.

A jagged rip in the mountainside marks the entrance to the Silverwater Mines.  Broken support beams, shattered lanterns, and deep gouges in the fine sand that lie around the opening are all that remain of a once prosperous establishment.  You can barely make out what lies beyond, save for a few dark shapes and odd snickering noises.

A shattered wood beam crosses your path here, the remnants of a house that has now long since vanished.  Fragments of rocks lie scattered across the ground, turning treacherously underfoot.  The ground creates odd embankments, as if the hand of a god pushed it back with one quick, idle brush.

Strange noises bounce off the ragged stone ceiling, amplified by the quiet air of the night.  The dark is so thick that you can hardly see ahead, and the only thing clueing you toward the exit is the lapping sound of the lake shore coming from the south.  To the north the tunnel is choked with debris, but maneuverable.
Broken stones, abandoned tools, and wooden beams choke this bottleneck passageway.  The smooth stone walls rise up to either side, constricting movement and creating a pretty place for an ambush.

The mine opens up into a somewhat larger room here, the walls extending up some fifty feet before shading off into darkness.  In the center of the chamber is a deep shaft that plunges as far down as the walls climb up.  The floor is oddly free of the debris that litters the rest of the mines.
The smooth walls of the mine shaft rise up to either side, a glossy black color.  Some fifty feet of sheer wall rests between this platform, the opening above, and the next platform below.
Luminescent fungi on the walls manages to lend light to this small, damp chamber.  Deep gouges cut through the ground, leaving glassy tracks and making the floor uneven.

The tunnel dead-ends here, choked by a wall of rubble and stone that blocks all further passage.  Chunks of rock lie strewn around you, and from beyond the stones you can hear a faint snickering sound.  A fine layer of dust lies over everything, and here and there you notice the faint tracings of footprints.

A rusting steel track is embedded into the cave floor here, running east ten feet before vanishing behind a wall of solid rock.  It is apparent from the stops at the visible end of the track that it began here, but hard to determine how it came to go through a wall, or how a wall came to grow up around it.  In the distance a repetitious dripping sound echoes through the cavern, doing nothing for the nerves.

Ambient light dances across the face of a large crystalline formation that stretches from floor to ceiling, teasing ever-changing shadows across the room.  To the left of the crystals, a flow of smooth limestone has shaped itself into a natural staircase leading up to the rock lip encircling the chamber.

An array of intertwining crystalline vines laces the jagged rock walls, their smooth, dry surfaces gleaming dully in the ambient light.  Crude steps chiseled into the walls lead up to a wide stone ledge.  A fine patina of dust covers the floor, roiling into brown clouds with the slightest disturbance.

Velvety limestone draperies flow down the far wall, adding a superficial appearance of softness to the rock's surface.  A number of flat, grey stones have been stacked into a tower of precarious steps leading up to a wide rock lip that encirles the entire cavern.

Milky-white deposits of limestone cascade down the northwest wall in formation created long ago but long since dried and dead.  A casualty of the near-total darkness, a spindly, single-leafed stalk hangs limply over the edge of a cracked clay pot that squats near one of the doors set into the walls of the cavern.

Rows of stacked stones surround a deep firepit in the center of the dirt floor.  A mass of ash, pieces of blackened wood and small bits of fire-greyed bone fill the pit, their presence adding a slight scent of char to the air.  Several large stone benches line the walls, chiseled from the cave's native limestone.

Silent stalactites glint far overhead with an eerie iridescence that lights the entire cavern in a pale, green glow.  A pile of large boulders along one wall give shelter to a tiny opening nestled in the rock face.

A stream of cool water trickles from a narrow crack in the rock wall and onto the floor, forming a small pool.  An even smaller rivulet dribbles from the other side of the pool, spreading across the nearby rock to evaporate into the warm, dry air.

A painting of a huge, four-legged creature dominates the near wall of this section of the chamber.  A plethora of runic symbols encircle the figure, interspersed between them the outlines of several large handprints.  The entire piece has been painted in the same, unvarying ochre hue.

A row of stalagmites form a natural railing along the lip of the stone walkway underfoot, lending a modicum of protection against falling to the cavern floor below.  The air is slightly warmer here than the rest of the cave.

A pile of discarded skulls and bones lies at the base of one wall, gleaming dully in the dim light.  The walls here are stained a smokey grey, darker near the lower areas where an abandoned firepit is slowly being consumed by the steady accumulation of dust on the cavern's floor.

This large stone ledge, wide enough for a yak caravan to travel, circles the entire rim of the cavern.  A series of crude drawings have been sketched along the walls, their images showing miniature Gor'Togs standing in an endless battle against creatures frozen in time.

The dull, listless waters of Silverwater Lake spread out before you, a rippling matte mirror.  Except for the choppy slap of the waves against the black sands of the shore, the lake is quiet and devoid of any sign of fish or wildlife.

A steep bank of rocks and dirt climbs up to the east, creating a short but unclimbable wall.  To the west the water of Silverwater Lake thrashes in its death throes, sucking away at the pebbled sands of the shore.  The stillness is unsettling, and a little frightening.

Quarry piled along the shore and the remnants of a deep channel that leads up to the mines indicates that this may have once been the place where the miners dumped the remains of the day's excursions.  A fine, gritty layer of black covers everything, and the water is noticeably darker by comparison to the rest of the lake.

The shoreline becomes more and more rocky until it finally turns into the treacherous mountainside.  Tall and majestic, the range cups the lake in a halfmoon shape.  An earthquake from time immemorial has split the part of the mountain's side that faces Silverwater, leaving a sheer wall of granite that dives straight down into the water with reckless abandon.  A splendid and awe-inspiring cataract topples aimlessly over the straightest cliff, feeding the lake but never dispelling its grim hue.

A river-rock wall extends east to west, protecting the northern end of a rambling village.  The open village gate looks out across a vast stretch of the fields worked by the villagers.  A dirt pathway winds southward through a collection of cottages, shops and huts standing at odd angles, most with a fence or ditch fronting the path.  Farmers, returning from a day in the fields, find fellowship and food in the conveniently-located pub, The Pig's Pannage, its open doors just a short walk from the gate.

The clang of a blacksmith's hammer comes from the doorway of a stone building fronted with a large shoeing yard.  A Gor'Tog farmer works at shoeing an ox suspended in a leather sling.  The uncomfortable ox rolls its eye to look at you and lets out a protesting bellow.

A willow-framed building with a thatched broom roof faces the path.  Strutting proudly across the front of the house is a family of geese.  The youngest stops to peck at something on the ground, until he is nudged onward by his elders.  A carved signpost stands at the pathway.

Colorful flowers and bushes laden with berries grow in a wild, brilliant display around a stone cottage topped with a roof thatched with heather.  A small grey donkey pokes its head out of the open doorway and gazes at you inquisitively.

A colorful wagon is parked alongside the pathway, red and gold banners flapping in the breeze, the rippling cloth nearly drowning out a faint snoring coming from within.  Clustered together at the nether end of the village are a small village green with an impressive manor house and an old mill just beyond it.

From somewhere off to the south you can hear the rumble and splash of the miller's waterwheel.  A straw thatched house is set off from the path with clay pots, bowls and urns displayed in its windows.

A rickety wagon lurches past you, pulled by wide-horned oxen.  A Gor'Tog wagoneer walking alongside the rumbling vehicle nods and tips his hat as he passes by.  Clouds of dust eddy about the deep ruts left in the dirt roadway as the cart passes.  A sturdy wood and stone building marks the local Trader's Guild outpost.

A booth with a wooden table and benches is tucked into the alcove, offering a quieter spot for private conversation.  Occasionally the loud thunk of a metal tankard being slammed onto the bar makes you aware of the activities in the central part of the pub.

A huge black and gold banner dominates the wall behind a massive stone bar.  Several Gor'Tog farmers are huddled together at one end, muttering to each other in low, rumbling voices.  Gurta, the alewife, slams a tankard on the bar and sends it sailing down to the farmers.  A platter of bacon and beans follows the tankard.

The smell of hot iron assails you as you enter the domain of Havor, the Gor'Tog blacksmith.  A massive anvil and stone forge stand side by side on the hard dirt floor, and tools of the blacksmith's craft lay neatly arranged on a wooden bench.  Several grinding wheels and a bin holding lengths of iron make up the rest of Havor's shop.

This outpost is a replica of the great Trader Guild buildings in the larger towns.  Designed for easy buying and selling of bulk goods by Guild members, it is crammed and jammed with crates, boxes and packages of all manner and value.  A worried-looking Guild trade minister is at hand to expedite transactions and to make sure none of the goods leave without the proper fees and monies being exchanged.

Every inch of this roomy covered wagon has been used efficently to store an amazing array of trinkets, colorful clothing and carryalls.  The peddler Posimur reclines against the back of the wagon half asleep midst a pile of discarded cloth, leather and string.

Squeals and giggles come from a group of Gor'Tog children who are running around a small, blindfolded lad.  The lad stumbles around, flailing his arms, trying to tag one of the others.  A wooden bridge spans across a deep moat to the south, where a large manor house stands proudly overlooking the surrounding area.  The village stocks are set off in the far corner of the green.

The dirt pathway ends at a small, neatly-kept toft that fronts a quaint cottage.  Bees buzz industriously around the tall shrubs of sage, rosemary and nutmeg geranium that border the yard, attracted by their spicy herbal fragrance.
A column of smoke spirals out of the tall stone chimney of a simple brick building.  The dirt path to its door is trampled hard, and a delicious aroma wafts from the open doorway.

An old mill looks over the shoreline of the Segoltha River, its massive waterwheel splashing and churning the river's deep water.  Tall grasses and willows grow abundantly around the mill grounds.  Village women stand in groups collecting bundles of willow wands and grass.
A neat line of flat white stones paves the pathway leading up to the door of an old church.  A small cemetery has been set off in the churchyard, bordered by low hedges of lavender.

A massive brick and iron oven fills the small shop, leaving barely enough space for the portly baxter Fernar, who stands behind a narrow wooden counter.  The delicious aroma of baking bread emanates from the oven, along with waves of intense heat.  The bulky Gor'Tog removes a tray of plump buns, and squirms back around to place them on the countertop.  A village woman enters the shop, hands Fernar a bowl of rising dough with brisk instructions, then lumbers purposefully out the door.

The croft behind the stone cottage is a bountiful herb garden overflowing with clumps of hyssop, angelica, liverwort, monkshood and sweet woodruff.  The abundant growth partially obscures a stone birdbath where a family of purple larks sit, sipping at the water and cheerfully chirping to each other.

The scents of aromatic smoke and drying herbs hang in the air in this tidy one-room cottage.  A tall drying cupboard stands against one wall, conveniently near the stone hearth.  An odd assortment of vials, flasks and copper pots line the mantel.  Bunches of herbs hang from wooden pegs mounted into the ceiling beams and window frames.  The floor is beaten earth covered with fresh rushes.  A stooped old woman works a set of bellows, keeping the hearth's fire going at full blast.

Chickens, pigs and donkeys roam freely in the yard, penned in by the high shrubs that surround them.  A quaint little stone cottage with a roof thatched with rushes sits at the far end of the toft.  Bunches of herbs hang in its open windows.  A purple lark hops back and forth along the roof's edge, eyeing you suspiciously.  Perhaps it guards a nest up there in the rushes?
A neat row of barred windows faces you along a marble counter.  Several patrons are already busy but there seems to be one window available.  The clerk smiles at you and beckons you over.

Marble tiled floors covered with heavy rugs and walls of polished jasper that gleam a cool blue mark this bank as solid and secure (and expensive).  An official money-changing booth is to one side and a row of tellers windows faces you.  Several guards, armed and armored, stand ready for trouble of any sort.  Near the tellers stands a table of fine wood for those who need to do some writing.

This small booth holds the official money-changing office for the town.  The clerk works behind a thickly barred window and you pass your money in and out via a small drawer that can only be worked by the clerk.  A well-padded chair is placed for your comfort while waiting for your money to be processed.
The ferry rocks gently as you step aboard.  Surrounded by the cool, briny air of the Segoltha, you take your place on the deserted deck and gaze up into the night sky.

The southern bank of the Segoltha River presents a wide, flat flood plain far to the east and west.  The alluvial soil here is deep brown and fertile, nourished by the unpredictable rains that cause the river to rise rapidly and without warning.  Off in the distance to the south, you can spy the crests of trees.  This marks the boundary of the Endrus Forest, which surrounds the fabled Elven stronghold of Leth Deriel.
