rooms.desc: A wide, smooth portion of road leads down to the northern bank of the Biiskbowr, which flows at a stately pace just to the southeast.  The tracks from numerous wheels, hooves and boots indicate that much of the local traffic passes this way.
The evergreens begin to close in again as the road marches northward away from Archer's Ford and the river to the southeast.  A rush of water splashing over stones is audible in the distance.

The packed earth underfoot bears a bit of moisture, making it soft enough that many of the fallen pine needles have been stamped into it so that they have become more than merely a covering but rather a part of the road itself.  On this green carpet, even heavy boots and hooves pass as quietly as slippers.

Downhill to the southeast, the gurgle of the Biiskbowr River, or as the local Gor'Togs call it, "The Wet River," can be heard.  That sound seems to wrap a soft blanket around the area, rendering it otherwise silent save for a barely-heard birdsong every now and then.

A spiky canopy shelters the lush forest, seemingly enforcing a hush upon all within it.  Even the insects feasting upon the remains of a rotten tree trunk observe a certain degree of decorum, and the occasional snap of a twig caused by some passing animal has a curious muted quality.

An enormous spruce lies fallen across the packed-dirt road.  In what must have been a heroic effort, some hardy soul has chopped a slice several feet wide through it.  Although it looks to be a tight squeeze for a caravan, passage is once again possible.

As it winds its way upward, the roadway crosses over slabs of rock, which serve as a reminder that, although the region is forested, it also abuts a mountain range.  The remains of a small campfire can be seen on one such piece of stone, a handy spot on which to cook, devoid of flammable vegetation.

Tiny pale blue and white wildflowers dot the roadside, poking intrepidly between fallen pine needles.  A fringe of small mushrooms circles a tall larch.  Sheltered beneath the tree's branches is a flat, moss-covered rock, which looks to be an ideal location for a summer picnic.

A small pool with vegetation floating on its surface is situated within sight of the road.  Varied hoof and paw prints lead up to the water's edge, suggesting that the local fauna come here often to drink.  On the far side, there are occasional stirrings and flashes of movement from creatures too wary of travelers to come out into the open.
From far above the treetops, an occasional hawk sounds its harsh cry as it soars down from the northern heights.  The undergrowth rustles as small land-bound creatures scurry for cover.

A clump of firs stands at the top of a short rise.  One tree in particular is marked with a yellow blaze, perhaps put there by one of the local trackers.  Nearby is a pair of flat-topped stumps, cut off at an ideal height for them to serve as stools.

A jagged ridge rises to the east as the road climbs northward.  The trees give way to chunks of stone as they approach the edge.  As it passes, the road leans slightly away to the west as if it were leery of a fall.

A wooden signpost, bearing two carved arms pointing in opposite directions, is planted solidly in the ground by the side of the road.  Puffs of dust are kicked up as travelers pass over the crumbly surface of crushed stone mixed with dried pine needles.
Stones battle tenacious roots for supremacy as the land climbs northward.  The evergreens of the forest persist here, but the mountains that rise to the east make their presence known.

A cacophony of bird calls echoes down from the trees, where raucous jays bully wrens and sparrows, and warblers sing, oblivious to the fracases.  Flashes of color peek through the greenery periodically as bright tanagers flit among the tops of the firs and spruces.

The road appears to be blocked by a clump of cedars; however, it merely loops around to either side.  Evidently, the Gor'Togs in the region were unwilling to cut the fragrant trees down, which they prize because "they smell nice."

Although there is packed dirt sufficiently wide to accommodate a caravan proceeding smoothly up the slope to the northwest, next to it there is a rough log stairway that leads the same way.  The reason for this is not apparent.  Perhaps someone was bored.

The roadway cuts its way through the woods, continuing its gradual climb.  Alongside it is a peculiar stairway that appears to lead just down the road a bit.  Near the head of the stairs is a roundish rock with a bit of paint on it.

Situated at the peak of its steady, gradual climb from the Biiskbowr River, the land is relatively level here but begins to descend to the southeast.  A ring of firs circles a small clearing, which houses a stone bench upon which weary travelers can rest.

A fresh scent of pine greets one's nostrils upon passing through these dense woods.  The air in this unspoiled region is clean, though often brisk, and there is seldom a sound other than those made by animals, birds, the wind, or cones crunching underfoot.

Far from large cities or towns, animals in this forest have little fear of passersby.  Here and there, one can see deer browsing shoots of grass unconcernedly or a hare twitching its nose in curiosity.  A sound in the distance is more likely to be the growl of a prowling bear than a hammer striking an anvil.

The reek of skunk cabbage wafts from a clump of thick leaves growing at the edge of a tiny creek that trickles from the north.  From a distance, the smell isn't very strong, but when the leaves are bruised, crushed, or otherwise damaged, they release an intense odor that attracts insects and may cause eyes to water.

Meeting the road at a right angle, a moss-clad stone bridge leads over a shallow chasm through which a thin creek flows.  The road narrows substantially as it continues to the northeast, becoming little more than a path and showing far fewer signs of passage than the wider, well-trodden section leading southeast.

The road is lonesome here, with few birds or other feral visitors.  Diminutive blue flowers sprawl along the roadside and provide cheerful company in the warmer months, but in the winter there is only the stark white pall of snow playing counterpoint to the deep shadows of the woods.

The evergreens flanking the thoroughfare are tall and straight with high crowns of thickly needled branches.  Tight clusters of shiny-leaved azalea dot the understory amid sprawling groups of feathery fern.

The land dips down here in a small, damp valley where rainwater drains, and the dense woods keep it from evaporating too quickly.  Mosses of all varieties thrive in the moisture, with thick blankets of it cloaking rocks and tree trunks.  Patches of it spot the roadway, especially at the edges, making the ground slippery even for the sure-footed.

Long pine boughs reach down from above to brush the pates of the road's taller travelers.  The wind plays in the branches and releases their clean, crisp scent.  Occasionally, the trees' movement will liberate sap-sugared pinecones that fall to the ground with a dense "thud."

The road bends around a massive basalt boulder clad in a monochrome palette of green lichen.  Vines climb from out of the crowd of shrubs surrounding the base of the rock, as though the ground were trying in vain to reclaim its former tenant.

Tangles of vines twine through the understory and twist up tree trunks.  Eventually, they cloak so much of a tree's greenery that its arboreal host browns and dies from lack of sunlight.  The vines reach their leafy tendrils out across the roadway, seeking unwary travelers to trip.

To one side of the road grows a copse of dogwood, its pebbly bark and meandering growing habit distinct from its evergreen neighbors.  In the springtime, the copse celebrates with vibrant pink and white flowers.

A break in the forest canopy reveals a broad patch of the daytime sky.  Below it, a swath of grass marred by a few wagon tracks sprawls out where the sunlight is able to spill down to the ground.  Along the edge of the roadway bordering the woods are wispy sprays of heather.

Amid the lushness of the evergreen forest stands the skeletal frame of a dead bristlecone pine.  The pine's bare branches knock and scrape against each other with each breath of wind, sending down a shower of splintered wood.  The tree's dry, brittle bark clings to the trunk only in small ragged spots that are host to conferences of termites.
Thrusting up from the thick underbrush flanking the road, tall fingers of timeworn stone loom like phantoms that watch life pass by with the cold and detached gaze of eternity.

The road is very narrow and uneven here, the forest leaning in from the sides and the craggy earth pushing up from below.  Gnarled tree roots snake through the stone-clotted soil close to the surface.  In places, they have been worn flat from years of accumulated foot traffic.

Clusters of hosta form a border at the edge of the thicker underbrush.  Their wide, deep green leaves are splotched with white, and in summer they send up tall shoots that bloom in decadent shades of purple and orange.  Occasionally, they rustle with movement, and a small grey coney or brown chipmunk emerges to see what visitors have come to its domain.

A sense of quiet and peace dominates the area, though birdsongs filter in from all directions.  The narrow dirt road that began as a thriving thoroughfare far to the south meets a wall of foliage and dwindles off further into the woods as a faint trail.

Brisk winds brush over the road, funneled by the rocks and trees that line the pathway.  Pine needles and leaves tumble from above with each gust, and the tiny flowers that peep from between the rocks bow their heads to keep their petals from being torn apart by the bitter blows.

Despite the wind funneling through the pass, the air is touched with silence.  No birds chatter, no rocks tumble or clatter, and even the wind, though sometimes blowing heartily, seems subdued in its passage.  From the trees hang bits of torn fabric, faded along the edges but still vibrant where they have been knotted to the branches.  Their frayed ends flitter and tangle with every gust.

A vicious gash in the earth's surface mars the landscape, with boulders and trees cracked and piled in heaps.  Rusted and dull chisels and picks lie scattered among the rubble, half-buried under the debris.  Thick boards are crossed over the opening, hammered heavily into place to bar entry to the old mine.  Though the boards appear weathered, some of the nails are freshly driven, their heads still shiny.

The path peaks in this spot, descending toward the Stelik Bridge in the southeast, and trickling to a narrow trail to the west.  Patches of rough grass grow among the rocks, and the trees are mostly undisturbed by the winds that rush through the pass below.  To one side, a stone block embedded into the ground holds a tall iron hook.  Attached to the hook is a solid iron ring from which a gold band dangles.

The trees and rocks crowd the path, making passage difficult as well as dangerous.  Sudden turns and steep drop-offs camouflaged by heavy underbrush as well as any light shifting through the branches overhead threaten the safety of even the most careful traveler.

The path ends abruptly here, overgrown with weeds and brush that eliminate any sign of which direction the path may have gone.  Silvery-green pricklebushes grow abundantly, their yellow needles bobbing against velvety leaves.

The hard-packed dirt road about a wagon's girth wide twists through the woods, its course determined by large, immovable trees that force travelers to go around them.  Though well-trod, the roadway seems locked in a losing battle with the viny underbrush that pushes in from all sides.

Young softwood trees make up much of the forest glade but there are also many broad hardwoods scattered throughout.  Deep grunting sounds echo from deeper in the glade, occasionally punctuating the arboreal symphony of birdsong, rustling trees and small animals' chittering.

A narrow ditch running alongside the roadway directs water back into the woods and away from the path of travelers, keeping the route from becoming muddy and rutted in even the heaviest rain or snowmelt.  Ivy twines up a tall post bearing the moss-patched yellow skull of a large boar.

A massive palisade gate guards the entry to a small village nestled within the forest glade.  Though sharpened points top the upright logs of the palisade, they appear to be the trees of the glade itself embracing the clusters of longhouses within.  Gor'Tog rangers flanking the gate open and close it as needed with a chorus of grunting and the scraping sounds of the wooden gate dragging on the ground as it moves.

A tall palisade wall of thick iron-banded tree trunks embraces the small village of thatched longhouses and bark-covered huts.  Split log walkways snake between the structures.  One rutted dirt path leads from the gate to a squarish building with deep eaves that shelters stacks of crates and barrels piled outside the door.

The sounds of a hunting party returning from the forest reverberate from somewhere close.  A few children carrying hide scrapers and curing salts run past you on the path to meet them, and in the small front yards of nearby homes, branch-frame drying racks are readied to receive the new batch of skins and meat.

Thick grey smoke curls from a run-down building set well away from the path.  The sharp sound of metal striking metal rings from its open doorway, accompanied by a steady backbeat of grunting.  A cracked shingle hangs on brass rings from two boar tusks mounted above the entrance.

Dirty straw litters a walkway branching off to the east toward some tall doors on a long, narrow building that rustles with the braying of animals.  The thatched roof is crowned with a carved wooden horse's head at the point of each gable.

Homes with small fenced-off front yards crowd between the pathway and the imposing palisade wall.  Some of the yards are planted with a few rows of turnips while others contain racks for drying meat or clothing.  To the southeast, an archway set back from the path frames a large open field in the center of the village.

The droop-roofed longhouses cluster in groups of three and four upon slight mounds to keep out rainwater.  Though similar at first glance, closer inspection reveals their unique construction.  While homes and shops have stone chimneys that rise well above the roof to keep stray cinders from the thatching, food stores are chimneyless and supported several hands above the ground by rat-proof mushroom-shaped stones.

Near the path, a large hide stretched within a cord-bound branch frame is branded with a few words in large block letters.  The acrid smell of tannin wafts from a longhouse with a leather-covered door studded with darkened bronze tacks.

Some of the logs in the pathway have been cut down by a third or half to make way for the bulging roots of a broad peregan tree that have burst up through the soil.  The only tree growing within the village walls, it soars above everything to impossible heights and the generous reach of its arching branches shelters several nearby buildings.

Facing the path, a bark-covered longhouse crested with carved boar's heads bustles with activity.  A steady flow of men and women pass through the stout oaken door and a low hum of chatter emanates from within.  Though it stands alone at this bend in the walkway, it appears to be the center of life in the otherwise quiet forest village.

Birds alight on the curved boar tusks that cap each of the thick logs forming the palisade wall surrounding the village.  They survey the thatched rooftops for plump insects and swoop from their perches to capture a meal.  To the east of the pathway, the ground slopes downward to a grassy vale.  A few of the birds investigate the grass for worms, but most find easier prey in the thick roof thatch.

The land tumbles down sharply from the level pathway above.  The slope is so severe in places that one or two thin slate steps have been set into the ground to ensure safe footing even when rain slicks the grass.

Sunk low in the earth and surrounded by the village, the small vale is protected from the frosty touch of bitter winds that scour the rest of the forest steppe.  Snow melts quickly here to reveal flower-dotted grass and pillows of bright green moss.  Nestled in the center is a patched hide tent stretched over a bent branch frame.

A gathering of longhouses cling to the sloped ground with the same tenacious determination as the clan itself has clung to survival in the unforgiving wilderness of the forest steppe.  Coveys of blue grouse occasionally alight upon a cluster of frostberry bushes growing nearby.

A large turnip patch surrounded by a low fence of woven branches stretches out between several of the homes, plumes of green leaves sprouting in neat rows from the dark soil.  Some leafy plumes lie tossed aside on the ground nearby, obvious evidence of snacks hastily eaten by hungry residents or passers-by.

Sounds of both the forest and village filter down from above, seeming at once surrounding and yet far away from this sleepy corner of the vale.  Stark white patches of snow cling to the grass and pillows of bright green moss that cover the ground.
Supported on thick stilts banded with iron, several bark-clad longhouses cluster along the snow-patched slope.  Stone-dotted tawny soil pathways worn through the grass connect each of the buildings.

Sunlight occasionally glints off of a verdigris brass water pump standing over a smooth stone basin amid the buildings.  Small-leaved variegated ivy twines up the shaft of the pump, enjoying the condensation on the metal and the moist soil at its base.  Birds perched on nearby homes wait for the basin to fill so they, too, may enjoy the cool spring water that flows from the pump.
The sharp slope levels off a bit here and stands of silver-white birch trees scatter among the thatched buildings.  In the springtime, tiny violet flowers bloom in their shade.

The trees of the forest grow tall and thin with branches that begin several stories overhead.  Most trees have had their bark rubbed and gouged off about a Dwarf's height from the ground.  Stuck into a thick thorn-covered fir is a long yellowed splinter of boar tusk.

The glade is a young and open pine forest brightened with sunlight and the sound of the river.  Birds call from their perches and occasionally swoop down from the boughs, either seeking a meal or in a game of chase with one another.  The crisp, clean scent of fir and spruce sharpens the cool air.

Stone outcroppings lining the steep descent into the river to the west echo the sound of the water playing merrily below.  The crags here are too unstable to climb and too wide to dive over, but father north, the forest edges closer to the river.
The thick, scaly bark of a nearby sikka tree secretes golden sap that wells in the cracks and crevices.  Unlucky insects become entombed in the gooey traps.

Thick clusters of blueberry bushes amble along the edge of the crags and quiver with the movements of birds perched within.  At dawn and twilight, when the sun's light is thinnest, small grey conies hop out from the shrubs in search of grasses and roots to augment their diet of berries.  The river is barely visible as it wends through the banks far beyond the bushes and the stony descent.

The land drops off to the west alongside the burbling Liirewsag.  The "plunk" of pinecones falling into the river from overhanging boughs punctuates the water's steady song.  Cones and splintered branches that fell short of the water lie strewn across the treacherous crags below.  Bloated and half-eaten by scavenger birds, the carcass of an unfortunate boar also lies broken across the rocks.

Saplings grow from slivers of earth caught in the crevices of the stony crags.  They cling tenaciously to the steep wall of shattered stone and arc gently over the water.  Their roots never grow very deep, and evidence of a hard rain's power to dislodge them lies cracked and broken on the rocks below.

A weeping hemlock droops over a weathered lunat log to shelter a patch of spindly puffball mushrooms that grow tall and top-heavy so that they bend over slightly beneath the weight of their pale caps.  From somewhere close comes the sound of grunting and something trundling through the underbrush.

The needle-strewn forest floor spreads out beneath a sky framed by spruce and pine boughs.  Seasonal flowers sprawl in sunlit clearings while juniper and laurel shrubs enjoy the shade where patches of snow linger throughout the year.

Slender evergreens grow tall and straight, with high, narrow crowns of branches.  The lowest limbs in this area belong to the longleaf pine, whose feathery boughs wave in the breezes about one story overhead.  Once their long dark green needles fall, they turn deep amber brown.  Frosty white wads of sap drip from their needles and cover the ground with globs of sticky goop that resemble hailstones.

Piles of stone and heavy boulders cap the craggy shore, blocking access to the river.  From between the stones grow woody plants that produce hardy orange blooms in late autumn.  Rather than wilt, they become straw-like and preserved into the winter months until blown away by a storm.  To the northwest, the earth slips down to the water's level.

The earth falls sharply downward from this perfect diving spot to dip its peaty edge in the river.  The bank leading to the river below is moist and fertile, making it an ideal home to a wide variety of hostas.  Most have variegated leaves of green streaked with yellow or gold, while others are nearly blue with blotchy patterns of white.  In spring, the leafy, low-growing plants send up tall spindly stalks that bloom in purple, white and orange.

A patch of green grows in this wide clearing amid the trees and pine needle-covered earth.  Tiny yellow waiku flowers huddle in the grasses and clover, their petals closed tightly against the sunlight.  The flora surrounding the clearing is as varied as a patchwork shawl.

Curious dark, rounded mammoth-sized boulders of basalt lie atop and project from the forest floor here.  They look as if they had been dropped in place, as they do not match the granite outcroppings or craggy shoreline.  Some have deep valleys filled with windblown soil and decaying matter in which weeds and small saplings grow, as though recreating the glade in miniature.

Here, the land is level with the water.  A permanent-looking puddle drenches the soil around the base of some tall cedar trees that cluster in a small depression.  Rain and snow feed the river that swells and ebbs with the seasons, changing the landscape and renewing the bank's fertile richness.  To the north and east, the earth rises again, pulling away from the sodden bank of the river.

A stand of pale slender-trunked paper birches grows along a ridge to the northeast.  Their bark is thin, white and smooth, separating into diaphanous strips that curl back from the trunk.  Skinny saplings growing amid the taller elders are reddish-brown but share the same delicate pointed-oval leaves that turn golden in autumn.

A line of ashen birches looks ghostly pale against the darker pines that surround them, like the spirits of fallen trees floating amid the living.  Their leafy limbs sway gracefully with each breath of wind and rustle a soft accompaniment to the river's song.

Beneath many of the shrubs and low tree branches are large saucer-shaped depressions.  The leaf-lined hollows evidence the forest's boar population.  In the day, the nests are filled with several boars piled together in sleep, but in the evening, all the nests are empty as entire drifts of boars roam the glade.

Slender needles from a stand of longleaf pine trees cover the ground here, making a crunchy matting that springs slightly underfoot.  Clusters of the tree's small cones lie scattered about, most having been pried open by squirrels for the seeds within.  A few undoubtedly opened before they fell, allowing their seeds to disperse and begin the forest's next generation.

The long, thick roots of a quaking aspen grow through the loamy soil and dangle down the steep bank to the cold waters of the river below.  The tree's broad, spreading crown sports leaves that are deep shiny green with silver undersides, and shiver in the wind, giving the tree its name.  In autumn, its foliage takes on brilliant hues of red, orange and yellow.

The river burbles playfully along the base of the steep and muddy bank, like a shimmering silver ribbon against brunette curls.  Birds perch on overhanging tree limbs to watch for potential meals swimming below and without warning, quickly swoop down to grab a struggling fish in their talons, then fly off with their catch.

A dead pine's skeletal branches knock together in the wind, and the dry rapping noises travel down the limbs into the trunk, sounding like a heart beating somewhere deep within.  The coarse, black bark clings to the weather-silvered tree only in ragged patches that crumble off easily, and in the crook of a low branch, the wood bears the lacy scars of a termite infestation.

A white-breasted nuthatch sitting in an overhead bough aggressively calls its mate with a nasal "ank-ank-ank" sound.  After a few calls, an answer comes in a shrill "kee-kee" from another limb.  Several other avian conversations begin, each with its own pitch, rhythm and emotion.  Rarely is there a moment of complete silence.

A charred and shattered spruce lies in a broken heap surrounded by several other fire-blackened trees, evidence of a lightning strike.  Periodic small wildfires help maintain the openness of the wood by clearing underbrush and encouraging growth of grasses and sedge.  Already life is returning to the scorched area as a few tender new seedlings sprout from a mound of blackened earth.

Beneath the tall conifers, the glade is open and park-like, relatively free of underbrush but for patches of shrubs that usually huddle close to the trees' shade.  Stretches of grass and sedge grow in small clearings, where older trees have fallen and the progression of the forest begins again with the smallest plants.

Ferns grow down the slope beside the river, softening the stony bank with their long, filigree fronds.  The water's swift current gambols along below, swirling around bends in the landscape and skipping over stones or fallen branches with a glad splashing sound.

Sunlight speckles the forest floor and wind sighs among the pine boughs, creating a sense of quiet solitude broken only by the sound of the boars that inhabit the forest.  A loud grunting sound usually precedes their barreling heedlessly through the area, snapping thin saplings and turning up the smooth brown carpet of pine needles.  Frequently, they stop to sharpen their tusks or just scratch themselves on the pines' rough bark, flaking chunks off and leaving the pale wood exposed.

Cold winds blow energetically down the northward slope and through the glade.  They cut through the strong smell of pine needles and dry, musty leaf mold that hangs heavily beneath the trees.  Each breeze renews the air with icy freshness.

Bristly spruce limbs cast filigree shadows that frolic over the ground as the trees sway in breezes scented with the clean smell of heather and pine.  The trees stand far enough apart that their branches do not overlap, and scrubby bunches of grass peek through the thin layer of pine needles covering the ground between the trees' canopy.

Soft pillows of bright green moss cling to the gnarled roots of some yews grouped on a low rise.  Between the trees, small piles of snow held in hollows formed by the roots melt slowly, providing a constant trickle to moisten the bark on which the moss thrives.

A grey and tattered bit of rope dangles from an overhanging tree limb, swinging back and forth in the wind.  Judging from the slipknots tied around the branch, the rope appears to be the remains of a trap.  The locals have long used this glade for hunting and trapping with such productive results that the only reason they've found to venture farther north into the dark, looming Paasvadh is foolhardy adventure-seeking.

The lunat's lowest, more or less horizontal branches typically die but remain on the tree for a few years afterward, giving it a scraggly look before they fall off.  These dead lower branches are generally encrusted with brittle splotches of grey-green lichen and pale shelves of fungus.

A ragged trench carved through the thick carpet of pine needles by flowing rainwater and melted snow follows the slope from the northeast down to the river's edge.  The bank is muddy and clotted with clumps of decaying debris, but climbable by an able soul to gain access to the chill river below.

A viny heap of small leaf ivy cascades down the bank to the river below.  Caught in the tangled tendrils are twigs, dried leaves and slender longleaf pine needles bundled together like tiny whiskbrooms.  Small brown chipmunks occasionally peek out from the ivy's leafy cover to scout the area for predators before venturing out.

Twin maple seedlings grow in a depression atop a very large basalt boulder.  A passing bird must have deposited the seeds, as there are no other maple trees in the glade.  Birds enjoy the rock because the shallow wells in its surface hold water high enough from the ground that they can drink and bathe here without being menaced by the glade's larger inhabitants.

Ivy envelops all but the skyward-reaching splinter of a broken stump.  It smothers the rocky outcroppings and covers the ground in deep green filigree throughout the seasons.  The sunlight plays hide-and-seek with shadows over the leafy blanket as it shivers in the brisk wind.

The land rises sharply to the north and east, stepping up in plateaus that seem supported by smooth chunks of granite mortared together with damp earth and moss.  At the base of each rise lies a line of trees washed away with the thin soil by rain or meltwater.  Twittering birds flit in and out of a gap in the lacy trim of deadfall.

Heather grows in wispy clumps between the widely spaced trees.  Its feathery texture contrasts with the stiff and dark-leafed boxwood growing nearby, and it celebrates each thaw with blooming sprays of purple and lavender.

A mature felenok pine reaches majestically skyward and seems to grasp the sun in its outstretched limbs.  Large, golden cones burden the ends of each branch, making them arc slightly downward.  Few felenok seeds survive to fulfill their purpose, as they are sweet to the palate of local squirrels that eagerly pry them from their cones before they drop to the ground.

To the north, the landscape fractures into a jumble of progressively larger outcrops and low cliffs.  Tall conifers crowd each other and cling with gnarled roots to the unyielding, stony soil.  On slopes too steep for trees grow azaleas that bloom red and pink in the early spring.  Several varieties of holly mingle with the lower-growing plants and adorn the glade's winter season with berries ranging from red and orange to golden yellow.

A scarlet-coifed woodpecker perched high in a nearby pine chips off loose flakes of tree bark with a staccato "rat-a-tat-a-tat".  The bark bits fall to the ground with a soft pattering sound, like a dry rain.  The litter of pine needles and leaves in the area is turned up from the recent furrowing of wild boars in search of something good to eat.

Birdsongs filter in from all directions, blending into a sweet arboreal symphony.  Some twitter staccato soprano parts and others caw contralto backbeats.  The owls and mourning doves add their long, slow tenor nearest twilight and dawn, when the sky's colors demand a bit more drama.

The trees become older, taller and closer as the glade wends up the broken landscape toward a dark line of towering trees to the north.  The underbrush also thickens noticeably as viny plants and scrubby bushes tangle amid the tree roots and timeworn stones protruding from the earth.

Squat bristlecone pines scatter along the steep rocky outcrops to the northeast.  Each pine, from young seedling to ancient relic, has an individual character.  Young trees are densely clad with glistening needle-covered branches that sway like foxtails in the wind.  Their bristled cones drip pine-scented resin and exude all the freshness of youth.  As centuries pass and the elements batter the trees, they become sculpted into astonishingly beautiful shapes.

The glade's omnivorous boars voraciously root in the pine litter for grubs, nuts, fungi, small animals and carrion, leaving upturned tufts of needles, soil and twigs.  Their furrowing is essential to both their survival and that of the forest, as they mix nutrients in the soil and speed the process of decomposition that is slowed by the cool climate.

The sloped riverbank yields again to steep, stony crags that climb away from the swiftly moving river.  To the southwest, the land dips its peaty fringe in the water, but to the northeast, it sits high on the rocky steppes.

The sunlit forest floor reclaims the remains of a fallen pine.  Blankets of heavy moss appear to drag it physically back into the earth.  The tree's cloak of bark has almost completely sloughed off, and the exposed wood is dark with rot.  In the cool climate of the forest steppe, decay is slow and deliberate.
Moss drapes from the sap-sugared pine branches above in wispy grey-blue tendrils.  They embrangle tall shrubs and fill in gaps in the tree canopy to block out almost all of the sky.
Patches of grass and moss cling to craggy outcrops that crowd stands of spruce and modwir.  Ivy and large shrubs tangle around the trees, further constricting the pathway leading upslope.

The tree branches twine overhead, covering the glade with cool shadow that chases the sunlight away.  Strange animal cries and sounds of movement that rustle in the thickening underbrush add to a sense of foreboding that fills the pathway.  It's little wonder the locals seldom tread this route.

The trees bend in over the slim pathway, casting it deep in shade.  Gnarled knotholes peering down through the bristly canopy of a fat spruce tree seem to watch every movement.  Shrill cries, unlike those heard farther south, pierce the dusky veil and seem to resonate in one's bones.

Thick shrubs push in toward the path and grab at passers-by like the small hands of a child tugging at one's cloak hem.  The sound of birdsong is strangely absent despite the thick mesh of branches above.

Cascades of ivy and other viny plants pour over each outcrop, concealing the stone-clotted earth and making the sharply rising landscape look more like a solid wall of dark foliage.  Fir and cedar trees lean into one another as they stagger up the slope, like old men walking home from a bar.

Leathery brown tripe lichen grows on many of the exposed rocks and looks like vaguely circular patches torn from a tanned hide.  The slightly upturned edges catch and store rainwater that keeps the plant supple.  Those with tears or insect-munched holes quickly dry up and become brittle.

Hardwoods gradually mingle with the conifers, giving the wind a slightly raspier voice when rustling through the branches.  In winter, the bare tree limbs whisper hoarsely as they rub against each other and sometimes sound like the grunting of boars.

Partially obscured by fallen pine needles, the soft earth holds the small paw prints of a fox.  Matted tufts of grey fur, the remains of some rodent, are strewn before a hollow between gnarled tree roots.  The faint scent of decay mingles with the sharp smell of pine sap.

Showing tell-tale signs of foot traffic, the narrow path creeps between the boles of ancient pines.  Many years' accumulation of rusty-brown needles and splintering pinecones carpet the ground, providing ample forage for squirrels and birds.

Cattails and bulrushes cluster thickly along the shores of a small pond nestled in a dip in the terrain.  Faint wisps of mist cling to the surface of the water.  The forest itself is quiet, the stillness broken by occasional birdsong and the wind rustling through the pine boughs.

Eternally mantled in snow and ice, the Arncharn Shel mountains rule the eastern horizon.  Soaring high above the dense forest, the stony windswept heights are painted numerous shades of grey.  The rugged trail continues its meandering way through the wooded foothills.

Fresh gouges bleed yellow sap where something has sharpened its claws on a giant pine.  The glistening sap-glazed bark contrasts with the muted grey-green moss mottling the trunks of the other trees.  Providing shelter to a family of bushy-tailed woodrats, a thick tangle of red currant bushes adds a bright splash of color.  The occasional shriek of a hawk brings about a temporary cessation of rustling in the undergrowth.

Heavily wooded hills rise on both sides as the road winds among them.  Glimpsed through the thinning trees to the north, a narrow valley nestles beneath the looming shadow of a snow-capped mountain standing silent watch over the terrain.  A fickle breeze sporadically rustles through the branches, cutting the scent of damp earth and leaf mold hanging in the air.

From the top of a rise overlooking the valley, the road affords a view of cultivated terraced fields divided by low walls of dark stone.  Goats dot the hillside, grazing on the tall grasses covering the rocky slopes beyond the fields.  Centered within this pastoral vista is a complex of buildings enclosed by fortified walls.

Dominating the view to the north, a mountain looms over the small settlement.  At once beautiful and forbidding, the crags and ice-capped peaks display a multiplicity of hues and textures.  Reaching endlessly for the sky, sheer bluffs and level terraces juxtaposed with jagged cliffs range in subtle shades between black, blue-grey and white.

In desperate need of realignment, the uneven jumble of cobblestones forming the road meanders down the gentle slope.  A sturdy wall rises to the north, the sharpened stakes along the top pointing skyward like a line of spears raised in defense.  Yellowing grasses, well nibbled by the goats which roam in the valley, cover much of the rocky ground.

Rising to intimidating heights, the fortified wall enclosing the compound is broken only by a stout ironwood gate.  The gate displays a bronze plaque engraved with the crest of the Clerics' Guild superimposed over a towering mountain.

Browning clumps of grass push up between cracked cobblestones, obscuring the edges of the roadway.  Low mounds of blackberry brambles cover the rocky slope to the south, grudgingly giving way to cultivated fields to the west.  Steeply pitched roofs can be glimpsed between the stakes surmounting the high, thick wall stretching east to west alongside the road.

The fortified wall enclosing the monastery grounds turns north here, sheltering the huddled buildings and those within from weather and wildlife.  Terraced fields rise to the south and west, scenting the vagrant breeze with mulched soil and cultivated vegetation.

The cobblestone road ends in a broad square crowded with thatch-roofed buildings and shops, their brick chimneys emitting wisps of bluish smoke.  Winding northwards, a packed earth track continues towards the mountains in the distance.

A high wall lines one side of the dirt road and prevents goats from wandering into the monastery's fields.  Orderly rows of stunted yet healthy plants peek over the top of the weathered stone.  Strung on a taut line stretched between two notched stakes, tattered scraps of cloth flutter in the fickle breeze.

Yellowing grass along the rutted track is slowly losing its battle with mortality.  Clumps of weeds skirt the stone wall enclosing a field with scarcely a break for the gate.  Towards the north, a dark line of trees is visible in the distance.

A patchwork of terraced fields bound by low rock walls spreads to the south.  Between the cultivated rows, a tidy grid work of paths is still visible forming a subtle brocade of dark earth against the less-than-verdant vegetation.  Inexplicably, the acrid tang of smoke mingled with a hint of decay lingers in the air.  The road ends here, dwindling into a weed-choked trail leading into dark forest.

The buildings within the compound have steeply pitched roofs that help ward off the elements during the harsher seasons.  A broad expanse of sere grass which lies between the gate and large buildings is littered with rock and boulders.
A dusty gravel path leads to the center of the courtyard where a small dark statue of a raccoon stands.  Hewn cedar benches encircle the area, providing a restful place for contemplation.

Carved granite urns filled with leafy ferns flank a silverwood door.  Octagonal tiles of silver-flecked black stone line the floor.  The walls feature frescos that depict the same landscape during each of the four seasons.

Partitioned from the rest of the building by folding screens, the size of the infirmary can be changed as needed to accommodate patients.  Shelves of supplies line the walls, while a battered worktable is shoved beneath a window.  A stack of stained pallets near a cast iron stove bears silent testimony to the work which has been done here.

A large stone fireplace dominates one wall of the windowless room.  A mismatched pair of shabby leather chairs huddles close to the hearth, while battered pine benches, with iron braziers placed beside them to warm chilled toes, provide extra seating.  Tables topped with carved slabs of granite, each boasting a pewter candelabrum, are placed within easy reach of most of the seating.

Worn smooth by the passage of time and countless feet, the floor is tiled with marble vela'tohr flowers set within black granite octagons.  Ceiling beams are carved with a series of bloom-covered vines that twist between evenly spaced chandeliers.  The curved walls of the rotunda are lavishly painted with a fresco that depicts a variety of animals.  By comparison, the marble altar in the middle of the room seems plain.

Polished copper pots and pans hang upon the wall on either side of a large stove.  Candle sconces are affixed to the other walls, between cluttered shelves stacked with culinary equipment and supplies.  A pair of large trestle tables fills most of the room, surrounded by threadbare runners lining the barely passable areas between the fixtures and the benches by the tables.

Wool hangings woven into geometric patterns cover the walls, creating a windbreak between the door and the rest of the guildhall.  Dried flakes of mud cling to a brass bootjack shoved halfway underneath a silverwillow wicker chair.  A wooden rack holds numerous pairs of footwear, most of which have been encrusted in various substances.

A small brick building faces an iron gate on opposite sides of the dusty courtyard.  A stout door on the south side leads back into the largest building.  Granite cisterns are wedged snugly against the various buildings, positioned to collect rainwater and snow melt funneled by drip channels cut into each sloping roof.  Sickly ivy clings tenaciously to the fortified wall curving protectively around the compound.

Freestanding shelves surround a large stone table in the center of the room.  Thick velvet draperies almost completely hide the walls from view.  At regular intervals wall sconces emerge from folds in the material, each bearing a softly glowing gaethzen orb.

Woven straw mats run the length of the hall, offering a measure of protection against the stone floor beneath.  Multi-colored wool hangings work as a similar buffer for the walls.  A brass telescope on a battered tripod points towards a large window.

Carved silverwillow beams run the length of the corridor, supporting the sloping ceiling.  Suspended at regular intervals from the elevated end of the hallway, chandeliers illuminate the cloisters with candlelight.  Laid end-to-end, woven straw mats speckled with drips of wax soften the stone floor underfoot.

Illuminated by candlelight from above, heavy wool tapestries are spaced evenly between numerous doorways.  Straw mats line the floors throughout the corridor, providing a buffer between feet and the stone.
A fresco occupies one wall, its ashen hues illustrating somber scenes.  The aroma of incense drifts up from a shallow copper bowl resting on a low table between two doors.

Rows of candles arranged on tall iron stands illuminate this end of the cloisters with a soft golden glow.  Dryads carved into the exposed rafters peer down, as if scrutinizing all who come and go in their domain.

Thriving plants in large glazed pots threaten to overwhelm the dusty courtyard.  Covered cisterns conceal most of a fortified wall.  Pathways paved with octagonal flagstones meander through a potted garden, connecting an iron gate, the door to the main building, and a small cottage.

An aged silverwillow desk sits in the center of the room.  Woven in shades of green and gold, a faded rug patterned with wheat sheaves stretches between the door and a pierced stone screen.  Scroll-filled shelves take up most of the space near the walls, leaving barely any room for a window.

A gate constructed from mismatched planks of wood is firmly wedged shut where two stone walls bordering the field converge.  The walls are pocked with deep gouges and blackened with streaks of soot.  Remnants of burnt vegetation crunch underfoot, although hints of green skirt the scorched tract to the north and west.

Stunted and withered stalks of wheat are strangled by thick greenish-brown vines armed with cruel thorns.  Running parallel to the weathered stone wall at the edge of the field, a broad swathe of bare, scorched earth cuts across the untended rows.  The scent of smoke lingers unpleasantly, and only a few tracks of small animals give evidence that there are still regular visitors to the area.

Curving west, the rock wall separates what's left of the field from the road and the edge of the forest.  Beneath a reddish-brown stain on the wall, a steel-bladed scythe lies forgotten and rusting in the grasp of the greenery.  Only patches of packed and scorched earth are bare of the omnipresent vines.

Withered amethyst bloom vines hang limply against the stone wall, nearly engulfed by the rapacious thorny green vines.  Stretching toward the sky, a few hardy weeds stubbornly struggle to survive the engulfing tangle of vines.  Over the wall, a dense forest stretches northwards, blanketing part of the slope of Asketi's Mount.

Bled dry of life and color, a sickly silverwillow tree glimpsed over the crumbling wall is pierced by the red thorns of the thick green vines coiled about it.  The weight of the vines is slowly pulling the tree down.  More vines spill from over the wall into the field, and no sign of the original crops remains.

Several forlorn stalks of wheat still stand, seemingly huddled against the wall for protection against the voracious vines blanketing the rest of the field.  Crows perch on the weathered rock, eyeing the abandoned bounty.  Occasionally something rustles through the greenery, causing the vines to seem to move with a life of their own.

Stunted and withered stalks of wheat are strangled by thick greenish-brown vines armed with cruel thorns.  Running parallel to the weathered stone wall at the edge of the field, a broad swathe of bare, scorched earth cuts across the untended rows.  The scent of smoke lingers unpleasantly, and only a few tracks of small animals give evidence that there are still regular visitors to the area.

A malevolent garden borne of secrets unknown to mortals, the forest's edge is inviting to the adventurous of spirit, yet foreboding to the strong of mind.  Dark red-tinged creeper vines drape across skeletal claw-like trees, evoking the image of poisonous adders writhing in the sky above.

The audible trickling of water beckons seductively from its unseen source.  A twisted myriad of dark vines stretch from the treetops above, blocking out all light -- whether by sun or star.  It is a wonder that anything grows on the forest's floor at all.

Thin veils of black widow's lace grass drape over the soft soil, silencing every step as if it were enfolded in its own void.  The foliage seems to stir constantly when glimpsed peripherally, yet no movement can be discerned in the immediate surroundings.

A severely knotted witchclaw tree rises in the center of the path, its barren branches entangled in pale silver amethyst vines blooming with vibrant violet blossoms.  The scene is a stark contrast of despair and beauty, one that is prevalent in this mysterious forest.

Soft patches of black lichen show up sparsely on the soil, intertwined with widow's lace and dark green moss.  Trees of all shapes, sizes and colors writhe up from the soil in all directions.  Woven amidst the branches of every tree are dark green vines tinged with a crimson gleam, a curious sign of foreboding to the experienced tracker.

Tangled masses of dark green vines dangle down from their perches, interwoven into the treetop canopy far above the forest floor.  The rustling of leaves is audible in the distance, yet the presence of wildlife seems strangely absent.

A teetering wild plum tree flanks the path, burdened by a shawl of the omnipresent green vines tinged with red highlights.  The thorns of each vine dig and pierce into the wounded tree's fleshy bark, as if feasting upon fallen prey.

The pungent aroma of jasmine perfumes the air, although no blossoms are visible.  Silvery strands of a tangled widow's web stretch between the branches of a stunted witchclaw tree, adorning it like a fine-jeweled platinum glove.

A single tree lies toppled in the pathway, covered with a carpet of red-thorned dark green vines.  With sporadic movements, the vines twitch and twist over the withering ironwood husk, as if sapping it of its very life.

Giant ferns sweep out into the pathway here, brushing passersby with their feathery fronds.  The distant sounds of trickling water cascades through the air, beckoning from the depths of the mysterious wood.

A massive black willow looms the height of twenty Gor'Togs or more, casting a pall of shade over the silent forest floor.  The sheer number and variety of shrubs, trees, and vines basking beneath it is startling, as if this lush forest was host to every variety of plant known to mortals -- and surely some that have yet to be discovered.

A pool of gleaming silvery water yawns open in the earth, its surface glassy and serene.  Blooming amethyst vines emerge from its depths to coil up the side of a nearby yew tree.  The darker crimson-tinted vines seem to shy away from the pool, rejecting the nourishment it supplies.

A curtain of undulating maiden's tresses is visible high in the treetops above, twitching about in search of warm flesh to devour in its deadly embrace.  All is quiet save for the rustling of the tress vines, as if the forest denizens avoid this area and the bizarre plant's seductive, predatory dance.  For now, it remains at its perch, granting passage to those who are swift.
Silvery dew trickles off of the dark green vines dangling from the verdant patchwork sky, forming small pools of glassy crystal that echo their muted cries of disruption at each intermittent drop.

A velvety carpet of flora explodes suddenly into being in this spot, bearing vibrant flowers and plants of all colors and shapes.  A sense of exuberance permeates the air here, as if it were charged with the essence of Life itself.

A single tree lies rotting and shattered amidst a colony of its healthier brethren.  The omnipresent thorny red-tinted vines are curiously absent around it, although what is left of its bark has been scarred horribly with gouge marks.

The sound of water dripping in the distance echoes quietly, steadily keeping the pulse of the forest.  The rhythm is fragile yet determined, as if the slightest tilt could shatter its equilibrium and end the balance of life in this oddly beautiful place.

Desiccated amethyst vines hang limp off the side of a nearby tree, their delicate forms crushed and dominated by the thicker green vines armed with thorny red barbs.  The cycle of life in this habitat becomes clearer, and it is certain that all is not as it may appear.

Tufts of dry, scraggly witchgrass nestle at the base of a nearby tree to garner shelter and shade.  This particular tree looks rather sickly, as if stricken with something that its neighbors have not yet caught.

The surroundings grow dimmer, the flora itself seeming more monotone than at the entrance to this bizarre garden.  Moving into the heart of the wood, everything seems to shift from vibrant, explosive colors into chalky, dull greys.

A soft buzzing sound emanates from a hollow beneath one of the silverwillows crowding the banks of a small stream.  Grass grows throughout, thinning and losing color as it approaches the waterline.  A narrow trail leads southerly towards a healthier region of the forest.

Stunted trees press in from all sides, grabbing at hair and clothing.  Tatters of grey moss caught in the branches flutter like shrouds snatched from the restless dead.  In curious contrast to the distorted trees, a lush carpet of black widow's lace grass provides a gloriously dark setting for colorful mounds of flowering adder's tongue.

The limbs of elder trees interweave overhead, blocking out any glimpse of the sky.  Somehow, a thick undergrowth of creeping vines and pale ferns thrive in the perpetual dusk, threatening to block the path at every turn.  Pale wisps of mists drift like aimless wraiths through the tangle of vines and trees.

Pallid streaks of daylight pierce the canopy to cast dappled shadows on the ground.  Crone's hair moss hangs in clumps from the barren, twisted limbs of a massive oak.  Gnarled roots reach out in all directions from the base of the hulking tree to trip the unwary.  From somewhere nearby comes the muted sound of running water.

A huge oak tree dominates the center of the clearing, lifting its great branches up to the sky.  Crone's hair moss hangs in clumps from the barren limbs while gnarled roots snake out in all directions to trip the unwary.  Wan light filters down to cast dappled shadows on the ground.

Festooned with ropy grey blankets of moss, the gnarled limbs of an enormous oak stretch overhead.  Deep gouges, the width of a finger or more, mar the bark of the forest giant.  The edges of the gouges are weathered, proving the damage occurred some time ago, yet the tree still weeps viscous dribbles of sap.

Thorned vines slither up and around the ancient oak trees like fanged vipers.  Broken, rotting limbs lay scattered over the ground like gangrenous appendages.  Standing out in the drear wood, red-capped mushrooms push up through the carpet of decomposing leaves, thriving in the moist decay.

Barely audible, the trickling of water whispers seductively from its unseen source.  Lush green vines armed with red thorns smother the eastern flank of the massive oak tree, yielding grudgingly to the grey moss swaying from the leafless limbs.  Rocky soils shows dark amidst scraggly patches of thin grass.

Spidery vines smother the sloping ground, tangling about the trunks of browning pines.  Murky light barely penetrates the layers of leaves and boughs.  A whispering rustle accompanies the slightest disturbance in the air.  The air is ripe with the scent of damp earth and faint corruption.

Cloyingly thick, the omnipresent stench of the stream permeates the area with a sickening miasma.  Icy fingers of mist slither around once prospering trees, as if groping blindly for victims to choke.  Dim reflections float on the dark waters, shattering and reforming with the slow moving current.

Hollow with distance, throaty ululations worry at the edge of hearing and then vanish.  The gnarled and diseased limbs of oak trees are being slowly strangled by black-thorned vines covered with blooms resembling purple spiders.  A small patch of weeds clusters around a large rock jutting from the ground.

Chill tendrils of mist rise from a malodorous stream coursing through the tangle.  The yellowish fog eddies eerily around the tree trunks, swirling in response to shifts in the air currents and movement of any living thing.  The bare limbs of sickly silverwillow trees stretch across the path, as if poised to scratch or ensnare the unwary.

Writhing like snakes, wisps of yellowish mist drift up off a rivulet to the east.  Half sunk in the soft boggy soil, storm-shattered trees lay strewn across the clearing; whether broken by wind or ice is hard to say.  Rotting stumps, covered with thick shelves of scabrous fungus, rear out of the deadfall.

Skeletons of once-thriving trees crowd together, their gnarled limbs sculpted by the harsh mountain winds.  Tangles of thorny red-tinted vines snake around the trunks and drape the chalky grey trees with a vibrant explosion of color.

To the north, the immense mass of the mountain emerges from pale wisps of mist.  Icy fingers of water trickle down from the snowpack above into small pools.  Blighted trees huddle close together as if commiserating with one another over their plight.  Occasional blasts of frigid air set limbs clattering against one another, raining desiccated leaves down to the forest floor.

A narrow track ends abruptly where a massive shoulder of black granite juts from the side of the mountain.  Part of the cliff has collapsed, leaving a great jumble of fallen rock that partially blocks a dark cave mouth.  Sheltered from the sun's cruel light by the stony slopes, a thick blanket of yellow-green lichen spreads over much of the area.

Grey and lifeless, a pervasive air of decay hangs over this region of the woods.  A number of trees lean precariously against one another, worn beyond endurance by the blight.  Limbs shattered, one pine has succumbed utterly and crashed to the forest floor.  A sickly growth of fungus has sprung up along its scaly bark.

What light filters through the dense canopy scarcely penetrates the gloomy shadows beneath the trees.  The trunks of the towering trees are splotched with some type of sickly fungus.  Reeking of death and decay, the forest floor is carpeted with dismal grey-green leaves on top and black rot underneath.

Icy fingers of water trickle down the sheer cliff and form a fetid rivulet that wends its way sluggishly south.  Chill winds tear at the brittle branches of dying silverwillows huddling close to the slow moving water.  Rotting leaves and branches form a loose tangle of debris in the rivulet, caught on stones slick with slimy black moss.

Skeletal tree limbs stretch imploringly up to the sky, withered leaves clinging tenaciously despite strong mountain winds.  A roiling mist clings to the surface of the stream coursing through the oaks and silverwillows.  The slick rocks bordering the stream are streaked with strangely luminescent lichen.

Sickly yellow-green scum covers the surface of a small pool.  Skeletal trees, bereft of leaves and life, lean precariously over the water like drunkards about to fall into a gutter.  The blight is especially virulent here, coating the ground and trees with a thick, oozing fungus reeking of rot.

Thin veils of mist chill the air.  Riddled with splotches of fungus, the scaly black trunks of pine trees rise up all around.  Overhead, thick branches lock together and support a tangled mat of moss and vines.  Brown needles cover the ground, hiding tripping hazards like protruding roots and treacherous stones.

A vast tangle of root and limbs, the wood is painted in shades of chalky grey splashed with splotches of reddish black where fungus oozes over the blighted trees.  Drifting up from the ground, yellowish mist thickens and thins inexplicably while carrying the scents of damp and decay.

Draped with tattered grey moss, the barren trees resemble skeletal black arms clad in the rotting remnants of winding sheets.  Reaching through the icy fog shrouding the forest, the dense tangle of vegetation forms an impenetrable barrier blocking passage at nearly every turn.

A ridge heaves up sharply from the forest floor, a long rise of stone and earth curved like a claw.  Trees cling to its flanks, their leafy canopies shrouding the world in grey twilight.  Smelling of crisp pine and the less pleasant scent of decay, pale mists rise from the black earth and curl through the scatter of rocks and trees.

Towering ironwoods spread their canopies over the stunted oaks and scrubby pines, the sparsely leafed limbs interlacing in a web of rot-riddled wood that hangs low over the narrow ridge rising up from the forest floor.  A few of the lower branches of the trees are broken, as if something large had passed this way recently.

Bent and twisted by strong mountain winds, an ambitious copse of witchclaw trees struggles along the sloping rise.  Huddled in solitude at the edge of the ridge overlooking the tangle, a scraggly pine draped with veils of crone's hair moss broods over its reflection in a dark pool.

A stand of blanched and bare birch struggles to survive in the stony ground as the path climbs up the sparsely wooded rise.  The air lacks the rich scents of earth, loam and decay while underfoot the land is sere, showing evidence of a blight terrible enough to bleed the very life from the land.

Curiously washed-out hues paint the landscape in stark and pallid detail.  Grass bleached to straw barely binds the soil together in the face of eroding winds and ice melt.  The trees growing on either side of the rutted track are stunted and spindly, roots exposed where exhausted earth has crumbled beneath the onslaught of the elements.

With the ridge dropping sharply towards the forest below, the narrow track hugs the mountain looming to the north.  Tenacious scrub pines cling to the stony ground, growing in defiance of strong winds and occasional rockslides.  Stubborn ice fills shadowed clefts in the granite cliffs.

Amidst this desolation of skeletal trees and barren crags, Asketi's Mount dominates the view as it thrusts skyward.  When the wind blows from the north, long plumes of snow fly from the high peak like banners.  A rough trail disappears beyond a switchback upslope from here.

A lone vela'tohr plant grows stoically amidst hard packed ground comprised of small pebbles and stone, tiny remnants from the mountain that looms above it.  It stands, a vigilant sentinel, before a rough trail that leads back to a denser part of the woods.

Small rugged pebbles and sharp rock splinters scatter the area, runoff from the majestic mountain towering above.  Random spots of green -- vegetation battling with the debris it's buried in -- offer muted color amidst the drab shards.

Partially obscured by the rock and crushed stone is the beginning of a steep switchback trail ascending upwards.  High overhead, rocky shelves and occasional overhangs mar the treacherous sides of the looming cliff that rises skyward.

A steep switchback trail from the foothills below ends abruptly on a small plateau.  Dead brush and thorny bushes partially obscure a crumbling path that continues the ascent up the mountainside.  The rocky ground is swept clean of the usual fallen debris by the strong gusts of wind whipping around the cliff edge.  No leaves or twigs crunch underfoot and the lack of scent normally associated with growing vegetation leaves the area feeling curiously sterile.
A crumbling path arises from the foothills below, opening onto a rather large rocky shelf.  Pieces of charred wood sitting within a circle of rocks give testament to previous hikers' campfires.

Scraggly clumps of sirese flowers, partially protected by the rising cliff, grow bravely amidst the accumulation of rubble scattered haphazardly on the hard ground.  Horizontal cracks striate the cliff -- strange handprints left by nature along the coarse stone wall.

Horizontal cracks rive the rock face below, offering scant finger- and toeholds.  The slope rising above this small ledge angles inward for a slightly easier climb.  Crumbling stone and small pebbles trickle down the cliff, careening and echoing noisily as they make their rapid descent.  The temperature begins to drop considerably in the higher altitude.

A thin layer of frost streaks the cliffside, creating a somewhat more treacherous climb on the rocky slope leading downwards.  The wind howls forlornly, lovingly embracing courageous climbers in an icy grasp as it fills the air with eerie laments.

Glimmers of blue-white frost soften the stark lines of the bare stone underfoot.  Nature's hand has carved a vast plateau from the cliffs that overlook the Vela'Tohr Woods.  Directly below, twisted skeletal trees huddle against the granite crags as if seeking protection from the icy winds that whistle down from the passes.  The Woods spread south and west, growing noticeably lusher further away from the mountain.  Far in the distance, the Liirewsag River can be seen winding its way towards Sawstwar Lake.

Narrow shelves and dark fissures riddle the jagged cliffs looming above, offering temporary relief for those who dare the ascent of the towering mountain.  Although the stone rises sheer here and offers no holds, an icy crevice that has opened in the mountain wall invites any would-be climbers to explore.  Strong winds buffet even the most tenacious traveler, threatening to remove all in its path in order to restore the sterile beauty of frozen stone.

Deep gouges formed by wind and ice mar the hard granite of the mountainside.  Rivulets of water that have dribbled down from these small crevices are forever frozen, forming strangely shaped ice sculptures upon the sleek rock.

A massive rockslide hinders easy travel to the north, partially sheltering the area from the bitterly cold winds.  The ground has been cleared of rubble and a few flat boulders are scattered randomly in small groupings.
Frigid winds caress the area with icy fingertips, leaving traces of rimy fingerprints upon the hard rock.  Icy pebbles and small stones litter the frozen ground like shattered pieces of cut glass.

The cold wind screams relentlessly, sending pebbled shards and icy gravel skittering across the frozen ground.  Powerful gusts cause even the strongest of hunters to sway precariously -- a false step would result in a very long fall.

Dead timber, perhaps stacked by previous hunters, is encased in ice and creates a snowy fence.  Strategically placed in relation to the steady wind currents, it provides a formidable barricade on the western edge of the overlook.

Light dustings of snow swirl upwards in odd shapes as tiny eddies sporadically shift and spin the white particles in all directions.  Occasionally, several of these unusual shapes group together and sprint across the frozen ground like deformed rabbits fleeing from an angry beast.

Shattered pieces of granite, finely dusted with tiny flecks of crystal, are strewn along the ground and encased in thin films of ice.  Occasionally, additional pieces careen down the mountainside, skittering to an abrupt halt to lie amidst the rocky debris that has accumulated.

A set of rusted crampons with rotting leather straps is half buried beneath a large ice-covered granite boulder surrounded by oddly shaped clumps of snow.  Packed with particles of granite and frozen twigs, the wind has molded the hard-packed snow into sculptured creatures -- malformed and strangely menacing.

A massive rockslide comprised of broken boulders and ice-covered granite rock ends abruptly against the mountainside.  Looming above is a completely vertical, unscalable cliff, its sides coated with solid ice.  Enclosed on three sides, this small area is sheltered from the omnipresent wind scouring the rest of the mountain.

The cave mouth opens into a broad interior passage that extends out of sight in the darkness to the north.  Slow drops of water fall from the ceiling, striking the floor with a splat that echoes off the rock walls.  A low, breathy chittering accompanies the rustling of leathery wings overhead.  Underfoot, bat guano covers the floor and holds the tracks of some large, bipedal creature.

A shifting flock of large bats blankets the cavern's ceiling.  Occasionally, one of the creatures flexes its wings with a papery rustle.  Other, less readily identifiable sounds tease along the edge of hearing, distorted by the echoing tunnels.

Although lost to sight in the darkness shrouding the ceiling, the scratching of claws on rock and the quiet squeaks of bats can be clearly heard.  Every visible surface of tunnel is streaked with guano that fills the air with an acrid odor.

The rough granite walls of the cavern stretch into darkness.  The faint tang of guano is carried on a draft from some deeper part of the passage.  A crude rope braided from vines tacitly invites exploration of the area above.

Illuminating patches of lichen cling to the walls, giving off a pallid phosphorescent glow.  A soft scratching sound can be heard coming from somewhere nearby, although between the echo of dripping water and the dim surroundings, the source cannot be easily pinpointed.

Signs point to something or someone bent on improving upon nature's design, transforming these subterranean tunnels from an uninhabited warren into a permanent lair.  Crooked timbers reinforce stone walls and some attempt has been made to level the floor.  A ragged hide flap covers an opening in the north wall.

A vile combination of wood smoke, unwashed bodies, rotting garbage and bat guano fills the area with a stomach-churning aroma.  The air itself has an oily feel, leaving a film on the skin and clothing of anyone attempting to pick their way through the piles that obstruct the burrow.

Dim light filters in through the opening.  The granite walls look different here, shifting from shades of black to light greys and blues.  The colors resolve into a faded mural emblazoned across the surface.  Though difficult to encompass with a casual glance, the image shows two groups: one is near the tunnel opening while the other is much farther away.  A two-headed adder separates the groups.

The tunnel narrows here, sloping sharply upwards to the north.  A thick layer of dust and guano coats the passage floor.  Tiny, glowing red eyes peer down from the cavern's ceiling, and a dry rustling fills the air like autumn leaves stirred by wind.

Narrowing significantly, the dark stone enclosing the tunnel seems to press inwards, and a whisper of chill air swirls through the area from above.  The high-pitched chittering of bats fills the tunnel, yet every so often the noise ceases abruptly for several heartbeats before resuming.

The tunnel slopes down to the south, gradually curving out of sight.  Trickles of icy water seep from the rock walls, collecting in thin rivulets that spill down the floor of the steeply slanted passage.  A broken spear shaft lies amidst a scattering of well-gnawed bones.  Faint scratching and rustling noises echo up the tunnel from below.

The geometrically precise tunnel forms a straight, if somewhat steep, passage through dark granite walls.  Scrapes mar the stone and disturb the dust lying thick on the floor, as if something large and heavy has been dragged this way.

The rough texture of the stone walls is further marred by gouges and scorch marks.  Splintered bones and broken axes give mute testimony to a battle here in the past.  Chipped columns support a lintel over an elaborately carved granite door.  Set heart-high on a tall Elf, a glowing crystal embedded in the door bathes the area with an eldritch light.

rooms.desc: Gutted from the mountain by wind and ice, the granite walls of the canyon pinch inward overhead to create scant shelter from the elements.  Powdery grey moss dapples the lower surfaces and the ground is carpeted with wind-blown dirt and leaves.  Chilly gusts whistle through the narrow opening to the south, carrying a faint scent of pine sap.  To the north, the cleft narrows further to form a tunnel leading deeper into the mountain.

Various stone and steel mining equipment lies scattered around the room, bearing the dents and scars of frequent use.  Well-braced crossbeams are spaced out along this section of the tunnel, occasionally creaking in reminder of the tremendous weight they are supporting.  A ragged hide flap covers an opening in the south wall.

The walls in this part of the cave are decorated with crude patterns.  Although primitive in design, the patterns are intricately painted in streaks of ash-black and rusty brown.  Bones have been attached to the walls, but the effect seems more decorative than structural.  Polished to a gleaming white, the bones glitter in the dim light of the banked fire in the center of the cavern.

Signs of intelligent life are apparent in the tunnels.  The ceiling of this roughly worked passage is more even, the cave floor more regular, than any natural fissure.  Long, sweeping femurs and radii reinforce the walls, cemented into place to give the impression of some gargantuan serpent's rib cage viewed from within.  A faint whiff of smoke drifts past, carrying the promise of heat to drive away the mountain's pervasive chill from weary limbs.

Chisel marks score the rock where ceiling and walls have been altered to enlarge the tunnel for easier passage.  Clumps of luminescent lichen illuminate the dark stone, causing flecks of mica to glint erratically like spirits trying to manifest just beneath the surface of the granite.

Spidery cracks run across the walls, and one of the larger fissures sports a small colony of moss.  The dust on the floor shows scuffed trails between a rickety ladder and the tunnel stretching to the northeast.  Anchored by a large boulder, a rope braided from vines leads down into the pit dominating the center of the room.

Compared to the rest of the living quarters, this area is neatly arranged.  A small pile of hay rests against one wall, and a pallet of furs is pushed up against the other.  Between the two sits a flat boulder covered with small bundles of twigs and a piece of flint.

Mounds of hides fill the modest sized cavern, each apparently a separate sleeping space.  The lumpy piles are all empty, with no sign of their residents' current whereabouts.  Crude boxes clutter the area, providing a modicum of storage.

Pile upon pile of poorly tanned hides cover the ground, making it nearly impossible to move about without finding some sort of skin underfoot.  In the center of the cave, an unscraped goatskin is stretched tautly over a makeshift frame.

Slow drops of water leak from the ceiling and strike the floor with soft splats that echo through the tunnel.  Luminescent lichen flourishes in the damp environment, splotching the wall with dimly glowing streaks of blue-green.  Tiny mushrooms poke up from the moss alongside the wall.  The top of a ladder rests against the ledge, secured to the rock with rusted iron spikes.

Sloping downward to the east, a narrow ledge runs along the wall.  Beneath it, a sheer drop-off plunges dizzyingly into darkness, offering no purchase to climb down into the depths.  Some steps have been crudely cut into the side of the cliff face above, rising in a series of narrow switchbacks.

Carved from the solid bedrock, a switchback of granite stairs zigzags up the northern wall while more steps cut into the cliff face lead down to the space below.  The wide ledge offers access to caves to the east and southwest.  Clusters of wickedly curved fangs decorated with black beads hang from the tops of poles leaning against the cavern walls along the ledge.

Swirls and scuffs in the dust on the floor testify to vigorous action by large feet.  Deep gouges inflicted by heavy objects wielded with unimaginable strength scar the walls of what can only be a training ground.  Riddled with broken arrows, a target dummy is wedged into a tight corner.

Wedged into the corners of the room, crude wooden bins hold withered carrots and moldy onions, wrinkled potatoes oozing reddish-brown liquid, and weevil-filled bags of coarsely ground flour.  Animal carcasses are slung from rusty hooks embedded in the ceiling.  The floor is sticky underfoot, though it's hard to tell in the dim light whether spilled food or blood is the cause.  Low benches surround a long granite block that serves as a table.  Some sort of brownish crust speckles the top of the rough stone.

Worn smooth over time, granite stairs lead down into the lower caverns.  A fraying rope ladder hangs against the wall, leading into the darkness overhead.  The corners of the cavern are filled with discarded rubbish.

Damp walls close in tightly, thin rivulets of water trickling and dripping into puddles on the stone floor.  The rough granite has been partially smoothed into angular planes of chiseled rock.  A flickering torch dimly illuminates the tunnel and provides evidence that this area is regularly traveled.

Various crude fletching tools and supplies lie scattered around the area, showing signs of frequent use.  Unstrung longbows are racked on the weapons stands lining the cavern walls.  Wood shavings and bone chips litter the floor around benches drawn up around the firepit in the center of the cavern.

Patches of lichen cling to the walls, giving off a pallid phosphorescent glow.  Deep gouges mar the surface of the rough stone where something made a futile attempt to extend this underground burrow.  Pile upon pile of ratty goatskins and straw cover the ground, making it nearly impossible to move about without finding some sort of makeshift bedding underfoot.

Moisture seeps through cracks in the tunnel's roof, filling the air with dampness and the sound of dripping water.  A rope ladder, lashed securely to a large outcropping, leads down into the lower tunnels.  Though frayed, it appears sturdy enough to allow more climbers to pass along its length.

Poorly tanned hides have been stretched over tall wooden poles to form a windbreak around a jagged fissure.  Dry flakes of snow swirl into the tunnel with each gust of wind.  Footprints on the dusty stone floor bear mute witness to others who have passed this way.  The passage narrows slightly as it inclines steeply downward, away from the fissure.

Damp walls close in tightly, thin rivulets of water trickling and dripping into puddles on the stone floor.  The rough granite has been partially smoothed into angular planes of chiseled rock.  A flickering torch dimly illuminates the tunnel and provides evidence that this area is regularly traveled.

A single boulder, too large to lift or move, sits in the exact center of the cave.  Scraps of food litter the uneven floor between piles of makeshift straw bedding.  The low rocky ceiling and cramped quarters leave little room to move around.

Mounds of straw are arranged haphazardly around this dank cave, heaped with crudely tanned furs to form warm, if somewhat smelly, beds.  Moldering piles of refuse, tossed aside by now absent inhabitants, collect in the corners.  The visible portions of the stone floor are streaked with ash, leftovers from past fires and attempts at fires.

Rocks and boulders slick with hoarfrost have made their home on a small shelf and partially obscure an icy crevice that leads to the overlook below.  Scant, unidentifiable vegetation -- blighted leaves entombed in a frosty glaze -- huddle against the leeward side of some of the larger boulders.
