rooms.desc: Imposing rock walls rise into the night sky, their suffocating closeness heightening the effects of nightfall.  Spreading tendrils of darkness creep across the bottom of the chasm devouring the last remnants of day.  A forbidding dark fissure, almost lost in the inky blackness, mars the rock face and plunges deep into the cold heart of the mountain.

Blazing torches punctuate the exterior wall of the chamber, lighting the rows of brightly burnished weapons and polished armor that rest in simple racks against the remaining three walls.  Ranks of stout shields hang from hooks beneath the torch sconces.  Ripples of dry heat emanate from the smoldering coals within a great iron brazier cast in the shape of a roaring dragon's maw.

Lit by lamps in stands placed in the corners, this somewhat square room is lined with trophies of past conquest.  Suits of Dwarven mail and old-styled armor from the other races have been set on stands.  Weapons and banners captured from various houses and cultures adorn the walls.  A large, serrated sword hangs over an arch of black obsidian.  A raised portcullis leads to the gatehouse.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, The Halls of Insanity]
rooms.desc: Half of the room has been caged off, restricting access.  Within the iron cage, several iron-banded barrels line one of the stone walls.  Half of the containers are filled with dragon-pommeled shh'oi'latas, while the other is half filled with bulging, leather belt pouches.  Steel hooks are attached to the ceiling, each holding a single piece of scale armor embellished with the image of a sleeping black dragon.  The only items not under lock are dozens of obsidian amulets that line one of the walls.

This circular grey stone chamber is lit by several torches that glow brightly within their niches.  Rising from the center of the room is an obsidian altar painstakingly carved to resemble a deep black dragon scale.  Small lines of blood, both fresh and dry, run down the slab in various areas.

Several torches that glow brightly within their niches light this circular grey stone chamber.  Rising from the center of the room is a huge slab of obsidian, painstakingly carved to resemble a deep-black scale.  Small lines of blood, both fresh and dry, run down the slab in various areas.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, The Halls of Insanity]
rooms.desc: The mingling odors of smoke and dried blood immediately assault the nose.  The poorly lit room is punctuated with dozens of small drab stone desks.  Each desk is surrounded on three sides by thick, granite slabs.  Most of the desks have large, misshapen patterns of dried blood that mingle with a black, powdery substance.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, The Halls of Insanity]
rooms.desc: Thin wisps of smoke rise from several braziers, giving the room a musty odor.  Thick wooden stilts support a mikkhalbamar loft, dividing the room into two separate levels.  A deep layer of sand covers both floors which the juggernauts use as sandpits.  Painted throughout the room are images of Peri'el lulling the World Dragon in an endless slumber, the last thing the juggernauts see when they sleep at night and their first sight upon waking.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, The Halls of Insanity]
rooms.desc: The smell of death and blood permeates the air.  The remains of two Dwarves lie against the back wall, one still in the chains holding him into a standing position.  Fresh blood is splattered against the back wall, and the other three have their share of older, dried stains.  Deep gashes have been cut into the stone walls giving testament to the strength of both the juggernauts and the shh'oiatas they wield.  Painted on the ceiling is a massive black dragon.

Sibilating torches spread an eerie glow across the soot-stained, stone walls of this long practice room.  Murals, depicting an army of zealots descending upon a band of Ru'atin Peri'el, stretch opposite an expansive tapestry depicting Dzree.  The dark stains that speckle the stone floor offer testament to the zealots' use of live steel for their practice sessions.

The dark masonry of the exterior wall abruptly gives way to the jagged, living rock into which the fortress has been built.  Training mannequins, rendered in various shapes and sizes, populate this room.  Between the scarred figures, sets of painted, concentric circles on the floor guide novice zealots while practicing their footwork and forms.  Upon the walls, dozens of parchment drawings illustrate the precise technique of different combat maneuvers.

Scattered, sputtering oil lamps cast barely enough light to navigate the space.  Rows of raised, masonry sandpits stretch the length of the room.  Those nearest the cliff face are small and lined with white sand suited to young, supple scales.  As the sandpits graduate to an adult size, they are lined with a mixture of coarse sand and crushed rock designed to harden their occupants, body and soul.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, Shrine of the Fang]
rooms.desc: The center of the chamber is dominated by a wickedly curved dragon fang carved from a single piece of deadly sharp obsidian.  Standing over a pace tall, the fang erupts from the floor within a circle of flickering, scarlet candles.  The accumulated wax surrounding the cuspidate stone creates the illusion of living flesh.

Half of the room has been caged off, restricting access.  Within the iron cage, several iron-banded barrels line one of the stone walls.  Half of the containers are filled with dragon-pommeled shh'oiatas, while the other is half filled with bulging, leather belt pouches.  Steel hooks are attached to the ceiling, each holding a single piece of scale armor embellished with the image of a sleeping black dragon.  The only items not under lock are dozens of obsidian amulets, which line one of the walls.

Dark and cavernous, the hall is clearly intended to accommodate all the residents of the fortress.  The floor is covered with a mosaic of multicolored tiles depicting the World Dragon menacing the orb of Elanthia.  Several benches sit to one side beside a raised platform.  Behind it, a large mural fills the entire wall and S'Kra Mur clan banners hang from the ceiling.

Orderly rows of tables and chairs fill this room.  On one wall, near the exit to the Great Hall, a list of daily duties and patrol routes has been posted.  A lectern stands in a corner next to a mounted slate board, which has been wiped clean.

A large hearth has been carved into the rock of the cliff face creating a deep, wide cooking space.  Hanging from a thick, iron lug pole, a large pot contains a bubbling, noxious concoction.  Centered in the room, a large table is heaped with vegetables and meats in various states of freshness.  Pots and pans sit in stacks underneath.

More a natural cavern than a constructed room, the storeroom contains rows of shelves holding grains and dried vegetables.  Barrels of ale and wine and crates filled with dried meats are stacked next to a large stone cistern.  The sound of slowly flowing water fills the room.

The parapet ends close to the steep ravine wall, heightening the defenses of the fortress.  Jagged rock protects the southern flank of the stronghold and the crenellations afford an unobstructed view to the massive corral in the distance.

The balcony stretches the entire front length of the fortress.  Wide crenellations give excellent vantage points to all approaches.  Several large pots, containing viscous oil and tar, sit nearby and are ready to be dropped on would-be invaders threatening the front gates.

The northern end of the parapet juts out toward the nearby forest, which has been clear cut some distance from the fortress' foundations.  The thick canopy of green leaves sways with the air currents flowing from the crashing waterfall not far away.

Large and unadorned by furniture, the hall serves as a rallying point for this section of the fortress.  The darkness here is broken only by the occasional flickering lamp suspended from claw-shaped hooks.  A set of double doors open out to the parapet and a narrow corridor leads southeast.

Restless flames from several torches illuminate the walls and send fitful shadows across the room.  Two walls are lined with tall racks that accommodate a large assortment of well-kept bows.  A third wall is studded with small wooden pegs from which hang dozens of quivers full of arrows.

Benches and tables are scattered throughout the area, and the floor is littered with wood shavings and bits of feathers.  Jars of oils and polish are strewn across the tables.  Reed baskets filled with assorted flights and bowstrings sit on shelves that line one of the walls.  On another, quivers, stocked with sticks of various types of woods hang on pegs.

Torches on an external wall supply light for this training room.  Woven reed wrestling mats cover the stone floor.  Against one of the walls are mounted wooden boards marked with what appears to be the outlines of Dwarves.  The figures are heavily scarred in the vital areas.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, Shrine of the Talon]
rooms.desc: A large, cast iron brazier lights the center of the large chamber.  The sanguine glow of the flames caresses a brutally sharp, black-lacquered talon of mikkhalbamar that rises about Dwarf height from a sunken pedestal in the center of an external wall.  A shallow trench in the stone floor surrounds the base and terminates in the wall to either side of the sculpture.  A large, eye-shaped skylight peers up toward the World Dragon Temple high above.

At first glance, the room seems to be full of oddly shaped mounds, but the sparse torchlight reveals them to be raised sandpits.  Surrounding a dimly lit brazier in the center of the room, smaller sandpits for the young are kept closest to the warmth.  Larger ones are scattered in a protective circle around them.

Dimly lit by a lone torch, the corridor looks like something out of a Gnomish nightmare.  Rocky protuberances shaped like teeth line the sides of the floor and ceiling.  All surfaces are painted to enhance the illusion of being inside a dragon's maw.

Plain racks line the thick, stone walls each filled with various types of swords and shields, some of which appear unused.  Bottles of various innocuous-smelling potions with no labels fill the stone shelves that seem to emerge from the wall.  A small, scorched framed window looks out on the forest below.

Along one wall are rows upon rows of bookcases that are filled with manuscripts on the history of the Dragon Priests and magic.  Nearby is a large desk filled with various ingredients and alchemy tools, above this are shelves filled with books on making potions.  Sketches adorn the wall and depict the various manipulations of nature that dwell in the forest below and serve the priests.

Rows of sandpits and woven mats hug the dark stone walls of the dimly lit room.  A small window near the door is the only light source, save for a crooked torch mounted nearby.  Sparsely decorated, there are only a few chests here for the storage of clothing.

rooms.t: [The Black Spire, Shrine of the Flame]
rooms.desc: The area is dominated by a large eye-shaped skylight that seems to be mounted atop a pillar of pure fire that fills the room with an intense heat.  A large metal shutter opens and closes with the billows of smoke, making the skylight seem as though it is alive and blinking while watching the occupants in the room below.  Words are carved into the walls around the room.

The far wall is dominated by a bookcase of tomes written by the Crones to detail the history of this sect of the Dragon Priests.  In the center of the room is a distorted mikkhalbamar desk with sheets of strange skin-like parchment and writing implements, whilst the focal point of the desk is a large book.  The floor is carved with images of the World Dragon.  A mouth-shaped window looks out on the forest.

The air, thick with smoke from dim oil lamps, is filled with the acrid odor of incense.  Stone steps rise into the gloom and descend to an oak door.  A dark shaft stretches upwards into shadow at the center of the tower.
The landing gives a good view of the stone steps that continue to wind up and down around the tower's central core.  Iron manacles attached to pins in the stone walls hang unused in the still air.

Oddly shaped to fit along the curved tower walls, chairs surround a modest table in the center of the room.  Pitted and marked by the points of countless knives, it is bare except for an elegantly detailed deobar box.  Near the table, an open chest contains short swords, serrated daggers, sharp pointed knives and bucklers of varying styles.

Two desks covered with parchments sit against the outer, curved wall of the room.  Ragged carpets soften the hard stone of the floor.  In the corner, a modified distillation apparatus, the glass blown in the shape of a coiled dragon, sits on top of a small, unlit stove.

The central core of the tower descends with a stone stair spiraling down its length.  A very steep stairway cuts directly across the precipitous drop to an opening in the lower floor's ceiling.  The risers show the marks and scratches of something being dragged up and down.

The dormitory consists of triple rows of three-high bunk beds placed to take advantage of all available floor space.  Each bunk is filled with coarse black sand.  An iron stove keeps the room at a high temperature.

Spanning the massive gap over a curving canyon that follows the lower contours of the Himineldar Shel, the bridge sways hazardously in the swirling breeze sweeping upward from the raging river below.  Massive icicles dangle from every surface of the rickety structure, occasionally snapping loose to tumble from sight.  The landscape beyond is shrouded by a thick opaque mist, giving the air a nearly tangible presence.

The eastern end of the Ratha warehouses stands like a wall at the side of the Port Walk.  Some very shady-looking characters pass by, maybe an uneasy blend of pirate and trader, legal when they have to be, otherwise when opportunity offers.

The Port Walk continues along at the rear of the warehouses.  In all sizes, all materials, and all stages of repair, they are the center of the hive of activity in the harbor.  In and out of their portals pass the merchants that channel the life-blood of commerce into the veins that branch and spread until the riches of Elanthia are delivered to the customer's door.

Some very bored but talented sailor must have waited here a long time.  One of the pilings has been carved into a very creditable likeness of a well-endowed mermaid, from flowing hair to fishy tail.  She's an alluring sight, despite the occasional seagull who uses her head to sit on.

Vendors of meat pies, tarts, and flavored ices stroll the crowded walk, calling out their wares in a sing-song rhythm that sticks in the memory.  Their cries blend with the splash of oars and the voice of the ocean wind to make a melody that identifies Ratha as clearly as a map or the high rock that juts from the harbor to the west.

The Port Walk curves inward, avoiding a galley-sized rock that rises from the water just over the side of the walkway railing.  A squadron of harbor seagulls has made the rock their home.  They perch on it, observing the goings-on around them with the keenest interest.  Now and then, one flies off on an avian errand, or lands with some scaly treasure stolen from a fishing boat.

At this eastern end of the port drydock, heaps of naval stores stand stacked behind a sturdy fence.  Timber for spars, decking, or planking, barrels of tar and oakum, sailcloth wrapped in oiled sheets, kegs of nails -- the hundred-and-one items that keep a ship afloat are arranged in orderly rows ready for use.

In the shelter of Ratha's drydock, water-worn or storm-shattered vessels find the craftsmen and material they need to make them seaworthy again.  High cranes stand at both sides of the drydock, ready to step a new mast, or lift a heavy spar into place.

The west end of Ratha's drydock commands the area, reaching out into the harbor with the machines to overhaul even the largest vessels.  At this end, a portly schooner is supported by beams while its bottom is being scraped of barnacles and worm-eaten planking is replaced.  On board, someone, probably its captain, is arguing with a carpenter.  Although their voices cannot be heard over the harbor din, their gesticulations make the disagreement clear.

The walk broadens into a wide platform lined with strong, iron mooring posts at wide intervals.  A vessel fills every slip, and others wait in the harbor, anchored until it's their turn to dock.  Somewhere a harbormaster must be issuing orders, because gangs of stevedores roll rumbling barrels along or shoulder sacks to and from the ships moored to the wharf.

The Port Walk skirts a small building jutting onto the path.  The traveler who moves to the water side of the walk to avoid it has a good view of the entire harbor, crowded with vessels small and large -- fishing smacks, the schooners of traders, galleys from far off -- an ever-changing, ever-moving testament of the wealth and power of Ratha.

The walk passes behind a small wooden building, either a vendor's booth or a storage shed for a company with very little inventory.  The blank wall fronting the water offers no further clues of its purpose.  On the harbor side, the hulk of a sunken fishing boat can be made out through the murky water.

An alley heads north from the walk, toward the streets where one needn't watch where one steps.  Here, the holes in the plank walk, the raised boards, and the slippery but unidentifiable patches along the way all demand attention.

The walk comes to an abrupt end in an angle between the water and the blank wall of a warehouse.  Rags and trash slowly molder against the board wall, which itself seems in little better repair.  Fruit rinds and a dead fish or two float in the water below.

Though seamy, dirty, and noisy, the Port Walk hums with life.  People from all the provinces, from all the races, stride past, each with his own goal and purpose.  They charge the air with a kind of energy and put on a dazzling show of the colors, the customs, the food, the dress, and the languages of every city and island under the triple moons.
Wide and well-built, this dock was made to accommodate the heavy caravans that pass over it daily.  Workers load and unload ships in an almost endless flurry of activity.

Yells and shouts fill the surroundings as dock workers communicate in the only way that is fitting for this noisy, hectic environment.  A couple young boys watch the work anxiously, planning their future and their torment.
Supporting the largest vessels from far-away lands, the dock has greeted both smuggler and prince, murderer and king.  It continues to perform its duty flawlessly though, without prejudice or regret.
The strong odor of seawater drowns out any other smells at this end of the street.  The road slopes down to the south, passing between two warehouses of moderate size before joining the Port Walk.
The backs of numerous buildings create shadows of sufficient blackness to hide any number of activities.  Muted scraping and scratching from all directions encourages wanderers to quicken their pace.
The close, tall buildings paint the street in deep shadow, barely affected by a single lit streetlamp.  A few dark figures scurry away sensing a stranger's approach.

w.5060: ;e unless DRSkill.getmodrank('Athletics') >= 615 then nil else 0.2 end

rooms.desc: The darkened street provides a haven for those that are more comfortable among the shadows.  Shops closed for the night leave the street in even darker shadows.  A tiny movement to the west proves to be a huge Gor'Tog man striding home through the dense blackness.

Poorly kept houses line the street, shuttered and closed for the night.  An apparently homeless Gor'Tog is curled up under a broken-down wagon, asleep.  No lamps brighten the area, leaving everything in shadows.
A mostly-intact fence completely severs the north and south sides of this area.  The gate has long since been torn down, and the well-traveled road passes directly through.

Buildings that were constructed too close together force the road into a narrow pathway.  Only the light of the stars and moons allow one to avoid tripping over the rubble and trash strewn haphazardly about the area.
A statue stands in the center of the street, dark with shadows.  Dim light falls on the street from the windows of several ramshackle houses.  An old Gor'Tog shuffles slowly across the street.
Old houses and buildings line the streets, though the quality seems to rise to the north.  A long line of cut-off fence posts stretches east to west.

Run-down houses are built against the tall cliff behind them, but still manage to look of superior quality to the houses south from here.  The street is empty of people, though signs of daytime activity indicate they'll be back with the sun.

The decent houses and fairly well lit street indicate that this is a step above the slums.  A few couples and lone Gor'Togs are out and about, though the couples don't seem too interested in anything but each other.

The street curves around a large flower-lined grassy area.  The locals stay mostly inside at night, though, leaving the lawn unused until morning.  Open windows in several buildings allow light to shine on the street, while sounds of laughter float in the air.
Dark shadows on the street reveal only two people, who both appear to be hurrying to their destinations.  Cracks of light around a shuttered window do nothing to ward off the darkness.

Stores of various purpose line the street, most closed for the night.  An abandoned streetcart leans against an available wall.  There are quite a few people on the street, huddled in the glow provided by the pawnshop's storefront lanterns, while others conspicuously avoid the light.

Stepping through an elaborately carved archway, one is transported from the filth and decay of the city streets to a simple but elegant square.  Tall iron lanterns illuminate the brick walkways and low walls.  Giant pots of greenery and flowers dot the square and cast long shadows on the meticulous brickwork.  The quiet of evening lends the square a serenity rarely found in the hectic bustle of the day.

The homeless shuffle toward the soup kitchen and the warmth of the doorways along the street.  Children play joyously here in the daytime, but come nightfall the area is once again filled with the harsh reality of poverty.

Hiding in the shadows, under awnings and in darkened doorways, the wretched and aimless seek shelter from the elements.  Broken and strewn about, the ancient trappings of a bustling market district paint a ghostly reminder of more prosperous times in Ratha's history.

Shadowy beings disappear into the recesses of a large abandoned building.  A favorite hideaway for thieves, this area is no place for the full of pockets to linger.  Echoing footsteps assail passersby from all directions, making safety no better than a vaguely familiar philosophy.

The artful brickwork of Redthorne Square is carried through in the design of this avenue.  Neither elegant nor stately, the street is clean and well maintained as part of an agreement made between area shopkeepers and the Redthorne family.

Feet and legs are a common sight, seen poking out of doorways, under bushes or benches, as the fallen drunk sleep off their revelry.  From somewhere in the vicinity, a heart wrenching wail can be heard, likely coming from a newly abandoned wife as her husband heads out to sea.

Shards of glass litter the street and boardwalk outside the Bosun's Whistle Tavern.  The favorite gathering spot for Ratha's rough dockworkers, this tavern on the edge of Tog town is center stage for the tawdry wenches who entertain the clientele as well as the heated arguments and fights that usually spill out into the street.

Clinking glasses, raunchy music and catcalls invade the otherwise peaceful night, the nightly activities at the local tavern in full swing.  The more sedate of the street's inhabitants stay inside with shutters closed to keep out the sound of revelry.
Darkness prevails as the shadows reach out from behind a broken fence.  Some unseen being lurks just ahead, waiting to prey on an innocent passerby, hence the name of this alley.

Long shadows wrap the facade of an abandoned market, and a quiet tenseness pervades the area.  The otherwise peaceful night is often disturbed by a muffled cry or a rift of drunken laughter, as those partaking in the quarter's night life wander towards home.

A decrepit fence surrounds the bare earth inside this vacant plot, its weathered slats often rotten or missing entirely.  Deeply worn into the otherwise featureless earth, a wide rut leads westward to disappear between two buildings on the other side of the lot.

The bumpy street stretches north and west, while to the east the cobblestones have been upturned by the roots of a pair of bloodwood trees, leaving only dirt marred by the occasional cracked stone.  Rotten wooden shutters hang precariously from the panes of ramshackle houses lining the road, and the faint sound of moving water can be heard to the west.

The cobbled street ends abruptly at a hole left by the fall of a massive ironwood.  The thick trunk has been chopped off, leaving only an upturned root ball extending from the recess.  Thick mud has filled the hole and now fosters dense growths of marsh plants.

Softly, a lone streetlamp lends a feeling of security to the occasional passerby, its glow illuminating the loosely cobbled street.  A single guard dozes lightly outside the larger of several warehouses, weapon at the ready, though easily circumventable by the stealthiest of prowlers.

Wooden crates are stacked several high along the rutted road.  Ratha's busy port is the lifeblood of this community, keeping the townsfolk busy all throughout the day and night.  The warehouse district to the north is full of goods and perishables, either making their way to Ratha, or being exported to other islands in the area.
Salt air and the smell of fish and decaying sealife fill your nostrils.  A large fenced lot is full of fishing nets, floats and other paraphernalia useful in the pursuit of a tasty morsel.

Traffic, both wheeled and on foot, wends its way up from the busy docklands and down from the commercial heart of the town.  Here and there, brightly colored awnings have been strung across the road to provide the occasional bit of shade.  Several children, S'Kra and Human, Elf and Gor'Tog, play a hearty game of ball with no discernable rules, discernable to the passing adult at least.
This dock is as sturdy and well-made as the others in the city, but has been painted a garish peacock blue, oddly out of place against the stark canvas and weathered wood of the rest of the area.

Reddish dust lies in a thin layer over the awnings which shade the walkway along the side of the street.  The dust dulls the colorful canvas, giving the scene an odd, monochromatic quality in the bright sunlight.  Nearby, a young S'Kra Mur woman saunters past carrying a terracotta waterjar balanced atop her head.  From the simple patterns of her face-paint, she seems to be a minor servant rather than the daughter of the house.

Abandoned houses line the broken street, shutters and doors hanging precariously from rusted hinges.  Round stones, stacked in a pyramid formation, sit in the doorway of one of the ruined buildings.  A large wooden barricade spans the width of the street, blocking further passage north.

Imble, the famous anchor merchant, has gone home for the evening, but the ironworks and foundry remain a busy place.  All else in the neighborhood is quiet, as a gentle breeze makes it's way from the ocean beyond the seawall.

Awnings are rolled up and soft lamplight illuminates the storefronts on the brickwork drive.  Echos of the day's activities still ring from the masonry shops and ancient lampposts.  The gentle lull of the ocean is barely audible above the muffled sounds of the sleeping city.

Not lavish by any standards, the patterned brickwork of this byway contrast sharply with the fetid decay of the surrounding neighborhoods.  A regular stream of customers can be seen darting furtively into the small shanty, set back unobtrusively from the road, that is home to the much adored fortune teller Magdha.

Barely passable, the deeply rutted road is one of the most frequented and favorite short cuts.  Carts loaded with goods and their ambitious drivers often race through the narrow lane in hopes of avoiding the giant potholes that threaten their equilibrium.

Mostly abandoned during the evening hours, the narrow lane is disturbingly quiet.  Passersby tread carefully, as there is never any assurance that the ramshackle fence does not hide some less than virtuous creature.
Wedged between buildings, the road seems impossibly narrow here.  Deeply rutted, it is truly a wonder that any wheeled vehicle is able to traverse the precarious passage.

The sky is nearly blocked from view by the closeness of the buildings bordering the road.  A popular fable tells of townfolk running frantically down the lane in order to avoid the buildings closing in and crushing them in their folly.

A network of roads converge from six directions, leaving traffic in a chaotic swirl not seen since the universe was formed.  Carters argue with sedan-chair bearers and small children and animals dart in and out amongst scurrying porters as they struggle to make sense of the maelstrom.  A harried civil official stands atop a small pillar in the center of it all, trying, and failing, to bring some order to the near-mob.
An abandoned store front serves as the residence for many a homeless traveller.  Several ragged looking men huddle around an open fire, exchanging muffled commentary on the plight of their comrades.

Littered and dirty, this alley looks little used.  Getting caught in this alley in the wee hours of the morning is not a pleasant thought, though there seem to be few places for mischievous miscreants to hide.

A wall of refuse brings an end to travel along this alley.  Rats, mice and neighborhood cats frequent the area in search of pungent victuals.  A broken door lies against the remains of a crumbling fence that partially covers a broken sewer grating.

The road rises to the northeast, where the great lifts bring people up and down between the tiers.  One sees richer robes and decorated tail-bands on many folks here, mingled with the poorer classes that inhabit the lowest level.

Terra cotta jars filled with rose-scented oil stand on either side of the entrance to a tiny shop.  A canvas awning is rolled back for the evening to allow the cool night breezes to flow into the dimly-lit interior of the building.

This busy intersection swarms with trade and traffic of all manner and description.  To the north, small shops for the lower classes vie with run-down hovels and the occasional soup kitchen.  The main road splits into three parts as it winds its way down to the docks.  A small park is visible amongst the stark stonework of the city to the south as well.

Colorful streamers decorate every street lamp and overhang as the bazaar comes into view.  The road transforms from common gravel to dark red brick as one nears the market area.  Trees, planted in large ceramic urns, are spaced evenly along the street, each providing a fair amount of shade on even the warmest of days.

A row of tumbledown shacks and low buildings marks one edge of the seedier quarters in this section of town.  The click of dice and low voices echo among the shanties as the occasional furtive figure darts out of one doorway and vanishes into another.
The wide road swings in a gentle curve, avoiding the dark stone bulk of the Merchant's Bank.  Lesser stone buildings rise on either side, like attendants on a noble lord.

This small room is filled with the subdued glimmer of many gems.  Locked cases of heavy crystal line the walls, each containing a staggering array of precious stones and gems of endless variety, cut, color and shape.  A soft white light falls upon a small table covered with black velvet.  It radiates from a curious lamp set in the center of the table.

A strong scent of burning food wafts through a wrought iron gate in a red brick wall.  Behind the wall, a brick courtyard leads to a rather neglected old house -- the mullions of its windows are stained with soot, and the door hangs half-off its hinges, while the plants in the terracotta urns beside the entry have long since withered in the heat.

An elderly S'Kra Mur woman, her features half-hidden by her voluminous black robe, sweeps the street outside a white stucco house.  As she works, she mutters under her breath and clicks her tongue, each syllable a sibilant imprecation against the dust or the ingratitude of her children.  Noticing you watching, she hisses angrily, before returning to her soliloquy to her broom.

Young traders bustle by with self-important expressions as they run errands for their masters.  A Halfling woman occupies her time berating a Gor'Tog laborer as he attempts to right an overturned tumbril before the local street rats can filch the delivery.  Though the cart is covered by a tarpaulin, the air is redolent with the aroma of dried ambergris and other less immediately recognizeable fragrances.

The walls of the cliff abut the road as it runs along the eastern end of the tier.  Birds build nests in the black rock surface, their raucous cries echoing about the area.  The buildings sport weathered grey wood shutters to keep out the wind and storms, while many roofs are designed with a narrow walkway around a cupola where women may stand to watch the sea, hoping for the return of loved ones.

Over the years, sculptors have exercised their talents and their chisels upon the rocky escarpment which shelters the town from the elements, covering the black rock wall with an intricate design of intertwined flowers and vines.  An opening in the wall leads to a cavern which houses a prosperous family of carpet weavers, one of whom evidently practices her trade on a loom outside the shop.

Built against the rocky cliff wall is the local inn, Jack Tarr's Rest, set back from the busy road.  The aroma of baking fish wafts through the air from the kitchens, while local traders relax as they recount tales of their voyages -- daring escapes from local pirates, successful bargains with the craftsmen of Mer'Kresh, the beauties of Aesry Surlaenis'a -- all these and more may be heard during the course of the day.

A cat darts down a narrow alley which runs along the back of the inn, between the building and the cliff face.  As the road meanders southwards toward the sea, the carvings on the cliff face change from flowers and vines to images of merfolk.  A vein of quartz in the rocky surface gives an illusion of cresting waves, enhanced by the clever chisel of the sculptor.

A small shrine stands in a shallow niche in the cliff wall.  The concave floor of the niche acts as a basin, currently empty, but streaked with rust-colored stains and bits of feathers.  Strands of shark's teeth dangle from an iron pole, clattering against each other in the wind.  Passersby hurry past, averting their faces from anyone gathered here.  At the back of the niche, a dark hole offers a faint glimpse of scattered bones, silent offerings to propitiate the sea.

The road bends to the southeast as it wends its way toward the docks.  A knot of pedestrians cluster around a pushcart laden with fresh fruit and juice for thirsty travelers.  Burly Gor'Tog porters jostle their way through the crowd, carrying heavy boxes and chests slung over their backs as they make their way from the harbor to the nearby inn.

Small homes line the street as it wends its way along the base of the eastern cliffs.  The black basalt escarpment towers high above, sheltering the town from the ravages of wind and sea.  Faint white lines of dried salt mar the solid black rock walls of the cliff, a grim reminder that their shelter is tenuous, at best.

Young children play beside a cozy whitewashed cottage nestled between two larger homes.  The smell of cooking wafts through the air from an opened window.  Lacy white curtains and window boxes filled with bright red geraniums complete the picturesque scene.

The road widens to the south to support the wagons and carts from the chandler's shop.  A warehouse beside the shop sees heavy traffic as burly Gor'Tog stevedores assemble orders placed by the quartermasters of ships in the harbor.  Each customer is sure that their order is most important, and their vociferous demands reflect that belief.

Quartermasters carrying bills of lading make their way to a dilapidated wooden shop set back from the road.  Though the shop itself is small, Captain Namazzi's Chandlery is well known for its extensive variety of preserved meats and other food for long voyages, as well as barrels, ropes and other supplies needed by any working ship that wishes to make ready for a voyage.

The evil smells emanating from a series of long brown huts made out of wattled stucco proclaim their allegiance to the leather trade.  A dozen Humans in grimy linen smear brown ointment on skins stretched tautly over wooden frames.  Others tend fires, fanning flames and feeding them chips of wood.  Dogs roam about the area, barking excitedly and occasionally yelping as a worker casually kicks one out of the way.

Groups of urchins clothed in filthy rags scramble about the badly pitted street, screaming with delight as they pelt passersby with small, hard stones.  Occassionally a rock connects with a target, drawing blood and howls of anger.  But when a guard shows up the children melt away, running swiftly through the alleyways they know better than anyone else.

A high lectern, reachable by a narrow set of steep steps, stands squeezed between two long-disused buildings to the north.  Several men take turns shouting out destinations, cargoes, quantities and prices to the jostling crowd, as messenger runners constantly whisper information in their ears.  Passing merchants stop, listen intently for a while, then continue swiftly on their way.

A low, sprawling building made of grey sandstone and blue mortar dominates the square.  A pair of roaring griffons carved in granite flank its arching entranceway.  Thrusting forward from its faded, white tiled roof is a banner portraying the movement of coins from hand to open hand, on a field of silver: the Bank of the Port.  Despite the splendor the bank is boarded up, a victim of poor times and stiff competition.

A sharp breeze whips a stinging fan of icy spray through the air over this short promontory that rises above the sea.  The smell of rotting vegetation clings close and heavy.  A few mold-covered, surf-worn benches lay alongside the path in shadows.

rooms.desc: The bustling dock areas provide a constant stream of traffic along the quays and up into the town proper along the main road.  Local militia, resplendent in plumed helms, their scales buffed and tinted with the town livery, keep a wary eye on foreign traveler and resident citizen alike.

The shattered remains of a fluted alabaster fountain squat immobile and unmourned in the middle of this busy square.  Well-to-do merchants dressed in fur and silk step lively around beggars missing assorted limbs.  Dingy, ramshackle houses line both sides of the road, furnishing cheap and seedy quarters for the unsqueamish.

The main road, broad and bumpy with ruts from thousands of wagon wheels, proceeds east and west between several large temporary storage areas.  Boxes, bales, barrels, chests and trunks of every kind are organized by lot and assigned their piece of ground.  Private guards stand watch, gazing suspiciously at every passerby.

The harbor at this end of the walk is crowded with small craft -- rowboats mostly -- in which the fishermen of the city bring their catch to shore.  The pungent smell of the fish lingers long after they've been unloaded, and the discarded bait and offal in the water is much enjoyed by the gulls.

Musclebound cargomen haul freight to and from the ships at this pier, using rusty chains suspended from twin poles of oak, stitched with sword moss.  They work under the watchful and none-too-friendly eyes of port overseers, who are quick to administer a warning lash when the cargo lists to one side.  Gangplanks creak, and the dock itself shudders beneath the onslaught of never-ceasing breakers.

Frowning warehouses, several stories high with projecting cranes, front the winding road.  Covered with pale, peeling blue paint and caked white in places with encrusted salt, these shuttered buildings are barred and triple-locked against poachers.  Each lock bears the seal of the municipal guard, in some cases vigorously defaced with a knife by some previously frustrated burglar.

A freshly scrubbed edifice of white brick lies to the north.  Above its stately teakwood gate is a sapphire blue shield bearing crossed yellow keys, the symbol of the Traders' Guild.  Many citizens of substance regularly enter and leave its premises, glancing around proudly at the well-trimmed hedge of peregan trees.  A stone statue poses majestically before the guildhall's entrance, gazing out over the open ocean.

To the south looms a wooden building, painted a leering red.  Its gaudy, golden window shutters are closed, but the door has been jammed open.  Raucous screams of rage and pain and laughter, shouts for drink, and scraps of music flow unceasingly from inside the doss-house.  Guards glance away self-consciously as they pass by, and merchants perceptibly quicken their pace on the road northeast or west.

To both sides of the path, tall, narrow houses with dark slits for windows lean precariously against one another, like old people gathering strength from close company in a blustering wind.  Their red-shingled roofs have rotted to brown, and their windows are boarded shut.  From somewhere to the southwest a ragged scar of jumbled music and laughter rises incoherently, then falls away to nothing.

Sturdy longshoremen use hooked poles of iron and thick gorse ropes to lever ship cargoes onto and across this dock.  The constant wash of brine scrubs the pier and posts like a rough razor.  Tax assessment officers regularly appear, checking off arrivals and departures, blandly ignoring the stares and poorly hidden curses of passengers and crew alike.

The road skirts its winding way between the roaring turquoise-colored surf to the south, and the weatherbeaten cliffs and scrag-oaks to the north.  A few piles of wooden debris would pass unnoticed if not for the tiny vegetable gardens outlined with small, irregular stones that adjoin each.

The Port Walk's fractured cobblestone paving gives way to a broad sand path strewn with broken shells, strands of seaweed, and driftwood drying in the breeze.  A small trail heads north toward the cliffs that hem the narrow band between true earth and salt sea.  The ocean's voice, ranging from soft whisper to beast's roar, sounds across the beach.

Shrill cries from ospreys nesting in the cliffs mix with the slap of the surf on the beach.  The huge nests, woven from driftwood, seaweed and assorted debris, are clearly visible against the light color of the cliff's face.  Every so often, one of the great birds launches itself into the breeze to soar over the waves.  Oceanward, pinnacles of rock carved by the sea's touch rise from the water.

Sweeping between the ocean and cliffs, the serpentine curves of the beach reach toward a towering cliff in the distance.  Wind-sculpted dunes parallel the beach, but the tide prevents them from encroaching past the highwater level.  Burrows in the dunes and nests wedged in the tough grass provide homes for a variety of creatures.

Small groups of sandpipers play tag with the waves as they dash along the beach.  The little birds occasionally pause in their game to investigate bits of seaweed or gobble up sand lice.  The waves, forced to travel around an offshore jumble of rocks, hit the beach at an angle.

Delicate red and yellow sandflowers nestle among clumps of hardy dune grass.  Several stone slabs have been arranged, either by nature or landsmen, to form a table and seating.  Trash near one of the stone seats suggests that someone has dined here recently.  The beach narrows as it curves north toward the cliffs.

The beach deadends at the cliff's face -- not even a thin ribbon of sand separates the water from the massive rock slabs that tumble against each other and into the ocean.  Spume washes the formations of stacked rocks as each wave strikes on their endless roll landward.

A small shrine in the shape of a cobra, its hood flared wide, sits to one side.  Bits of feathers and fragments of skin show the remains of small animals sacrificed for one reason or another -- to gain favor perhaps, or to give thanks for some minor success in life.

Cheap perfume and over-loud laughter wafts from behind deep-shaded windows hung with heavy curtains that line the upper story of a whitewashed stone building.  An almost exclusively male patronage seems intent on avoiding notice as they hurry into and out of the interior.

The traffic swirls and forms small tangled knots as the road splits, one path leading to the solid facade of the Merchant's Bank, while the other roads lead down to the docks and up into the center of town and the higher tiers.  A brace of heavily armed guards watches over the roadway leading to the bank, keeping a wary eye out for trouble.  The throng of pedestrians mingles with the occasional dray or laden caravan in an ever-changing kaleidoscope of colors and textures.

Guttering lanterns set high on poles shed a watery glow along the steep road leading to the Bank of Ratha.  In a land where business never sleeps, the bank keeps late hours for the convenience of all.  The wise traveler keeps well away from the deeper shadows along the wayside though, for legitimate business is not all that never sleeps.

The wide road leading from the docks to the lift makes a sharp bend as it passes a ruined pile of stones that was once a building.  Apparently ravaged by fire or some other disaster, the occupants have deserted the shell.  The remaining stones are cracked and blackened, the good ones having been removed by the local denizens to build their own houses.

Dim candles flicker behind ill-fitting shutters on the few windows to be found on the squatter's shacks and run-down houses along the road.  The occasional burst of coarse, sibilant laughter, or the sleepy whine of a child rises into the night air as other travelers, cloaked or hooded against the sea damp, hasten past on their own errands.

The heavy stone slabs used to pave the road as it winds its way along the curving shoulder of a small rise have been painted in patterns of color meant to resemble the scales of a giant serpent.  The pavement, though faded and dusty, still shows a glimmer of brightness here and there.  This part of town once knew a better life it seems.

From the east, the stink of death floats on the cool damp air.  The faint strains of a dirge echo among the stone walls of the nearby buildings.  Death comes to all, high and low, rich and poor, and all will end the same.

This pleasant square marks the center of social life for the down and out of Ratha.  Despite the noise and confusion and occasional screams from the great intersection to the south, a certain calmness pervades this spot.  A tiny park forms a rare green space in this cramped city of stone.

As you step into the room, your feet sink into plush carpets.  The walls are set with numerous locked display cases.  A well-dressed guard gives you a polite visual once over and steps aside so you may enter.  Gems of every sort and size, from slivers of plain looking crystal to a massive heart-shaped gem the size of a Gor'Tog's fist are displayed.  Grisgonda herself sits at a plain black marble desk with a bright lamp upon it inspecting gems that have been brought in for sale by other adventurers.

This short, narrow alleyway is used by the merchants coming to the bazaar from the shipyards.  Just a step or two from the larger avenue, wheeled carts with heavy loads can avoid the long arduous trek up Mission street.  Children often gather at the intersection to wait for stray goodies to fall off the wagons.

The crowds are thick here, near the lift which leads higher into the city.  Street vendors ply their wares while jugglers and musicians collide with people in a hurry in the eternal dance of life that is a crowded city.  To one side a crippled beggar shakes a leather cup, seeking alms with a certain air of quiet dignity.

Muffled sounds erupt into clamoring furor as the alley reaches the level of the bazaar's lower entrance.  The crowds that gather here are mostly visitors from other ports, and merchants who do business on this tier.  Among the throngs lurk the young pickpockets eagerly learning their craft.

Sandy and loose, ancient cobbles amble past a white mud and stone house that sits back a few paces from the road.  Bleached by the sun and in stark contrast with other buildings in the vicinity, the old house and manicured gardens surrounding it appear orderly and well cared for.

Steep cliffs rise high above, directing ones gaze toward the heavens.  Cliffside dwellings with dramatic ocean views can be seen from this vantage point.  Scanning the meager surroundings at this elevation, one can only imagine what it would be like to live the blessed lifestyle of Ratha's privileged class.  A rickety fence marks the northern boundary of this section of town.

Wretched poverty, brazen and offensive, assaults visitors to this small plateau.  Wanderers head past toward the bazaar, as the homeless find rest under any number of trees.  The slums of the city loom larger than life, just a few hundred yards below.

As the incline steepens further, solid granite cliffs loom larger than life just beyond the northern fenceline.  Removed from the rotting stench of the streets below, the breezes here are fresh and futures seem bright.  A stone wall provides a nice place to rest and enjoy the magnificent view.

Old women with bundles and buckets labor up the hill toward the dwellings that lie below the cliff face.  Row upon row, these makeshift shelters taunt the ocean into challenging their worthiness.  The sweeping vistas here simply take the breath away, and many find the cares of the day diminished by the awesome power and beauty of the ocean.

Along the oceanside avenue, the gentle incline gives way to a more dramatic rise in elevation.  From this part of Upper Mission street one has a commanding view of the towering cliffs to the north.  An interesting little shop wraps itself around the trunk of an enormous ironwood tree, just this side of a large open field.

Long lines of indigent and hungry await a warming morsel outside Nadamian's Mission.  A thin gruel the usual fare, the delicious smells and promise of a meal are half the experience for many of them.  Of course, along with the meal comes a helping of the Nadamian family's tenets and teachings.

A low wall and a space between buildings here, offer the onlooker a view of the rugged shore and the crystal blue ocean beyond.  A few diligent souls comb the rocks for edible gifts from the mother sea.  Delicious smells coming from somewhere nearby are a welcome relief to the rotting stench to the south.

The sharp stench of putrefaction and raw sewage assails the nostrils, sending all but the comatose into fits of retching.  Making its way across the road, a deep trench lays claim to the awful smell.  Rats and flies abound while children frolic and naked babies toddle at their mother's sides.

The once crowded, chaotic bazaar now stands silent, both merchant and shopper resting with the sun.  The colorful pennants marking the marketplace are now nothing more than shades of black, waiting to regain their luster in a new day.

The scents of the day mingle with the silence of night as the smells of the bazaar linger long after the merchants have turned in.  Shards of lamp light sporadically pierce the confines of the marketplace, causing both illumination and shadow.

The festive tents are darkened, awaiting the chaos of a new day.  Workers saunter through the grounds, cleaning and raking the gravel walkways as they go.

Scintillating aromas waft through the air.  Meats roasting, spicy concoctions brewing in some merchants stall, the scent of freshly cured tobacco and a thousand other olfactory offerings beckon even the weariest of shoppers to turn around and have another look.

The air is abuzz with the sounds of the bazaar.  Merchants of every description scream out the virtues of their wares while citizens try to dodge the more aggressive salesmen.  Scarlet-colored banners on the north side of the road point the way deeper into the bazaar.

The main part of the temple is dedicated to the goddess herself.  Entering through the arch, the first thing your eyes rest upon is the wall directly opposite the entrance.  An awe-inspiring mural of Hodierna, made out of thousands of tiny colored tiles, covers the entire length of the sanctuary.  Each tile is carefully placed, detailing the goddess' features, giving her an almost life-like appearance.  The altar is made of a pure white marble and polished to a lustrous shine.
The sounds of the bazaar, though faint, can be heard even this far away.  Citizens from all walks of life make their way to and from the merchant center of the city.
Guardsmen patrol this area heavily since many of the city's wealthy frequent the shops along this road.  Nearby stone benches provide a place for weary shoppers to take a moment's rest.

Children run up and down the sidewalks of this street, following parents that slowly make their way to the bazaar.  Whitewashed buildings line the cobblestone road like soldiers on parade while storekeepers stare out of their windows at travelers on the road.

The road narrows here, but luckily the number of supply caravans has also dwindled, making the traffic easier to navigate.  The pavement itself looks to be of a much better condition, too, as it has seen little abuse from iron-shod wheels.

The sounds of the nearby bazaar buzz in the background.  A gigantic memorial arch towers over the surrounding buildings.  The road continues south under this archway, which is supported by marble columns that line the sides of the street.

Guardsmen stand watch at every intersection, keeping a wary eye on all who pass in and out of the bazaar.  The mouth-watering scent of pastries and sweetmeats dazzles even the most finicky of palates.  A bright yellow banner hangs over the street to the north, pointing the way deeper into the bazaar.

Worn out shoppers lounge about on wooden benches, taking a short rest before diving once again into the maelstrom.  Children play ball on the side of the road under the watchful eyes of their parents.  A shimmering green banner to the north directs citizens into the bazaar.

The once crowded, chaotic bazaar now stands silent, both merchant and shopper resting with the sun.  The colorful pennants marking the marketplace are now nothing more than shades of black, waiting to regain their luster in a new day.
Treasures abound at every turn.  Among the throngs of prospective buyers lurk the shifty-eyed experts at sleight of hand, waiting in the shadows to share the wealth with the prosperous merchants.

The scents of the day mingle with the silence of night as the smells of the bazaar linger long after the merchants have turned in.  Shards of lamp light sporadically pierce the confines of the marketplace, causing both illumination and shadow.

The road is crowded with people making their way into the bazaar.  A community fountain at one intersection is a very popular spot for friends to meet before going off to shop.  Over the north road is a large blue banner that directs citizens into the bazaar.

Fabulous marble colonnades line a regal plaza of tremendous proportions.  Elegant fountains flow in a series down the exact center of the pavilion and provide a sparkling backdrop for enormous pots of ornamental palms and brilliant flowers.  Throngs of merchants and visitors mill about in the grand foyer of the Ratha Bazaar, waiting to reconcile bills of lading or gain entrance into the festive marketplace.
Out of the west, sounds from the bazaar fade to a faint thrum.  Traffic is heavy as people travel the road to reach their favorite merchant.

The scents of the day mingle with the silence of night as the smells of the bazaar linger long after the merchants have turned in.  Shards of lamp light sporadically pierce the confines of the marketplace, causing both illumination and shadow.

The great lift to the second tier rises from the humble beginnings of the first to the loftier levels above.  People of all classes and habits mingle, each intent on his or her own affairs.  A militia guard keeps an eye on the surroundings and occasionally dissuades some disreputable looking person or another from ascending without some proof of honest business above.

The darkened facade of a large building casts a shadow on the street below.  A wall of wooden crates blocks passage along the walkway, forcing pedestrians into the street and the path of trotting hoofbeats.

Buildings press in on both sides of the road.  Shoots of dark grass poke their way through the cracks of the cobblestone street.  A number of wealthy citizens stride along this thoroughfare, keeping a wary eye out for pickpockets.

Bright awnings and colorful pennants adorn the facade of a neat mud and brick building.  A lovely portico dotted with delightful iron chairs and matching tables offer weary shoppers a place to stop and catch their breath.

The road widens as it meets two others coming in at odd angles.  The resulting tangle of streets is set about with a curious variety of tiny shops mingled with somewhat ramshackle cottages and small storage yards for bulk goods.
Several small gardens, each with a tidy stone border, line the road along the edge of a genteel residential area.  Several tall stakes control long strands of curling vines, laden with pea-pods.

The smells of cooking and the sound of cheerful laughter emanate from a rambling tavern on the west side of the road.  The otherwise drab stone of its roof has been worked along the edge into a series of brightly-painted cameos depicting comically absurd portraits.

The backs of several large warehouses present a blank facade along the road.  Rough grey stone rises on both sides, cutting off any breeze and fencing in the noise and smells of a crowded town.  Faded chalk outlines on one wall are all that remain of some forgotten children's game or picture.
Traffic is quite heavy, despite the hour.  A few lanterns placed on rocky perches cast a feeble light on the crossroads.  A sleepy-looking guardsman leans on a pike, keeping half an eye on the road.

As the throng of citizens heads north from the lifts, this delightful little road heads west over the ridge toward some of the most beautiful scenery Ratha has to offer.  Weeping bloodwood trees form a graceful arch over the roadway, while neat white pickets surround a cluster of tidy homes.
Sweet scents float through the calm night air.  Glowing embers from the cooking fires die slowly, the residents long taken to their beds, and slumbering peacefully.
Spectres of the afternoon hustle and bustle are called forth by the soft whinny of a horse nearby.  The sparkling night view of the city below and the roiling ocean beyond is a joy to behold.

The neighborhood garden is silent, resting after a busy day of cultivation and activity.  A bustling center of activity by day, the garden lends quiet comfort to this quaint community in the long evening hours.

Several people gather around a large brick firepit outside a neatly trimmed cottage.  Billowing smoke wraps around the stone chimney as a wild boar turns slowly over the coals, fat dripping into the flames.  On smaller spits, a number of plump birds roast slowly, and large pots of bubbling liquids add their steam and delicious smells to the atmosphere.
The well worn stone wall nearly rings with the day's conversations.  Now quiet and peaceful, this delightful lane wends its way through the slumbering community.

Fingers of starlight filter through the lush canopy of bloodwood and sana'ati trees as the avenue broadens.  Protected from the frequent wind and rain sweeping off the ocean, the drive takes on an almost dream-like quality.  On the north side of the reach, gentle rolling knolls are host to a variety of well kept homes with dramatic views of the sparkling sea beyond the cliffs.

The denseness of the arboreal adit gives way briefly, allowing an unobstructed view of the shipyards far below, and the jetty beyond.  From this vantage point one can clearly observe the traffic in and out of the harbor.  It is said that the Odalva family purchased property on this bluff to keep track of the vast Redthorne fleet.

Veering close to the precipice, the avenue broadens slightly to form a small viewpoint.  The sights, sounds and even the smells of the city below can be experienced when the wind is blowing just right.  Scuffing and footprints can be seen just over the sturdy retaining wall, not two feet from a very obvious warning sign.

Enveloping the avenue, spreading masses of lush greenery play about the gnarled wood and sinewy branches.  Long, protective arms reach downward, toward the decorative stones along the fenceline.  Just ahead, a rolling meadow unfolds, hugging the north side of the road.

The softly rolling hillside whispers with the hushed sounds of grasses and flowers blowing in the gentle evening breeze.  Worn down by many a footfall, a trail meanders away from the road towards the quiet meadows.

Skirting along the meadow, the road ambles toward the cliff's edge and two large homes, perched precariously close to the precipice.  On the opposite side of the road, stables and gardens make best use of the grassy knoll and ample acreage.

Subtle fragrances waft through the air, hibiscus, cherry blossom, something else not quite identifiable.  Carstens, the florist, has gardens nearby and often roams the neighborhood selling his delicate and fresh-picked wares to the eager locals.

Breezes blow stronger here, as the road approaches the western overlook and the windward side of the bluff.  The thick stand of sana'ati gives way to smaller, sculpted pine trees.  Though still ornamental and pleasant to look upon, the plants and flowers here have adapted to the elements, taking on a distinctly squat and sturdy posture.

Diamonds of light sparkle off the surface of the ocean.  A stiff breeze blows constantly here, whipping the salt air against the side of the cliff in playful whorls.  Far out in the harbor, various ships lay at anchor, awaiting their turn in the busy port of Ratha.  Below, one needs only spy the griminess of the lower tier of the city to be reminded that all is not as unspoiled as this panorama proclaims.

The road leading into the town from the great lift crosses a large east-west road that serves the merchant quarters that make up the bulk of the inhabitants of this level.  A continual rush of traffic scurries about in all directions, taking little heed of anyone foolish enough to stand and gape at the hubbub.  A tall flagpost rises in the center of the crossroad, pennon snapping in the sea-breeze.

A tiny shed sits at quite a peculiar angle just off the avenue, adjoined to an equally peculiar little cottage.  Sumptuous smells often linger in the air here, making the cottage the frequent subject of local prattle.

Tall houses crowd together along both sides of the road, their half-timbered second stories leaning towards each other until they almost meet overhead.  The sky is nearly blocked, giving a gloomy feel to the passage between them that is offset by the cheery color schemes and sprays of greenery set in vases along the window ledges.  Somewhere, a sibilant voice is singing, accompanied by a less-than-skilled ocarina player.

One and two-story houses press close along the avenue.  Through shuttered windows, one can hear people going about their night-time activities.  A small lantern hangs over each door, as required by local custom.  Somewhere, the heavy tread of a watchman on his rounds echoes in the night air.

The road winds a bit between tidy cottages set between neat stone hedges.  One or two appear to be shuttered and empty, but most show signs of being occupied and maintained.  Each has a small brass or bronze night lantern set over the door.

A few houses, set back from the road, seem to brood in silence.  They are shuttered and look unkempt, their gardens gone to seed and their paint is peeling.  The damp night air thickens into fog and swirls about the dim wooden shapes.  There is evidence of a fire not too recently, to judge from the rain-streaked soot around the windows and doors and the smoke-stained walls of one house.

Two roads meet between rough-hewn stone buildings.  The obvious debris of a crowded roadway full of horses and mules have been swept to one side in untidy piles, awaiting the nightwagon's arrival.  The few pedestrians keep to the center of the way to avoid rude accidents to their footgear.

From here, looking over the tops of the far buildings, one can see the eastern lift that travels between Ratha's second and third tier.  Most of the road's traffic is heading westerly towards the city's bazaar.

The gravel road is tightly packed with citizens as they make their way through Ratha's merchant district.  Tall stone buildings line the thoroughfare.  A stone bench provides the weary a place to sit down amid the hustle of the city.
Pedestrians must keep a sharp eye out for supply caravans as they move down the road with little regard for those on foot.  The occasional braying of a donkey shatters the otherwise quiet street.

Tired laborers, craftsmen and merchants make their way towards some of the city's best inns that have their custom in this part of Ratha.  Some lean wearily against street lamps, resting in the pools of light, before continuing onward.

A small grove of trees has been planted here, in soil carried at great expense from more fertile lands.  They have done well despite the salt winds off the sea.  Some enterprising vendors have set up stands beneath their branches, selling cool drinks and roasted meats and boiled candies.

A pair of buildings appear to have been torn down, making a wide spot in the road just south of a busy intersection.  Some few stalls remain open despite the hour in what is a busy bazaar during the day, eager merchants hoping perhaps for a few more coppers before they turn in.  Then there are those whose primary business is best done in the dark of night or shadow.  Those hooded and cloaked figures that skirt the few guttering lanterns or grease-soaked rushlights, for example.
From the east, the stink of death floats on the cool damp air.  The stink of ash as well, perhaps from a crematorium.  Death comes to all, high and low, rich and poor, and all will end the same.

Normally a quagmire of people, wagons and carriages, Zeh'ra Boulevard is uncomfortably empty.  A light dusting of ash on the ground reveals no other footprints or wheel tracks.  The surrounding stillness and an odd scent in the air makes loitering an unpleasant prospect and relaxation unattainable.  Long shadows reach from the cliff above to shroud the street in uneasy murkiness.

A small cluster of stones juts above the boulevard's surface, which would make maneuvering through this area difficult in heavy traffic.  A slamming door can be heard off in the distance, which only serves to reinforce the complete absence of noise or light in this area.  The scent of seaweed is oddly intense for a location this deep in the city.

rooms.desc: Barrels and crates line both sides of the boulevard, stacked haphazardly in front of narrow doorways and windows.  Mounds of used packing straw and sawdust spill from broken containers, muffling any sound of passage.  The distinctive odor of urine emanates from one particularly large pile of sawdust.  Utter silence reigns among the deep shadows that crisscross the road.

The overpowering reek of rotting flesh wafts from a battered gull carcass kicked to the side of the boulevard in front of an abandoned looking warehouse liberally stained with streaks of white.  Several dozen gulls have gone to roost on the building's sagging rooftop.  The ill-fated gull apparently chose the wrong person to anoint during the hectic crush of the daytime.

Bits of broken shell crunch underfoot, the sound reverberating hollowly between the stark line of buildings and the cliff face.  An eldritch glow filters down from above, limning the outlines of tightly locked windows and doors in a sickly yellow light.  A momentary inspection of the rock reveals the source of the glow to be thick encrustations of lichen that blanket the stone.

The boulevard is nearly choked off between the ever-present stone to the north and a solid line of large warehouses to the south.  The high warehouse walls lend the street the look of a dark, narrow canyon, leaving any trace of moon or starlight far beyond reach.  A brisk wind howls from above, carrying the distinctive tang of salt along with the mournful cry of a solitary gull.

Two rows of small warehouses crowd the boulevard as it curves southwards to avoid an impressive slab of stone slanting outward from the base of the cliff.  Three figures standing in front of a brightly lit doorway are cast into silhouette.  While it is impossible to make out their features, the shadowy outlines of weapons and armor coupled with their alert stances serve to discourage casual interest.

A lengthy stretch of road running directly westwards is cast into perpetual shadow by the massive wall of rock to the north.  No light filters in from above, making passage precarious at best.  Heavy gloom collects under overhanging eaves, offering ideal concealment for those whose trade is best conducted in the strictest confidence -- and where shouts might go unheard.

Used primarily as a means to transport goods from one side of Ratha to the other without braving the mire of the Bazaar itself, the boulevard is an important link for the merchants located at either side of the city.  The heavy traffic of daylight is gone, leaving behind a more subtle rhythm of business and dealings ripe to catch the unwary and incautious.

Looming buildings built close to the cliff cast this narrow stretch of road into profound darkness.  Eerie echoes cascade down from above while furtive figures move quickly along the edges of the boulevard, giving each other a wide berth.  A sense of being watched is impossible to ignore.

Still predominantly residential at this point, Zeh'ra Boulevard curves languidly around a gigantic bulge of stone thrust out from the towering cliff to the north.  Without the distraction of the thick crowds found here during the day, the stench of refuse collecting in gutters is overpowering.  Fresh droppings from yaks, mules, ponies and other more exotic beasts of burden lend the odor an immediacy that quickens the step and makes deep breathing a thing best avoided.

A lissome S'kra Mur man stumbles up a short walkway leading to one of the townhouses built here.  Judging from his unsteady walk and the amount of trouble the latch causes, he's returning from more than a hard day's work.  No lights are visible in any of the windows facing the street and a cool wind blows in from the bay bringing with it the quiet susurration of the surf.
