rooms.desc: A solitary light glows from behind a sheer curtain in the upper story window of a neat townhouse offset from the street by a small sidewalk.  An occasional figure, indistinguishable in the darkness of the boulevard, passes on its way to or from the third tier.
The road forks here, southeast toward the Ratha bazaar, still open at this late hour and southwest toward the quaint homes of Amakra close.  Weary townsfolk make their way toward the comfort of home.

Ornate fencelines, white-washed trellises replete with meandering rose vines and fragrant lily blossoms adorn the walkways.  Spectres of the day's traffic seem to hang in the still night air, ready to descend once more onto the streets below.

Sparkling water commands the horizon beyond the cliffs to the west.  From these homes along the bluff, ships lanterns can be seen tracing a line toward the safety of the harbor below.  Fragrant jadsem blossoms lend a dream-like quality to the cool night air.

Whispers of a breeze linger in the trees that line the roadway, a stone archway leads to a dramatic overlook at the cliff's edge.  Elegant stone benches are placed on either side of the quaint roadway providing a pleasant place to sit and enjoy.  Enormous hanging baskets filled with weeping blood-red iera flowers and bright blue violets complete the picturesque walk.

Over the top of the surrounding buildings there is a fairly decent view of the western lifts that ascend to Ratha's temple district.  The acrid scent of a tanner and the faint sound of a hammer striking metal comes from the south.

Carriage traffic is very sporadic during the quiet hours of the evening and early morning.  On occasion a group of drunken sailors ambles through, lost from the main thoroughfare and creating a disturbance in the quiet neighborhood awaking angry residents from their slumber.

A pair of stone nagas rise to either side of the great lifts that lead to the third tier and the seat of power.  Liveried messengers hurry past, bearing important documents for the traders and merchants who do business on this level.  A nearby barracks holds a complement of guards, ready day and night to secure the approaches if rioting or rebellion should break out among the lower classes and threaten the island's trade.

A young family makes their way along the stone walkway toward the south and the beautiful views of the ocean.  A sturdy stone wall abuts the walkway and provides a safe barrier from the treachery of the sheer cliff beyond.

A row of neatly trimmed buildings sits back off the road, warm lamplight radiating from the windows.  Most businesses, which are closed for the night, leave a lamp or candle burning to inform townsfolk that the owners are in residence and available for emergencies.
A darkened home sits back from the road, surrounded by a high iron fence.  The gate is bolted shut as if the owner had been away for a long while.

Broad ironwoods grow tall on this side of the island protecting many small homes nestled under their protective foliage.  Like giants standing guard on this ocean-side knoll, they weave an eerie atmosphere as the shadows of moonlight play hide and seek.

The avenue is broad and decidedly residential.  The homes are not overly large or elegant, but well kept and nicely appointed.  The children who often play in the gardens and along the walkways, are tucked into their beds slumbering now as the stars come out to play.

Charming cottages and small homes sit close together, tiled walkways and neat gardens setting one apart from the other.  Residents can often be seen sitting on porches late into the night, puffing on pipes, drinking cider or just watching the stars play upon the ocean.

A quiet, tree-lined lane meanders off toward the west.  Unable to wander past the confines of a locked gate, the passerby is left to wonder what manner of mystery lays beyond the iron scrollwork.  Birdsong and laughter are carried aloft on a soft breeze, reminders of a carefree existence somewhere closeby.

A wide brick walkway commands the eastern side of the bluff, as the drive takes a turn toward the most beautiful of scenic finery on Ratha.  Stretching as far as the eye can see, a sparkling crystal ocean lays like a blanket surrounding the island.
Fields and walkways are quiet and settled for another night's slumber.  Come morning, the eager voices of children at play will once again carry aloft on the gentle breezes.

Both spectacular and dangerous, the view at this point is nonetheless exhilarating.  The stone wall protects the average traveler from the perilous cliffs, but too eager a spectator could easily find themselves awash in the churning surf and the rocks below.

A cluster of homes is set back away from the traffic of the avenue, taking advantage of the view from atop a slight rise.  A dirt lane serves as a drive connecting the homes to the road, forming what could be construed as a cul-de-sac.

The smell of straw and the occasional whinny of a horse heralds the presence of a livery service someplace closeby.  Hired out for pleasure or in service to specific delivery services, horses play an important part in the transportation of people and goods around town.

Beyond the safety of a low stone retaining wall, a cliff divides this level of the city from the lower warehouse district below.  With a slight adjustment of the eyes, the onlooker can forget the toil and chaos of the city below, and become lost in the depths of the crystal sea beyond.

Interesting serpentine patterns adorn a low stone wall on the cliff side of the avenue.  With access to goods from distant ports of call, it's not surprising to find foreign art and cultures influencing much of the Rathan architecture.

A small monument rests here, overlooking the busy port district of the city below.  To this day the Tierskel family, long involved in the development of seafaring trade in this region, controls the docks and shipyards.

The avenue sweeps toward the south and east and a lovely view of the city below.  The sparkling ocean, ever present from nearly every spot in Ratha is a constant reminder of the hard working way of life the town has to offer.
A few steps off the road, atop a slight rise, a bevy of small cottages beckon the weary home for the evening.  Clean and well cared for, the homes in this area are neither shabby nor elegant.

Traffic along this section of the busy road is typically limited to carriages and supply wagons destined for the homes on the tier.  The larger section of the road to the west and north, takes travelers toward the great lifts of the palace level or the portside district below.

A row of small storage yards are neatly filled with crates and bales stacked two and three high.  Traffic in and out of the area suggests that it is used by merchants as a clearing house for goods sold at the famous Ratha bazaar.

Cool sea-breezes sweep across the rocky precipice that divides lower Ratha from the higher class districts.  The massive lifts work day and night, hauling people and goods up and down between the levels.  The view from here is considerable, with many ships in the harbor below displaying all manner of construction and decoration, hailing from a dozen different ports of call.

A brick and timber building rises three floors above the avenue, small paned windows taking advantage of the southwest exposure.  The muted clang of a ship's bell, belies the presence of the busy port somewhere in the distance.
Several lovely homes find themselves ensconced amid neatly clipped shrubbery and tidy walkways.  Serviceable if not attractive fencing provides a bit of security to the urban neighborhood.
The dark street is quiet except for a few Dwarves that are sitting around a cart, standing guard and warning off the curious.  Travelers avoid eye contact with one another as they swiftly move past.
Many craftsmen gather on the stoops of their various shops to watch the passing citizens.  Others sit on nearby benches discussing the day's labor or just gossiping with their friends.
The street is free of all but a few people, making it easy to get from place to place.  Most of the buildings that line the road are dark.  Travelers avoid eye contact as they swiftly move past.

A pair of stone nagas rise to either side of the great lifts that lead to the upper tiers.  The constant drone of the lift is only intermittent now during the quiet hours of night, and guards in nearby posts doze sporadically.  Sailors and merchants frequent the bazaar at this time of night, seeking trinkets for the lovely ladies that catch their fancy.

Couples from all over Ratha frequent the overlook, making it a favorite spot for a romantic afternoon or evening stroll.  Slowly and happily, most that visit here soon wander north toward the merchant district and the ever popular bazaar.

Windblown grasses cling to sandy cracks in the walkways that bypass several tidy homes along the road.  Iron gates and covered porticos offer security and protection from the evening elements.  Tall and stately street lamps perform their nightly ritual, offering a ray or two of warm light to the evening stroller.

Tempests and whorls of salty air whip past, sending sand and dust flying inland.  Gnarled and deformed by the constant wind, a stand of dwarf pine hum as if goading the spirits of the wind into a battle of wits.

Spicy and aromatic, the scents of a growing herb garden drift past.  Rich and loamy, the soil and climate here are perfect for growing everything from brilliant flowers to flavorful vegetables.  Just ahead the welcoming lights of the Carstens farmhouse can be seen towering over darkened gardens.
Wild grapevines along a rickety fence cast strange shadows from the lamplight in the dark.  Sweet smells from the gardens beyond lend to the intoxicating environment along the tree-lined road.

A high stone wall, meant to protect the street from wind and erosion, blends with the outer walls of an impressive home at the cliff's edge.  For several hundred paces along the roadway the old fortress towers, appearing abandoned, yet ever watchful.  Folks say that the Odalva family owns the property and that sometimes, late at night, strange activities can be observed in and around the mysterious manse.

Continuing the inlaid stone motif, a high wall protects the street here from the whipping winds that frequent this side of the bluff.  In the distance, the tinkle of chimes plays an erratic melody in harmony with the constant drone of the city, and the crashing surf beyond the cliffs.

Hand quarried stone, inlaid with onyx tiles, form a handsome pattern on the floor of the overlook.  This delightful viewpoint is enclosed with sturdy matching walls and the ancient stone archway to the east.  Benches line the walls, and an ancient telescope, atop a small raised dais, offers the viewer a chance to observe the heavens.

This room appears to hold the failures of the clinic's work.  Several shrouded forms lie stacked on metal shelves along the back wall next to a stone table that angles down to a large drain.  One dim sconce is the only light source, and the changing, flickering light makes the shrouded forms seem to waver or move.

This open air porch looks to have been constructed by drunken Halflings.  Every plank of the deck creaks loudly.  The stoop sags low, making many a customer duck their head.  Benches on either side of the tavern's swinging doors give people a place to sit when it gets too hot inside.

The bar's taproom has sawdust covered floors and dirty wood planks for walls.  Flies swarm around open ale casks and piles of trash.  A dirty counter is piled with unwashed ceramic mugs and tin cups.  Stools are set up around a few beat-up tables.

The back room is falling apart along with the rest of the tavern.  Dirty wooden planks atop battered crates are the only seats, besides the floor.  A group of ragged S'Kra Mur throw daggers at the vermin which infest the shadows of the room.

The roof slants down sharply, almost reaching to the floor on one side, showing that this room has been created by the simple expedient of leaning planks against the building and knocking out the wall leading to the tap room.  The ever-present breeze off the harbor whistles through the gaps in the walls, creating background music for the more raucous cries of the patrons.

A lone table, propped under one leg with a wad of paper, sits under a hanging black iron lantern.  Rough wooden chairs with unidentifiable stains on the seats are scattered about, most of them covered in half-empty glasses and the knocked-out ashes from pipes.
This room is full of empty crates and barrels.  A number of dead rats lay among the other refuse.  The sour smell of ale gone bad fills the air.

Boxes and crates are stacked up solidly against the walls, and it appears that in places, they may be all that stands between you and the harbor.  The rough planks and logs from which the room was built seem to be random driftwood that has washed ashore and been scavenged for use as building materials.

The ledge widens slightly, creating a resting spot and a high vantage point.  To one side, a very steep slope formed of tumbled gravel forms a precarious path upward.  Far in the distance, tiny golden lights glide on the shimmering black expanse of ocean, creating streaks of brightness on the night-lit water.

Seaweed and algae coating the rocks make footing on the uneven surfaces even more treacherous.  Cracked shells lie scattered about, seemingly out of place, at this height above the tide line.  The stone mounds offshore reach toward the high slab ridges, further confusing where land ends and ocean begins.

The cliff edge drops abruptly, plunging vertically into the ocean far below.  Frothy waves crash against the rocky footings.  Farther downshore, a thin band of sand reappears, hugging the cliffs as they wind northward.  The sea stretches east, unbroken to the curved blue-grey horizon.

rooms.desc: The crevice widens to become a long channel of high-walled stone.  Stalks of dune grass push through the broken shells and splintered rock which clutter the sandy floor.  Faint impressions, barely recognizable as footprints, head off to the northwest.

A tiny shack shoulders against the rocky wall at the back of the channel.  Thatched with sea oats, and constructed of vine-lashed driftwood embedded in mounds of stone and shells, the structure looks too frail to withstand the weather or offer much shelter.  A piece of scrap canvas hanging crookedly from a break in the driftwood serves as a door.
Strewn with sandstone and driftwood, the path heads off towards the base of the cliff.  Footprints in the sand appear recent.

Abruptly, the short path comes to an end at the base of a sheer cliff.  Sand and rock crumble with each step as scattered debris, rocks and, what appears to be crushed bone, lay strewn about.  From this vantage point, the cliff appears unclimbable, with barely a hint of a hand or foot-hold discernable.

With a start you find yourself standing on the lip of the narrowest ledge imaginable.  The face of the cliff rises before you, disappearing as quickly under your feet.  The slightest movement causes a cascade of small stones to plummet the remaining distance to the rock strewn ground below.

Despite the warning sign posted plainly at the cliff's edge, there are signs that a few foolhardy individuals have tested their climbing skills.  Peering over the edge of the cliff, one can imagine that a number of those fools have perished in the attempt.  Passersby linger just over a sturdy retaining wall, taking in the view.

Tourists lounge under the monument's marble arches, enjoying the shade and the marvelous carvings on the memorial's columns.  The artwork depicts many points of Ratha's military history, particularly battles in which members of the Zsikiel family played an important role.

An immense memorial arch looms high across the alleyway.  Built by the merchant guilds of Ratha, the monument is a testament to the military achievements and patriotic sacrifices of the Zsikiel family.  The street does not bypass this feat of architecture but actually runs under its sweeping columns.

This part of the alley must run adjacent to some craft hall, because a number of barrels, filled with an assortment of scrap materials, line the side of the street.  Cured leather, pulped wood, and heated iron are the most prevalent scents that fill the air, all with the underlying aroma of mold and rust that comes from sitting out in the weather too long.

Many owners of the nearby buildings seem to use the alley as an open trash barrel.  Piles of refuse further impede those that travel this route, and few fail to leave the area without smelling a bit worse than when they entered.

The backsides of a number of shops and homes close in this road from both sides, throwing everything into shadows.  Traffic is thin, as most prefer the wide thoroughfares to the claustrophobic and perhaps more dangerous alleyway.  A few citizens still brave the passage, keeping a wary eye on all who pass near.

The street lies desolate, ruined husks of buildings lining the street like giant skeletons.  Wide claw marks have been gouged into the scattered remains, further shredding the weather-damaged wood.  Massive wooden beams brace a wide barricade to the south.

A large house has collapsed into the street, blocking most of the intersection.  A large skeleton, its huge skull bleached white against the darker wood, lies crushed under one particularly large beam.  The rough ground around the skeleton is scarred deeply, as if scraped by large claws.

The road ambles north and south, but a small alley leads west between two crumbling houses.  Broken glass and chunks of worked stone litter the street, surrounding an upturned granite bench in the middle of the road.  A wide smear of dried blood leads from the bench, into the alley, and out of sight.

Broken cobbles make up the road that surrounds a wide stone fountain.  Rubble lines the bottom edge of the dried-up reservoir, fallen from the exposed lip.  A large plaza, seemingly untouched by the weather, spreads out to the west, and collapsed in one of its corners is the wooden skeleton of a merchant's cart.

The remains of tall ruined houses line the western side of the street, unable to withstand the constant ravages of the tropical weather.  Wind-worn beams lie crisscrossed amidst the wreckage, nearly obscuring a small hole underneath.  To the east, a dried-up fountain stands as a scarred memory of the former residents.

Two overgrown strips of grass line a small gravel path leading up to a stone statue resembling a muscular Human grasping a shark.  Countless bone fragments contrast sharply against the lush grass and weeds, and a scattering of humanoid skulls serve as a grim suggestion of what may have happened here.  The street continues away from the statue to the northeast and southeast.

To the east of the street, a small house lies in abject decay.  The face of the structure seems mostly secure and its door and small window still seem functional despite apparent abuse.  Near the roof, the southern wall has been destroyed, revealing another possible entrance to the house's loft.  A dried stone fountain rests in the plaza to the northwest, while the road continues north and west around it.

A rusted iron fence lines the northern perimeter of the street, which continues south and west.  Weeds and briars have taken over what could have once been a viewing garden just through the fence.  A dried and aging fountain dominates the plaza, a cobbled pathway leading southwest through its center.

An oppressive heaviness weighs on the air here.  The crumbling remains of a white gazebo lean against the rusted iron fence lining the northern side of the street.  Several pieces of the lumber have been dragged about the area, some sporting unsightly crimson blotches or smears.  One particularly long post still bears a skeletal hand loosely wrapped around its base.

A thick oaken table dominates the center of this room and the skeleton of a small dog rests curled up on the middle of it.  Ash and partially burned logs lie scattered about the room but seem more concentrated in front of the open wood-burning stove sitting in a corner.  All of the cabinets have fallen off the walls, leaving shattered dishes and flatware strewn about the floor as well.  A large window looks north onto a garden overgrown with weeds.

A row of four rusted beds lines the back of the room, each covered in a dark red crust.  Two skeletons, sprawled across the pitted frames, are covered in stained crimson sheets.  The east wall bears a faded painting of a proud knight and a small window with a broken pane peers west onto the abandoned street outside.  A shoddy ladder leads to a loft, the entrance obscured by tattered grey curtains.

The smell of refuse and molding linen clings to the still air in this loft.  Scattered piles of composting cloth are nested about the room, giving the impression that the space was once inhabitable.  Tattered grey curtains dangle from the west side of the ceiling, ending just above a shoddy ladder leading to the living quarters down below.  The south wall of the loft has collapsed, leaving an opening to the desolate street below.  A collection of rotting wood figurines lies jumbled in a corner.
The sewer drop under the grating is a small, tile-lined room.  Rainwater from the street above flows into it and exits through a big bronze valve that seems oversized for that purpose.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: something noiselessly brushing past or an odd whiff of incense becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only the click of claws on stone breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the feel of soft, yielding mud or the stench of refuse and worse becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a low-pitched rumble breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the slip of a loose brick underfoot or the smell of fish, fresh and otherwise, becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a sound like a sigh breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the slip of a loose brick underfoot or the reek of mold long in the making becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only an occasional splash breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a drop of water -- surely it's water? -- or a pungent, spicy aroma becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only what might be a footstep breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: something noiselessly brushing past or a pungent, spicy aroma becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a continual dripping breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a feathery, sticky strand or the tang of the salt sea becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only the click of claws on stone breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the feel of soft, yielding mud or an odd whiff of incense becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only what might be a footstep breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a feathery, sticky strand or the smell of fish, fresh and otherwise, becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only an occasional splash breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the chill of a clammy breeze or the reek of mold long in the making becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a continual dripping breaks the silence.
Beneath the drain is a small, tile-lined room, part of the main sewer and water supply system, from the look of the big bronze valve that takes up most of one wall of the room.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: something silent brushing past or the stench of refuse and worse becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a sound like a sigh breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the feel of soft, yielding mud or the tang of the salt sea becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only an occasional splash breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a drop of water -- surely it's water? -- or the smell of fish, fresh and otherwise, becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a continual dripping breaks the silence.

A faint light from the grating above shows this small, tile-lined room, hardly more than a wide connection in the system of pipes that regulates the flow of water that cleanses and refreshes Ratha.  A big bronze valve is the only noteworthy feature in the place.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the slip of a loose brick underfoot or a pungent, spicy aroma becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only what might be a footstep breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a drop of water -- surely it's water? -- or the stench of refuse and worse becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a low-pitched rumble breaks the silence.

The dim beams from the southwest, gleaming weakly on wet brick and rough walls, reveal three ominously dark entrances to the room.  They stand like the gaping mouths of monsters into whose gullet one would not willingly travel.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a drop of water -- surely it's water? -- or the tang of the salt sea becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a sound like a sigh breaks the silence.

A large circular opening -- curiously shaped like a big pipe -- dominates the ceiling of the room.  From the southeast comes the light of flickering torches, contrasting sharply with the darkness to the northeast.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the chill of a clammy breeze or a pungent, spicy aroma becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a low-pitched rumble breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the touch of a feathery, sticky strand or the reek of mold long in the making becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only what might be a footstep breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the slip of a loose brick underfoot or an odd whiff of incense becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only the click of claws on stone breaks the silence.
A light flickers to the southwest, its beams reflecting off the damp stones of the passage.  Compared to the black tunnels, no long night's dawn could be more welcome than this faint glimmer.

The tunnel broadens into a kind of anteroom where more care than usual has been taken to dress and smooth the walls and floor.  The opening to the east is flanked by flaring torches in bronze holders shaped like lions' heads.  It appears to pierce some kind of thick stone wall.

A red glow flickers in the distance to the northwest.  Its light lends a sense of motion and distance, and dispels the oppressive feeling that the walls are closing in.  The light, obviously from flames, wavers -- growing brighter one moment, dimmer the next.

A few glowing wicks in wall niches cast dim light and dark shadows in a circular room lined with red tiles.  From an opening in the ceiling big enough for a wagon, an occasional drop of water splashes to the floor.  It trickles over to a matching hole in the floor and runs down the steeply sloping channel.

A few glowing wicks in wall niches cast dim light and dark shadows in a circular room lined with green tiles.  From an opening in the ceiling big enough for a wagon, an occasional drop of water splashes to the floor.  It trickles over to a matching hole in the floor and runs down the steeply sloping channel.

A few glowing wicks in wall niches cast dim light and dark shadows in a circular room lined with yellow tiles.  From an opening in the ceiling big enough for a wagon, an occasional drop of water splashes to the floor.  It trickles over to a matching hole in the floor and runs down the steeply sloping channel.

The tunnel broadens into a kind of anteroom where more care than usual has been taken to dress and smooth the walls and floor.  The opening to the north is flanked by flaring torches in iron holders shaped like trolls' hands.  It appears to pierce some kind of thick stone wall.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the feel of soft, yielding mud or the stench of refuse and worse becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only the click of claws on stone breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: something noiselessly brushing past or an odd whiff of incense becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a low-pitched rumble breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the chill of a clammy breeze or the smell of fish, fresh and otherwise, becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only a sound like a sigh breaks the silence.

In the darkness, senses other than sight press for attention: the chill of a clammy breeze or the stench of refuse and worse becomes ominous when eyesight fails and only an occasional splash breaks the silence.

The tunnel turns at odd angles and disturbing slants, a distorted mirror-image -- if stone can be called a mirror -- of the room to the north.  Torchlight flickers to the northwest, while the darkness waits at two other yawning entrances.

The tunnel broadens into a kind of anteroom where more care than usual has been taken to dress and smooth the walls and floor.  The opening to the east is flanked by flaring torches in brass holders shaped like trader logs.  It appears to pierce some kind of thick stone wall.

The tunnel walls have been built of a random mixture of brick and stone, as though the builders utilized whatever came to their hands at that moment.  A small heap of bricks, stone, and dirt has fallen from the ceiling in one place, exposing raw dirt.  The stability of the rest of the ceiling seems questionable.

A chill wind brushes by, blowing softly past from the black-throated tunnels stretching off in several directions.  The rusted rungs of a ladder climb the north wall, disappearing into a narrow hole cut into the ceiling from which a constant stream of water falls to the floor.  From a distance can be heard soft rustlings and movements, but from which direction, or whether from all directions at once, is impossible to tell.

Water falling from a line of pipes along the wall echoes unbearably loudly in the almost total darkness.  The noise and lack of light make it difficult to either see or hear anything approaching until it is virtually next to you.

The atmosphere is icy cold, and tendrils of chill air seem to reach under clothing as if seeking warm flesh to feed upon.  The light is very dim, and the walls of the tunnel are lost in shadowy darkness.

Water flows in from the north, falling into a hole in the floor leading straight down.  Iron rungs have been fastened to one wall of the dark pit, forming a slippery ladder.  The constant moisture has ensured that the rungs are well-rusted, in some places pulling out from the wall.

The walls are narrowly within a dagger stroke to either side, curving seamlessly into the ceiling and barely giving enough room to stand upright.  Along the center of the floor a stream of dark water flows south.

A fitful light filters through the bars of the grate overhead, and the air is unpleasant with odors probably best not identified.  The walls and floor of the cramped space are built out of tightly fitted stone.  A thin sheet of water flows southward down its center into a large pipe, just big enough to squeeze into.

The travel-worn road narrows, and the caravans that frequent it tangle in the crowded way.  Camels snort, donkeys bray and traders curse in the congestion as they all push for a place at the marble watering trough at the side of the road.

At this crossroads, travelers can choose to enjoy the splendor of the Palace to the west and southeast, or head on through the banking district to the northeast.  Guards stand rigid at their posts guarding the Palace grounds day and night.  Government officials and financial experts make their way southeast to the Palace entrance and the tax collectors.  To the west is the beginning of the grand Processional Way and the continuation of Promenade Way with its temples and shops.

The south end of the great Processional opens onto the Palace grounds where the trees spread their branches as if in greeting.  They beckon one to take the pleasant stroll northward to the Great Waymeet and Angels Flights.  Several stores and guilds can be found down the Promenade to the east.  The west path leads off towards the temple grounds.

At this juncture, a traveler can choose to enjoy the splendor of the Palace to the southeast, or head on through the temple district to the northwest.  Guards stand rigid at their posts guarding the Palace grounds day and night.  Government officials make their way down to Regents Circle and the entrance to the Palace.  To the east is the beginning of the grand Processional Way and the continuation of Promenade Way with its guilds and shops.

Travelers move quickly along the weathered cobblestone road which bridges the palace district and the temple district.  The lush greenery and trees found to the north and east fall back to a more open-air route of grass and small bushes.  An occasional glimpse of the elegant temple gardens to the north is possible through the ivy covered fences.  A large, ornate ironwork facade decorated with the image of a panther marks the entrance to Damaris' Temple.

A favorite place for the clergy to gather, this section of the Promenade widens on the north side where it encroaches onto the temple grounds and provides a beautiful garden setting to sit and relax along one's journey, or to just find some quiet place for personal meditation.  Several small statues of local deities line the fence as if to bless those who pass.

Promenade Way opens to the east where it skirts the southern border of the Temple district and provides easy access for commoners, the elite and the clergy.  Well traveled by foot, as well as caravan, the cobblestone street is replete with ruts and holes desperately in need of repair.  The grass along the fenced edges, however, is well maintained and allows for easy foot access to the temple grounds to the east and north.

Handsome brick walkways round the corner from the spaciousness of Palace Drive to the formality of Regents Circle.  Ornately wrought, iron balustrades are capped with gleaming brass and circumscribe the vast gardens that surround the palace.  Perfectly matched and richly appointed, the accoutrements of the palace guards are no less formal, lending a sense of impending royalty to the area.

The drive is hushed now, as the business of the day is left behind in exchange for the peace of the evening hours.  Pilgrims are often seen huddled in groups just off the drive, silent and seeking warmth as they wait for the dawn of a new day and the missions they've come to complete.

Great iron poles line the drive on either side, supporting brightly glowing lanterns.  The stately carriages and regal equines that traverse the drive during the day are now tucked safely into their stalls as even Ratha's royalty sleeps the night away.

Wide and expansive, this elegant drive parades east toward Regents Circle and the magnificent Ratha Palace beyond.  Down the center of the avenue, a lantern lined median channels carriage traffic east and west in an orderly flow.  All along the regal boulevard, handsome wrought-iron fencing and sculptured topiaries create a formal garden-like atmosphere, as administrators and clergy mingle with Ratha's upper class citizenry along the wide plazas on either side of the street.

Temples to the gods meet temples to paperwork where the districts of each coalesce.  Three roads converge in a small crossing among the stone and wooden buildings.  Far off, the sound of the sea echoes dimly and the bell of some ship rings faintly as it rocks at anchor.

Government offices rise cheek by jowl, poking out above the road as their teetering upper stories lean toward each other for mutual support.  Somewhere nearby can be heard the heavy clanking of lift chains as uniformed couriers race by, each carrying some tiny bit of paper to add the ever-growing piles needed by any bureaucracy.

The great oaken lift wends its way up and down, hauling people and cargo all the hours of the day and night.  Being closest to the government quarter, all manner of petty officials, couriers, hangers-on and an endless stream of petitioners make their way here, each wrapped in his or her concerns and heedless of the bustle all about.
Imposing granite statuary casts eerie shadows along the grand drive.  The exquisite details so pronounced in the daylight are lost, as the inanimate sentinels loom larger than life in the half light.

The gardens are lit beyond the elaborate iron fencing, small brass lanterns ablaze along the pathways and courtyards.  Two massive S'kra guards, replete in their offical finery patrol the circle all through the night, monitoring entrance into the palace grounds.

The stately Palace Drive meets Regents Circle in a celebration of wide plazas and decadent appointments.  Tall brass standards bear baskets of hanging flowers and foliage while brass capped fences frame the perfect gardens of the palace to the west.

Herbs and roses grow in a tangle along a bordering, low stone wall.  The shrine itself is built in the traditional Halfling style, as adapted to Ratha's rocky terrain.  The squat stone structure resembles a small bump of a hill, and a bright blue door leading inside stands ajar.  Three old island pines shelter and shade the shrine.

Bordered by a plethora of trees and bushes, a short walkway is visible that leads to the verandah of the Empath's Guild.  Somehow the dust of the roadway disappears, giving way to a welcome and pleasant spot in which to relax surrounded by the fragrant smells of herbs and potions from both the plants themselves and from their use by the guild members within.  One can usually find a kind member of this guild here to tend to any health problems.
Whispering boughs overhead sway softly, and dried needles underfoot rustle with each step.  The path skirts the southern side of the small building dedicated to the god Glythtide.

A large common green stretches out over most of the northeastern section of the tier.  The grassy area is an excellent spot for athletic activities, for a meal on the soft grass, or contemplating the sky above.  Chadatru's temple lies to the south.  A narrow path winds under a row of pine trees on the western border of the field.

A large common green stretches out over most of the northeastern section of the tier.  The grassy area is an excellent spot for athletic activities, for a meal on the soft grass, or contemplating the sky above.  The western edge of the field backs on to the temples of Chadatru and Glythtide, and a fountain dedicated to Truffenyi stands to the east near the intersection of the eastern-most road and East Palace Drive.
The great height of the palace looms to the west.  During the quiet of the evening hours, one can ponder the great structure in relative peace and safety.
Pilgrims and clergy alike mingle along this stretch of the drive.  Temples are situated througout this section of Ratha and offer the reverent a peaceful refuge wherein to learn and worship.

Imposing granite statuary can be seen all along the grand drive.  One in particular, is that of a young S'kra Mur trader.  Dressed in flowing robes and precious gems, he appears remarkably life-like, examining the crates on a waiting caravan.

Ornate brass standards fly colorful penants, in tribute to local heroes who have brought honor to the city and province.  Two massive S'kra guards glance about warily, alert to any sign of unwarranted entrance into the palace grounds.

From the well kept stone of the walkways, to the ornate iron fencing surrounding the lush gardens of the palace, the atmosphere is one of utter order and beauty.  The amazing architecture of the palace itself is a joy to behold.
Ivy covered iron fencing culminates in an elaborate gate that opens up onto a wide plaza.
The vendors have gone for the evening, the circle is now quiet.  In the morning, they'll be back offering warm drinks and luscious treats to the privileged citizens who travel this route.

rooms.desc: Wide and expansive, this elegant drive parades west toward Regents Circle and the magnificent Ratha Palace beyond.  Down the center of the avenue, a lighted median channels carriage traffic east and west in an orderly flow.

A large common green stretches out over most of the northeastern section of the tier.  The grassy area is an excellent spot for athletic activities, for a meal on the soft grass, or contemplating the sky above.  To the southeast a large circular fountain sprays water into the air with a hiss and soft patter of falling drops.

The scent of pine resin and decaying wood permeates this dark stand of trees.  The sky is completely blocked from view by the overhanging boughs, and the air is still and suffocating.  There is a sense of being watched, by something.

The air is still and muggy beneath the drooping limbs of tightly meshed pine boughs.  Sounds deaden and echoes die at the approach to a shadowy doorway cut jaggedly into a jumble of black basalt boulders mounded as a solid mass as tall as the surrounding pine trees.

Monks and clerics pass one another with nods or bows or barely concealed glares, depending on the relative state of relations amongst their deities and congregations.  Overhead, two grotesque gargoyles, one on each of two otherwise dissimilar buildings, seem to be glaring at each other in mimicry of the unspoken tensions below.

Tucked snugly in among the high and mighty temples is a quaint and curious shop, from which wafts an inviting tendril of incense that tugs at passersby.  Nearby, a lone mystic sits in a curious posture, knees intertwined with legs in what seems an uncomfortable pose.  He seems almost asleep until the twitching of one nostril, as it is tickled by the smoke emanating from the shop, shows that some attention to the mundane world exists within that ascetic shell.

Despite the general tone of wealth shown by the nearby Temples, the facade of the Clerics' Guild is modest to the point of being shabby.  Made of humble materials in a modest state of repairs, it sits alone, taking quiet pride in the essence of those it serves rather from the transience of mundane decoration and frippery.

The confluence of several disparate roads among the temples has been dubbed the "Threefold Path" by local wags.  The rich decor of the buildings and the many finely garbed holy workers reminds one that the business of serving the gods is oft a profitable endeavor.  The presence of the lavish Imperial Palm Inn also gives credence to the relative wealth of the Temples.

The tall, cool walls of the Imperial Palm Inn rise along the north side of the road.  Yards of shell-pink plaster cover the cold stone behind which twin towers, tiled in dark red, rise above the other lower buildings.

The stately entrance to the Imperial Palm Inn graces this stretch of roadway.  Pink stone walls surround this haven of charm and taste, frequented by the better classes of Rathan society as well as the discerning traveler with the coins to match his taste.

The road passes along the heavy, almost stolid flank of one of the city's many banks.  High leaded windows, set with stout bars, show glimpses of an elegant ceiling within.  City guards keep careful watch on the premises night and day.

Many roads converge here, north of Processional Way, the great route leading to the palace.  A large fountain rises at the center of the roads, and it serves as a gathering spot for all classes and races, a place where one can pause and enjoy the calming sounds of flowing waters and enjoy the marvelous aspect of the grand palace to the south.
A gold-trimmed lift carries its loads with quiet elegance.  Even the chains have been tinted a gold color in keeping with the high-ranking passengers who ride it.

Tucked between the pretentious facade of the Warrior Mage Guild and the great Waymeet, this tiny angle of road holds little charm.  Throngs of people hurry this way and that, regardless of the hour, ready to trample the idler.  Meanwhile, horse- and mule-borne cargoes stand poised to crush the less agile or those who may take a moment to pause and observe the rush of daily life.

Fluted stone towers rise towards the heavens, their surfaces engraved with images of twining snakes.  On the northern side of the street, a large wooden gate is bracketed by two defensive towers.  Engraved on the gate is the crest of the Warrior Mage Guild.

A few straggly patches of grass seem to be the only reason for the somewhat pompous name given to this patch of road.  Rough gravel strangles the grass and what little grows here is scraggly and drear.  Somewhere though, the cheerful sound of birdsong resonates and there is just the faintest whiff of true greenery.

A small, red tile-roofed shop sits deep within the shadows of a nearby grove of small trees.  A curious air pervades the tiny store, as if there were unseen comings and goings on some higher plane than normal senses could perceive.

From a small garden surrounding a curiously-shaped building comes the muted song of many birds.  A pleasant change from the omnipresent cry of gulls, it has a strangely soothing effect.  Cares and troubles seem to fade and a warm sense of security and warmth pervades the air.
A few torches glimmer from a small park nearby.  The scent of growing foliage is rich in the moist sea air, a welcome change from the dusty air in the more crowded sections of town.

A rare bit of open land among the crowded tiers, this patch of sandy soil has been taken over by someone trying to grow herbs and such.  The ground is hard and rocky, the crop sparse and the return poor.  However, for some it may mean the difference between poverty and starvation on the one hand, and survival on the other.

A small patch of open land among the drab backsides of nearby buildings offers a welcome bit of space.  A few straggly plants have found a way through the hard-packed, rocky soil, their tattered leaves making curious shadows against the darker background.

A narrow path begins a winding descent from the streets down the western cliffs of the city.  Saltbrush and stiff grasses block the view to the south and the climb down takes some careful foot-placing.  The main avenues of the city lie further to the east.

Below a steep section of the cliff, the path winds around some large bushes that glisten palely with white salt crystals on their thick leaves.  The city lies upwards over the cliff rocks, which rain a splattering of loose gravel with every movement over them.

A narrow alley runs among the temples, providing service access for deliveries and such.  Even the gods need their trash hauled, it would seem.  Rats and such skitter amongst small piles of debris while rag-clad scavengers of the two-legged sort pick over scraps of food and stubs of candles that can be resold in the lower tiers.

A wooded area shielded by a hedge of firethorn shrubs surrounds a tall barrel-shaped building.  A bench huddles beneath a low bough of a small tree heavily laden with bright red berries.  Many different kinds of songbirds flutter through the dense shrubs, snatching from the tree's feast.

The soft sounds of water from the fountain to the north create a peaceful and comfortable atmosphere as you saunter down this grand boulevard.  Lovely trees line the street almost creating an arch overhead and providing shelter from the elements, allowing a pleasant stroll at any hour of the day or night.

The wide boulevard is impeccably maintained with clean, almost white cobblestones, bordered on each side with grassy walkways creating the feel of a small park.  Nestled between the ivy covered fences lies a small white house.

This is a perfect place to sit and savor the grand splendor of this great processional.  Several benches, surrounded by small, delicate rose bushes giving off a heady, almost heavenly scent, abut the back fences of the temple grounds to the west and the bank to the east.

During state events, this halfway point down the Processional is the perfect location from which to view the dignitaries and their entourages as they proceed grandly down the boulevard anticipating the great events to follow.  The elegant temple gardens are visible through the ivy covered fence to the west.

Onlookers from all over the realms gather here to enjoy the spectacle of the Palace as well as all the official activities taking place around the Palace itself.  Even the trees seem to stand at attention, creating the atmosphere of great decorum.  Most people rarely speak over a whisper here so as not to disturb the natural beauty and awesome ambiance of this glorious setting.

The Oracle Veraclese's Cleric shop stands at this, the eastern end of Promenade Way.  More shops and guilds are found to the north on Three Fold Path along with an Inn which eagerly awaits the visit of folks in need of sustenance and sleep.  Journeying westward, the route borders the banking district and the Palace, and finally leads to the temple district.

The dome of Phelim's Temple rises against the sky in a gentle curve that offsets the harshness of this rock-bound city.  The air is rich with the sea tang from far below and the sound of sonorous chanting from within the sacred precincts blends with the distant wave song of the open ocean.

rooms.desc: The Temples of Ratha rise on both sides of this immaculately clean roadway.  The sacred architecture of a dozen different sects and cults vie with each other in what could have been a tasteless clash but somehow has managed to blend itself into a curious harmony.  Even the varied clouds of incense that drift about manage to combine into a strangely invigorating scent.

The road forks as it passes near the Temple district.  High walls protect the estates and offices of the tax gatherers to the south, and heavily-armed guards stalk along the walls, secure behind stone and iron.  The street itself is spotlessly clean, each scale-shaped cobble has been set with consummate skill so that the path resembles the endless coils of some enormous serpent.

The wide roadway wends between the blessed realms of the temples and the cursed domains of the tax gatherers.  Like the proverbial rock and a hard place, one must steer a difficult course between two such powerful entities.  To the south, the great lift descends to less heady heights.

Golden Scale Road leads from the lifts into the elite heart of Ratha.  The road is paved with stone blocks cleverly carved to resemble large scales, carefully set with gold-tinted mortar.  The effect is one of gaudy elegance.  The motif is reflected in the massive pillars that carry the iron chains that control the great lift.

The grassy green surrounds a large, sparkling white marble fountain.  At the fountain's center is a statue of the god Truffenyi, in mortal form, rendered by the carver as a strong muscular human warrior.  The water arcs from the rim of the fountain and rains down from above on the statue which gazes patiently on the mortal world.  Within the pool of the fountain are smaller carvings of the deity's aspects, the weasel and the magpie.
A simple building is designated as the temple to Everild by the threshold stone at the entrance.  Two carvings stand guard at the doorway, one of a centaur, the other of a wolverine.

A slick, steep incline of shale is slippery with sand that has blown across the path, though a break of bushes gives some handholds for steadying.  A clatter of rocks from above frightens a rabbit hiding beneath the brush.

A tall, dark wooden building lies ahead through an avenue of cedars.  The approach is a mown grassy field bordered with white Ratha cliff thistles.  The wind blows through the trees, creating a rush of soft sound.

A six-tiered temple, still under construction, faces the bay to the south.  Made of wood, instead of stone, it resembles a large sailing ship, with its wooden timbers and tall crow's nest perched high above.  Each dormer of the roof holds a carved wooden raven, wings outspread, that appears to both guard the entrances and to catch the ocean winds and nearly bear the whole structure aloft.  The flag of the Nadamian family flaps briskly from the the highest "mast."

A six-tiered temple, still under construction, faces the bay to the south.  Made of wood, instead of stone, it resembles a large sailing ship, with its wooden timbers and tall crow's nest perched high above.  Each dormer of the roof holds a carved wooden raven, wings outspread, that appears to both guard the entrances and to catch the ocean winds and nearly bear the whole structure aloft.  The flag of the Nadamian family flaps briskly from the the highest "mast."

A six-tiered temple, still under construction, faces the bay to the south.  Made of wood, instead of stone, it resembles a large sailing ship, with its wooden timbers and tall crow's nest perched high above.  Each dormer of the roof holds a carved wooden raven, wings outspread, that appears to both guard the entrances and to catch the ocean winds and nearly bear the whole structure aloft.  The flag of the Nadamian family flaps briskly from the the highest "mast."
A silver-trimmed lift carries its loads with quiet elegance.  Even the chains have been tinted a silver color in keeping with the many elegant personages who choose to ride it.

The red brick street runs eastward towards the prosperous theater which is one of the favorite entertainments of Ratha's upper class.  Colorful lamps, strung from pole to pole and kept burning around the clock, line the road.
Made of bleached granite, the Hotagi'rath theater is a renovated temple of sweeping arches and architectural flair.  Colorful pennants hang from every available outcrop on the building.
A large drainpipe, running up the side of the theater, connects to the roof's gutters.  The pipes empty out into mildew stained rain barrels that are placed conveniently beneath.

The brick street circles around the side of the Hotagi'rath theater.  Flower beds skirt the building, with a blaze of color and scents.  Benches amidst the small gardens provide a peaceful place to rest and contemplate.

The back of the theater looks to be in need of a bit of upkeep, with the bleached granite fading to its natural grey in many places.  The street is cluttered with debris.  Torn remnants of pennants, defaced by both the weather and vandals, hang on the building in need of replacement.

This pathway leads off towards the western cliffs and the sea beyond, and back towards the main streets of the city.  Sandlilies line the trail, their deep blue blossoms waving in the fresh sea air.  A gull cries in the distance, and the wind puffs in drafts blowing the sand in little clouds.

The path ends at a low building made of sandstone bricks, and the cliffs behind it fall off to the western sea below.  The temple's gently-sloping roof is made of slate tiles arranged in a fish-scale pattern.  A triangular-arched doorway, just tall enough for the tallest mortal to enter is capped with a splendid carving of a life-sized albatross.   Steps inside the doorway lead down into a cool, dark passageway.

Smooth, dark wooden walls curve around this tall narrow room.  The only window is a skylight above a pale statue of Faenella, sculpted kneeling before a basin of water placed in the center of the space.  One half of the room is strung with golden wires that run from the floor to the ceiling, and sound in the chamber vibrates them to a pleasing tone.
This cluttered room is filled with rolls of sheet music and instruments.  A S'Kra Mur priest, his black scales painted with silver wrens, sits beside a large harp, humming a hymn to his goddess.

Littered with the forgotten remanent of former treasures, this brick pathway winds past some of the more fashionable parts of town.  Light flickers from lanterns above unmarked doorways as it battles against the darkness that forces it to remain a mere pool of warmth at the doorsteps.  Ominous shadows seem to lurk within every nook from the depth of the cold night.

The sounds of the city are muffled from the high walls that parallel the alleyway.  A sense of movement and soft whispers are imagined from deep within the dark shadows.  Warm light from the windows above fail to win over the powers of the night to illuminate the alley.

Weak pale blades of grass and weeds fight to break through portions of the red brick that have become cracked and broken along the alley's path.  Formerly a soft pink color, the granite walls have become faded to a grayish-pink from rain and lack of care.

The walls close in upon the alley rendering dark foreboding shadows even at the peak of the day.  Empty barrels and crates choke the passage to a mere trail through a forest of debris and refuse.   A small pool of muddy and scum covered water has become the final resting spot for the drainage of a broken gutter above.  Slow thick concentric ripples slowly radiate outward from the center of the pond with each drip of water.

Years of neglect have rended this former bricked alley to a rutted dirt path with scattered embedded shards of broken brick.  Stacks of broken crates lean precariously against a rain streaked granite wall.  A couple of cracked stone steps lead down to a shadowed alcove.

An unmarked door is set within this dark alcove along the grey granite wall.  To the left of the door, a small dingy window hints of a brightly colored curtain on the inside.   A set of stone steps lead back up to the alley.

rooms.desc: The temple to Phelim is a domed building silhouetted against the night sky.  The sound of the sea beyond rumbles far below nearby cliffs, and the treeless, expansive sky floats overhead.
The domed roof of Phelim's temple is open to the night sky with a large telescope pointed towards the heavens.

Open to the sky above, this quiet enclosure is dedicated to Phelim, Lord of Dreams.  Odd sigils adorn the arches forming the shrine and a raised pedestal at the center of the shrine supports a Halfling-high statue of the deity.  Though no censers are apparent, the scent of sandalwood permeates the air.

An austere shrine of blue-veined marble stands at the edge of the lagoon's mouth.  Concentric rings of willow spread out from its circular base, the scent of spiced incense drifting from within.  To either side of the cove's entrance, jagged teeth of dark grey stone rise up to guard the northern shore.

This sheltered cove, bordered by a narrow stretch of white sand, offers an egress to the island for smaller sailing vessels.  To the northwest, at the tip of one of the lagoon's protective arms, lies a small outbuilding.  Southward, the spire of a conical building dominates the sky.

Approaching the building, its true nature becomes apparent -- it is the horned shell of some enormous sea creature.  Dotted with windows and narrow terraces, the central portion of the shell spirals into the sky.  Towering glassine doors lead through the mouth of the deserted husk.
The island trail rises from the east to turn and follow the coastline southwest just before plummeting into the sea.  A rocky cliff looks over the ocean toward the main continent, far from view.
A small stand of trees lines the inland side of the pathway with a wall of tightly knit branches.  The ocean view is quite startling, with the sea spread like a thick azure carpet to the horizon.

The trail is divided here, leading east toward the island's interior and continuing along the barren coastline.  Grey seabirds wheel against the heavens with faint screeching cries carried on a salt-tainted breeze.

A particularly tall spire of granite rises from the waves at this corner of the isle like a frozen sentinel.  Thick coats of dark lichen over the weathered stone provide testimony to its age.  Smaller jagged teeth of grey rock along the shore prevent a suitable landing for any ocean travellers.

A translucent obelisk, the small island's namesake, dominates the center of this silent grove.  Oddly, no sounds of wildlife penetrate the thick foliage surrounding the small meadow.  A slab of reddish-brown stone lies to one side of the obelisk.

At the crest of the hill, an odd structure is visible beside a narrow stretch of beach.  The white sand is stark against the deep blue of a small lagoon.  Southward, the trail wanders back along the shoreline.

Crushed stone grates softly underfoot as the path ascends a small hillock dotted with willow and brambles.  White-winged birds flit through the sky overhead, while gentle breezes whisper from offshore.  From somewhere out of sight, the faint sounds of a violin drift in the salty air.
This pebbled trail winds roughly south and north, beside a high bamboo fence that stretches along the eastern shore.  Unseen woodland creatures scurry through the thick underbrush toward the west.
Manicured trails lined with small dark stones wind along the coastline of the small island.  Wide bamboo gates set in a matching fence to the east permit access to the sailing docks.
The walkway winds through a small grove of willows and the sea glimmers through the foliage to the south.  The soft murmur of the ocean against the shore is muted by their trailing branches.

There are several boats harbored here, all festooned with dangling bells, glass and gaethzen lamps, wooden figureheads, and assortments of colored cloth and canvas.  The uptempo strains of a violin drift across the salty air, rising and falling in conjunction with the sloshing waves.  Strands of smoke drift up from the brightly painted fleet of vessels, no doubt the origin of the potent scent of spiced meals cooking.

A long dock, lined with pillars made from delicately carved cherry wood, stretches along the eastern shoreline.  Surmounted by a sign lettered in silver script, a wide pair of bamboo gates stands open to visitors.
The celestial light of the heavens sparkles across the ocean waves even on the darkest of nights.  Seabirds occasionally wheel across the skies with a screech.

Bordered by a beach of silver-white sand, the small lagoon is just large enough for a relaxing swim to the edge of the open sea.  Currently guarded by a coarse bamboo gate, the lagoon provides safe harbor for smaller seacraft tied along one side of the shore.

Smokeless burning torches emit a soft light, accompanied by a heady herbal scent, bathing the guild entrance in a soft glow.  Sounds of guild activity echo from farther along the broad corridor that curves out of sight to the northwest.  Two towering glassine doors lead out of the guildhall.

The Walk of the Winds slopes upward gently as it winds clockwise through the interior of the guild.  Gleaming waves, created with an intricate pattern of blue and white tile on the floor, sweep toward the spire.  A soft breeze blows along the corridor from somewhere above carrying the scent of the sea and some faint musical tones.
Another inner chamber is accessed here through a sweeping arch with a lintel of silverwood.  Faint lights glow beyond the doorway, but little else is visible in the subdued lighting of the corridor.

A tall narrow window, very nearly like an arrow slit, overlooks the western arm of Crescent Cove.  An ocean breeze whispers along the opening, producing a faint melody.  In less convivial surroundings, the wind song would be haunting.
A low corridor snakes off southwest between two ridges of gleaming shell.  The main passage begins to narrow and the walk steepens slightly as it continues to wind clockwise toward the spire.

Waves of blue and white tile race along the hallway as it winds out of sight to the south.  The intricate floor mosaic gives the illusion of increased speed as the passage narrows, with gleaming white-capped waves bordered by rushing patterns of foam.
One of the guild's tall windows sings softly along the corridor.  Just opposite, a particularly wide arch opens onto another central room.  The smells of fresh-baked bread drift from within.
A small section of the outer wall has been carved away here, leading to a narrow terrace.  A brisk breeze blows through the opening and down along the passageway to the northeast.

Overlooking the high bluffs along the western coast of the isle, a tall window whispers sea songs to passersby.  The corridor narrows even further as it ascends, but still not quite enough to make two-way foot traffic a problem.

The salt-scented breeze along the corridor picks up as the grade of the climb increases, adding a slight chill to the air.  The walk passes another sweeping arch into the heart of the guild that has been boarded over.

This narrow terrace, protected from the weather by a long overhang of horned shell, offers a breathtaking panorama of the island and the shimmering waters beyond.  Windswept grassy hillocks roll away from the guildhouse, and beyond it, a sailing ship glides slowly across the crystal waves.  A brass telescope has been mounted at the edge of the deck offering an enhanced view of the sea and sky.

The glistening mosaic of tiles begins to rise on either side of the passage, covering the lower section of wall with whitecaps.  The passage glides upward and around another turn in the spiral of the shell to the southeast.

Waves of azure rise up along the walls, threatening to engulf the passage as it funnels further into the heights of the guildhall.  Flecks of silver upon the blue, sparkle like tiny grains of sand caught in the fury of the rushing water.
The wash of water closes in overhead and begins to turn in a dizzying funnel of waves.  Tiny fish of silver and gold are swept along with the maelstrom as it pours into a central chamber.

The flood of blue and white spirals into the chamber and a mosaic whirlpool threatens to engulf those seeking knowledge as they cross the hall to the lectern of Guildmaster.  A natural curl of the shell curves up around the outer wall to an opening far above.

From above, the swirling vortex of tile is incredibly lifelike, threatening to pull observers from the narrow walkway.  The thin ledge of shell has a slightly unnerving resiliency that belies its strength.  Just before dropping off into the eye of the whirlpool, it turns up through a natural opening in the ceiling.

A slender spiraled horn of iridescence rises from the top of the guildhall to meet the sky.  Below, the island spreads out to the south and the lagoon is no more than a small puddle splashed upon the shore.  A narrow railing of brass guards the careless observer.

Lined with long communal tables made from dark-stained cherry wood, the exotic scents of spiced meat and herbal concoctions fill this luxurious dining hall.  No kitchens are in sight, the builders having gone to some trouble to conceal any evidence of the mundane.  Nonetheless, servants periodically bustle in and out with heaping trays of food or empty dishes, coming and going through doorways that vanish from sight the moment they're closed.

Light chases away the darkness of the room from highly polished niches along the walls.  An occasional rustling from among the rows of high bookcases betrays the presence of at least one researcher.  With every footstep, the scents of dust and moldering paper fill the air.

Windowless and dimly lit, a few scattered cushions provide seating for those who come to meditate and collate information they've gathered.  Incense slowly burns in hanging sconces, filling the dusky chamber with the soothing scent of sandalwood and a faint sheen of wispy grey smoke.

This enormous chamber is a gathering spot for visitors and general meetings of guild interest.  Natural seating is formed by a low ridge of pearlescent shell that runs around the edge of the hall.  Glowing spheres in ornate sconces, set high along the walls, illuminate the azure carpet like sunlight on the island shoals.
The walkways here become expansive plazas lined with potted trees and assorted floral finery.  All is quiet now, an occasional sweep sauntering by intent on ridding the area of unsightly refuse.

The wondrous smells of a nearby kitchen mingle with a refreshing light breeze, tantalizing all who pass by.  Roving musicians are often seen along the avenue lending a festive environment to the otherwise busy thoroughfare.

The tinkle of music and chimes intermingle with a pleasant breeze upon which floats the smell of something incredibly delicious.  Exclusive shops and artisans offer services to the privileged residents of the Shh'o'kumu Terrace.

Perfectly polished walkways and matching marble balustrades reflect just a portion of the incredible finery found on this tier.  Liveried carriages roll past conveying their occupants toward the sumptuous estates on the eastern side of the terrace.

The marble of the balustrade is used to create a series of arches that offer a bit of protection from the constant breeze.  Elegant rose vines climb their marbled surfaces and paint a pretty picture against the azure of the sea beyond.

The expansive facade of a large columnar building overshadows the elegance of the walkway.  Commanding a sweeping view of the eastern ocean and the bustling palace below, the building is set back from the roadway atop a small knoll.  Ornate fencing surrounds the property and a large gate, emblazoned with a royal coat of arms, marks the entrance to graceful driveway.

rooms.desc: Large marble arches shelter the walkway from the brisk evening breezes.  Crystal highlights glance off the ocean to the west lending an almost dreamlike quality to this section of the promenade.

A pair of stone nagas rise to either side of the great lifts that lead to the upper tiers.  The constant drone of the lift is only intermittent now during the quiet hours of night, and guards in nearby posts doze sporadically.  Sailors and merchants frequent the bazaar at this time of night, seeking trinkets for the lovely ladies that catch their fancy.

The occasional drone of giant pulleys is heard over the howl of the evening breeze.  Even in the wee hours of the morning, carts and wagons wearily enter or depart the lift heading toward the ports or the city gates to the north.

Perfectly patterned brickwork adorns this wide avenue that pierces the heart of the terrace.  Tall, gold trimmed lamp posts display large, colorful hanging baskets filled with sumptuous flowers and variegated ivy.

The neatly trimmed hedges and arboreal canopy frame the wide avenue that channels the majority of traffic north and south.  This is a favorite spot of neighborhood ruffians who enjoy sneaking away from their rigorous studies and nosy nannies to throw rocks at passing wagons.
The lane dips here to pass under the main arterial above.  Brass lanterns cast a warming glow that completely illuminates the lane, casting long shadows on cascades of draping foliage.

A jewel encrusted escutcheon adorns a large gate leading into the Zsikiel estate.  Jade and lapis have been crushed and inlaid into the stone walkway, forming a colorful sea-green mosaic.  The Zsikiel family plays host to hundreds of visitors a year, the elegant walks and grand entrance a showcase for Ratha's sterling upper class.

Lingering smells of the evenings repast waft through the air, the scent of cinnamon and coffee still strong.  Somewhere closeby, warming fires and relaxed conversation enfold the hard-working staff of any of the nearby estates, as they relax a bit and focus on their own families.

The soft tinkle of chimes and the scent of roses mingles on a breeze.  Alongside the lane, a low white fence marks the sumptuous boundary of a formal garden.  A series of elaborate fountains punctuates the sculpted greenery as it spans east toward some incredibly beautiful homes.
Lovely brass lanterns light this portion of the lane, near the beloved park that is now a likely subject of many a child's dream.
The bustle and chaos of the day is now only a distant memory.  Traffic continues along this stretch of avenue all through the night, but the pace is more relaxed.
Ivy draped walls rise to contain the clamorous traffic along the avenue, protecting nearby property from the sights and sounds of one of Ratha's busiest thoroughfares.

rooms.desc: Brightly colored pennants on polished brass poles herald the entrance to the much loved Deversham Park.  During the day, the park is filled with delighted children and their guardians who enjoy the festive accoutrements, and roving artisans.  In the evening hours it is a popular spot for romantic picnics by the pond.

Chaos and confusion is typical at this intersection between the main gates to the city.  A large sign directs the traveler to one of two possible exits.  Nadamian Avenue to the south is the main thoroughfare leading to the lifts and the city below.

A handsome stone and timber kiosk stands back from the road, the crossed swords identifying it as the guard station.  Wagonloads of goods arrive in a steady stream heading toward the Sur'oson gate and the distant towns beyond.

Tall timbers and rough-hewn stone form a giant gate in the great wall.  Standing open for the streams of wagon and foot traffic to pass through, the entrance to Ratha is carefully guarded by observant sentinels who watch every passerby with trained eyes.

Traffic is kept to a minimum along the drive as guards siphon the majority of travelers through to Nadamian Road.  The large wall opens up to the east allowing an expansive view of the lush greenery of the terrace.

The low half wall is replaced by a high, stone and timber wall which serves as a barrier to the great wilderness beyond the city limits.  To the east, the regal drives are darkened, and soft lights dot the expansive acreage as the community slumbers.

Shining tiled roofs, lush topiary gardens and manicured grounds present the onlooker with a beautiful view.  As gorgeous as the surrounding neighborhoods are, they all pale in comparison to the timeless beauty of the ocean to the west.

A stiff breeze blows here constantly, on the windward side of the terrace.  A gentle slope rises from the road toward the east covered with softly waving grasses and wild flowers.  An old stone bench allows travelers a chance to sit and enjoy the view.

Fine marble arches of the promenade loom to the south, their polished surfaces glinting with reflected light.  Families often stroll here, taking in the crisp air and the remarkable sights.  Several exquisite homes are nestled back from the road amid lush, manicured lawns.
A delightful lane is paved in perfectly matched cobbles, and bordered by low whitewashed fencing and sculpted hedges.  Draping willows form an arch over the roadway.

The drive is quiet this time of night, an occasional traveller wearily plodding down the drive toward the lower reaches of the city and the comforts of home.  Soft lamplight radiates from the polished lanterns burning along the great wall.

The great wall culminates here with the large and stately Por'oson Gate.  Day and night, streams of travelers find paths through the gate to the agricultural lands and great forests to the northeast, or find access to the ports of the city below.  A pair of wary guards watches the comings and goings here, constantly alert to potential trouble.

The pace of traffic is chaotic at times as the drive approaches the Por'oson Gate.  Travelers mill about asking directions to their destinations or seeking transportation to the distant locales beyond the city limits.
Bleached timbers and stone form the retaining wall that channels a constant flow of travelers to and from the great city gates.

A low ivy covered wall brings the expansive greenery of the terrace into view as the drive skirts the northeast border of the lovely Deversham park.  Toward the southwest the beauty of the ocean catches the eye of all who traverse this section of town.
