The stench of rotting paper emanating from two ceiling-high bookcases makes the thick air difficult to breathe.  Standing like a sentinel against the ravages of decay and time, a massive ironwood desk dominates the western wall.  Moldering black velveteen drapes, having failed in their task to shelter this room from the elements, hang in tatters about a stone archway leading out onto a balcony.

Providing a view of the wilderness and the temple gardens below, the scene from the balcony gives one pause to contemplate the workings of the gods.  Simple in construction and design, surrounded by a crumbling stone railing, this north-facing balcony was intentionally exposed to the harsher elements.  Blowing winds from the north reach through the slits in the railing and swirl about the balcony in a harsh whisper, speaking of long-kept secrets or messages forgotten to the living.

The forest clearing is devoid of life -- not a single plant, bird or insect can be heard or seen.  Skeletal remains of careless animals lie at the edges of the clearing, silent reminders to the supernatural qualities of the area.  Rising in the center of the clearing is a small mound, atop which stands a structure made of polished black onyx.  Thirteen stones, each carved with a symbol, make a rough staircase up to the entrance of a mausoleum.

The stale air mixed with the scent of desiccated flesh is overpowering.  This corrupted odor, one that only the dead are wholly familiar with, threatens to leave living intruders gasping for breath.  Faint light barely penetrates into the structure, creating spectral shadows that dart about with every move.  Simple plaques, green with verdigris, are fitted to the capstones that line the walls.  A stray ray of light reflects upon a golden urn resting atop a serpentine pillar at the head of the chamber.
A large bramble patch seems to block any hope of movement to the south.  In the thick loam beneath the trees a barely visible path heads northeast.

The trees thin out a little here giving more light to the undergrowth.  Several clusters of bright red, sharp yellow and deep blue flowers help break up the green and brown monotony of the forest.  To the north through the tree tops some mountain peaks are barely visible.

A jagged stump as large around as a table sticks dangerously out of the ground.  It looks as if a group of mad lumberjacks hacked at a tree with hand axes before the upper portion finally ripped away from the stump.  Leading from the stump, deep ruts in the ground head northeast.

The path is marred with deep ruts which lead to the ragged end of a large felled tree.  Some of the tree's branches have gotten caught on the surrounding bushes preventing it from being dragged any further. Fortunately, the tree was shoved somewhat off the northern side of path giving barely enough room to continue northeast.

The path disappears here amid small bushes and tall trees.  High overhead, a battered hip boot swings casually in the wind apparently caught at the ankle by a snare.  More tripped, but empty snares dangle from various tree limbs, silent testimony to their makers lack of skill.

Broken and trampled branches are the only signs of a trail winding through this large bramble patch.  The torn and bloody remnants of a cloak snagged on the sharp bramble needles mark a failed attempt to forge a new path.

An intrepid bird has made a nest high up in one of the stunted trees.  The nest is a marvel of engineering, clinging to the branches with grass and vines and mud-plaster.  That it's survived the steady, strong winds way up here speaks well of the stubborn bird who built it.

Wind-blown grit has sculpted the stone into fanciful shapes, scouring out the softer stone and leaving the harder layers ridged and twisted.  One spire looks rather like a chess piece from the right angle.

The road gets thinner and less worn here, with only a few small wooden houses at its side.  Children play on the lots in front of homes, running and laughing, making the whole area have a relaxed atmosphere.  Curls of smoke rise from homes carrying with them the smell of meals being prepared.

Buildings thicken this area of the village, making it seem larger than it really is, but the forest still looms at the edges as a reminder that this is still nature's part of the world.  Hammers banging and the smell of tanning oils penetrate the air giving the feel of work and little leisure.  The occasional trader or inhabitant walk down the road, intent on their destination.
To the north, the dense forest is interrupted by a dry creek bed running roughly east and west.  The edge of the creek has eroded creating a gentle slope down to the bed.

It's been some time since water has flowed through this creek bed.  The hollows and low points of the bed have filled with leaves and dirt.  The southern lip of the creek has eroded creating a gentle slope up.

In sharp contrast to the thriving forest to the north and south, a small, lanky flowering bush clings to life on the rocky bed.  Though sunlight is plentiful, there is barely enough soil or water to sustain it.

From the west, the sounds of flowing water and a flash of blue indicate that a river is close by.  The silt and sand partially covering the creek bed and a few small pockets of fresh water suggest that the river level sometimes raises enough to allow water up this far.

A wide band of smooth rocks and pebbles runs between the placid river to the west and the dense forest to the east.  When the river is at its fullest, this area is probably underwater.  A couple of fishing poles have been propped up near the water's edge, their lines trailing far downstream.

Completely oblivious to any other activity, a pair of ravens argue over a single shiny rock embedded in the creek bed.  At various times, each one manages to land briefly and work at prying the stone loose before the other swoops down and knocks its competitor away.
Dusty footprints weave back and forth between the banks of the creek bed.  The partly exposed roots of a tree up on the north bank serve as a reminder that once water flowed swiftly through here.

The ground slopes abruptly down from the creek bed into a small fen.  Once a large pond, a slow decrease in water has allowed marsh grasses and flowers to flourish.  The sounds of crickets and frogs fill the air with a pleasant melody.

The foul smell of long standing water and decaying plants fills the air.  A boot lies half buried in the thick, goopy mud that covers the area.  To the north, a mountain range looms over the tree tops.

A shallow algae-filled pond occupies the center of this area.  Dragonflies buzz around, darting up and down over the water before disappearing amid the tall marsh grass.  To the north, the upper peaks of the mountains can barely be seen above the forest.
The forest to the north is eagerly encroaching on the marsh grasses and flowers.  Several young saplings compete for sunlight and air with a variety of bushes.

The remnants of a beaver dam occupy much of this area.  Marsh grasses and a few small bushes push up through the graying tangle of tree branches and sapling trunks.  Amid the wreckage are signs of bird nests and small animal burrows.

A high bank overlooks the dry creek bed to the south. At some point the bank eroded, partially exposing the roots of a tall satinwood.  When the breeze tugs at the tree's upper canopy, the tree creaks ominously and the ground shudders slightly.
The air is heavy with the vanilla-sweet smell of some flowering bushes that cover the area.  Hummingbirds dart among the pale yellow flowers, stopping now and again for a sip of nectar.

The trees line both sides of the path, arching together to form a mottled green canopy overhead that looks more like the ceiling of an elaborate temple.  Flowers and ferns carpet the area beneath the trees.

A few blackened tree trunks stand in a large burned out area.  The tallest among them has been split in two apparently by a lightning bolt.  Half the trunk remains standing while the other half lies twisted and scarred among the burned out undergrowth.

A large wilted bramble bush looks oddly out of place among the ferns and satinwood trees in the area.  Even more odd, what looks like its roots, still partially covered in dirt, stick out from the top of the bush.

The path ends suddenly in a large pit.  Part of the pit is covered by a motley arrangement of tree branches barely concealed by a thin layer of dirt, leaves, and uprooted bushes.  At the bottom of the pit, sharpened poles and jagged edged rocks point ominously upwards.

The southern end of the path disappears abruptly under a large wilted bramble bush.  A few shriveled berries and flowers still cling to the bush.  Around it, the other vegetation grows strong and lush beneath the satinwood trees.
Bramble bushes compete with cinnamon ferns for light and space between the trees.  Something has been helping the ferns along by ripping out and discarding some of the larger bushes.

The tall trees thin out, allowing the mountain range to the north to come suddenly into view.  In the forefront a long ridge heads sharply up towards the closest peak.  In the far distance to the east, the top of a smoking volcano can barely be seen.

Crude drawings of hunts, battles, and weapons cover a large outcropping of rocks.  Those drawn with chalk or paint are faded and partially gone, while others, carved into the surface, seemed destined to last forever.
A loud crashing and thrashing from the bushes startles you.  Suddenly, several deer come leaping across the area.  In the distance can be heard a cougar's snarl, then an all too-brief bleating.
The path again disappears as the bushes and other undergrowth close in beneath the trees.

The rocky outcropping contains a small pocket of fresh water.  Around the water, bold red and creamy white lilies flourish.  Tracks of animals large and small can be seen in the mud at the water's edge.
The path threads its way through, over, and around large rocks and boulders.  If it weren't for the looming ridge to the north, it would be difficult to keep track of directions.

Part of the ridge has given way, partially covering the path.  A wedge of land slid down the side a little way, leaving the trees and bushes in the wedge still standing, while those at the edge lean precariously at different angles.

The path turns sharply here heading to either side of the ridge.  On a small hill to the northeast, a couple of large figures seem to be observing the path from a look-out platform built among the trees.

The ridge is not very steep here, but dense undergrowth still prevents anyone from climbing it.  The trees are not as tall or as dense as in the lower forest, but there are still satinwoods and oaks mixed in with redbuds and dogwoods.
The path begins to slip away from the ridge towards a small valley nestled between the mountains.  In the distance, a couple of smoke plumes rise above the forest before dissipating in the wind.

There is a rustling sound in the undergrowth beyond a fallen tree.  Suddenly, up pops a squirrel.  He climbs up on the tree, stares around for a bit, then starts licking and cleaning his fur, pausing only to sniff at a tree beetle crawling nearby.

An old wooden fence blocks the path continuing west.  A half-open gate barely hangs on a post with a couple of shredded leather hinges.  A gust of wind or a swift kick would probably knock the whole thing over.

The path crosses a large grassy clearing with a few scattered fire pits.  Off to one side, the bed of a wagon lies abandoned on the ground.  A broken axle and a couple of wheels are half-hidden in the taller grass nearby.

The chirping and chattering of hundreds of sparrows in the trees above is almost deafening.  Startled by something making noise in the bushes below, they suddenly take wing.  In several large groups, they fly in and around the trees before settling back down.
The trees and undergrowth are so thick that little can be seen beyond the faint path.  Ivy has grown at least part way up most of the trees, and sometimes between them, forming living veils.

An occasional glimpse of distant peaks can be caught through the leafy canopy to the north.  The sounds of birdsong are muted, with only a faint melody breaking the silence.  A dry streambed cuts across the forest floor, spanned by an old rope bridge that sways gently in the breeze.

The bridge creaks ominously underfoot.  Jagged rocks fill the gully below, waiting for anyone foolish enough to tempt fate.  Rolling hills are evident to the north, while a wall of trees presents itself south of the bridge.

A lone Gor'Tog stands motionless, his dark leathers rendering him almost indistinguishable from the surrounding underbrush.  The sentry's eyes scan constantly for signs of danger, the slightest movement instantly drawing his attention.  A low wooden building can be glimpsed off to the west, while to the north the thinning forest gives way to hills.  A rope bridge spans a dry gully south of here.
An array of weaponry, mostly clubs and spears, lean against the side of a dilapidated shack.  Muffled thumps from inside betray the presence of at least one occupant.
This beaten dirt path threads its way over lightly wooded hills.  Outskirts of a small settlement can barely be made out to the north, against the backdrop of jagged peaks.

Several fierce-looking Gor'Togs loiter about the entrance to a small cave.  Dressed in brightly dyed leathers and carrying an impressive amount of weaponry, the Gor'Togs appear ready for battle at a moment's notice.  The crackling of an open fire to the east fills the air.

Rolling hills give way to wooded plains, the sounds of the forest a welcome relief from the bustle of the Gor'Tog settlement to the north.  A beaten dirt path, worn from years of heavy use, leads deeper into the primeval wood.

Scorching heat rises from a roaring bonfire at the center of this sandy pit.  A huge boar slowly rotates over the fire, sending the scent of burnt flesh wafting into the air.  An elderly Gor'Tog, immensely strong despite his years, turns the spit with a steady rhythm.

Caves honeycomb the rocky hills, providing shelter from the elements for the many warriors who inhabit the area.  Gor'Togs cluster about, yelling to one another in booming shouts.  Boisterous laughter splits the air, its origin impossible to determine.  One particularly large cave entrance draws the eye.

Wooden buildings, a rare sight among the many cave dwellings, huddle about a clear pond.  Though unadorned, their construction seems sound enough.  Fingers of grey smoke curl into the air from the top of an unobtrusive shop.

Towering mountains block out the sky and create a natural barrier protecting the Clan's flank.  A wrought-iron gate, undoubtedly imposing in any other setting, pales in comparison.  The portal seems oddly out of place amidst the rocky crags.

Knives of all shapes, sizes, and descriptions occupy every available surface in this tiny shop.  Care must be taken to avoid any sudden movement, or painful consequences may result.  But despite the eccentricity of his establishment, Tobb the smith is almost revered by his patrons for the detailed craftsmanship with which he goes about his work.

Gnarled branches claw at the air, and tangled roots seem intent on tripping the unwary.  The fresh spoor of large game is apparent, a sure sign of plentiful hunting.  A beaten dirt path leads back to the settlement.

A circular clearing has been carved out of the dense wood, the lumber apparently used to construct the cabin that fills most of this break in the forest.  Constant battle is obviously waged to prevent the surrounding underbrush from encroaching into the area.
The wind lends a biting chill to the air as it whips through the trees.  An eerie whistling originates from some oddly-shaped reeds.  Perhaps because of the sound, wildlife seems to avoid this area.

Ancient trees soar skyward here in the heart of the primeval forest.  The mammoth trunks dwarf even the Gor'Tog hunters that frequent the glade in search of game.  One blackened stump pays testament to the violent storms that sometimes frequent these lands.

Pale grey mosses grow in curtains among clustered trees.  A black squirrel chirrs happily to himself as he scampers across an overhead limb.  With a heroic leap, the squirrel hurls himself through the air, only to land triumphantly moments later on a distant branch.

A few taffelberry bushes have managed to find a niche here in the shadow of looming trees.  From the bushes' rather barren appearance, the local wildlife has acquired quite a taste for the sweet berries.

Low tables are pushed up against bare rock walls in this natural cavern.  Carefully tanned furs and leathers are arranged haphazardly about the area, no thought having been given to a proper display.  Bukor, a Gor'Tog of great skill but suspect taste, is well known in the Clan for his temper.  He knows his work is excellent, and expects to be compensated accordingly.

A pine counter liberally spattered with a muddied rainbow of colors blocks passage deeper into the room.  Near a dark curtain at the back of the shop can be seen several barrels of pigmented metallic powders stacked carelessly next to a large bucket of half-dried paint.  Klurge, the proprieter of the operation, stands behind the counter, watching incoming customers with suspicious eyes.  A color menu list is nailed to the wall to the left of the exit.

By far the largest cavern in Trefan Iltesh, this vast cave serves as both a central meeting place and, more frequently, as a giant arena.  Opponents square off in the middle of a roughly circular pit carved into the rocky floor while onlookers gather about the edge and hurl insults or cheers as their champions' fortunes change.  Smaller caverns breaking off from the main cave lead in several directions.

The sharp "CRACK!" of clashing weaponry echoes madly through this rocky chamber.  Almost palpable waves of heat roll off grim-faced Gor'Togs as they flail at one another in preparation for their trials in the arena.  Despite their bulk, opponents dance nimbly through the natural obstacles formed by thrusting stalagmites.  A few heavy boulders have been pushed into one corner of the cavern.

The dim light from a few flickering torches is not enough to cut through the gloom that pervades this cramped alcove.  The cold stone walls seem to close in on all sides.  Against the far wall leans a carved granite statue of a fierce weasel, its small size oddly out of place among the giant Gor'Togs that inhabit these caves.

The cramped room smells of baked goods with fading notes of an antiseptic.  Standing torches illuminate the whitewashed floor and matching stone walls.  Darker stains can be seen beyond the coating of both, a testament to the lifetime of surgeries and triage that were once performed here.  Now, the sounds of such medicine are replaced with the rhythmic pounding of herbs in mortars and stirring of medicines and batters in large bowls.

Sagging cots are strewn about this tiny shack.  Off duty sentries catch a few precious moments of sleep while they await their shifts.  Only a few of the mattresses are presently occupied, but the sheer bulk of the slumbering guards is impressive.

Rough-cut logs with sharpened peaks reach across the rough stone walls to block further passage though the pass to the north.  Thick curls of black smoke spiral into the sky from beyond the makeshift walls of the outpost, the air filled with the pungent aroma of blood sausage and smoking cedar.  In the direct center of the fortification, a massive gear gate has been sandwiched between the sharpened log walls, reaching across the valley to slide seamlessly into the black rock walls of the valley.

Massive rough-cut logs span the gap between the black walls that frame the valley, slipping neatly into reinforced niches cut into the rough stone facade.  Discolored patches of grey wood have been hammered into the frost-covered surface of the log walls, mending countless cracks were the frost has managed to split its unfinished grain.  The dull chatter of life within the outpost is carried upon the air, rumbling just above the distant howl of the icy mountain gales.

The sheer wall of black stone curls high overhead, ending in several rows of curved spikes.  A thick layer of frost covers the uneven ground underfoot, and is lightly littered with rubble of various shapes and sizes.  A bitter wind sweeps along the curving wall of the valley, carrying shimmering flakes of snow upon their unseen currents.  Curious formations of ice rise from the ground at skewed angles, their mirror-like surfaces refracting the available light.

The valley grows narrow as it curls southward, splitting the path into a jagged pattern as it weaves back and forth between the blocky stone sides of the gorge.  A thin layer of frost-covered rubble is haphazardly strewn about the remains of a few tents left in ruin.  Small flecks of grey and black ash cover the small drifts of snow resting at the base of the wall, slowly swirling across the ground in the invisible currents of chill air.

The valley grows narrow at the southern end where a section of wall has collapsed, cutting a pathway though the black stone.  Softly shimmering in the available light, ice crystals cling to the black rock outlining the passage though the jagged stone.  To the north, the walls of Raven's Point rise in the distance, dwarfed beneath the massive slopes of the white-capped Himineldar Shel.

The twisted passage meets abruptly with a dense forest, the tangle of branches winding amongst the razor-sharp pinnacle of stone.  An icy wind sweeps briskly though the narrow passage with a low howl as it cuts through the stone to the north, causing the foliage of the canopies to rustle softly.  Thick creepers wind over the exterior of the stone walls, forming a natural archway over the gaping maw of black stone.

Stones and rubble near the midline of the valley are cleared to make way for the battered remains of a war camp.  Battle-worn tents, partially collapsed and decayed from extended exposure to the elements, are arranged in narrow rows around frozen remnants of campfires carved into the ground.  The chill wind sporadically sweeps from the heavens to meander though the valley, hitting the frost-covered fabric with a dull rustle.

The frost-covered remnants of several broken crates rest in a heap along the back valley wall, their weather-worn surfaces painted with a faded blood-red insignia.  Small patches of slowly shifting snow rest in wind-lashed drifts.  Gentle wisps of white crystals dance across the ground with each errant breeze.

Countless pikes, splattered with rusty stains, are partially buried at the foot of the rough-cut wall that surrounds the outpost.  Narrow gaps are cut in the black stone of the valley walls, just large enough to allow the sharpened logs to slide securely into the stone niches, giving the structure added stability.  Weather-worn Dwarves patrol the parapets along the interior of the walls, several of them sporadically resting to take a long drag from the curved pipes clenched between their teeth.

The frigid wind slides smoothly across the rock walls that enclose the valley, pulling shards of ice and compacted snow from the rough surface.  A massive boulder of the same black rock found within this valley rests securely in a narrow divot cut into the ground, covered in narrow gouges that crisscross along its rough surface.  In the gentle dusting of snow covering the ground several clawed prints follow the shadows along the edge of the valley leading northward towards the outpost.

The densely packed trees tower above the winding path, their canopies growing together to cast shifting shadows along the rocky trail.  The rustle of leaves trickles down from the lush treetops as flying squirrels leap from branch to branch, chattering noisily as they jump though the sea of green leaves.

Rugged roots from the surrounding trees protrude from the ashy brown soil underfoot, having been exposed by rainwater flowing down the slanted pathway.  A cracked leather boot rests lodged between two intertwining roots the size of a Gor'Tog's arm, giving warning to those who choose to incautiously traverse the pathway.

Every so often wind rolls though the area, sending several of the leaves lining the ground rolling along the reddish-black and burnt amber leaf cover.  A distant floral aroma lightens the overbearing musk of earth that hangs like mist on the air and slowly meanders though the wood upon the soft breeze.

Following the snake-like curves of the rocky pathway, the mammoth trees press in close to one another as they fight for any available space on the forest floor.  A gentle rain of leaves slowly drift to the rocky ground from the canopy above, landing amongst the carpet of organic decay already underfoot.

Through a narrow gap in the canopy to the north, a monstrous snow-capped mountain dominates the sky.  Gentle beams of light trickle though the random breaks in the deep green canopy overhead as its swings gently in the breeze.  Distant cracks and snaps echo in the distance, their source remaining undiscovered in the thick tangle of brush and leaves.

The pathway widens somewhat to the south, as the trees file close to the rocky pathway cut though the dense forest, forming a living wall of wood.  Near the center of the clearing, a small rock shrine rests amongst numerous colorfully painted stones and several bundles of dried flowers.  Bamboo wind chimes, hung with a several black crystals, dangle from a low-hanging branch above the center of the clearing, clacking softy in the gentle wilderness breeze.

Northward lies a heavily forested region cast in shade so deep it's hard to see more than a score of yards in that direction.  To the south the forest is not so dense, although the trees and the ridges still limit the line of sight.

The road dips slightly between the path north through the forest and a steeper rise to the southeast.  Off to one side, victim of some misfortune, sits an abandoned wagon -- or what's left of it after passersby have stripped it of usable parts.

The top of the ridge has been cleared of trees where the road crosses, revealing a sweeping vista of jagged, snow-capped mountains to the west and north, the Himineldar Shel and its Dark Pass.  To the southwest, a lone hill rises above the plain.

A steeply inclined road joins the top of a ridge to the west to the stream that runs through the valley.  The ridge is thickly forested with long-leaf pines, hemlocks and some mountain laurel, but the woods seem thinner toward the top.

The mud of a lower bank to the west is marked with footprints and wagon tracks, evidence of a pretty steady flow of traffic.  Probably many of those feet, sore from their wayfaring, have found refreshment in these waters.

The comfortable current and the pebbly bottom of the shallow stream make about as good a road as any on this long trek.  The bank is high and undercut to the west, and the water deepens to the south, making both of those directions look chancy.

A pool of friendly dimensions is a welcome spot for a dip or a bath, if one doesn't mind the chill mountain water.  Green fronds ripple on the bottom of the pool, clouds of minnows scatter and form, and now and then a larger fish swims into view, all distinctly visible through the clear water.

A shallow stream running down the valley crosses the road, its banks decorated by leafy ferns.  Frogs call, birds sing and dragonflies dart and hover over the water.  To the southeast, the road runs uphill through a big meadow.
Scrub brush and low saplings flank the road at the lower, western end of a big clearing, not far from a stream in the valley.  Higher up, the meadow looks freer of the encroaching forest.

The road crosses the eastern end of a big clearing, an unusual sight in the wooded foothills.  No mark of axe or saw can be seen, so the lea must have resulted from a natural event, perhaps a forest fire.  Downhill to the west, saplings around the edge show the slow return of the trees, and in fifty years no trace will remain of the meadow.

A mountain spring has been cleaned out near the road and piped into a stone trough, making the cold water available for man and beast alike.  The overflow from the trough runs downhill into the forest, away from the road, which follows higher ground.

The tread of many, many patient boots and hooves has worn the roadway down, and it crosses the top of the ridge several feet below the shoulders on either side.  The sunken path and the surrounding forest dim the light guiding the traveler's way, even on the brightest day.

Although the road is not terribly steep, a dislodged stone or a kicked pine cone may well roll a good distance before coming to rest.  One might enjoy a good view of the countryside from here, midway up the side of the ridge, were it not for the thick stand of pines that lines the road.

Obstinate ridges run north and south, frustrating travelers whose journeys go from east to west and back again.  One such ridge to the west forces the road through several switchbacks along a forested hillside.

The road occasionally greets a tilled field, but for the most part, scrub grasses separate stands of trees.  The groups of sumac, laurel, birch, and a few firs are denser and more numerous to the west than to the east.

A boldly carved wooden figure stands on a polished sandstone slab in the middle of the road, surrounded by piles of drying flowers, food, and other offerings.  A circle of benches surrounds the statue for those who wish to break their journey for rest or reflection.

On each side of the road is a colonnade of yew trees whose lines extend a fair distance to the east and whose fallen needles hush the noises of the road.  Whoever planted the big trees wanted something impressive, even showy, and they serve the purpose well.

A short avenue of yew trees leads to a low pile of rubble.  It must have been a noteworthy manse at one time: the extent of the remains, the carriage drive before what was its entrance, and the circle of sheltering trees all bespeak a residence of importance in the region.

Yew trees line the road, bordering it in a stately procession to the west.  A carpet of their fallen needles cushions the wheel or foot that travels in their shade.  Judging from their size, the trees have a few years on them and were obviously placed by design rather than nature.

Fields to the north and south of the road look cultivated, or at least were tilled some short time in the past.  The road is in good repair, which argues for a local population that takes on the task of maintenance.

Rolling plains stretch to a range of faraway mountains on the western horizon.  The road, however, links the bluff and the rising ground to the northwest, a region of low ridges and small groves of trees.

Scattered groves of pale-barked white oaks yield to seemingly endless waves of golden plumegrass and threadbrush.  With a slight swish and hiss, the grasses quickly close over any evidence of passage.

The lilting song of a savannah sparrow drifts occasionally through the air, the notes falling in a crystalline cascade so sweet and sharp that the sound lingers for long moments.  Passing breezes move through the thin-bladed grasses to create a constant soft whisper that just touches the edge of awareness.
A basalt-studded bluff looms over the savannah, lifting above the ocean of grasses.  Scrub oaks cling tenaciously to its sides, obscuring the base of the sun-blackened boulders at its crest.

A barely visible game trail climbs the bluff, threading between sun-scorched slabs of basalt thrust upward by some ancient upheaval.  A canopy of oak with an understory of shrubby hawthorn crowds the trail as it reaches a level stretch of ground that is churned by cloven hoofprints.

The barest trace of a game trail wends its way through undulating waves of grasses, their green-gold hues punctuated by the dusty orange of globemallow blossoms.  Gusty breezes whisk brittle seed pods along the ground, transporting the embryonic plants to some distant new home.

Each of countless blades of grass is gilded by sunlight, creating a shimmering vista that spans the earth in all directions.  A sprinkling of fast-moving clouds scatters a changeless yet ever-changing pattern of brightness and darkness over the landscape.

The tall, lavender-spiked plumes of windfeather plants rise in thick clusters, their silvery-green stems anchoring the gossamer strands of hundreds of spiderwebs.  Given the blossoms' attraction for moths and butterflies, the little webspinners have made a wise choice of location.

Thick-spiked windfeather and mature bluestem create a tapestry of purple and russet that stretches to the horizon, competing with the vastness of the sky.  Occasionally, the joyful, raucous yips of coyotes can be heard as they hunt for field mice or create their particular and unique brand of trouble.

Patches of ricegrass peek out from amongst the loftier bluestem, ruffled edges heavy with the whitish buds that create its name and attract foraging antelope and bison.  Overwhelmed by the heavy growth, the trail ghosts almost entirely away.

The trail fades into a narrow channel left by the course of a long-ago flash flood, though a network of tracks on the other side indicates that it continues.  Nearly overgrown with a lush tangle of evening primrose bushes, the channel still bears the marks of the torrent that created it.

Ridges in the earth mark the place where water once flowed, and will likely flow again if rains are heavy.  Thanks to the presence of a bare trace of silt left behind by the flood, ghostflowers inhabit the sides of the channel.  The rounded, bushy plants are crowded with translucent, pale yellow blossoms in branched clusters.

Screens of grass part to allow passage but quickly close ranks again, as though reminding travelers that they are merely visitors in this place.  Trilling through the bright air, the sonata of savannah sparrows and meadowlarks accompanies the sun as it stakes its claim on the prairie.

The tawny expanse of grasses is broken by the dark crowns of several oak trees nearby.  Clumps of coyote mint thrust themselves up amongst the grasses, permeating the air with a sharp-sweet scent when crushed underfoot.

Goldenbell vines swirl along the ground in intricate patterns of jade and bright yellow, sending long, delicate runners of pale green in all directions to establish areas of new growth.  Cloven hoofprints stamp their own design around the borders of the living tapestry as the game trail widens slightly.

A litter of acorns and leaves cloaks the ground beneath a prairie grove of venerable white oaks, their bark like burnished silver in the light.  Beyond the grove, the plains are awash in the cheerful yellow blossoms of brittlebush and the burning red blooms of firefall vines.

The faint smell of burning wood can still be detected from the scorched innards of the oak.  Snapped like a gidii's wishbone, one half of the gallant tree still stands while its counterpart lies listless upon the ground.  Small birds have taken up refuge under the fallen branches and dart to-and-fro through the newly created underbrush.

Despite the violent event that cleaved it, the upright half of the tree remains strong and firm as if it were standing by sheer will alone.  Like a stage prop, the western face of the tree appears to be as normal as any other tree, while the flat eastern face is nothing more than splinters and the charred innards of a once mighty oak.  The upper leaves and branches dance with the wind and clearly appear to be less stable.

At the highest limbs, the impact of what must have been a massive lightning strike and the resulting fracture of the great tree can be measured with dramatic sways caused by the slightest of breezes.  The remains of a bird's nest is tucked amongst the top branches, but the former tenants are nowhere to be seen.

Chunks of basalt lurch at an angle along the side of the bluff, providing a set of natural steps descending from the crest to the rich soil of the surrounding grasslands below.  In the far distance, stands of oak and aspen form prairie groves -- shaded islands of darkness against the moonlit background of grasses.
The constant whisper of grasses rides the soft wind, carrying with it the tangy scent of sage.  Looking down toward the base of the bluff, low-growing soapweed clings tightly to the dark earth.

White clover and wild indigo huddle under the tall canopy of bluestem and switchgrass.  A few overturned pebbles appear scorched -- mute evidence of the lightning fires that sometimes sweep across the steppes to force their constant cycle of destruction and renewal.

Low-growing grackleberry bushes cluster close together, their white fruit tucked securely within a weave of thorns.  At their base, a warren of little holes indicates that some creature of the steppes has taken advantage of the bushes' spiny protection to make a home here.

Thickets of golden currant bushes cluster in a grouping so dense at the center that it is nearly impenetrable.  Occasional rustling noises hint that some small nocturnal denizen of the steppes is making a meal of the crimson-gold fruit.

Some creature of the plateaus came to the end of its life here; all that is left is an arch of bleached ribs rising stark and oddly graceful above a ridge of vertebrae.  Only the wind knows what manner of death this was -- and it is not telling.  Grasses and sedge grow in a tangle between the bones, pulling them relentlessly back to the quiet earth.

A yellow fawn lily creates a sudden blaze of color against the more subdued golds and greyish-green of the surrounding grass and sedges.  Barely visible through the heavy weave of vegetation is the soil of the grasslands, so rich that it is almost black.
Faint trails wind through the grasslands, leading from nowhere to nowhere.  The ground beneath the undulating stalks rises and falls, gradually sloping downward toward the north.

Foxweed sends a profusion of slender, branched stems in all directions to stake its claim, so determined and pervasive that it even climbs nearby shrubs.  The branchlets are tipped with countless tiny white flowers that send a heavy lemony scent through the air.

Tall lanceleaf plants reach skyward with spires of pale yellow flowers that loft above the steppes.  A spider has taken advantage of their height to craft a web at the corollas' upper reaches, and the number of silk-wrapped forms dotting the gossamer strands give silent proof of the little weaver's good hunting instincts.

Russet-tipped plumegrasses feather passersby with a fine scattering of pale yellow pollen when touched.  Whispering eternally in a dry sibilance perhaps understood only by the earth itself, they loom so high in some spots that the rest of the world nearly seems to disappear.

The runners of a prairie rose sprawl among the grasses, its sturdy thorns creating an effective defense against any browsing antelope or bison that might be attracted to its tender buds.  Occasionally, the scent of woodsmoke fills the air, sharp with the tang of sage.

Soaring above the steppes, the top of the bluff provides a view that affirms the vastness of these lands.  Silvered by moonlight, tallgrass and plumegrasses sweep away in all directions, rippling like a windswept sea broken by occasional islands of trees.

Clover sprigs, thistle clumps, and small bushes break the surface of the grass.  Each variety of plant battles for its share of sunlight and water -- competition is not reserved to those that go on four legs.

A valley unfolds beneath the crest of a rise.  Weeping willows and cedar trees surround the streambed that snakes through the low-lying ground.  A profusion of wildflowers dots the expanse, and trees of various types grow in protection from the wind that lashes the grasslands above the depression.

Clumps of savannah grass mingle with bluestem, their paler stalks forming a pleasant contrast in texture and hue.  Tiny paths tangle and criss-cross through the grasses -- perhaps a colony of field mice or some other small prairie denizen lives nearby.

Groundwater must be closer to the surface in this particular spot, as the vegetation shifts just slightly to more moisture-loving types.  Little clusters of purple saxifrage form dense cushions here, their distinctive maroon-tinged leaves flattened close against the earth.
A tangle of blackberry bushes sends tendrils of new growth along the ground.  Occasional rustles can be heard from deep within the mounds of vines, but the inhabitants stay well hidden.

A low hillock is cloaked with a heavy growth of blackberry bushes.  The thorny vegetation creates a formidable barrier that effectively blocks access to the top, but thins just enough at its base to allow passage.
The cadence of cicadas thrums on all sides, persistent even in the disturbance created by passersby.  The earth is strewn with the matted, grassy carpeting of the previous seasons' growth.

A tracery of delicate cloven hoofprints weaves back and forth over a small patch of clear ground, then disappears again into the shelter of the grasses.  Too small for cattle, the tracks must be from deer or antelope that take advantage of the wealth of vegetation available for grazing and browsing.

Golden plumegrass surges and breaks like waves around a large grouping of blue ash trees not far away.  Underfoot, several prairie dog holes partly hidden by the vegetation make it necessary to step carefully.

Cooling the air slightly, a steady breeze carries with it the subtle combination of scent and taste that signals water somewhere in the distance.  Soft chittering noises from several directions provide a reminder that one never travels unseen across the grasslands.

A large stand of blue ash and sycamore forms a prairie grove -- an island of trees in the midst of grasslands.  Spaced just widely enough to allow passage between them, the trees provide shelter, shade, and the sense of a world apart within their shadows.

Starlight filters down through the canopy of leaves overhead to create a haze of misty illumination that softens the edges of all it touches.  The night drops her velvet cloak over all, and the occasional sleepy chirping of birds in branches high above lends the grove an atmosphere of tranquility.

Thriving in the shelter of the sycamores and ash, bluestem and bear grass grow sweet and thick.  Purple asters and bright yellow fawn lilies are scattered like gems on the heavy carpet of greenery.  Petals turned inward in the dreamtime of flowers, their color is dimmed but not extinguished by the darkness.

Pellets of white bone and silvery-grey fur scattered around the base of two of the largest sycamores indicate that owls have found a home in the deepest part of the grove.  The masters of silent flight are nowhere to be seen -- darkness has swept them away on their nocturnal hunt.

Graceful blue ash and sycamores gather at the edges of a prairie grove, their leaves forming a lacy mosaic of light, shadow, and shades of green that shifts with each passing breeze.  From within the grove cool depths beckon, while in the meadows beyond, vast stretches of grassland provide an invitation of a different sort.

The trees thin out slightly, giving way to plumegrass that flows up the side of a rain-softened ridge of volcanic ash and red earth.  Cresting the ridge, a scattering of wild indigo and goldenrod feather their silhouettes against the sky.

Greyish volcanic ash blends with darker soil as a series of gentle ridges drops away to meet level ground occupied by closely crowded tufts of bluestem grass and coyote mint.  Tiny spine-fringed seeds cling to some of the grasses, carried there by the ceaseless breezes that play across the steppes.
The trail takes a precipitous drop from the top of the ridge.  Bushes grow along the ridge side, their roots combining with the loose rocks and dirt to make the descent treacherous.
Thick-rooted bushes choke the steep trail.  Many generations of creatures have worn the path down the side of the ridge, traveling the quickest route to the running water in the valley below.

Murky water flows to the west, funneling in from a crevice not much wider than a hand.  Silty gloom lurks at the bottom of the water, and long-feelered fish wriggle through the muck at the bottom of the stream.  A thin coating of green algae coats the bottom of the stream bed, clinging between low rocks worn smooth by the current.

Overhead, the stars seem brighter than on the grasslands, the high valley walls bringing the expanse into focus.  A parliament of owls sometimes wings by, looking for richer lark-hunting on the plains above.

Sinuous shapes occasionally flicker through the tall, thick grass as bright-eyed ferrets scour the area for food.  A half-cropped tuft of buffalo grass shades a hole in the ground that leads to the creatures' burrow.
The tough tops of the towering grass have been broken and chewed in places, but the resilient stems persist in growing.  The greenery sways with every breeze.

The tall grasses are thicker to the east and west, but a faint path is worn northward where large animals have made for the stream.  The air is redolent of lush greenery, and one can almost hear the roots unfurling within the earth as the plants grow.
Closer to the stream, the grass becomes even more lush and stands just a few hands high -- perfect for grazing.  A few vedda trees provide shade and, in times of desperation, food.
Tall, head-high grass mixes with short, broad-bladed grass emerging from the detritus at the base of the slope.  Some of the blades are crushed and broken, but most simply spring back when disturbed.
The trail leads up from the valley floor, winding along the slope of the ridge to the grasslands above.  To the northeast, the path tapers off within the grasses and trees covering the river valley.

Underneath a tumbled rock, a small nest of twigs and grass makes a cozy home for some field mice.  The creatures dart about looking for seeds borne by the wind, but scatter rapidly if anything larger than a rat approaches.

The current flows upward lightly as it hits a large bank of rough feldspar that houses numerous small fish and pockets of green algae.  Murky silt churns up from the streambed, filling the water with plumes that briefly resemble stormclouds before dissipating.  An occasional minnow darts here and there, creating a disturbance in the water and a flash of silver in the gloom.

A portion of the ridge bows into the valley, where the water curved around the hard granite that underlaid the softer limestone.  Near to the edge of the ridge, the soil is more arid.  The taller grasses begin to give up ground to their more sedate, shorter cousins.

Starflowers and wild carrots spread along the valley floor side by side with sedge and buffalo grass.  Faint trails of hoofprints meander through the grasses in no discernible direction, though to the south a trail leading up the ridge can be seen.

A few cedars stretch north toward the water.  Short-bladed grass and some sedges vie for ground cover.  A meadowlark's nest is almost hidden within the grass, its woven roof a patch of brown among the green.
Southwest, the shorter grass gives way to a taller variety as the valley rolls in a slow dip.  The grass is a thick, cropped carpet here, with divots turned up by the hooves of fast-moving horses.

Red cedar trees cling to the stream bank, surrounded by weeping willows that vie for the water.  The cedars' gnarled roots protrude into the rivulet, both stabilizing the bank and providing a convenient seat.

Weeping willows stretch their boughs over the water at the stream's head, providing shelter for a small flock of ducks whose nests dot the bank.  A number of rodents also dwell by the trees, receiving shelter from the elements.
Saplings have taken root among the tenacious grass.  The young trees are not faring well -- tufts of hair are caught in the ragged bark where horses have used them as grooming aids.
Wind whisks along the path, moving from the top of the ridge to the valley below.  It brings with it the dry dust and chaff frisked from the grasses above, and the scent of the earth.
The trail broadens from the east, until two horses could pass abreast.  The rocky path is bordered by clumps of grass and weeds on either side that cling to the sides of the ridge.
Meandering along the ridge, the trail widens to the west as it begins its descent to the valley.  Loose rocks, disturbed by passing wildlife, skitter a few feet before coming to rest again.

A gentle breeze whispers through this small space, lightly ruffling the tendrils of the thick emerald green moss that covers the ground like a rich velvet cloak.  The canopy of leaves close in protectively above, allowing only a small patch of night sky to be visible.  Emerging from the shadows, a masterfully carved totem in the image of an antelope guards a fine-grained ash altar from any peril the darkness may bring.

Crystal clear water trickles down a shallow trench in a rock like a miniature fountain, shaped over many long years of erosion.  No pool forms however -- the emerald green moss greedily soaks up every drop like a sponge, causing it to grow more densely at the end of the stream.  A detailed totem carved in the image of an antelope bows toward the thick moss, as if daintily nibbling the velvety plant.

Silhouetted against the moon-silvered sky, tents are arranged in an orderly grouping that takes maximum advantage of trees that will provide shade in the heat of the day and the partial shelter of a few low ridges.  A nearby clump of juniper lists slightly to one side, almost excavated by something that has dug underneath its low branches to create a hollow in the shadows.

Though the grasses in this area grow thick and abundant, they are closely cropped in many spots.  Even the thorny runners of prairie roses and heavy, furred bark of mesquite show signs of determined nibbling.  The air is filled with the musky scent of sheep and goats, and only the occasional stamp of a hooved foot or the call of a ewe to her restless lamb mark the quiet passage of the night's hours.

An occasional quiet growl can be heard from the herding dogs that drowse nearby, protective of the flocks throughout the night.  Moonlight glints off the edges of tender new blades of grass springing up even in heavily grazed areas, a reminder that given a chance, the prairie will prevail over this temporary intrusion.

A few young white oaks provide shelter for any of the flock that wants a resting place for the night.  The oaks' weathered bark bears a meshwork of scars in spots where rams and bucks have rubbed their horns or butted the trees in play.

A rough but clean and carefully mended blanket lies on the ground under a black oak tree, the gnawed rib bone at its center the only evidence of the blanket's regular occupant.  Wooden buckets and woven-grass ropes are stacked neatly near the entrance of a deep green felt tent with a narrow row of gamboling lambs embroidered on its entry flap.

Placed close to the shepherd's tent both for the safety of its little inhabitants and the convenience of their caretaker is an osage orangewood pen used for orphaned lambs and kids.  One end of the pen has been covered with a lattice of bent willow and juniper boughs, and the ground beneath spread with a heavy layer of soft grasses, the whole providing a fragrant nursery that is well-protected by the heavy osage thorns.

A pair of coyote pelts, each stretched taut on a bentwood rack, has been placed to dry and season in the nighttime air.  Their soft buff and silver-tipped fur ruffles in passing breezes like a warning banner to any of their kind who might consider taking an interest in the taste of lamb.

Cardamom and thyme add their spicy notes to the smell of grilling lamb carried on drifts of smoke emerging from two deep barbecue pits that flank a pale gold tent.  Designed to handle large cuts of meat, each pit is lined with river stones that must have been carried here for just this purpose.  Almost hidden behind the large turnspit placed over one of the pits is the diminutive and fierce proprietor of Horse Clan's finest eating establishment, 'The Lamb's Shank'.

A square of dirt has been carefully cleared and smoothed.  At its center a miniature fence of twigs surrounds some stick figures that, given their adornment of haphazardly placed tufts of wool, may represent sheep.  The childish pen is currently deserted, though a partially constructed twig animal left nearby hints that the young shepherd may not have gone far.

Fluttering multicolored ribbons wrapped around the poles of a midnight blue felt tent create a welcoming frame for its embroidered entry flap.  The lower sides of the tent are spangled with tiny, bright handprints, looking for all the world as though someone encouraged a flock of children to dip their hands in paint and leave their cheerful marks.  Nearby, a large mortar holds a mound of crushed nutshells that are likely being used in the process of creating dye.

Their warm golden hues blooming against the earth like flowers against the dark earth, several split willow and yucca baskets have been set out to dry before their weaver adds the traditional finishing touches of quail and meadowlark feathers to the edges.  All around are the subdued sounds of the village at night -- a woman crooning to a fretful child, the quiet laughter of a group of men chatting in a nearby tent, and the occasional bark of a watchful sheepdog.

A narrow path wends its way between the tents reserved for visitors, the carefully maintained area demonstrating that the denizens of Horse Clan clearly understand the importance of maintaining the comfort of guests who have traveled there to purchase goods or trade in horseflesh.  Near the wood-framed entry of an azure tent is a stack of neatly cut juniper, and bundles of feathers and sage wrapped in crimson yarn are hung around the entrance.

Tucked against tall fronds of plumegrass, a sage-green tent would fade nearly out of sight but for the flutter of leather-wrapped juniper sprigs tied along its sides.  Set just outside the wood-framed entrance is a large yucca basket holding a bright arrangement of yellow fawn lilies and stems of lavender windfeather.

Lacy-leafed tamarisk and yarrow huddle around the path, a composition in dusty green and dark gold.  Their slender leaves dapple a sand-colored tent with translucent shadows that flicker with movement in the playful breezes swirling constantly through the grasses.  A mat of fresh rushes near the wood-framed entrance holds a flat willow basket with an array of apples and nuts arranged on oak leaves.

A beaten path weaves between clumps of saltbrush that have been cut back to assure clear passage.  From the visitors' tents nearby comes the rich scent of fresh coffee -- a treat often offered to guests.  Just to the north, an occasional high whicker comes from the pen holding orphaned or weanling foals.

Low-growing juniper bushes form a natural hedge bordering the path.  Beneath the shelter of their bluish vegetation, a row of firewheel flowers slumbers through the night, their showy petals curled tightly shut.

Alder and spiky osage timbers form a large pen that confines orphaned foals or those in the process of being weaned prior to sale -- a traumatic process for all involved, but necessary nonetheless.  A hollowed log filled with fresh water, the pen's careful placement near a few tamarisk trees and a large patch of sweet grass are evidence the youngsters' comfort has been carefully attended to.

Birchwood stakes have been driven deeply into the ground and braided grass rope stretched between them to provide a small tethering area.  Next to the tether stands an elegant charcoal-grey felt tent with black kidskin stitched along the edges and a deep crimson doorflap.  Hanging on either side is a pair of ornate bridles crafted of tan leather and set with rows of white cowrie shells.

Climbing prairie roses have taken advantage of the presence of a few clumps of sagebrush to create a tangle of deep green leaves and pale pink blossoms, nearly obliterating the more austere sage from view.  Around the bushes the ground is nearly clear of vegetation, worn down by the constant footsteps of passing villagers.

Clay pots and jars stand everywhere, leaving just enough room to reach the entrance of a saffron felt tent painted with fine-lined geometric patterns in black and white.  Flat willow baskets hold potshards in readiness for mixing with the next batch of clay, and from somewhere behind the tent, a thin line of smoke rises to the sky.

Flanked by long planked aspen benches, a tall white tent is placed to face the tower of spears at the center of the camp.  The entrance flap is embroidered with a stylized sunburst pattern and is tied securely shut at the moment, though the size and location of the tent as well as the tracery of footprints leading to and from the vicinity indicate that it may be used for large meetings.

Painted with symbols of the hunt, a tall white tent stands behind an assortment of perches that appear to be freshly cleaned -- each constructed in the half-circle shape used for birds of prey.  Their immaculate condition and their variety, ranging from the slim arcs of woven willow that suit merlins or falconets to the heavy branches wrapped in rope that must hold eagles, indicates a culture that values its hunting birds.

Bells jingle softly, the sound resonating through the air as the hunting hawks and falcons put out to weather shift about on their perches.  None of the birds are hooded at present, so their perches have been placed well away from each other to ensure that the larger hunters don't make meals of their smaller relatives.

A half-circle of spears wrapped in white and saffron silk and topped with crimson-beaded cougar skulls arcs around the entrance to a stately tent of white felt with a flow of shaded blue beadwork along its sides.  Streamers of white horsehair and brilliant azure feathers tied with black silk cascade from the entrance poles, and near the doorway is an oak stand holding a tall sandalwood bucket with silver crocodile heads affixed to the rim.

Growing thick and fragrant, a tall hedge of prairie roses crowns an embankment that drops to a dense stand of sycamore trees, signaling water somewhere nearby.  A narrow pathway pierces the vegetation to form a shadowy tunnel that meanders down through the thicket, a secret highway nearly hidden from view.

Rising above the grasslands is a dome-shaped tent of dazzling white felt cloaked with panels of heavy gold silk embroidered in blue, black, and scarlet -- the Wind Elf colors of sky, earth, and the spirit world.  Angled to face the rising sun, the entrance is flanked by a pair of jade jaguars.  Perched atop tall aspen poles with their tails gracefully looping downward, the great cats, amber eyes watchful, crouch in eternal vigil.

Placed between the four white tents at the heart of the village is a stack of horse skulls, each gleaming with beadwork of black, gold, and scarlet.  Arching over them are six great silver-tipped spears wrapped in white and yellow silk and lashed together to form a tower that lifts imposingly against the sky.  At the tower's apex, long streamers of silver-beaded white horsehair flutter in the passing breezes, casting a veil of moving shadows over the ornately decorated skulls beneath.

Behind the horse-trader's tent a moonlit stretch of grassland beckons, level and wide.  At the near end, an oak wagon wheel and an alder wagon wheel mark the beginning and end of an obstacle course inviting those who wish to put a mount through its paces.  Just past the course, a beaten track laced with hoofprints provides an opportunity for checking gait and speed, or simply enjoying a gallop.

A great fire pit dominates this area, as wide as a small cottage and deep enough to hold a stack of cordwood topped with a thick layer of pinecones and nettles, the whole crowned with a dome of smooth river rocks.  Just behind the pit is a low hut crafted of bent green aspen poles and covered with layered hides and juniper boughs.  A narrow channel has been dug between the double row of logs forming the base of the hut.

A single sycamore stands in the midst of the settlement, somehow having grown apart from its fellows in nearby prairie groves and more distant streambeds.  Someone has hung a few small wooden platforms suspended by braided leather cords from its lower branches, and the scattering of little seeds underneath reveals them to be bird feeders.

The ground slopes away into a shallow furrow cut by the flow of water during heavy rains.  Its edges are softened by tufts of sedge and shortgrass, the fast-growing plants wasting no time in establishing their domain.  The haunting call of a nightbird echoes periodically in the distance, its resonance somehow deepening the silence amongst the surrounding tents.

Propped against the side of a silvery-blue felt tent, a willow rack is draped with the long strips of marsh cane and juniper that are used in bowcraft.  Errant breezes send curls of shavings skirling about the ground near the tent's entrance, and the crisp, pleasant scents of wood and resin hang in the air.

Heat radiates steadily from a firepit just behind the potter's tent.  River stones have been piled up above the hot coals, and a planked pine framework placed over them with a second fire burning on top -- the whole creating an inferno from which the distinctive Horse Clan pottery is born.  Nearby, large baskets of cedar kindling and dried horse manure stand ready to replenish the hungry flames.

Brilliant colors flash against the ground, revealed to be bird skins stretched to dry on cane circles laid out neatly on lengths of clean felt.  Bright gold, scarlet, velvety black, and iridescent blue feathers are destined to become vivid embellishments on weapons, clothing, or baskets.

Just behind a sprawling bank of morning glory vines stands a handsome black felt tent, its entrance draped in a fall of creamy cashmere worked in a fanciful white-on-white arabesque motif.  Off to one side, a swathe of shrubs and grasses has been cleared, perhaps to make room for the rows of cashmere fleeces neatly laid across alder racks.

Opulent bands of amber and scarlet embroidery are crosshatched against the deep brown felt of a large tent that has beaded streamers of chestnut and black horsehair flowing from the tops of its entry poles.  Several low willow camp chairs with supple kidskin seats have been placed in a half-circle a slight distance from the entrance, perhaps to provide a bit of privacy for haggling and the all-important analysis of horseflesh.

Sycamore poles, still bearing their mottled green and white bark, support a canopy of deep brown felt with an underlining of pale, filmy netting that can be dropped if insects become troublesome.  Willow camp chairs and a small brass table are placed beneath, and the whole arrangement has been invitingly arranged to provide a good view of the osage pen that holds horses available for sale.

The sweet sound of water bubbles nearby as the pathway drops into a grove of sycamore, their lower branches ornamented with an assortment of felt and kidskin pouches.  Around the base of the trees, ornate yucca baskets trimmed with quail and meadowlark feathers hold fragrant sage leaves and bundles of delicate bird bones wrapped with braided grass.  A small altar crafted of deep purple osage heartwood holds a beaded hawk-wing fan framing a brass bowl filled with milk.

A grove of white-barked aspens lifts to the sky, their leaves a dance of moon-silvered green and gold.  Lashed between them is a canopy of alabaster felt edged with a row of tiny silver bells and amber-beaded feathers.  An elaborately carved sandalwood bucket filled with grain sits amidst a drift of the sweet grasses that grow thickly around the tree trunks.

Flinging rainbowed prisms of mist as it tumbles along, a little creek rushes from the grasslands beyond.  Coursing over polished stones that gleam through the clarity of the water, it finally drops into a wide, rocky basin encircled with a natural garden of moss, cinnamon fern, and wild iris.

Wooden latticework lines the white felt interior of the spacious chadir, its slats running upward to the 'sky-door' -- a circular roof opening covered with azure silk.  In this central area meant for greeting visitors, the crisp scent of grass floor mats mixes with the welcoming aroma of warm aszal and other treats set out on an oak table.  Vivid colors cloak the walls in scenes of clan life depicted on a series of tapestries, while clouded arzumos furs cover the entrances to the living areas.

The rich simplicity of the personal quarters of this aristocrat of the steppes reflects the wild beauty of his world.  One entire wall is covered by the gleaming pelt of a snow leopard hunted down on some remote, icy peak, and an amber-beaded spirit wheel hangs from the ceiling, the eagle feathers at its center swaying gently in the air.  Along the floor, the starkly elegant patterns of Horse Clan tapestries surround an oak table and a sleeping pad strewn with lush black-and-gold jaguar furs.

Quiet descends in this chamber designed for work or silent thought.  The entrance is sheltered from visitors' eyes by the ivory and gold fur of a clouded arzumos, and whirlwind-patterned baskets against the wall are filled with white sage leaves that fill the air with the warm scent of the open steppes.  A low table and chairs are the only furnishings.  Almost stark in their simplicity, they are yet as regal as any courtly furniture thanks to the rare osage heartwood from which they are crafted.

Just visible past a series of low ridges, a long plateau looms against the horizon like a cresting wave.  The steppes seem to want no part of primly terraced hills, choosing to be graced instead with this chain of bluffs stratified in thick red layers of ancient lava alternating with multicolored bands of ash-based rock.  These cliffs were born in fire.

The land surges into low, rolling hills interlaced with a gallery forest.  The startling fringe of deep green, startling against the subdued hues of the plains, indicates places where streams coursing through give rise to stands of cedar and juniper trees gathered along the water's edge.

Asserting its presence, the high desert begins to slip in amongst the grasslands.  The country eases into the color of old broken pottery, the faded green of sage, and the sunbleached white of rice grass.

Prophet trees stand tall and austere, cloaked in silvery channeled bark and multiple limbs that are upturned to the sky as though in prayer.  At the end of each branch are heavy, daggerlike leaves surrounding tiny bursts of red flowers like exploding candles.

Flowing up to the edge of a deep ravine, the land has the long, gentle lines of all ancient ground.  Distant cliffs -- reefs of ages past -- are banded in the bright red of fire coral.  The occasional call of a canyon wren trills through the air, a descant against the theme of the constant breezes.

Bordering the ravine, the track meanders to an overlook that opens over a grotesque landscape.  Ancient deposits of mud and clay have been deeply eroded by the elements, and sharp ridges have been cut into side-ridges and then further divided, as if by some mad sculptor, into intricately torturous shapes.

Angling sharply, the track dips just below the ravine's edge, as though yearning for whatever lies beyond.  The soil here is powdery and unstable, crumbling away at the slightest pressure and sending constant little torrents of sand plummeting downward.

Abruptly, the track switchbacks into the abyss of the ravine and comes to the edge of what elsewhere would be a waterway, but now is only sand.  Current once flowed here, leaving sculpted channels and riffles that look almost as though they could cascade downstream.
Fanning wide between the ravine's sheer walls, the streambed courses along deep, V-shaped gouges scoured out by flash floods and past debris piled up where it was flung long ago by tumbling water.

Upstream, a side trail crosses the streambed, dappled with a myriad of tracks mingled together in the traffic of the ravine.  The shadowed walls of rock and clay channel cool breezes along the dry watercourse.

The ravine walls loft higher, now more rock than earth.  In a flow of sand that sparkles with tiny fragments of eroded quartz, the streambed disappears in a maze of narrow sandstone passageways with perpendicular walls.

There are little worlds in the streambed -- burrows holding creatures that become active in the cool of the evening, inch-high flowerbeds of dense sedge, and tiny castles of eroded stone.  The canyon walls drop a cloak of cool shadow over everything, and the vast expanse of steppes above seems distant in this place.
Stalks as tall as javelins, a group of blue yucca tower over the dry watercourse, surrounded by a thick bed of golden poppies.  Each yucca stalk is heavily flowered with waxy white blossoms.

Where the sand is coarse it throws up dark edges, forming paths that radiate around sculpted stones or delicately paralleling cutbacks.  High above, the cliffs become surreal -- boulders are perched atop eroded, sandy spires, the whole construct looking as though it could collapse at the touch of a breeze.
Steadily, the canyon walls deepen, forking upward to the sheer cliffs and unclimbable overhangs that make up the formidable palisades of the high plains netherworld.

Further upstream, a tall wall of quartz blocks the way.  At its crest is a lip worn smooth as glass over which flash floods have poured for countless eons.  Below it is a splash basin where thundering water has hollowed out the bedrock.

At the base of the wall the still air seems charged somehow, as though waiting for the torrents of water that have so often filled this canyon with their deafening roar.  The sheer wall lofts high, with a gloss that lends the illusion of a slick of water flowing down the cliff face, though this is simply the result of stray beams of light refracting off the translucent quartz.

The wash meanders along the base of the wall as the cliffs on either side gradually gain height, throwing deep shadows that chill the air regardless of time of day or season.  Like shatter lines in glass, a delicate webwork of cracks shroud the face of the dark quartz, some widened into deep clefts in the side of the rock.

High on a grim rampart of stone, a skeleton has been suspended from a crude bolt driven deep into the rock.  Tattered robes, perhaps once red but now faded to the color of the sandstone itself, dangle in long shreds from the remains.  Its skull angles up towards the distant sky, jaws gaping in a soundless scream and empty eye sockets eternally gazing toward unattainable freedom.

Faint clattering echoes periodically between the canyon walls, a sound like stones being dislodged from somewhere above.  The shadowed spires of rock provide no hint of what may be causing the disturbances.

Sand glitters in elaborately flowing ridges and spirals as though the breezes themselves have been playfully crafting designs with its water-smoothed grains.  Yellow-flowered clusters of coyote mint grow in thick bunches alongside the streambed and gather around the base of a weathered platform.

The cleft opens into a wide passage that arches dark and smooth overhead.  A few beams of ambient light flicker in from just outside, but are quickly quenched to wavering threads, as though the passage itself forbids their presence.  The sand of the canyon floor gives way to finer silt, and cool, faintly sour air drifts in from somewhere in the darkness beyond.

The passage ceiling and walls seem to pull closer, and the air grows thick with a sickly-sweet scent overlaid with the odor of decay.  Papery rustling sounds come almost constantly from overhead, though the pervasive darkness blocks any sight of whatever is moving about.

Standing in relief against the darkness, faint streaks of sickly yellow phosphorescence glimmer along the walls, somehow eerie even though their source is just a humble moss that clings damply to the stone in great, furry patches.

Chill air whispers along the passage, plucking insistently at passersby like a petulant spirit before dissipating as quickly as it arose.  The darkness lifts enough to limn the outlines of a grotesque, towering figure incised into the rocky walls.

Like a cleansing draught, the crisp scent of sage flows in through the jagged cleft that leads back out into light and air uncontaminated with whatever has imbued its noxious presence into the stone of the passage.

On either side of a cliff face that is broken by deep clefts and jagged cracks, sheer sandstone lofts upward to explode in a myriad of spires, pinnacles, eroded flows, and delicately balanced stones.  Between the parallel walls of rock, the air is immediately still with the intricate quiet of contained space.

Water on stone, day by countless day, sculpted this honeycombed labyrinth crowned by the rim of the sky curving over the steppes above.  At its upper end, tucked among a few trees stubbornly rooted between bare rock, water pours from an underground spring that courses down the canyon and then sinks into the rocks as suddenly as it appeared.

Chanting canyon frogs, elegant white-barked aspens and lacy willows, and the maze of rock shaped like elaborate turrets all conspire to create a world apart.  Someone or something has lingered here, though -- one of the wind-smoothed walls of stone is distorted with complex etchings.

As though called down by the water, a heavily-tracked game trail drops from deep clefts in the sheer rock of the canyon wall to flank the stream bank.  Beside the trail, the stream flows like a guide.  Only inches deep in some places, it flows over a cool bed of sparkling sand.

Dividing the valley from a rolling plateau, the bluff drops down into rich lowlands and bogs that surround a winding river.  A narrow path laced with hoof prints traverses the striated bands composing the rocky face of the bluff and ends at the higher steppe beyond.

A thin band of aspen trees laces the borders of a seep -- a deep, waterlogged mat of dead moss and leaves underlying the forest-ringed wetland.  Cinnamon and royal ferns thrive in the damp, insulating detritus, and wild calla lilies lift their heart-shaped white faces to the sky.  A long bluff stretches out to the west, marking the border of higher lands.

A crude stone bridge crosses the Ilaya Gish, its surface worn nearly smooth from repeated seasons of freezing, thawing, and floods.  The riverbanks themselves have been reinforced in some places with stones placed behind heavy netting in an effort to keep the waters at bay when snowmelt runs high.  Marshy lowlands span the western banks, edging a long bluff.

Under the shadow of the Himineldar, the icy waters of the Ilaya Gish come surging out of the mountains, winding their way toward the south.  Milky with the burden of suspended minerals carried from the heart of the mountains, the river sprays fans of fine mist in the air as it sluices through the valley.

A stone croft sits near the road, its doorframe gaping empty and one wall collapsed.  Time and the icy winds have partnered to do a through job of erasing any signs of the original inhabitants, and a tangle of silverleaf vines have climbed the remaining walls, ready to begin their patient work of pulling the stonework back down to the waiting earth.

Nestled between the Himineldar Shel and the dense forest to the south is a secluded valley quilted with glimmering stretches of marshy fens.  From the valley's center, nighttime's subdued illumination merely outlines bits of trails and game paths that are quickly lost in the darkness.

The road slopes over the edge of a band of rolling hills, providing a view of the darkness-cloaked valley basin below.  Drifts of white mountain heather, blossoms slumbering through the night, grow along the hills that crest like emerald-green waves to curve behind the lowlands that stretch along the base of the mountains.

Along the edges of a lowland valley, the grassy knolls surrounding the road are so closely cropped that they must be used for grazing.  As if in confirmation, the horizon is dotted with tufts of white, grey, and brown that appear to be herds of some kind, though they are too distant to make out clearly.  Rocky hills continue to the east, tumbling up to the feet of the mighty Himineldar Shel.

A roughly-cut hillside to the west stretches to meet the tall grasses and aspen of the eastern slopes.  From somewhere beyond the hill, the wind carries the sounds of goats and sheep bleating and the occasional bark of a sheepdog to echo off rocky slopes in an oddly harmonious duet.

The road bends around the base of one of the hills, traveling through an area of thick bear grass and golden switchgrass.  Softened by the hillside, a cool breeze whispers through the brush, filling the air with the crisp scent of forests and icy peaks.

The jagged slopes of the Himineldar Shel have peppered their lower reaches with blocks of stone that somehow slipped from its grip.  Attempts to offset the toll of winter freezes and heavy rains on the road have utilized these fragments of the mountain for repairs and though perhaps a bit bumpy for cart or caravan, they provide a comfortable walk through otherwise rugged terrain.

Grassy hills to the southwest roll to meet the sweeping base of the Himineldar, their rugged, icy peaks looming over the entire northern landscape and stretching east toward Wyvern Wood and the Dragon Spine Mountains beyond.  The road is fairly well maintained, carefully curving around the base of the mountains as it navigates its way through the rough terrain.

The rocky road leads around the base of a sheer mountain, surrounded by the greenbriar brush and bear grass that cling to the stone-ridden foothills.  Nearby lie the remains of a cart, forgotten long ago by the wayside.  Only planks from the sideboard and a heavily damaged wheel are left to decay in the chilling winds that claim this trail.

The side of the mountain has been sheared away.  Shattered blocks of rock scattered among the overgrown brush hint that this area may once have been a quarry, though the lush growth of lupine among the fragments show that it is long abandoned.  To the east, thin young saplings mark the beginning of a spanning forest, while to the west, rocky grasslands roll down into a basin nestled in the shadows of the Himineldar.

Flurries of chilling wind sweep down almost constantly from the snow-packed peaks, their icy fingers seeming to search for warmth to destroy.  To the north are the majestic Himineldar -- rocky giants laced with ribbons of green trees that grow sparse and then fade away at the uppermost reaches.  A dense mist hangs around the heights, giving the mountains a hazy, dreamlike aura from this distance.  Among the wind-gnarled pines of the foothills, the road continues along its winding path.

The Himineldar Shel adorn the northwest skyline like a massive sculpture of granite that trails into the far distance.  Conifers stunted by icy winds huddle around their base, sometimes scaling up the rocks in nearly-perfect lines.
