rooms.desc: A squat, dark tunnel bored through the footings of the massive Zirelga Bridge connects the southern quadrant of Pearl Circle to the western quarter.  Barely big enough to allow two merchant wagons to pass side by side, those afoot must take care to avoid being crushed.  Oil lamps held high by heavy metal sconces illuminate the moss growing on the ceiling, and the trickle of moisture that perpetually dampens the walls.

The arc of the road sweeps west toward a cluster of buildings shouldering against the Zirelga Bridge.  Narrow wrought iron balconies and window boxes bright with flowers adorn the shopkeepers' homes built above their businesses.  The bay window of one shop, usually the stage for young women to display clothing, is dark with the curtains partially drawn.  A chink of candle light from one corner of the shop casts wavering shadows upon the mannequins clad in the fashions for tomorrow's models.

Waxed paper covers the trays of chocolates, dishes of gumdrops and bowls of marzipan prominently displayed in one of the shop windows.  A dim light filtering from the back of the store reveals the shopkeeper inside, busily scraping fudge on a marble tabletop in preparation of the next day's business.  The cobbled road curves west toward the Zirelga Bridge and away from the sparsely populated southern quadrant of Pearl Circle.

The dim light from the street torches flicker off the canal waves.  A shabby gondola landing spanning the width of the ring draws a fair business from couples desiring a romantic evening boat ride.  "Rent Here" proclaims a sign, with paint so badly flaked as to be nearly illegible.  Northward, a set of wobbly steps creaks down to the gondolas docked in the inner canal.  Across the street, a stairway southward descends to a half-sunken dock where boats tie up in the outer canal.

Tufts of wiry brown grass push up through the cobbles, and flowering weeds edging the roadside gutters wave in the gentle breeze flowing from the outer canal.  Several shadowy figures pick through the rubble littering one side of the road, no doubt "salvaging" items left in the pile created when some buildings were torn down to make way for fresh construction.  Across the street, sparkling new paint and crisp curtains adorn MAMAS, the local assay shop.

Fewer buildings jam the roadway as the cracked cobbles curve toward the end of the circle where the middle and inner canals meet.  The yards grow from tiny to small, and some homes have little lawns carpeted with neatly trimmed grass.  An old store, shaded by faded blue and green striped awnings at the windows, sags toward a young oak tree whose roots have found purchase deep in the alluvial soil beneath the city.

Night has silenced the raucous squawking, barks, growls and braying that normally screeches forth from the pet shop.  The parrots in the store window have their heads tucked beneath their vibrantly plumed wings, and the small furry animals are curled into slumbering balls.  Northeast toward the end of the ring, where few people travel or care, the cobbles gradually become loose and rutted.

Shadows from the street torches streak the nearby Dajere Bridge and canals.  The waves striking the ring's stone foundation seem loud without the normal noises of day, and the night breeze off the canal is brisk with cold and brine.  Savory aromas waft from a modest wooden building nearby.

A set of stone steps rises upwards into the terraced lawns, flanked by the waving stalks of cultivated orchids and lilies.  Opposite, a white-washed arch leads out to the street, twisted rose vines entangling themselves lovingly within the gaps of the arch's trelliswork.  Even at such a short distance, the sounds of the busy road begin to fade, absorbed by the flora as a sponge absorbs water.

Brilliant orchids dance along the edges of raised terraces, performers on natural stages that would make many a landscaper proud.  Each morning, the tiny flowers unfold to catch any breeze and sway in their dance, while each night they fold slowly and graciously for slumber.  The scene is repeated on many of the planted terraces about the lawn by a multitude of different plants, some brightly colored, others simply green.

The potent scent of brine mingles with fragrant orchids in an exotic combination, whipped by the coastal winds that swirl up from the waters of Torbis Sanhalas Bay and over the terraced slopes of the lawn.  Adding to the white of the heady flowers are silk memorial ribbons, tied at intermittent heights in the trees and shrubs and shuddering slightly in the sea breezes.

Pale and unobtrusive, a portrait of a demurely smiling Elven woman nestles snugly against the walls of foliage.  At the foot of the stand it rests upon, flowers lie, and fluttering in the trees all around are white ribbons.  A glimpse of pink winks from behind the painting -- not a flower, but the side of Torbis Sanhalas Hospital next door.

The curving walls of a one-story building embrace the lawns, the building itself closely surrounded by the lush gardens.  A few audacious vines crawl upwards, reaching vainly for the eaves.  Centered in the side of the concave structure is a mahogany door, adorned with a solemn assortment of white ribbons and a few bows.  Above the door a wreath hangs, the visible symbol of a loss.

Simplistic in design and function, the foyer serves as both a reception area and main hall, curving off in either direction.  At the apex of the curve, a multi-paneled door resides in the wall, etched with an unusual pattern and guarded by a birch-topped desk.  A white banner stretches over the door, and small bows and wreaths hang from the ceiling rafters.

Shelves line all but one of the walls, each filled with books, memorabilia, and assorted odds and ends.  A large picture window takes up the space of the remaining wall, revealing a sharp slope cluttered with orchids and day-lilies, some of which droop as if in mourning against the backdrop of the bay's waters.  The shore of M'Riss lies far beyond, details lost to distance.

A double row of bricks runs down the base of the corridor, butting tight against the exposed support timbers.  Diagrams and pictorial sequences of healing in process do a poor job hiding the unfinished walls, the parchment curling up in the miniscule breezes set into motion by passing students.  Abruptly, the papers and the hall stop, the rough timbers replaced with the smooth handrails of an open-air walkway leading to a pink structure next door.

Two ship's masts stretch between the hospital and the crescent-shaped Empath's hall, lodged firmly in the walls of each.  A sturdy walkway connects the two buildings with the mast's firm support as the pink walls of the hospital stare beneath at the slope dropping away from the Empath's hall.  Those areas of the horizon that aren't blocked by the dual structures exposes Mer'Kresh in all its splendor as well as the far shores of M'Riss.

If only for show, a thin wooden arch marks the point at which the balcony cuts into a tight angle and then changes into an open-air walkway.  The far side of the walkway collides into one wall of a pale crescent-shaped building.  A simple wooden plaque gazes across as a few dried rose petals swirl in the air beneath it.

The balcony curves around the street-facing side of the hospital, hugging tight to its arching pink surface, while the large windows that surround the hospital's domed top loom overhead, too high to reveal a sight of the interior.  Mer'Kresh is not difficult to see, as this lofty vantage turns the streets and roads into ripples on the surface of a puddle, radiating outwards from the Carillion at the center of town.

Far across the waters lies the coast, dotted with buildings and dwellings along the Ring Road.  Angling towards that shore is the aqueduct, a marvel of engineering that provides fresh water for the city.  A glance eastwards bestows a more natural scene of the far-off lands of M'Riss, while below, the waters of the bay for which the hospital is named lap against the stony rocks of the shore.

Near the domed roof high above, a circle of windows floods the hospital with natural, healing light during the day and gives a relaxing view of the dark sky during night.  A curved bench offers those tired or ill souls a place to rest and enjoy the sky that lies beyond those lofty windows.  Apartment doors along the walls show that some resident students make their homes here, near enough to be called upon at a moment's notice in an emergency.

Squares of thick glass, stacked in place of windows, distort every simple motion outside into a flailing and pulsing mimicry of light and shadow.  Copying this in static form, blue and grey stripes dive up and down the contour of the walls, only splitting apart once the ceiling ascends into the domed central hall.  The design is a potent sight, and may explain the vacancy behind the receptionist's desk.

A cushioned sofa rests under a dazzling painted landscape that graces the walls.  The vivid colors flow up from the floor in bold dashes and streaks, encircling the sofa as if each of the brushstrokes were moths flying about an open flame.  A simple red shelf is treated in similar fashion by the design, yet the artistic swirls on the wall give it a wider berth than they do the neighboring sofa.

A single gaethzen sphere serves as the area's only light source, sending soft bird-like shadows spinning slowly around the room as it twirls gently.  Directly below it, a padded wood and steel table awaits to serve the wounded, as do the white sheets hanging in the corner await to provide cover to those beyond help.  Near them, a sealed cabinet mounted on the wall faces those sitting on the table.

rooms.t: [Warrior Mage Guild, Under the Aether Dome]
rooms.desc: Thick cut-looped carpets cover the floor and a circle of cushions scattered around the water pipe provide a place to talk and watch the aquarium fish.  A tile walkway edges the walls, allowing passage through the area without leaving boot-dirt on the rugs.  One corner holds the guild leader's desk and a set of bookshelves.  The great dome of the guild looms overhead, its interior decorated with a flowery lattice-work in gold leaf and azure.

Triangular raised planting beds are set in a rough triskele with smooth ocean pebbles and crushed shell providing a walkway through the garden.  A potting table rests against one wall, with a large wheelbarrow of loam parked next to it.  Skylights in the dome above ensure enough light for healthy plants.  The aroma of floral and herbal fragrances has banished the scent of brimstone and naphtha, leaving this as the only room in the guild that doesn't smell of something burning.

Tattered bits of burned carpet have been pulled together to cover the floor at one end of the hall.  Scorched chairs and singed tables are clustered near the carpet.  The other end of the hall is starkly empty, the walls burned and gouged and the floor coated with ash.

Several knotted hangings, each worked in the shape of an animal, are tacked to the walls.  Cushions and crumbs surround a low rosewood table that matches the corner bookshelf.  The hardwood floor is uncarpeted and unremarkable, except for a splattering of green paint near the stair.

Dark tiled walkways surround a shallow octagonal pool with a fountain set in its center.  The pool's blue and green tiles create an intricate, repetitive geometric mosaic that gives the impression of looking through a kaleidoscope.  The fountain's water trickles into the pool with a lulling patter.  A cypress bench rests against one wall, with a cluster of potted palms on either side.

Airy and open, the landing's archways give a clear northwesterly view over the city and toward the carillon.  The smell of cultivated earth and growing plants wafts up from below, and partially obscures the ever-present scent of something burning.  The dome was designed with skylights to provide plenty of sun for the plants.

Airy and open, the landing's archways give a clear northeasterly view beyond the inner canal to the colorful homes and businesses nestled on the middle ring.  The sound of splashing water rising from the fountain mingles with the slosh of the canal to drown out any conversation from the lower room.  The dome is painted in blues and greens, its geometric motif a mirror of the pattern in the pool below.

Airy and open, the landing's archways give a clear southeasterly view beyond the inner canal to the break in the middle ring and the Dajere Bridge.  An occasional murmur from people passing below rises up the stairwell to mix with the sounds of the canal and "Screeee!" of the gulls.  Each quadrant of the dome's ceiling is painted with a view of the sky.

Airy and open, the landing's archways give a clear view over the city toward the carillon, and of the northern end of the Dajere Bridge.  Smoke and noise drift up from below, accompanied by the smell of naptha, brimstone, and incense.  Every so often, the conversations of people below can be heard over the racket and rumpus downstairs.  Despite regular cleanings, the dome overhead is covered with a sooty film that obscures the decoration.

A stone relief of a young barbarian dressed in fur-lined leather straddles the door.  Several raging polar bears circle the young lad, their snarls etched with meticulous care.  Behind, a tremendous fortress rises from a snowy plain and blocks some of the mountains that line the horizon.

Along the southern wall, a remarkable frieze depicts an exploding volcano flinging blazing orbs into the bay.  Several boats are lashed together in the water, just out of reach of most of the fiery lava chunks, and a wall of stoic-looking barbarians, with weapons drawn, deflect those few projectiles that threaten the vessels.  Clearly, some liberties were taken by the sculptor.

Four large statues bear the weight of the domed ceiling upon their shoulders, each at the corner of an area cleared of obstructions.  A thick length of rope encircles the area, affixed tightly to the floor to cordon off a sparring section, and to mark a boundary for contests of skill.  Clearly known as "The Pit" for esoteric reasons, there is actually nothing here that resembles a pit or sunken area.

Two large basalt statues lean forward from the wall, flanking a simple oak podium.  Both of the stone forms are identical, and each statue's face is curled in a cross between a snarl and a grin that bears rows of flat, square teeth.  Nestled on the wall between the two is a portrait of a young barbarian holding a gleaming broadsword aloft in triumph.

Textured stone lines the walls between the massive columns supporting the roof.  A fresco of a straining barbarian, struggling to drag a giant-sized catapult across the burning sands of a desert, stretches across the wall.  On one side of the barbarian, a horde of jeering Gorbesh soldiers screams.  On the other side, a small group of wounded warriors cluster, pinned down by Gorbesh arrows while they await the heroic barbarian's salvation.

More a landing than a true hallway, there is little in this tiny alcove at the top of the stairs except a reed mat on the floor and heavy cypress door.  Even the whitewashed walls are bare of everything but a few fingerprints.

White sand embedded with chunks of black volcanic rock covers the ground like soot-streaked snow.  Raised beds of esturi fruit bound one side of the courtyard, and figs grow in the bed opposite.  An obsidian fountain sits in the center of the area erupting not with a geyser of water, but one of flame.

Slate stepping stones are harmoniously laid to create a winding path through the neatly raked sand floor.  Reed mats offer a place to sit and study -- or lie and snooze.  Books are neatly arranged on a bookcase resting atop a large, flat-surfaced rock serving as a desk.

Twists of morning glory cling to the bamboo arch, nearly obscuring it in a green shadow, and a stone threshold separates the courtyard's sand from the neatly clipped common yard where these homes rest.  Each bamboo hut's exterior is nearly identical to its neighbor, giving a serene and ordered look to the small neighborhood.

Heavy double doors open onto a large, rectangular foyer.  Two stories high, the entryway to the Cleric's Guild is dimly lit by several wall-mounted lanterns.  Two thick, fluted pedestals guard each side of the chapel's double door to the east.  Low padded benches line each wall between the pedestals and the doorway to the guildmaster's office on the north wall, and the meeting room on the south wall.

The windowless meeting room holds a long, narrow table surrounded by chairs, as well as several smaller tables.  Several people sit at a corner table discussing a private matter.  Benches line the walls underneath three large tapestries depicting various gods.

Tall windows high on the north and south walls allow plenty of light into the chapel.  A plainly carved altar sits under two beautiful stained-glass windows in the east wall.  Thick red carpets hug the walls, leaving the center of the stone floor bare.  Each corner holds two floor-standing braziers for the ritual burning of sacred writings.

Neat bookshelves behind a large desk hold Eydtha's private library.  The office is brightly lit by a hanging lamp in each corner.  A thick, dark blue carpet covers the stone floor, and two padded, straight-backed chairs sit in the corners nearest the door.  The large desk holds neatly stacked papers and a small statue of a dolphin.

Tall and stately, the entrance to the guild proper looms just ahead.  Giant slabs of quarried stone support a gabled entrance which frames a door of immense proportions.  As long shadows cast their quiet presence on the arched porticos, a sense of peace and tranquility settles over the darkened building.

A magnificent room of great breadth and height is set off by smooth alabaster walls and tall arched windows that suffuse the hall with moonlight.  A huge stone fireplace commands the entire north wall with several large chairs placed strategically to take advantage of the warmth of the roaring fire.  Footfalls are subdued by several skin throws on the cold stone floor.

A beautifully carved display case fills most of one side of this narrow room.  Razor-sharp blades atop the case glint with reflected light, emphasizing their flawless condition.  Shields of all types hang closely together along the opposite wall, many bearing the crest of the Paladin guild or the D'Sel family.

A long room, appointed with dark hardwood mouldings and a beautiful woven carpet, the office exudes a quiet sensibilty.  A massive cherrywood desk commands the far end of the room, the long walk agonizing to any young squire summoned to speak with the Guild Mistress.  In each corner of the office, a large iron stand supports a fat, scented candle nestled among silver ivy vines.

In contrast with the otherwise stark architecture, the portico is softened by latticework and silvery vines.  An open window offers a glimpse of fresh cut flowers and the unmistakable smell of roasting meat.  A dirt path leads toward the east and the training fields.

Cobbled stones are precisely set into a swirling pattern around a central garden.  A large iron gate separates the courtyard from a shaded portico that leads back toward the living quarters.  Sounds of soft music, and quiet laughter punctuate this otherwise peaceful enclave.

At the top of the steps, the noise from the courtyard lessens and can only faintly be heard.  The cobblestone steps end at marble flooring.  A large ornamental rug, which almost encompasses the entire hall, lies in the middle of the floor.  This passageway does not have the look of a room with heavy traffic as dust has built up on several of the surfaces.  Several benches and chairs are scattered throughout the hall as if it were a waiting area.  A lone door sits in the far northwest corner.

Flat and black, the basalt foundations for future shops and homes fill either side of the road, their edges lined with wood guiderails.  The dark grey streaks of ash and lime mortar between the stones creates the illusion that the surfaces are cracked deeply, when in fact the specially made mortar keeps a tight grip on the individual stones.

Though the road is completed, no structures stand but for one run-down shack huddled quietly off to the side.  A constant sloshing from the canal behind the shack replaces the sounds of workers and townsfolk, and only the occasional cry of a hungry seagull breaks through the noisy water's gurgle.

Unobstructed by buildings or people, the coast of M'Riss lies serenely across the bay, Torbis Sanhalas.  Beyond the ash-colored sands of the beaches, Undogoz Mountain towers over the woodlands of the main island, a perpetual haze clouding details due to the distance.  Much closer, a series of broken and shattered fences run a circle around one of the finished basalt foundations along the street.

Thin patches of ashen dirt cover some sections of the road's flagstones, lending the area an unkempt appearance.  The assortment of tools and construction supplies remaining after the workers were done doesn't add to the concept of tidiness.  A stack of leftover bricks sits to one side of the main causeway, no longer needed now that this section of Gull Circle is nearing completion.

The most prominent feature of the end of the road is the massive bronze-wrapped tower that will, once finished, hold the northern half of the canal gate in place.  Practically a work of art, the tower stretches high overhead, holding several colorful banners aloft.  Taut ropes run from the midsection, the top, and a point inbetween, down to several metal loops along the ground.  A pile of jagged rocks, discarded from the construction of the road, lean against the ring from inside the canal.

Veering off, this section of road still needs a lot of work.  The flagstones stop abruptly as the land drops down into a shallow path, dug to create a route through the ashen soil.  Chunky gravel lines the ditch's base and is topped by another layer of rocks the size of peas in an attempt to provide good drainage under the flat stone surface when it is completed in the future.

Marbled granite boulders have been used to create a retaining wall that shores up the land along one side of the road.  Stones once carefully stacked by size and secured with mortar form a solid mass that should stand the test of time despite its rundown appearance.  Along the top, wires running between wooden fence pickets have been added to discourage the local children from exploring.

Weatherworn pallets of flagstone sit waiting for workers to return and lay them out as pavement on the sections of unfinished road.  Weeds grow in scraggly patches around the stacked stone, managing to spread despite the hardened soil.  Broken and discarded masonry tools litter the area, suggesting it has been some time since a cleanup crew has been by.

In preparation for paving with flagstones and mortar, this section of the road's gravel base has been covered with a bed of sand carted in from the island's shoreline.  Having been left too long, the once packed and graded surface is now covered in uneven ruts.  A collection of rakes has been tossed into a haphazard pile that passing seagulls have liberally decorated with excrement as they've flown by.

The trail of gravel runs alongside the waterway then swerves off towards a section of open land.  Rolling waves can be heard slapping at the footings of the Nelyn Bridge located a short distance away, filling the air with the salty scent of the water in the nearby canal.

Crunching underfoot, the hard-packed soil is covered in chunks of broken mortar and its dusty residue, carpeting the land in construction debris.  A broken-down wooden wagon stands tilted at an angle, its cargo of granite blocks slowly shifting to one side of the bed as time goes by.  Several planks, piled haphazardly nearby, are starting to show signs of rot from the island weather combined with the occasional damp mist that travels over from the canal.

Surviving despite the poor soil conditions, a tall oak was left standing to provide some shade from summer's heat to the otherwise stark lot.  A makeshift bench, built from a stack of black basalt slabs, sits close to the tree's gnarled trunk.  Judging by the trash left scattered around, workers took full advantage of the slight comfort offered to eat and watch the entertaining scenery of gondolas gliding by in the canal or fishermen struggling with their catch at the water's edge.

Granite markers subdivide this large lot into smaller sections, mapping out a strip of plots suited in size for future shops.  The ground limestone once used to connect them has now mostly worn away, leaving only a slight shadow on the hard, ashen soil to show the builder's original intentions.  In one corner, a black basalt foundation remains unfinished, waiting for mortar to secure the back wall in place.

A dented wheelbarrow lies beneath the unfinished lip of Zirelga Bridge, its handles cracked and its contents long gone.  At this stage of construction, the bridge is little more than a glorified dumping ramp, used by workers to unload their hauls of garbage.  A stone block, halfway up the support of the bridge, channels the dumped rubbish to one side.  From there, the debris is carried off to fill in holes along the road.

The swirling and foaming waters of the ocean churn against the black basalt exposed from beneath the road as a sudden transition takes place.  The rock and wooden framework of a construction in progress yields to the intermittent placement of dark stones rising from the sea.  The rectangular walls are representatives of the first stages of ring-building, and are designed to be platforms to support both workers and the later layers of stones.

Here, the road is nothing more than the top of several closely packed stone walls.  Shiny from the sea waters washing over them, the largest of the walls flank either side of where the finished road will be, and the spaces between will eventually be filled with rubble, rock and garbage.  The western most wall is severed from this section of the road by a water-filled channel, so any travel to the north must take place across the surface of the eastern one.

A huge bulge curves out of the wall, filled with gently rocking sea water.  The dark pool of water gurgles with every thrust of the waves, but the walls of its confinement keep it mainly separate from the freedom of the wide ocean.  One large stone, reinforced with wooden supports, sits directly across from the bulge on the other side of the channel that guts the middle of the road.

Beyond the mirrored twin of this road atop the walls, the ocean heaves, white-caps dancing atop its shifting surface.  Swept away by the tides, bits of driftwood bob in the currents, occasionally rapping against the sides of the stones in the walls before being pulled away and back into Eluned's caress.

The foul stench of uncovered garbage rises from a wide hole in the surface of the road, overwhelming the salty sea breeze.  A circle of gull feathers surrounds the refuse-filled pit, left behind when their previous owners swooped in for a quick meal.  Along one side, a wooden plank has been fastened down to keep the hole from swallowing runaway wheelbarrows.

Unless hidden behind the miscellaneous construction tools or stacks of cobblestones, there are no laborers working on the ring.  The deep gouges scarring the edge of the road may have something to do with this, as they are obviously not the result of any shovel or hammer.

The remains of a seagull lie dead-center in the road, torn to shreds by some predator.  Around the kill, the stones are jagged and cracked, as through something massive collided into them from above.  Wide and open, the sky is unobstructed by buildings or other structures, lending no credence to the concept that the murderer of the gull came from on high.

Looking more like a letter in Gamgweth than a street, the road splits into two halves that straddle a rubble- and water-filled pit.  The walls of the pit reveal the layered construction of Mer'Kresh: the cobblestones rest on a bed of crushed stone that in turn overlays a mass of rubble and broken rock.

Jagged basalt clamors in the surf around the bases of the stone walls, wet and sharp.  Northwards, room to walk is virtually non-existent, replaced by the chaotic piles of the black stones.  Above the rocky clutter, a wooden walkway allows workers to continue with their tasks in relative safety.  Here and south, only the flat tops of the water barrier is available to stand upon.

Except for a handful of simple tools such as shovels and hammers, there are few signs of a construction in progress.  The cobblestones are in place, and the edges of the street are lined with stone guardrails.  Only the lack of buildings betrays what work is needed, but meanwhile the empty spaces reveal an unobstructed view of the ocean.

Soldiers of the construction world, wheelbarrows line the edge of the road in tight rows.  Most of them wear the grey and white scars that a load full of stones would leave behind, while others are marked by reddish flakes of rust from exposure to the salty sea air.  For now, the burden they've carried is gone, and rest they will until they are called upon again.

A covering of dirt and pebbles partly masks the cobblestones.  Aside from a good sweeping, this section of the construction area looks in complete readiness to be opened.  Westwards, the gaping maws of open pits and unfinished street surfaces tells a different story, while southwards only the eternal rising and falling of the ocean's waves awaits.

Planks and temporary fences become border guards as Gull Circle curves along its path.  Each of the guardians vigilantly watch over one of several open gaps in the street, protecting both the workers from a fall and the pits from unwelcome additions to their contents.  A clearly defined line cuts across the road where the cobblestones stop and the underlying ridge stones are revealed.

The sounds of waves crashing down upon the stones on either side of the road is as regular as a heartbeat, pounding out a steady and noisy rhythm that drowns even the sounds of the ever present sea winds.  Though they can not be heard clearly, the winds make their presence known by whipping at whatever loose objects they find.  Far to the south of this nearby combination of sky and surf, the hazy line of the horizon lay.

The backs of the buildings and homes of Pearl Circle look across the canal at the construction in progress along Gull Circle.  Many of the structures are reinforced with stone and wood, and few have low windows despite the fact that a thief would have to risk drowning to manage a break-in.  Odd marks along the walls appear to be some form of damage, but a closer examination -- difficult to do from here -- would be necessary to be sure.

A fair distance to the northwest, the arching form of Zirelga Bridge rises easily from behind the nearby stacks of brick and stone that litter the unfinished street.  One end of the bridge disappears behind the buildings across the canal while the other abruptly stops as it juts out over Gull Circle.  Duplicating the function of the bridge in a small scale, a thick wooden board stretches across one of the pits that are so common along this section of the road.

Each of the dark flagstones paving the Carillon path has been carefully shaped for fit and appearance, which, along with the meticulous care of the plants, lends a formal grace to the gardens.  A low border of phlox edges the pathway as it continues north toward the Carillon.  Bright hued flowers to the east and west beckon visitors with their color and aroma.

A small footbridge spanning an ornamental brook interrupts the winding flow of the flagstone path.  Roses mingling with honeysuckle climb the bridge's posts and stretch across its handrails.  Tangled vines grow along the banks of the stream and knee-high shrub parterres filled with flowers border the path.  As the path curves, the carillon can be seen rising to the north east.

A barrier of hostas and ferns set between the flagstones and a fountain is wide enough to block visitors tempted to leave the path but narrow enough that with a favorable breeze someone could toss a few crackers into the water.  Speckled carp swim lazily in the fountain, some weave among the lily pad stems and some nudge against the curved bowl as if looking for a crumb of bread.  A thicket of forsythia grows between the path and the carillon.

rooms.desc: Night fails to darken the sparkle of the quartz flecks of the Carillon's sandy granite exterior, and a glow from within lights the stained glass windows.  Only the bells, normally visible through the arches beneath the roof during the day, are hidden in shadow.

Curving from the south, the flagstone path continues its tour around the Carillon, still visible as it rises above the trees lining the inner side of the path.  A small herd of metal oxen grazes among stands of ornamental grass.  Garlands, each woven of vines, bits of paper, and flowers have been placed around the necks of the sculpture.

Soft cooing floats from a dovecote sitting on the outer side of the path, and periodically a curious bird pokes its head out to gaze at the passersby.  Light glints off the breeze-rippled surface of a shallow reflecting pool.  At the end across from the dovecote is a bronze statue of a woman kneeling as she sets a toy ship into the pool.  The carillon is visible to the southwest.

Several black basalt slabs surrounding a sphere sculpted from lava sit near the inner edge of the path.  A flame flickers from atop the ball, an eternal reminder of the fire warming the heart of M'Riss.  A curved bench rests on the outer edge of the flagstones, providing a clear view of the carillon rising in the distance behind the garden's stone sentinels.

Tree roots burrowing under the path have caused several of the flagstones to buckle.  A tulip and iris border fails to brighten the drab-colored mosaic set outside the path.  Untrellised, straggling wysteria dot the area between the path and the carillon, their slender switches lashing in even the slightest breeze as though a gale were blowing through them.

Bamboo chimes dangle from the branches of a grove of rosewood trees that separates the path from the carillon.  Lilies ring the trunks of the rosewoods and between them, a vibrant carpet of crocus paints a sea of color.  On the opposite side of the path, a bed of tiny, multi-hued shells holds a large bronze chime and a statue of a sitting jackal.  Dull basalt stepping stones skirt the shells and disappear into a stand of mimosa.

Light from the glow of burning votive candles banked around the room rises upwards to illuminate the massive stained glass windows set high in the carillon.  Thick, angular lines form a complex, intersecting pattern which nearly spans the length and breadth of the pale marble floor.  A staircase zig-zags upward above the doorway toward the belltower.

A slender handrail and low ledge on the outside of the narrow stairs are all that prevent someone from plummeting to the marble floor below.  A gilded framed landscape adds a splash of color to the sand-toned wall.  There is a small landing at the top of the staircase, just wide enough to turn to climb the next flight.

A slender handrail and low ledge on the outer edge of the narrow stairs are all that prevent someone from plummeting to the marble floor below.  More steep than the last flight, the stairs cling precariously to the carillon wall.  There is a small landing at the top of the staircase, just wide enough to turn to climb to the next flight.  From this height, the lines on the floor resolve clearly into a mariner's compass.

A slender handrail and low ledge on the outside of the narrow stairs are all that prevent someone from plummeting to the marble floor below.  There is a small landing at the top of the steep staircase, just wide enough to turn to climb to the next flight.  Midway, one of the treads has become loose and wobbly.

A slender handrail and low ledge on the outer edge of the narrow stairs are all that prevent someone from plummeting to the marble floor below.  The angle of the staircase pitches more sharply between the landings than the previous flight.  A tapestry, the linen frayed and wool faded with time, hangs on the stairwell wall.

A slender handrail and low ledge on the outside of the narrow stairs are all that prevent someone from plummeting to the marble floor below.  At this point the staircase is nearly vertical as it scales the inside of the tapering tower.  At the summit of the ladder-like stairs is a small landing leading to a door.

Eight bronze bells are suspended from the carillon's rafters.  Each bell is a different size, and each plays a different scale note.  A series of arched openings cut through the walls allow the sea breeze to flow in and the toll of the bells to ring out.

Two simple altars, one of rosewood and the other of stone, nestle within the stand of close-set mimosa.  Fluttering slowly to the ground, feathery blossoms settle to the earth like a carpet of pink snow.  Overhead, soft murmurs whisper through the leaves, perhaps the counsel of the gods, perhaps the entreaties of the dead.  Dull basalt stepping stones lead out of the grove.

Dark shapes of waiting goods and passengers loom against the backdrop of the bay and sky.  Toward the shore, a few flickering lights dot the dark outline of M'Riss.  They reflect off the waters of the bay, touching the waves that lap against the dock.

rooms.desc: Nocturnal calm contrasts with the daytime bustle on the road past the pumping station and its shed to the dock.  A small night-watch stands vigil on both the station and the dock, a few of its number turning to eye a Gor'tog with a pike who eyes them back.

rooms.desc: The road, rutted from traffic of carts and draft animals, turns south toward the bay.  The farmer's oxen plod alongside the trader's caravan in a moving free-for-all up and down the gentle slope, past the pumping station, to the dock at the water's edge.

Moonlight shines on a small bay to the southwest, and the distant lights of Mer'Kresh glitter beyond in the darkness of Torbis Sanhalas.  A brook trickles between rich farms on either side of the road, down to the bay.

Small farms flourish here in lowland soil close to the market in Mer'Kresh.  Some of the richest soil on all M'Riss makes crops grow vigorously and the road even sprouts a remarkable crop of weeds.  Lights in the windows of large farmhouses attest to the agricultural wealth of the region.
The road passes between a large field and an orchard which climbs a small hill behind a farmstead.  Poorer ground along the farmyard gravel is used for a pasture and a woodlot.
A large farm is carved from the heavy forest, rich only by virtue of its size.  A nut orchard loses itself in the native deobar and oak, while a field of cotton grows right to the verge of the road.

The small farm here is in obvious disrepair.  A small tree grows through the roof of a tumble-down barn and someone has attempted to thatch the branches in an effort to re-roof the barn.  Several small fields are rapidly vanishing as the forest reclaims the land.  A few chickens are visible bedded down against the farm buildings for the night, and a small flock is asleep, head under wing, right in the middle of the road.
A vigorous creek tumbles through the darkness under a timber bridge on its way to Torbis Sanhalas.  A small trail runs along the stream bank to join the Island Ring Road here.

A small clearing at the top of a low hill reveals two dramatic vistas.  To the northeast loom the rocky crags of Undogoz Mountain while to the south is the expanse of Torbis Sanhalas.  A chipmunk sitting on a rock scolds visitors incessantly.

An inlet juts into the low hills, bringing the saltwater close as the road skirts the fjord.  Deciduous trees predominate and the few farms are poor and scattered.  Grain waves gently in a few nearby fields, but darkness obscures most crops.

Deciduous forest predominates here.  A small farm cleared from the forest provides an extreme example of the Rissan ideal of self-sufficiency.  A large kitchen garden, a small plot of cotton, an orchard and a pasture are plenty large to feed a hard-working family but too small to earn much silver from the distant markets of Mer'Kresh.

Heavy underbrush crowds the road.  Tall oak, deobar, and halmik trees lean across the road forming a canopy which deepens the shadows on the moss-covered road.  Faint traces of an old trail heading west are visible through the heavy brush.

The faint scent of deobar oil oozes out of the heavy dark forest.  Freshly cut logs are stacked near the road.  Darkness obscures much of the grove, but the trees appear to be in good health and undergrowth is lacking.

Halmik trees dominate the dark forest along this stretch of road.  A solitary farm struggles for existence against the forest, the farmhouse sited to provide glimpses of a small bay through the trees.

Forest gives way to swamp as the road traverses broad, marshy mudflats along a raised roadbed.  A strong smell of salt marsh tickles the nose, while clouds of small, biting insects assault the ears and skin.

rooms.desc: Frogs hum and crickets chirp in the marsh.  A larger creature grunts unseen along the mudflats as something splashes at the water's edge.

Through a cedar grove winds a path covered with feathery needles, where the traveler's tread stirs a balsamy fragrance with each footfall.  An owl hoots unexpectedly somewhere in the distance.  The light from a welcoming window shines here and there among the trees.

The grassy pasture the townsfolk call the West Commons is empty, deserted for the night by all but the wandering fox or hunting owl.  A barking dog off in the distance wakes a rooster, who sends up his challenge in the darkness.

The silhouette of tall cedars forms a dark wall at the south side of the Commons, broken at only one place by a path leading beyond it.  Although light shines from a few nearby windows, the path lies in deep shadow.

The community well, ringed by a low wall of mortared stones, stands at the east end of the Commons.  Deserted now, it will become the center of the grove's social life when the sun rises and women come to fill their waterjars.
At the north end of the pasture is the grove's communal oven, a big brick beehive-shaped structure still warm after the day's baking.  A pile of wood stands next to the oven.
The path lies on a gentle incline from the heights to the northeast to the entrance to the grove below.  At a bend in the path, almost hidden by tree roots and groundcover, is a low stone.
Neat homesteads lie on both sides of a wide, sloping path that descends from the Commons in the northwest.  Logs placed at intervals across the path form easy steps down to a bend in the southeast.
At the bottom of a hollow, the cedar-lined path takes a sharp turn to avoid a spring that bubbles up into a shallow pool.  A shadowy figure stands next to the pool, half-hidden in the darkness.

Homes of weathered planks or shakes peek from between the cedars atop a wide ridge whose arms enclose the Commons of the grove.  A narrow path leads down the hill to the south, an obvious shortcut to the well below.
Many of the homes of the grove cluster along the top of this encircling ridge.  Below to the south is the open area of the Commons, mostly empty now as the village rests.
A little clearing stands among the darkness of the trees.  A path leads off to the west, wandering along the ridge.

From the lower end of this sloping path comes the sound of trickling water.  To the northwest it rises toward the crest of a hill topped by what looks like several houses.  A light in one distant window is a welcome guide in the darkness.

A gravel walkway lies beneath a pleached arbor, its leafy roof turning the walk into a dark tunnel.  Halfway down the arbor, wooden benches sit facing each other in circles of light from bright paper lanterns hung above each resting-place.
The entrance to an arbor stands at the northwest side of a spacious clearing in the trees.  The grass of the lawn is thick underfoot, and here and there in the darkness loom strange shapes.

With the trail ending abruptly at this serene grove, shrubs and ferns surround a lone oak tree which stands as a monument to the artistry involved in the creation of Elanthia.  Small creatures play hide-and-seek from you as they look for a place that makes them feel safe from your sight.

Straw dust and the sweet scent of horse manure coat the air.  The brush and twig walls keep out the worst of the weather and any night-roaming creatures.  Overhead, the soft glow of a lantern dangling from the thatched roof disperses the dark.  Low straw barriers protruding from the walls section off individual stalls for the horses, and a corral is visible through a split tarp hanging across the back wall.
Forest abuts mudflats here.  In one of several small openings at the verge, a rundown cabin sits on higher ground.  A shell midden indicates the occupants are probably shellfishers, not farmers.

A small inlet is visible far below and Torbias Sanhalas can be glimpsed through gaps in the trees as the road crosses this highland.  Pines intermingle with the occasional stems of oak and deobar, their presence betraying the poor local soil.

rooms.desc: Looming spires of volcanic rock throw shadows along the verge of the road.  At the horizon, moonlight glints off Torbias Sanhalas through the sparse trees.  Nearer and below, moonlight is reflected by the twin bays of the Two Fingers.

A small brook babbles in the darkness of this narrow valley.  Steep hillsides obscure moonlight, deepening darkness.  Weak candlelight from a cottage window provides the only illumination other than the stars directly overhead.

Moonlight glints off Torbis Sanhalas to the east as the road skirts the brow of a rocky headland.  Scattered shadows of rock outcrops interspersed with oak and pine above give way to the inky blackness of the thick forest below.

Vague rounded shapes of deciduous trees below yield to the angular shapes of conifers above, while the road feels slightly rougher and steeper.  There is a sense of change about this stretch of road, but blackness obscures most visual cues.

The road twists and turns in the moonlit darkness, crawling around outcroppings like some giant serpent crawling up the mountain.  One road cut has uncovered a great gash of soft dark stone which breaks and crumbles to the touch.

Sparse trees and large rock outcrops cast disorienting shadows as the switchbacks dodge the steepest slopes.  Pools of blackness may be shadow or pothole, making an already rough road a serious threat to ankle and axle.  Moonlight glinting on a rock spire above only adds to the treacherous shadows on the road.

The steep switchback road cut into the side of the slope snakes dramatically across the incline, twisting through the shadows of large outcrops.  The road is well into the high country, but still sheltered from the constant winds of higher elevation.  Those trees that find purchase in the rocky ground attain respectable stature.

Constant wind whistles through the needles of trees unseen in darkness and howls across the spine of the island where three roads meet.  The Island Ring Road leads north along the spine toward the Penal Colony and east to Torbis Sanhalas and M'Riss, while a small spur leads south to Fever Point.

Swirling dust scatters violently in the wind that howls angrily in the night.  The dust almost seems resentful as it attacks the eyes and nose, stinging as though the air were filled with tiny wasps.  The curving edge of a bluff vanishes into the gloom.

As the road curves over the crest of a hill, a view of the deep ocean fills the horizon.  The pines trees that populate the upper elevations of M'Riss thin out as they approach the coast, replaced by smaller shrubbery and brush.

Grey fragments of rock sprawl down the side of a sudden slope beside the road, ending in a pile of rubble and pebbles.  The hazardous incline is populated by small scrub pines that cling to the occasional ledge, their trunks and roots surrounded by bits of stone.  Its a simple reminder that the mountains of the Undogoz chain will not yield willingly to the gradual plains of the Fever Point peninsula.

Vague waving movement across the tops of the rows of scrub pines develops under the push of mountain gusts.  The trees bow submissively as they move, giving rather than battling the forced motion.  A desperate chirp rings out from somewhere within the depths of the trees as some hidden bird awakens from its slumber, stirred whenever a particularly churning wind attacks.

The nearest mountain blocks sight to the east, replacing the lost view with an indeterminate blur of grey and black shadows.  The road uncaringly twists its way down the side of the mountain, dodging the unclear silhouettes of tangled vegetation and straight shafts of pine trees.

An unilluminated incline drops westward, an empty tiered seating arena pointed out across the sea.  The evening sight of the ocean then becomes an empty stage, stretching to the far reaches of the horizon, longing for a watchful audience.  It only need look upwards to the clouds, the stars, or the moons to fulfill its wish.

A distant twinkling of light betrays the location of ships on the murky puddle of shadows, which in reality is the bay of Torbis Sanhalas.  The sound of rushing water adds an appropriate feel to the sight, despite the difference between the noise of a brook and a breaking bay.  Somewhere in the darkness, the gurgling stream falls and sends echoes of splashing water up the mountainside.

Thin pale shapes huddle in the safety of the darkened terrain, tangled limbs rasping as the potent drafts blow.  Some, close enough to the road to inspect in passing, show themselves to be malformed pines.  Those closer do not refrain from joining in the cacophony of their comrades, and crackle with glee in every shuddering gust.

The gentle lapping of waves from somewhere west carries up to even this high a section of the mountain chain.  At night or day, the ocean works to have its way with M'Riss, modifying its outer contours or cleaving its land with inlet and gulf.  For now, the road is solid, despite the attempts of the ocean and the blindness of nightfall, and travel will continue.

A grave-like lump of debris lay pushed out of the path of the road.  Long and twisted skeletal shapes make bed-mates with rugged mounds of something cold and hard, all of it discarded in a mass of identity swallowing shadow.  A villainous murderer could not find a more appropriate place to leave his victims.  A shriveled limb from the pile stretches out toward passerby's -- and unmasks the harsh reality of the dead pile of pine trees.

The blanket of darkness eliminates the reliance on visual cues while enhancing the other senses.  As if nature wished to test the hearing of those in her embrace, an occasional racket of falling stones rings out from the shadows before silence rejoins its companion, the night.

Only a few darkened grey columns poke themselves skyward, each one a pine that has decided to grow in spite of the rough surfaces.  Beneath the court of pines, scrubby brush thickens the ground, but does little to muffle the crunch of the gravel that hides on the road and in the gloomy crevices.

A dark veil fills the horizon, obscuring what must be an impressive daytime sight.  Northwards, the keen eye captures the occasional blink of light from the now dormant volcano Undogoz, piercing the night with a brief contrast before winking out of existence.

Shades of black and grey disguise granite outcrops and rocky shelves which crouch alongside the road, prepared to reveal their presence as damaging bandits of wheel and boot.  Between two massive shadows that can only be mountain peaks, the scattered winking of lights across the eastern landscape mark individual homes and farms while a gathering of similar twinkling lights displays the distant location of Mer'Kresh.

A subtle depression between the upper rims surges with hardy ash and pine.  A particularly wiry pine points rebelliously against the general direction of growth and toward the uphill trek to the south.  Incredulous, the other trees ignore this young upstart, angling themselves socially toward the north.  Allying with the pine, a number of fiddlehead ferns casually lean the same way.

A huge stone, a miniature scale mountain in its own right, has proven itself resilient to the choking roots of several pines.  Though invulnerable, the stone has become prisoner to the trunks of the very trees encircling it.  Beyond this vignette of internment, one of the smaller peaks of the island towers, confined by its own scale of timberland.

A petite sign is the only survivor of the collapse of a roadside waystation into the keen-edged crags awaiting at the bottom of the slope.  A blank space, devoid of tree, stone, or brush, overlooks where the small shed fell, and it now includes an unobstructed view of the coast.  This same view may have been what led the builder of the ill-fated shack to construct it in the first place.

A jagged shadow threatens to be an obstacle in the road, but turns out to be a kind guardian, saving the precious soil from the theft of the winds and keeping night blind travelers from stumbling off the road and to a certain doom below.  One section of the shaded stone circle is missing, a lost victim to gravity, showing that even the large and sturdy are likely to face a potential fall.  The largest shape, that of the massive Undogoz Mountain, glares from the north horizon.

At some point, a good-sized boulder from the higher cliff slammed into the this tier and cracked from the impact.  Now it rests, the split in its middle a crafty smirk, acknowledging that nothing can maintain an eternal hold on a lofty residence.  Several of its fellows remain in place, awaiting their chance when they, too, shall plunge to rejoin their lost brother, or perhaps skid beyond and tear a new path through the woods as they tumble towards the coast.

A hissing updraft sets the grass that tenaciously clings to the stones into a constant frenzied thrashing.  Surrounded by the berserking grass, a lone and sickly scrub pine digs its roots into the cracks in the stone, sending fragmented chunks spilling to the forest below.  Between the wild movement of the weedy grass and the slow but constant squeezing of the pine's roots, the elements will have an easier time weathering away the road as the seasons pass.

The mammoth bulk of a grey ridge arrogantly fills half the sky above, and the road, challenged by the task of passage, determinedly winds its way up from this plateau.  In comparison, the road leisurely slinks down in the opposite direction and into groves of short pines.  Collections of pine saplings here attempt to duplicate the groves below at least in mockery if not in size.

If this dip in the road were any sharper it would be necessary for any walking wanderer to succumb to travel upon hands and knees.  Several paths weave alternate routes from the main road in crooked dashes among indifferent pines.  Only some of the trails appear to be as safe as the road itself while others come precariously close to a severe fall.

A procession of stunted pines lines the grade, suggestive of a parade of Dwarves heading toward some secretive mountain worship.  Ominously, two slightly larger pines watch over the line of smaller trees, much like two imposing Gor'Tog bodyguards.

Struggling pines somehow find enough soil to sink their roots and grasp onto the edges of the granite surface of the slope.  By no means sparse, this rocky incline is not friendly to the larger plant life as the proximity to the ocean, and the winds birthed of it, have a tendency to sweep clear any rich soil to the lower elevations.  This doesn't seem true of the neighboring peaks, as each sports a full growth of rich green as proudly as a dwarf sports a beard.

Weather and time have exposed sections of the road to be nothing more than soft dark soil caked atop a shelf of grey granite slabs.  Moss and lichen now squeeze their way into the cracks of the revealed stone, the traffic in this area not near frequent enough to crush their growth.  Southwards, and up the sloping hills, walls of the grey rock cradle the road, quite the opposite of the increase in soft groundcover and downward slope to the north.

As the road corners around a pitted boulder nestled in the brush, the wider side of the route opens into an expansive sight of the ocean.  Upon the waters, white crests dance upon the tips of the waves, riding and falling in little twirling displays before splashing themselves against the cracked granite along the shore.  An inlet from the ocean lances toward the mountains, forcing the road to bypass or be consumed.

The road banks dangerously toward the gorge and bears deep scars from sliding wagon wheels to prove it.  An unobstructed view of the road capping the other side of this gaping pit is convenient from this vantage point, but quite possibly one of the last things on the mind of anyone struggling to maintain a filled wagon of provisions from slipping into a deadly fall.

A precipice that plunges into a watery bed of sharp stones forces the road into a tight hairpin curve.  Aside from one oddly bare spot in the brush, the thick shrubs and growth would have allowed the forgers of this path no other option but to yield to the demands of nature, and bend their route accordingly.

The mixed canopy of ash and pine trees, to the east, dips between two mountain peaks.  Though not nearly as large as Undogoz Mountain, those peaks are obviously part of the same chain, sharing the same color and texture as the infamous inert volcano.  The angle of these sloping mountains, however, is not unlike that of the water-filled canyon dipping down beside the road only a few feet away.

Some kind soul has staked posts of wood into the ground along the southern lip of the road in an attempt to add a touch of safety for those brave enough to peer over into the canyon beyond.  The construction is good, but woefully unlikely that it would stop a speeding horseman from plummeting into the deep gorge.  Indeed, several of the posts are split from some unknown collision.

A runoff parallels the road for a short way before cutting a sharp angle away and then down toward the ocean.  Wagon tracks, ruts, and hoof prints marr the ground where the ditch carves a path across the road, the cause of many a stumble.  The tiny crevice vanishes into the gaping maw of a large cloven boulder that sits askew, striking the pose of a slack jawed fool drunk after too many drinks.

Somewhere close, waves are slamming into a rocky shoreline with enough force that the sound echoes off of trees along the road even here.  With all the underbrush along this hilly terrain, one false step could send a clumsy explorer tumbling into the source of that sound, vanishing beneath the waves and adding his own spectral cries to that of the ocean.

Ash trees crowd in upon the road, shouldered together, limb to limb.  When the wind hustles through, the sound of branches creaking against one another overshadows that of leaves and foliage rustling.  If only the trees were clothed in guild cloaks could the scene be anymore reminiscent of the crowded streets of a town.

A sudden break in the brush and foliage reveals an incline that drops smoothly away from the road and to the west.  A glance down the slope quickly unveils a surface crammed with ferns, bracken and sharp thistles, as well as a splendid look at the naked sea.

Deep scars across the road trail to a heap of dense trees, obviously felled by a directing intellect.  Spear heads have been deeply embedded in the trunks, business ends outward, and durable, waxy rope has been lashed around the whole lot.  Surely, if left in its place of design, this obstacle would be the end to an already difficult voyage that wagons must endure here.

Mushrooms dot the shade beneath the brush, stark white bubbles in a sea of green and black.  Beyond the mushrooms, rows of gnarled reeds stand at attention, defending nothing more important than the gradual slope up the hills to the east.  Above, indifferent to the posturing of the little weeds and fungus, an alder tree perches, home to a family of sparrows that dart through the air with liquid ease.

The crumbling remains of a way station slouch off to one side.  Too much time has passed since its usefulness ended.  Its shutters and doors are now nothing more than rotted scraps of wood laying in the soil and its walls are not much else but split rocks as common as those that fall from the mountain chain.

The multiple points of Undogoz Mountain peek through the breaks in the trees, ever watchful for events transpiring in his domain.  The fiddlehead ferns and moss lining the road may make a temporary respite from his gaze for the random traveler, but there is no permanent escape for those who tread on the Elven mountain's lands.

The creaking of wood on wood sounds out from a pair of dead trees arching over the road, their wispy wigs of moss swaying in the night air.  Waves crashing against some nearby shore create a rhythmic sound of sobbing as the pair shift, and a branch dangling from one of them grasps blindly for comfort from passersby.

A gaping maw of vegetation swallows the road in shifting gloom while the beach sand covers it in the opposite direction.  A broken wagon sits abandoned beneath the dark foliage, its wheels buried in the soft sand.  The wagon may be stopped permanently, but the hiss of waves sliding across the sands rises and falls, unmoved by the drama of passing travellers.

Shady and jagged fingers of stone poke from the southern shore of the inlet, ready to prod and bash even the most skilled swimmers and send them to a dark grave.  Further out, the waves of the open ocean lap and swirl, uncaring of those lost within their embrace.

The slow erosion of the beach is apparent even at night.  Jagged stones, dark shadows in the wet, white spray, hunch defiantly in the surf, asking no quarter from the eroding waves and giving none without a fight.

White curls of ocean waves dance at the far end of a rock-lined inlet, amplified in both sound and power, as they are forced down the inlet's gullet to wash upon the sands of the beach.  Sharp and jagged rocks, visible as vicious dark shades along the north and south shores, jut into the waters.  Combined with the night, the stones become twice as deadly as they would be during the day.

Despite the somber cover of darkness, flecks of white and grey speckle the sandy floor.  Small obsidian stones, half-buried in the sand, threaten to trip the careless beachcomber.  The stones are lonely remains of the volcanic flow that long ago burned a path here and eventually added its own body to that of the sands.

The gentle echos of breaking waves drift through the air during pauses in the night breeze, revealing by sound if not by sight the nearness of the ocean.  The road, veiled by the blanket of night, slants toward the unseen source of the sound of the waves.

Pinpricks of light, barely visible through the thick umbrella of desert-ash leaves, betray some form of activity upon Undogoz Mountain.  Though this sand is more forgiving than in the featureless desert, it still scurries mercilessly into boots and clothes, stealthy in the dark until felt upon the skin of its victim.
Dark shopes mark shadowed clusters of trees along the roadside.  One lone, curving silhouette stands apart from the goups, looking oddly out of place.

Weaving about the dark forms of swaying palm trees, the road skirts the deeper woods which begin at the volcano's slopes and end here.  The slight taste of salt is carried on an occasional breeze, a subtle clue the coast is merely out of sight and not too far away.

The rustling sound of the wind through the darkened treetops precedes an occasional frond falling from the sky like a dying spirit, casually cast out from the heavens.  Several dried fronds, now little more than decaying husks, flutter helplessly away from the trees which spawned them.

Even at night, the slow meshing of desert and wooded hillside is clear from this point in the road.  The dark trunks of palm trees thicken to the south and east, and conversely lose density as one gazes to the north.  A deep shadow on one side indicates a rut or ditch of some sort.  Thin plants within wave their fronds when touched by the most gentle of night breezes.

Black columns rise ominously on either side of the road.  Travellers, if they intend to make use of the stable footing of the road's packed surface, must walk between the massive dark shapes.  Only upon a closer look do the shapes reveal themselves as rough-barked palm trees.  The inky silouette of a discarded wheel can be seen at the foot of one of the palms.

The sundered peaks of the volcano region are visible as a differing shade of deep grey against the background blackness of the sky.  A traveller may find himself longing for the shade of the distant forest under the burning glare of the sun.  However, in the darkness of night, the shifting lights on the slopes of the mountain hint that the safety and comfort of those woods are nothing more than wishful thinking.

A makeshift cairn of fist-sized stones lies abandoned in the gloom.  Sagebrush bristles around the stones, offering the long-dead inhabitant nature's condolences.  The fate of the traveller beneath the stones remains a mystery, a reminder that the dangers of the island remain, even in the coolness of the night.

Small and hardy brush pokes up from the bed of sand, and only then with obvious challenge.  Far to the southeast, the peaks of a tremendous mountain are outlined against the night sky.  Dim specks of light can be clearly seen up and down the mountain's slope, flickering and blinking like a thousand leering eyes looking out over the desert's floor.

Any step off the road is noticed in the darkness, not by sight, but by the sudden feeling of loose sand gripping ankle and foot in a desperate attempt to add victims to the desert's environment.  A claw-like cluster of thistles stretches longingly upwards, beckoning the night sky into a deadly embrace.

The dim outline of a large, felled tree resides at the edge of a curve in the road, a casualty of the harsh daytime environment.  Sand, blown by the wind, threatens to engulf the tree, making an already vague and shadowy shape even more indistinct.

A handful of weathered posts border the way.  Perhaps they were intended to define the edge of the route from the surrounding desert sands, but at night they become a series of obstacles to trap unwary travelers.
Cool sands and cold air do not make the desert any less threatening, as it is still parched.  The winds have died down for the night, but will return with the heat in the morning.

The smell of salt air is strong, with a hint of an ocean breeze.  To the south, the road leads into the desert -- assuming that the line of posts diminishing in the distance marks a road.  To the northeast, the road ascends a slight hill, high enough to block sight in that direction.
Cool sands and cold air do not make the desert any less threatening, as it is still parched.  The winds have died down for the night, but will return with the heat in the morning.

From the top of a slight rise, the road reveals the reason for its change of direction: the coastline bends inward, forming a bay that extends out of sight to the north.  Down the slope to the north, there appears to be some sort of structure beside the road.

A small guardhouse painted with broad black and white stripes stands beside the road.  Next to it, a post supports a stout wooden bar, pivoted so that it can be lowered to block the way.  On the side of the guardhouse is a large sign.

The road rises as it heads toward the fortress on a hill in the distance.  To the northeast it issues from a narrow covered bridge and stretches toward the bay to the southwest until, in the distance, it bends to the south, following the coastline.

Beside the lower roads below, a figure stands motionless, details vague and unclear from this distance.  Beyond him, the fields of the southern peninsula checker the lands in shades of tan and green, descending to the coast.  Many miles further away, at the point where the land juts into the sea and ends, dark specks of houses cluster together in what must be Fever Point.

Legends along the peninsula often spoke of a dashing Rissan who broke from the normal low-key behavior and risked his own life for those of his beloved neighbors.  Though never officially accepted as a quantified hero, Th'darzt is still revered by locals, as evidenced by the rather crude wooden statue erected in his honor.  A simple bench stares up at the statue from across the track.

Waving rows of ferns line a rundown segment of fence.  The fence is no longer enough to protect the fields it once surrounded, nor is the ragged scarecrow that hangs in wide-eyed vigil above the long gone harvest.  On the other side of the road, however, a newer and sturdier barricade safely corrals tall stalks of corn and wheat.  Drowning in the ocean of crops is a barn, visible only from the shingles of its roof that manage to peek over.

The whisper of the wind in the tall grasses creates a chorus of voices that discuss travelers upon the road, hushing in a rustling hurry whenever the breeze stops.  During the pause, animal calls and cries ring out across the land, and then stop as well, buried in the silence of their wake.  A small group of pines cluster alongside the road, a safe haven for the creatures that issue the natural sounds, and an additional set of gossips joining the grasses.

Tilted on its side, the skeleton of a plow sits alone in the overgrown fields.  Seasons of absent farmers have aided the weeds and shrubbery in their slow takeover of the plow's corpse.  A complete fence still encircles the out of control growth in the field, but its days of functional service have long since passed.  Where the wood slats have not fallen from neglect, garden spiders have virtually covered it with sticky webs.

Fishing poles, nets and signs proclaiming sales on bait are clear clues that this minuscule village's survival depended on the fishing trade.  Only a handful of homes still stand after so much time exposed to the elements without upkeep, and the doors on most swing open in the sea breeze.  A pier, some distance to the south, juts out into the sea, desperately attempting to escape whatever memories it holds of this deserted village.

Sharp bends and angles in the road lend credence to the story Sailor's Ramble was named for the path stumbled by drunken sailors from pub to beach.  Unlike the seedy, derelict town center, this area has been enjoying a revival of care: fresh paint, colorful curtains, and even a few flowerbeds to replace the weeds.

The road winds back upon itself in a hairpin bend, then slowly straightens as it curves downward toward the ocean.  A few cabins, once temporary housing for sailors awaiting their next berth, rest among the scattered weeds and leaves that edge the dusty path.  Splashes of whitewash here and neatly raked lawns there show the buildings have received renewed care.

Careening northwest, the road makes an abrupt jog toward a massive oak standing at the end of the forest, then abruptly veers just short of the tree's roots to run along the forest line.  Two cairns are set side-by-side on the road.

Hooking west, the road makes an abrupt turn into the forest and meanders among the trees.  At one turn, the path splits before a large camphor tree as though no consensus could be made upon the preferred route, then merges on the opposite side.  A prickly ravelthorn hedge intermingled with esturi bushes bounces the road sharply back toward the south.

Gently swinging southeast, the road dips into a gully and narrows to little more than a footpath used as much by animals as by men.  Brush growing from the gully walls reaches out to tickle passersby, and the occasional thorn to sting them.  Gradually, the sloping walls of dirt flatten to a trail that deposits travelers onto a sandy beach.

Jewel-like shells are nestled in the crooked line of seaweed that marks the beach's high tide line.  The beach curves westward, stopping at a meadow of sharp-bladed sawgrass.  Eastward, the Fever Point Pier juts out over the water, and the soft sand gives way to rocks and stones dumped to prevent erosion.

From the size of the building, the inn, ironically named "The Lost Sailor's Refuge," was obviously a mainstay of the fishing village.  A large picture window, now but a boarded-up frame, stares out at the street.  Unlike other structures, the inn's front door has been sealed securely with lengths of rusty chain.

The inclined trail rises from the beach and curves northwest toward the village.  Holes have been dug near the roots of many of the trees -- whether by rodents or residents is unclear.  Scrub pine grows among the larger hardwoods, nearly overwhelming the sea's scents with the smell of resin.

Emerging from the gravel and rocks beneath the pier, the beach continues its graceful arc before disappearing into the line of trees above the beach.  Tufts of yellow flowers grow in the shelter of a tumble of boulders close to the trees.  Footprints dotting the beach, as well as other unnatural disturbances in the sand, hint this is a frequently used area.

Gravel and colorful chunks of split rock dumped beneath the pier interrupt the sandy beach's east-west course.  The pier above stretches a large ship's length into the ocean, ending where the water is deep enough to dock a vessel larger than an island skiff.  A slippery coating of salt moss clings to the pilings and hangs from cross-braces overhead.

To the southwest, the road runs through a covered bridge that crosses a deep gully.  The bridge, barely wide enough for a wagon, has been laboriously pieced together from odd-sized planks cut from driftwood -- signs of both the scarcity of wood and the abundance of free labor.
Torchlight throws black shadows on the looming bulk of the Colony fortress to the north.  A lane leads up the hill to a deep-set gate, cast in shadow by flaring lanterns hung on either side.

A little south of the fortress walls, the road already shows signs of its disuse.  A well-travelled highway is always marked by litter, old campsites, fresh wheel-ruts, and animal droppings, none of which are in evidence here.  To the west, a lane leads uphill to the fortress gate, and to the southeast, the road curves to avoid an inlet.

The ancient road, once a thoroughfare along M'Riss's north shore, is surrendering to the elements.  Paving stones cracked and heaved up by frost lie half-buried in sand blown by the constant northwest winds, and a grey-green moss covers their leeward side.

To the east the road disappears abruptly: the tides have washed away its foundation, and a big section of the paving has simply slid into the encroaching sea.  Not that anyone seems to mind -- there's no sign that traffic has headed eastward in a long, long time.

A few torches burn atop the Colony Fortress's South Wall.  The shadows they cast partly hide the deep-set Desert Gate.  A lane leads from the gate downhill to where the Island Ring Road bypasses the colony, southwest to northeast.  Aside from a large flat rock and a few scrubby patches of sea-oats, the area is barren.

Just to the west of the Desert Gate lies a small flowerbed outlined with whitewashed stones.  Someone has tried to nurture a bit of color in the shelter of the wall, providing the daily water and weeding needed.

This shadowed corner where the south and the bay walls meet has become the home of weeds, the seeds brought by passing gulls and sheltered from the desert winds.  The land slopes steeply down from the fortress wall.

The ground drops off below the south wall, almost as if someone had planned a moat and begun the digging, only to abandon the job.  Now the desert sands have sifted in, leaving only a curiously regular depression like a dry riverbed.

The high tower of the Desert Bastion faces rank on rank of dunes receding into the distance.  The wind picks up swirls of sand from their tops, shifting the sands in a slow procession.  If not for the hazy mountains to the southeast, one could believe that the desert went on forever.

A wide cleared area stretches along the wall from the beach to the north to the desert in the south.  Here, some lazy or careless hand has tossed rubbish from the fortress, and it lies piled at the base of the wall, buzzing with flies.

As the coastline curves to the east, the dunes give way to a barren, rock-strewn headland, dotted with shallow dips and hollows.  Only an occasional stunted tree or low bush has been spared the clearing of the ground outside the fortress walls.

The wind whistles and swirls around the Lee Bastion to the north, scouring its seaward face, but in the shelter of the eastern wall huddle a few greyish-green creepers.  The vines, none thicker than a little finger, scratch out a meager living among the rocks, shells, and sand.
The mighty Lee Bastion anchors the northeast corner of the fortress.  Arrow slits pierce its walls high above and the deep shadows in their recesses hint at the thickness and strength of its masonry.

Clumps of sea oats rise from dunes as high as a Halfling.  The dunes follow the shoreline to the west, curving gradually around the prominence on which the fortress stands.  Its walls rise to the south, weathered from the steady ocean winds.

Just a step into the verge of the forest, the trees become taller, stronger, more majestic, and the undergrowth thins.  The ground looks more open to west yet contradictorily seems darker.  Somewhere overhead, a bird warbles, and its song is answered with a like melody from deeper in the woods.

Giant red oaks and pines stand widely separated, rank on rank.  Their crowns spread high above, almost blocking out the sky and dimming the light that penetrates to the forest floor.  Travel is easy, the path underfoot softened with a thick layer of needles that hushes each footfall.  The path, perhaps a game trail, follows a small stream that extends from the brushier east off to the west.  A grey, furry object lies near the trail.

Along its way down the gentle slope, the stream widens into quiet pools as if for some sylvan ritual.  It curves to the southwest, gliding through a forest cathedral dappled with beams of light lancing from the forest crown high above.  The scent of balsam sweetens the air, and even the birds seem hushed in quiet reverence.

From the northeast the stream eases its way down a shallow valley.  Here and there along its banks a willow or a birch overhangs the edge.  What looks like a reddish stone near one tree proves to be a rusty bascinet.  To the southwest the ground levels again, and the trees look smaller and less imposing.
A shelf of rock rises from the soil, angling the brook sharply northeast and northwest.  In the pond below the shelf, a small turtle catches flies and contemplates whatever turtles ponder.
