A mixed wood covers the hillside -- fragrant hemlocks and an occasional slash pine stand on the higher ground and broader-leafed, moisture-loving trees in the lower areas.  The stream meanders around hillocks, sending an exploring arm bubbling into side channels here and there, descending the slope to the south and west.  The path mostly hugs the firmer ground but sometimes crosses a softer, wetter patch.

The ground slopes and the stream ripples down a gentle decline, twisting and turning with the lay of the land.  Fewer firs and oaks rise from the moist soil, and more willows and river birches droop slender branches along the path.  The tangy scent of evergreen sap, strong on the steeper slopes to the east, is fainter here.

Appearing and disappearing, the stream splits and breaks into pools and puddles.  Small rivulets run off right and left, half of them seeping into the forest mulch.  The fallen leaves are wet and slippery underfoot.

A sharp rise in the forest floor allows a good view despite the dense vegetation: to the east the forests rise, and to the west a vast land lies shrouded in blue mist.  In the distance to the north, though it's difficult to make out through the trees, looms a large outcropping of rock, its peak thrust high above the thick forest.

The path is dim beneath the thick cover overhead, and dimmed further by mist drifting from occasional low-lying patches of ground.  Where the path crosses these dips, the moist earth slightly gives way underfoot.  The drone of mosquitoes has replaced the humming of wild honeybees, and the air feels warm and humid.

Signs of wildlife are everywhere: squirrels scamper in a stunted elm, rabbit warrens hide in its roots, and the trails of small game lead off into the brush around it.  To the west stands a low knoll that offers a way around the bottoms to the southwest and an escape from the clinging mud.

At the top of a firm, dry knoll, a curious oak with twin trunks rises high into the air.  Its high, dense crown has held down the undergrowth and allows a view to the west of what looks like an upthrust cliff.  The cliff itself is hard to distinguish from the surrounding vegetation because of its own thick covering.

Over the years, water has soaked a deep depression between the hills, making every step a chore.  In the dark water, a silvery cypress tree stands like a monarch, scores of roots and knees anchoring it, its limbs covered with moss and vines, reaching up toward the trees on the surrounding hillsides.

A massive cypress grows on a slight rise just above the waterline.  Its upper branches form a second storey high above the forest floor.  Occasionally something stirs in the canopy above, sometimes raining a shower of leaves and twigs, but nothing ever seems to show its face.

One of the younger cypress trees stands near the bottom of a slight rise of the land, small only by comparison with the giants to the east, yet one of the few that doesn't seem wrapped in vines.  Still, the lower branches are within reach, and it looks climbable.

The sound of water splashing comes from the northwest.  A stream curves out from around the base of the outcropping of rock, heading south toward the marsh.  Here at its base, where the cliff looms high overhead, the trees are noticeably thinner than the bigger ones to the northeast.

A good hundred feet up, a small stream of water spills over the edge of the cliff.  It has worn a slippery channel down the slope, but the channel looks far too slick and steep to climb.  The run-off gathers in pools along the path before seeping into the surrounding bog.

On the border between the forest giants and lesser trees, water trickles along the ground in innumerable ribbons, heading generally south.  The path is nearly mud, and walking is difficult as it winds among the bushes and vines that swarm up the face of the outcrop.  And the mosquitoes are especially hungry.

A fallen log lies across the path, sunk half-way in the moist ground.  Moss covers its trunk, softening the outlines, and its upper branches are coated with a hard, white fungus.  A puddle has collected on the eastern, upslope side of the trunk.

A curious mixture of trees and undergrowth lines the trail: where the path rises, the ground is a bit firmer and drier, with oaks predominating.  But in the hollows, the going is slower, the earth damp and yielding, and alder and willow saplings thrive.  To the south and west, the land is lower still.

To the west looms a great outcropping of rock, tinted green and grey with moss.  Great trees rise in all other directions but southwest.  On that side, the ground slopes down to a wet, marshy bog, out of which comes a din of frogs croaking and insects buzzing.

The path has become a yielding muck, hampering movement but not greatly slowing it.  Swarms of the tiny black flies that breed in the marsh are more numerous, almost everywhere, and they all seem to be just at eye-level.  Still lower ground lies through a thicket to the southwest.

A grove of cypress trees of all sizes spreads in all directions, rooted in the soft, wet bog.  Insects hum and buzz, bubbles rise from the ooze and pop with every step, and unfamiliar cries of birds or animals sound on all sides.  A bramble thicket on a slight rise running northeast to west, or possibly an opening in the trees to the southeast, looks like the only chance of dry, firm footing.

The ground is soft underfoot, making a liquid sucking sound with every step.  A discarded boot, now a permanent resident, is lodged nearby, half submerged in the mire.  The surrounding woods are full of birdsong, and every so often comes a rustling in the brush or something like a muffled footfall.

The trail winds between the marsh and the rocky slopes of the Forlorn Hope -- the fabled mountain, Galduta Isharon, visible to the northwest through breaks in the tress.  The stench of decay hangs over the murky brown water lapping along the edge of the path.

On the crest of a slight rise a massive white oak towers into the sky, a stalwart sentinel.  The ground around the base of the tree is littered with empty acorn caps.  A few slender oak saplings find purchase here and stretch to the sky but are hard pressed to find sunlight in the shade of the behemoth above them.

A rocky outcropping like a tilted tabletop stretches far to the north to a jagged peak jutting into the sky.  Through the ravelthorn bushes to the south and west comes the flash of sunbeams on the Altanen River.

A thicket of alder surrounds a big willow tree, then stretches off to the east -- a pleasantly shady resting spot if the biting flies ever left the swamp.  Occasionally, the wind blows fresh air and the smell of life from across the Altanen, momentarily masking the reek of the bog.  A piece of cloth caught in some ravelthorn bushes flutters in the breeze, near a trail following the rising ground north along the river.

From the west comes the noise of rushing water -- no small stream, by the sound of it.  Here, in the midst of a thicket of alder and willow trees, the water is still and knee-deep in some places, but a path can be traced by stepping carefully across the roots of the trees.  A shaft of sunlight flashes a reflection from something at the base of a willow.

A game trail, a path for something between the size of a badger and a deer, struggles through a patch of dense underbrush.  The path is wide and well-trampled, but to each side, saplings as thick as an arm have been broken off and scored with deep gouges.

A fair-sized clearing allows the light to reach this one small part of the bog.  One of the giant cypresses has fallen, pulling its neighboring trees down with it, and the tangled remains of broken trunks and shattered limbs are slowly sinking into the mire.  Spindly saplings sprout in the gaping hole and struggle to capture the precious sunlight.

A gnarled cypress, bent into a wooden parody of a giant bowed under a heavy burden, stands in the muddy soil.  The tree even bears something that resembles a wound: a gash has been ripped into the bark along one side.  Beyond it to the west is a large pool of dirty brown water, home to who knows what kind of creatures.

Scum-covered waters swirl around a moss-shrouded cypress standing in a murky brown pool.  Unknown and unseen inhabitants lurking below the surface stir the water, from which an everpresent fog slowly twists and dances despite the deathly still air.  Rumors say the fog holds the spirits of the fallen, forever trapped in the mist.

The water deepens, making the footing even more uncertain in front of a large cypress tree slowly being strangled by greyish-green vines with big, plate-sized leaves.  The vines drape the tree like a shroud and will eventually pull it down, but for the creature that climbs the tree, they offer a secure handhold, almost as good as a ladder.

A few faint tracks of small animals wander, seemingly at random, among the broken fragments of dry mud that form the old watercourse.  Thorn bushes and scrubby trees overhang the banks, futilely seeking moisture in this dry place.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A dense thicket, full of thorns, rises suddenly in the sun-baked mud of the old streambed.  Perhaps tapping a lost spring, the deep green of the twisted branches is a marked contrast to the drier shrubs along the banks.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: The hard surface of the streambed rises noticeably to the south.  Crumbling chunks of rough-hewn stone along the banks show that someone once managed this watercourse for some long-forgotten purpose.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Stones and gravel from the sides of the streambed have fallen down into untidy piles.  One massive boulder rises up above the rest like some patriarch among his flock.  Given its rough edges and lack of softening, this huge rock likely fell long after the stream dried up.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A dry streambed ends in empty air.  The crumbling lip of a long-dead waterfall hangs out over a small pond some distance below.  Broken chunks of shaped rock lie to one side, their purpose unknowable to a casual look.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Several large rocks and small boulders form an untidy pile along the edge of a dry streambed.  Nearby, a huge growth of thorns and brambles arises.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A tangle of thick bushes covered with long thorns creates an interlocking mesh of spikes and vine.  Two narrow paths intersect, beaten through the stubborn shrubs, but even the crushed branches and thorns underfoot are an obstacle.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A hill slopes up to the west, and from the curve of the land, you can see the thornberry patch reaches to the western horizon.  A brown rabbit scurries quickly across the path before diving to disappear into the growth.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A high, level plain of knee-high brambles unfolds, without a tall bush or tree nearby.  The relentless sun and fierce storms have destroyed all but the persistent growth of thornberry shrubs, which are able to survive under almost any condition.  They cling to the hard rocky soil and hold this wilderness in place.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Soft siltstone and sandstone washed away by rain through the ages, have created a sheer slope that starts as a large gully and descends rapidly into an impressive arroyo.  Sculpted by the elements, large knobby boulder-like outcrops project upward from the rock forming oddly shaped sentinels to watch over the small canyon.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A shattered bridge once provided a safe pathway from the mill to the southern side of the ravine.  Now, however, the chasm appears uncrossable as thick rotting ropes trail away from termite ridden support posts to disappear over the canyon edge.  Bits of frail wooden planking still litter the steep slope near the supports and the chasm bottom far below.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A deep chasm opens almost beneath your feet.  The remains of an old grist-mill sit beneath the faint shade of some scruffy trees nearby.  A broken millstone lies against the side of the mill, complete with an empty bird's nest in the center hole, though no birds appear to have used it in a long time.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Small clumps of crabgrass and scraggly shrubs give way to a gritty sandstone promontory, forming a sheer cliff that plummets down to the deep gorge below.  Across the chasm, on the far wall, layer after layer of herring-bone shaped laminations alternate with one another in the rock forming a curious pattern.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A cluster of small slender trees rings a sparser area of the thicket. The shrubs are dwarfed here, but the thorns are even sharper.  Sticking to the paths is the only option.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: The ground has broken away and tumbled far below to a chasm of dry rocky soil.  Some remaining fat plump thornberries cling fiercely to their protective branches, just as the shrubs themselves hold fast to the slowly eroding ground.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: An open area has been cleared from the thicket recently, but the voracious shrubs have begun growing back, their branches trailing into the clearing.  Rubbery shoots of new growth have pierced the bare ground, and biting green thorns already make the tender growth hostile.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Thick brush surrounds everything, rising taller than the tallest elf.  Narrow passages through the thorns fan out in several directions, but what lies around each bend is hidden from view.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A dense wet smell of rotten fruit permeates the air, as thornberries protected from any beast hang overripe and decaying on the branches.  Swarms of midge-like flies fly in and out of the thorns -- if the thorns don't bite you most likely the flies will.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Rising out of the thickets of thornberry shrubs is a lone pine.  Blighted by the dry land and poor soil, it still climbs to an impressive height.  Some distance away, past a totally impassible wall of brambles, a few other trees can be seen.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: The shrubs grow thicker and taller here, the way east a solid wall of dagger-thorns.  The path leads into an area hollowed out within the brake, with the shrub branches arching overhead to form a latticed roof.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A wild plum tree struggles upwards from the choking thorns, as the thorny vines reach upward for support.  Though the tree struggles for air and space, the remaining plums are protected from any but the swiftest and most agile birds.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A long-abandoned grist mill lies beneath the weak shade of a scruffy maple tree.  A surprisingly stout lock holds the sagging front door closed.  Mouseholes gnawed into the wooden siding give shadowy glimpses into the dark interior.  A rotting pile of empty grain sacks shows obvious use as nesting material for some now-gone animal.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: You cling to the thick and heavy trunk of an ancient maple tree.  Below you, a ruined mill sits in the scattered shade.  To one side, the millwheel waits for the stream that once turned it.  Cliffs rise to the northeast where the thin thread of a waterfall descends to form a small pool.  Perhaps this is where the old mill stream has gone.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: The heavy branch you crouch on sways near an upper story window set into the weathered side of the old mill.  To one side, the mill wheel waits endlessly for the water that no longer turns it.  Only dust now fills its rusting scoops.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A thick and twisted limb sways underfoot uneasily.  A gnarled branch from a creaking pine tree brushes this limb, making footing even more uncertain.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Grey bushes bristling with hundreds of small, pointed thorns stand like giant sentries at silent attention in this tunnel, ready to strike at the first sign of invasion.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Ravens tap and pick at the engulfing net of thistle branches weaving across several defoliated oak trees.  They carefully avoid the sharp thorns, but blackened blotches underfoot reveal their occasional lack of past success.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Thorny brambles engulf everything in sight, forming both rug and canopy.  Through the latticework of grey branches you can dimly make out lights winking their message of cheer and warmth from distant cities.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A horde of dense brambles crowds in upon this area from all sides, and from above.  Gusts of wind send its nettled branches snicking loudly with sinister emphasis.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A small animal thrashes about in the all-encompassing vegetation, trapped, reduced to anonymous pulp by the action of innumerable thorns.  The bushes that hold it seem almost alive, their scraggly branches clinging with single-minded frenzy.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A small metal cart lies on its side, its wheels broken, its spilled contents a rotted, unidentifiable mass.  Spread over its surface is a heavy layer of brambles speckled with vivid red thornberries.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Several caves open into the side of a enormous, moss-covered mound.  They were once occupied by intelligent creatures, judging by the rusty tools which lie scattered about their entrances.  However, an impenetrable wall of bramble now prevents any access.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A dark green moss expands along every curve of the sloping hills of this region.  The moss in turn is completely covered by a patchwork blanket of brush, its thorns glistening with dew.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: The thorn thicket crests like a giant grey wave, engulfing several dead black oaks.  Wisps of nests can still be seen in their higher boughs.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: Tendrils of snakeweed wind endlessly through mounds of dagger-thorn bushes like the work of some sylvan weaver.  The result is a clogged thicket of grey branches striped bright green, shimmering in the air as it stirs with every passing breeze.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A few variwinkles peek out from the wild tangle of surrounding thorn bushes.  Their small purple flowers nod among the briars, dancing innocently in the fitful play of light.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A bristling net of thorns covers the stump of a silverwood sapling.  The remaining bark gleams in all its primal glory, but dried black stains on the thorns testify that travelers have tried to remove a few souvenir splinters from the stump in the past.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: A grove of white birch trees stands opposite the prayer gate dedicated to the Goddess Peri'el.  Watching over the wild inner slopes to the south, a golden king snake perches atop the gate.  Two guards, taking their duty very seriously, stand to either side of the gate watching those who approach.

Patterns of light bloom within the glossy black stone of the prayer gate's walls.  Etched in gold on one side, a wounded S'Kra Mur woman sings to a sleeping dragon, her tail held gently above her ankles.  On the other side, the same woman holds a sleeping S'Kra Mur baby in her arms, her tail undulating in the air.

This old passage once connected the main hall with the southern towers of the keep, but has been converted into a sitting room.  Well-padded benches cluster around imported wooden tables to give the bank patrons a place to smooth out any disagreements in their planned financial deals.  A large old painting of a group of S'Kra hangs on the back wall, looking sternly down upon the room.

At first glance it is difficult to tell you are in the renowned healing arts' hospital of Martyr Saedelthorp.  It looks more like a battlefield healer's station.  Blood, gore, sweat and mud streak the tiled floor and the wooden benches.  Groaning adventurers in various states of shock and consciousness await tending by concerned but fatigued healers.  You gingerly step over a patient with a severed limb sprawled out on a canvas stretcher.

You stand on the bank of a tiny pond in the middle of the square.  Cool water laps against the soft, velvety silt that covers the shore, and in the distance you can hear the bustle of the town.  Sitting in the middle of the pond is a massive gelapod, looking content and not the least bit aggressive.

This metal platform waits defiantly for the frequent storms that batter the walls of Muspar'i, as it huddles down in the sand.  Thick coils of rope, wrapped around the platform's steel pillars, stand ready to tie off the barges traversing the desert sea to the isolated city, and a wide ramp allows easy access for boarding and disembarking the flatboats.
A deep shelf is carved into the wall, in which is stored locked chests bound by chains.  Strange symbols are crudely etched into the rock wall above each one, though their relation is unclear.

The water of Lake Ratamipak is dark with a greyish tone, owed to a dense concentration of suspended salt.  Here away from shore, the bottom drops off rapidly, making it difficult to move further out into the lake.

Unlike the teller windows across the hall, the exchange of coins is handled a bit more openly.  An old stone-topped table has been set out with all the tools of the exchanger to allow the customer to see that everything is as they wish.  The exchange official confers with a teller behind an iron screen from time to time in order to keep the number of coins on the table to a minimum.

A strong breeze pulls upward past the well-traveled balcony forming a wide half circle around the perimeter of the lightwell at this level.  Daylight streams down from the skylights above to brighten the area, despite being nearly in the center of the great stone keep.  Off to the side of the balcony is a set of carpeted steps leading up to the top floor.

Sandstone floors have been rubbed smooth and lightly polished to a soft, rosy glow, then covered with a luxurious scatter of thick carpets patterned in a white-on-white arabesque motif.  Light glints off the glass fronts of tall rosewood cabinets filled with rows of velvet-lined shelves holding an array of precious and semiprecious gemstones, and a long table that is covered with a length of white linen is scattered with magnifying lenses, forceps, and other tools of the gembuyer's trade.

The dusty track continues to follow the great wall of the city, pounded out by the generational tread of gleaners that were unwilling to stray out into the merciless desert.  Sloping gently to the northeast for a number of yards, the ground suddenly drops away sharply towards the vertical, a potent natural barrier between the city and the arid plain below.

A great tower of black stone rises high overhead with a pair of massive double doors leading within.  Its buttresses and outrunning columns cast long shadows across the courtyard, which is occupied primarily by two long tables of black oak set up to either side of the lane, displaying various wares to passersby.  The bright buntings draping down from the tables' canopy create a daring splash of color, offsetting the other rather austere surroundings.

Long tapestries sewn in deep, rich colors drape the polished stone walls of the preparation hall.  Stools and straight-backed chairs are scattered about for the use of those entering the arena and those waiting to join the line.  The scent of sandalwood hangs in the air, drifting from incense burners placed in the four corners of the room.

The stone walls are dense and thick, draping the hall in a curtain of heavy, reverent silence.  Every other panel in each wall is carved with images, alternating with clear crystal oil lamps that burn with strange blue flames.  Those buried in the Hall of Masters lie at rest beneath the stone floor, their names engraved atop granite slabs turned dark with age.

The entryway to the guild is sparse and utilitarian, but its seamless stone walls and heavy floor tiles are undoubtedly crafted from the finest of materials.  A pair of massive double doors dominates the south wall, directly opposite the heavily carved archway leading into the Guildmaster's office.  Two towering cobras with glittering emerald eyes watch over the hall from either side of the arch.

Three tall arches lead out from the armory, one on each wall opposite and adjacent to the eastern passageway.  While the floorboards here are sanded, they are not polished, offering better traction when the weapons that line the walls are tested.

Dark mahogany paneling lines the walls but is barely visible, for every scrap of space against the wall is covered with shelving stacked neatly with books.  A special crosshatched wooden shelf stands just to the right of the entryway, full of scrolls.  Heavy curtains, made of a material that makes them seem to shimmer, drape over the three stone arches leading into the gardens, helping to keep dust and debris from outside at bay, preserving the precious stock of the library.

A heavy humidity hangs in the air in defiance of the garden's desert surroundings.  Shallow pools weave around the round-cobbled paths, sprouting several varieties of fragrant water lily.  Huge blue irises twine around one large stone archway that leads down to the south.

A cool radiance sparkles in the clear, refreshing atmosphere of the Air Garden.  Twisting, careless paths weave in easy elegance around the area, curving in fanciful spirals and grandiose arcs.  The flowers here vary in size, but all are snowy white and speckled toward the center in pale primrose-blue.

A smooth stone walkway passes through the tall metal gate that opens here, dust and sand giving way to small green shrubs and blossoming succulents.  Stretching east and west, stone walls serve to protect the area from the harsh Velakan winds.  Faintly carved into the sand-worn surface of the walkway lies the image of a goblet, pointing north further into the oasis.

Walkways from three directions converge in this area, meeting along the perimeter of a deep spring of saltwater.  Protruding from the center of the splashing water, a large limestone fountain bears inset pieces of carved zenith spinel.  Gnarled cacti rise out of the ground, surrounded by large sand-worn rocks.

Clusters of desert lilies huddle along the bottom edge of a layered stone wall that shields the surrounding area from the harsh desert winds.  The dusty walkway extends north towards more houses and east further into the oasis.  Barely visible beneath the sand on the path is the carved image of a stylized knife.

Bursts of green wildflowers litter the walkway, providing stark contrast to the muted color of the stone.  On the east side of the path rests a massive smooth rock chiseled to depict the image of a male S'Kra Mur.  A small opening cut into the sand-worn walls allows visibility of the sweeping dunes on the other side.

The north and east walls meet here in a sharp corner marking the boundary of the area, naturally lined by piles of sand of various sizes.  Near the north wall stands a large rock carved to depict the image of a male S'Kra Mur.  The unmistakable sound of trickling water drifts through the area, enticing in the unrelenting desert heat.

Enough sand has been cleared away to expose an intricately carved female S'Kra Mur along the full height of one wall.  The walkway branches southeast further into the oasis, where tall shadows waver in the desert heat.

The light plays sparkling games with the crushed obsidian that lines the weaving pathways here, dancing in faerie-like jocosity across black marble benches.  Tiny wood violets take shelter beneath them, spreading their vivid petals in the comfort of the shade.

Candlelight twinkles from the many windows of an enormous manor house that is sprawled across the southern end of the village, hugging the shoreline of the Segoltha River.  The low sound of snoring comes from the house, and you notice a large pig laying sound asleep next to the massive hardwood door.

A grove of trees covered with deep green, glossy leaves and laden with plump fuzzy peaches stands just east of a large manor house.  A cobblestone path winds through the trees toward a group of buildings to the south.

A Gor'Tog housemaid emerges from a stone building carrying a huge silver platter of roasted meat.  She hurries it through a side door of the manor house.  Opposite the stone building is a brick structure with neatly-trimmed rosemary and lavender hedges surrounding it.  Several women in servant's garb hang freshly washed garments and linen on the hedges to dry.

A strong, unpleasant odor comes from a stone-block building where bits of bones and brownish stains cover the entryway.  Dozens of flies buzz and crawl over the strong mesh covering the building's window.

The unmistakable odor of putrefying meat assails you when you enter the larder, lessened only slightly by the breeze flowing through the mesh-covered windows that are arranged all around the building.  A large iron wheel mounted in the ceiling supports several slabs of meat and carcasses of game birds.  Brine barrels and salting tubs are placed alongside a stone chopping block.

The tantalizing aroma of roasting meat and herbs emanates from a massive brick hearth on the far wall.  An iron spit revolves slowing over the fire, powered by a strange contraption.  Sitting conveniently at the hearthside are a tinderbox and a huge wooden bin.  Shelves on the walls are covered with neatly arranged supplies, and sturdy wooden pegs mounted in the beams of the high vaulted ceiling hold hanging bunches of garlic and onions.  A long deal table occupies the center of the stone floor.

Enormous coopered tubs fill the room, some filled with clothes soaking in soap-filmed water.  Several washboards and an assortment of wash-sticks hang from the wall.  An earthenware soapdish holds a few greyish lye-balls.

The gentle fluttering of wings and occasional cooing come from the dark huddled shadows of sleeping birds.  A stone dairy and great barn overlook the yard, and some wooden steps lead down toward the Segoltha River's edge.

The deep waters of the mighty Segoltha River lap against the wooden planks of the Grandmaster's boats that are securely tied at the shore.  Across the river and far off to the south, you can see the treetops of the massive Endrus Forest.

The soft lowing of cattle mingles with the more strident sounds of yaks and mules being unharnessed by strapping Gor'Togs.  A similiar group can be spied through the stable door, swiftly unloading caravans and pack animals.  Tired traders troop towards the manor house and a meal, passing beneath a large painted sign.

The gurgle of trickling water resounds pleasantly in the peaceful tranquility of this ceramic-tiled room.  Slate shelves trimmed with marble edge the walls, providing a cool surface for the flat pans of separating milk.  A Gor'tog dairymaid wielding a pair of grooved wooden batlets deftly shapes a portion of butter, then adds a decorative Tiger imprint with a butter stamp.

This short hallway contains a wooden entryway leading out to the curia on the west side and a servant's door on the east.  A young serving girl comes through the door, carrying a covered platter toward the buttery to the north.

The west wall of the larder is covered with an enormous blue cupboard, while the east wall holds an equally large purple cupboard.  Birdcages containing blackbirds, larks, plovers and thrushes hang from the ceiling among muslin bags of drying herbs.

This dimly-lit larder is cool and damp.  A light breeze wafts in from mesh-covered windows, easing the strong fishy smell that hangs in the air.  The brick floor slopes downward toward a drainage hole in the center.  Thick slate shelves contain fresh fish, cuts of meat and vegetables covered with muslin and handfuls of wet rushes.
This cramped passageway connects the servant's areas.  Some stone stairs lead down to the manor's ale cellar.
The clanking of iron comes from a wooden door, as a weary-looking Gor'tog maid passes through it, heading up some rickety steps for a much-needed break.
Dishes and cups are arranged in piles and stacks atop wooden shelves that line the walls.  Loaves of fresh baked bread wrapped in clean cloths are lined up on a table, awaiting the morning meal.
A large fitted cupboard takes up most of the space in the little linen closet.  A wooden mending table, set off to the side, holds a frayed monogrammed sheet with a threaded needle still stuck in it.

A massive copper dominates the cellar room.  Ale barrels stand in rows on the sawdust-strewn cobbled floor.  A Gor'Tog woman, her head covered by a purple kerchief, uses a wooden paddle to stir some malt into the liquid held in a large mash tun.  A shelf holds casks of yeast and tubs of malt.  By the foot of the stairs, a wincing elderly Gor'Tog man holds a stringy wig between two fingertips as if he were disposing of a dead rat.

This large attic room holds several curtained bedsteads that are tucked into the eaves of the manor roof.  Short stools and a single table holding a metal wash basin are the only other furnishings here.

The clang of iron against iron jars the peaceful night in this open-air courtyard.  Two young men from Ortug's team of guards train with massive metal clubs.  The sweat on their hefty Gor'Tog arms glimmers in the dim light from their candles.  A large archway leads into the main part of the manor.

The heavy blue velvet drapes that cover the many windows in the room are trimmed with shiny gold fringe.  A long mahogany dining table is surrounded by highback chairs, with a large throne-like chair occupying the master's place at the head of the table.  A massive sideboard runs the length of one wall, its surface laden with food.

A Gor'Tog dressed in servant's garb drags a leashed goat out of a wood-framed opening in the south wall.  The animal, stubbornly munching on a candlestick, tosses its head in irritation as it follows the man.  Delicious aromas of roasted meat waft through a wooden arch to the west.

The high-ceilinged vestibule leads from the manor's entry to an ornately carved wooden archway that opens out to the central courtyard.  Tiers of purple velvet with gold fringe top the vestibule and connecting passageway walls, adding a garish touch to the otherwise attractive room.
The walls topped with tiers of purple velvet continue down the east-west stretch of corridor.  A Gor'Tog housemaid, wielding a broom, chases an angrily clucking chicken around a bend to the south.

Several prosperous-looking Halfling traders emerge from an iron door, stepping aside gingerly to avoid a mother pig who has chosen a central spot on the corridor floor to nurse her young.  They chuckle to each other about the hazards of finding good caravan guards these days, as they head north.
The corridor ends at an enormous purple door that fills most of the south wall.  A smaller blue door leads to the west.  This end of the hall seems much quieter, with not a pig or chicken in sight.

The Borthgar master bedroom is a visual disaster!  The purple paisley bed quilt clashes with the red floral rugs and blue checquered draperies.  Resomba, the manor mistress, sits in a massive rocking chair trying to do some embroidery.  She glowers at her work and impatiently yanks out some stitching, ripping the fabric in the process.

This small bedroom belongs to the family's son, Grob, who is sitting on the floor studying something.  He quickly shoves a piece of paper under the bed, giving you a furtive glance.  Toy war clubs and shields are strewn around the room, and a small version of the Tiger Clan guard uniform hangs from a peg on the wall.
Several cloaks and greatcoats belonging to the manor's guests hang on wooden coatracks.  A collection of muddied boots have been tossed in a discarded jumble in a dark corner.

Impressive acanth wood bookshelves line the walls here.  Several books reside on the shelves, but most are heaped in a pile on the floor.  A young goat stands over them, contentedly munching on some pages.

This richly, but rather garishly furnished drawing room contains an ancient central hearth where a hearty fire crackles.  Vivid purple and blue flowers cover the long couches and chairs, and equally bright matching flowers spread across the carpeted floor.  The furniture has a dusty appearance, as if the room has been unused for awhile.

The Grandmaster Ortug lumbers slowly around a group of Gor'Tog guards, proudly examining their bright purple uniforms.  The guards listen carefully as Ortug instructs them.  He recites, "Some person mess with caravan, you bash them!  Some critter mess with caravan, you bash it!"  Several of the guards nod thoughtfully, while another carefully scratches a reminder note on a crumpled piece of paper.

Chaos rules in this unorganized jumble that Ortug calls a study.  Unsteady piles of papers and books cover the floor and desk, forming the Grandmaster's preferred filing system.  A brown and white feathered chicken makes her way through the maze of stacks, squawking and flapping her wings when a single paper drifts down from the desk, sailing over her head and onto the floor.

The ivory-colored balustrade surrounding the belfry is carved with stylized representations of birds and animals.  The view below is of the church cemetery to the north, and the village green off to the west.

Some rows of wooden pews are set before a simple altar.  A symbol carved in the shape of a dove rests on a dais, and a quiet peace fills the space in tribute to Albreda's blessing.  Candlelight casts a tranquil glow over the walls and pews and gives the space a safe and warm feeling at any hour of the night.

The final resting places of individuals and entire families are marked with carved stones.  The history of the village is written in the epitaphs.  A tiny mound of freshly turned earth covered with flowers gives testimony to the continuing function of the cemetery in the cycle of life and death.

The headstones here are plainer and newer than the section of the cemetery closest to the church.  A lavender hedge separates the sacred ground from the surrounding countryside, with a Halfling-high stone wall stretching across the northern boundary.
Cold, clammy, damp dark surrounds everything.  An odor of decay permeates the stale air.
The quiet surroundings of this picnic area give weary travelers a short break before moving on.

The sounds of travelers can be heard from the main road, but the voices are faint and hard to distinguish.  Though touched by civilization's hand, the encroaching trees and chattering critters leave no doubt that nature rules here.  A small log cabin rests on the edge of the path.

Cutting through the forest's vegetation this packed path is used fairly often, if the numerous footprints are any indication.  The trail rises slightly to the northeast and levels out to the southwest, connecting two small log cabins.
At the end of the path rests a small cabin, cradled gently in the arms of ancient firs.  Though the way is neatly cut-back, it appears that the wilds could take this place at any moment.

A pair of stone pillars mark the edge of the neighborhood named Temple Hill.  A freshly graded, crushed-stone street carries traffic south into the heart of the community.  Running along one side of the lane, a low stone wall, cut with a prominent wrought iron gate, borders the grounds of Temple Hill Manor.  Across the street are a row of neat stone cottages.

The crushed stone of the lane leads between several stone cottages, winding its way deeper into the district.  Young locust trees have been planted along both sides of the road in the hopes that with the passage of time they will shade the way.

The Mycthengelde Flatlands encroach upon the base of Temple Hill just below this stretch of Hero's March, with the tallest trees almost an extension of the hill.  Stone cottages cluster along the gravel surface of the way, the solid houses and well-maintained street lending a sense of permanence to the area.  Children shout as they sport among the cottages, their noises echoed by the noise of stone falling in a nearby quarry.

Yellowish-green lawns and shrubs stretch in front of cozy stone cottages, green only where the owners have imported soil or planted raised beds.  In spite of the yellow color, the residents of this area are enthusiastic gardeners as shown by the attention to their landscaping.

Pristine cottages line each side of the path and enjoy a pleasant view of a tall marble fountain and the surrounding flatlands.  A memorial plaque upon the fountain hails warriors from seasons past.  Thick shrubs and pale flowers grace each home with sweet smells and a touch of elegance.

Lazy clouds of dust occasionally billow out from a large stoneworking shop dominating the south side of Temple Hill Lane.  Behind the workshop, loose rock and unprocessed rubble tumbles down a large chute from a partially visible quarrying area.

Carefully tended lawns and young trees provide evidence that the residents of this neighborhood are planting and planning for the future.  Stone and brick cottages line the lane, with somber colors predominating -- mostly dark greys, dark browns, and dull reds, although the trimmings and trappings suggest the inhabitants are not nearly as gloomy as their dwellings.

Grass surrounds a small reflecting pool in this wooded park at the top of the hill.  Strategically placed low stone benches surround the pool, allowing peaceful contemplation of life.  Roses twine along a fence that separates the park from the quarry to the east.

Jagged stone makes a staggered path through this restful park.  Tall trees reach out to the sky and give homes to squirrels, rabbits and a variety of birds.  A lone stone bench, flanked on each side by a pot of fragrant flowers, offers a place for quiet reflection.

Lawns and gardens stretch out alongside stone cottages that stand in rows along the lane.  Small trees and plantings decorate the well-tended lawns, but none are of any immense size.  Evidently, the temple rubble provides better building material than soil for planting.

Cozy, sturdy white cottages line the crushed-stone street, with the exception of one cordoned-off lot.  The fence surrounding it is quite sturdy, and has been patched and reinforced to prevent even the most agile of children from wandering into the area.

The street turns to follow the contour of Temple Hill, providing a good view from the high vantage point.  Downhill lies a small court with a statue in the center.  Rising behind it are the earthen ramparts of the Crossing, the roofs of the city peeking over the top of the wall.

Cottages surround a simply carved stone pedestal in the center of the lane.  A glass case surmounts the pedestal, with a bronze plaque mounted firmly on the front.  Downhill to the east, a great expanse of rooftops stretches out behind the earthen mass of the Crossing city wall.

Scents of fresh bread and baked goods drift upon the air, perhaps from one of the nearby homes.  Sounds of children playing mingle with bird song and form a pleasant melody.  The cozy cottages here have a sweeping view of the Crossing wall below with the city beyond.

The low, yellowish vegetation of the lane gives way to deeper greens and larger shrubs, partially masking the gentle slope to the south.  One young lunat tree seems to be thriving, although it still stands only about as tall as a Gor'Tog.

The stately manors constructed high on Temple Hill enjoy a broad view of the Mycthengelde Flatlands and the roofs of the Crossing.  Rows of colorful flowers and shrubs encircle each manor and give them a distinctive look.  A narrow stone path leads south towards Finch Cottage Path.

Cottages lining the crushed rubble surface of Hero's March have expansive views of Finch Cottage Path and a tiny glimpse of the Crossing's western wall.  Clusters of homes, visible as roofs and chimneys, poke through the lush vegetation below while birdsong drifts on the air.

A heavy cast iron sundial is centered in middle of the crushed stone path, surrounded by a narrow ring of low-growing herbs.  Occasionally a bird swoops down to land on it, as if checking the time.  Between two cottages, a grassy path winds uphill.

Colorful cottages line the crushed rock street and enjoy a panoramic view of the Mycthengelde Flatlands.  Young trees, freshly planted, lift up their scrawny limbs to the sky.  One such tree enjoys a ragtag doll hanging haphazardly from its highest point.

Finch Cottage Path represents a drastic change from Temple Hill proper.  The soil is old and deep here, and vegetation flourishes.  Care was taken when building the cottages to leave as many of the original plants as possible.  Numerous songbirds flit and chirp among the abundant shrubs and trees, a living reward for the careful preservation of plants.

A number of paths converge upon a wide tan circle of crushed stone surrounded by twisting wyndwood trees.  Snug cottages tuck themselves beneath the tangled tree limbs that reach out over the circle.  Birds dart about from tree to bush to shrub, pausing frequently at the cedar platform birdfeeder on a tall pole that stands at the center of the circle.

The clamor of commerce from around the West Gate carries from beyond the city wall, but this tranquil court is well screened from view among the trees.  Graceful cottages cluster around a huge iron bell hung from a decorative stone tower.

Lunat trees line the elegant path meandering between the comfortable-looking cottages snugly situated in thick stands of shrubs.  The tree-lined path continues to the south, while a smaller path branches off to the northwest.  Birds dart between shrubs and trees, while birdsong rings out in a near-constant flow of music.

The path dead-ends into a cozy circle of homes clustered around a small clearing edged with wildflowers.  Comfortable cottages are nestled among native plants and lush landscaping tended with loving care.  Birds flit about the luxurious vegetation, pausing at a cedar platform birdfeeder on a tall pole.

The graceful path winds between stone cottages nestled in comforting thickets of vegetation.  Chirping echoes around the cottages as birds dart in and out amongst the shrubs.  A long sunflower feeder hangs from a sprawling old oak, providing a royal feast for visiting birds.

Lunat trees line the elegant path that narrows as it continues toward the southwest, slipping between cozy cottages pleasantly located in stands of tended vegetation.  Birds gambol in the air between trees on either side of the path and birdcalls ring out with a merry chatter from the surrounding undergrowth.

The Finch Cottage grounds are carefully landscaped to attract birds.  Shrubs and berry bushes provide food and sanctuary, and nest boxes hung about the yard provide cozy homes.  Finches abound, attracted to a long hanging feeder in front of the cottage's window.

Native plants and bird-friendly vegetation grow in lush profusion around cozy stone cottages.  A large oak birdfeeder on a tall pole creates a focus for the cabins -- evidently bird watching is a common local interest.

The path ends in a grove of trees containing a small circle of cottages centered about a tall cedar platform birdfeeder.  The cottages are nestled beneath the canopies of tall old trees and surrounded by luxuriant stands of low plants.  Birds sprint from place to place in a flurry of wings, pausing from time to time at the birdfeeder.

Laughter rings loud as children play with boats upon a small pond.  Each cottage in this pleasant court faces the pond and has a different flag hung from its eaves.  To the south grows a more densely wooded area that offers the children more exciting play.

Workers sort the salvaged stone of the quarry into piles of similar size and color.  Along the west edge of the pit, stone is pounded and poured through stacked sieves to make various grades of sand and gravel.  Finished materials are stacked along the side of the quarry until needed, when they are slid down a large chute to the stone works.  Every few minutes, warning shouts precede a great tumbling of raw materials from a cliff to the south.

Tall faces of variegated stone loom above the observer on three sides of the quarry.  Workers pry mixed stone and rubble from these rock walls, sending it tumbling into piles which are then shoved over a small cliff to the north for sorting.

Framed by a low stone wall pierced with a wrought iron gate, a grand lawn stretches out along three sides of Temple Hill Manor to gracefully encompass the elegant abode.  Small plantings dot the grass, drawing attention toward the young maple trees flanking the door of the manor.  Two bronze statues set on stone pedestals hold places of honor on the great lawn, further enhancing the elegant setting.

Sheltered under the watchful eye of the mountain, towering walls and craggy parapets rise like a ravenous serpent from the rock that composes this end of the ravine.  Wrought of mikkhalbamar and thick, iron bands, the massive gates of the fortress mark the end of the valley road.  Silent evidence of battle litters the ground; riven siege towers, wrecked onagers and shattered scorpions have been trodden nearly to splinters by time and the footfalls of great beasts.

Unadorned except for two large torches in plain iron holders, the gatehouse is empty and clear of debris.  Many years of tramping boots have worn a smooth path across the flat stones of the floor.  Thick, iron-banded gates, made of dense mikkhalbamar, provide an exit to the valley.  A stout crossbeam sits nearby, ready to secure them against invasion.  Two openings and a raised portcullis lead further into the fortress.

From this vantage point, high above the trail below, the view would be spectacular -- if only the constantly wind-whipped snow would clear long enough to allow a good look.  The mountain rises with a sheer slope, curving slightly overhead so that this ledge is somewhat protected, but also preventing any possible climb further.  The ledge itself is wide enough for comfort standing, but not so wide that one is tempted to remain for any length of time.

Dim light from the passage filters through the foliage, illuminating an opening in the forest that's barely wide enough for a Gor'Tog to pass through.  The sounds of animals and insects come from the underbrush, along with other, unidentifiable sounds.
Raucous calls of birds ring out overhead from the unseen sky.  Vines and creepers dangle from the soaring canopy which stretches far above the shrubs and saplings of the forest floor.

Standing tall and straight in the forest opening, a mighty durmast stretches skyward, its spreading branches reaching like outstretched arms to the surrounding forest.  The opening in the canopy allows for grass to struggle with the ever-present vines and shrubs.

Growing up over a clump of saplings and shrubs, a particularly exuberant creeper has all but obscured one path through the woods here.  Further paths are less overgrown, and show evidence of being used by something, although the tracks are not quite like any animal recorded.

Fallen leaves lie like forgotten children's toys along the forest trail, tattered and strewn about with the passage of animals.  The faint scent of decaying foliage lingers in the air, everpresent beneath the smell of the forest.

Seeping from the ground, a tiny spring burbles within the forest, its waters making the area more humid while providing a source of moisture for delicate plants.  One bank of the pool shows signs that the waters are also used by the forest's denizens as welcome refreshment.

The game trails that wend their way through the heavy undergrowth come together long enough to split apart again.  The rustle of leaves gives evidence of something lurking just beyond sight, but nothing gives any clue as to the unknown creature's identity.

Falling like a curtain from the canopy, a wall of vines has interwoven itself so tightly that it blocks further passage in some directions.  Game trails twist their way through the rest of the trees, joining and parting like a meandering stream.

Mountain peaks, reminiscent of castle turrets, cast a persistent shadow over this region.  Rarely does the sun's warm embrace penetrate the chilly gloom.  Blasts of wind charge down the mountainsides to assault the glacial plain with unbridled fury.  Deep-throated rumbling echoes across the plain, the voice of the ancient icy river speaking on its slow, ponderous journey through the mountains.  Rising from the plain, a dark stone pillar stands resolute against nature's fury.

Underbrush crowds up against the taller trees, almost choking out any passage.  Forest creatures, however, have left their mark and a few twisting passages allow for travel deeper within the wilderness.

Resting in the shadow of taller peaks, the mountainside is subjected to frigid temperatures.  Cyclonic gusts tear down from the summit to race across the landscape, causing a banshee-like wail to issue forth from the deepest crevasses and chasms marring the terrain's icy blanket.  Blinding clouds of snow and ice, stirred by the constant winds, serve only to disorient the unwary.  A dark stone pillar, unstable as a result of glacial tremors, leans to one side.

Towering mountain peaks rise high above this glacial plain, their tops lost in swirling clouds of windblown sleet.  A nearby peak casts a shadow over the ice field, creating a noticeable difference in temperature.  Large snowdrifts cover the mountainside, similar to the dunes of a desert and equally difficult to traverse.  The bleached bones of an unknown pack animal and its owner lie exposed at the base of a dark stone pillar.

Little can survive the constant onslaught of the bitter cold winds rushing across the exposed mountainside.  Towering drifts of snow have formed to either side of a small rocky outcropping, providing limited shelter and respite from the elements.  Partially buried in one of the drifts stands a dark stone pillar, perhaps a route marker for a lost trail.  In the distance, shrouded in clouds of blowing snow and ice crystals, the tallest peaks of the range are visible.

Surrendering long ago to the onslaught of a glacier, the mountain now lies buried beneath an impenetrable blanket of ice.  Frigid winds whip across the glacial surface stirring thousands of small crystals, each tiny shard capable of flaying exposed skin.  Feeble rays of sunlight are useless in dispelling the unyielding bitter cold.

Covered in a perpetual winter, the high mountainside has proven to be inhospitable to all but the hardiest of explorers.  Frigid temperatures, constant winds and sudden snowstorms are all part of the daily experience in this region.  Perhaps, in some distant past, this mountain range was exposed to warmer temperatures and seasonal changes, though only the spirit of the mountain knows.  A solitary dark stone pillar stands in resolute silence.

Blinding, swirling clouds of ice crystals further compromise the already treacherous footing on the slippery, glacial ice.  A deep crevasse gives rise to concern for one's safety in this region, as only incredible stresses could cause such a fracture.  Leaning drunkenly, a dark stone pillar stands silent watch over the snow field.

Crashing against the mountainside has caused the ancient glacier to become broken and shattered.  Crevasses crisscross the glacier, their icy blue hues deepening with their distance below the surface.  Gigantic shards of ice, thrust up from the depths of the glacier, twist as they reach for the sky.  Toppled and lying on its side, a dark stone pillar has proven no match against the forces of nature.

Blue-tinged monoliths rise from the shattered glacial plain, a result of the relentlessly slow grinding process of ice against stone.  An insidious pattern of crevasses and trenches lies buried beneath a blanket of snow, their presence betrayed only by slight depressions.  Occasionally the great ice field is wracked by violent tremors as the mountain surrenders to the tremendous weight and pressure of the frozen river.  A dark stone pillar stands in solitude on the desolate plain.

An unusual copper and bronze sculpture consisting of crescent moon shapes bobs silently at the base of some wide steps.  Surrounding the metal moons on all sides, the walls are covered with a painted depiction of Moon Mages in various stages of stargazing.  The three moons -- Xibar, Katamba and Yavash -- smile down upon the watching mages from their locations high in the painted sky.

Directly opposite from an ironwood door is a massive portrait of a hunting expedition, though this is far from the only indication of the manor owner's inclinations.  The walls are decorated with an inordinate number of trophies, ranging from snowbeast heads to bearskins and leucro tails.  A snarling boar's head stares down the hall from its perch high above the glazed marble floors.

High above, a colorful awning peeks out from the edge of the rooftop between hanging strings of spider vines that cascade down the manor's walls.  At regular intervals along the upper ledges, stone gargoyles leer downward with mouths gaping open, some of their number wrapped in cloaks of vines.  Far closer to the ground, an ironwood door allows entry into the building.

Brown and red bricks set into the basalt of the manor outline each of the arched windows and emphasize the building's rich opulence.  Spider vines struggle across some of the sills, winding down toward the ground from their source on the rooftop.  Additional victims of the strangling vines are the gargoyles of varied design that stare from the heights into the gurgling canal.

A mound of slimy-green refuse coagulates here, providing a shaky foothold and limited view beyond the moat's filthy walls.  The gatehouse looms overhead like a gaping maw, and a narrow ledge leads upwards through a patch of slippery moss.  Brackish water oozes east and west, shallow enough that even a Halfling could wade through without much difficulty.

A massive catapult stone protrudes from the water like the bald pate of a Gor'Tog giant.  Its unsavory green hue pales in comparison to the blackened mildew that plagues the embattlement, spreading upwards through imperfections in the stonework and fractures left by siege missile fire.

Frothy white globules erupt from an unknown source beneath the muck and drift slowly in all directions, tainted with grime and residue.  An underwater current sucks them under near a curve in the wall, but they pop right up with stubborn buoyancy.

Standing well over twice the height of a Human, the moat's stone walls muffle all sounds except the faint trickle of water.  The mildewed waterlines reflect the barony's decline and seep lower with each passing year, falling into decay and corruption like the wizard-kings of the Seven Crown Empire.

Thriving stoneworts nestle amongst hardened lime deposits against the wall, their whorly stalks striving forth in defiance of the brackish water.  Intermittent splashes disturb the silence, and darkness blankets the channel which curves around the southeastern edge of the Keep.

A nearly imperceptible current flows from north to south, bringing with it a nagging infestation of hungry mosquitos.  Bobbing along the surface, a discarded chamberpot teeters to one side, revealing a dark, foul-looking liquid.

Thick vines entangle this portion of the keep, from the topmost parapet to the murky waters swirling afoot.  The long, twisted tendrils obscure the stonework completely, gathering at the waterline where striders and beetles skitter between the leaves.  Oddly, the temperature seems somewhat cooler in this location.

The moat halts abruptly, obstructed by remnants of what was once the northeast Keep.  Even from this poor vantage point, the devastation is frightening.  The northeast tower lies sideways across the moat, as if uprooted from the ground by a wrathful god and abandoned like a child's toy.  Undoubtedly, no conventional army wrought this awful destruction.

A luminescent gel-like substance coats the stone embattlement along its roughly-hewn face, pulsing softly with an eerie glow.  The mass tapers off southward, but appears much more prevalent northward where garbage chokes the passageway to just a few feet.

Discarded rubble, lumber and common trash compose a daunting heap to the northeast, blocking the moat entirely in that direction.  The combination of filthy garbage and stagnant water elevates the stench here to heights no mortal should ever experience, and the narrow, slime-ridden passage southwards looks like it offers little, if any, relief.

Broken masonry and trash clog the moat at this junction, forming a makeshift dam that prevents stagnant water from spoiling the northern Keep.  The upper ramparts stand in ruin, clearly the source of all the rubble, but still high enough to thwart intruders despite its dilapidated condition.  Unlike the dank, water-logged channel southwards, the moat looks dry and solid to the east.

Long iron spikes line the moat's bottom, spaced far enough apart that a nimble thief could walk between them, but sure to impale any fool falling from above.  Gazing upwards, a dark tower pierces the nighttime sky, soft torchlight flickering from its windows.

The moat descends through a gap in the foundation, the site of a massive cave-in where attackers undermined the castle's embattlements.  Ramparts once thought impenetrable lie about in shambles, blocking further progress beyond the exposed mining tunnel.

Crumbling stone slabs rise from the earth like misshapen gravemarkers, lamenting their downfall from what was once a mighty bastion.  Other fragments choke the very mining tunnel that induced their ruin, as a final act of defiance in a war the descendants of long-dead soldiers can't even recall.

Roughly carved stone walls meet the hand cut blocks of the keep's outer wall to the south.  Moisture creeps down the tunnel walls to gather in a pool on the floor and begin its journey deeper into into the darkess.  An opening, half-heartedly covered up, appears to have led out at one time but is now sealed.
Light seeps through small holes in the ceiling of the tunnel and reflects dimly off the stone walls.  Thin rivulets of water trickle along the rough passage floor, flowing slowly to the north.

Broken strands of cobwebs lifted by an almost imperceptible current of air brush against mildewed walls.  A splintered oak door hangs precariously against the inner wall of a tunnel that splits to the east.

An oak door hangs in ruins against the stone wall, held in place by one twisted iron hinge.  A collection of rubble has been piled up against the tunnel wall to form what looks like a battle barricade.

Although not visible in the darkness, a steady dripping can be heard as water makes its way from the ceiling to the floor.  A slippery slime covers the floor, requiring each step to be made with caution.

A few weapons and armor lie on the floor, rust and decay being a testament to the years that have passed since they were last used in a battle.  A garrison banner, still attached to its staff, lies buried under rubble and mud.

Brewer's vats and barrels reveal the past purpose of this room.  Crossbeams still support the pulleys once used to move barrels from the racks to transportation carts.  Tired and frayed ropes hang from the crossbeams, dangling just out of reach.

Empty burlap sacks, long ago robbed of their grain by the smaller vermin that run these tunnels, lay rotting in the moisture of the floor.  The storage racks where the bags were once stored are now little more than splinters tossed about recklessly.
A caved-in section of the ceiling allows light and air to enter this section of the tunnel.  Sporadic patches of moss growing along the stone walls glisten with moisture in the dim illumination.

Any movement to the east would require stepping on an odd looking slab of rock embedded in the floor of this passage.  A large tapestry depicting a battle of archers versus horsemen hangs on the wall of the tunnel.

Any movement to the west would require stepping on an odd looking slab embedded in the floor of the tunnel.  A large tapestry depicting a scene from a battle hangs on the wall.  A soft glow of light winds its way down the tunnel from the eastern end.

High in the ceiling, troughs have been carved and a low burning fire finds residence there.  Obviously fed by some type of fuel, the light makes it very easy to see in what would normally be a pitch dark area.  Interestingly, there is a small opening in the lower portion of the north wall.

To the northeast is the view of a richly decorated room that is quite out of place in these deep, dank tunnels reeking of wet soil and stone.  A glow of light filters through the iron door but reveals only darkness on the other side.

Time and abandonment have not destroyed the beauty of the lavish tapestries and thick carpets that adorn this underground room.  Designed to be self contained, the room contains a four poster bed, a pair of well cushioned chairs, a dining table and a polished mahogany dresser.  A bookcase large enough to hold several month's worth of reading material stands empty against the furthest wall of the room.

Gravel and rock piled about the floor almost hide the expensive tile laid on beneath the rubble.  A shredded tapestry hanging on the wall makes a feable attempt to hide a hole carved out of the rock near the floor.  Studying the tapestry for any indication of what it might have depicted in its better days, your eyes follow it to the ceiling where you notice another hole that is definitely out of reach.

Old meat kegs, now empty, fill this room.  Still present on the stone floor is the salt that was once used to pack the meat.  Now dirty and caked, the salt has managed to keep the room completely dry which in turn has made this part of the tunnels one of the few areas without a mildew smell.  In a divot carved into the wall, sits a wooden box.  A hole, about three feet off the floor, has been bored in the stone wall.  The tunnel continues to the east but gets very low.
A low ceiling makes standing impossible in this section of the tunnel and the sharp edged stones of the roughly chipped passage makes crawling particularly uncomfortable.
Sticky cobwebs cling to everything that passes through this tight space.  Faintly glowing patches of lichen provide the only source of natural light.

You find you must twist and turn your body to to maneuver through here.  There will be no turning around at this point, you must ever continue forward or back your way out.  So close are the walls that you can feel the heat of your own breath.  The cold stone is almost welcome as sweat drips from your brow.

Any effort to stand in this portion of the tunnel would be futile.  Movement further north will require a bit of twisting and turning.  The passage to the south, just a few squirms away, appears to be a little more spacious.

Several bones and skulls lie scattered about the floor along with remnants of armor and weapons.  A fire to the northeast has scorched the walls about half way into this section of the tunnel.  White streaks of ash reveal something was drug across the floor and to the south.

A fire raged in this room at some time in the past.  A fire hot enough to turn the surrounding rock to a molten slag now cooled to glassy smoothness.  A few inches of grey ash on the floor is all that remains of whatever objects were once contained here.

Faint tracks of white ash run from the north and into a hole in the east wall.  A make-shift iron plate which once covered the small opening is now pryed up and allows entry.  Occasionally a slight whisp of fresh air floats in from the south cooling your face just briefly.

Cobwebs trail from shelf to box to rotting bag in this underground storage room. Several old chairs are stacked against one wall, and a pile of splintered crates blocks a portion of the exit to the north.

This portion of the tunnel has been converted into a storage area for the furniture of the keep that no longer has a home.  A good size hole now covered by a tapestry at one time must have provided access to the keep itself but it is now sealed.

An old single hole privy fills the majority of this room.  A mirror frame with no mirror inside hangs crookedly on the wall.  Stone and pebbles are piled about the floor making it difficult to find a comfortable place to stand.  A large gaping hole in the ceiling is well out of reach.
Dim light seeping through the gloom from the south provides a welcome alternative to navigating through these dark, web-riddled passages by touch.

Weblike threads dangle in artistic patterns from the ceiling and walls.  The scent of dust, trapped in the sticky strands, hangs heavy in the air.  To the south an arch, now bricked up, silently tells of a time when this passage was part of the Keep's floorplan.
The rough stone walls of the tunnel are covered with a sticky substance that would seem to be spider's silk, were it not so inordinately thick and heavy.

Ants seem to have taken up housekeeping in this part of the tunnel.  As they crawl about and over your hands you can't help but wonder how they could build a nest in what appears to be almost solid rock.  Light makes its way across the stone floor from a low opening to the west where the area on the other side offers an opportunity to stand and stretch.

As you move through this tunnel your mind pauses to reflect on the workers that dug it.  Just moving through them is difficult, the thought of having to chisel and pick inch by inch and then haul the debris out boggles the imagination.

Your knees ache with the pain of supporting the weight of you and all your gear.  Your clothing and other items snag on the razor-like edges created through the impact of metal picks on hard stone.  The passage sweeps from a northern darkness into a western darkness.

As you crawl along this passage, sharp rocks and gravel give way beneath your hands making it difficult to stay on all fours.  The low ceiling traps your breath and makes it hard to breathe, as you fight the sweat that runs off your brow and into your eyes.

Bricks, shovels, lime and mortar are piled near a bench with other mason's tools, and a stack of smoothly-cut blocks eclipses the basement's rusticated facade.  Additional space opens to the south, and a crude stairway climbs upward on dimpled steps which look like a blind man attacked them with a pick.

Distorted sounds echo down this pock-marked tunnel, carried on a frigid draft whipping around your legs like a disgruntled poltergeist.  Flickering torches maintain a somber light as the passage descends sharply to the west.

Chilling darkness permeates the chamber despite a glowing firepit, churning sparks like a mage's bungled spell.  A long wooden rack replete with chains and manacles awaits traitorous thieves or murderers, and heavy tongs, branding irons, and leather whips round out the torturer's modest collection.

This end of the basement remains bare of supplies, excluding a dusty barrel tethered against the wall.  A trail of footprints marches back and forth between a storeroom door and a sturdy ladder, but seems loath to proceed north any further than necessary.

Sealed crates and pallets cram the room from floor to ceiling, most marked as one sundry item or another.  From lumber to furs to perfume, you can bet it's here if traders find it worth the journey to Riverhaven.

Multiple levels of shelves expand the storage capacity here at least twofold, accommodating a stockpile of iron rations which could probably support the keep beyond a thirty-day siege.  Casks of low-grade wine settle in a far corner, as tasteless now as they'd be in a hundred years.

Deft craftsmen have fitted massive blocks of new stone, rebuilt cabinets, and added several shelves to these kitchens.  Only faint smudges of indelible black and mild bubbling at the edges of some of the old masonry show that these kitchens were anything other than pristine.  Large kegs of ale and tapped barrels of wine now line the eastern and northern walls.  Pitchers and ladles hang from long brass hooks, and the wide shelves are crammed with preserves and bottles.

If the victuals taste as good as they smell, the current Baron follows his predecessor's tradition and keeps a lavish table.  Fresh fruits and vegetables garnish shelves along the wall, and strings of garlic, dried peppers and sausage dangle from handy hooks overhead.  A scarred cutting board proudly displays an array of dishes ranging from poultry to exotic seafood imported from the Eastern Seaboard.  Each dish bears the hallmark of the chef's culinary brilliance.

Barely large enough to accommodate the deobar table and matching cabinets for which it was built, this modest room serves as a staging area for elaborate feasts before their presentation.  Southwards, master chefs prepare renowned culinary recipes foretold by the mouth-watering aromas wafting from that direction.

Seven columns span the chamber in a vast semi-circle of burnished black marble, the middle three curving around a broad dais while the outer pairs brace high, spectacular balconies.  Striking blue-gold banners and silken tapestries proclaim the royal colors of Therengia, but these minor ornaments pale before the tiled dome ceiling and a massive, seven-sided table which dominates the great hall.

Voices and laughter echo throughout the gallery, originating from a granite archway and the keep's central hall beyond.  A majestic standard hangs upon the wall in plain view, so that all who enter or exit the Baron's court shall know who it is that offers them hearth and hospitality.

A row of evenly spaced torches burns brightly to illuminate the way along this long gallery that stretches to the east.  A large tarpaulin, nailed to the wall, has replaced the old tapestries.  Blue-marbled tiles lead southward through a well-lit entry hall.

Twin rows of gleaming plate armor stand along the lengthy hallway, resplendent in shimmering surcoats of blue and gold.  A heavy wooden beam protrudes from a nearby pedestal, placed so that it won't disrupt the pristine view, but still close at hand should the entrance need to be barred.  The polished marble floor radiates a soft, blue luminescence as it ripples northward into flickering shadows, like moonlight on the open water.

The corridor halts before a drystone wall, recently constructed in a manner unlike that of the surrounding masonry.  A broken shovel litters the ground, quite out of place considering the rich tapestries and extravagant weapon displays to either side.  Southwards, a crude stairway leads down to the lower levels.

Nothing more than a recess in the exterior wall, the latrine's cleanliness speaks well of the servants who attend it.  Sweet-scented jasmine mollifies the air, and a bucket of wash water stands prepared to flush out the chute.

Modest but comfortable, the servants enjoy excellent quarters considering the restricted capacity of the keep.  Woven rush mats blanket the cold floor, and soft bedding comforts the hand-picked personal staff who retire here after toiling in the yards or kitchen.

A few steps or so above the polished marble deck, this raised platform nevertheless grants a commanding presence over the great hall.  Glowing braziers flank the Baron's throne, infiltrating the chamber with feeble, reddish light and the pungent smell of burning herbs.  Gazing downwards, the hall seems barren and quiet despite its restoration, mourning the ancestral knights, ladies, battle songs, and ballads that echoed through the keep so long ago.

Spanning roughly ten feet across, this dim corridor ranges southward to a guard's antechamber.  Thousands of opaque tiles form a vivid mural illustrating the keep before it was razed, silhouetted against a clear blue sky and the rising sun.

Light and heavy crossbows hang from a convenient rack, each weapon accompanied with a score of deadly quarrels.  A simple table and chair are the only other furniture in this spartan guard post, yielding to a lengthy corridor northwards.

This expansive bay accommodates a score of professional soldiers, though ample space remains for twice that number if needs be.  Judging from the perfectly aligned cots and footlockers, the Captain of the Guard keeps his charges orderly and well-disciplined -- even mattresses reserved for infrequent mercenaries lay neatly in the corner.

Greatswords, battle axes and maces join an immense inventory of weapons staged around the room, and elaborate suits of plate and chain await champions bold enough to don them in Theren's name.  Somehow, a small writing desk littered with scrolls and ledgers squeezes midst the armaments, where a scribe reluctantly logs every piece of equipment.

This cramped alcove is packed with the raw supplies necessary for the ardous task of smithing.  A single torch casts a dim, flickering light on the different metals, causing faint reflective wisps to dance in an ever-shifting pattern upon the dark granite walls.  A bored Dwarven attendant sits off in a corner in front of a stained and torn velvet curtain.  From somewhere down below comes the faint sound of the pounding of metal.

Thin moonlight strays through a rough, cross-shaped arrow loop, betraying a flurry of dust stirred up by your movements.  A sturdy oak door leads out to the parapet, and a spiral staircase winds downward to the first floor.

Dull, featureless stone marks this interminable hallway, and a glimpse in either direction promises little if nothing better.  A flight of short steps ascends to the keep's upper echelons, straining half the corridor's length just to reach the next floor.

Heads, horns and furs from beasts both mundane and monstrous decorate the freshly-painted walls of the Hall of Knights, where the Baron's warriors congregate when not feasting in the Great Hall or sparring in the courtyard.
