The castellan's office looms beyond an acanth table strewn with local maps and games of strategy, and the keep's chapel lingers to the east like a dull afterthought.

Tapered candles provide a warm light for the Chapel of Chadatru despite the dark of night.  Even in the dim light the stained glass window can be viewed.  A richly embroidered tapestry serves as a backdrop to a polished ash altar carved with the image of a golden lion upon its surface.  Oak benches have been placed here so the devout can come and observe the first rays of dawn blaze into existence across the face of the window and cast its fiery light across the altar of the god of justice.

This particular corner of the parapet sulks below the northwest tower, rising overhead with all the majesty of an emperor's palace compared to the outer ramparts.  Unlike the weathered stone deck, the tower shows signs of half-hearted maintenance where mud and grime was scraped away by either reluctant servants or guards caught sleeping at their post.

The sound of boots striking stone echoes across the parapet whether you step or stand still.  Perhaps a despondent ghost or lone watchman, the source remains obscure though a clear line of sight bares the passageway in both directions.

Disjointed boarding provides a makeshift roof over this squat drum-tower, the ancient wood half-charred to a brittle crisp.  Safeguarding the entrance and western courtyard, the embattlement provides fields of fire ranging beyond the outer ramparts, and machicolations to hinder assailants below.  If not for the keep's warlike implications, the picturesque view of the surrounding countryside might even be considered romantic.

A tiny bird's nest rests between two square-cut merlons, protected by a wooden shutter still dangling from a few arrow-riven splinters.  Almost laughable in this place of war, the nest's owner has gathered shreds of hay, cloth and fletching to build its new home, now an old souvenir of long-dead men and forgotten battles.

Ages ago, the parapet encircled the northeast tower and continued south to protect the vulnerable flanks.  But now the walkway greets empty space where the tower once stood, its pitiful remnants strewn across the landscape a thousand times over by unfathomable powers.  Even time takes its toll in the aftermath, slowly eating away the weakened embattlements year after year.

Colorful frescos beautify the walls with bright pastels and soft earthtones, quelling the drab ambience of a stairwell angling down to the second floor.  An assortment of gold and indigo curtains introduces a broad balcony to the east, overlooking the great hall but largely concealed from the occupants below.

The southwest tower harbors a solid, steel-bound door, bolted shut with broad bands of metal.  Its dark grey fixtures pulse in and out of shadow as if suffused with a restless spirit, foregoing the Starry Road to fulfill a tragic life.  Eastwards, the hallway ventures through the infamous guest quarter, while blithe embellishments illuminate the north.

A fine oil painting distinguishes the quaint foyer to one of several apartments reserved for honored guests.  Despite slender arrow loops housed in the embattlement, the trappings here look every bit as comfortable as the finest inn in Riverhaven.

The passageway halts before a reinforced ironwood door with elaborate figures etched around the frame.  Faint scuffmarks blemish the door's threshold, and a stout lock ensures the northwest tower remains offlimits to all but the Baron himself.

The scent of recently painted wood lingers where a restored architrave has replaced a severely damaged doorway.  The sturdy door is made of carved deobar, graced with a shiny, new brass doorknob.  Fresh rush matting muffles every footstep ensuring that guests are not disturbed as bustling servants go about their daily chores.

Woven rush matting cushions your footsteps as the hallway veers past the southeast tower and west beyond the common guest suites.  Framed paintings of charming pastoral scenes line the walls and a fine porcelain vase, complete with fresh flowers stands on a marble pedestal.

A side balcony to the west provides a lofty perch for spying on the great hall, visible through a tasseled silk curtain fluttering from a burnished brass rod.  The sconces along the wall remain empty for one reason or another, throwing the walkway into near darkness.

Sturdy wooden planks nailed across the northern wall of this room block off all access to the ruined Northeast tower.  A large tarpaulin stretches across the wooden barricade to keep the worst of the wind and moisture out.

The damp of the stone wall is somewhat mollified by the vivid tapestries that grace this balcony.  The flickering light of a single torch sheds a pool of feeble light onto the gleaming mahogany deck.  A handsome banister gleams with freshly applied polish, the smooth lines of its curved posts testifying to its newness.  Down below, the hall thrives with newfound effervescence.

Sunlight filters through panes of shimmering crystalline glass, spanning the entire roof of this secluded loft.  A sloping bedframe swept with layered down comforters provides guests with a luxuriant cradle for romantic diversions or a simple hideaway to enjoy the pristine skyward view.

More queen's parlor than baron's guest chamber, this comfortable apartment could kindle a romantic spark between the most frigid couple.  Rich blue-gold curtains frame a shuttered window, and an exquisite sandalwood dresser offers sumptuous edibles fresh from the kitchen.  Lush floral carpets shroud the stone floor embellished with soft pink rose petals, while a comfy loft lounges below a skylight of crystalline glass polished to a breathtaking sheen.

Smelling of lavender and polish, this room bears the hallmarks of refurbishment -- fresh paint and obviously new furniture.  The four-poster bed is resplendent with satin covers, plump pillows, freshly laundered bed linen, and small petal-filled muslin satchels tied with a silk ribbon.  An elegant high-backed chair stands in one corner next to a small glass case.  A candelabrum with tall candles stands on a glossy cabinet with brass hinges and handles.

More honeymoon suite than common guest room, the romantic ambience tantalizes your senses.  Freshly laden herbs cover the floor, their sweet scent mingled with jasmine and lavender, and a cozy fireplace contributes to the heady aroma, crackling at the foot of a large canopied bed.  Soft satin pillows shimmer in the light, awaiting their lover's embrace.

This elegant balcony stands midway between the tiled ceiling and marble floor of the great hall.  Seasoned mahogany enhances the decor with its deep, reddish brown hue, and luxurious chairs offer the hospitality one would anticipate in a prince's theatre, much less a stone-walled keep.  Nestled in shadow, you have an excellent view of the hall below.

Everything in this room speaks of a sharp, well-organized mind.  Not a yard of floor space goes unoccupied, and the castellan wastes no effort on frivolous artwork or tapestries.  Instead, books and ledgers line the shelves, all neatly aligned according to size, and a wide desk bears a detailed floor plan of the Keep.

The knights enjoy a private latrine reserved for their use.  Fresh herbs are scattered about the floor that give up their scent when crushed underfoot.  Bundles of straw lay handy and a half-filled wooden bucket of water stands to one side of some overturned chamber pots.  While the narrow chute has been scrubbed as far as is possible, the rest is mercifully obstructed from view.

Once used as a storage place for ceremonial vessels, the aumbry now serves as a home for rats and other vermin.  Dusty cobwebs flutter in every corner, anchored by dessicated husks of spider's prey, and in a few instances, the spiders themselves.

Sunlight is welcomed into the Chapel of Chadatru by the rainbow colors of a stained glass window set in the eastern wall.  A richly embroidered tapestry serves as a backdrop to a polished ash altar carved with the image of a golden lion upon its surface.  Simple oak benches have been placed here so the devout can come and observe the first rays of dawn blaze into existence across the face of the window, casting its fiery light across the altar of the god of justice.

Sturdy wooden planks nailed across the northern wall of this room block off all access to the ruined Northeast tower.  A large tarpaulin stretches across the wooden barricade to keep the worst of the wind and moisture out.

At first glance, this chamber appears quite innocuous.  Grey stone steps lead down to the courtyard, and huge, black walnut doors welcome guests like lethargic watchmen.  However, machicolations disguised as lion's gullets and cleverly concealed murder holes reaffirm this stronghold shall always be prepared to defend itself.

A squat drum-tower overlooks the forebuilding, warding the entrance with ruthless crossbow fire from arrow loops along its battle-scarred walls.  Ascending through engraved marble arches, a series of chiseled stone steps leads into the Baron's resurging stronghold.

The persistent sounds of hooves clomping on solid earth and of neighing signals the presence of the Baron's stables.  A deep-rutted path leads north through patches of dry grass, and a small tower hovers to the east, guarding the stone entryway.

An aging heavy catapult lies abandoned at this junction in the courtyard, with only a broad, wooden frame and broken crossbeam to distinguish it as a siege engine.  A junk pile near the outer rampart reveals the splintered catapult arm and its water-logged skeins, useless now, but at one time capable of raining death far beyond the barony's walls in the form of massive boulders or fiery concoctions.

Buttressed towers stand to either side, housing the drawbridge mechanisms and a half-raised portcullis rusted in place from years of disuse.  The main keep looms to the north beyond an open courtyard, stretching northwest toward some exterior buildings and east where a small grove of trees brightens the landscape.

While the walls of Theren Keep bear telltale scars of siege and war, a newly-constructed ballista assumes the charge of her inner defenses.  Skeins of twisted cord notch the weapon's deadly ammunition -- a half score of long, razor-sharp arrows aimed southward should the mighty gatehouse fall to attackers.  A tall wooden rack contains more lethal shafts beside a crumpled tarpaulin, used to protect the ballista during inclement weather.

The dirt trail gradually turns to mud as it passes a small shed protruding from the western parapet, and a tall, fractured rampart lingers to the north, opposing the parapet's even crenellations with jagged edges that bruise the daytime sky.  Towards the east caravan tracks lead to the Trader stables.

Not a single horse graces the empty stables -- no saddle or harness hangs upon the wall.  If chargers or warhorses ever paced these dusty grounds, they are long gone with the stalwart knights who bridled them.

The outer wall runs diagonally from the northwest parapet, turning southward as it skirts the main courtyard.  Here, the upper rampart has fallen into complete ruin -- first weakened by enemy bombardment, then broken off in the final assault and toppled into the moat.  In spite of the damage, a rickety wooden ladder still leans against the crumbling wall-walk.

Lush grass and tiny wildflowers blanket the ground beneath a small grove of sicle trees, offering a pleasant diversion from the stark backdrop of Theren Keep.  A well-branched young sicle tree is securely rooted beside an old gnarled stump, a symbolic motion by the Baron and his garrison to reestablish the honorable name of Theren and restore the keep to its former glory.

A slight haze of red dust coats the split rails of the small paddock connecting a long thatch-roofed stable to a squat red brick office.  Standing in the shadow of a lone tree, a small herd of horses of varying shade and size patiently whisk away flies with their tails.  One battle-hardened horse remains alone near the water trough, stomping imperiously as he glances repeatedly toward the gate.

Boxes, crates and barrels of all sizes line the walls from corner to corner midst a thick layer of dust and unsightly rat droppings.  An uprooted floorboard reveals a possible underground passage, but the opening is far too small for even a Halfling.

Crumbled stone shifts underfoot with granulated mortar, but the rampart's sheer width makes it safe enough that a drunken bard would have trouble slipping over the side.  An awful stench rises from below, and glancing into the moat you'd guess this is where most of the Keep's refuse is discarded.

Lurking underfoot, the remains of a gravel path lie below sprawling weeds and uncut grass.  A few wooden pikes, their shafts rotting and soft from years of neglect, border the route, still managing to direct pedestrians to and from the field beyond.  Wind rustling the leaves in the nearby forest sounds eerily like the breathy cheers of a faraway crowd of enthusiastic togball fans.

A tall hedgerow blocks the view of the field to the west of the path.  Once neatly maintained, the shrubbery reflects the general sloppiness of the winding, weed-strewn walkway.  Discarded like yesterday's newssheet, a torn pennant left near a large wooden pike shifts gently with every footfall upon the unkempt grass.

An overturned barrel separates the gravelly route from the large field on the western side.  Trash mingles with the grass and bushes as if the group were lifelong friends, inseparable from birth.  It's not hard to imagine a bustling throng navigating the path on the busiest of days despite the current state of affairs.

Hunched astride a bend in the road, a dilapidated wooden shed creaks and groans with every gust of wind.  The curmudgeonly structure looms like an unwanted eavesdropper, interrupting the natural greenery and imposing its dark presence.  While its gravel dies near the shack's entrance, the pebbled path resumes its course to the southwest, retreating to the more welcoming grasses.

Scraggly branches protrude from the bulky hedgerow to the south like a centipede's legs.  The shrubbery crowds the path somewhat, but the tall, flowery grasses along the northern edge balance the scene.  A rut divides the rocky path in an uneven line, likely caused by a wheelbarrow's habitual journey.

Shattered and askew beside the road, a rotting oaken plank slowly succumbs to the torture of both time and nature.  Deteriorating food scraps and empty bottles abound near a barrel tipped on its side, a gooey sludge leaking from the mouth like regurgitated bile.  All signs point to this area formerly housing the field's concession stand, particularly the faded banner labeled 'SNAX' in faint red paint.

Quite literally, this is the end of the road.  The gravel fades into rugged brush grasses and spindly saplings, likely taking root in more recent years when constant activity in the area ceased.  Surrounded by log fencing, a small patch of land is sectioned off to the west, a crumbling stone well visible through the shafts.

Next to the door, a remarkably intact wooden sign shows a curious but effective stick figure of a large biped wiping its feet on a mat.  Two walls are lined with hooks and cubbyholes, where togballers and the grounds crew could store their muddy gear.  Tattered bits of once-bright clothing and rotted muddy boots still remain, although the main occupants of the compartments now are a few weasels and a surly raccoon.

Racks along the wall contain implements for the care and upkeep of the field.  Rusty rakes, shovels and the like stand at wobbly attention, but a few have fallen out of formation -- especially those where the wooden handles have completely given up the ghost.  Some bins in one corner may have held grass seed meant to fill in divots and bare spots on the field after a round of mayhem, although there is no real evidence of this, and they may have actually held turnips or rum for all the observer can tell.

A ring of rusted keys still sitting on a peg on the wall hints that this may have been the guard room for Togs posted to watch the togballs penned in the adjacent room.  The remains of a table with three collapsed legs and several oversized broken chairs, none of which are still functional, lie in a jumble in the middle of the floor.  Indicative of the seriousness with which guard duty was taken, a pair of dented iron tankards completes the decor.

The roots of an immense tree have broken through the floor here, bringing with them a host of mosses, lichens and fungi.  As a result, the footing is tricky, requiring one to high-step, duck and be wary of slipping.  It is not immediately obvious what this room was used for, but whatever the case, nature has surely claimed it back.

The shattered remains of a door frame along with some badly tilting shelving indicate that this small nook was probably a closet of some sort.  Splintered chunks of wood, most of it liberally gnawed, cover the floor.  Piled on the shelves and slipped off onto the ground nearby, shreds of jerseys lie as if they were still freshly washed and awaiting the next match.

Tattered banners hang from the rafters.  On some one can still see the figure of a boar's head; others are merely limp shreds of fabric.  Little else distinguishes this area other than a fallen length of roof lying atop a fractured skull.  The skull appears too small to be an adult Gor'Tog's, but aside from that, there are no clues as to its origin.

A badly decayed woven rush mat covers nearly the entire floor here.  This must have been the practice room, where players could try out their moves with only a modest number of broken bones and smashed heads.  Lying askew in one corner, a large skull grins as if proud that it remains intact.

Battered wooden crates and barrels are scattered throughout the area, creating a sort of obstacle course to walk through for any but small animals.  It seems likely that they once held foodstuffs, but anything that remained has long since decomposed.  The occasional chittering and the faint scrape of claws suggest that some critters have indeed made this place home.

This appears to be the remains of a large pen.  Rusted, cross-hatched wire presumably once kept unfortunates assigned to be togballs inside, although given that the balls were frequently smarter than their jailers, it's debatable whether they really stayed inside for very long.  A flimsy door swings on one intact hinge, but it is now unnecessary due to wide gaps in the old wire.

Once lush and verdant, the thick grass sprawls unchecked along the ground.  The massive hedgerows loom over this corner of the field to create an abundance of shadows for all sorts of creepy crawlies to seek for shelter.  Most of the soil is intact here due to the relatively infrequent use during game days, though a giant felled tree creates an imposing dent.

Trash accumulates upon the ground in staggered clumps, blown onto the grass by errant winds or simply discarded by careless spectators of the past.  The corners of a few benches tossed onto the field jut through the tangle of brambles slowly invading the area.  Sticky mud underfoot emits immodest sucking sounds as people and creatures traverse the turf.

Dense thicket grasses make a play to claim a pair of overturned benches strewn sideways on the ground.  Whether the bleachers were ripped from the sidelines by a terrible storm or a pack of rabid fans remains a mystery, though both scenarios are equally as likely.  Whatever the reason, the long wooden seats inhibit passage westward, but other trailblazers' footsteps and weapons have cleared the brush in other directions.

Years of abandonment transformed the field's southeast corner into a marshy swamp.  Stagnant liquid refuses to absorb into the water table underground, and since the grassy floor descends slightly, the earth degrades into muck and filth.  Splatters of mud cake the surrounding hedgerows as if out of spite.

Two dilapidated posts lie willy-nilly upon the ground.  Once designating the brown side's goal, the rotting shafts serve no more purpose now than to give termites and fungi a place to call home.  Debris in the form of jagged branches and decaying leaves restricts passage through the field where there formerly was open space.

From this high point it is possible to see quite a distance out over the grasslands that slope westward, while to the east a mystical quiet radiates from the forest cloaked in its dark finery.  A plume of smoke drifts over a distant hill, possibly from an unseen chimney.

A tidy kitchen with whitewashed cabinets and a round oak table opens just beyond a short hall leading from the front of the house.  The scent of chocolate drifts in the air and a kettle of tea burbles over the fire.  Placed neatly near the fireplace is a green cushion with lumps and strands of fur in its cloth.  An occasional breeze moves curtains made of yellow gingham tied off with lace ribbon scraps that hang at the windows.  The table is set for company, and a plaque hangs on the wooden door.

An oasis of green in a city of barren stone and rock, this garden holds a concentrated subset of the many herbs and plants needed to refresh the working Empath.  Built by a master, the small space mimics a wild environment, with plants growing in a seeming haphazard fashion amongst their natural brethren.  Tall plantings hide the view of the town and mitigate the chill, damp sea winds.

Set on the roof of the clinic, this comfortable room is meant as a retreat for the staff and for visiting Healers.  One side opens out onto a small but well-tended roof garden where many herbs and useful plants are grown.  Inside, several comfortable chairs and sofas await the weary and work-worn.

Moans, groans, screams and the keening of still-conscious beings undergoing excruciating pain and terror emanate from three treatment rooms that open off this rotunda.  The air is cold and heavy with nervous tension overlaid with the stench of blood and the sharp, astringent odors of medicines.  Several coldly efficient S'Kra direct the entire facility, dispensing minor first aid, directing people to treatment rooms and arranging supplies for the harried surgeons.

Just to the northeast the road is rutted, with an obvious track passing crosswise over it.  This is where the farmers usually cross with wagons of refuse, and take their pigs to feed on the daaknuts, often in depressingly large herds.  Depressing for any travellers caught on the wrong side of the stream of porcine livestock, that is.  The farmers are doubtless quite happy with the fertility of their pigs.

This crude little stand has been here for some time, judging by the weathering of the wood from which it's built.  Essentially a large table with a few boards nailed up on beams overhead to provide some shade from the sun or protection from the rain, it doesn't look as though it would get much business, but it's a favorite gathering place of the area and the three children behind the table grin as they hand over mugs of ale and rolls of bread and whatever else they might have today.

The grand avenue that leads to the Palace is set with elaborate topiaries in the shape of mythical sea-creatures and stately coral formations.  Even the path here glistens like the sea-bed.  Well-manicured lawns sweep away to right and left, surrounding the edifice with a deep green carpet.

Two lines of statues of famous personages and mythical heroes line a wide carriageway made of crushed stone.  Each statue is twice life-size and formed with cunning skill, so that at any moment, they might step down off their pedestals and join the throngs around the palace.

A sweeping carriage drive runs up to the very base of a magnificent stairway carved of white stone.  Day and night, grooms stand ready to assist the nobility in alighting and caring for their horses, while sullen guards stand ready to deal with anyone who causes problems.

A wide, sweeping stair of gleaming white alabaster carries the eye from the grandeur of the Palace grounds to the equally imposing portico.  Giant guards flank the doors, immobile as if cast from stone.  The portico itself spreads across the front of the palace offering cool shade from the heat of the day.  Several fountains spout from bronze grotesques set into the wall, their streams running down into stone basins where the traveler may quench a thirst or lave dusty feet.

The western portico looks out across the city and ocean to the far horizon.  When the weather is right, spectacular sunsets can be watched from the comfort of stone benches conveniently placed to enhance the view.

Gazing out across the city towards the sunrise, the eastern portico offers an inspiring view to the early risers of the town.  From time to time, services are held here to welcome the day.  A low altar with a sunrise carved into the pale yellow stone is set here for that mission.

The roof rises far overhead to disappear in a glorious chandelier made of hundreds of rows of polished crystals in the shape of fanciful sea-creatures.  The floor is a tesseract of cleverly interlocking tiles of sea-foam green stone alternating with pale alabaster shapes that together form endless rows of breaking waves.  To one side, a hallway leads to the public offices accessible to everyone.

Stained glass in the colors of the ocean is set into crescent-shaped windows high overhead.  Bright light falls on the hushed rows of shelving holding fine matching leather-bound books with embossed gold lettering on the spines.  Dark walnut tables with matching chairs provide places for readers to sit and spread out their research materials.

Understated elegance is the theme of this, the premier bank of the province.  Carpet thicker than the bedding in many a cheap hostel muffles every sound.  A golden light filters down from giant lamps set with stained-glass, while a gentle perfume scents the air.  Deep banquettes, upholstered in richly embroidered fabrics provide a comfortable resting place for those waiting to conduct business.

Quiet elegance is the theme here, that and the sort of luxury only huge piles of money can buy.  Thick carpet, rare fireflame-patterned silverwood paneling, polished stone counters and trim emphasize the common theme of material wealth and lots of it.  Elegantly liveried tellers quietly handle each transaction with a minimum of fuss and delay.

Stark white walls and plain grey stone leech all feelings of warmth from the hallway.  Unlike the grand ceremonial parts of the palace, this area is purely functional with no accommodation made for luxuries for the citizenry who must attend to legal matters here.  Offices extend along the hall and are open to assist even those who keep late hours.

This is quite obviously a waiting room for some high-ranked official's office.  Dark wood paneling covers the the thick stone walls and the furniture, though sparse, is of heavy construction.  A door set with brass studs leads into the inner sanctum while an iron-bound door that would do credit to a bank leads to the hallway outside.

Two features dominate the room: a massive safe big enough to hold a Gor'Tog and a desk easily large enough to serve as a small cottage for a pair of Halflings.  The windowless room's only decor is a pair of silk hangings that depict banking scenes.

Stark white walls and dull grey stone floor tiles suck any vestige of warmth from the very air.  Grim-faced folk pass by in both directions, and from behind heavily barred doors comes the sound of clinking coins and the scratching sound of quill on parchment with the staccato clicking of an abacus adding a disjointed rhythm to the sounds, not unlike dry bones clacking in some bizarre parody of a dance.

There is a sense of repressed tension and anxiety in the air.  For all the rich decor, this room seems cold and spare.  A few people huddle along a hard narrow bench along the far wall.  A circular counter surrounds several bored-looking clerks who seem to be engaged in almost any activity other than helping those pathetic few who approach them from time to time.

The plain but serviceable decor extends along this part of the hallway with not so much as a picture on the wall to distract busy citizens as they go about their day.  A hastily thrown-up barrier prevents further travel down the hall to the south, but the offices all seem open for business.

Dominating the tiny room, a large mahogany four-poster bed stands against the wall, nearly blocking the door from swinging open fully.  A homemade quilt is folded neatly at the end of the bed, the bright red and yellow prints contrasting with the darker reddish brown of the wood.  In one corner sits a table, dwarfed by the oversized bed.  A small wooden chair crowds in another corner, an embroidered shawl draped over the back.

Small, dark, and dust-filled, the room is lit only by one ceiling-hung lantern that seems not to have been cleaned in some time.  Piles of rocks lie scattered in corners and on the scratched and stained counter, sorted by color or weight, or in some cases, by whim.  A frayed map is mounted on the wall behind a hanging set of curiously dust-free scales.

A thin film of grease and dust vies with the cobwebs to cover the floor and counter in the tiny shop.  Old Mother Magpie is a familiar character to residents of the area commonly known as 'Tog Town.  Dealing in gems and precious metals, rumor has it she also sponsors a band of street rats who bring her some of her... rarer items.

A gaethzen stand-lamp hovers over the large walnut desk which divides the constable's area from the rest of the room.  A rich carpet covers the polished granite floor, but only behind the desk.  A gold plated door leads to the holding cell where the Malk'smo entertain their more serious visitors.

Calls from the guards above echo down to a narrow strip of sand beneath the soaring walls of Shard.  The river laps quietly at this beach, marked heavily by footprints leading right into the water.  The prints head toward a sandbar rising barely above the surface about fifty feet out.

The river flows by on all sides of this narrow sandbar.  A number of footprints lead west, pointing across the water to a narrow beach beneath the walls of Shard.  To the east, a row of stone pilings rises a few feet above the water's surface, with the nearest one not far away.

Wide stone pilings sunk into the water look like they might have been placed there for a bridge which was never built.  Now they provide a precarious walkway across the river beyond the town walls.  The pilings stop about fifty feet from the far shore, but from here you can just make out a narrow sandbar that should indicate a place to ford the last stretch.

Long tables lined with matching benches fill the roomy pub, standing over a sawdust-covered floor swept clean every day.  Bunches of drying herbs hanging from rafters add spicy scents that mingle with the aromas of meats roasting on spits and the freshly-popped corn kernels that fill wooden bowls.  A small stage has been set up in one corner for minstrels, storytellers and other entertainers.  Contrasting shouts of glee and groans of dismay come from rooms set off to the east and the west.

Feathery ferns and seasonal flowers grow abundantly in beds that circle the courtyard, surrounding numerous tables, each with its own canvas umbrella to shelter customers from inclement weather.  A half dozen tall torchieres are imbedded in the ground giving off light and warmth.  Bowls of crunchy popped corn, a longtime tradition of Kygar's Pub, sit on each table.

Curious spires of rock, whether native to the spot or carved by some forgotten artist, form a bottleneck to the busy streams of traffic flowing up and down the roadway.  Over the years, passersby have carved names, initials and colorful (and sometimes off-color) slogans on every aspect of the rocks.

rooms.t: [The Raven's Mask and Leatherworks, Sales Room]
rooms.desc: Display cases holding leather armor and masks fill much of this tiny shop, but one corner is set up as a comfortable nook beside the stove.  An overstuffed chair sits beside the fire, occupied by a brightly garbed young Halfling man.  The noise of a hammer on metal may be heard from the nearby work room, along with an occasional muffled curse.

Black laquered cabinets line the walls of the shop, their open fronts displaying an assortment of hair care items ranging from razors to combs.  A small catalog rests on a marble counter that stretches from one end of the room to another.  Tiny iron smoke pots, perched on brass tripods in the corners, are giving off a strong odor from the incense burning within.

A fire crackles merrily in a cast iron stove mounted in an alcove along the rear wall of the shop.  The remaining walls are covered with shelves lined with colorful glass bottles and vials.  Dozens of cloth bags hang from hooks attached to the rafters, each of which gives off a distinctive fragrance.  Two elderly S'Kra Mur women dressed in identical enveloping black robes potter about the shop, occupied with their daily routine.

The massive slate roof of the bank overhangs the wide entrance, forming a deep pool of shade relieved by a pair of bronze and crystal flambeaux half again as tall as an Elothean.  A quartet of well-armed guards lean on wicked-looking tridents, while their cold ophidian eyes watch every person carefully.  The doors are open to the night and the energetic sounds of commerce waft out from within.

A wide expanse of cool sea-foam green marble stretches across this noble room.  Far overhead, crystal panes set within a spidery framework of gilded wrought iron provide ample light that in daytime, will flood the room with brightness.  Lofty arches on three sides lead to the various banking departments:  The Bursar for foreign currency exchange, the Cashiers for regular banking transactions and the Bourse for private sales.

The soft jingle of coins mixes with the sharp "click" of an abacus being rapidly worked.  A low counter separates customers from the moneychangers and a brisk business ensues at all hours.  Cool efficiency suffuses each transaction and there is little or no exchange of courtesies or bonhomie beyond the minimum necesary to complete the task at hand.

Pale buff marble walls frame an equally bland beige counter where cold-eyed tellers process transactions with a plentitude of speed and accuracy but a notable lack of warmth or attempts at false friendship common to other such institutions.  Business is the order of the day and that which interferes has no place in these cool and efficient chambers of commerce.

This large room has been set aside by the bank for those wishing to do business among themselves and to prevent the regular transactions from being disrupted.  Heavy velvet drapes line the walls and a thick carpet covers the normally bare marble floor to muffle the sound of buying and selling and the not-infrequent disputes that arise over same.

Flowers line the thick, green grass.  A small opening between the flowers provides access to the lawn from the street.  A pleasant breeze stirs the flowers, while bees industriously fly from flower to flower.  The feel of the grass between one's toes brings people trickling in throughout the day.

Cracked glass doors block access to the cluttered shelves which line the walls of the shop.  A thin film of oily dirt covers everything in the room, leaving a repulsively tacky finish which clings to boots and sandals with each step across the grimy floor.  The burly figure of the owner stands behind the counter, half-hidden by the shadows which fill the area.

A musty dampness pervades this cavernous room, and a faint salt breeze flutters down from a gaping hole in the roof where decades of neglect have caused the weathered beams to collapse.  Faint smudges of paint on the peeling plaster walls evidence the prior existence of proud frescoes, but all that now remains is the occasional hint of a sword arm raised in combat, and the grimace of a dying warrior disembodied from his once-glorious likeness.

Tall, drooping trees form a protective circle around a tiny cove on the riverbank.  Scorched pits in the sand mark old campfires screened by the trees from the walls of Shard.  The reason for the campsite is obvious -- a row of stone pilings stretches out into the river, providing a way across that avoids the heavily guarded North Gate.

The scents of old sweat and dried blood have been worked into the wooden floor of the salle with the passage of time.  Hundreds of students have walked these polished boards, their skills ranging from inept to masterful.  Blademaster Antellius, the school's patron and head teacher, stands in one corner of the room, appraising his students.

A small platform wedged between two large limbs provides a stable resting place high in the apple tree.  A canopy of leaves blocking out most of the view of the sky and the ground below gives the perch a feeling of privacy.  It is not exactly quiet here, but the bright song of birds and whisper of a breeze passing over verdant green foilage is pleasant and soothing.  The sturdy trunk of the tree has a couple of steps hammered down the side to aid climbing to the ground below.

Traders gather on the porch of the inn, sipping mugs of ale and puffing at carved bone pipes as they discuss their latest successes or bemoan the loss of a venture.  A bench swing rocks back and forth with a creaking noise as the chains rub against the hooks in the ceiling, and a pleasant breeze from the sea carries with it the sharp tang of saltwater.

Discarded junk fills almost every inch of the space along the adjoining privacy walls.  Makeshift footpaths weave through the garbage for a navigable route, though one might question the rationale considering the repulsive stench.  A short awning hangs over the broken door facilitating access to the building's interior, holes in the canvas revealing glimpses of the sky.

The walls of the foyer are covered with stippled whitewashed plaster and polished teak wainscotting.  A brass bell sits atop the front desk.  From the dents and scratches in the metal, it sees much use as patrons demand service from a harried-looking clerk.  A hallway leads east toward the stairs, while sounds of merriment echo from the nearby common room where guests can enjoy a snack or meal at any time of the day.

Exposed oak beams, darkened with smoke and age, crisscross the whitewashed plaster ceiling of the hallway.  The scent of fish wafts from the door of the nearby kitchen, where a cook can be heard berating a hapless assistant.  Seascapes and pictures of sailing ships line the walls, while dark oak stairs lead up to the second floor.

A narrow table stands at the northern end of the long upstairs hallway.  Above the table, vases filled with creamy white starflowers hang on either side of a painting of the late Josiah "Jack" Tarr.  Black gauze draped above the painting trails down to pool in soft heaps upon the floor.  Nearby, darkened oak stairs spiral down to the first floor.

A wide brass bed with a lace coverlet and frilly pillows nearly fills the tiny chamber.  Beside the bed, a crystal vase filled with an arrangement of rosebuds stands atop a nightstand.  An intricately woven carpet covers the floor, muffling the sounds from the common room below.

A vibrant floral carpet covers the polished oak floorboards of the tiny chamber.  The colors of the carpet are echoed in the quilted coverlet atop the dark oak sleigh bed.  The quilt, a traditional "storm at sea" pattern, was at one time believed to be a binding spell to protect those it sheltered from Drogor's anger.

A red and gold runner covers the dark oak floorboards of the hallway, the colors vivid against the polished wood.  The gilded frames of the paintings which hang on the whitewashed walls gleam dully in the light.  Each painting depicts a ship on which Captain Josiah Tarr had served before his unfortunate death at sea.  A trapdoor in the ceiling leads up to the widow's walk on the top of the inn.

Tiles of gold and silver-flecked marble line the floor.  A gentle breeze swirls through the room, rustling papers stacked on ebonwood tables.  Carefully watching the bank's customers, a well-armed guard stands beside the paper screen door leading out to the courtyard.

Bright light shines through an opening in the thick paper walls of the building.  A young acolyte of Kertigen sits behind a tall wooden counter, carefully recording the deposits handed to her.  To the west, a moneychanger awaits those in need of his services.
Sitting behind a dark ebonwood table, a bored-looking Dwarf awaits those in need of a moneychanger's services.  A large board, listing currency exchange rates, is propped on one end of the table.

The pungent smell of curing pelts fills the air, coming from several large vats along one wall of the courtyard.  A paper-screen door leads into the furrier's shop.  To the southeast, a crushed shell pathway lies beyond the yard's wooden gate.

Dira'ela Egani sits behind a counter piled high with assorted pelts and body parts of the animals which roam the island.  Busy sorting and cataloging the furs, she always has time to speak with an adventurer about purchasing a new hide.  An open screen behind her leads to the leather repair shop run by her husband.

Several small tables support an array of bottles, jars, patterns and leather working tools.  A delicate counter of darkly polished teak runs across most of the room, behind which sits an aging clerk.  Long shelves line the walls behind the counter, stacked with assorted material.

Racks of leather armor in various stages of repair fill the room.  Sefu himself sits at a long wooden workbench, laboring over a piece of armor for a customer.  Many of his tools, though still sturdy, are worn from years of use.

Windchimes of delicate crystal hang from the ceiling of this elegant jewelry shop.  Intricate Elothean shesegri are painted in blue, red and green upon the paper walls.  Shoiya stands behind an ebonwood counter topped by mottled marble, running her business with a serene smile.

Plump seating cushions and plain low tables are scattered around the room.  Bronze lamps overhead provide bright illumination for scholars interested in browsing through the merchandise.  Zenastara, the proprietress of the shop, bustles about straightening and dusting, pausing to answer the occasional inquiry.

This is a mine shaft drilled horizontally into the mountainside.  Particularly noticeable is a blue moss that coats most of the ceiling and wall.  The strong smell of a recently deceased animal forces an involuntary wrinkle of your nose.  At one end of the shaft is a narrow crevice.
Rubble and loam cover the ground and all that remains visible in the sparse light filtering through the crevice is a decrepit old ladder with rusted rungs.

The strange blue moss throws out an eerie light making it possible to see the surroundings.  Water has corroded the ceiling and the walls, but not enough to erode what looks like a set of mysterious markings.  From this point in the tunnel, there is only one possible direction.

Stalagmites and stalactites reach out trustingly to touch one another.  Helictites high above amaze you with their beauty.  Glowing in the dim light and resting on the floor of the tunnel are sinister formations.  Other than being in awe of the wealth of natural treasures, the predominant sensation is one of cold as the dampness and chill air start to pervade your body.

Curving walls and dim piles of rock continually hint at hidden alcoves and endless corridors.  Your muscles complain as you endlessly sidestep piles of rocks in the bed of an old streamlet.  Any attempts to speed through this place are prevented by numerous depressions.

This is a gallery with a basin-shaped floor, where channels have been cut into the roof by swirling waters.  In the center stand several broad cone-shaped stalagmites, most of which are supplied by several smaller stalactites.  A huge unnatural pile of rubble stands off to one side.

Weaving in and out of large blocks of stone, you stumble across an old fire site.  On most of the walls, the dripstone has formed beautiful cascades, resembling either petrified waterfalls or curtains.  To the north are three identical-looking tunnels.

It is difficult to keep a sense of direction in this stony labyrinth.  Chambers and tunnels open up in every conceivable direction.  The eerie silence is broken only by the crunch of rocks and crystals underfoot.

It is difficult to keep a sense of direction in this stony labyrinth.  Chambers and tunnels open up in every conceivable direction.  The eerie silence is broken only by the crunch of rocks and crystals underfoot.  You also see some scattered bones.
Atop this pile are an odd collection of bones and crude tools.

A large dripstone saw-blade is visible on the ceiling.  Caught in the dim glow of the lights recessed in the wall, it resembles two jaws waiting to clamp down on the next unfortunate soul that chooses to pass under them.  The walls glisten with moisture and are cool to the touch.  A slight breeze wafting across your face carries air both cool and fresh.

Flickering lanterns cast enormous wavering shadows on the pocketed walls.  Despite the frequently placed sconces, the tunnel recedes into nightlike blackness in both directions.  Unknown sounds whispered from all directions cause you to frequently stop and determine their location.
Several small structures all possessing a similar design are dotted around this area and appear specifically built for dwarves.  Passing by, the architecture appears spartan but functional.
The damp and the cold of the cavern that you had previously relegated from your thoughts suddenly becomes more noticeable as a violent shiver takes hold of your body.

Drawn to this location by contagious laughter and hearty singing, you happen upon Forkbeard's Brodger.  Pausing briefly and sniffing the air, smells of home made food and strong ale tempt you to enter.  The possibility of exchanging information and hearing some new rumors also acts as a lure.

A huge stalagmite rises up towards the cavern ceiling, its top disappearing into the darkness.  Dangling loosely from its sides are several thick ropes inviting the would be climber to explore the darkness.  Pitons hammered into the side offer a more challenging climb.

More houses are located in this area and with one exception, they share the same spartan functionality that is reflected throughout the entire dwarven community.  A larger home, known locally as Vinquoy Brach, is the dwelling of the chieftain and his wife and is the focus of a great deal of attention.  Two armed dwarven guards, one on either side of the door of the chieftain's home, scrutinize everyone entering and leaving.

Unlike the rest of the cavern, the floor here has been made purposefully smooth in places.  Pikes, shields, lances and other types of weapons have been placed against the large rocks off to one side.  Several dwarves, suited up in armor are stretched out on the floor off to one side.

Large boulders litter this portion of the cavern, yet it is easy to skirt around most of them.  Off to one side, several boulders have been chiseled, fashioned into seats and placed in a semi-circle.  A larger stone is shaped like a podium, suggesting that this is either a teaching or meeting place.
On either side of the tunnel to your north are two especially bright lanterns.  The tunnel, regular and smooth, bears all of the hallmarks of traditional dwarven mining.

Along the east wall, a multitude of glistening milky-white stalagmites rise up in their delicate beauty like rows of candles waiting to be lit.  The whole area possesses a fairy tale quality, providing a multitude of hiding places.  Occasionally you catch a glimpse of a young dwarven face peeking out from between the stalagmites.

Looking closely at the wall, hairline fissures in the rock are noticeable.  It is unclear whether these are recent or several centuries old.  You resolve to ask someone as quickly as possible.  Hewn into the wall of the cavern are several benches inviting the weary person to take the weight off their feet.

Flickering lanterns cast enormous wavering shadows on the pocketed walls, their light slipping off the surface of a smooth boulder that fills one of the many indentations.  Despite the frequently placed sconces, the tunnel recedes into nightlike blackness in both directions.  Unknown sounds whispered from all directions cause you to frequently stop and determine their location.

Heavy encrustation of magnificent flowstone is located in the recesses of the walls along this tunnel.  At every step, strange and beautiful objects sweep into view.  Reddish wormlike growths coated with quartz and glistening crystals of white gypsum dot the ceilings, walls and floor.  Lanterns have been placed in small alcoves at regular distances.

A small, well lit chamber suddenly comes into view, compelling both humility and silence.  Four vertical monoliths, each owning a corner, buttress the roof.  In the center of the chamber a set of smaller grey stones has been placed in a circle.  The chamber is completely silent, all sounds from the cavern have died away.

Carefully chiseled into the floor within the circle of stones is the hallowed image of Kertigen.  Unlike other areas of the dwarven settlement, where some of the floors have become worn and smooth with age, the surface here appears unchanged from its original state.

An unknown odor makes you sniff as you enter the workshop and it is unclear whether it is originating from the bottles of reagents and solutions on the shelves or the fine dust resembling charcoal that covers the floor.  Colorful crystalline bull's-eyes, crystals and other polished gems have been placed on Goi's display case.  A huge grinding wheel stands off to one corner, surrounded by various other tools used for polishing, sanding and cleaning.  Close to the wheel is a large trough.
A thick layer of dust lies on the floor.  This hut awaits a new occupant.

Heat, noise and the smell of sweat assail your senses as you enter this busy workshop.  Hung on one of the walls is an ornate suit of armor, several pick axes, sturdy helmets and other mining accessories.  Muckele Rognvald stands at the forge, fashioning yet another suit of armor.

Gigantic boulders are strewn all over, steep rock faces surround this area and a large hole lies in the ground.  Firmly secured to several of the boulders is a rope ladder.  Other than the sinkhole, there do not appear to be any obvious exits.

rooms.desc: More shining deposits glitter before your eyes.  Making a mental note of the exact location, you consider returning with the correct tools to mine these rich deposits.  High above shines a faint light, possibly the exit from the mine.  A rope ladder dangles above you.
More rich veins of ore and crystals in the rock face attract the eye and emphasize the wealth of unmined deposits in this tunnel.  Hanging from the ledge is a rope.
A large pile of boulders stacked in the passageway and an overturned wheelbarrow force you to edge by the wall and skirt around these obstacles.

Sturdy timbers at this juncture are in stark contrast to the disrepair that you have witnessed elsewhere.  Similarly the boulders, rocks and pebbles in this room are different.  Although weathering and constant erosion have taken their toll throughout the mine, for some reason this area has been spared.

A ghastly sight confronts you entering this portion of the mine.  Poised to attack, battle axe in one hand, shield in the other, stands a dwarf frozen in all of his glory.  What he was about to fight or defend himself from or what left him in this sorry state, can only be the subject of conjecture.

A strong smell of rotting flesh fills the air.  The source appears to be a rodent that met its demise here, its corpse still partially preserved by the cold temperature.  Mounds of crushed rock that do not appear to be the result of mining litter the floor.  A huge natural bridge stands to the south.

Thin translucent sheets of calcite punctuated by brown streaks hang down from the ceiling.  Unlike most of the mine, there are no timbers that have been used to shore up the roof or walls here.  An eerie, dark silence pervades the gloom.  To the east lies a narrow passageway.

Walking quietly through the dark slippery passageways is claustrophobic.  Turning a tight corner, you almost bump into a large solid slab of ice which stretches across the entire tunnel and prevents further passage.  Encased in the ice is a huge seemingly perfectly preserved creature.

Standing on the long stone bridge, you take a moment to peer over the sides only to see a deep dark chasm that appears to have no end.  Fighting a brief moment of vertigo, you struggle to steady yourself and catch your breath.

The light thrown off by the ever present moss is reflected by a myriad of small crystal fragments embedded in the walls of the tunnel and is reminiscent of the nighttime sky.  A huge natural bridge stands to the north.

The beams that shore up the tunnel have been eaten away in places.  Icicles line the wall and trails of a slimy substance line the tunnel floor.  In the faint glow, the exhalation of your breath momentarily forms a fast dissipating cloud.
The passageway levels off here allowing you to slow down and catch your breath.  The guiding light is even scarcer causing the occasional stumble, stubbed toe and silent curse.

Stepping over piles of rock, debris and abandoned tools, the entrance to a wider passageway starts to open up.  The loud reverberating echoes of the crunching sounds made by your footsteps announce your presence.

A chill in the air forces a shiver and the realization that the temperature has dropped.  The bluish moss on the ceilings and walls is less abundant which makes it harder to see and forces you to concentrate on your surroundings by using your other senses.
Small creatures scuttle away at your approach.  Large rocks placed in a semi-circle and remnants of litter suggest that this was an ad hoc eating area.  Overturned metal containers litter the floor.
Carts still filled with ore, rich veins in the rock face, pick axes and shovels all provide further evidence of a hasty departure by the miners that plied their trade here.

This long corridor appears to be an old abandoned mining tunnel that runs east to west.  The timbers shoring up the low ceiling are all reminiscent of traditional dwarven mining.  The south wall has a very smooth surface.

The corridor comes to an abrupt end here.  A rock fall has sealed the route, preventing further progress.  The pattern of the rocks suggest that the rock fall was caused purposefully to prevent something from getting out rather than preventing something entering.

The path underfoot is overgrown with weeds and almost completely covered with dried, fallen branches yet still feels surprisingly firm.  A few pine saplings off to one side struggle to push up through the heavy soil.

Meandering rows of saplings impede your progress as the path seems to try to envelop you in foliage.  Glancing northeast to get your bearings you see mountain brush beginning to take over the landscape.  Occasionally, as you trudge along, your feet scuff up bits of dirt and clay.
The rusted remains of an iron wagon, long abandoned by its owner, lay to one side of the path.

The road's never-ending battle to survive the onslaught of the foliage seems to be a losing one at this particularly overgrown stretch.  The rhythmic buzzing of insects serves as a reminder that, to some, this place is home.

A single pine stands, aloof and deserted, like a lone soldier after the battle, forgotten but yet on guard.  Gnarled and twisted roots cling to the poor soil in a desperate grasp, yet this guardian still manages to provide a place for a small nest.  The road widens as it winds to the north.

The road here is composed of a chocolate-brown clay, cracked and chipped in places where it has dried after a season of heavy rains.  From here it wends its way through hills covered in dry scrub, dropping from sight as it ducks behind a bend in the distance.  To the north rises a range of stony mountains, their heights dominated by one particularly tall, looming crag whose shadow falls heavily upon the lesser hills around it.
A rockslide of mud and stone almost seems to have brought an entire mountain to its knees a few paces to the west.

The hard-packed dirt of the road has been broken into a thick layer of loose dust by the passage of many feet and hooves.  An occasional roadside footprint, nearly knee-deep in hardened clay, indicates that mud must be a real problem in times of heavy rain.

Tree-dotted hillsides rise on both sides of the path, providing ample high ground and cover for would-be attackers.  The road here is mostly flat as it meanders along the valley floor, although there is the slightest incline to the north.  One especially large tree lies fallen near the edge of the road, its roots helplessly exposed.

The road takes a sharp bend here where it begins to slope more steeply to the west.  The rough hew of the road's northern wall and the beginnings of a dropoff to the southern valley floor indicate that the path here was not created by the simple passing of travellers, but was instead purposely cut into the hillside.

The hard, brown clay of the road is pitted and rutted where it has been traveled during heavy rains.  Although most of the footprints in the road are from human-like creatures or domesticated animals, there is on occasion a large print of a four-toed creature which appears to have a set of rather pointy claws.

The path takes a sharp east-northeast turn where it contorts to follow the ridge of the hill above.  The bend offers a fine vantage point for watching the brush-covered valley to the west, far past which can be seen the stony fist of Sorrow's Reach, thrusting angrily into the sky.

A tall, regal pine stands watch here over a bend in the road formed by the tapered end of a ridgeline stretching off to the east.  The vegetation in the valley below, somewhat dry and brown to the southwest, transitions into a deep green as it nears the valley floor to the north.

A thick jungle of dry brush covers the hillside bordering the southern edge of the road, while downslope to the north lies an impenetrable mass of vine-laden oaks.  Although the gathering of trees seems somewhat thinner to the east, the dense vegetation makes travel via the road your only real option.

Tall, moss-covered conifers rub shoulders with lush, green oak on the slopes bordering both sides of the road.  An occasional glimpse through the curtain of trees on the northern downslope reveals the path to be paralleling a river.  To the east you can see a break in the trees where the road turns to march down the hillside below.

Tall pines stand in silent vigil at a sharp west-north curve in the road.  Steep hills curve protectively above to the south and east, while to the north the landscape drops sharply as it descends to meet the river below.  A slight smell of charred wood hangs upon the air.

Charred branches and the occasional ring of blackened stones indicate that this area is used as a campsite.  The lack of ground vegetation and presence of many footprints in the soil suggest that the grounds are well-frequented.  A wide dirt path runs through the campsite, leading from a steep hill to the south down to the riverbank.

A clear blue river flows shallow and wide over a multitude of rounded stones.  On the far bank, a great jumble of earth stretches up to a stone road paralleling the river to the west.  A wide path of hard-packed soil climbs its way uphill towards a small flat area to the south.

A small game trail runs here among the clumps of reeds sprouting between the stones along the riverbank.  Majestic trees of pine and oak thrust high overhead from an upslope to the south, providing cover from the elements.  The far bank, by contrast, is a barren, rocky waste of a cliff which stretches from the riverbank up to and beyond a stone road cut into the hillside.

Tall patches of grass and an occasional clump of reeds grow here among the smooth stones of the riverbank.  A small game trail wends its way among the grasses, trailing from the flats to the east up a small incline running west along the beginnings of the southern canyon rim.

Securing a comfortable perch, you survey the vast wilderness below.  A sea of foliage blankets this part of Elanthia to protect it from the ravages of the seasons.  To the south, the road below gasps its final breaths in the distance as it decays into oblivion.  Beside you a nest of pine needles, long grass and scrub brush rests in the arms of its host.  A sudden breeze causes a slight bending of the tree top as it resists yet another force of nature.

An ancient oak tree crowns the top of this hill, its wide branches arching high into the heavens to provide shelter for man and beast alike.  Whatever kind soul planted the acorn from which it grew knew much of the magic within the earth, for here all seems a little kinder, a little quieter than whatever may occur on the hillsides below.

A large cut-out of mountain and earth opens up near the southern edge of the dell.  Granite rubble, too small to be of any use to the Dwarves who once worked this old quarry, marks the path through the tree-lined foothills.  Up ahead, the opening to a dark cavern is blocked by a small wooden shack, its rickety door hanging limply from rusted hinges.

Cutting through the thick pines, an unkempt path climbs the hill southward at a steep incline, while to the north it descends to a dusty road.  Gnarled, brittle branches reach out at all angles, threatening to grab and trip at any opportunity.  Light filters through skeletal limbs, casting shadows on the ground litter in random patterns that change as the sun moves through the sky.

The angle of the path gives travelers a workout, navigating through the trees that thin toward the rise to the south.  Ground litter makes footing treacherous at times as well as noticeably muffling noise underfoot.  Despite the obvious lack of use to the area, the abundant sounds of wildlife indicate it is quite a thriving environment.

Pine trees line the slope to the north, heading downhill along a trail to the dry road barely discernable through the trees.  A wide field opens under the daytime sky, where soft grasses sway with the breezes rushing over the open plain.  Soft grasses sway with the breezes rushing over the open plain, a path pressed into the ground leading from the tree line to a meadow in the distance.

Wildflowers circle a leafy bush and a large, flat boulder, the surface of which is rounded due to years of exposure to the wind and rain.  Lush grass blankets the ground like a living carpet that softens footfalls.  A faint path heads toward the tree line to the north, while the field drops off elsewhere in the other directions.

Icy-cold water flows smoothly past the stones underfoot, adding its whispers to those of the winds blowing up the river canyon which stretches off to the west.  The jumbled mass of a collapsed hillside on the north riverbank provides a stark contrast to the neat, rocky shores of the south.  A fine view of the sheer eastern face of Sorrow's Reach is afforded by the open space of the river.

It appears that part of the northern hillside has recently given way, for a large tumble of rocks and splintered trees leads from the riverbank to a small ridge above.  A few steps to the south flow the stony, cold waters of the river.

Small scraps of cloth, driftwood, and various unidentifiable pieces of jetsam line the walls and floor of this dank, fetid burrow.  A heavy odor almost seems to squeak 'Rodent!' in your nostrils with every reluctant breath you take, and the occasional scrabbling you hear in the recesses of the hole is certainly more than just your imagination.

The road angles steeply here in its cliffside trek through the mountains, making travel an exercise in caution.  Occasional washes of dried mud, the remnants of water runoff from melting snows on the high slopes to the north, dirty the otherwise smooth stones.  Several of the road's mighty flagstones appear to have fallen to the canyon floor below, victims of a long-ago collapse.

A crumbled tower of black stone, pitted along its once smooth face, lies here in a great heap along the southern edge of the road.  Several large, charred timbers jut from the pile like skeletal fingers, pointing at the heavens in mute accusation of a long-ago crime.

A wide stone road which stretches off to the east ends here at a sheer cliff wall, giving way to a decrepit wooden bridge that spans southward across a small gap in the canyon.  From the cliff heights far above juts a small promontory of stone, behind which you can see a small cave leading into the mountains.

The smooth, grey flagstones of a well built road abruptly end here in a massive jumble of stone and broken trees, the remains of a hillside which has tumbled into the river below.  Although there are signs someone has been digging to clear the debris, the only way the road may be traveled for now is to the west.

A black granite arch looks out upon the remains of a flagstone road that stretches west towards a tall spire of grey and black rock.  Paired doors carved of solid onyx hang askew on broken hinges to either side of the arch, held upright by the remains of an avalanche recently tumbled down from the nearby hillside.  The road continues through the arch and on into the darkness, with light from the outside dimly illuminating the way in and downward.

The smooth, finished walls of this tunnel mark it unmistakeably as a Dwarven clan home.  Small, musty clouds of dust rise at the slightest movement, their presence attesting to the long-ago abandonment of this area by its creators.

The spirits of an ancient people mutter softly with the echo of every sound that reverbrates through the tunnel.  To one side of the path lists an abandoned oxcart, its axle rusted and split by long years of neglect.  The highway makes another downward turn to the east and widens into a natural cavern.

Sparkling gems embedded in the ceiling high above refract torchlight upon the surrounding walls in bizarre, kaleidoscopic patterns.  A starburst constructed of varying shades of marble dominates the center of the chamber floor, its surface curiously clean in stark contrast to the surrounding dust.  Three small passages to the east lead further into the depths of the clan home.
Water trickles from a hairline fracture along one wall, across the floor and under one of the doors lining the tunnel.  A strong smell of decaying vegetation hangs in the air.

A long, low table set with several wooden chairs curves before the forward edge of a slightly raised circular dais.  Rotting tapestries hang behind the dais, their colors muted by age and further sullied by the great clouds of dust that kick up with every disturbance of the floor.  A large steel door, covered with lime and streaks of rust, sits in a recess at the back of the chamber.

The passage narrows here, the weight of the hillside seeming to bear down from above.  Several doors are set seamlessly into the surrounding walls, distinguishable only by slight color variations in the stonework.

The soft burbling of an underground spring whispers from somewhere beyond the tunnel walls.  A long patch of phosphoresecent scarlet fungus climbs one wall of the tunnel, the dim light it emits casting sunset hues upon the doors set into the granite.
The light dims considerably at this juncture of the corridors.  A tunnel leading to the east has collapsed into a massive pile of rubble, preventing further passage into the clan's stronghold.
Gaezthen spheres in finely-worked silver sconces line the walls of the corridor at regular intervals.  Vague outlines of doors mark the entrances to private dwellings.
A collection of finest Dwarven stonework fills this shop, stout furnishings that, while simple, will last several lifetimes.

The bridge on which you stand has definitely seen better days.  Wide as two men are tall and the length of a large, fallen pine, it has dry-rotted from too many years of wet snows and blistering summer suns.  A number of holes in the decomposed floorboards offer glimpses of the river below.

A decrepit, flat wooden bridge crosses the canyon to the north.  The bridge appears to be a hastily assembled substitute for the original stone bridge, the remains of which arch a few feet over the canyon on either side.  A road of wide, grey flagstones winds southwest into the mountains.

The ancient stone road winds ambitiously along the southern face of the mountain range, turning frequently in its effort to bypass obstacles thrown up by the steep, rocky slopes.  Clumps of small stones and the occasional large boulder line the northern edge of the path, silently watching your passage.

At times wide and flat, but most often a steep, winding path, the road here writhes snake-like in its travel through the rocky heights of the mountains.  Much of the road is cloaked in shadow, as what light comes from above is oft blocked by the high, stony crags on either side of the twisting path.

Great peaks of craggy grey stone, devoid of vegetation, rise above on all sides save for a steep, winding road that stumbles its way northeast down the mountain.  The road's builders apparently decided at this point that passage over the mountains was impossible, for here the flagstones enter the gaping black maw of a tunnel.

A soft glow emanates from the tunnel mouth before you, but the light quickly fades as it filters into the tunnel's malevolent, grasping blackness.  To the west climb the silent, grey flagstones of the ancient road.

Like a Will-O-Wisp waiting to lure the unwary to their doom, the dim circle of the tunnel exit glows in the distance below.  Your only choices are a heavy eastern descent to freedom, or to trudge into the sucking blackness which lies a steep climb to the west.

Darkness swirls and eddies about you like a malevolent fog, clutching greedily at your clothing as you feel your way along the ancient road.  The stones underfoot are slick with moisture, and with each scrape of your feet whisper of unseen chasms ahead.

A faint, glowing circle squats stolidly in the western firmaments above, indicating a steep climb to the freedom of open skies and fresh air.  Other than your erstwhile lunar companion, the darkness here is absolute.

What faint light manages to filter from the nearby tunnel mouth is quickly absorbed by the hungry blackness all around you.  There is an odd rushing sound, akin to that of strong winds blowing through the tall trees of a forest, coming from outside the tunnel.

You are on a wide plateau of stone, high above a mighty river gorge which slashes its way east into the distance.  All around you towers the treeless, rocky spire of Sorrow's Reach, its stony roots curving protectively down around the canyon's western limits.  A mighty river of white water bursts eagerly from a cavern mouth high upon the north face of the Reach, roaring forth to plummet into a wide pool in the depths of the canyon below.

The path here is barely wide enough to accommodate a single person.  The wall to the west offers little in the way of support, being nearly devoid of handgrips and just as slick as the rock below your feet.  One slip of a foot to the east lies a drop into the reaches of infinity.

A road of square grey flagstones begins here in a corner guarded to the west and north by the sheer cliffs of the Reach.  The assembly of dull grey stones, shiny black where they have been chipped or worn smooth by passing traffic, stretch behind the waterfall to the east before winding their way up the mountainside.

The great roar of the river beast rushing from above beats upon your ears like a winter storm battering a coastal village.  Although this small stone grotto would at first glance seem an ideal hiding place, its algae slickened floor and body soaking humidity make it unlikely anyone would use it as such.

A sharp bend in the road provides a good vantage point for monitoring traffic passing near the waterfall to the west.  Several large boulders border either side of the path, providing ample cover for would-be assailants.

A slight sound of rushing water reaches your ears, complementing the smooth whisper of the winds which blow up the canyon and across the stony face of the Reach.  The road here, level to the northwest, begins to climb slightly as it stretches to the east.

A gnarled, twisted pine, bent with age and stunted from a life far above the treeline, hangs precariously over the edge of the canyon rim as if considering an end to its pitiful existence.  Something seems to have taken the signs of the tree's weakness as an invitation to attack, for most of its bark has been shredded away from its trunk in long, thin strips.

A sharp bend in the road has been rendered treacherous by the collapse of most of its surface into the canyon below.  Only one width of flagstones remains at the narrowest point, and it appears that a great deal of the earth underneath has already washed away.  Long, sharp scratches in the mountain wall bordering the road almost appear to be the frenzied digging of some creature intent on widening the passage.

Tall piles of small, black stones lie on either side of the road here, slowing passage along mountain.  Several of the stones have been used to create a crude fire ring on the uphill side of the piles, and a few animal bones, picked clean of flesh, lie scattered about the area.

Weeds choke the cracks between mighty flagstones of coarse grey rock.  The road here rises slightly to the north, while a bend to the southwest begins a torturous descent to the hills below.  A rope bridge can be seen in the distance, stretching across the canyon from a rocky outcropping to the northeast.

You are standing on a massive slab of flat, grey stone cut into one side of the Reach.  The north and west walls are soaring towers of granite, while to the south and east lie sheer cliffs which stretch a lifetime's fall to the canyon floor below.  A rope bridge, attached to a natural outcropping of stone, sways in the breeze above the canyon.

A sharp, cool wind tugs at your clothing as you stand upon this modest bridge of stick and rope.  Far, far below you can see a small wooden bridge spanning the canyon, and even further beyond stretches a slight band of blue which you can only assume to be the river.

Ringed by dark clouds of grey, the massive, stony crag of Sorrow's Reach looms above you to the north like the thrusted fist of an angry earth-god.  A deep river gorge has ripped its way through the lands at the base of the Reach, creating a formidable barrier to those who would scale its heights.  The canyon would be nigh impossible to cross, were it not for a simple rope bridge which stretches across to a stone plateau in the mountainside.

A small footpath wending its way from the north ends here at the top of what must have been a mighty avalanche indeed.  Splintered trees and boulders the size of small houses lie jumbled together in a great rockslide which seems to reach all the way to the foothills below.
A small trail leading west through a tangled morass of weeds and brambles ends here at a soaring cliff wall, rent open by a narrow crack in its craggy face.

The pass winds and twists between rugged walls of dark stone, boulders precariously balanced on the cliffs far above.  The numerous craters on the overgrown path, where chunks of rock lie embedded as deep as a foot into the stony soil, bear silent testimony to the danger here.

The narrow pass through the mountainside changes shape here, widening into a valley to the west and squeezing into a narrow, rocky passage to the east.  In the shadow of western cliffs stands a ruined village, ramshackle huts and crude wooden buildings standing empty and silent, not even the chirping of birds or the buzzing of insects relieving the eerie, dead stillness.

A broad trail, weeds shooting up though the pebbled road, leads west into the center of the silent village.  The mountain pass stands to the east, and a narrower, less-traveled path runs far to the southwest.

The eastern boundary of the village proper is a tangled mass of dry grass and weed grown between piles of splintered boulders tumbled from the cliff face above.  Tiny abandoned homes, most of them long ago flattened into kindling, lie scattered about the landscape.  The tip of a black obelisk can be seen poking its head over two still-standing homes to the west.

The eastern trail merges with a wide, circular boulevard here, broken cobblestones littered across upturned black soil.  A tall, black obelisk looms in an open plaza to the west, encircled by the road that arches protectively around it.

North of the village monument, this part of the boulevard runs past a small, ramshackle building with two small obsidian obelisks sitting on its front porch.  A smaller footpath, all that remains of a larger road, wends to the northwest through tall, dry grasses.

This path leads through a tangle of ruined and fallen huts, the only fragments and reminders of a once prosperous village.  The worn footpath, fresh tracks still evident upon it, curves from the south to the northeast, where it disappears from view behind a ramshackle wooden building.

The west end of the boulevard runs before the tallest building in the village, a church sided with clapboard and peeling white paint.  Several ruined homes stand in the shadow of the building's tall bell tower.
South of the village monument, this part of the boulevard passes by the burnt-out shells of sad, empty houses.  A smaller road stretches off to the south.

A tall obsidian obelisk, chipped and cracked and sunken into the earth at a jagged lean, stands at the center of the village.  Broken and abandoned buildings stand silently around the boulevard, dwarfed by the tall, crumbling facade of a church to the west.
This narrow, overgrown trail winds between rows of collapsed rubble mounds that might once have been homes.  The trail continues southwest, and rejoins the main boulevard to the north.

Unlike the utter desolation due east, this street shows slight signs of rebirth cropping from the earth.  Grass patches clump in front of the run-down houses.  Above the squat shacks lining the south side of the road appears a modest-sized knoll, crowned by a building seething with plant growth.

In stark contrast to the rest of this section of the lane, one whitewashed cottage stands snug and whole in the midst of the squalor, proving that is indeed possible to rise against and to conquer adversity.  A deep-grained walnut door, graced with delicate unicorn and panther carvings, acts as entry into the abode.
Clumps of daisies peek out of the earth, dwarfed by the remains of burnt buildings lined along the sides of the dirt path.  A lone wooden sign dangles from the remains of one of the houses.

The dirt road ends at the base of a knoll, changing into a cobblestone path leading up the tiny hill to a thatched-roof house.  Vines choke the whitewashed structure in a tangle of green tendrils.
