Stray wildflowers dot the hillside, struggling to create a spot of brightness amongst the remains of the rest of the village.
The lane comes to an end at a morass of bramble thickets here, rubble vanishing in the tall, wavering grass.
The path cuts through a grassy field, away from the village and towards a cluster of low, grey stones to the southwest.  Deep gouges cut into the ground betray the passage of a heavily laden wagon.

Dozens of grey stones, many toppled flat and half-buried in the overgrown grass, lie scattered about the ground.  Although most are faceless, half-legible inscriptions on one or two show them to be gravestones.  The number of markers seems abnormally large for such a small village, and it is apparent from the crowds of newer stones jammed between the neatly ordered rows that many of the graves were dug in a short period of time.

A multitude of smooth grey stones peep above the sea of grass here in the shadow of the cliff wall at the southern end of the valley.  The dark mouth of a cave stands at the trail's end, a pair of deep wagon tracks leading right inside.  A fetid smell drifts from the cave, something like a dead animal rotting.

The footpath ends behind a large wooden building, where a refuse heap piled high with obsidian chips, broken hammerstones and various other garbage sits in silence.  A long, ash-white bone juts from the bottom of the pile.

Large slabs of crudely cut obsidian lie stacked in careful piles along the walls of this oak-paneled workshop.  Small chips of flint-knapped stone litter the floor, ready to slice the feet of the unwary.  A sign on the far wall invites attention.

The ancient timbers of this one-room house creak and sway dangerously every time a wind blows through, as if it may collapse upon itself at any moment.  The furniture has disintegrated into wooden shards and scraps of cloth, and the old fireplace is home to a massive spiderweb from which tiny scarlet eyes gleam.

Queued up like a line in a Carousel, the cobblestones sweep in a broad arc from the bottom to the top of the knoll, ending at a quaint house.  Several snakeweeds grow thickly around its perimeter, their oblong leaves jutting outwards as if to guide visitors away from the chestnut door leading inside.

The welcome light of day streams in through the mouth of this dank tunnel where it exits to a small, grassy valley.  Further south, the rough stone floor slopes sharply downward, out of sight and closer to the stench of decay that pervades the gloom.

The tunnel levels here from its steep slope to the north and turns sharply to the east.  A pair of wagon tracks end abruptly at this point, their depth in the hard-packed earth suggesting the cart's burden was a very heavy one.

The tunnel ends here at the brink of a vast pit, piled high with the bones of the dead.  A sea of ashen bones and skeletal remains gleams in the dim light, eyeless sockets turned up to the earthen roof as if searching for release.  From far beneath, perhaps at the bottom of the pit, comes a chorus of slithering, clicking noises, like a million wriggling centipedes nesting in the bones.

A lofty wall of some oddly colored green metal blocks the view west.  All other directions lead to grim reminders of death and mortality.  A low, creeping vine has taken over much of the open ground, but here and there, broken stumps of stone or metal protrude unevenly.  A bare path made of thousands of tiny, rough pebbles leads northwest towards an irregular, slab-sided chapel.

Numerous rows of grave markers stand side by side in oddly close array.  Most are broken and overturned, but a few still stand upright.  Tiny flowers grow amongst the stones, pale white and delicate.  Their clean, sweet scent seems so out of place in this grim setting that it disturbs rather than uplifts.

Surrounded by dozens of tiny grave markers, an elegant alabaster fountain stands, a monument to the silent dead.  Here and there, some of the graves have been disturbed in a curious manner.  The earth has been overturned, as if pushed up from below by some unseen force.  Several tiny caskets lie tumbled about, broken and empty.

Many small gravestones here are ruined and destroyed, perhaps by time and the weather, yet the wreckage seems systematic, as if someone had been searching for something buried.  To the north, a long row of massive and elaborate obelisks and other shapes rise along the high wall of the cemetery.

Running along the high wall, many strange, even bizarre stone monuments rise, each striving to outdo the next in elaborate paeans to the forgotten dead rotting beneath.  Many-winged beings raise a pot-bellied figure dressed as a Trader in mute exaltation.  Dying warriors make bloody obeisance to a stoop-shouldered figure clad as a mighty warlord.

Numerous rows of grave markers stand side by side in oddly close array.  Most are broken and overturned, but a few still stand upright.  Tiny flowers grow amongst the stones, pale white and delicate.  Their clean, sweet scent seems so out of place in this grim setting that it disturbs rather than uplifts.

Numerous monuments to the dead rise all about, each its own testament to the long forgotten corpses that lie buried beneath.  The wind sighs in a hollow dirge, perhaps in keening tribute to the deceased.

Northwards, the land falls away rapidly in a sheer drop-off, leaving naught but an echoing vista of open air.  Nearer at hand, one huge monument dominates the garish row of memorials along the high wall, though the heroic figure surmounting the pile of stone seems oddly distorted.  The ground around it is dry and bare of dust and dirt, yet faint marks of something heavily-clawed mar the surface.

The ground here is bare and devoid of all, except for faint marks etched in the stone paving here and there.  The remains of numerous wooden and latticework frames still stand along the edge of the precipice, and in one place, a stone platform juts out over the edge.
The ground here is barren and untended.  Oddly, not one piece of grass or one flower grows anywhere.  The walkway is mainly dirt and gravel, the footing at times treacherous.

Tall wooden poles are set in regular groups deep into the stone.  Many bits of bone and other identifiable remains lie scattered about.  The air is heavy with the nearness of death, as though some great power or ritual had once been worked here.  Far off in the sky, a huge black bird glides on motionless wings, rising in slow circles, yet never straying far from this place.

Underfoot, the ground is hard and stony.  No grave or monument rises here, as if the space had been left unused when this place of the dead was abandoned.  Faint lines etched into the rock indicate where monuments might once have been placed.  Nothing grows in the desolation, save one tiny tree that grows in a scant pocket of earth in the cracked stone.

Soft earth rises in low mounds all about.  Some are topped with standing stones, but most are bare or scattered with rubble.  There is a sweet smell of ancient mold and rot seeping into the air.  Scabrous yellow flowers grow among piles of broken rock, and lichen the color of dried blood spatters the stony surfaces.

A series of dark green grassy mounds run along the cemetery wall.  Some seem recently created, an oddity in this place that appears otherwise abandoned, while others appear to have existed for quite some time.  A sense of uneasiness fills the air, perhaps caused by the heavy silence that permeates the area.

Along the high wall protecting this place, many low, mossy burial mounds stand.  Few are marked in any way and fewer still seem intact.  Almost all of them have been dug up, unearthed, or otherwise disturbed.  Whether the desecration took place long ago or more recently is impossible to discern, and there is no hint as to its cause.

One mound, higher than all the others, looms over the cemetery like an ominous guardian.  The top is crowned with a single massive standing stone of dull black slate.  No grass grows here, yet the earth appears darkly rich.  Faint footprints run across bare loam, and many drag marks criss-cross its surface, yet the silence that reigns over all yields no hint as to the source of the activity.

Footing is treacherous here, as loose earth slides with each step.  Bits of bone glint white against the bare dirt, and many broken weapons lie scattered, lost perhaps in some ancient battle.  Slightly to the west stands a dull black slab that rises from the mire in the low center of the mound.

Here at the top of the mound, the center of Promado Village is seen.  The church steeple is barely discernible, its white clapboard sides almost pristine as it stands next to several abandoned and demolished homes.  The black slate slab stands in the center of the mound, larger than life.  Around the base, someone has arranged rocks and sticks into some oddly-shaped symbols, their meaning long forgotten.

A series of dark green grassy mounds run along the cemetery wall.  Some seem recently created, an oddity in this place that appears otherwise abandoned, while others appear to have existed for quite some time.  A sense of uneasiness fills the air, perhaps caused by the heavy silence that permeates the area.

A series of dark green grassy mounds run along the cemetery wall.  Some seem recently created, an oddity in this place that appears otherwise abandoned, while others appear to have existed for quite some time.  A sense of uneasiness fills the air, perhaps caused by the heavy silence that permeates the area.

A huge granite boulder from Outer Hibarnhvidar leads into this sharply sloping tunnel.  Bricks of red-streaked granite populate the grey stone of the walls, floor, and ceiling more and more until nothing but the granite bricks frame a black iron door at the lower end.

Enormous granite blocks, fitted with no visible mortar, create thirty-foot walls and a vaulted ceiling.  Thick veins of ore meet in a whorl in the center of the floor.  In the east wall, a wrought iron keystone twenty-five feet above the floor supports a red granite arch which is flanked by two fifteen-foot-high granite arches, one black and the other grey.  Flames that light the chamber rise from a trough along the top of each wall.

Curving granite blocks form the circular walls for this huge chamber.  Thick veins of brick-red hematite emanate from the wrought iron keystone that supports the arch in the west wall.  Long low benches have been hewn from the granite floor and surround a huge map constructed from fine metals and gemstones that is inlaid into the floor.  A broad set of low stairs leads to a dais to the east.

The veins of hematite change to solid iron in the granite blocks nearest the dais.  A raised square of granite holds the Guildleader's seat, and a nearby pedestal holds the Guildleader's tankard.  A table at the rear of the dais holds an oaken hogshead.  Stairs lead down from the dais.

Bright silver strata flow through the granite blocks, catching the torchlight to illuminate even the far corners.  Training dummies are scattered about, obviously rended and repaired many times, and makeshift weapon racks stand along the north wall.  Stones of various sizes protrude from the floor at different heights, no doubt meant to keep warriors mindful of their footwork.
Dozens of alcoves in this broad corridor keep an arsenal of weapons and armor at the ready.  Torches are set into the wall between each pair of alcoves.  Guild guards keep watch over the alcoves.

Eleven statues of barbarians line the walls, each on one knee and facing the flaming brazier in the center of the chamber.  Triangular stones inlaid in the floor point from the edge of the brazier to the statues honoring it.

Polished granite walls surround a massive iron chain that is sunk into the inlaid marble floor and climbs into the darkness above.  Stairs lead up the north wall around the chain and into the Guildhall's famous tower, and a brushed bronze door is centered on the east wall.
Whorls of copper, malachite, and azurite run from the black granite arch in the northwest corner to the open stone doors in the east wall.  Large racks line the south and west walls.

An occasional cry of pain can be heard through the loud laughter echoing around the circular bar that dominates this room.  Stone stools of varying heights surround the bar, and tankards of numerous sizes clutter it.  Midway between matching sets of stone doors to the west and northeast, a set of steps climbs the wall to a raised balcony.

Stone steps climb the wall from the drinking hall below to this wooden balcony.  Large squared mikkhalbamar timbers are cantilevered from square holes in the stone wall, and thick red oak planks are laid across them.  Simple stools line the stone wall, and two low oak chairs in the center of the balcony face each other across a table set with blocks and handles.

Silver runs in veins throughout the walls.  Intricate patterns guide the eye to stairs that continue upward around the walls from the steps below.  Torches are pushed through the large links of an iron chain that hangs through the center of the chamber from high above.

A yard-tall rampart, punctuated with large stone slabs, surrounds two-thirds of the circular area carved from the mountainside.  The jet-black granite of the floor and rampart sets off the smooth grey of the stone slabs.  The architecture amplifies every footstep into an echoing clatter.  Two spears stabbed into the granite mark the sides of an opening to stairs leading down.

The platinum spiderweb below gives way to a lace of silver and grey animite that covers every block of this chamber's twelve walls.  The heavy lace embedded in each step and makes the stairs hard to discern from the walls.  A massive iron chain is set into the granite ceiling and torches have been shoved into its links.  The stairs continue around the walls and upward from the steps below.

Streaks of gold glitter in the blocks of stone carefully fit together to form the six walls that the stairs continue to spiral around.  The walls smoothly transition from the four walls below into what appears to be eight above.  The massive iron chain, laden with torches, continues above and below.

Eight granite walls are covered with a web of platinum threads inset into the stone.  Stairs, due to their lack of platinum embellishment, can be clearly seen to continue up and around the eight walls.  The platinum glitters in the light from the torches jammed into the iron chain hanging through the center of the chamber.  The torches barely light the steps leading down the tower.

This long, wide room appears to be a partially converted brewery, the air still filled with the scent of ale.  Rows of casks line the walls, leaving the center of the floor clear to make room for business.  Clerks, traders and commodity brokers intermingle with local farmers and miners to discuss the ever-changing prices of commodities, while the noisy sound of braying animals can be heard to the east.

rooms.t: [Hibarnhvidar Trader Guild, Office of Interprovincial Trade]
rooms.desc: A foil map hangs across the back wall, tinted and textured to show the five provinces of Elanthia.  Other than that single piece of elegance, the room is completely utilitarian with a wooden plank floor and a single desk of neatly stacked paperwork.

Mountain hardy beasts of all sorts find themselves in neighboring stalls in this slightly cramped but serviceable stable.  Bales of alfalfa and hay have been pushed against the wall, leaving only the bare minimum amount of area needed to lead caravans and carts in and out from the road.

This long abandoned portion of the brewery has been cleaned up and turned into an exquisite rock garden.  An intentionally meandering path of carefully pieced slate rock connects the stables and cask room, as well as a shiny brass contraption in the western garden.  Old ale casks, cut in half, have been used as picturesque flower boxes, while other pieces of cask have been used as trimming around individual beds nestled within colorful collections of polished stone.

The dazzling rock garden occupying the wide warehouse portion of this old brewery has been muted by the presence of a lone working still that takes up the western portion of the wall.  Several Dwarven workers tend to the still, oblivious to the beauty of the arrangements of colored rock and crystal around them.  Channels of water run through the garden both to further beautify the area as well as to keep the room at a comfortable temperature.

The Guildmaster's office has been carefully coordinated to incorporate the vision of a sun rising above the mountains.  Purple and gold silk drapes hang loosely against the stone walls with light from wall sconces peeking through behind it like the first rays of a new morning in a cloudy sky.  A large gold-inlaid rosewood desk glows in the reflected light from the smokeless candles set about the room.  On a small shelf behind the desk rests a crystal decanter and four matching wine glasses.
Damp and cool, this room acts as a tasting room for guests and a break room for clerks, although it is hard to say who is actually doing the most sampling.

The confines of a low ramshackle building converted to living quarters are furnished haphazardly.  Doors, arch, hallway and alcove branch off from the long squat common room without symmetry, giving the appearance of being tacked on as needed.  A wood stove burns brightly, mismatched benches and chairs pulled in a cluster around it.  Only windows on the street side of the building contribute light or fresh air, and although the room looks frayed and made of collected discards, it is clean and neat.

A shelf holds writing slates and chalk for lessons, and long backless benches stand arranged in symmetrical rows.  At the far side of the room is a table displaying student efforts.  Of note is a large, chipped ceramic bowl furnished with water, pebbles and turtle.

The Headmaster's chamber is no more elaborate than any other area of the orphanage.  His battered desk is missing a drawer, and his chair's rungs are reinforced with twine.  A window - a luxury - looks out into the street, and behind a screen is a small cot.  Drawings pinned to the wall only add to the clutter.  Nevertheless, there is a hint of good will in his disorder, that there is too much work for one man, but what is left undone has been put aside for the priority of affection rather than neglect.

Tucked in the front corner of the common room, the library bookshelves form two of the walls to divide it as a separate room.  The largest window in the whole orphanage looks out into the street, so during daylight hours it is the brightest lit and cheeriest of nooks.  A comfortable chair is a favorite spot, and its faded cover and squashed cushion suggest many children have retreated here.

A semicircle of lumpy overstuffed chairs faces a roaring fire crackling in a large flagstone hearth set into the rear wall of this spacious chamber.  The remainder of the space is covered by heavily scarred oaken tables, most of them replete with massive frothing tankards and wide platters heaped with the hearty fare favored by Toggish laborers.  Based on the relaxed postures of many of the patrons, it is clear that they consider this their home away from home.

Unlike the atmosphere in the rest of this establishment, there is an air of formality here.  The enormous long table that runs nearly the entire length of the room is draped in white linen, and there are centerpieces of freshly cut flowers at regular intervals.  The chairs are in markedly better repair than those found in the common room.

Several thick-legged stools, braced for the weight of the pub's massive patrons, line the front of a long wooden, slightly warped bar.  On the barkeep's side are stands supporting three large kegs and a shelf filled with a motley array of bottles and jars.  A large rectangular mirror covers most of the back wall, affording drinkers the opportunity to make faces at themselves while they enjoy their libations.

This room has been set aside for 'Togs who wish to divert themselves with something other than mere eating and drinking.  Mounted on the back wall is a well-used two-colored dartboard.  Numerous nicks and gouges beyond the border of the target silently testify to the fact that the contestants are often more enthusiastic than skillful.  A few scattered armchairs are provided for the comfort of those waiting their turns to cause structural damage.

A perpetual haze of tobacco smoke hangs just under the low ceiling, illuminated from beneath by the orange glow of the roaring fire in the flagstone fireplace that takes up most of one wall.  Opposite it, a long bar runs the length of the room.  Rough wooden tables and chairs are scattered about, of wildly varying sizes to accommodate travelers of all races.  Day and night, the room is filled by those stopping for a bite to eat or liquid refreshment.
A single glass-enclosed lantern on one wall provides the only light on the narrow landing.  The flickering flame inside wavers and gutters, casting moving shadows along the wood-paneled walls.

Warm golden highlights glint from the deep brown wood-paneled walls.  An immense four-poster bed dominates the room, covered in thick, clean-smelling down comforters and piles of fluffy pillows.  A small table is placed conveniently close to the bed, holding simple refreshments.

A faint scent of baking bread drifts through the small room, apparently located somewhere near the kitchens.  The knotty pine paneling's warm yellow hue is matched by the bed coverings on the low, thick mattress.

Though the path widens and descends as it curves southwards, the other end crests over a hump of earth and dirt and vanishes.  The identifiable sounds of rural civilization leak over from the other side of the barrier, but all of the muffled noises dance just at the edge of earshot.  All around, waist-high lengths of barley sway gently in the wind.

A simple wooden plow rises from the rippling ocean of barley, contrasting as starkly as would a dark warship in a sea of crystal blue.  Nesting birds have built their homes in the joint where the handles meet the blade.  Even though the farmer has abandoned the plow to the weather, its usefulness shall not end.

Green barley makes a miniature wall to the north as the path fades within the stalks of the waving crop.  Here, at the edge of the fields, the fine topsoil gives way to a stony and pebble-covered surface, the defining line nothing more than a mud-filled irrigation ditch.

An odd series of rounded stones poke up from the dirt as the trail curves northwards, indicating that this path may have once been used frequently enough to be at least partially paved.  Except for the few stones still clinging to the vestiges of what was once a road, they've all fallen down the side of a steep slope.  Occasionally, one of the smaller stones bounces down the rock slide and vanishes from sight.

Tattered remnants of faded cloth shiver in the wind but are not pulled from their half-buried locations at the base of a rock slide.  Shifting any of the stones to discover what else may be hidden beneath the stones is naturally discouraged by the frequent crunching of the stones as they shift under the slightest provocation.

Wind tears across the barren surface of the rocks, changing direction and force often enough to maintain a constant state of turbulent drafts.  A handful of sickly weeds find purchase in what little ash ridden soil the wind has failed to claim, unusually curved from their lives in the overbearing gusts.

The deep scars of a washout gut the trail across the center, splitting the route into two halves before swallowing it completely.  Bits of black rock and tiny showers of grey dirt patter down the washout's slope, dislodged with every touch of the wind and every stray movement of a landing bird.  The peak of the volcano rises above the swirling wind, completely indifferent to the travelers braving its rocky routes.

Narrow to the point that it very nearly is non-existent, the trail clings tightly to the side of the volcano's slopes.  Glassy black rocks jut from their perches along either side as though they were hands reaching out to the sky for salvation.  Some of them have received their deliverance, having fallen to new resting places far below.

All semblence of a proper path have vanished, and only the sharp angles of massive stones embedded in the surface of the volcano guide those who are not of avian descent.  A wispy grey fog curls serpentine-like around the bases of the blackened rocks, adding an even greater element of treacherous risk.

The crumbling features of an obsidian rockface are nearly disguised by the tendrils of smoky mist that rise from below.  Though the grey twisting shape of the ever-present fog is hardly opaque here, it thickens quickly as one gazes off the edge of the sheer dropoff, hiding any and all things that may be lurking there.

A dark mass towers above, its details masked by the heavy fog settled over the area.  Judging by the glossy black stones that are close enough to be unconcealed by the murky grey, the shape can only be that of one of the volcano's jagged obsidian rockfaces.

Gentle breezes from the nearby coastline carry the scent of brine, mingling it with the scent of dirt and stone for a hearty combination of natural smells.  The stirring of air also keeps the clouds of coastal fog from thickening, but a heavy bank of grey looms some distance away to the northeast.  The stones underfoot are not quite sharp enough to tear through a boot, but those that hide within the mist may have an augmented chance of doing just that.

Wisps of fog float gently up and over the cliff's edge, twining together, then separating and dissipating in the cold salty breeze.  Overhead, a lone albatross flies in never-ending spirals.  In the distance to the southeast, the outline of a lighthouse is barely visible through the fog.
A knee-high rock wall lines the path on the cliff-side, blocking access to the edge.  Among the rocks, red and gold poppies bob in the sea breeze, nodding a merry "Hello!" to all who walk by them.

The cliff has crumbled away, taking part of the path and the rock wall with it.  A makeshift fence of old branches lashed together with stout fishing line leans precariously towards the edge, offering only the illusion of security from a sudden plunge into the murky fog below.

The path threads between some rocks and a lone acanth tree growing at the cliff's edge.  The constant sea breeze has limited growth on the seaward side causing the tree to lean inland.  Its long lean branches and sparse leaves flutter like streamers in the breeze.

The rocky cliffs give way to a flat prominence covered in short grasses.  At the far eastern end of the prominence, a white lighthouse rises up against the pale blue sky.  Grey fog continues to obscure whatever lies at the bottom of the cliffs.

Wild red roses are slowly overgrowing the remains of a greying picket fence.  Beyond the fence lies a child's playground, desolate and empty.  A gate, ripped from the fence, lies discarded in the grass nearby.

The prominence falls away sharply from both sides of the path, turning it into a thin dividing line between the grey foggy nothingness to north and the lively blue sea to the south.  A muted buoy within the fog murmurs endless mantras of "no pain, no sorrow, no loss" while the sparkling sea entices the senses with promises of hope, freedom, and laughter.

Make-shift gweldalmaen mark the site of three graves placed carefully on the southern side of the path looking towards the wide open sea.  A small mound of dirt lies next to a fourth, still open grave.

An alabaster lighthouse rises high against the backdrop of sea and sky.  A heavy wooden door leads into the base of the structure.  The roar of crashing waves rises up from below the promontory along with hearty scent of salt air.

A picnic bench, a broken teeter-totter and flattened playhouse are lingering signs that a playground once existed here.  The playhouse looks like it might have been a child-sized version of the lighthouse to the east.

Pegs alongside the door are hung with the rotting remains of several woolen cloaks.  Through an arch to the east, there's a small sitting room.  A staircase, caked with years of grime and tarnish, spirals upward to the next level of the lighthouse.

Oil to feed the beacon is stored in the large iron drums stacked here.  A thick black morass spills across the floor where one of the drums has split along its seam.  A confusion of muddled tracks follows the soft curve of the southern wall further into the storage area.

A series of copper pipes, greenish-white with age, are poised over some oaken barrels.  The conduits angle upward and outward through the base of the tower in order to collect fresh rainwater for washing, drinking and bathing.

This room was once homey and comfortable.  A decayed basket of knitting lies forgotten beside a light blue divan and upon the wall hangs a family portrait and a rack of hand-carved pipes.  A woman's touch is evident in the lacey curtains decorating a long window overlooking the sea.  That touch is long past, as dust lies heavily over the entire room.

A cast iron stove remains untended, topped by a rusting teakettle.  Three chairs sit around a small table, the remains of the last meal uncleared.  A curtained alcove lies to the north and a narrow eastern window keeps watch over the ocean.

Shelves lining the walls once held cooking supplies but the perishables have long since collapsed into dust.  Flour spills across the floor where a canvas sack has burst and soft white bootprints leave tracks to the base of some stone steps leading upward into the spire.

A beautiful mahogany bed and wardrobe are carved with matching scenes of Lemicus spreading her arms in a benediction of protection over a raging sea.  A trundle bed is pulled out from one side of the larger, and upon it sits a toy galleon with a broken mast.  The ever-present eastern window overlooks the sea.

In the center of the room stands a four-foot tall oil lamp on a low directable platform.  The lamp's reflector, an unblinking silver eye, keeps watch for ship and storm through the heavy glass walls of the spire.

The sea spreads out from the base of the tower, chasing the horizon.  Seagulls ride the air currents, diving with a cry to grab shellfish from the shoals.  The promontory is scattered with debris where the gulls have smashed open their meals upon the rocks.

Thick roiling mists cover the northern shore heedless of wind or weather.  Occasionally the mists thin and vaguely menacing forms can be made out stalking along the beaches.  Unearthly cries rise up from within the fog, the wailing lament of those lost forever on a foreign shore.

Far to the west, a range of mountains peeks over the horizon.  A wide blue band of water meanders from near the base of the peaks toward the river delta.  Sailing hazards lie on either side of the promontory.  To the south, craggy rock formations peek from beneath the waves and to the north, dangerously shallow shoals could cause the unwary seafarer to run aground.

Jagged rock formations jut from beneath the surface in the southern cove.  The danger is made evident by a schooner mast lying broken across the rocks.  The shoreline stretches southward them pulls back inland and out of sight.

Here at the northern end of the temple, an aisle stretches forward to the altar at the south.  Every inch of the wooden walls is covered with painted images of the history of the island and the various representations of the aspects of the gods in their role in the universe.  Wooden columns support narrow galleries above and clerestory windows of leaded glass filter light to flood the temple.

The center of the temple allows a good view of the galleries above and the timbered ceiling.  Painters have not completed the ceiling artwork, but the basic outlines of a large raven in flight is roughly painted in.

The ceiling of the west transept is painted with the image of a young Dwarf holding a mining hammer and discovering a large vein of silver ore.  A silver-plated door leads out of the temple.  Lanterns of polished silver hang from the walls which are painted with other scenes from the long life of Tarteran Nadamian.

Although there are no pews for worshippers to rest on, here at the front of the temple are several long wooden benches.  A curved railing shaped much like the bow of a ship encloses the altar, protecting and framing it splendidly.

The ceiling of the east transept is painted with an eternal battle.  A small welkin, the symbol of Divyaush struggles with a raving raccoon, the manisfestation of Zachriedek.  A stormy sea scene frames their conflict, as waves of foam-crested spume fling up the walls toward the supporting ceiling beams.

Filigree iron stairs spiral around a large wooden pole reminsicent of a ship's mast.  A polished deobar railing is carved with images of ravens and raccoons which intertwine around anchors, mining picks and the crest of the Nadamian family.  Dark aged oak carved into the shape of a leaping welkin forms the newel post to anchor the railing to the steps at the bottom and top of each section.

The pinpoint brilliance of a candle flame is the only light within the chamber.  Rustling movements and whispered chants are the only sounds to fill the blackness.  A flight of wooden steps leads to the main section of temple above.

The limestone floor, inset with various shells to create a mosaic border with images of cresting waves and swirling currents, is an unusual feature of this entry hall.  The walls are painted with elaborate murals of the sea, each a vision of a calm, clear ocean.  Nothing suggestive of disaster or misfortune exists here.

The main portion of the temple is a large pool surrounded by a border of smooth raked sand.  On the western wall, a waterfall tumbles merrily into the pool and splashes clear water that foams and froths gently on the surface.

Rough-hewned granite walls that form two-story arches create a sheltered walkway for this grand inn.  The ornately carved mahogany double doors hang heavily from highly polished brass hinges and bear the inn's crest.  Tall potted ferns line the walkway beneath the towering arches.

Pale grey sandstone bricks create a smooth passage toward an elegant inn to the northeast.  Travelers casually rest upon cool white marble benches beneath the towering palm trees throughout the lush terraced gardens.  Shell-pink granite walls rise above the trees to the red clay tiled roof of the building.

A walk through this shady garden can be a rewarding side trip.  Stately trees form green walls along winding gravel paths that bisect the gardens from large expanses of manicured green lawns.  At the crossroads is a white gazebo surrounded by three symmetrical reflecting pools.  Standing on a small moss covered mound, the little structure seems to blush in the sunlight.  Stepping stones create a path through the clear pools to the small marble structure.

Majestic palms line this sandstone drive.  A large crystal dome sparkles with the colors of a rainbow as it rises serenely amidst the red barrel tile roof of the inn.  Tall open archways of the building's facade can partially be seen through lush gardens that cover the face of the inn.

The aroma of roasting meats and simmering soups wafts through the tiled area.  The sound of whistling tea kettles from atop an iron stove mingles with the barking orders of a chef to a line of lads as they chop vegetables upon scarred wooden tables.  Frazzled looking waiters scurry through the room carrying large platters full of filled plates to waiting guests.

The oak floor has become worn down the center of the pantry to a dull luster from the constant traffic of waiters running through.  Tiled pantry shelves line one wall, filled with the inn's custom china and various baked goods.  On the opposing wall, a wine rack holds myriad beverages.

The lime-washed carved oak walls and an intricately inlaid oak parquet floor create an inviting atmosphere.  An oak footbridge beneath the wide arches to the east and glassed doors to the west create an outdoor feel within these walls.  Composed waiters dressed in deep blue velvet livery move silently around a blue silk tapestry screen that stands near a dark oak sideboard.  Ferns separate the area to provide quiet corners and secluded tables for those private dining moments.

Tall palms in ornate brass pots stand before two-story arched windows that illuminate this grand lobby.  Rich burgundy tapestries hang from pale beige painted walls that have been polished to a porcelain lustre.  This immense room is dominated by a bronze sculpture in the center.  Muffled voices can be heard from a dark arch to the west.  A small teak footbridge crosses a narrow stream that surrounds an atrium at the center of the inn.

Thick redwood beams frame the rough white plastered walls of the pub.  Heads of various creatures and weapons are mounted on the walls for display.  Near the door a gleaming suit of armor stands with blazing shield in one hand, a greatsword in the other.  Booths line the interior walls while redwood trestle tables surrounded by padded leather barrel chairs are scattered throughout the tavern.  The heady scent of ale mingles with the musty smell of oak burning in the stone fireplace.

A thick burgundy carpeted runner climbs the beige marble steps of a grand divided staircase.  Magnificient crystal candelabras on brass stands line the staircase rendering bright illumination on every step.  Large bouquets of vibrant pink lilies stand as sentinels at the base of the stairs in white halfling-size porcelain vases.  A small teak footbridge crosses into the domed atrium.

This room is aglow with candlelight from the gold chandeliers that hang at measured intervals from the beamed ceiling.  Silk brocade drapes cascade gracefully down the back wall to pool upon the gold-veined white marble tiles of the floor.  Soft music seems to float all around the room from a small lattice window.  A low marble footbridge crosses a tiled streambed into the atrium to the south.

Tall palms rise to tickle the base of this balustraded balcony that encircles the inn's lush center courtyard.  Crystal and brass chandeliers enhance the lighting from the stained-glass dome above.  Highly polished carved doors line the gallery, each inlaid with a gold design.  The grand divided staircase continues its climb toward the towers.

Tall palms rise to tickle the base of this balustraded balcony that encircles the inn's lush center courtyard.  Crystal and brass chandeliers enhance the lighting from the stained-glass dome above.  Highly polished carved doors line the gallery, each inlaid with a gold design.

Tall palms rise to tickle the base of this balustraded balcony that encircles the inn's lush center courtyard.  Crystal and brass chandeliers enhance the lighting from the stained-glass dome above.  Highly polished carved doors line the gallery, each inlaid with a gold design.

Tall palms rise to tickle the base of this balustraded balcony that encircles the inn's lush center courtyard.  Crystal and brass chandeliers enhance the lighting from the stained-glass dome above.  Highly polished carved doors line the gallery, each inlaid with a gold design.

The soft sounds of clinking crystal glasses and muted voices can be heard from the dining room that lies across a footbridge to the west.  Soft light from the dining room strays into the garden lighting the nearest foliage before fading into the shadows.

Tall torches planted among the foliage create a blazing glow around this section of the garden.  Shadows cast from the light upon the plants waltz slowly across the leaves and paths as if to music only they can hear.

Within a sea of lush plants and sandy path reefs is an oasis of cool inviting water that bubbles musically from a stone fountain.  Large delicate pink water lily blossoms rise above platter-shaped leaves and float undisturbed upon the crystal clear water of the sparkling tiled basin at the fountain's base.  A stone statue rises from the center of the basin beneath a misty spray.

The sweet scent of alyssum wafts gently through the room.  A single lantern sits near a stone bench rendering a softly illuminated resting spot amidst the lush tropical atrium.  Soft music and gay voices can be heard from the ballroom across a low white marble footbridge.

Sleepy flowers nod lazily among the shrubbery.  Light from the lobby's chandeliers silently inch into the garden creating flickering shadows along the path.  A blue mirror ball seems to glow from the lanterned light as it reflects its surroundings, nestled within the flowers and shrubs.

A soft breeze rustles a forest of bright green leaves that provide a sheltering screen, hushing the din of the world outside the foliaged walls.  A narrow stream meanders musically past boulders and stone paths through lush ferns and tall grasses.  Pristine white gardenias peek through the low-lying foliage around a small bamboo pavilion, their heady scent lingering on the air.  A small stone bench is nestled within a nook of tall ferns for those quiet moments.

Voices are hushed from the dining area behind the tall ferns that give seclusion to this private table.  Soft blue silk cushioned oak chairs surround the crisp blue linen-covered lime-washed oak table.  At each place setting, gleaming silver and clear crystal glasses sit at their appointed positions near china with lapis lazuli borders.

Pink and white sand is packed within a framework of narrow creamy white marble bands across the floor.  Sparkling flecks within the sands create a glistening diamond mosaic that catches the faintest light.  Matching marble benches stand between the columns offering restful seating.  The roof of the gazebo is forged from delicate strands of iron.  Shaped into ivy vines and leaves, it twines around a metal lattice creating a lacy silhouette against the sky.

An air of anticipation runs through this room as people shuffle their papers and tiredly smile to one another, a nice change from the cold reception outside these doors.  A yawning clerk slowly waves everyone to the small, comfortable-looking couches lining the walls.  Several sleepy patrons lounge about, nodding off from time to time as they wait their turn.

The central junction of Haizen Cugis is little more settled than the most remote outskirts of many other cities.  A handful of leaning tents and huts huddle together for support in the gale-force winds that the hamlet is known for, managing despite all odds to remain standing.  At the exact middle of the intersection, a tall post with a tattered piece of red cloth tied atop it stands guard, constantly swaying and bending in the breeze.

Settled between two of the dunes bordering the hamlet, this trail like many others owes its continued existence to the rocky shelves of sandstone that manage -- just barely -- to hold back the shifting desert.  The sands whip about, leaping across the path and dancing in the wind only to settle again, leaving the landscape ultimately unchanged.  Few structures reside too close to the mounds, revealing the cautious nature of the residents here.

Tall pillars of stacked sandstone joined at the top by narrow beams of dry timber form the Dune Gate, bordering the path as it dwindles to little more than a valley leading westward into the great star-shaped dunes.  To the east the sands recede ever so slightly, becoming shallow, manageable hills of earth.  Along the side of the trail rest a half-dozen rounded boulders, unmarked and smooth, their purpose not immediately apparent.

Dark and oppressive shapes loom on all sides, the shadowy nocturnal visages of the towering star-shaped dunes which dominate this portion of the Velaka Desert, stoic and silent.  The horizon in every direction is blocked by the hulking mountains of sand, making navigation by landmark an impossibility, the dunes themselves changing shape in the passing wind.  Overhead, visible only over the peaks of the darkened hills, the sky serves as a reminder of the depth of the valley.

The sands nearly close the path off, blocked by a combined effort between a great sandstone boulder and several low tents, many of which are partially buried.  Evidently earning far fewer visitors past this point than other portions of the hamlet, signs of foot traffic dwindle significantly toward the west.

Formed in some sort of natural windfall, the path widens into a tear-shaped paddock lined by modest tents.  Few formations like this are common in the desert, making its seclusion from the rest of the hamlet somewhat peculiar.  At the center of the clearing stands a slab of basalt supported on a sandstone boulder and surrounded by similar small rocks.

A shallow and narrow dead end reaches desperately out into the sands from the center of the hamlet, thwarted quickly by the ever-present dunes.  Setting it apart from most of the other areas of Haizen Cugis, the peculiar terrain here gives the impression that it was dug out rather than naturally formed.  Deep gouges in the walls of sand to the west, south and east reveal where the desert has attempted to reclaim the space, but has been pushed back by stubborn residents.

The sandy path turns at a sharp angle as it follows the shape of a nearby dune, curving past a ramshackle tent in the process.  Broad sheets of sandstone assist in keeping the sloping dune from pushing further into the hamlet, blending with the color of the sands almost flawlessly.

Like the claw of a slumbering desert behemoth, a broad sandstone shelf which hedges in the settlement juts upwards out of the ground to the side of the sandy path.  Gathered closely to others of its kind, the natural obstacles leave little room on the trail for passing travelers, and even less for the tents the locals use to gain shelter from the winds.

Beneath a rickety wooden frame referred to, perhaps humorously, as a gate by the locals, the path through the desert almost resembles a formal road, beaten down by the regular foot traffic that passes through.  Nestled between jagged shelves of rock that hold back the oppressive dunes, shanties and huts to the north form the outskirts of one of Heru Taipa's many hamlets.

The sweeping dunes of the Velaka desert slope downward here, forming a crude road that slants across the sands.  Over the next shallow mound, a ramshackle wooden archway looms, like a lonely guardian in the wastes.

A rarity in the diminutive hamlet, this section of path has a relatively unobstructed view of the skyline, albeit only in one direction.  Opposite the towering shapes of the star dunes, northeastward the desert opens up into a rolling landscape of endless golden waves, flickering heat dancing along their crests.

In the crook of two great arms of a massive star-shaped dune, this dead end resembles most any in Velaka, apart from the solitary structure residing here.  Typical of the brazen Sand Elves that settled Haizen Cugis, a rare few will apparently set down stakes in even the least hospitable locales.

Little is visible of the Velaka from the crest of this relatively small dune, nestled snugly between a shifting ocean of sand to the north and a lush green oasis, tantalizingly nearby to the southwest.  The desert beyond remains nothing more than waves of gold, immeasurable and unrelenting.

Curving through the sea of dunes, a deep trench cuts through the sand like a great gash in the desert landscape.  Though the trail curves and disappears around the shifting dunes in either direction, a gradual slope to the northeast offers a promising escape from the sinuous path, appearing almost inviting by comparison.

Perhaps one of the lowest points in the Velakan desert, this stretch of long trench seems almost like a basin, surrounded on all sides by walls of sand ranging from simply domineering to truly colossal.  The floor of the dusty canyon is uneven, with hundreds of oddly-shaped depressions making travel somewhat difficult.

Along the shallowly angled plane of the slope, a handful of rocks about the size and shape of S'Kra Mur skulls jut out of the sand, growing in concentration nearer to the sandstone crags to the south and west.  Northward, the mighty expanse of Velaka stretches on, daring even the most adventurous explorers with its majestic crests and valleys, shimmering behind a curtain of sweltering heat.

Several colossal formations stand sentinel to what remains of a towering passage in the cliff face.  Now crumbling and partially engulfed by the surrounding sands, the entrance in encased by a large stone archway covered with eroded images and symbols, barely discernable from the rest of the rocky fissures.

Two extended apexes protrude from the upper-most cliffs, nearly touching to form a grand archway over the desolate trail.  The crumbling remains of what might have once been massive, sculpted pillars flank the regal pass, while the billowing sands wend their way amid large chunks of fallen rock, one of them attempting to hide a scrap of tattered fabric.

Tiny patches of moss cling desperately to the cliff's edge, their near futile attempt thwarted by the harsh desert environment.  Deep hues of umber, gold, and amethyst line the surrounding walls, their odd formations appearing to take on a life of their own.  The perpetual, shifting trail winds its way around several fallen boulders as it descends further to the north.

Billowing sands swirl about the wide trail while several migrating birds flit in and out of holes and deep hollows that dot the cliff face.  The massive, time-worn walls bear deep crags and fissures that lend to the appearance of enormous, statuesque figures, their fragile layers threatening to crumble and collapse, crushing anything in their wake.

Mountainous sandstone formations rise from the sands at a graduated rate along both sides of the gusty trail, their ever increasing size providing somewhat of a barrier against the desert winds.  Layers of sedimentary rock color the walls in varied hues of gold, grey and rust, the surfaces dotted with small holes that spout dried mosses, supporting the scant few creatures able to survive the harsh environment.

Several, small boulders emerge from their ever-shifting crypt, the years of erosion mutating them each into curious, pitted formations.  The sandy trail descends to the north, while the surrounding landscape is desolate and barren with nothing in sight but the endless expanse of golden dunes that waver in the unrelenting harshness of the surrounding desert.

Tall palm trees sway and rustle in the desert wind, their wide green fronds half-browned and similar to their shed leaves that now lay cracked and dead, littering the sparse underbrush at the edge of the tree line.  A small spattering of plant life clings near the narrow trail which is nearly invisible amid the shifting sands.

Lush greens and dried browns mingled in the surrounding plant life are a reminder of the constant evolution of this rare reprieve from the more severe outer regions of the Velaka.  Migrating birds soar in from the heat of the outer desert, sharing the welcome shade with the local wildlife.

Bending sharply through the thick surrounding brush that appears to grasp at everything like the hands of small children, the vague trail hums with the sounds of the surrounding insects.  A weathered palm lies uprooted nearby, its once-thick foliage now cracked and browned by the arid conditions.

Forming a comfortable windbreak from outlying sands, the dense underbrush is scattered with thin patches of ghostflowers desperately trying to take a foothold amid the harsh conditions.  A long-tailed lizard basks on a trunk of the surrounding palms, patiently awaiting a nearby insect that carelessly travels too close.

Along the narrow trail, gusts of desert winds push their way through the surrounding trees, causing small whirlwinds of stinging sand that disperse over the underbrush as quickly as they come.  Several large rocks thrust from the ground throughout the area, their odd formations ever-changing in the eroding sands.

Tall, sheltering palms bob and sway in the winds of the surrounding desert just beyond the deep green fronds.  Small sand martins flit carelessly among the tree tops and the shade of the lower flora, their twittering song filling the air.

Beneath the thick overhead canopy, dense underbrush threatens to overrun the barely discernable trail with a multitude of thick shrubs, vines, spiny grasses and the occasional flowering cactus with its deep golden blooms.

Large, flat fronds hang low from the sagging trees above, their deep green complexion obscuring the desert which lies just feet beyond.  Life thrives here in spite of the inhospitable sand, with numerous forms of insect clicking and chirping from the underbrush.

Thickly packed foliage overhead blocks out the view of the sky and the sounds of the desert, making it easy to forget the harsh climate beyond the oasis.  The dense concentration of plant life does such an exemplary job of sheltering this trail that it threatens to swallow it whole, consuming the only evidence of civilization's presence.

A low point stands between two great dune fields, separated by an arm of tall, jagged stones.  Eastward stands an expansive sprawl of crescent-shaped dunes, the wide hills of blowing sand stretching out toward the far horizon.  West beyond the stones, relatively calmer winds prevail, forming low mounds that roll to and fro.

A high point in the sandy sea, this pinnacle of dusty ground stands over the rest to give an excellent vantage point of the surroundings.  Far to the east the Gemfire Mountains loom, while westward the walls of Muspar'i are just faintly visible, flickering like a mirage that may not even be real.

Tall trees with long, wide fronds stand all around this expansive oasis, offering a pleasant opportunity to escape the harsh desert environment.  As if in defiance of the Velaka, only a meager path of loose sand hints at the landscape beyond the gently swaying leaves, otherwise giving the impression of a tropical refuge.  A modest freshwater pond provides well-deserved refreshment for two teams of yeehars and the handlers that attend to them.

Low bushes and creeping vines stretch out along a downward slope from the oasis toward the desert wastes, accompanied by the dry husks of former vegetation that was not as successful.  A groove worn in the sand by the barge route skirts along the southern side of the tree line, halting the attempts of the small paradise to expand.

A seemingly endless expanse of sand dunes stretch out to the north from the broad oasis, untouched apart from the deep channel worn in the ground by the barge route.  Pale scrub bushes strive for survival in this transitional environment, not entirely exposed to the harsh terrain while not quite safe among the lush greenery.

Sinuous walls of layered sandstone enclose the canyon from its floor up to the narrow opening at its top, which reveals a narrow sliver of sky.  The orange hue of the rock resembles the glow of the sun rising over the dunes, serving as a reminder that this is just one more facet of Velaka's diverse terrain.

The canyon tightens overhead while bending outward near the stone floor, giving this section a unique bell shape.  Curving around at an angle, the path widens to the south, however grows narrower to the northeast.

A choke point in the uneven walls of the canyon completely blocks the sky from view, casting the sheltered niche into a murky darkness.  Only the pale light reflected from the pasty yellow sandstone provides any shred of illumination, though day and night are indiscernible.

Filtering in through a small gap in the otherwise obstructing vertical waves of sandstone overhead, a narrow shaft of light lances all the way to the canyon floor.  Thousands of layers of rock ranging from deep brown to blood red create the curvaceous walls, a mosaic of muted color that blends into a visual symphony of desert hues.

Bands of color stretch across the walls as the canyon curves gently from northwest to south, some as wide as a Gor'Tog's hand while others are smaller than a Gnome's toenail.  As if the sandstone were painted by hand, each unique shade of pale orange or murky gold compliments the adjacent layers, forming a cohesive whole.

A long, sloping plane reaches out from the slot canyon to the southeast like a serpent's tongue, even matching its hue with the reddish sandstone.  The ramp drops steeply off to both sides, forcing travelers to descend directly into a low trench, beyond which stands a tall plateau.

Far from the brilliant golds and oranges found in the rest of Velaka, the ground here is made of dark, greyish-brown stone, as if the color had been drained away.  An oily residue clings to the rocks and gravel, giving the entire area a distinctly unclean appearance.

Cold, grey walls of crumbling stone lift upward to the southwest, enclosing the trench like an arena.  All about the ground are scattered lumps of the same rock, a fine layer of oily residue clinging to their surfaces, giving the entire area a distinctly unclean appearance.

Giant vertebrae, teeth and skulls -- many of which are cracked and broken -- pile high into the air, closely matching the grey stones upon which they rest.

Massive shards of broken bone plates jut upward and outward from the grey stones like the teeth of a fallen beast beneath the heap.

Flickering torchlight from the adjacent vestibule reaches this modest entry chamber, though much of the room remains shrouded in darkness.  The narrow hall affords little more space than is needed to walk through into the deeper sections of the temple, with rows of benches on either wall only further discouraging loiterers.  Even the frail, wavering light that creeps in from the north has difficulty filling the room, cloaking the upper walls and ceiling in an impenetrable veil of inky darkness.

Cool stone walls of pale grey granite, trimmed in dark-stained oak, enclose the study in an atmosphere of careful, contemplative elegance.  A monstrous oaken desk dominates one wall, a thick silk rug stretching between it and the equally large fireplace across the room.  At the desk, the guildmaster sits in a chair that just barely falls short of being a throne.

Narrow alleyways spike through the crowded street like the quills of a dyrachis.  The road, filled with high stone buildings and tiny homes, clings desperately to the hillside, vainly clawing toward the wall for protection.  The wall, however, failing to reach these heights, offers no safety from the buffeting sands of the Golden Heights.

Smooth walls curve gently around the perimeter of the room, forming a modestly spacious conical chamber with a high, vaulted ceiling.  A small bargate statue of abstract design stands beneath a brass lantern -- the obvious centerpiece of the area -- the tilework pattern on the floor outlining a walkway that circumnavigates the sculpture.  Following the contour of the wall, the path branches out to the north, east and south through narrow hallways.

Curving around the perimeter of the temple in a wide arc, the narrow hallway is hedged in by a row of thick columns.  Two burning torches rest on the wall in the quiet corner beyond.  The stone pillars stand just wide enough apart to allow narrow shafts of pale light into the corridor, dividing the darkness and further enshrouding the unlit portions of the path in seclusion.

A pedestal at the center of the room supports a trio of brass oil lamps, whose frail light is solely responsible for providing enough illumination to read.  Woven from long reeds, a pale carpet stretches across the floor between the bare, sandstone walls, dampening sound and reflecting the flickering flames above.  Rows of deep shelves are occupied by numerous volumes and grimoires, all attended to and arranged meticulously by the elderly monk seated behind a long, oak desk.

Large, stone pillars separate the cramped hallway from a quiet nook in which two torches quietly burn.  The radiance of the flickering flames reaches feebly out between the columns, unsuccessful in its task of illuminating the shadowed passage and managing only to subdivide the area into corridors of pale light and pools of tenebrous shadow.

Rough sandstone walls and a feeble wooden bench function as the most comfort this desolate sanctuary can offer, eerily characteristic of its patron.  The flickering torches attempt to reach beyond to the east and south, blocked largely by the stone pillars that separate the area from the corridor.

Standing at the center of the oblong chamber that yawns from northwest to south, brass candelabras festooned with desert-thistle wreaths surround a low altar of carved quartz.  A fine crack runs diagonally through the glossy stone, splitting it neatly in half, though the two segments remain pressed together.  Ghostly tallow candles -- the only permanent light source for the small room -- burn atop their respective perches, working desperately to illumine the paintings that line the curving walls.

A musty odor of still air and dust envelops the room, made all the more poignant by the quiet of the desert night.  Resting on the arm of an oak-framed settee, a tarnished silver oil lamp casts the glow of its dancing flame out in all directions.  The frame of a stained-glass window looms overhead, glinting in the meager light like some odd skeletal guardian.  A creased, calligraphic vellum has been attached to a plaque on the wall.

Long wooden benches line the walls of the meditation room, spaced just far enough for a tail to rest comfortably behind them.  An intricate Sun Maze mosaic has been laid into the floor, and six expansive windows permit soft sunlight to gently illuminate it and the leafy palms that sit in each corner of the room.

Dried desert roses hang in garlands from the low ceiling to frame the small room, and a modest Musparan silk rug lies upon the floor.  No more than a squared hole, a glassless window carved from the sandstone wall is shaded by a pair of painted wooden shutters, offering some respite from the city noise and desert wind.  The young S'Kra Mur woman, Muspar'i's local locksmith, sits behind a clean sandstone counter, occasionally pointing out the shelf and hook of wares behind her to interested parties.

Swaths of grass cover the interior courtyard, broken only by a rectangular reflecting pool that doubles as a trough and bath for the horses.  The field is hemmed by brick buildings on three sides, with the facade wall and gated archway forming the fourth enclosing structure.

Hungry -- or bored -- horses have ignored the stacks of baled hay nearby in favor of cropping several bare patches into the grass.  A low set of fieldstone steps leads up to a red door.  A plaque next to the door reads, "Stablemaster".

A large brick stable stands here with its dark wooden doors thrown wide open.  A nearby well is festooned with buckets and rope, with young children often seen sprinting from the stable to the well, enhancing their daily chores with a race.  Some slightly trampled climbing rose bushes grow up against one side of the stable.

Just off the courtyard stands a red brick building with a profusion of roses guarding its entrance.  Stone steps that lead to its dark doors bear the print of horses' hoofs, giving them a faintly whimsical look.  A wooden sign peeks out from behind one of the thorny rose bushes.

Shelves filled with tastefully arranged trophies and ribbons line one wall of the Stablemaster's office, and the wall opposite is taken up with books describing all aspects of horse care and instruction in equestrian skills.  An ornate desk, set upon wood carved horse-hoof feet is pushed against a window overlooking the stableyard.
Crisp, clean smells emanate from the freshly polished chestnut floor.  An archway to one side of the entryway leads to a cozy sitting room while on the other is a mahogany door.

The air is filled with the scent of fresh grass and the smell of horses.  A narrow pathway opens into a practice field for trainers and their spirited horses.  High fences covered in ivy and moss offer jumpers a challenging course.  The field also features a row of barrels and a low brick wall that gives the horses variety of tasks as their handlers put them through their paces.

Another practice area opens up, with the scent of fresh grass and the smell of horses in sharp contrast to the fragrant roses planted against a nearby brick wall.  Wooden barrels and fences provide the perfect opportunity for practicing jumps and turns.

Sectioned off for more strenuous training, this jousting field offers benches for watchers to be comfortably seated.  A ring of tall oak trees forms a natural stadium for horses and their riders to showcase their jousting abilities.  Not a day goes by that some poor soul isn't led off the field by helpful spectators.

The pungent smell of horses is kept at bay by a wreath of dried herbs and flowers hung on the stall doors of this huge stable.  Made of the finest of maple and oak, each uniform stall is pristinely kept, with nary a straw out of place.  Various instruments of the trade are hung upon one wall, all in neat order.  A trough of fresh water is kept full by young boys, often seen carrying buckets from a nearby well.

Dark oak-paneled walls adorned with oval mirrors and lace-covered shelves enclose this room.  Wide arches on each side of the room lead to more merchandise.  Burgundy velvet settees and chairs are comfortably situated to offer customers a place to rest while contemplating their purchases.

The fresh smell of leather permeates the air adrift from the newly made saddles and gear that reside in this room.  Sturdy racks and shelves hold various items, from simple horse's brushes to elaborate flanchards polished to perfection.

Eager young clerks stand behind a dark oak counter ready to take orders and handle the horse's feed that is being sold.  From stacks of hay to bags of oats, they lift and haul them from the nearby loading dock and neatly place them along the wooden paneled walls.

A cheerful fire blazes from a brick fireplace along the far wall, a cast-iron teakettle warming inside it.  Brown leather armchairs standing before the fireplace offer a perfect spot for a break.  A narrow stairway at one end leads up into the second story.

rooms.t: [A Bit For Horses, Top Of Stairs]
rooms.desc: A narrow stairwell leading back down to the main floor is covered with a well-worn carpet.  Set between a green door and a blue door is a painting of a stunning black stallion.

The inside of the lobby here is breathtaking, unlike anything else you have seen so far in Leth Deriel in terms of its display of wealth and worldliness.  The interior of the ebonwood tree has been polished and grooved to resemble rich paneling.  A brass sign along the far wall points up.

Here at the inside of a large fork is a chamber that houses the tellers for local currency transactions.  Despite their rather conservative nature, the local merchants, traders and citizens seem to be conducting a fair amount of business.  A sign points up for the Foreign Branch.

Here is the foreign exchange window at which one province's currency may be exchanged for that of another.  Exchange rates in Leth Deriel have always been governed primarily by the forces of supply and demand - if you want supplies here, the town's merchants demand local currency.

Hedges of varying heights have been grown in amazing patterns throughout the garden.  In various corners small white tables, chairs and benches are set to provide a resting spot or a site for intimate conversations.  A bronzed statue of a man is in the center, its base ringed with vibrant roses and myrtle.
The forest gives way to the banks of a swift-flowing river.  No bridge crosses the water, and the far bank is too steep to clamber out.

rooms.desc: Bark curls in pale strips from the trunks of birch trees.  Wide-leafed hosta grow in a circle around their base, thriving in the dim light of the forest.  The undergrowth is thinner, with fewer thorns, and you can hear the rush of water nearby.

Feathery ferns crowned with thick, cinnamon-red spikes nestle in the shade of the trees.  The trail winds around in the lazy meandering pattern typical of deer paths everywhere.  To the north, the faint burble of running water can be heard through the brush.

As the trees grow further apart, the path becomes more narrow.  Thick mounds of brush crowd the trail, competing for the sunlight and catching at passersby.  Clumps of fur caught in the grasping branches hint at others who haunt the forest.  Since the fur is about waist-high on a Gor'Tog, these others are perhaps more dangerous than an occasional thorn.

Leathery dark green leaves flutter on bushes that grow beneath the trees, twisting to reveal a thick-veined bronze underside.  Birds swoop amongst the branches, carrying bits and pieces of grass and vines to mend their nests.

Birds chitter in the branches -- the warbling song of a wren, the shrill scolding of a scarlet jay, the hoarse call of a large crow -- all competing in a cacophonous clash of sound that masks the rustle of dead leaves as you move.

Clusters of river birch grow in pale grey stands along the edge of the clearing.  Beyond, the forest looms, tall and dark.  Mossy green vines dangle from overhanging limbs, modestly concealing the tree's trunk from view and masking the approach of anything that might be moving within the woods.  It's impossible to see which way to go to find the path in the forest.

rooms.desc: The rock face angles outward above the ledge, making it impossible to climb past this point.  Below, you can see the deer paths' meandering track through the forest, twisting and turning in a logic known only to the deer.

At the top of a rocky outcropping, you can look down onto a thicket of menacing briars.  No way down is readily apparent, and the thought of dropping thrice the height of a Gor'Tog into the thorns is really not something a sane person would wish to entertain.

Narrow cracks in the rock wall provide precarious hand- and footholds as you climb.  Sharp-leafed shrubs cling tenaciously to the surface, their roots threading fragile tendrils into almost invisible cracks in their search for water.

High above, the trees' spreading branches are silhouetted against the star-lit sky.  On the forest floor, the land is cloaked in a perpetual green-tinged darkness broken from time to time by silvery shafts of moonlight piercing the canopy overhead.  Leaves crackle underfoot, a dried carpet over the thick, rich mulch.

Blight stalks the forest, leaving behind it a meandering track of dead trees, their bark peeled away in ragged curls to reveal weathered grey wood beneath.  Birds nest in the branches and hollows, and foxes or badgers lay claim to the burrows beneath the roots, but eventually the rotted wood will fall and join the decomposing leaves that carpet the forest floor.

Still and somber, pine trees lower their branches to brush the ground, drooping like dejected suitors mourning their lost loves.  The melancholy limbs show a distressing tendency to clutch at travelers trying to make their way through the forest, jabbing sharp needles into exposed skin.

Red-leafed vines twined around the trunks and lower branches of the trees lend a splash of vivid color to the dark greens and browns.  The leafless limbs of a dead tree let in dim light to brush the forest floor, heightening the shadows.

Crystal clear water tumbles, icy cold, over the rounded pebbles of the streambed.  Spray slicks the dark grey rocks on either side.  The current pushes you toward the south bank where, despite the wet surface, an agile climber could probably scramble out of the water.  Just downstream, the creek flows over a pile of logs tumbled higgledy-piggledy like some giant's jackstraws.

The water surges with renewed energy as it passes the end of a long, low rock in the river, swirling around as opposing currents meet.  Half-sunken logs shift and groan as the current pounds against them in an ongoing battle to dislodge the obstructions in the river's path.

Long and low, a lichen-streaked grey boulder rises from the current.  Lumpy ridges along the top resemble nothing more than two hands crossed on the breast of a massive corpse laid out at a funeral, giving rise to the original name of Giant's Pyre River.

Deep grooves etched into the rocky bank mark the passage of years as the water gouges wide, rippling channels beneath the overhanging rock.  Branches and logs floating down the river catch on the sides of the creekbed, causing them to swing around with almost lethal force before the momentum jars them free.  A traveler attempting to ford the stream must be wary of such hazards.

A wide, sandy ramp flows up from the north bank of the creek, certainly shallow enough to allow you to scramble out of the water.  Clusters of pale birch trees lean out over the banks, their silvery bark peeling away from the wood in curling strips.  Dappled sunlight filters through the trees' green leaves to sparkle against the water's surface.  To the southeast, a brook branches off from the main waterway, leaving the river flowing more gently as it continues to the west.
