The only branches leading upwards are too far for even the tallest Gor'Tog, so that one cannot climb in that direction.  A wide hole in the side of the trunk looks broad enough to squeeze through.

A deep recess in the face of the cliff gives travelers bit of freedom to move about.  A huge oak tree on one side of the depression looks slightly lopsided, having grown so close to the face of the cliff that it is stunted on that side.  The lower limbs of the tree grow close to the ground, granting access to some of the higher limbs.  The tree shades the recess, and nearly hides a wide crack at the back.  Handholds have been carved into the face of the cliff, leading down.

Moisture trickles down the face of a sandstone cliff, gathering in a shallow pool at the base.  Year after year, such trickles wear away at the smooth surface, leaving behind striated chimneys carved out of the surrounding rock.

Leaves whisper in the wind, twisting to reveal their red-veined undersides.  Quiet and peaceful, the serenity is belied by scraps of blood-stained fur caught on the rough bark of a tree trunk and the marks of claws in the damp loam of the forest floor.

The trail twists around, crossing and recrossing its path in an aimless meander.  A low buzzing sound draws your attention to a papery grey hornet's nest in the branches of a mistwood tree, fortunately out of reach.

Patches of bark litter the forest floor, fallen from a dead tree across the path.  The exposed wood is riddled with tiny holes left by insects and larger holes left by the birds that prey upon them.  Despite the damage done by animals, the wood has aged to a lovely shade of silver-grey with dusky green veins.
A fox darts beneath a mistwood tree, disappearing into a tangle of thick roots.  Shadowed by the overhanging boughs, it's hard to see whether it went to earth in its den or lurks there, unseen.

Leaves rustle in counterpoint to a melodic twittering and chirping, a near-constant concert that falls silent from time to time as some threat is detected, only to begin again.  The birds themselves remain unseen, hidden by the dense foliage.

Past years' leaves lie crumpled and brown beneath the sheltering branches of the mistwood trees.  Every footstep and shift in position evokes a dry crackling noise as the fragile remains crumple underfoot.

Bits of fur and broken bones litter the ground at the base of a tree, evidently the perch of an owl or some other bird of prey.  Overhanging branches sport a pale green fall of maiden's tresses that block your view of the upper reaches of the tree.

Dull red needles form a dense mat around the base of a pine tree, one of the few left in the forest.  For the most part, the quick growing conifers have been supplanted by the slower-growing grey mistwood so highly prized by lumbermen.

For the most part, the forest is painted in shades of grey on grey, from the dull charcoal bark of the mistwood trees to the pale, almost white lichens that cover fallen logs.  Occasional splashes of color break the monotone palate -- vivid scarlet leaves on a dark wyrdwood tree, or deep purple berries on a chokeweed bush.  The air is redolent with the smell of decaying leaves and rotting wood mingled with the faint sweet scent of blood.

rooms.desc: A pockmarked boulder glitters with tiny garnet chips half hidden beneath flaky grey-green lichen.  Vivid moss clings to the northern side of the rock, smoothing the bumpy surface with a carpet of sharply scented greenery.
Musty leaves slip and slide underfoot, made slick by rain and slow decomposition.  Falling in graceful green veils, maiden's tresses drape over the branches to catch at the limbs of passersby.
Spiky cinnamon-brown stalks jut up from clusters of ferns that thrive in the shadows of the forest.  Here and there, a deep maroon trillium raises its face to the dim light of the sun.

Pale yellow against the forest floor, a few shy lady's slipper orchids sway in a slight breeze.  Overhead, squirrels leap from branch to branch with gleeful abandon as they go about their search for seeds and nuts to tide them over the winter months.

The forest crowds up against the base of a tall cliff to the east.  Angling out to loom over the huddled forest below, the sandstone surface looks almost impossible to climb.  High overhead, a raptor circles as it hunts.

A steep-sided ravine breaches the forest floor, leaving a wide gash spanned by a pair of ropes tied to trees on either side.  It's hard to dignify the arrangement by calling it a bridge, but it looks like the only way across.

Packed earth trails, wide enough for a wagon, wind through the trees and stumps of the forest.  A charcoal burner's hut stands in a small clearing, surrounded by smoking mounds of earth that cover stacks of slowly smoldering wood.

Grey barked mistwood trees line the trail, their broad leaves cupped to cradle the dew.  The moons, filtered by overhanging branches and dense foliage, cast more shadows than illumination, an effect that is only heightened by the faint, pallid glow of phosphorescent mosses clinging to the tree trunks.  From time to time, a hunting cat gives off a hoarse yowl of frustration, presumably to curse the escape of its prey.
The ground underfoot is soft with layer upon layer of decaying leaves.  A fine haze fills the air, reflecting every beam of moonlight that manages to penetrate the forest canopy.

Tall spikes of pale purple flowers sway above the broad leaves of hosta growing in the shade of the forest.  Grey-barked mistwood trees grow close together, broken here and there by clumps of river birch or oak.

Motes of dust dance in beams of moonlight that filter through the tree branches.  The trail narrows as it passes deeper into the forest.  Though the chitter of birds may fade with the setting sun, the forest is never silent, as even the leaves whisper against one another in the wind.

An occasional dark grey-barked mistwood tree jostles for space amidst the faster-growing birch and pine here on the edge of the forest.  The sharp needles and gum-laden branches of the pines tend to catch at the hair and clothing of those passing beneath the trees, as if some wood sprite did try to cling to those who travel through her domain.

Cloaked in the forest's pale twilight world of greenery, you can see the brighter greens and golds of the fields to the north and the dark browns and greys of the forest to the east.  The road grows rougher as it enters the forest, rutted and churned by passing wagons and lack of maintenance.

A winding ravine blocks travel to the south.  There's no way to cross at this point, but you can see a pair of ropes spanning the divide a bit further east.  The trees are sparse near the edge of the cliff, and the ground underfoot is crumbling in places.

Wide swathes of oats and wheat, their colors faded in the night, ripen in fields on either side of the road.  A split-log fence prevents cattle from straying into the crops.  To the south, trees grow thickly together as the road enters the shadows of the Mistwood Forest.

A few small thatched-roof cottages cluster beside the road in a bucolic setting.  Assorted livestock move restlessly within a pen -- a bristle-maned grey donkey, a pair of oxen and a swaybacked nag with a shaggy coat.  The animals' legs are coated in mud or some other, less appealing substance.

A spring wells up from the ground beside the road, trickling down a rocky outcropping to pool in a stone basin.  Local residents rely on it for their animals and crops, as the overflow from the basin runs into a ditch used to irrigate surrounding fields.

Cattle lowing in a nearby pasture break the silence of the surrounding countryside.  Flowers and herbs bloom in small gardens between the houses that border the road.  Though quite similar in construction, each building each has some feature to distinguish it from its neighbor.  One house has fruit trees, another a pen for a pig, while yet another is home to a box-like shelter mounted atop a pole in front.
Rolling hills stretch out on either side of the road, covered with a thick mat of wild thyme and rosemary.  Tiny white and purple flowers dot the fragrant greenery.

A wooden tower at the crest of the hill offers a view of the surrounding countryside.  In the dry season, the Baron's foresters keep a careful watch for fires that could destroy the prosperous fields.

To the south, the rolling hills give way to orchards and neatly tended fields.  The road to Mistwood Forest stretches out to the south and east, branching off from the main North Road that connects Therenborough with the village of Langenfirth.

An ancient empath putters about the shop, tending small pots of herbs.  He seems to mutter constantly, either to himself or to his plants.  His goods are stored on shelves in various clay jars and, since none are labeled, it is hoped that the good Yorgi knows what is in them.
A few ferns have sprung up here, owing their life to damp soil.  The water must percolate from below, for there is no evidence of a running spring.

The steep grade of the trail doesn't seem to bother the wildlife that use it daily, but for adventurers used to flatter lands, it is a sweaty climb.  The path continues its relentless rise to the north.

Briar bushes encroach the small path, reaching to rip at passersby.  At least one beast failed to escape the thorny grasp, as evidenced by the thick strands of wool, which hang lifelessly entrapped.  The game trail branches here, the directions most worn from travel climbing sharply to the north and cutting along a side slope to the southeast.

The trail winds its way through the brush and rises steeply up the face of the hill to the east.  The trail does not appear to be heavily used, and the soil underfoot is loose, making ascent difficult.  To the northwest, the trail descends at an easier angle.
Faint, barely surviving upon the wind, is the scent of blood.  The smell seems to arrive from the east, hinting at a fresh kill.  Grass covered ground continues to descend slightly to the south.

Pressed into the soft dirt alongside this steep trail are an animal's tracks.  It doesn't take a ranger to discern that these large, deep paw prints are the work of a predator.  Although the trail descends steeply to the south, a change in grade can be seen towards the east, over the next rise.
The vegetation thrives here, apparently unaware of the presence of a steep cliff.  Down the abrupt drop-off, loose rock and dirt promise an impossible climb and a deadly fall.
The game trail is wide, level, and holds few trees atop this hummock.  Sounds of the wild are unnervingly absent here, save the occasional rambling beast.
Sparse trees and shrubs mingle with short, fragile grass beneath the open sky.  Small, criss-crossing paths cut through the grass, revealing the heavy use creatures give this place.
The view from atop this hill is quite limited due to the trees, which surround this lush meadow.

Alone, in the ground covering grass, stands a tall, proud, yet oddly colored oak tree.  Spreading wide its thick limbs, the tree offers shade and protection from the elements.  Beneath the tree, the grass is broken, trampled, and torn.  Bone, hide, and the distinct odor of blood mark this place as home to the wolves of 'Neer's Hummock.
A few rogue wildflowers dance among the grass, daring to claim their place.  Leading through a break in the trees, an exposed path veers off towards a small glade.

Rising to the calf of a human, the grass of this plain, quiet meadow spreads forth in a sea of yellow-green.  The temptation to lie and take rest is strong, but not advised when the local carnivorous beast happens along.

The ground in this open square is trampled flat, aside from one young deobar tree which stands in the middle of the yard.  Ragged target dummies bearing crude parodies of the guild crests are tied in nooses from a branch.
Low benches are pulled up to long wooden tables.  Some sort of greenish crust stains the tables in spots.

Mistwood trees press in around the edge of the cliff, a few clinging rather tenuously to the ground.  A stout rope has been tied to a nearby stump and leads through an open knothole in the side of an oak tree which begins somewhere below the edge of the cliff and towers up over it.  Older layers of leaves, nearly decomposed now, have been kicked up in various places by someone, or something.  A series of low limbs offers a route to the upper branches of one stout tree.

The ground is thick with foliage fallen from the trees.  The trees seem to huddle together, forming a thick canopy and almost completely blocking the sky above.  A narrow path winds through the trees, running north and angling sharply east, with the occasional gnarled root or branch nearly blocking the way.  The densely packed trees form a highway of branches overhead with access from some of the limbs closer to the ground.

The forest is quiet, broken only by the sound of the occasional bird chirp, which is then quickly silenced.  The trees have been badly damaged, with what would appear to be claw marks on almost every tree in the immediate vicinity.  Game trails stretch in the four cardinal directions, dodging between the trees.  Low limbs on one tree look particularly stout and good for climbing.

Dense clusters of brush and scrub mark this part of the forest.  Game trails run from southerly bearings and begin to scatter in a large number of directions heading north.  The northern trails disappear beneath the local chaparral, making them impossible to follow.  The bones of some small animal, partially hidden at the edge of a bush, have been gathered into a pile and the skull placed on top.  The limbs of one tree almost form a spiraling staircase as they circle upwards to the top of the tree.

A small clearing has formed in the midst of the dense trees.  The trees grow a respectable distance away from a large pit that has been dug in the middle of the clearing.  The sides of the pit are smooth, which would have made escape impossible if one of the walls had not collapsed into a large pile of rubble, partially filling the pit.  One tree has fallen over onto another so that it leans at an angle perfect for scaling to some of the higher branches.

A weathered pile of rocks has been stacked rather carefully, marking the boundary between a game trail leading west and a stone road that winds through the forest to the east.  Off the beaten trail the ground is thick with foliage, carpeting it in a fresh layer of green leaves.  The rough bark of one mistwood tree makes natural places to grip when scaling the trunk, creating a possible place to climb.

The trees clump together in groves, densely packed, but with visible differences from what can be seen to the west.  Fallen leaves nearly cover a pile of stones off to one side of the road.  At the base of the pile one of the rocks looks as if it had been inscribed, though the words are too faded to make out.

The woods press in on the road oppressively, forming a thick canopy overhead.  A small portion of the road is virtually untouched by the ravages of time, as the stones are still tightly fitted together.  The superb construction demonstrates the care and hard work that the laborers put into the road's assembly.  Weeds and grasses have grown between most of the stones that once formed the road.

The trees are fewer and far between towards the edge of the forest.  Smaller varieties of plant life flourish with little competition from the larger trees.  The undergrowth continues out past the last of the trees and a short ways up the slope of a rocky hill.  A mistwood tree near the road offers a way up into the canopy.

Thick growths of underbrush rule this part of the forest.  Interspersed between the thickets are a few sparse clusters of mistwood trees.  A small brook gurgles as it meanders through the forest and crosses the path of the road.  Alongside the brook grows a single lilac, a stranger among giants.

Briar roses grow in profusion around the palisade walls of a small village.  Sweetly scented as they are, nothing can mask the stench of rotting meat that emanates from the charnel heap of dead and decaying carcasses piled outside the gate.  Scraps of flesh cling to the gnawed bones of deer, wild boar and an unfortunate Human or two.

Pale pink roses blossom against thorny green leaves, growing in profusion in the dense thicket.  The trail twists and turns, following the hoofprints of countless generations of deer.  An intense fragrance perfumes the air, but all the roses in the world can't conceal the sickly-sweet stench of rotting meat that underlies it.

The village palisade, trimmed saplings bound together with rope and rusted iron bands, offers little protection against invaders.  From the looks of the shells of houses that residents once called their homes, there is little to attract bandits to prey upon the town.  Broken pottery, offal and other, less appealing substances line the sides of the dirt street, turning the packed earth into a reeking mud that clings to clothing and skin.

At one time, this must have been the site of a more conventional village, for a chimney and fireplace stand a lonely vigil amidst the ruins of a burnt-out house.  Rude wooden benches, little more than split logs, offer seating for residents to gather around what is now used as a communal cookfire.  A rusty cauldron swings from an iron hook over the sullenly burning logs in the hearth.

Fragments of colored glass litter the grass outside a small stone chapel.  Once a center for worship and a meeting place for the town, the building is now just a ruin towering over the tumbled-down cottages.  Splintered pews litter the small graveyard beside it, evidently used to knock down the markers on the graves.

Stone walls survive, but the thatched roof has long since blown away on the largest house still standing in the village.  Broken shutters surround the unglazed diamond-paned windows, still marred by black soot from the destruction of the village itself.
Round wooden silos once stored grain for villagers.  Now the boards bow out as the wheat or barley held within swells from exposure to moisture, and a heady scent of fermentation fills the air.

Streaked with rust, an anvil stands beneath a lightning-blasted tree.  Iron and steel bars lie in a tumbled haystack effect, melded together by the metal's oxidation to form a madman's sculpture.  Nearby houses are in no better shape, missing their roofs, their doors broken down and shutters swaying aimlessly in the breeze.

Splintered stiles sag from weathered fence posts surrounding a muddy common, no longer a barrier to the passage of people or animals.  The canted remains of a small hut sway precariously in the breeze, perhaps once a manger for the animals that grazed here.

In the midst of the burnt-out cottages and broken fences, a sign still sways outside the doorway of what was once a small store.  The sturdy construction has left the building mostly intact, though its thatched roof, like all the houses in the town, has long since blown away.

Built up against the palisade wall, the stable seems to have survived the destruction almost intact.  No glass remains in the structure's windows, but the split-shingled roof, while scorched from fire, displays little other damage.  The village well stands nearby, a broken bucket overturned beside it.

Old doors and close-growing saplings form the walls of one nearby shanty.  The trees themselves, still solidly rooted in the ground, are long-since dead from the noxious condition of the soil, but some enterprising resident has threaded willow withies between the trunks to form a rude shelter.

Long oak trestle tables with matching benches line the walls, ready to be pulled out for the manor's evening meal.  Or so the hall was used in the days before the town's destruction.  Now, sticky with filth and spilled ale, the tables are piled high with straw to form rude beds for the invaders.  The rushes that cover the floor give off a sour smelling stench of mildew, mold and worse.

A broken loom, still half threaded, stands near the long windows that overlook the orchard at the back of the manor.  Although frayed and tattered, the pattern of the unfinished tapestry is still visible beneath the accumulated dirt and cobwebs.

Empty wooden racks once held swords and crossbows.  A barrel, half-filled with coarse black sand, would have been used to polish chainmail, removing the rust as a man at arms sweated to roll the barrel back and forth.  Now, the room holds naught but a few broken arrows and some bowstrings wrapped in oiled paper in a storage bin.

No fires burn in the great hearths at either end of the kitchen.  Now, they hold only cold ashes and the bitter memories of the once-thriving population that resided here.  Thick trestle tables are littered with broken pottery, some upturned against the wall and used as target practice, to judge by the splintered scars and broken arrowheads lodged within.  The flagstone floor is marred by sticky brown stains.

Rodent bones have been heaped in a pile in the corner of the pantry.  Marble shelves line the walls, so chipped and tilted as to be unusable.  Wooden barrels hold spoiled remains of wheat and oats, and an unbroken earthenware crock gives off a stench of rancid oil.
Stove-in barrels and the stale smell of ale fill the buttery.  Once used by the hall as a storage room for drinks, little remains but broken bottles and shards of earthenware tankards.
The hall runs along the outer wall of the manor, lit only by narrow slit-like windows known as arrow loops.  Finely woven clothing, the expensive fabrics little more than tatters, litters the floor.

Shredded hangings sway from the posts of the carved mahogany bed like dull grey ghosts of the past.  Moths have been at the draperies, leaving behind cobweb-strewn fabric that more closely resembles fuzzy lace than the original rich green velvet.  Pale brown feathers drift in the air, swept up from holes in the mattress ticking by the wind.  An iron-banded chest at the foot of the bed lies open and empty.

Chill white walls and dingy white damask drapes make the cherrywood bed seem to glow a deep, rich red color despite the lack of polish and exposure to the elements.  The mattress is missing -- dragged off to use for bedding elsewhere or simply eaten by rodents.  Nothing else remains in the room but dust and dirt.

The hall runs along the outer wall of the manor, lit only by narrow slit-like windows known as arrow loops.  Empty torch rings frame the doors along the inner wall, and a dimly lit staircase leads up to the attics.
Torn strips of sapphire-blue wallpaper sag to the floor, revealing the whitewashed walls behind it.  A dark blue braided rug is the only furnishing in this empty bedroom.

An overturned cot lies sprawled in the ashes of the fireplace, seared and crackled by heat.  Nearby, two small cradles hold scattered bones amidst the linen bedding.  Less damage was done here than in the other rooms of the manor -- the dressers remain standing, and the flames were confined to the fireplace itself.  Dirt has settled into the corners, veiled by a year or more of spider webs, and choking clouds of dust rise up with each movement.

The roof is missing, burnt by the fires which ravaged the village or simply lost to time and weather, leaving the attics open to the sky.  Dark rafters tower overhead, and a narrow staircase leads down to the lower floors.

Wind and rain have swept the floorboards bare, leaving behind little more than warped and weathered wood.  Wooden rings on iron bars between the rafters are all that remain of the curtains used to divide the large room into smaller cubbies for the servants who worked from dawn to long past dark to keep the manor house running.

Toppled trunks, their sides bashed in, are scattered across the floor of the storeroom.  Open to the weather, the wood has swollen and dried, cracking a little more with each cycle until jagged splinters offer a hazard to anyone lacking sturdy boots.

You stand in the entrance hall of Riverhaven's famed hospital.  Tall sea-green marble columns reach from the floor to the ceiling. Moss-stuffed pillows line one wall for the minor wounded to sit in while waiting for the empaths to finish with the more seriously impaired.  Beneath your feet, a woven rug of soft fleece adorns the room.  To the east, a cream colored arch with the words, "For Their Pain, My Heart" inscribed on it, beckons those who need immediate tending.

An empath glances at you while scurrying over to help a wounded citizen.  All around you are wounded or dying from every walk of life, but the efficiency of the empaths keeps everyone calm and assured. The smooth cream-colored marbled walls lend a cool feel to the room, helping to keep down any fevers that may afflict the diseased or poisoned.  Peering through a small arch you see a glimpse of a garden outside.
An enormous slab of rock is upthrust in the river to the south, cutting the water like a knife.  Downriver of the formation a low, forested island lies, a green tail to a stony comet.
Placed in the wall of the sheer cliff is a huge stone door with an arched top.  Two large lifelike sentinels, one on either side of the door, stand at attention in silence.

The trees in this part of the forest are clustered together in sparsely populated groves.  Passage is difficult due to the wide distance between clusters of trees.  A chain of trees echoes a stone road below and allows passage to the west and northeast.  One of the taller mistwood trees offers a route down to the ground.

The trees begin to disperse noticeably to the east.  The trees are thinner than are those to the west, clumping together in small groves.  The smaller bodies are close enough together that passage between each cluster of trees is possible.  The sturdy limbs of the mistwood trees allow one with a good bit of skill or perhaps luck to climb down to the ground.

Branches form a thick canopy, obscuring the forest floor except for faint glimpses of the remains of a stone road.  The thicker, sturdier branches form a highway that echoes the path of the stone road.  One especially large mistwood tree along the path looks like a somewhat passable, if awkward and difficult way to climb down to the ground.

From your vantage point you can see a stone road below.  To the east, as the forest thins, the branches become less dense and tangled.  A series of blue rags, tied to branches, marks a route through the thinning forest canopy to the east.  The trunk of one tree is scratched on one side, as if it has been used frequently to climb between the ground and the treetops.

The branches overhead thin slightly, allowing a clear view of the sky above.  Below, dense thickets cover the leaf-strewn ground, possibly providing a bit of cushion for those who might fall.  Limbs form a spiraling staircase that provides a means to get down to the forest floor.

Broad, thick mistwood branches grow in a tangled mess and form a highway high over the forest floor.  Some branches do not lead anywhere, while others connect and form wooden bridges between trees.  The limbs of one tree lead down to a spot where it is possible to drop to the ground, though it might be difficult and could result in a fall.

The trees grow close together, a jumbled mass of branches and trunks.  Moving about is a bit difficult, but not impossible.  The ground below is completely obscured by branches and the sky is only visible in fleeting glimpses.  Small scraps of tattered white cloth have been conveniently placed to mark routes where it is possible to travel.  An assortment of red cloths hangs from a set of branches that lead down to the forest floor.

Broad avenues of branches stretch out in every direction, high above the ground.  Most of the branches look sturdy enough to support a good deal of weight, while others look like they could snap under the slightest pressure.  One branch has broken, and its fallen half now lies dead on the forest floor.  A series of stout limbs forms a natural ladder to the ground below.

The branches arch over the ground, giving one a view of a small clearing below where a pit has been dug.  The trees seem to shy away from the pit, none daring to grow too close to its edge.  One tree has fallen over, providing a steep ramp to the ground below.

At the edge of the forest the trees are few and far between, while to the west the growth thickens.  To the east a stone road climbs partway up a rock-strewn hill.  A series of connecting branches form a broad avenue high in the treetop canopy.  A mistwood tree at the extreme edge of the forest offers a way down to the road for those foolhardy or skilled enough.

Scattered feathers shift fitfully in the breeze, all that remains of some hapless bird.  The trees grow close together, blocking the faint light that might be shed by the moons.  Shelf lichens cling to tree trunks, glowing with a faint phosphorescence.

Spiky stalks jut up from clusters of ferns that thrive in the depths of the forest, catching at skin and clothing.  The shadows of night are filled with the rustle of unseen footsteps making their way through the darkness.

Fireflies flicker in the darkness beneath the forest canopy, briefly illuminating a few shy lady's slipper orchids, or reflecting against the yellow eyes of a marauding raccoon as it trundles through the shrubbery.

The forest crowds up against the base of a tall cliff to the east.  Angling out to loom over the huddled forest below, the sandstone surface looks almost impossible to climb.  High overhead, an owl circles as it hunts.

The sound of hammering and grinding is deafening in this cramped workshop.  The heat from a small forge nearly roasts you and you try to move away from it without getting in the way of an apprentice hammering out fist-sized dents in a bloody steel cuirass.  Unspiek, a squat and massive Dwarf, is filing the nicks out of a battle-axe nearly as broad as he is.  Sparks shower the floor from his rapid work and the noise, on top of the rest of the infernal din, makes your teeth ache.

Steeped in silence, the tenebrous forest seems to quietly consider the interlopers passing beneath its venerable boughs, reserving judgment for a later time.  A few clumps of stunted mountain laurel huddle in spots where the deep shadows cast by the forest canopy are thinnest and sunlight has struggled through the darkness to reach the ground.

The heavy canopy allows not even the slightest breeze to waft through the understory, so the smell of rot and mold hangs heavily in the unmoving air.  Bright crimson blood ivy crawls opportunistically up a nearby oak tree, a sanguine rivulet that contrasts sharply with the deep brown bark.  Occasional splotches of deep green marring the red leaves reveal themselves as small web-footed tree frogs.

Imbrued in darkness, the forest is thick with secrets whispered by the softly falling leaves and barely audible sounds of movement in the canopy far overhead.  Below, tangles of gnarled vines and tree roots twist through the layer of leaves, waiting to ambush the unwary traveler.

The twisted roots of the massive hardwoods look much like a clot of sleeping snakes.  When the canopy shifts enough to change the quality of light, they appear to move as though waking.  Niches between the roots harbor pools of stagnant rainwater or wet clumps of decaying leaves.

The cloak of darkness clinging to everything allows the imagination to remake the landscape in the form of its fears.  At a quick glance, a pile of broken branches to the south appears to be the decomposing carcass of a beast with splintered bones protruding at odd angles from torn flesh that are only broken boughs and rotting leaves.

In the dimness, the forest looks like a darkened cathedral with tree trunk pillars soaring upwards to arched boughs just beyond the reach of the sickly pale sunlight.  The cries of mourning doves echo eerily, sounding like a woman weeping at the altar of an empty church.
Movement rustles through the darkness above and occasionally sends down a rain of twigs and leaves.  It comes in fits and starts, as though the canopy itself were throwing restless tantrums.

A decaying alder limb lays wedged between the broad roots of the trees from which it fell.  The darkness itself seems to move across it as a stream of black-carapaced beetles makes its way along the surface of the fallen bough and into a rotted-out knothole near one end.

A ring of russet-spotted mushrooms encircles a particularly gnarled pin oak that twists its way up among straighter, thicker trees.  If the stories of faerie rings are to be believed, this oak must be well thought of among the fae to have gained the protection of their ring.  Indeed, the oak tree seems the only one of the forest's trees to revel in the darkness.

Color is a luxury afforded only by light, so it is nearly nonexistent here.  The understory is painted in deep monochromes of blacks and browns, and textures take the place of hues to vary the landscape.  Each tree, thick or thin, bent or straight, is clad in slightly different bark.  Some are smooth like taut skin, many are fine-grained like alligator hide, while others' bark is rough and squared like roof shingles.
The broken branch of a tremendous oak slopes down out of the pitch-blackness above and touches the ground.  Blood ivy and sathmoor moss crawl up the branch's sharp incline toward the forest canopy.

The burden of the forest's darkness settles down upon the shoulders of those who travel below, as if the trees wished to pass on the weighty gloom they've carried for too long.  From above comes the sound of sinister whisperings that rustle through the leafy canopy from tree to tree.

The great age of the forest is spoken from each bent limb, gnarled knothole and twisted root of the massive hardwood trees towering overhead.  Even the newer growth of young pines that feed on the rotting remains of their forbearers seems wizened in this forest.

As dark as the forest is, there are shadows even darker that dance through the trees like living things.  Mist rises from the damp ground like wisps of smoke and gives everything a ghostly, bleached-out look.

The feeble-looking saplings dotting the understory have obviously been growing slowly in the dimness for many years judging by the thickness of their bark.  They patiently wait for a larger tree or branch to fall and open a spot in the dense canopy.

The splintered bottom half of an ironwood juts from the ground like an enormous pointed fang from a blackened jaw.  Apparently the victim of a lightening strike, the tree's top half and branches have been shattered and lay in a wide circumference on the ground.

A gathering of torch rhododendrons clusters beneath a small break in the forest canopy where thin shafts of sunlight spill to the ground.  The bright red-streaked orange flowers are a celebration of life amid the dismal gloom of the understory.

Moss-clad stones and splintery, rotting sticks interrupt the otherwise soft ground.  The sound of dripping water seems to come from everywhere yet nowhere in particular.  Most of the time, the drips sound flat as if they have landed on leaves or other porous matter, but occasionally they ring with a higher pitch as they land in water.

Blood ivy cloaks the dark ironwoods with crimson filigree that shivers with the movements of tiny insects and tree frogs that live within.  The bright red leaves enable the vine to absorb more of the dim light available in the understory than their verdant counterparts.  Ironically, because it has become so adapted to the darkness, the blood ivy dies when it reaches the bright sunlit top layer of the forest canopy.

Buzzing black flies hover over what appears to be a moldy blue sack slouched against the broad base of a black oak tree.  The cloth sags limply over oddly protruding lumps and a rotted leather boot peeks out one end.

Pale fungus growing in small shelves spirals around the thick trunk of a locust tree like a tiny stairway leading upwards into shadow.  Local legends say they are made by the woodfae that protect the trees of the forest and that harm will surely come to anyone who interferes with their work.

Shadows hang from the bony limbs of the forest canopy in great dusky swaths that meet the rising mist and conceal the understory from the eyes of the outside world.  Sounds echo through the wood, reverberating and becoming so distorted that their sources are unidentifiable as anything of this plane.

The trees crowd close, their thick rope-like roots making the ground uneven and breaking through the leaf litter in spots.  Here and there, the roots frame murky holes leading down into the earth that look like open maws waiting to gobble an ill-placed foot.
The foul smell of dung rises from a rather large pile near the base of a towering hawthorn tree.  A conference of black flies begins to assemble for the occasion.

Spindly shoots adorned with only a pale leaf or two spring up from a low mound in the mulch.  Whatever lay composting beneath the leaf-strewn mound is nourishing the next generation of the forest that will compete for a space in the canopy when an elder falls.

The silence of the somber forest envelops you like the gulfs of night embrace a dying star.  Time here doesn't have the same quality as it does elsewhere, as everything seems either unmoving or at least very slow.

The muddy ground squishes sickeningly underfoot and makes traveling through the area very slow going.  Sodden earth and rotting vegetation form a sticky, spongy mat that is unwilling to easily release its hold.

The matted layer of composting materials littering the forest floor is disturbed here, as though thrown into the air during a scuffle.  Like a flag of surrender raised above the battlefield, a small scrap of dirty white cloth clings to a broken stick.  A spattering of crimson visible against the pale, freshly broken wood seems to indicate the fight did not end peacefully.
The dense forest seems thinner to the south, where color and the golden warmth of sunlight seem to live without the deadening pall of eternal darkness that envelops the Paasvadh.

Deepening shadows created by the thick leafy canopy soaring overhead foster a sense of forboding where the seeds of fear may be found.  Broad-leafed plants nourished on decaying vegetation creep along the forest floor seeking whatever dim light might reach them.  The acrid smell of rot and fetid earth hangs heavily in the air.

The ground here is sodden and squishes with each step, leaving small foot-shaped ponds of murky water.  Pale lichen-patched stones rise like islands from a dark sea of wet leaves.  A shallow pool of water to the south and east glistens faintly through the gloom.

Feather-leafed ferns cluster near a muddy frog pool.  Some broad cypress trees grow along the dirty edge of the water, their fluted bases connected to their reflections, but few other trees do.  The sparseness of trees in the pond creates a break in the canopy that allows thin shafts of sunlight to filter down into this otherwise shaded place.

Footprints captured in the muck from a recent passer-by slowly fill with muddy brown water and disappear.  They are quite large and appear almost humanoid but have a finger-like toe extending from the heel.  The tracks don't have a wide stride, but seem to belong to a heavy creature with a loping gait.

Freshly chiseled granite walls surround an area where forgers can quickly resupply.  A passageway covered by a leather flap pierces the wall to the south, and from the passage resound the clangs of an anvil chorus.  A simple wooden door leads back outside.

rooms.t: [Crossing Forging Society, Lobby and Maker's Mark Ordering]
rooms.desc: A chamber with stone walls and a lofty, vaulted ceiling links the rooms of the forge.  Its high arches help to subdue the clangor, letting it rise and echo in the space overhead.  Waves of heat and flickering reddish light from the foundries to the west strive with the scream of the grindstones to the east and the pounding din of metal on metal from the smithies to the south.

Waves of heat, blasting with an almost tangible force, roll from the flames of a brick-lined firepit.  Over the firepit, a blackened granite crucible hangs by stout chains from an oak beam high overhead.  Near the crucible's spout stand stone molds of different shapes, with a pile of fuel within easy reach.  Similar crucibles hang to the north and south.

Windows high in the vaulted ceiling ventilate the south corner of the foundry, reducing its oven-like temperature to something endurable.  The forms of a granite crucible and a pile of fuel shimmer in the heat waves rising from the orange bricks of the firepits.  Two similar crucibles hang to the north.

A chamber with stone walls and a lofty, vaulted ceiling links the rooms of the forge.  Its high arches help to subdue the clangor, letting it rise and echo in the space overhead.  Waves of heat and flickering reddish light from the foundries to the west strive with the scream of the grindstones to the east and the pounding din of metal on metal from the smithies to the south.
Masters and journeyman of the forging craft find a home in this room purchasing tools and ingredients.  Loud thumps and groaning accompany the loading and unloading of goods from storage.

The south end of the grindstone room has a few more of the big stone wheels, all in good condition.  Apprentices of Yalda inspect them daily, treating them with oil and checking for chips on the grinding face.  Other grindstones stand to the north.

Several large grindstones on wooden frames stand in the middle of the workroom.  From time to time, a Dwarven apprentice scatters sand over the floor, both for more secure footing and as a safeguard against fire from the sparks cascading off the grindstones.  A high-pitched keening and the smell of hot metal rise from those in use and from others to the south.

This area is the one most favored by the knowledgeable smiths in the guild.  Tall, narrow windows in the northern wall admit whatever breaths of air are stirring, occasionally fanning the flames beneath a granite crucible.  Like the two foundries to the south, this one has all needed implements close at hand.

Well-fitted granite brick encloses this space.  Thick oak doors exit onto the street, and a thick tarp leads deeper into the forging chambers.  To the side a burly guard limits entry through a narrow arch.  A rhythmic pounding echoes from inside the building.
Thick steel bars block access to a depot storing a multitude of resources and crafted goods.  Workers hoist larger pieces atop massive shelving using an intricate network of ropes and pulleys.

A selection of organized patterns, templates and designs for maker's marks line the walls.  A handful of prestigious crafters browse the possibilities and discuss selections with nearby attendants.  An arch leads back into the main lobby.

The ardent sound of anvil work carries from doors on either side of the hallway and echoes off the well-fitted granite floor.  A pair of masterwork weapons lines the wall as testament to the skilled work accomplished within.

A storefront backed up by boxes and cabinetry offers tools for sale.  Attendants rush back and forth helping customers and shout above the din of forging hammers smacking metal.  A stockpile of coal sits off to one side.
Bins of recently mined metal await sale next to eager attendants happily serving crafters' needs.  Several nearby crates contain additional materials for sale, including already smelted ingots.

A massive iron table decorated with pewter miniatures dominates this small office.  A soot-stained bookshelf and an oak chest with an ornate haralun lock sit nearby.  Three charts detailing the techniques for weaponsmithing, armorsmithing and blacksmithing hang from the wall.

Soot-stained stone walls rise up to a peaked roof where smoke and ash escape through several air vents.  To one side of the room a granite crucible hangs suspended over a glowing fire.  A pile of fuel lay scattered across the room from it and black footprints cover the stony ground.

Even the walls have accumulated moisture from the incredible heat rising from the forge fires.  A short distance away sits a hefty anvil with an extra long horn, a slack tub filled with water and a messy pile of fuel.  The clang of metal on metal assaults your ears as nearby forgers ply the trade.
Dents and chips line the walls as though someone once became careless with a forging hammer.  Placed diagonal to the wall is an iron anvil and a slack tub filled with water.
A large granite crucible hanging over a glowing fire rests in the center of the room.  The fire pit beneath the crucible forms a star pattern from the way in which its stones arrange.

Barely any soot remains on the walls or floor here, despite constant use.  A nice leather tarp holds a mountain of fuel, and nearby is a large anvil and forge fire that crackles and pops in the low light.

The freshly scrubbed walls of this smelting spot indicate it is the preferred place for upper class patrons.  An organized pile of fuel sits nearby, and a large granite crucible hangs from decorated leather straps above a glowing fire.

A rickety platform in the top of this huge, tall, ancient tree provides a good look-out point with a view which is unbroken for many miles.  It has given the towns folk, as they peer in many directions, fair warning of anything coming their way from the distant hills and early sightings of the barge arriving from Riverhaven.  The town below is hidden beneath the tops of shorter firs, but the view far out into Gwenalion Lake is clear for miles.

The ironwood platform has withstood the test of time.  Despite some loose and uneven planks, neither rot nor moss mars its surface.  Several scorched spots blacken the northern edges, and bent and broken arrows litter the surface.  A sinuous creeper snakes across from an adjacent cypress.
The bark on the limb is well worn, as if it has been traversed frequently.  The mosses and vines are dense here, hampering sight, though an overgrown platform is visible further down the limb.

The sad state of the cypress is even more apparent up close.  The northern side of the trunk is marred by deep burns that have not yet healed.  The once well-proportioned tree is crouched over, as if protecting its remaining, life-giving limb.  Vines and mosses have slowly begun to cover the wounded cypress, taking advantage of its weakened state.

Cobblestones line this small square, which is dominated by the large, stone building housing the Mer'Kresh Crafting Society.  A parade of sturdy wagons going in and out of the nearby alley is a common sight as artisans haul their hand-made goods off for sale at the local markets.  Wooden benches line the edge of the canal, offering a scenic spot for workers to rest and enjoy some fresh air.

A mule brays in surprise as you enter his domain, and several chickens flap their wings, annoyed at the intrusion.  Mounds of hay and nesting shelves provide sleeping places for the occupants.  A deep ditch separates the byre from the living area to the south, and a narrow wooden ramp provides access.

Sazu, the Gor'Tog dyer, works industriously at a table, pounding dried flowers into a fine powder.  She tosses the colorful powder into a black iron kettle, and stirs the liquid within.  Dozens of wicker baskets hang from the ceiling, along with bunches of the drying flowers.  The cottage windows are shuttered tightly against the night air.  A dye menu chart is nailed next to a ladder which appears to lead to a room overhead.
A simple straw pallet is the only furnishing here, but the loft has been festively decorated with bunches of lavender heather in earthenware pots and colorfully dyed garments hanging from wall pegs.

Plush seats lined up in rows face a hardwood stage raised four feet from the ground.  Red velvet curtains draped from the high vaulted ceiling cover the walls.  The acoustics create a warm echo which lends an air of nobility to the place.  A podium in the corner hints that the hall must be used for formal meetings as well as performances.

Though straight and sturdy, the trees lean with the sharp downward pitch of the land, each limb on their northern sides farther from the ground than those on their southern sides.  From those heights, a shower of needles, leaves and limbs falls, set into a whirling plunge of motion with every buffet of wind.  The debris races down the hillside, lost from sight as its descent takes it beneath the interposing branches of the valley below.

Covering the angled banks of the sloped ground, a lush beard of grass thickens the humps of the trail.  As real whiskers might hide an unsavory profile, so does the hefty growth in this wood disguise the rough, rocky surface of the land.  The trees have little problem with the stone-ridden ground, growing tall and strong, surely making for a different scale of metaphorical beard to viewers on the other hills and mountains.

Riddled with plant life as the trail may be, a hazy grey peak in the Undogoz mountains manages to rise into view and out of the trees' concealment.  Though distant, the glimpses of sheer cliffs and bare stone humble any comparison of the slanting footpath winding in these hills.  Folly it would be to travel upon those dangerous crags, and the thought makes the steep, northern descent of this land quite manageable in contrast.

A wide selection of vegetation clusters at the base of every tree in the forest, ranging from ferns and flowers to ivy and vines.  The ash enriched soil at the foot of the Undogoz chain is most likely responsible for the rampant growth, yet the view of the nearest slope through the trees reveals a relatively barren surface.  Sheltered from the high cliff's strong winds, the wooded path has become a botanist's dream.

Surrounded by a cul-de-sac of living greenery, thick grass blades wave in unison under the brisk mountain zephyrs.  Several types of brightly colored wildflower nestle in the grass, seen only when an appropriate breeze shoves the interposing blades out of the way.  The gentle rustling is constant, but rises and falls in tempo with nature, its conductor.

The building is constructed of stone, mined locally, to withstand years of abuse from the salty air that blows in off the ocean.  Tall, fluted columns stand near each corner of the room, helping to support the raised dome ceiling decoratively covered in silver leaf.  Tiny lights hidden within the roof's architecture reflect off the metallic surface to highlight an intricate, mosaic map of M'Riss inlaid into the tile floor.  A pair of crossed hammers adorns the top of an archway leading to the Forging Society.

Across the room from an archway leading to the main edifice are a pair of wooden benches, which are the only furniture provided for the customer's comfort.  Periodically, custodians hired to keep the area tidy wander through, occasionally muttering as they sweep the stone floor clean of all the grime people drag in with them when they leave the foundry.  On one wall, an artist has painted a portrait of the Undogoz Forge as a memorial to the now closed building where many Rissans learned their craft.  Insulating the space from the searing heat of the smithy is a heavy oak door, covered on each side with a sheet of steel for added protection.

A long, cypress counter serves as a partition between the bookstore and a much smaller office area, making it easy for Master Smith Kapric, who runs the facility, to keep an eye on customers when they enter and offer assistance when necessary.  Tall racks are filled with sample books for the shopper who prefers to peruse the merchandise.

Despite the building's thick, rock walls, the faint sound of metal hitting metal can sometimes be heard, its repetitive pattern becoming almost lyrical.  Clerks keep busy checking to make sure the displays of tools and supplies for sale are filled, often rushing to the backroom to load up on any stock that is missing.

Crude, wooden pallets stacked with recently mined ore create cramped aisles throughout the room, giving customers a chance to inspect the selection before making their purchase.  Off in the corner, several crates contain additional materials for sale, including already smelted ingots.

White paint coating the stone block walls serves as a neutral canvas for the sketches of sample designs aimed at helping potential customers decide on what aspects they desire in their maker's marks.  Tools, templates and patterns hang above a small work area where artisans construct the purchased orders promptly as they come in.  Heat emanates from cracks around a leather curtain leading to the foundry.

Once servicing the Undogoz Forge, select pieces of equipment, which still remain in good working condition, have found a new home here as part of the city's attempts to keep costs down.  In the room's center, a constant fire burns in the circular firepit with a small pile of fuel by its side, waiting to be added to increase the flames to a blazing inferno.  The clang of metal against metal drifts over from the smithy to the west and a heavy, oak door leads to the entry hall of the society.

Constant waves of scalding heat flow through the smithy, set into motion by the sizzling fires and red-hot metals being worked.  Even sounds seem warped and muffled, but somehow the echo of clanging tools and crackling of fiery sparks manage to cut through the thick air.  Nothing is spared the attentions of the temperature and dust, and both stone and metal tools wear the scars that the environment has delivered.

A combination of sweat and molten steel intertwine to permeate the air with a slightly acrid, sour smell that varies in intensity depending on the time of day.  Suspended by heavy chains secured to a blackened wooden beam is a huge granite crucible.  Piled high in the corner of the room is a large pile of crushed coal, waiting for the next forger to feed it to the fire.

The floor bears the burns and scars from regular sprays of stray sparks.  Should only the stone surface be an ocean, the equipment scattered about would make a parody of an armada of ships, possibly in mockery of the failed attempts of the Dragon Priest Empire to subdue Mer'Kresh.  In reality, though, the only subduing going on is that of iron and steel beneath a determined worker's tools.

Emanating from the fire, patchy clouds of soot cover the ceiling and form streaks down the walls like black rain during a tropical storm.  Ashy dust fills the air, spiraling up in the heat as it blows off a pile of fuel.  A rhythmic hammering sound drifts over from the smithy to the west, followed by an occasional curse indicating things probably didn't go the way the forger desired.

An oversized, glowing forge dominates the center of the stone floor, banishing all other equipment to the outlying corners of the room.  Nicknamed -- The Beast -- it's constantly consuming the red-hot coals in its belly and demanding more fuel from the pile, much like a ravenous animal.  From the smell of burning flesh lingering in the room, many craftsmen have felt its fiery bite.

Already dark by its nature, the stone walls of the forge are blackened further by soot, ash and dust kicked up by the constant stream of workmen the forge serves on a daily basis.  Custodians hired by the city wander in and out checking the large waste bucket, making sure the discarded pieces of metal are cleaned up off the floor and keeping the foundry as clean of trash as possible.

Despite being swept on a regular basis by diligent custodians, metal shavings and bits of broken steel litter the floor, creating a sparkling effect when lit by the flames of the forge's roaring fire.  The smell of burning coal and heated metal fight for dominance here, indicating the amount of work this room normally sees.

Along the top of one wall, a row of exhaust vents siphon off some of the oppressive heat generated by the fire in an attempt to make the room's temperature more comfortable for forgers busy at their craft.  An ingot cutter salvaged from the Undogoz Forge sits near a large pile of fuel and a leather curtain leads to the Maker's Mark shop.

The back wall of the smithy area is covered with a grimy grey and red dust from the constant attention of the grindstone.  Several small windows along the top of the wall vent some of the choking dust and heat from the forge, but solid steel grates prevent anything larger than a gauntlet from passing through and into the canal beyond.

The heady scent of soil and plant life fills the air, only to be whisked temporarily away with each swirling breeze.  As the wind blows, ferns nod and branches sway, as if to shoo the thick smells of earth.  Losing leaves and needles with the motion, the waving of the plants reaches a crescendo before stillness descends on the area, and the scenario repeats.

Twinkling sounds from a cowrie shell door chime hung above the entrance welcome visitors to this bustling shop.  Display shelves lining a large window are packed with an assortment of curious bottles, jars, and boxes containing healing remedies collected from several provinces that have been arranged between a collection of potted plants.  Small bundles of exotic herbs hang from the ceiling, thickening the air with their earthy perfume while partially concealing a set of stairs leading to the attic.

Faded whitewashed walls, painted with images of healing regents, serve as advertising for some of the items sold here.  An earthy, herbal scent wafts through the air, growing stronger near an iron cauldron hung above a copper brazier, which slowly simmers with one of Trintah's latest experiments.  Flashes of color dash around the room like elusive pixies as light from bronze lanterns bounces off strings of colored sea glass, collected from local beaches and hung to create a decorative beaded curtain.

Offered by the owner, this cozy salon may be a ploy to keep people spending coins in her shop.  The smell of freshly baked bread mingled with medicinal liquors wafts from a sideboard against the wall, masking the odd scent permeating the building while encouraging customers to linger and socialize.  Groupings of small tables, covered in colorful linens and surrounded by comfortable chairs, are strategically placed about the room to draw attention to a dolphin triskele mosaic set into the tiled floor.

Neat as a pin, Scupper's Furrier Shop still bears the disquieting scent of uncured hides and pelts.  An attempt has been made to mask it, not quite successfully, with large bowls of potpourri placed here and there.  Scupper busies himself about the place, moving stock from one pile to another.

The bank lobby has been roofed over and is open to customers, although the walls still show some scorching where the painters have not yet finished.  Scaffolding and building supplies lie here and there.  The staircase to the second floor, uncarpeted as yet, has been repaired and the polished wooden handrail replaced.

Quite out of place considering the environment, a broken stone arch rises from the weeds in the center of the path.  Missing a Gor'Tog sized chunk from its keystone down, the arch looks liable to fall over under the slightest provocation.  This may prove deceptive, however, as the steady winds and heavy growth of vines across its surface are seemingly unable to affect its position.

Stately guardians, two potted fiddlehead ferns of enormous size flank the staircase leading to the lobby below.  Obviously, some extraordinary measures were taken to promote the growth of these two decorations, be it magic or alchemical, perhaps for the purpose of drawing attention from the doors beyond.  An ash door peeks out from the behind the fern to the north and down the hall towards its ornate looking opposite.  The hall itself opens to a domed courtyard filled with a multitude of plants.

The timid beige hues of the walls peek out from behind the brilliant splash of the red and green foliage of the potted plants.  Pushed against one of the polished stone walls is a wooden bench padded with red velvet.  The indentations in the seat confirm that many a trader and bank employee have rested here, stopping to gaze upwards at the soft glow of daylight from the domed ceiling above.

Appearing to be little more than an afterthought in the construction of the bank, the coin exchanger's room is manned by a stooped, elderly Human.  He constantly kneads something at his chest as he sits behind the safety of the steel bars that seperate him from his customers.  The black metal and ironwood craftwork of the booth is in direct opposition to the softer hues and flowing architecture of the beige stonework elsewhere in the bank.

A dazzling array of multicolored plants with large, floppy leaves decorates every niche and recess of the walls.  Most of the plants have been set into heavy looking ceramic pots and all show signs of good maintenance.  A deep red carpet stretches across the floor, marking pathways through the flora and along the gently inclined stairs leading upwards.

A pretty Elf sits behind the teller's window, dabbing occasionally at the rose petal makeup daintly applied to her cheeks.  Every so often she looks towards the exit and past the velvet ropes that file customers to her booth and sighs.  A soft light flows in from the courtyard outside, as well as from the skylight above, keeping the area cheerfully lit for the benefit of easy transactions.

There is a definitive lack of the larger indoor plants that make up the decor in other parts of the bank's courtyard.  Where they might have been, large statues of crouching gargoyles sit.  Despite the tell-tale worn spots in the center of the red carpet, little business takes place here beneath the eyes of the grotesque stone forms.

Unadorned tapestries hang from a handful of thick bronze wall mounts encircling the room, doing little but adding to the already present gloom.  The tapestries have been arranged in such a way that they emphasize the solid oak table set centrally.  Without a skylight or window to shed any illumination upon the table, items upon it take on a similar murky quality.
Soft mud underfoot, not to mention the occasional ankle-deep pool, shows that the river is lower than usual.  But from the sound of flowing water, the Altanen is still wide and powerful.

rooms.desc: A strip of muddy bank lies between the river and the face of the cliff to the east.  A narrow crevice splits the rock face at a steep angle, carrying a trickle of water down the mountainside.
The water in the Altanen ripples in the current and laps at the bank underfoot.  Frogs thrum a deep bass accompaniment to the chuckle of the river.
A shoulder of the cliff looms up to the north as the mudbank comes to an end.  The sound of the river flowing past echoes from the near-vertical wall close at hand.
Insects drone in the dark, prey to the bat or night-flying bird whose passage is revealed by the beat of a wing.  The soft splashes in the river to the east suggest that the fish are feeding too.

Spray from the obstructed river casts a damp smell over the island.  The churning rapids to the west drown out all sound of movement through the high grasses that have sprung up to cover the island's muddy surface.
The roar of the rapids and the wall of mist above it lend a strange boundary to the west.  The buzz of a mosquito or the croak of a frog punctuates the background noise.
It's hard to see much more than the clumps of grass, like huddled figures in the darkness.  The splash of the rapids to the west masks all sounds.

A faint smell of decaying vegetation -- or perhaps a fish stranded when the waters dropped -- touches the air.  Swarms of insects have found a home on the island, although what they feed on is a puzzle, unless it's each other, or maybe whatever makes that snuffling sound heard now and then.
