The bustling main hallway of the large building provides a place for people to gather and discuss new ideas with one another.  Stone benches topped with soft cushions offer moderately comfortable seating for those who wish to rest their weary bones.  On either side of the benches stand intricate pedestals which bear carved marble vases filled with floral bouquets.

An elaborate gold birdcage rests on a large stand, placed next to a makeshift desk in the center of the room.  Along the far wall, a workbench bearing a variety of gadgets and tools display what Paarupensteen treasures most in life.  Upon the wall above the workbench hangs a picture of a plump Halfling woman next to an equally so Halfling man.

Marbled flooring surrounded by white walls, which are accented with brass lanterns, span the length of the hall.  Not as many crafters walk through this end of the building, though echoes of pounding hammers permeate the hallway.  A carved sign bearing workshop rules hangs from the wall before three doors.

Bustling back and forth from the shop's backroom, harried workers carry goods that are either in need of repair or have been completed.  Behind a long counter, which spans nearly the width of the room, stands the shop's repairwoman.  Upon the wall behind her are rows of shelves which hold repaired goods waiting for their owner to retrieve them.

Like most of the Society Hall, the shop is neat and clean.  Attendants bustle around with brooms and rags cleaning the marbled floors and smooth stone walls.  Behind the counter are crates of supplies to restock the tables and countertops so that any crafter in need of a specific tool does not go without.  Sheer black curtains upon a small oval window shield the shop from prying eyes outside.

Solid white stone walls encompass the marbled flooring of the shop.  A large double door guarded by two Gor'Togs allows workers to travel between the store and the outside of the building where they bring in new shipments or prepare to be transferred to one of the workshops.  Several raised platforms upon the floor bear heavy blocks of stone which are waiting to be crafted into furniture or unique decorations for the home.

Ill-fitted boulders jut at odd angles from the damp granite walls.  Even the ceiling looks a bit ramshackle here, as though the entry-way were built with speed more than safety in mind.  A slight draft blows from deep inside the building and carries a mixture of odd smells with it.

Tall oak supply crates flank an extended counter displaying various alchemical tools for sale.  A pair of robed individuals rush about helping customers restock.  You notice the overwhelming combination of smells is somewhat reduced here.

A haze of dust permeates the air and casts a glow about the wall torches.  A large bookshelf rests against the back wall and a robed figure scurries up and down a ladder to sell tomes and recipes to interested patrons.

A pungent odor combines with the powder-filled air to make breathing here more difficult.  Racks of spices, herbs, plants and other materials line the walls as attendants scurry about helping customers.  Pewter trays in each corner hold burning incense sticks.  Despite the size and large amount of smoke wafting from each stick, it is nearly impossible to detect even a hint of their scent.

Cut into the granite of the far wall is a shelf containing an elaborate collection of alchemical equipment.  The assortment overshadows the Society Master's desk, a simple piece of oak furniture pushed unceremoniously against the wall.

Grey marble walls give way to alabaster columns framing an open supply depot.  The northern hallway bears a sign indicating it leads to workshops, and a well-used road meanders out to the east.  Crisscrossing wagon ruts in the dirt remain from trips to supply the guild with stone and wood supplies.

Expertly fitted grey marble slabs frame the lower half of the shop's alabaster walls.  A sliver of light shines through a pair of squat windows bordered by well-polished oak molding and fitted with iron bars styled to resemble vines of ivy.  This area sells a variety of supplies to eager crafters and offers some shelter from the loud noises of productivity emanating from the east.

A small forge in the corner of this room basks everything in its warmth.  Adjacent to it, a long counter sits cluttered with numerous tools and devices for repairing things.  Bundles of repaired goods rest against the far wall waiting for pickup.
A long hallway cut from smoky alabaster echoes with all sorts of clinks and clanks.  Doors leading to solitary workshops line the walls, manned by attendants waiting to deliver on deed orders.

Mechanical components of all shapes and sizes lay scattered about the polished marble floor.  A large workbench littered with diagrams sits under a pair of shelves cluttered with widgets and gears.  The office's rear contains a row of overflowing bookcases lacking any semblance of organization.

Within the folds of the mossy shrouds the air is deathly still.  Sheets of moss compete with tangled vines for purchase on the steady limbs of the cypress.  Despite the clinging companions, the great tree seems unhindered in its growth.  It stands straight and proud, keeping endless vigil over the things that dwell in the bog.

A dark grey moss hangs from the branches above, making footing treacherous and soaking the traveler who pushes through its clinging, soggy curtains.  Water drips down with a recurring 'plop' that adds to the cacophony of sounds.  A warm glow from the east hints at a drier perch.  A weather-worn rope, nearly overgrown by the mosses, hangs from a branch higher up.

Above, the sun shines brightly though a hole in the canopy, and the moss is dry and almost brittle.  A dry branch snaps underfoot, and silence fills the air.  For a few moments not even the wind dares stir.  Slowly the chatter and whistles of birds return.  A thin vine dangles here, reaching over from a stooping, worn-out cypress.

Midway up the tree, big vines wind about the mighty cypress like ropes around a mast.  Two large limbs branch out like strong arms spread in welcome to the forest before them.  The marsh below is hidden by a sea of green leaves and fronds waving and glistening in the sunlight.

The branch threads its way through a nightmare of green strands, almost like soft, searching tentacles.  While they offer no real resistance to movement, their leaves block the view of the way ahead.  They wave in every breeze, threatening to distract and fray nerves already burdened with constant watchfulness.

Many of the creepers that hamper the view and confound the step trail down to the ground or are so caught in branches that they might almost be a web for a monstrous spider.  But something so menacing could hardly be possible.  One vine looks almost designed for swinging to a nearby willow.

The wide limb is all but invisible, completely wrapped in layer upon layer of twisting creepers.  Young green tendrils wreath around it, groping for a hold on the limb.  Strong vines cascade from above, reaching from tree to tree.  One of the larger vines nearby disappears into a big oak tree to the north.

Peat and muck cake the limb, and the smell of decaying vegetation is thick.  A small clump of bog grass has taken root in the crook of the branch, a dwarfed flowering weed growing in its midst.  A single yellow blossom leans toward the few beams of sunlight that make their way through the upper canopy.  It rocks back and forth in a gentle dance with the breeze.

Sunlight filters down through the canopy above, dappling with light and shadow a wide limb littered with twigs and leaves.  A small nest of sticks and moss nestles deep in a nearby crook.  Vines hang from above, draping from branch to branch in graceful, snakelike curves, some reaching to a neighboring cypress.

This room, located just off the main cavern, serves as a junction for the different locations within the hospital.  In addition to serving as the workplace for the resident healer Shalvarn, whose office is located through a small door to the west, the infirmary allows other healers to stop by and help with the demand for healing.

Located just off the entrance hall, this room allows members of the community a quiet space to sit and relax while waiting to be seen by Shalvarn.  Several chairs lie scattered about the room in small groups, enabling friends to have a quiet chat.

Small alcoves set into each of the four walls hold short canvas cots to raise the patients off the cold stone.  The center of the room is mostly empty save for several large pillows piled there.  A white cabinet rests against the north wall between two of the bays.

This small alcove off the main room is the work area of the resident healer of Hibarnhvidar.  Although many adventurers utilize the services of the primary Empaths' guild, Shalvard set up this small hospital to service those who do not desire to seek help from the guild.

The ornate entrance arch gives way to a long hall, filled with accountants and bookkeepers.  Opposing the arch, two tunnels lead deeper into the bank to the foreign exchange and teller windows.  Several Dwarven employees wander about, conversing with colleagues seated at the desks.

Two Dwarven guards stand at the entrance to the tunnel leading back to the bank foyer, insuring the safety and security of deposited funds.  Several alcoves are available in the cavern walls to allow for privacy as one converses with the tellers on the other side of the stone counters.

A small opening sits embedded in the wall opposite the tunnel to the bank foyer.  This part of the cavern claims only a narrow garbage trough and the exchange window as adornment.  A short Dwarven banker sits behind the metal grille, waiting to exchange patron's money into other currencies.

The smell of curing hides clings to the air, cloying the nostrils with a heavy unpleasant smell of decayed animal flesh.  A thick cord draped with various furs extends from one end of the room to the other, acting as a makeshift curtain that leads to the back room.  The shop owner Vandorf tends to his furs, stopping every so often to acknowledge customers that walk in to do business.

A glaes arch divides the public forge from the main cavern.  Owned by Juln, a master smith of Hibarnhvidar, the area resounds with the dull roar of the furnaces, the screech of metal against grindstones and the hiss of hot metal being quenched beyond the hatch in the south wall.  At the entry, tables and counters groan beneath the weight of books for both casual and master smiths.

Granite walls and arches support and decorate this hallowed hall of metalworking.  The crackle of fire from the forges and smithies and the sharp hiss of grinding metal echo around the area in a symphony for the senses.  A small hatch lined with soot leads back towards the main cavern and storeroom, and racks containing tools for sale line the walls.  The other tunnels lead to destinations most suited to a smith.

More suited to fine detail work than mass production, this room does not contain all the amenities the larger foundries possess.  However, it is much quieter, enabling smiths to concentrate on the projects at hand.

The fire in the small forge, primarily used to reheat weapons or to prepare smaller items, burns merrily in the south wall.  A large anvil stands ready for smiths to pick up the hammer and set to work.

The workbench, forge and anvil take up the entire west wall of this room, though there is plenty of room to walk around.  Smells of burning coal and warm metal vie for supremacy here, indicating the amount of work this room normally sees.

Two large counters bracket the forge and anvil located in the southeastern corner of this room.  An irregular layer of soot films the walls and counters near the forge and the smell of burning flesh lingers in the room.
A small alcove to one side of the room contains tables displaying tools for sale.  Several vents in the ceiling gently pull warm air from the foundries nearby.

Maker's mark attendants wait in a small alcove above which hangs a variety of tools.  Prestigious crafters mill about and eagerly discuss trade skills with each other.  An old grindstone sits off to one side.
Fashioned similarly to the rest of the forge, this room offers additional space for the storage and sale of crafting supplies.  Large wooden pallets display materials that can be ordered at any time.

The forging area feels warmer than most places in Hibarnhvidar due to a large fire kept constantly burning in the basement of the forge.  Heat from the blaze below bleeds up into a smaller standby fire in the room, enabling a well-trained smith to work with even the most difficult of metals.  A small pile of fuel sits by, waiting to be added to the fire.

A vent high in the ceiling helps to alleviate some of the heat circulating in this room.  A hearth has been set up against one wall, its fire fed from the blazes below, allowing work to proceed at all hours of the day.  A pile of fuel has been shoveled against the wall, allowing a smith to easily stoke the fire up to a raging inferno.
Various forging accoutrements line the walls, encircling the fire located in the center of the room.  Blasts of heat from below constantly surge through the room.

The forge fire takes up the entire northwest wall -- the roar of the blaze drowns out all but the strongest of noises.  A small access port in the center of the wall allows a smith to use the heat within for his own purposes.  On the opposite side of the room a pile of fuel waits to be used.

Sized like an after thought, this room has just enough space for the gemsmith to conduct her business.  Whether to give this area the illusion of space, or to provide something for Rasiya to rest her eyes on, the stone walls have been sculpted with flowers representative of the province.

The stairway pauses more than midway up the wall at a small landing before continuing up to the battlements.  Each step has a smooth valley worn from ages of boot traffic and since there is no railing that accompanies the stairway, the valleys are positioned closer to the safety of the wall.  Smoke twists from the chimney of a small lean-to below.

Each merlon and crenel of the parapet is the width of two men, offering ample protection to archers.  The crenellations cast alternating pools of colored light and shadow across the wall walk as the moons perform their celestial dance.  A torch flickers nearby.

A brass chandelier and matching wall sconces illuminate walls of white plaster and pale oak wainscot in this small, handsome shop.  A note and a brace of candles rest on a simple table next to some chairs for customers.

Stretching the length of the great wall, the battlements allow many men to stand along the top to keep the watch and defend when needed.  Here, the granite wall meets the sheer rock face of the canyon wall with cuts so precise there is neither need for mortar nor room enough for a scrap of paper to be slid in the seam.  A torch flickers nearby.

The stairway pauses more than midway up the wall at a small landing before continuing up to the battlements.  Each step has a smooth valley worn into the top from ages of boot traffic.  Since there is no railing that accompanies the stairway, the valleys are positioned closer to the safety of the wall.  At the foot of the stair is a pale muslin tent.
The porous stone is worn by the ages, yet dark brown stains mar the parapets and wall walk.  They stubbornly defy the weather and remain as silent monuments to the fallen who refuse to be forgotten.
The battlements have resisted the ages, their defiance against crumbling to the elements as strong as the will of men to defend them against the foe.  Torches flicker on the wall nearby.

A large section of the parapet has been rebuilt with coarse uncut fieldstone and pebbly mortar.  Though a much more recent addition to the wall, the materials used in the repair have weathered worse than the original granite beneath it and patches of moss have found purchase in the disintegrating fill.

Loose boards of white-washed wood and a collection of dingy tapestries that reek of dust and mold compose this small, windowless hovel.  Oddly, there is little detectable tell-tale scent of blood, although the walls are splashed liberally with bright red splotches.  A single oil lamp hangs overhead, and the only other light source is the open door leading out.

This eastern chamber of the smithy is equipped like the others, with a forge and anvil for heating and tempering the castings from the foundry.  From time to time, the din of hammers pounding on the heated blanks rings out from the anvils in the other rooms.

An iron anvil is mounted on a thick oaken stump in the center of the chamber.  Against the wall behind it is the forge, stoked by Yalda's apprentices, where the sword- or shield-to-be is brought to a red-hot glow before being hammered into shape.

These small rooms at the back of Yalda's establishment are the shrines of the smiths, housing the furnaces where the glowing metal is heated, tempered, and beaten into shape.  Just a step away from the forge is an iron anvil, bolted to a charred but solid wooden support.

The faint outline of your image is blurred on the sheen of the highly polished mahogany walls.  Short red carpeting, maintained in pristine condition, cushions the hardwood floors.  Hand-carved cherrywood cuts horizontally across the paneling halfway from the ceiling in a decorative trim.

The reception desk is stacked with letters, invoices, purchase requests, and a general stream of bizarre visitors, yet still maintains a sense of orderliness, due mainly to the young Prydaen man behind it.  He seems the sort who can keep control of even the most stressful of situations without blinking.

The faint outline of your image is blurred on the sheen of the highly polished mahogany walls.  Short red carpeting, maintained in pristine condition, cushions the hardwood floors.  Hand-carved cherrywood cuts horizontally across the paneling halfway from the ceiling in a decorative trim.

This is the nerve center of the Traders' Guild, a long narrow hall plunged into a state of utter chaos.  While harried clerks run to and fro collecting paperwork to assist the guild's members, others are busily calculating the ever-fluctuating exchange rates of nearby towns.  As your senses assimilate the free-flying information, you begin to notice a kind of method to this room's insatiable madness.

A sense of chaos mingled with urgency pervades the scene before you.  Harried stock clerks rush about, gathering orders and directing sweating laborers in assembling the contents of endless caravans.  The cavernous room echoes with grunts and banging and voices all shouting conflicting commands, each trying to drown the other out to be heard first.  Impatient traders try to catch the fleeting attention of the clerks and give vent to a varied array of oaths in many tongues when ignored.

This room serves as a social hub for the cherished members of the guild to gather and share their adventures and exploits with one another.  Highly polished mahogany walls open up to a large bay window overlooking the River Oxenwaithe.  The guild staff keeps fresh treats available on the serving cart.

Long imported silk drapes extend from ceiling to floor and are gathered on either side of a large area window that spans several paces in length.  From this vantage point the bank, gates and various guilds and merchants can be seen throughout Crossing.  An exceptional hand-spun silk carpet nearly covers the entire floor.  Positioned directly opposite the guildleader's desk is a large map of the province mounted high up on the wall.

The local traders guild runs its supply out of this dingy excuse for a stable.  Moldy hay is piled in the corners, while the pitiful sounds of cramped animals calls up from the stalls.  Perched on the latest shipment of flour is a greasy-looking boy who can only be the clerk.

Stopping the trees abruptly, a tall stone wall rises above the forest canopy.  Set into the wall's outward face is a small iron gate, and the courtyard of a monastery can be seen through it.  Far too small to be a main entrance, it appears to be a back way into the grounds and is a little rusted from years of weathering.

The path here splits in two different directions, each one branching off sharply.  Set at the center of the junction is a large sana'ati tree, much taller than any of the others in the forest.  Small white mushrooms dot the dirt around the tree's roots, although the area is otherwise quite clear of debris or undergrowth.

The forest path sharply ends here at a fallen tree trunk, although the trail looks like it once continued further.  Shining clubmoss covers the ground and some of the trees, and the area feels somewhat damp.  Tangles of vine, shrubs and other undergrowth cover the felled trunk and the space around it, making passage completely impossible.

A crumbled piece of white marble is set in a wide spot between two half-dead trees, the chunk of stone looking to be the broken remnants of a monument or statue.  No longer recognizable at all, the marble's surface is covered in the forest's climbing vines, making it their home.  Overhead, the branches are quite thick, the apple trees flourishing in this area.

Apple trees grow tall in this part of the forest, spread out between the maple and occasionally a willow tree.  Large knotholes in several of them appear to house nests for forest creatures, although many seem to have gone unused for quite some time.  Barely visible through the thick trees to the east is a small pond.

Large huckleberry shrubs somewhat obscure the beginning of this small trail, which winds its way between several tall maple and poplar trees.  Their branches tangle together overhead, forming a dense canopy.  In contrast, the forest floor is sparsely covered, with only a few small wildflowers poking through the cover of decaying leaves.

Within the crevice is a green oasis, hidden below the barren plains above you.  Water trickles from a spring in the gully's face, collecting in a series of crystal pools in the rock.  Reeds and a few small trees grow up around the water's edge and rustle in the cool moist breeze.  An old firepit built in the shade of the overhanging granite walls shows that you are not the first to seek shelter in this small paradise.

The narrow cobblestone path continues east and west, looking as if its surface was washed recently.  Visible through a wrought iron fence is a large covered greenhouse, rows of ripening grapes and other plants visible within.  A small wooden gate leads into the carefully crafted structure, and next to it sits a large washtub full of monk's clothes.

A tall tower stands at the end of the cobblestone path, made from the same stone as the other buildings dotting the grounds of the complex.  With a sturdy iron door that looks solidly locked, the structure's function seems to be a mystery, though the occasional window is visible a few stories up.  Lush vineyards can be seen through the wrought iron fence to the north, growing in neat rows on white trellises.

A well-kept cobblestone path runs through the center of a large green lawn, which appears to be very freshly cut.  Although a tall iron fence runs parallel to the pathway and cuts off passage, it's still easy to see several buildings through it, each of them made of mortared stone.  Standing next to the walkway is a single lamppost, also made of cast iron.

The expansive lawn is meticulously kept free of any weeds, creating a completely uniform sea of green on either side of the cobblestone path.  The view through a wrought iron fence shows several buildings, and each one appears to be set aside for a specific purpose.  Directly to the north is a modestly sized chapel, its stained glass windows and wooden doors a bit marred by the accumulation of dust and dirt.

The cobblestone pathway passes between two buildings, turning the space briefly into an alleyway.  Each structure is several stories tall, although it's hard to judge exactly because of the flat roofing.  Though the southern building has a small window facing the alley, the interior is fully obscured by heavy grey curtains.  A small wooden door leads into the northern building, apparently a side entrance.

The cobblestone pathway stops at a tall stone fence, which seems to be more for appearance than to keep out intruders.  A sign hangs above the entrance, marking it as the monastery's private cemetery.  Growing near the entrance is a small poplar tree, looking like it's not much older than a sapling.

The stone walls contrast somewhat with the polished white marble floor, which has a narrow strip of dark red carpeting running down the center.  Although careful work has gone into detailing and carving the architecture, the walls are completely bare and seem almost sterile.  Set into the eastern wall is a steepled window featuring plain glass in an iron frame, which looks out into a small graveyard.

Large portions of the hallway's walls are very smooth, divided by columns that break up the pattern of the flagstone.  Though these sections are almost completely bare, flecks of paint at the very edges imply that images once decorated the walls but have long since been scrubbed away.  Gaethzen orbs hang from the ceiling high above, illuminating the narrow hall in a somewhat dim light.

The hallway here bends slightly, a single raised step in the center of the floor.  Though the walls are made of bare mortar stone, elaborate borderwork near the ceiling and floor give it just a touch of elegance.  Placed upon a white stone pedestal at the slight corner is a small sword of polished silver, resting atop a dark red pillow.

A single raised step in the center of the hallway marks a slight bend in the passage.  Gold leaf adorns the top and bottom borders of the rough stone walls, which are spaced every so often with carved marble columns.  Securely bolted to the northern wall is a large lead sheet, which looks somewhat scuffed in various places.

Torches are set at periodic intervals on each wall of this wide passageway, flickering and sending tongues of orange light to play over the grey stone.  Crafted from polished steel, a small medallion hangs around the base of one of dark iron sconces.  The hallway ends to the east at an elegantly arched door, its surface covered with ornate carvings.

Very narrow and rather claustrophobic, the interior of this hallway is quite plain and unadorned, the walls crafted from mortared stones.  Thick red carpeting covers the entire floor, perhaps placed to mute the sound of footsteps.  The only light in the area is somewhat dim torchlight, filtering in from the passage to the north.

The cramped, curving hallway is difficult to see down, its southern end washed out by torchlight.  A narrow strip of red carpeting runs down the center of the stone floor, both kept very clean.  Twin torches burn on the walls, their red and orange light flickering and playing off the mortared stone.

Though the rest of the hallway is almost sterile in appearance, the northern wall opens completely out into a balcony, providing a view just over the treetops.  The nighttime sky is clearly visible, extending over the forest like a dark blanket.  Dim torches line the railing, burning with an orange glow.

Brightly burning torches set on the southern wall nearly obscure the view from a balcony to the north.  The sky appears pitch black, and the trees below look like little more than the vague outline of shadows.  A waist-high stone railing blocks off the balcony, preventing any serious falls.

Both walls are very smooth and completely bare, contrasting sharply with the arching ceiling overhead and its elaborate design.  A deep red carpet runs down the center of the marble floor, muting footsteps and adding just a hint of warmth to the room.  Blazing torches frame both sides of an ornately carved wooden door set in the northern wall.

Standing in the circular end of the hallway is an elegant statue crafted from white marble which depicts a woman in a long robe.  Coated in elegant gold leaf, the alcove's interior is designed to reflect a shower of light onto the figure, giving it a surreal feeling.  A small window on the southern wall looks out onto the monastery grounds.

Row upon row of volumes and tomes line several darkly stained cedar shelves, taking up the entire eastern wall of the room.  A dark mahogany desk stands in the center of the room, a large and comfortable-looking chair behind it.  Two narrow strips of deep red carpeting run along each side of the desk, simply accenting the black marble floor.
A set of rolling green hills rise up to the west, gradually flattening out into grasslands to the east.  A barricade blocks off further passage toward the east along the Journalai Route.

The old, abandoned Journalai Route runs through the rolling hills outside of the village of Kaerna like a winding brownish-green ribbon someone dropped and forgot.  A few stones that might have been road markers still remain, cracked and weathered and lying, forsaken, to one side of the road.

The Route continues to the east and west, while to the north you notice a dirt path that looks to have been tread by the passage of feet, not the passage of wagons.  A trickling stream passes over the road, leaving mud and muck in its wake as it vanishes into the grasses of the surrounding hillside.

The silence here would be peaceful, if it weren't so intrusive.  No birdsong, no movement of wildlife, just an empty, all-encompassing stillness, as if the green, wild hills that rise about you were holding their breath.
From here, the top of one of the tallest hills, you can see the lay of the land, rising and falling before and behind you.  The Route winds onward to the east, and dwindles slowly toward the west.

Slender, willowy trees grow along the side of the road on this part of the Route, their boughs intertwining to form a wild, beautiful arch of leaf and branch.  From somewhere in the trees you hear the soft twitter of a single bird, the first you have heard in your entire time here.

Large stones crop out from the sides of the hills, bones jutting from the round flesh of the earth.  Wild roses climb over the hillsides, their bushes tangling into one another, and their fresh scent encircling you.  It is not enough, however, to dispel the faint tinge of rot that seems to hang in the air.

The ground is extremely stony here, and the sides of the hills are dotted with the broken remains of boulders.  To the west you see mountain peaks, broken-edged etchings against the sky.  Patches of grass grow sporadically amongst the gravel and stones through which you pick your way, and it is hard to distinguish where the sides of the Route end, and where the hills begin.

A massive rockslide has cut off any further western passage along the Journalai Route by caravan, and the slide itself looks too unstable and massive to climb safely.  You can catch a glimpse of sweeping forested mountainside just beyond the barrier, the caps of the peaks frosted with eternal snows.

A dirt path cuts its way along the grassy bank of a thin stream, winding northwards to untamed hills, and southward back to the Journalai Route.  The size of the stream's bed suggests that it must have been bigger once, but upheaval has changed it to a fraction of the size it used to be.

The stream splashes its way southeast, springing forth from underneath a set of rocks that jut out of the hill in front of you.  A hollow log lies next to the creek, looking a tad out of place in this mostly treeless land.

The leafy treetop forms a secure if spongy carpet beneath you, fanning out in all directions like a shimmering umbrella.  Tantalizing vreeland pears hang just out of reach, golden brown and tempting.  You can climb down the way you came up, or rest here for a bit.

The grass grows thick and lush beneath your feet, while above you rise tall wiir trees in full flourish.  The only disturbances are a set of large, unusual footprints that have crushed the tall grass, and the long marks, as if something heavy had been dragged through here, that accompany them.

Dazzling green hues spread over the surrounding hillside, creating a rippling illusion of movement.  The side of the hill you stand on slopes downward toward a tiny vale, while to the east it climbs back toward a dip where several hills meet.

Dazzling green hues spread over the surrounding hillside, creating a rippling illusion of movement.  The side of the hill you stand on slopes downward toward a tiny vale, while to the east it climbs back toward a dip where several hills meet.

The grass grows in a dark, soft circle here, inviting you to rest and relax, while tall wiir trees make a ring around the patch of green, their boughs intertwining in defense against the wind and rain.  An opening in a set of rocks piled up by the side of a hill creates a cave-like shelter to further protect you from the elements.

The grass grows in lush clumps beneath your feet, carpeting the tiny hillocks that rise up from the ground.  A butterfly floats through the air as it makes its way from wildflower to wildflower, its wings bright and vivid.

The ground is sprinkled with bits of gravel and stone, making this steep slope an adventure in and of itself.  Split boulders strewn across the ground prove to be good for catching your balance when dexterity gives way to gravity and the slippery mixture of skree and grass.

The hills shoulder the Route, observing all that passes down its fading trail with silent, unseen eyes.

Mountains to the west loom protectively over their smaller siblings, the hills.  Somewhere to the northeast you can catch the occasional splishing sound that signals the presence of a river or stream nearby.

The hills rise like frozen waves, their slopes leading down to a grassy knoll, as if in homage to something or someone.  A brisk breeze gusts downs from the high, untouched hilltops, creating a lonely song that whistles through the stones of the knoll.

The hills close in about you, monuments to greenery and life.  A pool is cupped at the base of one of the hills, its surface constantly moving from unseen currents.  A good-size hole opens up in the ground by one of the largest, steepest hills.  It leads down into darkness, giving no hint of where it might go.

The log is surprisingly large inside, big enough for an Elf to crouch in without being cramped.  The faint scent of rot that fills it does not make it a pleasant place to stay, however, and you feel oddly relieved that it is too dark in here to tell exactly what it is you are stepping in that squishes so.

The path winds between giant oaks mixed in with a secondary growth of smaller trees of many types.  Your footsteps are hushed on a thick carpet of rotting leaves and pine needles.  The air is fresh with the smell of growing things and rich earth.  The only jarring note is an odd footprint in the dirt.  Of some size, it seems almost human but for its far longer toes ending in deep indentations that speak of non-human claws.

This small clearing is open to the sky but surrounded by a thick growth of trees.  The ground here is soft and shows evidence of recent footsteps.  There is a faint scent of burned wood and ash from the east while several other paths branch off in various directions.  A tall, grotesque totem carved of ironwood dominates the center of the clearing.

This path snakes between two close-set trees with low-hanging foliage.  A perfect spot for an ambush, you note to yourself, while trying to stay to the center of the narrow path, away from the shadows and their feeling of watchful menace.

The ground is low and swampy underfoot.  Each step leaves an imprint in the soil that oozes moisture.  There are heavy vines looped over everything and your footing is unsteady as you try to avoid tripping.  Every bare patch of ground sprouts colonies of dead-white toadstools.  From nearby you hear a deep croaking sound followed by several more in different directions until you stand in the midst of a chorus of frog calls.

From nearby you hear a deep croaking sound followed by several more in different directions until you stand in the midst of a chorus of frog calls.

Several willow trees grow close together, nearly choking off the pathway.  Somewhere nearby you hear flowing water.  Brightly colored flowers hang from thick-stemmed creepers along the tree trunks, while numerous dragonflies flit among them on jewelled wings.  From time to time a shaft of light fights its way through the greenery and strikes the fliers' wings, causing their intense colors to glisten and sparkle.

The path ends here at a small stream that sings softly to itself as it flows among mossy stones.  Midges and gnats swarm above the water in clouds and they react to your presence with hungry delight.  Looking north along the stream bed you see it flows from beneath a high stone wall.  A tiny fish breaks the water's surface to snag a minute insect for supper.

The stream flows gently from north to south, running along an obviously artificial course.  This place was once meant as a pleasant spot to sit and enjoy the sound, as there is an ancient stone bench, now overturned and broken, set along the stream's edge.  A small hole in the stream bank appears to mark the home of a badger or some other water-dweller.

A stream widens out as it approaches a small river.  The ground is soft and marshy and is heavy with reeds and sedge-grass.  Frogs croak loudly along the banks and one occasionally leaps into the water with a loud splash.

The stream runs down into a small muddy river, hard by a large grove of willows growing in the rich soil.  As they whisper to each other, long branches brushing the ground in a gentle breeze, it seems to you that there are words and meanings hidden in the idle sounds.  Beneath your feet, the boggy ground shows traces of someone or something else passing by recently.

Standing on relatively firm ground, you note a natural cairn of rocks from which a bubbling spring arises to flow down into the boggy ground south and west.  A tiny pond has formed at the base of the rocks and little water-skimmer insects dart across its smooth surface, dodging each other like frantic ice skaters.  There is a wild and untamed beauty here that earns your respect for whoever first laid out this abandonded park.

A large rock outcrop thrusts its way from beneath the boggy soil here, blocking all passage save back towards a nearby spring.  The outcrop rises alongside the outer wall of the preserve but a series of downward- and upward-pointing spikes set near the top discourage any thoughts of rock-climbing today.  Large patches of moss form abstract designs on the granite outcrop and one struggling tree has tried to make a home in a dirt-filled crack in the rock.

This outpost is built of heavy, massive rockwork in the Dwarven style, plain but durable.  Designed for safe storage, as well as easy buying and selling of bulk goods by Guild members, it is crammed and jammed with crates, boxes and packages of all manner and value.  A stern-looking Guild trade minister is at hand to expedite transactions and to make sure nothing leaves or arrives without the proper fees and monies being exchanged.

This outpost is a miniature replica of one of the great Trader Guild buildings in the larger towns.  Designed for rapid buying and selling of bulk goods by Guild members, it is crammed and jammed with crates, boxes and packages of all sizes and shapes.  A harried Guild trade minister is at hand to expedite members' transactions and to make sure none of the goods leave under their own power or without the proper fees and monies being exchanged.

Traders mill about in the foyer, dressed in fine clothing of colorful silken or woolen fabrics sparkled with gleaming gold and jewels.  You pick up bits of conversation about the current prices or the quality of goods in various areas, as the tradesmen wander past you.  Occasionally, a young student, notebook in hand, moves meekly among them with a wide-eyed, awed expression.

The walls of this large room are painted a rich, deep doeskin tan.  Finely detailed tapestries of deep red, midnight blue and forest green cover three of the walls.  Several prosperous-looking traders saunter over to a board mounted on the remaining wall.  They peruse it quickly and move away to make room for others.  A young Halfling lad scurries to the north, a notebook clasped firmly to his chest.

An explosion in a dye factory can best describe this cramped little room at the very back of Swotting Hall.  Brightly-colored curtains in asymmetrical patterns pick up the vibrant primary hues used to upholster some plush arm chairs, and a rainbow-inspired throw rug shields the pale wooden floor.  A rotund clerk occasionally peers up at the pricing board before making notes in a faded leatherbound journal.

Simplicity seems to have been the goal in decorating this room.  Plain chairs have been neatly arranged in a half-circle facing the center of the room.  Unadorned beige walls and bare windows surround you.  Hildegrim Hornbeam stands in the center, dressed in an austere style that matches the decor.  She nods curtly at you as you enter.
