Thick tangles of thorny brambles cover what little land is elevated enough not to be drowned by the brackish mud, blocking the path on the easiest of routes and making it necessary to trudge through the muck and mire.

Thick reeds jut upward from the murky waters, forming a small burrow for the harmless creatures of the region.  The omnipresent canopy surrounding most of the swamp breaks here, allowing the fumes to drift upward into the sky, escaping the festering quagmire.

Two clerks sit behind the counter taking orders and sorting through the day's various requisitions.  A pile of invoices and work orders are stacked high on the Society Master's desk in the rear of the office next to a tall book shelf.

Pine paneled walls are nearly covered by racks of raw cloth and leather that flank either side of the narrow hallway.  In one corner sits a mannequin completely destitute of any type of clothing.  Tailors of all kinds rush back and forth, busy with their wares, dropping a random pin on the floor adding to the collection of scrap.

The scent of tanning lotions lingers in the air from the hides covering the walls.  An overworked Elven fellow sits behind a small table scraping away at some leather that he pulls from the large pile on the table.  Several tall racks against a wall hold a plentiful supply of crafting books.

The supply shop projects an air of quiet efficiency at all times with clerks refilling the various empty slots with new tools for sale.  Bottles, fabrics, and canvases stand neatly arranged on shelves that line the wall behind a polished white granite counter.  Several workrooms nearby provide enough static noise to block out the clerks idle conversations.

Three finely crafted rocking chairs sit around a round table in the center of the room where denizens will often sit and play a quick dice game while working away.  Shelves line the room where someone can set aside their work for a moment of rest, although those come few and far between.  A counter stocked with many types of fabrics and furs dominates one side of the room to make crafting materials readily accessible.

The hallway comes to an abrupt end where it branches off into to three rooms separated by granite arches.  Scrap cloth and leather along with empty bottles litter the otherwise empty tile floor.  Busy tailors shuffle in and out of the rooms, avoiding the garbage on the floor, hurrying to get more supplies.

Smoke from several sconces lining the room swirl out of the dim skylights overhead, and create a smoky fog along the ceiling.  Stained glass windows line the wall, reflecting the warm glow off the colored panes back into the room.  A long, thin rug decorated with embroidered sunbursts stretches in front of a hefty loom, a threadbare trail evidently marking where most weavers stand to perform their craft.  An azure granite arch leads back out into the building.

Open prairies and grasslands are painted in a panoramic mural that cover the stone walls from floor to ceiling.  Planted pots of junegrass and lilies are set up in a horseshoe around a hefty loom.  A beige granite arch leads back out into the building.

Darkness pours through the expansive windows as small candles on the sill illuminate the area.  Beneath a hefty loom is a lumpy burlap rug showing signs of wear atop a large lump, which props up the rug, from the shoes of many a weaver propping his feet up as he worked.  A grey granite arch leads back out into the building.

Large panes of thick, frosted glass make up the ceiling of this room, reflecting flickering torchlight across the walls.  A large spinning wheel sits below the darkened skylight atop an intricate grass rug woven in a zig-zag pattern.  The workbench lining the back wall generally serves as a place to take a quick respite or work on a project that requires more attention to detail.  A puce granite arch leads back out into the building.

Hundreds of stained glass panels make up the ceiling of this room, allowing the occasional glimpse of the skies above.  A painted spinning wheel sits below the skylight atop a rug dyed in vibrant greens and blues.  The workbench lining the back wall is splattered with various colored paints to add to the visual effect.  A white granite arch leads back out into the building.

Alternating panels of ironwood and cedar surround the walls to form stripes of dark and light.  Torchlight reflects off the highly polished walls to showcase the large spinning wheel sitting atop a plush cotton rug near the center of the room.  Beneath it, the alternating woods come together in a point.  The only other piece of furniture to grace the room is a long workbench against the back wall.  A green granite arch leads back out into the building.

A narrow ledge has been hacked out of the side of one of the volcanoes that dominate Dirge.  Whether carved by nature or mortal hand none can tell.  The mountain falls away steeply below, and any attempt to traverse that slope would lead to a painful and lonely death on the jagged spires far below.  The route upward is as hopeless, so you remain like some spirit of air, poised between heaven and earth.

A precipitous ledge leads down into inky depths.  Cool air, tinged with a flinty dryness, drifts bits of dust and feather fluff about your feet.  The remains of numerous bird's nests lie scattered about on the ground and in every nook and crevice.  A wide crack in the rock leads to a painfully bright daylit exterior.

A faint breeze stirs the air, it appears to come from the direction of a twisting crack in the basalt wall.  Grit and dust covers the stony ground and a few dried leaves caught in a corner indicate a possible route to the outer world.

You are wedged into a narrow crack in the rocks.  Jagged edges chafe at every bit of exposed flesh.  Crablike sideways movement is all that is possible.  The floor below pitches at a steep angle and one would surely fall if not held in a stony embrace.

A vast echoing space swallows your senses into utter darkness.  Unseen air currents brush by with cold, clammy hands.  Faint gleams of bone amongst piles of rubble mark the narrow edge of a seemingly bottomless crevasse.  A huge mound of bones to the east rises up to a darker spot in the darkness.  Far overhead, a few specks of light shine like stars against the dark rock.  Apparently when the roof collapsed, rifts opened to the outer air.

Balancing on a knife-edge of rock, darkness hangs over you like a heavy cloak.  Mounds of bones and gravel-sized rock slope steeply downward to the east and west.  Straining to pierce the Stygian blackness, there is the faintest glimmer of light from the west.

The dark walls show signs of once having been smooth, but some upheaval of the earth has turned the arched dome into a jagged mass of splintered rock and shattered stone.  Mounds of bone lie heaped along the ruins of the walls, where their burial niches once held them.  There is little rest, even for the dead, in this world.

Broken and cracked rocks encumber your feet and the roof is a crazed mass of rotten stone that appears ready to crash down with no warning.  Splintered bits of bone poke out from among the piles of rock.  There is no way to tell if they are the remains of the ancient dead, or someone of more recent vintage who got very unlucky.

This is a large cavern, almost circular in shape, with a domed roof of worked stone arching high overhead.  A low altar rises in the center of the cave.  Hundreds of bone-filled niches tower on all sides, climbing up the curving walls.  One great stalactite descends from the shrouded heights of the dome like the accusing finger of an angry god.

Sometime in the distant past, this passageway was wider.  A huge slab of rock has forced its way up from beneath like a stony wedge, narrowing the path almost to uselessness.  Occasional bits of bone litter the cracked and fissured ground.  The air is curiously damp, enough so that the walls are covered with a thick fur of moss or mold that gives off a musty stench like rotting leather mixed with rancid butter.

Dozens of niches carved deeply into the wall contain an overflowing abundance of bones.  Skulls and femurs, finger-bones and kneecaps litter the stony ground and roll everywhere.  Centuries of burial have crammed every crack and corner of the cave with the grim relics of the departed.

A cramped and twisted passage leads from one cavern to another.  Bone fragments litter the ground and larger remnants lie heaped against the walls. Chill breezes, scented with a tinge of rot, stir the air.

This cavern is circular, with walls and floor polished smooth by time and human effort.  The air is thick with mingled odors and an odd white dust covers the floor.  The walls are crammed with hundreds of carved niches, rising far overhead on all sides.  Those nearest you are piled high with bones and skulls of all sizes and conditions.  A strong smell of decay and rot wafts up from a large pit in the center of the room.

A narrow, twisty passage wends among unclimbable mounds of broken rock.  Here and there, a skull rests upright by some chance upon a ledge or flat surface.  Each one seems to leer with silent mirth as you stumble and lurch on the uneven pathway.

A funnel-shaped area narrows to the northeast and widens out into a huge spherical chamber to the southwest.  The rock walls are featureless black stone, all texture melted and smoothed into a dull, glassy surface.

A narrow passageway opens out into a roughly spherical cave.  The walls are a curiously porous stone, resembling a petrified sponge.  The overall effect is that of being inside a bubble formed by some strange quirk of nature when the rock was soft and pliable.

A trio of spherical caves, like ebony pearls in a row, form a line one after another.  Shaped perhaps in the time of the volcano by hot gases surging outward, the inner surface of the rock is a mass of frozen froth.  In places it shows ripples and waves and flow marks, resembling custard stirred and left to harden.

A bubble-shaped cavern rises on all sides, nearly perfect in its symmetry.  The walls are a curiously porous rock, laced with millions of lesser bubbles.  The edges are brittle and sharp for all the seeming softness of the stone, caught in mid-flow and solidified.

What was once a large cavern, roughly spherical in shape, has collapsed into formless heaps of rubble.  Unlike its brethren to the north, there is nothing of graceful arcs and curves here.  Only hard and brittle boulders of dull grey and black rock, jagged and misshapen lie within view.

This large grey lump of ancient stone lies against the curve of the cave wall.  Above, on the wall itself, a dark pocket with jagged edges shows from whence it came.  Time has worn the boulder's surface into a series of pits and fissures.

The inside of this boulder is cracked and fissured, so much so, one can find a limited amount of room to move about.  Jagged slabs of broken rock form rude walls, blocking vision and hampering movement.  Gravel rolls beneath your feet, making the footing uncertain.

Stone walls curve in close above your head and jagged flakes of rock form shaky walls inside this oddly hollow boulder.  Something has made a nest here, tufts of rank hair and a few scattered bones attest to meals once consumed and dried droppings attest to their aftermath.

Chunks of crumbling rock litter the cramped floor in this narrow hollow inside a huge boulder.  The rough ceiling presses down on heavily and the air is thick with dust.  A rising sense of claustrophobia grips at your mind.

A few largish rocks and scattered pebbles litter the otherwise smooth floor. The cramped confines hem all movement and obscures vision.  The air is dead and still.  No wind has stirred here for ages and the air tastes of ashes and rock dust.  Dry and sere, it seems to lack any vitality.  It can be breathed, but it does not encourage one to linger.

There is scant space to turn or move, broken slabs of rock nearly pin you against a cold wall of stone.  Flinty dust rises in a dry choking fog all about.  Silence hangs thick like a musty blanket.  The closeness is oppressive, daylight and fresh air are all but forgotten.

This cramped space resembles a niche, someplace to place an idol or statue on display.  The entire weight of the massive, hollow boulder feels as if it might come crashing down at any moment.  Tiny flakes of rock drift everywhere in a constant rain, like dessicated snow.  They grate underfoot and coat every surface with a grey dust.

This narrow cave resembles a hallway of sorts.  A cool breeze filters up from the darkness but it bears a hint of foulness and corruption.  The walls and floor are smooth and dry, though cold enough to seem clammy.

The bottom of this pit is filled with a dark, thick liquid.  Viscous and foul-smelling, it fills a deeper pit almost to the rim.  Small waves travel across its surface though there is no wind to cause them.  Dozens of corroded bronze cages hang from the walls attached to long chains.  For centuries, the dead of Dirge have been brought here to have their flesh eaten away by the liquid in the pit and their polished bones laid in niches of remembrance in the room above.
A sharp movement in a low thicket sends stalks of stinging nettles sailing, slapping the air like angry insects.  A moment later, everything is silent.
An ambitious thicket of weeping hemlock reaches for the sky, casting odd dancing shadows on the ground.  A few twigs nearer the ground are broken, as if something had passed this way not long ago.
Tufts of goldenseal struggle amidst the tangled thicket of dry, scrubby boar-bristle bushes.  A faint trail of broken thorns leads off to the northeast.

Daylight clings like a fitful child to the thick forest and undergrowth.  Though it is possible to venture in most directions, it promises to be a frustrating, difficult and painful battle against the stubborn resistance of the woods.  Discerning the cardinal directions is a matter of guesswork and only close observation reveals anything of worth.
A huge dead oak overhangs the road.  One enormous crabbed branch extends directly overhead, its smaller branches splayed like a giant, outstretched claw.
You rest a moment in the crotch of a dead branch that sticks out at an acute angle midway up the gnarled and twisted tree trunk.  Nearby, other trees break through the heavy thornbrake far below.
rooms.loc: Northern Trade Road, Vipers & Rock Guardians

rooms.desc: One single candle lights the way in the interior room of the temple.  The light flickers as an unnerving cool breeze that seems to come from nowhere chills the air.  Reflections can be seen on the walls made of black glasslike material that is polished to a high shine.  Unfamiliar scraping and hissing noises leave the hair at the nape of the neck standing on end.

Sheer-sided and sandy, this massive crater is utterly bereft of life.  A sharp smell, like heated metal, permeates the area.  A faint track picks its way up the southern slope of the crater back toward the main road and a narrow lava tube on the northwestern face leads into darkness.
An uncomfortable heat radiates from the smooth, round walls.  The tube ends here with the southern maw opening into a massive crater.
An uncomfortable heat radiates from the smooth, round walls.  The tube slowly curves here concealing either end of the tunnel.
An uncomfortable heat radiates from the smooth, round walls.  The tube slowly slopes upwards towards the eastern maw.

Undulating sheets of long hardened lava flow forth from an old lava tube.  A few stray cobblestones have survived both the lava the more recent explosion from which the massive crater to the south resulted.

A crooked fissure brings the road to an abrupt end, glowing sullenly and casting forth an acrid sulfuric reek.  A collapsed black marble column serves as a makeshift bridge, allowing relatively safe passage to the northeast.

A crooked fissure blocks passage to the southwest, a fallen black marble column serving as a makeshift bridge.  The road continues to the southeast, though it has been almost completely obliterated by drifting ash.  A rocky trail leads northwards to the collapsed ruins of a stone building.

The ground here is blanketed in ankle-deep ash; the rocks and masonry hidden beneath making for treacherous footing.  A plinth from a massive black marble column lies shattered in two pieces; the scattered remains of the pillar stretching southward like an out-flung arm.
The road ends abruptly here, a treacherous jumble of massive rocks making passage onward all but impossible.  The volcano looms to the northwest, rumbling and muttering like a sleeping giant.
A precipitous escarpment rises directly off the canyon floor and up into the night sky.  A collection of dirt and rubble lies at the bottom of the cliff.
Canyons twist and turn through the shadowy bluffs and peaks, creating a disorienting sense of deja vu.  The path bends sharply around a corner and reaches a dead end.

The top of this mesa is broad and flat, offering spectacular views of the varied rock formations and surrounding savannah.  With overhanging cliffs around most of the plateau, the only way down is an unstable, crumbling cliff on the south side.

Canyons twist and turn through the shadowy bluffs and peaks, creating a disorienting sense of deja vu.  Upon closer scrutiny, a deeper gloom near the base of the cliff proves to be simply a large boulder.  A steep crumbling cliff rises to the east.

The crumbling rock on the face of this steep cliff is extremely unstable.  Clinging precariously in the dark, your slightest movement causes small avalanches of rocks and soil to go careening down the bluff.

Set up as a small celebration area, the festival area for the corn maze is surrounded by a wooden fence.  Any grass in the area is thoroughly trampled by the heavy foot traffic, and the smell of ale hangs heavily in the air.

A lone dogwood tree grows here, its white and red petals unexpectedly bright against the muted background of sand and silt at the bottom of the canyon.  A light, flowery scent wafts from the wizened tree.  Animal tracks mark the ground near the tree, evidence that these canyons are not as uninhabited as they appear.
Convoluted limbs shaped like skeletal arms extend into the narrowing canyon, grasping at passersby.  The path twists and turns until it reaches a dead end.
A long precarious ledge angles sharply down the northern wall of the canyon, dwindling as it descends.  Small holes chipped in the unforgiving granite above the ledge are worn smooth from use.

A narrow ledge ascending steeply from the canyon floor culminates at a dark vertical crevice that splits the thick granite wall, its depth indeterminable without closer inspection.  Small smooth holes are carved into the face of the cliff above the ledge.
A musty smell permeates this dark cavern.  Discarded rags lie along one wall, riddled with holes and infested with bugs.  Daylight is visible through a large vertical crevice in the granite.

Gnarled trees line the path in a row here, the handiwork of a passing traveler or nature's plan unknown.  Five-pointed leaves are scattered amongst the rubble of fallen rocks, their fading color dusted with the blue silt of an eroding stratum on the cliff above.
The chasm twists and narrows unexpectedly, the high cliffs closing in on the canyon floor.  Only a small patch of sky is visible beyond the steep walls.

Wind moans through the stark canyons and stone columns, the sound lonely and desolate.  Seemingly familiar sights, smells and sounds in this maze of canyons confound the senses with their disorganized patterns and could easily lead an inattentive wanderer astray.

Obstinately clinging to life, a cluster of gnarled cottonwood trees line the bed of an all but vanished stream.  A passing breeze rustles their leaves, exposing their silvery undersides to gleam in the light.  Dozens of small mounds near the roots of the trees swarm with red ants, moving quickly and purposefully about the canyon walls and floor.

A colony of prairie dogs inhabits this broad valley between low bluffs.  With quick darting movements, they take turns poking their golden brown heads out of their burrows and looking about with bright eyes.  Their chittering and barking oscillates in an intermittent rhythm.

Several desert ironwood trees with smooth grey bark and glossy green leaves huddle around a small natural spring.  A rich, spicy fragrance emanates from white blossoms growing singly on elongated stems while some fallen flowers float serenely in the placid water of the spring.
The ravine widens here and paths lead in three directions.  From this angle the surrounding geological formations look curiously like heads and faces engaged in an animated conversation.

The canyon twists unexpectedly through the bluffs in this stretch of the path, widening slightly here as it snakes its way through the maze of weather-sculpted stone.  Off to one side a cairn of carefully stacked rocks and pebbles has been constructed.

Fantastic arches and pillars of ruddy sandstone, formed over centuries by the slow work of wind and water, loom silently on either side of the narrow track.  The passing wind sings eerily through the stone.
Canyons twist and turn through the colorful bluffs and peaks, creating a disorienting sense of deja vu.  The cliffs taper off to the east, and the savannah can be glimpsed beyond the badlands.

Spectacular rock formations dominate the eroded bluffs looming to the west.  Vividly colored in stratified shades of tan, black, red, blue, and green, the steep cliffs and arches soar over the canyons like rainbows in the distance.

The crumbling canyon walls are bolstered in places by twisted and dwarfed trees that cling tenaciously to the nearly vertical surfaces.  Tiny birds flutter in and out of a small hole near one tree, the avian family choosing to make their home in solid rock rather than in the tortured vegetation.

Named for their vividly colored layers of soil and minerals, the heavily eroded Mosaic Bluffs loom to the north.  From the muted hues of dun sandstone and dark charcoal to brighter strata of red, blue, and green,  the steep cliffs form a harmonious chiaroscuro of light and dark.  Scattered patches of rock nettle and purple star thistle quiver with each breezy gust of wind.

Detailed maps of Ilithi's different roads and towns are painted on the walls.  The largest map depicts the city of Shard and the deep blue of the lake around it.  Two long tables of polished wood fill the floor space, while a thick black rug spreads from corner to corner.

Hard packed ground is littered with barrels, boxes and various conveyances awaiting the ferries' return to dock.  Smooth rock benches are scattered around the large area, for those travelers wishing to wait off their feet.  The dock itself is crafted from dark wood and braced by huge rocks and beams, while iron lanterns blaze from poles hung along each side.

The south fork of the Segoltha River surges steadily eastward.  Compared to the aspects of the river on the other three sides of Ain Ghazal, the flow is deep and calm.  The lantern-lit South Dock, perpetually busy with ferry traffic, extends south from River Road.  The road itself curves northeast and northwest, and a steep slope leads upward.

The well-built and durable East Pier connects to River Road at this spot.  Skiffs take the public to and from River Clan, loading and unloading people, animals and commodities on the wide, dimly lit pier.  This road arcs to the northwest and southwest, and a steep slope leads upward.
The Segoltha water that crashes deafeningly against Ain Ghazal rock renders the surface of the road damp and fills the air with a fine mist.  A moist cliff leads uphill.

The roar of the river is inescapable as it echoes between the soaring heights of the Journalai Range to the north and the mass of Ain Ghazal to the south.  The River Road, bordered by a low wall, curves southwest and southeast, and a sheer cliff lies directly above.

Subtle light gleams from bronze lanterns hung from a couple of tall poles, leaving shadows along a wood pier that juts off from the hard packed ground.  The pier provides a sturdy transition from road to river conveyance, with its beams wide enough for large beasts to go safely aboard.  The river's brisk waters beat against the rocks below with a wild rhythm, while a sign nearby warns of their danger.

The Spiral Road curves downhill to the northwest and up to the northeast.  A steep slope leads straight down to the river and the South Dock, where ferries carrying passengers, caravans, and cargo hustle back and forth.  Overhead is a sheer cliff.

A steep slope leads down to the River Road at its intersection with the East Pier.  The steady activity of passengers, skiffs, small boats, crates, barrels, and packages continues through the night.  A sheer cliff leads upward.

The sound of rushing water resonates against the mountain cliffs to the north.  Overhead is a perpendicular escarpment that appears difficult to climb, and a sheer cliff below would lead adventurous climbers down to the River Road.

The roar of the river is reminiscent of a powerful waterfall.  The road, which leads up to the southeast and down to the northeast, may be a longer journey between the docks and the chateau, but it appears to be much safer than attempting to climb the perpendicular escarpment above or the sheer cliff below.

With lights reflecting in sparkles on the surface of the water, ferries move busily between the South Dock of Ain Ghazal and the Haalikshaal Highway Dock on the southern shore of the river.  The perpendicular escarpment above looks like a very difficult climb, and the sheer cliff below does not seem much easier.

Visible from this location are the lights of the East Pier and the lit skiffs moving downstream and upstream, to and from River Clan.  The perpendicular escarpment above might be suitable for expert climbers, and a sheer cliff leads down to the segment of the road directly below.
A dim precipice overhangs the road, and an escarpment leads downward.
The crash of the river against the foot of the island thunders through the air.

Dimly illuminated ferries move quickly back and forth between the South Dock of Ain Ghazal and the dock at the terminus of the Haalikshaal Highway.  A precipice looms above the road, and on the other side of the road an escarpment may be a difficult shortcut to the section of road just below.

The distant lights of the East Pier and the skiffs it services are visible from this vantage.  A precipice juts out overhead, and a perpendicular escarpment lies between this section of the road and the section immediately below.
Directly below this section of the Spiral Road is an overhanging precipice that makes it difficult to see the lower curves of the road.  Off to one side of the road is a good-sized sinkhole.
The road curves down to the northwest and up to some iron gates in the northeast.  Directly below, an overhanging precipice blocks the view of the rest of the island.

The towering Journalai Range thrusts out from the earth just across the river from Ain Ghazal, obstructing the view of all areas farther north.  Directly below this section of the Spiral Road is an overhanging precipice that makes it difficult to see the lower curves of the road as it winds around the island.  Off to one side of the road is a sinkhole about twelve feet across.

A jagged hole high above shows the sky, making this cavern appear to be some sort of sinkhole.  Boulders of all sizes litter the area, perhaps flung there by some long-past cave-in.  Soft green moss spreads across the floor like a living carpet, growing thickest directly under the wide opening.  Many bones poke through the greenery, the remains of some poor, doomed animals that fell to their deaths.

A shallow stream runs along the bottom of a boulder-strewn passage for a short distance before disappearing into a narrow fissure running across the floor.  One wall of the passage is sheer rock, but the other is formed of tumbled boulders atop one another almost like tiered amphitheater seating.

Dark rock walls press close, forming a cramped tunnel.  The ceiling is festooned with rows of razor-sharp, blood-red stalactites that curve ever so slightly.  Fang-like stalagmites jutting up from the floor do little to dispel the impression of traveling down some monster's throat.

Boulders littering the floor have lain undisturbed for ages, as proved by the white flowstone formation that drapes across the top and down one side of a massive pile.  Out of the pile extends a pair of red pillars connecting it to the ceiling.

This narrow passage inclines steeply, making footing precarious.  A thick layer of loose rock and mud covering the floor compounds the problem, but with care and balance it is possible to move onwards.  Needle-like sprays of white crystal radiate from the walls and ceiling, adding a further impediment to travel.

Moisture percolating through the porous rocks above forms thin rivulets of water trickling across an immense and intricate white flowstone formation banded with shades of blue, grey and green.  The sound of water splashing as it drips into the puddles that litter the floor echoes incessantly in the large cavern.

Narrow and treacherous, the way becomes less like a path than a ledge on the face of a steep rock wall.  Over the rim of the ledge, the crevasse plunges almost straight down, without any cracks or crevices to provide a solid grip for climbing.  The far wall of the cavern is hidden in the darkness, and only the echoes hint at its existence.

Shattered remains of a rock wall that once divided two smaller caverns cover the floor.  The stone lies splintered, destroyed by some angry force.  Scarred flowstone remnants cling to the ceiling and walls, their broken edges curiously clean, as if cut with surgical precision.  A distant rumble shivers the rock underfoot, perceptibly stronger to the north.

A narrow shelf runs along the edge of a sheer precipice as it passes beneath a roaring cataract.  Bursting forth from a fissure high in the wall, the cascade of water falls in a thundering torrent into a churning black pool far below.  Mist wafts up from the depths of the gorge, slicking the rocks with condensation.

This narrow passage inclines steeply, making footing precarious.  A thick layer of loose rock and mud covering the floor compounds the problem, but with care and balance it is possible to move onwards.  Needle-like sprays of white crystal radiate from the walls and ceiling, adding a further impediment to travel.

Underfoot lie patches of thick mud and golden-brown sand, but the walls are slick and clean.  Overhead the flat expanse of the ceiling is marred only by a few tiny cracks which extend a few feet then disappear into the smooth stone.
Twisting and turning, the narrow tunnel weaves a circuitous and disorienting path between craggy rock walls.  The ground underfoot is a slippery layer of mud and stone that shifts with every step.

Moisture seeps from the walls in slow trickles, pooling on a slick floor of dark clay mixed with sand.  Anyone wading through the cavern is in danger of being mired by the molasses-like consistency of the knee-deep sludge.  Jutting out of the muck is a low flowstone formation which is relatively smooth and flat in places, making it possible to sit upon.

Every exposed surface -- the floor, walls and even the ceiling -- is coated with thick mud.  Sloping downward, the ankle-deep muck gives way to a still pool of dark water filling one end of the cavern.  One can only surmise that the mud was deposited by receding floodwaters which filled the cave recently.

A river once flowed freely through this tunnel, depositing a muddy clay residue which hardened over time.  Studded with chunks of white rock, the dark red clay covers the floor and rises halfway up the wall, looking much like a tile mosaic.
A broad open area lies between crowded ranks of stalagmites and massive, green-streaked columns.  With no rubble barring the way, it resembles nothing so much as a wide aisle in some great cathedral.

A thick vein of copper flows down one wall and runs across the floor.  The glittering metallic line has many spidery offshoots, each spreading for a short distance then tapering off into ever-thinner veins before disappearing altogether.
Odd bumps and protrusions cover the walls of the passage.  Some are smaller than a pea while others are larger than a boobrie egg.  The unusual formation gives the rock appearance of popcorn.

The passage flares high and wide into a cavernous chamber where heaps of rubble litter the broad floor.  The debris spills from an enormous rock fall in the center of the room.  Multi-colored layers of stone are exposed on the ceiling where the chunks of rock have recently broken off, adding to the pile fallen in past upheavals.

Stone walls press inward, constricting the passage to its claustrophobic narrowest.  Red-swirled flowstone curtains flecked with sparkling mica nearly seal the tunnel at one point, leaving a narrow opening to squeeze through.

Carved from the rock by an underground river, the tunnel walls are smooth rather than rough, and the ceiling and floor are barren of rocky growths.  Reduced now to a shallow stream, the clear waters cover a bed of fine sand with leaf fragments and water-polished quartz pebbles.

Shallow water laps gently at the edges of a tumble of boulders in the middle of the cavern.  The water-worn rocks, too heavy to be pushed any further by the river that carved these tunnels ages ago, are riddled with dark scars where erosion has eaten away the outer stone.

Walls of water-cut limestone are covered with jagged edges, ready to slice whatever might fall down upon them.  Hundreds of trickling streams of water pour from the holes in the ceiling high overhead.  The water gathers in shallow rivulets before spilling down the sloping passage.  An uneven fault splits the floor, forking into many more.  The fissures split and split again, covering most of the floor with a web of flaws.

Smooth stone walls are covered with beads of water dripping down with inexorable slowness.  Puddles and tiny pools cover the floor, some spilling over to merge with the stream that winds between green- and blue-marbled stalagmites before disappearing into a pile of rocks.

An extensive maze of cracks runs across the limestone walls and ceiling.  Dense clusters of calcite deposited by the mineral-rich water fill the intersecting fractures.  The resulting veins of white crystal stand out starkly against dark grey rock, as intricate as ornamental fretwork.

A tier of white stalactites festoons the ceiling like elegant chandeliers.  Jagged stone stalagmites mark a staggered path through the cavern.  The way is treacherous, littered with loosely piled mounds of pebbles and slabs that shift underfoot.

Soaring up from the mud, strangely shaped columns stretch into the dark recesses of the stalactite-studded ceiling.  Yielding to the pull of gravity, heavy droplets of water saturated with dissolved minerals slide down the needle-like rock formations, dropping from above and forming miniature craters in the mud on impact.

The rock walls and floor of this steeply sloping corridor are riddled with occasional splits and fissures.  Most can be stepped over with ease, but some would have to be jumped across by anyone shorter than an Olvi.

Draping from the ceiling to the edge of a blue-green pool is an expansive curtain of a creamy translucent mineral, dominating the small grotto.  Thin rivulets of water stream from cracks in the ceiling and flow down the curtain and into the pool with unusual quiet.

Outcrops of crystal spar interspersed among the formations that cover the walls and ceiling make the grotto sparkle.  Only the smooth stone floor remains free of decoration and is coated with a fine grit of pulverized rock.
Blue-grey stone glitters with mineral deposits, flecks of gold glimmer in veins of quartz in the walls, and still more quartz forms rosettes adorned with many large, lustrous, dark red needles.

Transparent stalactites grow from the ceiling, resembling glass more than stone.  Glittering like a glassblower's display, every surface is covered with curling streamers of crystalline minerals clustered together to form "cave flowers".

The passage widens abruptly to reveal a grotto whose ceiling is lost in shadow high overhead.  Creamy flowstone curtains whorled with blue and green drape the walls.  Flecks of pure white calcite crystals are woven into the flowstone, sparkling with reflected light.

Although the bulk of it has long since crumbled into the gorge, a natural stone bridge once spanned the stream rushing through a channel carved deep into the rock.  The swift-moving water cuts across the cavern before disappearing into a narrow fissure.  From the black depths of the fissure comes a disquieting sucking sound.

The walls slope sharply inward, narrowing and lowering the passage.  At the narrowest point the ceiling is low enough that members of the taller races would need to hunch over to keep from hitting their heads.

Stalagmites and rocky scree litter the floor and hinder the explorer in this long tunnel.  A pair of collapsed columns lean against one another for support.  Wedged tightly between one wall and a broken stalagmite, a slab of fallen stone rests at a near level angle, forming a natural table.

Fragments of the ceiling have collapsed here and there along the length of the tunnel.  The dark fissures exposed by the fall are jeweled with minerals that contrast starkly with the surrounding dull grey rock.

The walls curve gently upward and inward to form a natural hemisphere of dark grey, mica-flecked stone.  Crystal spar decorates the ceiling and walls, tracing some of the cracks in a glittering display.  Sand lies deep on the floor, save for a few small piles of crystalline debris, apparently the remnant of something once attached to the ceiling that now lies in shattered ruin.

Widening abruptly, the tunnel affords a view of stately stone formations.  Untold years of dripping water depositing layers of colorful minerals have resulted in stalactites and stalagmites streaked with shades of blue and green.  Some meet in the middle to form columns, demonstrating the great age of this hall.
Widening slightly into a long channel of high-walled stone, the ceiling is lost in shadow high overhead.  A dun crystalline crust covers the walls, powdering and flaking with the lightest pressure.

A narrowing of the passage forces air to flow past with increased velocity, producing a faint whistling sound.  Thick, twisted stone columns run the length of the tunnel, like a marble colonnade supporting the vaulted ceiling of a grand ballroom.

A large flowstone formation banded in grey and white forms one wall in this gigantic cavern.  Numerous rimstone pools hug the bottom edge of the stone curtain, spilling downwards in terraced sections.  The unusually clear waters reflect the stalactites hanging from the ceiling overhead, creating the illusion of ruined towers drowned deep within the pools.
Although this cavern must have once been fairly open, passage is now made difficult by rock formations jutting up from the floor and rubble where great stalactites have fallen in ages past.

Seams in the ceiling are lined with long, needle-like clusters of stalactites, commonly referred to as "cave straw".  At intervals, mineral-rich water gathers from above to drip down onto the point of one of the many stalagmites.  Fragments of broken crystal needles litter the floor, resembling splinters of glass.

Slanted walls and narrow passageways leave little room to maneuver without brushing against the delicate crystalline formations covering the rock.  Resembling fluttering ribbons frozen in a moment of time, twisting streamers of snowy calcite lend the grotto the appearance of a wedding pavilion.

The rock itself grows darker here, indicating a change in the nature of the stone as the passage winds its way onward.  Flecks of crystal glitter in the walls and ceiling.  The floor is uneven and covered with pebbles poking up through a layer of powdery sand.

Rock walls soar upwards, coming together gradually to form a natural dome enclosing a cavern cratered with hot springs.  The stone floor is wildly uneven, creating ridges and half-walls of buckled stone that pose a threat to anyone walking through.  Brown and red streaked columns rise like twisting trees to support the vaulted ceiling high above.

A hot spring roils and steams in the upper end of the gallery, rimmed by crowded stalagmites and flowstone streaked lemon-yellow.  The drab rock walls are smooth and damp, intermittently veined with yellow and red.  A faint, sulphuric scent rises from the pool.

A soft mist spills out over the ground, issuing forth from a number of tiny fissures along one wall.  The air here feels warmer than in the rest of the cave, and it smells slightly of rotten eggs.  Deep crevices in the walls are lined with sparkling white crystals studded with lemon-yellow mineral deposits.

Welling up from a crevice in the wall, a steamy trickle of water flows down a rock outcropping and into a shallow pool.  A creeping vapor clings to the surface of the water, filling the area with the stench of rotten eggs.

Water from a deep creek rushes into a small inland pond. Fresh from its passage over cleansing rocks and sand, the water is crystal clear and the shadowed forms of fish can be seen gliding through the darkened depths of the pond.

Piles of stacked skins, finished and unfinished, crowd the broad tent of calico patchwork hides and make it seem far smaller than it would appear from outside.  The overpowering fetid odor of the tanner's craft pervades the space within the tent, clutching at the throat and clinging to all who pass through.  Amid it all stands the tanner himself, apparently immune to the miasma from long exposure.

A vast tapestry of nine golden stars sprinkled on a midnight blue background hangs upon one of the painted turquoise walls, while a soft woolen rug blankets the floor underfoot.  A large spinning wheel stands at the back of the parlor, while a large workbench and padded chair rest nearby, providing a place to relax or work on a project that requires more attention to detail.

Set in the back of the large workroom is a hefty loom.  Hooks and shelves line the painted turquoise walls, holding various tools and spools of thread that are currently not in use.  Next to the archway is a simple workbench and chair, a place to take a load off and enjoy a cool drink, and enjoy the fruits of one's labor.

A sturdy anvil dominates the center of this small forging area.  Heat pours out from the glowing forge and permeates the room as a small ceiling shaft tries futilely to draw it outside.  A slack tub stands guard below the forge, waiting to cool off the anvil's bounty, be they broken pieces or masterpieces.

Two acolytes stand guard over a cold black marble altar, while others drag the deceased and pull them on top in offering to Urrem'tier.  The darkness is broken by the lone torch that stands next to the altar, casting a glow on the black glass walls.

Snickering noises echo in the alcove, or maybe it is the unknown breeze that chills the air even colder here than in the outer room.  Shadows dance on the walls yet there is no light source visible to cause them.  A larger than life onyx scorpion statue stands menacingly in the middle of the room.

The scraping noises are louder now and seem to come from all around.  An arched doorway is cut into the black rock that leads off into an endless tunnel.  Torches are placed over the doorway to help light the way through the darkness.

Darkness permeates the cave with the only light coming from some source to the north of the tunnel.  Trickling noises seem to come from behind the walls as well as an unfamiliar hissing sound coming from somewhere within.

Shadows flicker on every wall possibly coming from the torches reflecting off of the black crystal walls.  Tunnels branch off in many directions and show no signs of ending.  An unfamiliar sound, possibly hissing, is enough to make hair stand on end.

Formations of marbled white and black glass make up the interior of the grotto.  Less eerie here, light seems to filter in from cracks in the ceiling, giving an indication the exit is near.  The tunnel narrows down to an entrance leading north back towards safety.

An almost eerie quiet fills this part of the cavern.  No sounds seem to filter through except for the occasional echo of a footstep nearby.  Carved images in the cavern walls depict scenes of death in a more natural state.

The obvious end of the tunnel is a shrine to the goddess Eylhaar.  A featureless statue, somewhat feminine in nature but with a hint of masculinity, stands next to a gnarled doorway.  The feeling of death hangs in the air, but is one of a more peaceful, natural death.  The walls themselves are etched with memorials of those who have died and may be buried here.

Rusted chains, frayed rope, and fragments of wood litter the foredeck, the debris scattered across the slanting ship.  With its weight crushing the sea-torn starboard rails, the giant foremast provides a bridge between the ship and the shallows, its upper portion now partly wedged in the rocks like a toothpick between the teeth.  Occasionally a fierce wave crashes against the creaking vessel, spraying it with water but doing little to move the ship from its impaled position.

Heavily pitched mahogany rails along the foredeck of the ship converge on the pulpit just above the headless figurehead.  Rusted chains and debris litter the area, most piled upon the lower eastern end of the prow.  Occasional spray slickens the deck, making it slightly hazardous.  Nestled between the rails is a small shrine, constructed from sea stones and hardened sand.

Securely nailed, a row of small tables lines the port side main deck, slanting in unison with the angle of the ship as if their battered surfaces were bowing to the cliff-lined coast.  Large sections of greying planks show through chipped white paint, and disturbingly large cracks cross the wood from the stress of the crash.  In the center, the remains of the main mast stick out like a jagged spike.

Splitting through the deck like a giant tree stump are the remains of the mizzenmast.  Its once proud sails have long since disappeared, leaving only rusted rings, wood splinters, and rope fragments to remember them by.  A narrow, steep stairs matches the deck's angle, making them a little trickier to navigate.

Smoke fills the air as Ferashi'ini toils over his anvil in front of a massive brick forge, creating weapons with precision and skill.  His apprentice works by his side, keeping his master stocked with the supplies he needs and stoking the bellows to keep the fire raging.  Underneath a soot covered sign, several finished weapons have been mounted upon a display wall, their blades gleaming in the light of the fire.

The blended scents of oil, leather, and metal create the characteristic atmosphere of those rooms where the art of weapon repair holds sway.  Rough sandstone floors are kept swept clean, though occasional stray glints in the corners betray metallic shavings that have escaped from the workroom somewhere in the rear of the building that Fekoeti uses to ply his trade.

A pair of tiny windows in the vaulted ceiling far overhead capture every errant breeze, transforming the hollow of the building into the bell of a great stone whistle.  Low thrumming notes resonate through the chamber and out onto the cobblestone street, carried on the back of swooping gusts that cause the wares on a pair of heavy wrought-iron tables to quiver.

An unusually rancid aroma rises to meet the nostrils.  Lying farther back in a dark corner are the remains of some poor beast, once covered with a white downy coat but now disemboweled as fodder for scavengers.  Small rocks are arranged in a rather crude circle near the carcass, but no ashes are to be found within its perimeter.

Shaded almost completely by the heavy cover of lofty palm trees, this small manmade pool brims with crystal blue refreshment.  Daylight peeks through the verdant green leaves to stripe both the water and the bordering sandstone bricks.  The pool's gentle undulations artistically distort the elaborate mosaic of vibrant tiles lining the bottom.

A wild garden grows here with hawthorn and blackberry bushes that are plaited together by twisting vines of rambler roses.  Pale pink rose petals are strewn across the well-tended grass.  A stone urn filled with flowers sits on a pedestal in front of a wooden garden pavilion.
Faint moonlight streams through the translucent veil of rushing water that seals off this small cave, but does not provide enough illumination to reveal the surroundings.

Giant boulders are scattered haphazardly about the ocean near the beach.  Curiously, smaller stones have been collected to form a rocky path atop the water -- wide enough for a pair of horses and long enough for at least ten.  The ocean's floor drops away to invisible depths at the pathway's midpoint, leaving little doubt that the end is quite deep indeed.  Tufts of soggy, seaweed-matted fur cling to the stones.

Meticulously placed with care upon the cushioned shelves circling the walls of this small sandstone shop are a variety of musical instruments.  The tenaciousness of S'hhtrkith's gentle and tender hand in the care of his goods shows that he is a true believer in the bardic spirit.

Light from the desert sky pierces through an elaborate, imported stained glass window, spraying streams of rainbow luminance upon shelves of instruments.  A wide counter spanning the length of the store separates the shopping area from the work and residence portions -- a stairway in the shadowy recesses of the shop stretches up to what presumably is a bedroom.

This small shop is cluttered with stands and racks bearing all manner of scrolls made of dozens of type of parchments -- some leathery, perhaps from certain desert beasts, while others appear to be of the highest quality paper.  From somewhere, whether within the shop or one of the nearby buildings or from the street itself, can be heard a faint singing.

It is hard to walk through this medium-sized shop without tripping over the clay jugs splayed across the floor.  Eretesk's prized goods create something of a narrow, maze-like trail through the room as one navigates the stacks and piles of pottery products.

Despite its small size, or perhaps because of it, Uurlath's tiny shop is extremely well kept.  The tiled floor is swept clean of dust, and the clay walls show signs of recent washing.  Narrow shelves line the walls, displaying the potter's wares.

Small and sparsely decorated, the sandstone shop offers a welcoming atmosphere all the same.  A bright blue rug with golden tassels rests just inside the door, directly across from a liberally padded counter and a small painting on the rear wall.  A pillow-topped pedestal stands tall and proud just in front of hexagonal window overlooking the busy street outside.

Smoothly woven white cloth hangs in folds from the cool sandstone ceiling to the matching floor in this sparsely decorated room.  A single shelf draped with thick black velvet provides a sharp contrast not only to the light cloth around it, but also to the creamy white porcelain dolls sitting patiently on it, waiting for a home.

Wobbling uncertainly just above a crooked shelf is a lantern hanging from the ceiling, making the shadows dance oddly across the walls and giving the room a more claustrophobic feeling than it already has.

Unbelievably cluttered, the tiny shop has clearly seen better days.  The slant to the walls, visible from outside, is also clear from within, and they lean precariously inward.  Bits of dried plants and preserved animal parts are tacked to the walls at random intervals.  At least partially cleared, a stained countertop displays a small collection of identical pots.

In the shadow of the steep cliff rising to the north, the hemlocks grow close together, their branches entwined and woven in a matted mass of snarls.  The sky is barely visible overhead and only a wan light penetrates to the needle-covered forest floor.  The distant sound of tumbling rocks ricochets dully off the cliff face high overhead where something climbs, or falls.

The narrow trail plunges on into the dense trees, weaving amongst the scented, drooping branches.  The smaller trees show scars where the bark was stripped away, either by a gnawing animal, or cut and harvested for medicinal uses.

A cliff rises overhead as the northeastern slope of the island sweeps upwards at an impossible angle.  The initial climb up is a mixture of earth and protruding rocks, but not far overhead is a broken face of red-veined dark stone.  Hemlock trees crowd right to the base of the cliff, a few smaller specimens even encroaching up the lower reaches of the ascent.

This chunk of land hides in the overwhelming darkness, both from the structural behemoth and the presence of night.  Though it is hard to tell precisely due to limited visibility, the lot appears free of unnecessary objects and even the coating of sand upon the ground.  Everything about the area exudes separation and discretion.

Chiefly used as a storage facility, the rooftop houses dozens of crates brimming with shadows.  Gentle tings reminiscent of distant cathedral bells dance around the rooftop, seeming to come from the improbable musical stylings of the boxes themselves.  The enchanting scent of jasmine oil pervades the night air like a persistent perfume salesman.

The end of the sun's daily crusade slows the journeys of so many of the city's inhabitants.  A faint sulfuric aroma lingers within the hushed atmosphere, the odor a remnant of the secretive production processes carried on during the business day.  The night's cooler breezes dissipate the pungency, only to be faced with the same problem the following evening.

The singular melody plucked from a string instrument strains to eke out an existence amidst the quietude above the streets.  Several dark banners stationed in even intervals inflate with each gust of wind, adding a percussive beat to the periodic movement in the city.  The fabric also buffers rooftop loiterers from the all-too-observant eyes of law enforcement prowling through the shadows.

Pushed astray by sporadic desert winds, broken bottles and empty cartons roll across the rooftop in rhythmic fashion.  Squat ledges bordering the area as well as imperfect wooden lattices stand out, blacker than the deep blue of the night sky.  The sound of people is never far away, especially during the mad dashes in and out of the theater before and after each performance.

The rooftop's surface shifts underfoot, with its layer of confetti and sand grinding against the tiles with each movement from intruders.  Though quieter now due to the late anlas, music from the streets serenades the space high above the enduring crowds, the noise bouncing off the walls to fill each crevice with sound.  The festivities distract potential onlookers from gazing at the rooftop for very long, rather entrancing them with magic and song to keep them occupied with their immediate surroundings.

Hidden amidst the shadows harbored by the branches and fronds, a circular platform extends inconspicuously around the trunk, high above the street.  The location provides a bird's-eye view of all activity below, though the volume of travelers is lessened by the onset of night.  A string of glowing lanterns stretches across the road to connect the tree to the rooftop of an adjacent building.

Sturdy wooden posts frame the small box of land, the fencing intended to provide as much asylum as possible, keeping the area's activity away from the prying eyes of local authorities.  A low canvas spreads across one corner to create a section completely overtaken by shadows.  Improvised seating in the form of discarded crates delivers a modicum of utilitarian hospitality.

Situated in nearly the direct center of the city, the space here thrums with the pulse of urban nightlife.  A grand landscape of black and blue predominates, the regular desert hues painted over with shadow and darkness with a few twinkles of white from lit windows.  The silhouette of the Golden Heights towers over the rest of the streets, imposing an almost perceptible presence amidst the other structural inhabitants.

Despite the darkness, the distinctive buzz of the renowned bazaar below is still present, albeit more subdued.  Stacked wooden pallets produce a shadowy maze due to their inadvertent partitioning of the broad space.  When moonlight passes through the gaps in the planks, the illumination cast upon the ground mimics checkered tiles in a fancy salon.

Though the spiky clusters in the corners of the confined space are no more than shadowy in the night's dim, they radiate warmth likely retained from bathing in the heat during the day.  A few cylindrical pipes sprout from the sandstone like motionless statues in an outdoor gallery.  The desert breeze blows over the openings, transforming them into crude instruments that color the silence with low, windy tones.

Laid bare to face the glory of the night sky, the square of flat sandstone still retains the warmth from the desert sun.  The streets below lack their usual conversations of expensive treasures and rare finds, leaving the rooftop in marked silence.  Sand upon the ground manages to refract some of the available light, sparkling subtly like so many of the city's fantastic jewels exchanging hands.

Overflow from the dump floods the shadowy crescent of space between a tall wall and the back of the building.  Dimly lit by the city's nighttime haze, simplistic texturing upon the stone reveals several imperfect attempts at defying the judicial authorities inside.

The overpowering smells in this shop, some sickeningly sweet while others are of a more tingling scent, serve as a testament of alchemists' fortitude that would make even the finest tanner, with all the rotting, tarry smells of their work, proud.  As a stark contrast to the deluging nasal distinction, the shop is visually nondescript -- unappealing sandstone walls, unpainted wooden door, unremarkable wooden table.

Even the dullest and most congested nose would be overwhelmed by the staggering assailment of conflicting smells sealed within this bastion of olfactory strength.  Individually sampling the various perfumes within the shop's confines would serve as a virtual impossibility.

A haze of pungent oily smoke belches from a tangled mass of copper piping, stinging your lungs and leaving a sticky film over the glass vials and jars that line the shelves along the wall.  The counters are littered with dried herbs, spilled ink and bits of paper as the alchemist, Tobriash Merrybay, works at his craft.

Water trickles over carefully placed rocks in a fountain that overflows to irrigate the plants of the greenhouse.  Small trees are planted in the lush brown soil, surrounded by low shrubs and vines.  A border of jadice flowers surrounds the gravel walk that winds its way among the plants as novices of the Order of the Green Lady continue their struggle to raise the healing herbs in the desert city of Muspar'i.

This small shop is piled high with bizarre objects, stacked on shelves and racks encircling the sandstone room.  The odd ingredients and vials of unpleasant-smelling liquids are perhaps why Sevitei has a reputation for being the least successful alchemist and perfumer in Muspar'i.

Vibrant silk drapes obscure the rough sandstone of this shop's walls, while lively banners parade about the upper echelons, interrupted by a curtained archway leading to the back room.  Along the walls stand several large vats of dark, almost bubbling liquids and shelves of innumerable and quite unidentifiable alchemic concoctions and ingredients.  The materials, all of dazzling colors of a wide assortment, animate what might otherwise be dull in appearance.

Here at the edge of the Street of Cloth Weavers, those not so accomplished in the trade ply their wares from trays and an occasional stall.  The poorer denizens of Muspar'i, rarely bothering to penetrate further down the row, flock here in hopes of snatching up the inexpensive castoffs of the more opulent districts catered to by the shops further to the southwest.

Thick, heavily dyed area rugs give Yhhsakri's shop the sharp, pungent scent of cloth dye.  Her wares adorn each of the four walls, leaving very little space between them.  The slate floor and clay ceiling are the only surfaces providing any respite from the colorful assault on the eyes, resting carefully unadorned in a quiet counterpoint to the intricately detailed rugs.

A low-set table crouched down upon the rock floor glares across the small expanse of the shop toward a watery blue door.  Plopped onto and tossed about the table, numerous small pouches leave not a trace of wood uncovered.

A thick cloud of sandalwood incense engulfs your senses, hanging just below the low ceiling in a thin fog of blue smoke.  The shop is heavily decorated, trinkets of brass and drapings of colorful silk littering every available surface.  Imogen, though not present, makes her touch known through every nuance of her shop's vibrant display of undeniable -- style.

Small tassels edge a cream-colored rattan rug that contrasts with the dark, sparse furnishings.  A large chandelier holds dozens of small candles whose bright flames are reflected by the crystal pieces displayed around the room.  An open black walnut bookcase displays three crystal sculptures, each on its own shelf.

A wide table containing several sacks presents the weaver's craft to the browsers and shoppers while samples of her work hang from one wall.  Szilri, her work focusing on non-S'Kra formal clothing, runs a tidy shop with nary a speck of dust within her business.

Enclosed within these rough and coarse sandstone walls is a surprisingly formal and showy stock of clothing, woven with an appeal to the discerning eye of wealth.  The products for sale adorn a stone countertop in the center of the cramped room.  A narrow brown door leads to the streets outside.

Sunlight streams through the small shop's windows, casting a warm glow over the work area.  Low stools provide a place for customers to stand for a fitting, and a comfortable rattan chair near the window offers the seamstress a place to sit while she sews.  A colorful braid of embroidery threads bears dozens of tiny silver bells that chime with each breath of wind.

A cyclical row of mannequins vainly model a few decorative articles of clothing, pleading with passing purchasers to exchange their lirums for the proffered pieces.  The clothing, most likely stitched by the old S'Kra shopkeeper that resides up the sealed-off stairwell, is all done in the traditional racial style.

Bolts of many-colored cloth decorate this tiny interior, the silks and chamois and wool hanging from racks and poles.  As a stark contrast to the works-in-progress, a relatively long table displays the finished products.  The sedate and pacific Street of Cloth Weavers can be seen through a white door.

Intricately embroidered patterns are displayed on the walls on cloth strips framed in teak wood.  Threads of different colors have been laid out onto a low counter and covered with glass, showcasing the different types that can be bought.  Neidle, the shop's proprietor, stands behind the counter, smiling at all who enter.

A row of wooden mannequins displays fine sets of elegant green formal wear, the handiwork of the shop's proprietress, while a long table facing the shop's cream-painted door contains sets of the exquisite clothing bundled in knapsacks and backpacks.  Through the open doorway, the sounds of the city destroy any attempt at quiet in the shop.

The floor of this small shop is laid with an exquisitely woven carpet showing the three moons in all their phases against a field of night blue silk.  Several oil lamps are suspended from the ceiling on fine silver chains, their flickering light illuminating a polished teak case along the back wall.  Centered upon the carpet is a low mahogany table covered with an ornate damask cloth.

A catalog rests on the rough wooden counter that divides the front sales area from the work area in the back of the shop.  Knives, daggers and short swords in various stages of completion are heaped in baskets along the back wall.  A sullen orange glow outlines the ill-fitting door that leads to the back room, evidently the forge to judge by the waves of heat that seep around the edges.

Bright sunlight from the open door shines where it touches the silver wares inside this shop.  Silver plaques crowd one another as they perch on mottled grey stone shelves lining the walls, each silently vying for attention as they stand among fellows of myriad shapes and sizes.  A counter of the same stone divides the room near the far wall, preventing the casual peruser from reaching the more delicate wares beyond.
Wooden and metal racks littering the floor and hanging from the shop's sandstone walls display an array of well-crafted weaponry.  A banner reclining along the far wall carries several sinuous marks.

Unlike the owners of most shops in Muspar'i's many mercantile districts, this shopkeeper goes to great lengths to decorate his store.  The sandstone walls, normally a sedately tepid and uninspired color, have been painted in vibrant hues distinguishable, even from the street, through the store's two windows.  Several tapestries hanging above and beside a jewelry case serve to further set the establishment apart.

Shadows would drown the tiny room, were it not for the open doorway.  Various ragged rugs have been spread haphazardly atop each other on the floor, and brightly dyed gauzy fabric drapes from the ceiling to soften the stone walls.  Several rock pedestals are arranged in a semicircle on the carpets, each holding a silken scarf as backdrop for a piece of merchandise.  In the darkest corner, the attendant unobtrusively sips tea between customers.

Muted shafts of colored light dapple the interior of the shop, cascading down from the abstract pattern of jewel-toned glass insets carefully placed in the vaulted ceiling.  Dangling down from the room's peak is a twisted confection of silver and brass chains, from which hangs a caliginous tzgaa orb.  Arranged on a shimmering sandstone counter are a marble tray, slightly tilted to better display the contents, and an obsidian rack.

Bejeweled metal ornaments ostentatiously line the plush interior of a glass case, the display curving in a crescentic way across an otherwise drab and unadorned shop.  Fastidious care is obviously paid the jewelry case, its imported velvet pillows fluffed, its fine glass unsmudged.

Frosted glass lanterns fill the foyer with soft light, complementing the warm wood paneling and thick, dark rugs.  A polished oak table laden with champagne sits in one corner, its lamp shaded with blue glass that casts a sapphirine glow on the wood behind it.  There are no windows, the better to close out the street sounds outside, but the ceilings are vaulted, creating an illusion of immense space.

Two elegantly garbed mannequins dominate the center of the hallway, set to either side of a simple wooden door made of rare desert pine.  The wall paneling becomes more elaborate here, carved at floor and ceiling with tiny flowers.  The pattern seems to extend the full length of the long hallway without repeating.

Tiny wooden panels no larger than a Halfling's thumb cover the floor below from wall to wall, forming an intricate pattern of swirling waves.  A large cabinet carved in the same pattern presides over the room, set between two bright oil lanterns.  Before it sits a low table, and on the far end of the room a tall rack shares a corner with an array of wooden mannequins.

Paneled in dark, fragrant sandalwood, the room is tasteful and bordering on austere.  Its only decoration is a delicate herringbone pattern carved into the wood just below the ceiling, encircling the room.  Small brass censers emit thin strands of blue smoke, filling the air with the scent of tiger lily incense.

Wavering light from a wrought iron candelabrum fights the abundant shadows residing in this small corner, hidden away from the main showroom.  Wax drips from the metal branches onto the surface of a circular table, the congealing liquid forming splatter patterns around several items for purchase, obviously selected for an exclusive clientele.  Placed under a small wooden shelf, a comfortable-looking, albeit drab, leather sofa fills the entire wall opposite the door.

The dark stone staircase briefly halts its upward journey here at a small landing.  A brilliantly-colored green and gold patterned rug covers the stone floor of the landing, its surface slightly marred by the muddy tracks of a large cat.  A large tapestry hangs upon the wall, its surface depicting the aspects of Meraud.

Shaped like a hexagon, the Warrior Mage Guild's library is devoted to instructing members on the history of the Guild, as well as the arcane uses of their power.  Each of the six walls is covered in a mural inspired by one of the elements.  A stand of dark ebonwood holds many volumes of written lore, a treasure for all Mages.

The third floor landing is devoted to the Warrior Mage's eternal companion:  his familiar.  Statues and tapestries depict the countless varieties of familiars, from lizard to dolphin and beyond.  An arch to the east leads to the familiar infirmary, where Mages can tend their companions if they become wounded in battle.

Since most familiars are too sensible to allow their Mage to perform major surgery on them, the small room set off the third floor landing only contains the bare necessities to prevent bleeding.  Cabinets filled with medical bandages and flat wooden boards for splints line the walls.  A large stone table, its surface lightly stained with blood, rests in the center of the room for those familiars small enough to fit upon it.

The portion of the winding staircase that led up to the rooftop has been shattered beyond repair.  All that remains are a few fragments of stone that lie scattered about the landing.  A large glass window which once filled the room with light, is now obscured by a fog or mist outside the tower.

The Guild barracks is dimly lit, the only source of light being what can filter through a large casement window on the western wall, and the mist beyond.  Rows of thinly padded cots and small chests fill the room, provided for the use of junior members of the Guild, or those too poor or avoidable to have a place of their own to stay.

A portion of the cloud which surrounds Stormwill has solidified into a narrow walkway that circles the tower.  The mist looks as fragile as the rest of the cloud, yet seems sturdy enough to support a Gor'Tog in full plate armor.  Leading back into the tower is a small casement window, the only way to access the cloudwalk.
The narrow ledge of mist continues wrapping around the tower, barely wide enough to sidle along.  A small gap in the mist provides a bird's-eye view of the city far, far below.

The mist ledge broadens dramatically at the eastern side of the tower.  A small flight of stairs, each step made of the same mist as the ledge, leads up to the top of the tower.  The stormcloud rumbles and crackles threateningly above.

Where the other areas of the cloudwalk are sturdy as the ground itself, portions here have begun to weaken and dissipate.  The rest of the cloud is thicker than ever, its dark mass churning and rumbling as air currents sweep through it.

The top of Stormwill Tower, as well as its highest floor, is completely enshrouded in a massive stormcloud which never dissipates or moves from its position.  Created years ago by a half-mad mage drunk with power, the storm is now a permanent fixture of the Tower.  Each Guildmaster devotes every waking moment to keeping the storm in check, preventing it from growing large enough to destroy the city.  A small flight of stairs, shaped from the very substance of the storm, leads down to the cloudwalk.

The smell of herbs is strong in this small but well-kept garden.  Numerous herbal flower beds are laid out in rows holding Balm, Chickweed, Fenugreek, Basil and more.  An empath helps an elderly female dwarf slowly around the garden, all the while chanting softly to help ease the senior dwarf's old age ills.

The weather outside suddenly seems beneficent.  Once the frigid wind enters this cavern, whether howling through the cave mouth or swooping in a hole in the mountainside, it gets trapped and gains power as it spirals between gaps in the cavern floors, walls and ceilings.  Each gust spreads a damp, brittle cold that chills even through the thickest armor while appearing to caress a variety of ice formations.  Depth perception is erratic as ice walls almost act like mirrors, reflecting what may not be there.

A slight slope to the ice floor results in a slipping hazard that has been somewhat alleviated by battles fought in the area.  Constant melting and refreezing has mercifully ruined the smoothness of the cave floor, barely visible in some spots under clouded ice protrusions.  Gouges and ruts in the ice allow for last minute balance corrections, saving many a sore behind.

Slippery tunnels, narrowed by ice, seem to twist and turn in no ordered direction.  A huge stalagmite forming here hampers progress even further.  Slick deposits of lime and frost coat the floor so thickly that in places only the most agile can safely pass between it and the ceiling.

Frigid air stiffens anything warm-blooded and makes navigating the slippery cave more treacherous.  The thick ice encasing an extremely narrow passageway to the northeast seems pearlized, as if it was exposed to outside light.  Close inspection of some dark spots in the floor reveals rusted items trapped in the ice.

Claustrophobia easily affects those susceptible, as perspective in here is skewed: the floor slopes slightly upward while the ceiling seems to plunge suddenly, looming just above a Gor'Tog's head.  Protrusions of thicker ice along the tunnel-like walls narrow the passageway further.

Shards of ice litter the floor and crunch into tiny crystals under foot.  A few strands of matted hair are half frozen into the floor.  Puddles of water covered in a frigid glaze mask what lies beneath, increasing the challenge of choosing safe footing.  The slick walls act like mirrors, reflecting what may not be there.

Thick frozen spires jut up from the slick floor, never quite meeting those that hang down from the roof of the cavern but coming close enough to force a change of direction.  Gaping holes in the cave floor plunge into inky depths below the frost line causing passage through the area to be slow and careful.  In some spots, newly formed ice tentatively creeps over old holes, but counting on its ability to hold weight is for the foolhardy.

The sounds of industry are mysteriously quiet in this small alcove of the mountain.  Since many of his potential customers can perform their own repairs, the proprietor of this small shop, Ladar, has much of his time to himself.  He sits on a stool at the side of the room, moving only to take care of the rare customer who wanders in.

Heavy boulders leap out from the middle of the trail and hinder passage through the chasm.  Some stand proudly, reaching toward the sky, while others topple over to lean one against the other like a pair of drunks reeling home after a night at the tavern.

Off to one side of the faint trail through the chasm, a towering silverwood tree stands out amongst the otherwise barren and rocky landscape.  At its base is a stone marker etched with faintly visible lettering.  A lone chicory branch, withered and brown, lies next to the simple landmark.

Silence settles across the chasm, broken only by the occasional soft shower of pebbles down the cliff face.  Retreat continues to remain a viable option against whatever unseen foe might await in the blackness ahead.

Old bones lie in haphazard piles along the cavern floor.  In one far corner, a weathered and eyeless skull peers out from beneath the hood of a tattered grey cloak, its bony mouth agape in silent laughter at your courage.  Cold drafts creep along the floor, seeking out every gap in clothing or armor with a bone-chilling touch.

The only decoration in this bland chamber is a raised dais, on which sits a single chair.  Used by the king's appointees to dole out justice, when they deign to make the trip to this room, the dais almost has the appearance of a throne.  On the far side of the office, a ring of bars surrounds the area where the prisoners are kept, and a heavy iron-bound door leads to the front of the building.

One side of this small stone building is occupied by a large pile of sacks.  Periodically, guards in the red and black uniform of Muspar'i carelessly and haphazardly toss additional sacks, containing some hapless prisoner's belongings, onto the pile.  Near a narrow door, painted to match the justice officials' uniforms, sits a lone wooden desk.

Neat rows of headstones fill three quarters of this small cemetery, which looks to be kept clean and regularly maintained.  Set into the stone at the front of each grave marker is a simple medallion bearing the names of the monks entombed in the area.  Small poplar trees planted in each corner of the cemetery give a bit of shade.

Moss, lichen and bare stone compose the surface of this broad rock, providing a pinnacle from which to view an extensive amount of surrounding land.  Pine to the east contrasts with the large wall to the west and the river beyond, separated only by the rock-strewn earth between.  Below, gouges in the soil are more discernible from this vantage point, seeming to concentrate around the base of the boulder.

The ceiling rises upward and toward the northeast to form a dramatic arched dome, a large marble obelisk centered exactly underneath it.  Puffy white clouds are painted onto the dome, giving it a very open feeling.  Several granite benches line the southern wall, providing a convenient place for a brief respite.

Overshadowing everything else in the room is a massive set of double doors in the northern wall, marking the main entrance to the building.  Although it appears to have been carved with many deities, all of the work is very abstract, making it impossible to recognize any individual one.  The rest of this corner of the commons room is quite bare, with no furnishings at all except a tall marble obelisk standing in the center of the room.

A dramatic arched dome rises in the center of the common room, a large marble obelisk positioned underneath it and standing quite tall.  Muted wisps of cloud are painted onto the dome, mimicking the noontime sky.  Several prayer mats are lined against the north and eastern walls, providing a convenient place for worship.

A curious arrangement graces the southern wall of the common room.  Three arched windows rise high in the stonework, two of them filled with clear, textured glass.  The third is crafted from elaborate stained glass, seeming a little out of place next to the others.
