The tough shrubs littering the side of the ridge give way to wildflowers and lush grass that thrive on the moist soil of the valley floor.

Sinuous shapes occasionally flicker through the tall, thick grass as bright-eyed ferrets scour the area for food.  A half-cropped tuft of buffalo grass shades a hole in the ground that leads to the creatures' burrow.

The tall grasses are thicker to the east and west, but a faint path is worn northward where large animals have made for the stream.  The air is redolent of lush greenery, and one can almost hear the roots unfurling within the earth as the plants grow.

A morass of rocks and dead trees filters the water that flows to the ridge from to the valley floor, creating a natural dam that widens the stream.  Although the stream is murky, the water at the surface is clean and untainted.  Cedar trees shade the stream and keep it cool, and toads croak along the bank in a cacaphony of noise.

The wide stream runs through the small valley, bordered on each side by jutting feldspar stones constantly dampened by the fresh spray.  Tiny minnows dart here and there under the surface, constantly playing in an underwater dance in the clear water and sometimes darting downward and out of sight.  Occasionally leaves and twigs float downstream, carried by the rushing current.

Flowing water eddies against the side of the ridge that walls the small valley, slowly eroding the rock.  Dark blue water below hints that the stream is quite deep, the murky depths disappearing before the bottom is visible.  Small reeds line each side of the bank, small insects jumping back and forth between them.

Overhead, the sky seems bluer than on the grasslands, the high valley walls bringing the span into focus.  An exaltation of larks sometimes sings by, looking for a greener bit of grassland on the plains above.

A curious and unsettling silence hangs heavily over the fog-shrouded countryside.  What little light there is succeeds only in creating eerie phantoms that dance wildly in the lingering mists.  A single oak, tall and majestic, crowns the summit and remains unmarred by the fiery devastation afflicting surrounding areas.  A series of deep marks are clawed into the bark of the tree.

The sky to the northwest is aswirl with burning, shifting colors, reflections of the fire blazing at the heart of the Greater Fist.  Fine ash and drifting embers eddy and swirl with each gust and breeze, moving through the air like swarms of fireflies.  The ground is littered with cracked masonry and bits of shattered mosaic, their colors dull and flat beneath a heavy coating of soot and grime.

The parts from a shattered humanoid statue are scattered here, interspersed with jagged blocks of pumice and tile fragments from ruined murals.  A slender, long-fingered marble hand juts upward from a mound of debris, seeming to wave cheerfully at those who pass this way.

Some rubble-choked steps dominate this area, the massive, black marble blocks that comprise them scattered about like a child's abandoned toys.  The scent of brimstone is more pungent here, the fickle breezes that play through the area stirring the ash that blankets the ground.

A small, bright-red flow of lava oozes across the edge of the courtyard, stretching forth like a questing finger.  Varicolored tiles are scattered everywhere, their bright hues dampened by the ubiquitous ash and soot.

The floor here is almost totally obscured by a long-cooled lava flow, rucked and wrinkled like the skin of an elderly human.  Only one part of the mosaic is visible and unblemished -- a cracked, unblinking eye staring blankly skyward.

A massive black marble plinth dominates this area, largely intact, if empty.  The bits of floor visible despite the ash and dust are deeply scarred and gouged, the mosaic here almost completely destroyed.

Overhead is the loose cover on an abandoned well on the surface, to judge by the muffled footsteps and hoofbeats coming from above.  Directly below the opening, a wooden ladder descends into a shaft in the earth.  A tunnel leads north just under the surface, and another tunnel in the western wall slopes sharply down out of sight.

The tunnel walls are noticeably damper here  -- possibly because the passage lies beneath one of Shard's many waterways.  The steady dripping of moisture calls up frightening visions of the tons of water overhead.

The tunnels widen into a broad oval area where three tunnels converge.  It looks like someone has made their home here at some time in the past.  Debris is scattered throughout the room, and a long unused firepit sits in the north corner.  A pile of mouldering crates near the firepit looks like it might have served as a bed frame.  Perhaps some thief on the run sought shelter here from the forces of law and order.

Brick arches support the foundation of the street overhead, where a barred sewer grate provides easy access to the surface.  Reeking piles of rancid produce have been dumped here by the bazaar vendors above, and the stench discourages any curious surface dwellers from paying this area too close attention.  The sewer tunnel slopes steeply downwards to the southeast.

A stream of refuse flows through a rough channel cut into the floor, reeking of sewage and things better left unexplored.  A rough-hewn shaft in the ceiling rises toward the surface, spotted with slippery but useable stone handholds.  The tunnel continues into the distance to the northwest and slopes upwards slightly to the south.

Once inside, it is obvious that this abandoned carriage barn is not as abandoned as other buildings in the neighborhood.  Although unpainted, the walls are shored up with sound wooden planking, and the flagstone floor is swept clean.  A ladder pokes from an opening in the floor.

The tunnel changes from bare rock to brickwork along a smoothly paved corridor.  The skilled masonry contrasts with the rough, unfinished stone passageways to the west and southwest.  Overhead, an open well climbs far into the shadows, lit by torches attached to the wall every few feet.

The fissure widens slightly into a narrow passage, one that has obviously been worked, but not by skilled hands.  The walls are rough and badly chipped, and the floor is covered with fragments of stone that make the footing treacherous.

This corner of the market runs up along one of the cavern's walls, the black stone inscribed with old Imperial records but the glyphs long since obscured by crude graffitti and chiseled obscenities.  A large stall stands nearby, its billowing sheets woven of purple thread instead of grey like all the others, and the locals give it a wide berth.

Every sort of intelligent being and every walk of life can be seen in the aisles of the Grey Market, from urchins and cutpurses, to adventurers and lesser nobles, the crowds churning in an elaborate dance that only the locals seem to understand.  The best an outsider can do is try to move with them, and cut your own path without starting a brawl.

The few merchants in this area feature items of a different nature and the tempo is much more subdued.  Workmen move large crates, their contents carefully concealed behind closely spaced wooden slats, over the edge of a dark causeway.  Loosely tied bales surround a rag merchant who sits propped against the wall, his hat covering his face as his assumed pose cries easy mark.

Every footstep, man-made or otherwise, reverberates through the cavern.  Hanging from the ceiling, flocks of bats rustle their wings as they slumber quietly.  Glistening webs, some still fresh and damp to the touch, fall in graceful swags against the walls, as if some lunatic decorator has tried to brighten the dark surroundings.

Half-domed, a large underground chamber opens out, formed from eons of erosion through an ancient earthquake fault.  Water bubbles gently from an effervescent pool at the bottom of a towering cascade, accounting for the cool dampness of the grotto.  Diminutive cave fish, devoid of eyes, intermittently thrust sensitive whiskers into the air from the surface of the frothy waters.

Cool, dank air flows through the caverns, dampening fur and hair, and weighing heavily against skin and scale alike.  Shadows pool in the corners, making it hard to see, but an occasional wink of red eyes or the glint of a discarded longsword makes it hard to pretend you're all alone.

For centuries, feeble trickles of mineral-laden water have run down the walls of the cavern, leaving behind them voluminous calcite "draperies".  Folding and curling back and forth along themselves, the shimmering curtains are carefully arranged by the hand of nature.  Even the most talented of artisans could not likely have painted such a display upon a mere canvas landscape.

Tiny rivulets of ice-cold water drop from the ceiling to fall uncaring against the cool stone floor and exposed skin alike.  The dampness of the grotto seeps into your bones to make the cavern seem several degrees colder than it actually is.

Darkness envelops all who venture into the dimmest recesses of the grotto.  A loud shriek, full of agony, echoes from deeper within the cavern.  The sound is distorted by distance, making it impossible to clearly distinguish whether it is produced by man or by some beast about to expire at a hunter's blade.
Rivulets of water trickle down the walls, causing a soft drip to echo throughout the cavern as the tiny droplets splash against the solid rock floor.

Disorientation begins to take a firm hold as the passages twist and turn in all directions.  Shimmering webs of silver lace dangle from the walls and ceiling, gently but firmly tangling the limbs of any who attempt to make their way through the caverns.

Masses of carrot-shaped stalactites descend from the ceiling, forcing one to weave precariously in and out to avoid a sharp welt on the head.  Columns make navigation even more difficult where the low-hanging stalactites flow into stalagmites rising up from the ground.

Darkness envelops all who venture into the dimmest recesses of the grotto.  A loud shriek, full of agony, echoes from deeper within the cavern.  The sound is distorted by distance, making it impossible to clearly distinguish whether it is produced by man or by some beast about to expire at a hunter's blade.

Every footstep, man-made or otherwise, reverberates through the cavern.  Hanging from the ceiling, flocks of bats rustle their wings as they slumber quietly.  Glistening webs, some still fresh and damp to the touch, fall in graceful swags against the walls, as if some lunatic decorator has tried to brighten the dark surroundings.

An unnatural silence settles across the chasm, broken only by the occasional soft shower of pebbles down the cliff face.  Retreat continues to remain quite the viable option against whatever unseen foe might await in the blackness ahead.

Standing guard against heedless entry by less cautious explorers, heavy boulders loom large before a series of dark caverns ahead.  Distinct, sinuous markings that cross over themselves in the dirt floor of the chasm reveal the recent passing of those creatures that crawl along on their smooth underbellies alone.

Now drab and browned by the sun, clusters of once-bright orange paintbrush ramble across the landscape.  Rolling and tumbling in the breeze, like dice in a chance game of hazard, the now tangled vines scratch mercilessly at any bare patch of flesh they may encounter as they flit swiftly past.
From its leisurely perch atop a rock-strewn crag, a small brown lizard lightly tastes the air with its tongue and then quickly scurries across the chasm floor with any encroaching footstep.

Boulders of all shapes and sizes litter the landscape, forcing one to have to weave and climb in and around the chasm.  Dust springs up in heavy swirls without warning, bringing tears to the eyes and evoking more than one fit of coughing.

From somewhere off in the distance comes the mournful hoot of an owl, awakened uneasily from its peaceful slumber.  The intermittent shadows overhead appear to have confused the otherwise nocturnal creature as to whether or not nightfall has, at long last, arrived.

The occasional call of a lone eagle in flight through the abandoned canyon remains the only sound to break the solitude.  Steep slopes covered in loose rubble known as scree are too treacherous to climb, leaving only this twisting path for travelers to make their way through the canyon.

The breeze echoes with a faint creaking sound as large, black shadows wheel and turn overhead.  Heavy boulders grow denser and crowd out the few sprigs of dry, brown grass that so valiantly attempt to rise from between them.

Parched grasses line the winding path and leave one to wonder how far away the river must be for these simple plants to unable to sustain any nourishment.  Rows of large boulders loom menacingly along the horizon.  Perched atop one of the heavy stones sits a scowling grey vulture, furtively scanning the area in search of the next tasty morsel to scavenge.

Settled unobtrusively beneath a lone spruce tree is a narrow bench of sorts.  Formed of two small boulders with a rough log placed across them, the rigid seating silently offers a welcome pause in an increasingly arduous journey.

Tiny brown saplings peer up from amongst patches of withered grass, fruitlessly attempting to gain some lease on life.  Clusters of rocks spring up across the path, rudely interrupting any view of greenery along the trail.

Thick taffelberry bushes reach out along the sides of the trail, inviting further exploration deeper into the chasm.  Sparrows chirp noisily to their mates as they flit from bush to bush in their search for any of the dark, juicy berries to take home to their hatchlings.

Towering stands of silverwood and fir trees line the riverbank, their massive trunks dominating the earth and providing a welcome nest amidst their roots for the weary adventurer.  Peeking out from his burrow with beady black eyes, a furry mole cautiously plans an escape route to the water's edge.

Currents begin to abate and footing is once more attainable as the waters shallow and the icy film floats away in ever-widening parcels.  A much-welcome rush of fresh air fills the nostrils and inflates the chest with sweet relief upon stepping up out of the deeper waters.  Tall clusters of cattails and fronds of eelgrass line the riverbank.

A quick glance upwards reveals a noticeable thinning of the heavy ice sheet across the water.  Light filters through in patches to reveal a school of tiny minnows attempting to conceal themselves among the hairgrass and coontails lining the silt floor.

While the frigid water remains crystal clear, nearly impenetrable beds of bristly muskgrass and stonewart rise up from the river bottom.  Stealthily entwining their slender branches around arms and legs, they quickly become a nuisance making movement through the brisk currents even more perilous.

Dark shadows overhead take the form of an ice hut bored into place, quite likely the favorite hunting ground for some nearby fisherman.  Barely discernible beneath the shadow is a small, though perfectly formed circular opening, expertly carved into the ice sheeting above.

Maneuvering effortlessly along on the swift current, a bevy of large multi-colored trout dart in and out amongst each other.  Vision dims even further as the unrelenting frosting across the surface of the water thickens.

The icy river takes on a mind of its own as the merciless waters become increasingly difficult to navigate.  Great care is required to suppress the instinctual urge to replenish the lungs with air.  Shivers crawl up and down the limbs of the weary traveler.
Fingers and toes are numbed by the bone-chilling cold of the waters.  A large hatch of tiny, newborn salmon floats by, carried along by the ever-strengthening current.

Chilling currents grow ever stronger with further navigation along the river bottom.  Overhead, a solid sheet of ice covers the water, trapping you underneath.  One can only hope for the appearance of an occasional pocket of air near the surface.

Icy fingers crawl up your spine upon entering the frigid waters.  The overwhelming desire to hold one's breath overtakes all other coherent thought.  A small hole in the thick blanket of ice overhead drifts just barely within reach.

Ringed by succulent bushes dotted with flowers kept blooming by the gentle ministrations of skilled lifesculptors, the personal glade of Lady Atladene is canopied by twining ivy and interwoven leaves of the tall birch and willow trees that grow here.  The Lady herself sits at the center of the glade, waiting for the wounded with tireless patience.

Thick blue carpet covers the floor of the entryway, a strip of rich purple down the center to accent it.  Painted murals cover the walls, alive with vibrant hues that pull at the eyes.  The faint sound of talking and laughter echoes down the corridor that leads into the parlor, where the upper class of Shard gather to chat and dine.

A simple church of crumbling brick and dark, aged pine stands here surrounded by walls of rough-hewn stone.  The bare earth leading to its entrance has been pressed flat by the passing of countless generations of worshipers, leaving not even a hardy weed to break the brown vista underfoot.  Despite the poverty of the building, a warm, inviting glow beckons through its open doors.

The city's tiny chapel is a simple square room furnished with polished oak pews facing a raised altar.  The small stained-glass window over the entry door casts a subdued light upon the altar, causing the embroidery on the altar cloth to sparkle with a silky bluish glow.  A single brass candlestick rests in the middle of the cloth.

The sandy soil shifts easily underfoot, sending small landslides down the uneven slope.  Straw-like tufts of grass grow from cracks in rocks and on any vaguely horizontal surface.  Above, a thin trail winds inland through the grass.

Protruding stones provide more solid footholds than the loose and sandy soil.  Further down the slope, the soft loam gives way entirely to large slabs of broken rock.  The soothing sounds of surf washes up from below, pierced now and again by the cry of a sea bird.
Gulls reel and swoop through the sky, crying out soulfully to each other.  Occasionally, one dives and plunges into the sea and emerges triumphantly with a struggling fish in its beak.

In the distance, great masted ships look like splinters of brown and white slipping over the horizon and out of sight while others emerge and gradually draw closer.  Long before the bluffs greeted the ships of mortals, it is rumored they were home to the island's fae.

The wind ebbs and flows like the waves below, but with a rhythm all its own.  Sometimes the soft breezes sound like a ballad quietly whispered between the land and sea, while at other times the wind sings shrilly across the crags like a bitter song of mourning.

The sheer bluffs soften to a sharply sloping talus of rock slabs either broken off of or dislodged from the cliff above.  Water seeps up between the large stones, creating calm tide pools where small schools of tiny silver fish dart about in search of food.

Mist-laden air sprays and swirls around the stony bluffs, slicking the already slippery rock.  Pearly little crustaceans about the size of walnuts cling to the safety of a slim crevice in the rock face.

Light and shadow play against the surf.  Sunlight catches waves as they grow from the sea and rides the crest above little pools of darkness that bob in and out of view.  As the waves crash against the stony shore, both are lost in a jubilant spray of white foam.
An algae-stained precipice littered with broken rock and shells reaches out from the bluff in a broad arm that seems to hover just above the waterline.
Briny water left by the receding tides fills the slim aperture in the stone.  Slimy strands of seaweed cling to the rock just above the waterline.
The deep grey, mica-flecked stone walls have been worn smooth by ages of tides flowing through the narrow fissure.
The uneven walls grow close, making the passageway more difficult to navigate.
Thin light glows vaguely above and diffuses shadows lurking within the fissure.
Most of the encroaching sand has been cleared away, leaving the once-smooth paving stones exposed anew.  The air is heavy with dust and the acrid smell of hot rock and sand.
Jumbled stones lie heaped in disordered piles where buildings once stood.  A few withered weeds sprout from cracks, struggling to survive in the blasted environment.
Piles of broken rock and sand snake across the otherwise barren stones of the plaza, the forerunners of the blasted surroundings ready to rebury the ruins under debris and dunes.
Partially cleared spaces vie with the aggressive sand that keeps trying to return the reclaimed concourse to dunes.  Paths lead to various stone buildings reclaimed from the desert.
A single lantern casts a fitful light over the musty chamber.  Sand drifts in small rills on the stone floor, piling up in the corners.

Piles of sand and rocks show where efforts at beating back the badlands have borne fruit.  The cleared areas include a couple of stone buildings which have been reclaimed for habitation from the wasteland.

Broken boards and other debris are swept against the walls, clearing a space in the middle of the room.  A hastily assembled shelf holds a flickering lamp which sheds an irregular light throughout the building.
Makeshift sconces line the walls, holding flickering candles that barely beat back the gloom.  Although the room has been cleared of most obstructions and debris, some still fill the corners.

Tumbled stones litter the platform, refugees from higher on the structure.  A trail has been hacked out of the surrounding vegetation, allowing access further around the edifice.  The middle and upper platforms, covered with tangles of foliage, loom over the crude pathway.
A few blocks have fallen from the heights, providing obstacles for the path hewn from the jungle.  The upper platforms tower over this, the lowest terrace.
Most of the encroaching sand has been cleared away, leaving the once-smooth paving stones exposed anew.  The air is heavy with dust and the acrid smell of hot rock and sand.

Hewn from the surrounding flora, a crude pathway zigzags between jumbled rocks that cover the platform.  The upper platforms tower over this, the lowest terrace.  Some of the stones have been cleared off in the beginnings of attempts at archaeological work.
The upper levels soar in vertical stone walls above the lower level.  A few blocks have fallen from the heights, providing obstacles for the path hewn from the jungle.

The two upper platforms, covered with tangles of vines, loom over the crude trail zigzagging between fallen stones.  Some of the stones have been cleared off to the side in the beginnings of attempts at archaeological work.
Hacked from the surrounding undergrowth, a narrow trace zigzags between fallen rocks that cover the platform.  Some of the stones have been cleared away to begin the process of excavation.
The middle and upper platforms, covered with vines and trees, loom over the trail hacked out of the surrounding vegetation.  The constant calls of insects and birds fill the air.
Fallen stones litter the platform, refugees from higher on the edifice.  The middle and upper platforms, covered with trees and vines, loom over the twisty pathway.

The ever-present jungle growth crowds in on the narrow path, threatening to once more reclaim it.  Puddles from prior rains stretch across the footpath, settling into the depressions in the stones of the pyramid.

Buffered by forest to the north, this meandering trail is shaded by towering deobar trees high overhead.  Sparsely laid out, the trees provide an attractive shelter to the homes nestled amidst the foliage, while a large meadow opens up away from the forest.

The occasional clanging monastery bell sounds in the distance, summoning monks from their various tasks for service.  A crowing chicken waddles along the narrow path trying to assert its dominance over the mellifluous bell.  Wildflowers stretch in every direction giving each house that lines the path a vibrantly colorful lawn.

Wooden pallets form an uneven trail through the thicker woods.  Massive blueberry bushes dot the area creating a dense canopy for small skittering woodland animals.  Tucked into the overgrowth, thatched cottages melt into their surroundings, creating harmony between habitation and the natural world.

The soft babbling sounds of a nearby brook mingle with the occasional scuffling of small creatures and the ever present chirrups of local birds.  A pair of benches line the cobbled brick pathway that encircles a massive pagoda tree surrounded by tall grasses bent to either side from the traffic of local residents.

Solid rock walls curve gently toward each other and come together somewhere above but the peak has been lost in the shadows.  Torches line the walls at regular intervals, their illumination nearly drowned out by a more intense light coming through an ogee arch.  The other end of the tunnel fades into a murky darkness to the north, only visible because of the torches lining the walls.

A pinprick of light to the south is the only indication that this tunnel has any end.  The darkness is held at bay by a number of flickering torches bolted to the wall.  Carved into the rock wall, small arrows next to the crest of the Warrior Mage guild point north.

A narrow staircase plunges at a sharp, but passable, angle downward into darkness.  Torches bracketed to either side illuminate both the tunnel leading southward, and the rough stone of the first few steps down.

A set of narrow stairs leads up at a sharp angle towards a doorway in the distance.  The climb is steep in comparison to a set of broader steps which lead gently downward.  The air is damp and algae has grown in the cracks between squared stone blocks which form the staircase walls.

A long hall separates two sets of steps, the algae-covered walls flanked by plain stone pillars.  Broad stone steps gently slope upwards towards the south while to the north narrow stairs ascend steeply to an archway high above.  The air is rank with a musty scent caused by stagnant puddles formed in low spots in the floor.

Two large, fire-filled bronze bowls sit on either side of a small archway, working to light up the large tunnel.  The flames are bright enough that they illuminate the smooth stone walls which slope upwards into a tapered point as well as a set of narrow stairs which lead down on the other side of the arch.

Two torches are bracketed to the unnaturally smooth stone walls of an arched tunnel, dimly lighting a crag which juts out above a body of water.  The feeble light does little and shadows press in oppresively as the walls fade away into oblivion, giving off a sense of vastness.

A stone bridge rises out of the lake and traverses the gap between an arch in the southern wall and the shore, leading up to a gateway.  Tall wicker torches line the small beach, illuminating the stone fortress' walls and giving it a menacing look.  Two silver banners hang down from the crenellations and flank the gateway, each bearing the crest of the Warrior Mage Guild.

Torches line the beach, flickering and sputtering in the damp cavern air and illuminating the fortress walls.  The dominant sound is that of water lapping against the sandy shore, but occasionally there is the drip of falling water elsewhere in the cavern.

Torches line the beach, flickering and sputtering in the damp cavern air and illuminating the fortress walls.  The dominant sound is that of water lapping against the sandy shore, but occasionally there is the drip of falling water elsewhere in the cavern.

Large stone blocks stack atop one another to create a dull grey wall that surrounds the courtyard.  A steel portcullis is raised, allowing access to and from the courtyard through an arched gateway.  Large slabs of green slate pave the ground, covering nearly every square inch.  Care has been put into maintaining the area as none of the slabs contain cracks or even pitting.

A variety of mushrooms, ranging in size from pebbles to large Gnomes, fill this section of the courtyard.  A drainage ditch reveals a thick layer of soft loamy soil that spreads across the stone plateau, giving the mushrooms ample fertilizer.  Tightly fitted stones form what looks to be a low wall, ending almost a foot above the courtyard floor.  A sign is placed at the edge of the garden bearing large, white letters.

A catapult sits broken in this corner of the courtyard.  The wood shows signs of rot and the throwing arm is completely smashed beyond any repair.  A ladder has been set up next to the catapult, leading up the south wall.

A flight of white marble steps leads from the courtyard to a limestone hall.  Two large brass braziers sit outside the door of the hall, casting off light and a generous amount of smoke.  The limestone walls are highly polished, gleaming even in the light cast off by the braziers.

A covered stone well sits next to a tall wall, which surrounds the courtyard.  The well looks to be no longer in use as a large board covers up the mouth and the bucket is missing.  A sign bearing large, white letters sits next to the well.

Iron sconces, bracketed to the walls outside the fortress just below crenellations in its fortifications, dimly illuminate the battlement and the lake below.  Small pinpricks of light illuminate a bridge that leads to an arching entrance in a rock wall across the water from the keep.  The top of a ladder can be seen peeking above the inside of the wall, leading down to the green slate floor of the courtyard.

Iron sconces have been bracketed to the walls on the outside of the keep and provide a dim illumination.  The battlements stretch from east to west, overlooking a stone bridge that leads to the southern wall of the cavern.  The entrance of the Warrior Mage Guild is visible here, the crenellations angled so that a casual glance down would allow one to see anyone entering or leaving the guild.  Two silver banners are visible through the crenellations, each bearing the crest of the Warrior Mage Guild.

Iron sconces, bracketed to the walls outside the fortress just below crenellations in its fortifications, dimly illuminate the battlement and the lake below.  Water from the lake laps up against a sandy shore near the base of the fortifications while a large rock wall rises up to the south.  Occasionally, a loud dripping echoes from elsewhere in the cavern, disturbing the soothing sounds made by waves upon the sand.

Smooth stone walls have been polished to a glassy sheen.  The smell of smoke is heavy in the air and comes mostly from the direction of a leather flap in the northern wall.  A Dwarven attendant mutters to himself as he goes about his business of arranging and re-arranging the same items for no apparent reason.

A smoky smell from years of burning torches mingles with the smell of roasted food coming from the direction of a long table.  The polished oak table spans the hall, sitting directly below the peak of the thatched roof.  Flanking the table on either side is a row of thick stone columns that support wooden crossbeams.  A large bronze-banded oak door leads out to a courtyard paved with green slate.

A long, polished oak table sits in the center of the hall.  On either side of the table are benches where a few weary looking warriors sit, eating food slowly from plates set before them.  Columns artificially partition the area into three segments, creating a wide walkway on either side of a long table that makes it easier to traverse the hall without bothering feasting warriors.

A large space has been cleared at this end of the hall where a tall throne sits.  The gilded chair bears the Warrior Mage Guild crest on the back.  Behind the throne, two elaborate tapestries flank a small door that seems plain in comparison.  A polished oak table spans the length of the hall.

Upon the table sits a large feast, the aroma pleasant and inviting.  Several warriors sit at various places on long benches to either side of the table, their boisterous voices carrying throughout the hall as they chat animatedly with each other.  Occasionally an apprentice silently scurries up to the table and cleans up a spilled goblet or picks up a used plate.

A high-backed wooden chair, bearing a large pair of antlers, sits behind a cluttered desk so that it faces a small door.  A large gilded bookcase sits squarely against the northern wall and has been stuffed near to bursting with various books, tomes and scrolls.
Surprisingly, the little lake is no more than ankle deep, hardly fit for any type of carousing.  The water is a pleasant, deep blue color and wonderfully cool to the touch.

Banners representing every Elothean house hang from the ceiling, and one massive one of the House of the Steel Dove serve as the backdrop for the justiciar's dais at the far back of the room.  No forms of seating can be seen in all the chamber, a gesture that implies one should not loiter here long.

Three gleaming desks create an open-ended rectangle here, one for each of the patrol leaders of Shard.  A glass display case holds the names of the criminals foolish enough to have attracted the attention of the elite watchmen of the city.  A painting of the Ferdahl hangs over the doorway, some words written in gold ink beneath her face on the frame.

Indefinable odors waft from various mortars, pots and cauldrons on tables and shelves throughout the shop.  Herbs, carefully dried and cured, hang in bunches from a drying rack suspended from the ceiling.  Everything the serious alchemist could possibly want or need can be found in here.  A section of shelving separates a tall ironbound door from a smaller wood door on the opposite wall.

Pure white alabaster offsets a striking multihued fresco dominating the rear walls of this majestic foyer.  Thirteen shimmering gaethzen lamps dangle from the edge of a circular opening midway between a naturally formed pool and the expansive dome overhead.  A crystal weer telescope sits amid a framework of ironwood beams and brass machinery.  The telescope's tremendous tube angles upwards, providing it access to the heavens.

Hanging from a chain attached to the ceiling's center beam, a crude votive lamp of murky wine-colored glass spills muted illumination upon a low rosewood table.  Charcoal woolen curtains and a padded bench draped with purplish-black felt enhance this shadowy atmosphere.  As if escaping the darkness, an occasional draft flees whistling up a wide circular staircase.

The drab stone walls of the shop are given dazzling color by an assortment of tapestries and banners hanging throughout.  Resting to one side, a solid table displays a loom alongside bolts of smooth, regal silk and a bundle of thick wool.  Carefully arranged near the material on the wooden tabletop are glass jars of oils, paints and dyes.

Sturdy oaken shelves, wicker baskets, and a wooden counter display a variety of clerical wares and necessities in the shop of Sister Nongwen.  The air is heavy with smoke from sputtering oil lanterns and incense burners that flicker eerily, casting dark shadows on the shuttered windows.  Bundles of herbs and wild grasses hang from exposed rafters, partially obscuring a dimly lit corner of the store.

Motes of white drift through the air, dusting patrons with flour or coating them in sugar depending on what is baking at the moment.  A wood counter, built of peeled logs thick enough to support the weight of customers peering over at the merchandise, displays pans with the shop's offerings for the day.

Tiny and dark, the shop is lit only by a smoke-darkened lantern hanging directly over the tall counter dividing the room.  In front of the counter is only a bucket and an expanse of wood-planked floor, dirt-blackened in the corners but with a polished trail leading straight in from the doorway.  Behind the counter are heaps and piles of used goods, some sorted and others simply stacked.

Hibarnhvidar's lamp and lantern shop is either cozy or cramped, depending on one's outlook.  Three or four customers would crowd this tiny establishment, but almost all of the wares are within arm's length, except for the flammable stuff.  That sits behind a high counter out of reach of the public.

The cliffside chateau dominates the view.  Its entrance was designed to face the sun as it rises and the exterior architecture, with steep-angled gables, wrought-iron embellishments, crenelated cornices, and myriad turrets, captures the feel of an alpine castle.  The road leading west from this gatehouse to the chateau is paved with neatly inlaid flat limestone slabs.  Beyond the tall iron gates in the other direction, the limestone gravel road leads east and down to the docks.

The mighty Segoltha River surges toward this island from the west.  On a clear day, the sparkling waters of Sawstwar Lake are visible in the distance.  As the Segoltha meets Ain Ghazal Island, immense boulders placed either by plan or by fortuitous fate block the vital force of the current and split it into two fast-moving forks that pass to the north and south of the island.  Directly below, an overhanging precipice blocks most of the view of the other western segments of the Spiral Road.

The vast forested expanses of the Himineldar Shel lie to the south.  Miles of obscuring atmosphere between each range of mountains make it appear that each row of mountains is floating slightly above and beyond the nearer mountains.  To the southwest looms the colossal eminence of Mount Hibarnhvidar.  This road curves down to the northwest and up to some iron gates in the northeast.  Directly below, an overhanging precipice blocks most of the view of the other southern sectors of the Spiral Road.

The gravel road that spirals down to the river and the docks passes through tall iron gates to the west.  Beyond the gates, where the chateau looms, the gravel is replaced with fitted flagstone.  To the east, the vigorous Segoltha River continues its journey toward River Clan and the Reshal Sea beyond.  An overhanging precipice directly below blocks most of the view of the other eastern segments of this road.

This covered walkway between two rows of slender marble columns leads to the massive front doors of the chateau, which dominate the west side of the portico.  Tall lanterns flank the magnificent doors.  The mosaic marble terrace is bordered with violet glowstones, which emit a dim light, while flowerpots and planter boxes add a fresh scent and a splash of color to the area.  An animite arch carved with the words "Ain Ghazal Auberge" leads north and a small path slopes down to the south.

Tucked against the soaring stone walls and towers of the chateau, a small haven of tranquility has been lovingly created.  Gracefully carved wooden benches line the pathway from the arch to double doors crafted of subtly incised walnut that lead into the auberge.  A tumble of stones falls from a slice of exposed cliffside, and a babbling stream of water falls with the stones, lending a musical counterpoint to quiet conversation.

Chairs and couches upholstered in tasteful burgundy silk brocade are scattered in clusters around this large reception area.  Dark wooden beams curve upward, meeting at the apex of the lofty ceiling, and finely detailed murals grace the walls between the beams.  The faint aroma of fine cuisine and a low hum of conversation drifts from behind some elegantly draped curtains, while the front desk lies just to the west.

Tables covered in snowy linen are scattered across a plush brandy-colored carpet, with centerpieces of flowers and candles lighting each table.  The pale glow of overhead chandeliers, along with dim light from the floor-to-ceiling windows creatively framed with gossamer burgundy drapes, maintains a subdued ambiance.  The soft hum of conversation and the clink of heavy silver cutlery on fine china provide the background for an intimate dining experience.

Low tables surrounded by plushly upholstered chairs fill the room, spaced just far enough apart that conversations can be private.  Thick carpeting on the floor and burgundy velvet drapes contribute to the hushed environment.  Some patrons stand near the tall windows on the east side of the room, sipping drinks and gazing down at the river.  An occasional discreetly dressed waitress glides across the room, taking orders and serving drinks and light meals.

Just west of the main entryway, a long marble counter serves as the inn's front desk.  The Innkeeper works behind the counter, maintaining the register and controlling room keys that hang from a golden pegboard.  Travelers come and go, some arranging lodging for a night or two and others staying longer, presumably to study and contemplate with the community.  A sana'ati wood staircase with a plush, deep-burgundy carpet runner sweeps upward to the guest rooms.

Warm peach sponged with subtle shades of pink and cream paint adorns the walls, harmonizing with the rich orange-red tones of the flamewood arch.  A hint of sandalwood perfumes the air with its exotic fragrance.  Mirrors in carved teak frames reflect the flattering glow of the bayberry tapers positioned atop the counters and shelves, brightening the room.

Ensuring that each of the well-appointed staterooms through the doors on the east wall has a river view, this hall runs north and south deep into the rock of Ain Ghazal.  Airy and spacious with a high ceiling, despite being effectively underground, the broad corridor is well lit with several chandeliers and numerous wall sconces.  The sana'ati staircase leading down to the front desk continues upward in the form of wide, plushly carpeted sana'ati steps.

This spacious landing has abundant room for luggage, and the specialized furniture required for some guests, to await moving in or out of the luxurious suite at the top of the Auberge.  The vaulted ceiling rises high above, but a bright crystal chandelier adorned with dozens of Eluned's tear sapphires chases away even the thought of any gloom or darkness.

This sumptuous suite affords deep-pile chestnut carpet with lush cherrywood paneling and furniture.  Detailed in gold-embroidered amaranthine silk bedding filled with eiderdown, the wide four-poster bed has a matching canopy and adjustable drapes.  Silk upholstered chairs and settee gather around a low table, while a desk and chair are available for letter writing.  A wide balcony offers a panoramic view of the Segoltha River, with River Clan skiffs constantly moving to and from the East Pier far below.

Rare adderwood paneling, with its swirling and weaving grain, lends a fanciful touch to this large room.  The four-poster adderwood bed, covered in rich rose and platinum brocade, is embellished with a matching canopy.  Tall windows draped with silvery lace curtains fill the east wall, and a cantilevered balcony extends a pace or two to a filigreed platinum rail.  From the balcony, there is an excellent vista of the Segoltha River flowing downstream, with the East Pier and the River Clan skiffs far below.

Warm goldenoak paneling on three walls embraces a fluffy and inviting oversized feather bed with a burgundy silk duvet embroidered in gold.  Light streams through the lightly curtained windows that comprise the entire east wall, picking up highlights in both the weave of the bedding and the wood of the walls.  A small, buttressed balcony, guarded by an ornate golden rail, allows one to open the window and take a step or two out to a view of river and sky and skiffs.

In this cozy room, a large bed covered with a silver-embroidered burgundy comforter uses most of the space.  Plush rugs add warmth to the polished hardwood floors, and sheer white drapes cover the tall windows along the entire east wall, allowing plenty of light while providing privacy.  In the center of the glass wall, a tiny balcony juts out so that guests may open the window and take a step or two out of the room before encountering the sturdy silver rail.

Well-tended plants grow alongside the paths, decorate the walls, and hang from the ceiling.  Marble steps lead down into the renowned mineral baths, and numerous oak benches and chairs offer comfortable repose between soaks.
Half a dozen comfortable seats and recliners with headrests are carved into the submerged white marble.  The soothing cadence of trickling water invites carefree relaxation.
Framed by lovely climbing honeysuckle vines, a sturdy narrow door leads into the chateau.  A small stone path leads north and up to the portico, while a faint trail heads farther south and down.

In this protected glade, surrounded by thick vineyards, tall green grass sways in an ever-present soft breeze.  An oval bed of densely-blooming daisies lights up the center of the glade, and a faint trail slopes up to the north.

This entryway has plenty of room for residents to hang cloaks on pegs and several racks on which they may place wet or dirty shoes and boots.  Benches allow sitting while removing footgear, and a neat stack of soft slippers is available for anyone who might need them.

This brightly-lit study hall provides chairs in partitioned nooks along the walls, chairs in individual carrels, and solitary desk chairs.  Only the scratching of pens on paper and the rustle of book pages being turned break the absolute silence.

Stuffed chairs line the walls and numerous small tables surrounded by simple wooden chairs are set up in the middle of this large room.  Bright wall lamps allow reading and studying throughout the room, although quiet conversation sometimes turns to animated discussion here.  Serious study is best left to other areas of the chateau.

This quiet dormitory is filled with rows of spartan and austere cots, about half of which are occupied by sleeping forms.  Most of the cots are about six feet long, but there are a few that are longer.  Widely spaced wall lamps offer dim light.

Like most institutional dining rooms, this room is simple and functional.  Nevertheless, the long rows of tables and benches are smoothly sanded and polished, curving gently to support the average human form.  There are a few taller tables with significantly bigger benches, and a few tables and benches that are much smaller.  Simple glass lamps mounted on wall brackets provide ample light.

This capacious kitchen is constantly bustling, like a beehive disturbed by a fool.  Every inch of wall space is utilized by ovens, stoves, counters, sinks, and an icebox, with waist-high islands in the center of the room and appetizing aromas coming from every direction.  Cooks, servers and dishwashers hurry about their business, weaving in and out around each other without ever colliding.  Despite the energy of controlled chaos, the room is exceptionally clean and maintains a functionally low noise level.

This room is an extension of the kitchen to the east -- equally busy, equally functional, and equally clean.  The foods cooked here suggest simpler fare than the gourmet dishes created in the adjacent room, probably because the stairway and dumbwaiter that lead to the banquet room connect directly to that kitchen.  Nevertheless, delectable aromas fill the air.

Nevertheless, the long rows of tables and benches are smoothly sanded and polished, curving gently to support the average human form.  There are a few taller tables with significantly bigger benches, and a few tables and benches that are much smaller.  Simple glass lamps mounted on wall brackets provide ample light.

This quiet dormitory is filled with rows of spartan and austere cots, about half of which are occupied by sleeping forms.  Most of the cots are about six feet long, but there are a few that are longer.  Widely spaced wall lamps offer dim light.

The vaulted ceiling far above is painted to resemble blue sky with puffy white clouds.  Eleven tables with lace tablecloths, exceptional place settings, fresh flowers, and an elegant chandelier over each table, seem prepared for a banquet.  One table is prominent on a raised dais at the end of the room, and ten longer tables lie perpendicular to the head table.  The Grand Staircase is to the east and a smaller service stairway to the south, next to a spotless dumbwaiter, leads down to the kitchens.

Crystal chandeliers high in the gold vaulted ceiling light this spacious area, and heavy tapestries soften the cold hardness of the stone walls.  Fluted marble columns line the hall, reflecting lightly across the crystal arabesque floor, and a plush red carpet leads up the Grand Staircase to the west.  Sisters and visitors pass along a cloistered balcony high above that encircles the room.  A marble rose and a statue stand in the middle of the chamber, and a number of busts are displayed on pedestals.

The masterfully crafted cherry wood floor is clearly the centerpiece of this elegant ballroom.  Lit candles in dozens of niches form arches along the indigo marble walls, creating a twinkling atmosphere.  A platform at the west end of the room could easily accommodate a small orchestra.

As visitors enter the chateau through this enormous circular foyer, their first view is of sweeping dual stairways that lead upward in elegant curves to a gold marble balcony.  Through a dreamstone-inlaid arch to the west, between and beyond the stairways, is a lofty Great Hall lined with fluted marble columns.  Reddish light from a score of oil lamps creates a glow that warms the sky blue marble floor.

rooms.desc: Comfortable furniture is scattered throughout this elegant theater lobby, just south of the Chateau Foyer.  Gilded theatrical masks frame the amphitheater doors, and an empty marble counter, covered now with a white linen cloth, acts as a refreshment stand when the theater is in use.

To the west, this gold marble balcony continues around the walls of the Great Hall, high above the floor.  Sweeping dual stairways lead in elegant curves down to the foyer, a steep spiral staircase leads upward, and a cherry wood door opens to the south.

Rich reddish brown cherry wood paneling, a deep-piled wool carpet, and dramatic drapes that flow in graceful curves across the entire ceiling cover every inch of the stone that encases this room.  Locked display cases showcase some of the instruments acquired by the Sisters over the years.  In one corner a huge concert harp stands behind a burgundy velvet rope, and behind another rope is a magnificent harpsichord.

rooms.t: [Ain Ghazal Chateau, Balcony Above Great Hall]
rooms.desc: This cloistered balcony circumnavigates the perimeter of the Great Hall, far above its remarkable floor.  The elaborate crystal chandeliers are almost within reach.
Rich wall hangings and a thick carpet deaden sounds in this room.  Through a carved stone arch, rows of audience chairs fill the four balconies overlooking the Synod Chamber.
This audience balcony overlooks the dais of the Synod Chamber.  The individual, carved and polished mahogany seats are simple yet comfortable, with smooth armrests.
This long hallway leads north and south along the east side of the chateau, sloping slightly upward to the north.

Two long halls intersect here.  One leads west, sloping slightly upward, and the other leads south, sloping slightly downward.  At the inside corner an enclosed stairwell with steep steps tunnels upward toward the southwest.

This is one of the rare areas in the chateau that seems uncomfortably confined and almost claustrophobic.  A long vertical ladder with rungs carved into the stone leads up, and a steep enclosed stair leads down.

A crenelated wall girds this outdoor platform surrounding the bell tower at a height from which one can see far into the distance in all directions.  The Journalai Mountains loom to the north, the Himineldar Shel to the south flaunt their lush green forests, and the Segoltha River flows from far to the west to the Reshal Sea far to the east.  A short stairway goes up to the bell chamber itself, and a wooden door is visible under the stairs.  Rungs carved into the stone lead down into the chateau.

The walls, ceiling and floors are paneled with rare burled thuya wood, oiled to a lustrous sheen.  A raised platform with a restraining banister allows visitors to observe the carillonneur from a short distance, so as not to interfere with the musical performance.  Two banks of batons, one at waist level and the other at the feet, form the musical keyboard for this centuries-old carillon.  Connected to each baton is a thick wire that leads through the ceiling to the bell chamber above.

Dozens of bronze bells of various sizes are bolted to huge wooden beams and obviously remain stationary during performances.  Movable metal clappers, connected to thick wires that disappear through tiny oval slots in the marble floor, carry the impulses of the carillonneur from the batons below to the bells above.  A short stairway leads down to the bastion.
This long hallway leads east and west along the north side of the chateau, sloping slightly upward to the west.
This long hallway leads east and west along the north side of the chateau, sloping slightly upward to the west.

This classroom has many individual deskchairs, with a lectern and easel at the front of the room.  Next to the easel is a neatly-organized cupboard filled with rolled-up maps and documents and pointers of various lengths.  A pitcher and glass of water rest on a silver tray on one corner of the lectern.

Set up to service several meeting rooms with concurrent sessions, this room is the staging area for conference refreshments.  Foods and drinks, soon to be balanced on the silver trays of the attendants, are organized on wide counters and tables.  Dirty dishes are quickly whisked off to the kitchen for cleaning.

This large and functional meeting room has a polished oak table, a number of matching wooden chairs, and a chalkboard with many pieces of colored chalk.  On the long table, there is a silver tray holding a pitcher of water and some glasses.

The thick woolen carpet and lustrous wood paneling absorb any small noises that might be made in this quiet vestibule.  The Archive Docent sits reading a book behind a mahogany desk with a small sign on it.

Deep within the silent rock of Ain Ghazal, the Archives proper have the same thick woolen carpet and lustrous wood paneling as the vestibule above.  Like an optical illusion, countless rows of bookshelves seem to taper off in the distance, but never quite disappear.

A fine mist of water floats above the Segoltha as the river crashes into a cluster of towering boulders and cleaves to flow in two branches around the island.  The surface of the road is damp and the air reverberates with the constant thunder of the battle between Segoltha water and Ain Ghazal rock.  A low wall borders the outside edge of the River Road and the Spiral Road branches upward to the southeast, heading toward the chateau at its apex.  A moist cliff also leads uphill.

Waiting for a skiff is made interesting by an intriguing placement of rocks.  Though many try to climb down to decipher them, they are warned off by a large, brooding Gor'Tog.  A dark wood pier juts off from the hard packed ground.

The river surges past, merging at the eastern end of the island in white-capped eddies that swirl around the pier's pilings.  Dead fish and waterweeds mingle with the aroma of cookshops to the west.  Coils of tarred ropes lash the pilings to the base of the pier, leaving dark streaks against still-bright patches of new wood that mark this as a recent extension to the main dock.

Another ring of the Spiral Road is visible below, and below that the northern arc of the River Road curves around the island.  The north fork of the Segoltha River leaps and plunges from west to east along the bottom of the gorge, and across the river the Journalai Mountains rise abruptly from the river's northern edge.  An overhanging precipice shades the road, and an escarpment leads downward.

Moving with prodigious force toward the island from the west, the Segoltha River creates magnificent sprays of water wherever it encounters boulders rising above the river's surface.  At the foot of the island, a formation of spectacularly large boulders bifurcates the rush of water into two branches, generating huge fan-shaped geysers and a near constant rumble.  When the sun shines on the spray, dozens of rainbows play across the airborne water droplets.

The tiny fires of hundreds of candles placed in all corners of the room cast gleaming warm highlights that reflect off the polished wood from which the bank lobby was built.  Thick beams criss-cross the ceiling, and solid pillars -- looking as though they were made of whole tree trunks -- march along all four walls.  The wood is a medium shade, neither oppressively dark nor so light as to appear freshly cut, and has been lovingly polished until it glows.

Raw wood and sawdust litter the floor of the Assay Office, and scaffolding, loose timbers, planks, and tools lie everywhere.  Amidst the noise of hammers and saws, an assay clerk stands impassively behind a tin-topped counter.

A stately oak staircase ascends to an airy second floor gallery, proving an overlook to the milling crowd below.  Through the railings that prevent people on the upper story falling to the Reception hall, traders and shoppers can be seen haggling and handling merchandise.  Above the noisy mob rises the vaulted wooden ceiling, its crystal chandeliers lighting the entire building.

The frigid water gambols along the steep and muddy river's edge, so clear it catches whatever starlight fills the sky and twinkles like liquid silver.  The tree branches hanging over the river are much higher than during the daytime, when birds perch above the water looking for fish to eat.
The cold currents steal whatever warmth they touch, flowing strong and clear as crystal.  In the darkness, the river seems endless.

The cold currents steal whatever warmth they touch, flowing strong and clear as crystal.  In the darkness, the river seems endless.

Piles of stone and heavy boulders cap the craggy shore, making it inaccessible from the river.  From between the stones grow woody plants that produce hardy orange blooms in late autumn that become straw-like into the winter months until blown away by a storm.  To the north, the earth slips down to the water's level.
The cold currents steal whatever warmth they touch, flowing strong and clear as crystal.  In the darkness, the river seems endless.
The cold currents steal whatever warmth they touch, flowing strong and clear as crystal.  In the darkness, the river seems endless.
The numbing waters of the Liirewsag chase foamy whitecaps that rollick over the ragged river edge.  Crickets chirp in the darkness from the bushes dotting the crags alongside the water.

The *plunk* of pinecones falling into the river from overhanging boughs punctuates the water's steady burbling.  Cones and splintered branches that fell short of the water lay strewn across the treacherous crags along with the bloated and half-eaten carcass of an unfortunate boar.

Saplings growing from slivers of earth caught in the crevices of the stony crags lining the river arc gently out over the water.  Their shallow roots extend over the surface of the stone and dangle in the river, embrangling whatever debris or unlucky swimmer the current sweeps too close.

The water laps against the steep crags to the east, tugging at the inaccessible bank like a child pulling on its mother's apron strings for attention.  Greys and browns paint the layering of generations on the face of the rocky wall.

A large rock rises from the river's swift current like a small island in a storm-tossed sea.  The rollicking water splashes and swirls around the base of the rock, but the top is dry and well above even storm swells.
The cold currents steal whatever warmth they touch, flowing strong and clear as crystal.  In the darkness, the river seems endless.

Were it not for some lanterns that someone has hung from the ceiling of this burrow, you wouldn't be able to see a thing.  The total silence that pervades this underground tunnel isn't helping much, either.  What little you do see of the architecture is expertly made, possibly even Dwarven in construction.

There is a strong light leaking in from a hole above you, and weaker lantern light to the east.  Roots stick out from the wood-braced dirt walls, the glittering minerals in the earth catching what little light there is and reflecting it back.

Here a dirt path leads to a dark grove of trees.  A tree stump, its trunk featuring a sizable hole and the base covered with odd carvings that would appear to be symbols, stands where the trail terminates.

Around you grow trees in a circle so even and perfect they warrant suspicion.  In the center of the grove is a deep pool, its surface smooth and glassy, undisturbed by the wind.  Sunlight slants through the leaves and falls in dappled pools of light.  A nest has been built in one of the tallest trees, its occupant a sleeping night owl, its head tucked under its wing.

A shady clump of sicle saplings cluster around a large, moss-encrusted fragment of pink coral.  Carved into a hollow in the center of the coral landmark is a crude yet moving image of Tamsine, one of the patron goddesses of the town.  Before the simple shrine is a low limestone bench, where the weary traveler might take some rest in the shade, leave offerings of flowers or food, and contemplate matters of the soul and spirit.

Water burbles over rocks to fill a shallow stone basin, conveniently positioned for visitors wishing to wash their hands upon entering the garden.  Thick cushions of green moss soften the stones and carpet the ground underfoot.  Red azaleas, deep purple irises and white chrysanthemums add vibrant touches of color against the velvety moss.  At the center of the garden, ribbon-tied parchment scrolls flutter from a red maple tree, celebrating the memory of loved ones lost.

Small gaethzen spheres line this foyer leading to the city's offices.  Atop a pedestal, a marble statue of Hexoch, the Dwarven king, supervises all the work that goes on in the offices to the south.  During business hours, various denizens of the mountain city rush about to do business in the city's administrative center.

Desks line the walls of this room, though only one is occupied.  The others are piled high with what look to be architectural drawings and other documents.  The one clerk on duty continues looking over a pile of papers on his desk, glancing up only briefly when someone enters the office.

A squat counter stretches from wall to wall, behind which a lone Dwarven clerk sits smoking a pipe.  The smoke from his pipe winds its way up through a tiny slit in the ceiling.  Occasionally, another Dwarf will run in and hand something to the clerk, but the exchange is too fast to see what is being passed.

The Debtor's Office for Hibarnhvidar stretches off into the mountain, its back wall obscured by pipe smoke and distance.  A lone Dwarf sits behind the service counter, taking the money of the citizens of the province of Forfedhdar.  Behind him, rank upon rank of desks are placed in neat orderly rows, where, during the day, clerks sit updating the accounts of all the citizens in the land.

The glow cast by oil lamps set into the rough granite walls fails to bring any warmth to this grim cavern.  A bored looking Dwarven constable sits behind a slate desk covered with neat stacks of papers.  The walls narrow toward the rear of the chamber, but a glint of light indicates that there is something more beyond.

A squat grey marble dais sits in the center of one end of this room.  Cold stone walls add to the foreboding aura of the chamber.  From here judgment is passed upon those who run afoul of the law in Hibarnhvidar.

At night, young people gather beneath a rose-covered gazebo in the center of the square.  Lively strains of music float through the air to set toes tapping and tempt even the most conservative matron to remember the carefree days of her youth.

The streets are quiet in the evening, the shadows partially dispelled by the warm glow of candle light which streams through the windows of nearby cottages.  The stillness is broken only by the faint clatter of footsteps against the cobblestones, or the occasional barking of a neighbor's dog.

The exchange clerks sit behind a low counter, separated from the entry area by a thick pane of glass with a small hole cut in it at mouth-level, and a scooped-out area cut into the wooden counter underneath it so coins can be pushed through to the other side.  The bored-looking clerks scurry to and fro within their glass cage, moving papers from one desk to another with a great show of efficiency.

Bored-looking Gor'Tog clerks sit behind a high counter topped by a bronze railing, wakening as people come and go.  Large, solid wooden desks fill their area, and sturdy file cabinets line the walls.  On the customer side of the counter, the floor is covered with plush carpeting and the walls are covered in rich brocade cloth and wainscotted below.
The precipice offers an unobstructed view of the rippling ocean of frost-nipped green and brown.  Wrapping around to the northern face is a narrow ledge while the rocky slope leads to the top.

Gouged from the cliff face under a small overhang, the cave mouth offers shelter from the elements but little else in the way of creature comforts save for a lonesome wind-torn torch that casts a panoply of shadows throughout the cave.  Set directly into the stone of the southern wall is a worn granite archway and a narrow ledge wraps around to the eastern face of the plateau.
This small tunnel is barely high enough to accommodate a Gor'Tog.  Chiseled directly from the stone, the rough walls have grown dark and stained with the passage of both time and people.
Hewn into the stone is a series of cubbies interspersed between severely faded paintings depicting the early history of the tribes.
Thick hides layer the floor connecting the southern end of the corridor to the northern.  Carvings of ancient shamans are worked along the length of each wall.

Plush furs ring a squat, circular table that fills the bulk of the room.  Smoke rises in a steady column from the large stone firepit nested into the table.  Leaning against a wall is a sturdy ladder leading to a wooden loft above.
Hangings of heavy skin and hide cover the stone walls, and assorted tools of Azdara's trade cover a large worktable that sits between a series of occupied tanning racks.

Freshly hewn timbers form the circular loft, and an assortment of hides and furs provide sleeping space for a dozen or more.  Smoke rises from below towards the painted ceiling, escaping into the ventilation shaft bored into the stone.  A study ladder leads to the chambers below.

Clearly a man-made extension to the cavern, the stone balcony juts from the side of the plateau.  The Arid Steppe stretches for countless miles north, a flatland of uninterrupted frost and tall grasses.

The hallway walls are lined with portraits of the Guild leaders and tapestries depicting beautiful scenes and ancient heroes hang from the ceiling.  A set of brass-bound ironwood doors stands at the end of the hall.  Flanking the doors are two Gor'Tog-sized suits of gleaming silver ceremonial plate armor, complete with gigantic pole-axes sporting nasty serrated blades.

The training room smells of sweat and the air is hot.  Large posters are tacked to the walls amidst racks for weapons and hooks for shields.  The floor is heavily scarred and notched and, although it looks as though it's been swept clean, the deeper gouges are still caked with blood-soaked sawdust.

Tapestries and flickering torches line the walls of the circular meeting room.  Eight sets of silverwood benches, arranged in ascending rows, face a central speaker's podium.  The topmost row, a full three Tog-lengths above the main floor, sits at eye level with a large chandelier that hangs from the ceiling.

A well-polished ironwood banister guards the narrow walkway that overlooks the Grand Hallway.  Spanning the length of the wooden floor is a tightly woven rug of forest green that slips beneath a pair of massive wooden double doors, each set with a bronze knocker fashioned into a roaring lion's head.

A small table surrounded by chairs rests in the center of the room, enclosed on all sides by towering shelves stocked full with books and journals.  The colorful spines of the manuscripts depict the names of masterpieces collected over the years, and some bear tell-tale signs of wear and age.  A large sign with gold-foil lettering hangs behind a mahogany book return desk.

A covered breezeway, this portico connects the main guildhall with the courtyard and outer buildings of the compound.  The tiled roof covering the long corridor is draped with softly twisting vines and offers shade from the sun in summer and shelter from the elements the rest of the year.  Weary combatants in training are often seen resting here among the greenery.

Supported by iron lattices, wild rose bushes cling together forming a dense wall of brilliant scarlet against a backdrop of lush evergreens.  Veins of ebony streak through the grey marble flagstones, their pattern spiraling in towards a bronzed statue.  Beyond it, a stone bench with ornate armrests stands watch over an open, iron gate.

A simple, marbled pathway winds its way around the spacious grassy yard, breaking off in many directions.  Casting a canopy of shade over those engaging in contests of skill is a massive flamethorne tree with a leather-wrapped target dummy swaying from a low, sturdy limb.  To the east, a series of wooden rails peek above the horizon, tracing a distant line of fencing.

A large vine-covered edifice, this building looms over the courtyard and is matched in height only by the guild proper.  Ivy, speckled with tiny violet flowers, twines around the flagstones as they broaden into half-moon shaped steps before a polished ebonwood door.  Hanging from the entryway is an inlaid wooden sign, its darkened lettering set upon a lighter field.  A cobbled drive winds behind the building where artisans are often seen unloading new wares and custom crafted armor and weaponry.

Embellished with golden accents, the marble walls glitter to life, highlighted by an overhanging chandelier.  An elaborately woven dark blue rug lies before the polished ebonwood door and stretches towards a simple wooden counter that displays a golden plaque.  A nearby set of winding stairs curves its way to the second floor, its gilded gold banister polished to a soft sheen.

The staircase gives way to a circular landing, halved by two soulstone arches that shimmer softly, their radiance glimmering off the smooth, polished, marble flooring.  High above glitters a stained-glass skylight portraying a noble Paladin brandishing a silvery sword in combat against a menacing stone gargoyle.

Smooth, multicolored river pebbles line the ground before a large wooden barn.  Tufts of grass peek between the gravel at the stone foundation, the tips of their blades just grazing the redwood slats.  An overhanging chute juts out from above and bits of straw and hay cling tenaciously to the metallic mouth as if afraid to let loose and tumble to the stony floor below.

The scent of horse sweat and well-oiled leather lingers in the air, carried on a gentle cross breeze.  Sunlight filters through the redwood slats, dancing over a thick layer of straw strewn on the aisle floor.  Lined on both sides of the aisle by a series of wooden stalls, shadows emitted from their hulking height fall more heavily on the far end, nearly concealing a stone-encased corner.  A pair of heavy wooden doors leads to the stable's side yard.

Bale upon bale of yellowed hay is stacked eight-high against the roughened walls, each one bound by heavy twine.  Scattered bits litter the floor to mix with a fine layer of dust.  An opening in one wall reveals a metal chute overlooking the gravel entryway, its wide mouth large enough to fit two simultaneous bales.

Marred by heavy hoofprints, the dirt is uneven and clumpy.  A three-rail wooden fence surrounds three quarters of the perimeter, its slating painted a bright white.  Various equipment is neatly stacked against the back side of the barn just beside a pair of heavy doors that lead inside.

Velvety grass surrounds the back exposure of the two-story edifice.  From this perspective the pristine marble building looms imposingly against the horizon, the acute angle of the barracks roof lending an illusion of extended height.  Ivy clings to the side of the building, slowly meandering towards the sky and a tall iron staircase, bolted securely into the moldings, runs diagonally from the ground to a tiled archway on the second floor.

Dozens of footprints score the ground from heavy use and continual traffic.  On one side, tall stands provide spectator seating, crowned with brightly hued pennants that splash the sky with color.  A heavy gate leads into the arena proper, guarded by a burly S'kra Mur in full plate mail.

Surrounded by a split-rail fence, the arena floor is a mixture of sand and dirt.  Marred with deep hoof-prints and churned completely in areas, the ground bears the telltale signs of frequent use.  Rows of wooden stands line the far end of the rail for spectator seating, and a wooden observation box towers above them, providing safety for the officiator.

Despite the height, the view is blocked by the barracks and all that can be seen is the yard below and the bustling street beyond the gate.  The landing is narrow, but what lacks in width is made up for in length and can easily hold a large group of people.  A solitary guard stands at the door, carefully eyeing all that pass.
A colorful archway stands at the end of the hall, providing a view of the balcony beyond.  The murmurs of city life drift through, a constant hubub of activity at all hours.

The wooden floors remain unmarred despite the heavily armored feet that often traipse across it.  A green glass vase sits atop a small three-legged table, displaying a preserved bouquet of jonquils, their vibrant yellow color as bright now as when they were freshly cut.

An emblazoned shield hangs upon the wall, framed by two small brass oil lanterns, their flames enclosed in glass flumes.  Their dim lighting casts a warm yellow glow over the doorframes throughout the hallway.  A deep scar mars the surface of the oaken floor, remnants of a careless footstep long ago.

Young squires bustle up and down a secluded stairwell, their arms heavily laden with pieces of their master's armor.  From behind a nearby door, the lingering scent of cabbage wafts through the air, tell-tale signs of a home cooked meal.  At the end of the hallway hangs a painting of a golden lion, its head thrown back in a deep roar, mane flowing wildly around its massive head.

The soft beige walls are embellished with a golden filigree pattern and contrast tastefully with the deep green rug laid over the wooden flooring.  Interwoven with silvery threads, the plush woolen floor covering bears the Zoluren provincial crest.

An armored figure stands at attention in the corner, its heavy sword raised to its metal-clad brow in a respectful salute.  Hanging lanterns cast a soft sheen over the highly polished wooden flooring and illuminate the dark mahogany walls, highlighting their intricately grained pattern.

Long wooden flats have been sanded to a smooth finish and comprise the flooring and handrails of this enclosed porch.  Covered by a tiled roof, the enclosure provides a sheltered place to rest and relax after a long and tiring day.  A long bench rests against one rail, directly opposite a hanging porch-swing, both upholstered with soft cushions.

The path ends abruptly before an elongated, neatly trimmed building, its tiled roof overhanging rows of double windows that gaze over the courtyard like pairs of unblinking eyes.  Long benches placed on the porch offer a place to sit while removing muddy boots, and young squires are often seen sweeping the long porch under the careful watch of an armored guard.  Standing near the oaken doors, a silent protector and observer, he casts a dark shadow over a nearby bronze spittoon.

Scarce handholds are offered by tiny juts of obsidian for those who wish to brave the upward climb, while occasional fissures in the sheer ice wall offer scant footing for a careful retreat from the icy ascent.
Flakes of snow and ice crystals casually float by in abject defiance of both gravity and the still air as any trace of warmth is quickly extinguished.
