Flakes of snow and ice crystals casually float by in abject defiance of both gravity and the still air as any trace of warmth is quickly extinguished.  Irregular flickers of light dance from the darkened entrance of a cave to the east.

The obsidian walls of the cave are absolutely smooth, and form a mathematically perfect arc above.  Tiny flecks of ice float in from the mouth of the cave, gracefully swirling about in an otherworldly dance.

The Assay Office looks like a contractor's storeroom: scaffolding, loose timbers, planks, and tools lie everywhere, as carpenters and plasterers work away.  Behind a tin-topped counter stands the assay clerk, who is adjusting the beam of the smallest of three graduated scales.

Logs form concentric half-circles in front of a large peregan tree altar that dominates the far end of the tent.  Sweet bearberry candles line the perimeter of the humble tabernacle, flickering softly and chasing the musty smell of dampness from the air.  A leather pennant branded with the image of a rampant boar hangs from above.

This tasteful entry hall is paneled with a variety of exotic woods.  The parquet floor is patterned in alternately light and dark diamond shapes, surrounding the Estate Holder crest in the center of the room.  Lining the walls are several plush couches for the comfort of those awaiting appointments.

This wide hallway is somewhat less opulent than the entry foyer and the rooms dedicated to council meetings, reflecting the fact that this is where the day-to-day business takes place.  Several offices open off from here, with frequent visitors coming and going.  The walls display portraits of prominent estate holders, past and present.

This is a large office with a well-worn counter, several windows each with a "Use Next Window, Please" sign and apparently one clerk actually working.  Every town in the land seems cursed with lines and waiting and fees.  This office is for the obtaining of permits, licenses and similar matters.

Tiny, stuffed with old, dusty furniture, and smelling like yesterday's laundry, this office is anything but a testimony to bureaucratic efficiency.  Large piles of yellowing papers spill from cracked file cabinets and lie scattered upon the floor, fallen from large, ungainly stacks on what little desk space is not taken up by piles of mouldering food.

Maps cover practically every inch of available wall space, with overview maps covering all of Kermoria ranging down to ones detailing individual neighborhoods.  Trays labeled "IN" and "OUT" are filled to overflowing, although the "IN" box is piled deeper by far.  Government officials, landowners and couriers seem to form a parade of traffic through the office.

This office is like a cousin to the Acquisitions Office without all the hubbub.  There are a handful of maps on the wall, with pushpins marking areas for development.  A few office workers are engaged in conversation with merchants and artisans, discussing potential development opportunities.

The dim passage is a good deal larger than it looks from a distance.  From the texture of the walls and the chips of granite covering the floor, it's apparent the tunnel is not a natural formation.  Someone carved a trail between the cul-de-sac and whatever lies beyond the wall.

The path underfoot is treacherous and strewn with gravel chips painstakingly carved from the rock wall.  This end of the tunnel opens through a granite arch onto a limestone valley.  The scent of burning charcoal is much stronger here.

A granite arch opens into the base of an unusual stone wall.  Nearly thirty feet tall, the granite wall is encrusted with shimmering quartz crystals.  Although the crystals have been removed as high as can be readily reached, the remaining strip extends along the southern wall of the valley in brilliant display.

The crystals end abrubtly at the eastern wall of the valley, refracting pinpoints of light against a limestone backdrop.  The slight inward tilt of the limestone cliffs precludes any possibility of scaling them.
The greyish-white wall leans in over the tar pit where the path narrows to a few feet across.  A fine rain of chalky powder continually drifts down from above, dislodged by stray breezes.
Thin striations of pure pink marble can be seen embedded in the limestone.  The veins are scarce, but time will create a rich harvest for future miners.

A tall arch is carved into the wall and set with a solid marble gate.  Although there's no apparent locking mechanism, the gate is solidly closed.  Fresh air drifts through the narrow crack around the slab carrying a hint of pine.

The skeleton of a mid-size feline lies here in disarray and several large chunks of limestone are shattered beneath the remains.  It appears the edge of the cliff gave way while the luckless animal investigated the valley from above.  A far quicker death than the slowly suffocating fumes of the pit.
The path here is thick with spatters from the pit, making each step a challenge.  An extremely large bubble of tar hisses and burbles, slowly releasing a steady stream of gas and black ooze.

Between the crystal-encrusted granite and the chalky lime runs a thick vein of pure ivory marble.  An ambitious Halfling miner was unsuccessful in attempts to reap some of nature's bounty before being overcome by the fumes.  Nothing but a skeleton and a few tattered scraps of clothing are left.

Squeezing through the small gap is hard going as the rough walls seem to grasp for exposed skin at every chance.  The fissure extends back a good distance into the northern cliff, then vanishes around a corner.

Someone has used this small hidden cavern as a refuge in the past.  There's a circle of stones containing the remains of a campfire and a narrow vent in the ceiling provides ample ventilation for escaping smoke.

The tree-lined trail winds an erratic route along the riverbank, eternally muddy and smelling of fish.  The bank drops off steeply into the river below, a deadly climb for anyone foolish enough to try.

The vegetation grows thickly here, fertilized by the steady stream of birds and wildlife attracted to the nearby river.  To the west, the riverbank subsides into a more gradual slope, easing entrance into the water for animals and fishermen alike.  Here however, the man-made bank drops off treacherously, its slippery slope inviting the sounds of the river to permeate the area.

Surrounded by lush ferns, an expansive flagstone patio supports several smokewood benches and a small table of refreshments.  Vibrant crimson blossoms spangle the clematis vines that cover the trunks of a pair of dwarf maple trees standing guard at the courtyard's archway.  Glowing gaethzen orbs are tucked neatly within the fragrant lavender bushes that line the surrounding fence.

Tiny gaethzen globes light the room, adding a soft gleam to the silks draping the displays and tables that feature some of the luthier's more intricate work, available for his most discriminating clients.  A settee provides seating, and a small tray offers beverages and snacks to entice those shopping into staying longer -- and buying more.  A heavy lined curtain leads back out to the main shop.

A shelving unit gleams from regular polishing, their shelves laden with supplies and wares both available for sale and those yet to be unpacked.  In the center of the room, a short table sits before a glass display case, both of which hold sparkling treasures.

Racks and shelves are filled with a kaleidoscopic display of small clothing for men and women.  Phoebe Woodcock, talented village seamstress, is standing in front of a rack methodically arranging shirts according to color.  She pauses to give a flirtatious smile to an attractive male Halfling customer.

A gilded birdcage containing a wind-up parrot is suspended near the doorway.  Glass cases line the walls, displaying practical items alongside rare oddities.  A stuffed leucro head, which has been mounted on the wall, stares down at you with its sharp teeth exposed.  The owner of the shop, Rufus Tanglefoot, looks up from combing his foothair and smiles at you expectantly.

Huddled amongst the gulls that scream noisily atop the wooden pilings of a nearby pier, a local wag has placed an articulated wooden pelican.  Its deep bowl-shaped beak bobs up and down, spilling dribbles of rainwater as it does, to reveal a golden fish swimming within, while its wings are poised to spin in the breeze.

An occasional metallic clang echoes beneath the boardwalk, drawing attention to a rope tied to the harbor-side railing.  At the other end of the rope, flies congregate, thick and black, around a bucket of chopped fish half-submerged in the water below.  The rope holds the bucket in place, keeping the fish cool until it is needed for bait later in the day.

The backsides of stalls and wagons press in against the road, forcing it to narrow slightly in passing.  Bright and festive banners flutter madly in the breeze while colorful signs beckon passerby with promises of exotic wares at affordable prices.  The cry of an auctioneer echoes out from somewhere down one of the alleys that cut between the wagon carts.

An over-scaled wooden hammer nods in the wind from atop an oddly-angled building nearby.  Displayed in the windows of the shop are a wide assortment of tools and construction goods, and the painted image of fat crowned face gleefully peers out into the street.  Tacked above the door, a sign proclaims "King's Hardware and Fine Goods" in bright, flowing colors.

Thick strands of honeysuckle dangle teasingly over the top of an iron fence, blocking all but scant glimpses of a stone building on the other side.  A bell tower rises proudly from the building, dwarfing the fence and the surrounding structures.  Attached firmly to one of the brick supports for the fence is a brass-plated plaque.

Squeezed snugly in an alley between two apartment buildings is a descending series of stone steps.  Makeshift handrails flank the steps and a banner flaps from above the alley's entrance.  Someone has kept the narrow side street swept clean of most debris, but the nostril-flaring scent of rubbish still wafts through the air.  On the other end of the alley, the tops of gondolas can be seen bobbing on the canal waters.

Several seagulls strut and flit along the ground, snatching scraps of garbage and discarded food before hopping off to devour their meals.  The gulls are considerably braver here than elsewhere in Mer'Kresh, though this may owe as much to the abundance of loose trash as it does to any courage the birds can muster.  The flaking paint and broken windows of some of the buildings here echo the street's condition.

A broken board has been mended with a support brace, carefully secured with bent-over nails.  The new wood is lighter in color than the surrounding slats, not yet greyed by exposure to the elements.  Sailors and merchants brush past on their way to and from the ships swaying beside the nearby pier.

Most of the floor has been swept free of debris, revealing a mosaic of faded pastel tiles.  Black dirt, spared by the broom, still clings in the corners of the room.  Hung crookedly on one wall, a message board wears an assortment of smudged papers proclaiming long-past resident meetings.

A set of rickety stairs ascends to the next floor as the giant-sized face of a smiling Rissan beams down the hall.  Originally painted in extreme colors, the face is now partly veiled by a thin layer of soot and dust.  Tightly clutching to a foaming mug with one hand, the happy Rissan indicates his prized drink with a pointing finger.

A few steps lead down to a hot, brightly lit room packed with sailors in every state of consciousness from keen-eyed alertness to drunken collapse.  Somewhere in the crowd, a reedy concertina accompanies one or another of several songs being sung in cheery disregard for each other.  Behind the mahogany bar, the owner Deeper presides over the tumult, disappearing into the throng from time to time with an armload of mugs.  Above the bar hangs a hand-written menu.

A yard-thick, floor-to-ceiling wooden pillar dominates this corner of the tavern.  The mast, as the regular patrons call it, rises like a tree trunk through the center of a circular table.  Here the boastful and the optimistic gather to test their strength of arm.

Kegs empty and full, mugs for the filling, and the tools of the trade (including a solid-looking bungstarter) line this long, narrow space between the bar and a rear wall hung with trophies of the sea.  At the end farthest from the entrance is an open trapdoor.

This secluded corner of the tavern contains the favorite table of Rancois Sendaque, the most famous part-time poet in Mer'Kresh.  Many of the song scrolls he sells are his original work, and well known among the discriminating (and the stingy).

The dim lantern-light reveals a room filled from the floor to the low ceiling with the supplies and furnishings of the tavern.  Here stand broken tables and benches awaiting repair, boxes of crockery mugs, framed paintings that appear to have been used as weapons, and even a stuffed marlin that has seen better days.  Stacked kegs of rum hide one wall completely, and a large wine rack filled with bottles stands a little ways out from another wall.  Stairs lead up to the tavern's main room.

An engraved oaken sales counter sits prominently in the back of the shop, providing a surface for merchant and customer to haggle or exchange goods for coin.  A ironwood rack and some steel shelves hang on the oaken walls, with a black oak armoir along the edges of the room.  A granite table sits on the granite floor, with a lunat trunk placed nearby to provide a variety of browsing options.

An engraved oaken sales counter sits prominently in the back of the shop, providing a surface for merchant and customer to haggle or exchange goods for coin.  An oaken table sits alone on the stained oak floor, while the granite walls are unadorned.

Several oval paintings line the off-white walls of this office, and a faint scent of old paper fills the air.  A bored clerk sits behind a semi-polished desk occasionally glancing at a book entitled, "Rules and Regulations."  A couple of plush wine velvet couches provide seating for those waiting, while a colorful fringed rug entertains a kitten that seems to have found its way through the doors.

Ventilation grates provide a slight breeze that assists in drying bundled herbs hung from the rafters but do nothing to relieve the oppressive heat.  The air is thick with a strange odor, not floral and not spice but definitely unpleasant.  Large storage barrels stacked alongside wooden crates provide seating for the weary.  Light from a lantern outside a small window falls on one of these containers, marked with a skull and crossbones, fueling rumors that not all of Trintah's concoctions are for healing.

Perched at the apex of the gardens' central spire, this carved crystal platform commands an all-encompassing view of the adjacent grounds.  Floating terraces encircle the monolith below, surrounded themselves by a larger ring of airborne islands.  Further out, a wall of constantly shifting light enfolds the lofty gardens in a massive sphere, obscuring everything beyond its boundaries.
Glittering stairs wind along the inner wall of the crystal tower, spiraling about an elaborate gyroscopic device curiously suspended in midair over the rotunda below.

Rays of prismatic light filter through thick quartz walls, bathing the grand circular gallery in an ethereal glow.  The chamber interior is sparse and utilitarian, unfurnished aside from an aetheric distillery centered on the floor, the gurgle of the strange apparatus echoing softly throughout the rotunda.

The cobbled road widens as it curves past a gondola landing.  Tall blue and purple striped poles topped with golden streamers and set with large metal rings are moored near the slips.  The frayed remains of rope used to tie off the gondolas hang off one ring.  The only barriers to Shell Circle and Gull Circle are the salty stretches of water and the massive terracotta planters marking the entrance steps to each gondola slip.

Staggered gaps between the colorful buildings give plenty of room to gaze at the canals and the slow moving barges hauling cargo.  The area boasts few shops -- residences surrounded by patches of lawn dominate.  Above, ropes strung between the upper stories flap with laundry and birds.

Burlap bags filled with old rags cast a sharp scent throughout the shop.  Several fine mesh screens lean against a large square tub filled with thick, grey liquid.  Colorfully glazed jars, brushes, and sheets of raw paper are neatly arranged on the work table in the center of the room.  Above, finished paper is hanging to dry on rough cord strung from wall to wall.

Splits of leather, replacement hilts and blades, rivets and metal scraps are jumbled together in crates.  A box of broken shields, armor and weapons sits in one relatively clean corner.  Two barrels with a plank of wood across them serve as a makeshift counter.  In the back of the small lean-to, a scruffy-looking Elf with tobacco-stained teeth and fingers works at his trade.

Dark wood paneling runs the length of the upper hall, split by contrasting trim nearly halfway up the wall.  A carved sandalwood door breaks the monotony of the paneling along the southern wall.  Tacked to the center of the door is a curled note, pierced through the middle by a bent nail.  At the far end of the hall, a spiral staircase rises through a covered opening in the roof, while opposite, a set of wide steps descends to the lower floor.

Stone troughs along the edges of the rooftop serve a dual purpose as homes for flowering plants and as guard rails to keep sky-watching mages from stumbling off into the gardens two stories below.  Spider vines arc over the ledges and flow downward, unafraid of the height.  To the west, the roof of the commodities building stares into the sky in poor imitation of the scholars that use this manor.

Heavy growths of plants and vines drape down the side of the building, wrapping themselves lovingly around the stone gargoyle statues protruding from the ledges.  A blank spot some distance below hints that one of the gargoyles may have lost its mortared hold on the wall and plummeted into the canal.  Poking out over the edge of the rooftop, and uncaring of the canal's rushing waters, is a polished blackwood telescope set neatly onto a raised pedestal at the southern end of the roof.

Heavy double doors open onto a large, rectangular foyer.  Two stories high, the entryway to the Cleric's Guild is well lit through tall, narrow windows high on the walls.  Two thick, fluted pedestals guard each side of the chapel's double door to the east.  Low padded benches line each wall between the pedestals and the doorway to the guildmaster's office on the north wall, and the meeting room on the south wall.

Neat bookshelves behind a large desk hold Eydtha's private library.  The office is brightly lit through two tall windows on the east and west walls.  A thick, dark blue carpet covers the stone floor, and two padded, straight-backed chairs sit in the corners nearest the door.  The large desk holds neatly stacked papers and a small statue of a dolphin.

The windowless meeting room holds a long, narrow table surrounded by chairs, as well as several smaller tables.  Several people sit at a corner table discussing a private matter.  Benches line the walls underneath three large tapestries depicting various gods.

Tall windows high on the north and south walls allow plenty of light into the chapel.  A plainly carved altar sits under two beautiful stained-glass windows in the east wall.  Thick red carpets hug the walls, leaving the center of the stone floor bare.  Each corner holds two floor-standing braziers for the ritual burning of sacred writings.

Low steps, each the entire width of the room, climb at evenly spaced intervals to the large door at the far end.  A long, narrow, black carpet lines the center of the room from one door to the other, hugging the steps closely.

Several long-suffering guards stand on the other side of a large table, arms crossed, frowning and nodding at the supplicants across from them.  Occasionally a guard will turn around and pick up an item of some sort and hand it to the person across from him, but more often than not, the people leave empty-handed.  The unwilling are forcefully escorted out of the room.

High arches in the eight cardinal directions meet in the center to support a large, circular skylight.  Behind a curved desk on the far side of the round room sit the judges, stern-looking men and women with a reputation for rapidly deciding the fate of the accused.

The high arch of the Grand Foyer is pierced by huge stained glass windows illustrating the aspects and heroics of the thirteen.  White marble columns anchor the majestic arch to the grey marble floor.  Great oaken doors along the north wall lead to various city offices and the formal Council Arch on the south wall leads to the Grand Hall of the Council.

The Grand Hall of the Council is extremely formal.  If the Rissan oak beams and white marble walls could speak, they would tell tales about the founding of Rissan tradition.  A huge oak council table dominates the hall.  Council chairs surround the table at precise locations.  The council president's chair looms like a throne above one end of the council table, adding to the sense of awe the room inspires.

At the far end of a spacious room with a polished oak floor sits a large, ornately carved desk and a high-backed oak chair with a velvet cushion.  On either side behind the desk are floor-to-ceiling stained glass windows.  A brightly colored rug is draped over the desk.
This little room, barely bigger than a closet, is crowded even more by crates, boxes, racks, and bookcases overflowing with scrolls and papers.  In front of a tiny window is a folding desk and stool.

A small vestibule lit by ornate bronze lamps occupies the space between an ascending flight of stairs and the street door.  All the furnishings, from the polished lamps to the soft carpet underfoot, set a tone of quiet (and expensive) good taste.

At a large landing at the top of the stairs, several gleaming oak chairs face each other across a dark blue carpet with deep pile.  In the far wall, paneled double doors stand open, in limed oak matching the chairs.  To the right of the doors is a window with a dark blue drape, and to the left is a smaller door that says "Repairs."

The light gleams off polished glass in the showroom of Bergen Perobler, Elanthia's foremost chronometrician, where the wares of this inventive and artistic genius are displayed.  The buzzes, hums, chirps, cuckoos, chimes, and ticks of his astonishing creations are a background to every conversation.  A competent-looking guard by the exit doors keeps a wary eye on the customers and merchandise alike.

This tiny, almost bare room -- the workroom of Knobby Snaggle, Perobler's repairdwarf -- has only a small counter with a high stool behind it.  What light there is comes from a small window in the rear wall, on which hang a handsome sign and a framed certificate.

More cramped than cozy, this conference room has seen a fair amount of use.  The carpet has lost its color in an arching trail from the ash door to the chair at the head of the glossy black table, and the walls are brown from years of cigar-smoking inhabitants.

Thick woods gradually thin to light forest and, finally, to occasional close growing clumps of trees in the northern wilds.  The ground begins to rise rapidly and steeply to the north.  Vanishing up in the hills, a faint path winds its way through the tall grasses.

Rising gently, the footbridge's arched shape is barely noticeable as it spans the narrow brook.  Spilling from the bridge's railing, roses and honeysuckle trail into the water and are tugged by the current.  Within the brook, glints of golden fish flash among the plants and sparkling coins thrown from the bridge by wishers and seekers.  The path away from the carillon parts the tufts of grass and cattails vying for space on the stream bank.

Sheltered beneath a camphor tree, a proud basalt lion watches over his stone pride as they lounge in the flower-speckled clearing.  One lioness rolls on her back, one sniffs at a clump of lilies, while yet another sculptured lioness licks her cub.  Several stone cubs gather around a bronze paladin seated upon a basalt slab.  At the north end of the clearing, a grass and bamboo gate closes the path from further exploration.

Towering above the city, the Carillon tolls the sailor's watch and serves as a look-out for those who wait for a mariner's return.  Centered on the innermost disk, this slender obelisk is home to those who seek comfort and counsel.  Flecks of quartz in the sandy granite exterior sparkle in the light, and stained glass windows, like a jeweled belt, encircle the building midway to the top.  Atop, bells hang in the open arches supporting the roof.

Higher in the hills, the forest sounds die away as the thick southern woods thin to sparsely wooded highland.  The scattered growths cling tenuously to the earth, their wind-twisted trunks and branches betraying misery in the face of the surrounding greenery.

The air is thick with motes of dust dancing in the dim light and the scent of lemon polish nearly masks the smell of musk.  Heavy oak shelves lining the walls from floor to ceiling bow under the weight of countless items of undeterminable value.  A stack of crates holding hundreds of used cards and wedding invitations rests against the end of a scarred counter.  In one corner, a canvas sack full of dull jelly beans lies against a box overflowing with used shapers.

Exotic tapestries of every possible description drape the wall ringing the Carousel's core.  A circular roof supports a vast framework of iron and timbers rising to the building's apex.  Countless gears, pulleys and weights within the structure form the strikingly complex and beautiful mechanism which drives the Carousel.
A long wooden desk spans the width of the western wall.  Brass lanterns hang from the ceiling, and the floor behind the desk is covered in spotless red tile.

A temporary pier of scaffolding mounts the walls and tapering dikes to provide workers with sure footing.  Hanging from one of the support beams, a bucket sways in the wind, its contents clattering as it moves.  Just beneath the planking of the makeshift walkway, the explosive sound of the ocean washing over the jumbled stones shakes the wood, and sends the bucket into yet another shifting motion.

Most of the pilings and posts that support the wooden walkway lean askew, pushed off kilter by the movement of the heavy and keen-edged boulders underneath.  The boards, glossy and green from the constant dampness, shudder under the slightest weight or the most gentle push of the wind.  Whenever a particularly potent wave slams into the barrier, some unseen part of the walkway growls angrily as it shakes and repositions itself.

Abruptly stopping over a mound of pointed basalt, the walkway lacks any safety features such as guardrails or warning signs.  One heavy black stone in particular is a favorite spot for the waves to dash, if only because its great size presents such a good target.  Just poking from the surface of the waves, another series of black basalt curves in mimicry, shielding this one from the worst of the ocean's assault.

Only slightly more stable than its twin to the west, this heap of rock and rubble is at least saved from the most dramatic of swells flooding over both.  All manner of rough stonework is half-buried in the mounds, from cracked sculptures and friezes to the remnants of support columns and paving stones.  Some are glaringly apparent, the white of pitted marble contrasting sharply with the dark basalt.  Others are more subtle, like the mostly-covered face of the statue gazing from the shattered rocks.

The wet, black stones underfoot shift menacingly in the tide, every so often uttering a muffled plop as one of their number slides into the sea.  Thick pilings struggle to keep the pile of stones from vanishing completely under the onslaught of the ocean's power, but their barnacle-encrusted forms betray the weakened state that their time in the water has brought.

Solidly mortared and built from heavy blocks of basalt, the base for the planned canal gate is closer to completion than the surrounding ring, and stands out from the surrounding pile of rough and loose rock.  Ebbing waves slicken the stones on top of the base with spray and foam.  Caught only by the most violent splashes, a brilliant red banner flutters from atop a wooden pole.
Light from the city's buildings reflects off the rippling water, but doesn't cast enough illumination to navigate.  Only the current, tugging toward the southeast, hints at where you are.
Light from the city's buildings reflects off the rippling water, but doesn't cast enough illumination to navigate.  Only the current, tugging toward the southeast, hints at where you are.
Light from the city's buildings reflects off the rippling water, but doesn't cast enough illumination to navigate.  Only the current, tugging eastward, hints at where you are.
Light from the city's buildings reflects off the rippling water, but doesn't cast enough illumination to navigate.  Only the current, tugging eastward, hints at where you are.
Light from the city's buildings reflects off the rippling water, but doesn't cast enough illumination to navigate.  Only the current, tugging toward the northeast, hints at where you are.

The willow, not nearly as tall as some of the giants around it, has some of its branches tangled in a mass of vines hanging from a nearby cypress.  One in particular looks like a way to get to the larger tree.
A barren, rocky clearing slopes slightly up to the north.  On lower ground to the south, a heavy thicket of ravelthorns blocks the way, broken only by a few faint game trails.

On the high side of a steep ditch, the ground rises almost to the tops of the trees in the bog below.  Cypress branches and tangled vines conceal the view to the south, but to the west, the way seems clearer.  Already the air feels drier and cooler.

The view to the north shows a rising field of broken rock, a jumble of odd shapes and strange conjunctions.  In one place, the path skirts boulders that look for all the world like trolls.  In another, it avoids the smaller rubble scattered at toe-stubbing, ankle-twisting, and shin-barking heights.

The trail swings through a half-turn as it threads its way among the sharp, loose stones.  A few ravelthorn bushes spring up in the soil collected on the high side of the larger stones, but for the most part, the slope is barren of plant life, left to the wind and the rain.

The trail stands at the last switch-back in its steady mounting of the hillside.  Red and brown stones from the size of pebbles to cottages cover the ground, and the trail cuts back and forth between the largest of them like the path of a bouncing ball.  Each Spring rain must change the path as the smaller stones wash southward to the bog.

The rock, sloping gently to the south, suddenly rises high above the treetops.  A massive ridge looms against the northern sky, its front like the prow of a gigantic ship cresting the green billows of the forest.  A side-trail leads off to the northeast, passing along the foot of the ridge.

The path ends at a sheer face of rock with a small pool at its base.  Water from a chimney in the rock face has worn a shallow basin in the ledge, and it spills over the side, trickling down a mossy channel that drops to the ground far below.  The chimney looks like it leads to higher ground above, but might be a tough climb.

High above the knees of the cypress, a wide limb offers firm footing to the creatures who spend most of their lives among its leaves.  They are born, hunt, mate, and die in this green world above the forest floor.

The wide limb spreads its branches to either side, moss cascading in grey-green strands to left and right.  A world of birds and beetles, caracals, squirrels and snakes -- a whole aerial menagerie -- whistles, growls, chitters, and hisses a welcome.

The limb of the cypress tapers, and with each step it flexes underfoot.  This aerial path is clearly at an end, but a cluster of vines from nearby trees entangles the end of the bough like a weaver's nightmare.  One sturdy vine in particular drapes over from a massive cypress.

Pink flowers with a cloud of feathery petals dot the end of the branch, a startling sight on a cypress.  A closer look shows that the flowers only appear to be sprouting from the limb: they are blossoming on a dark green vine swooping down to a smaller, younger cypress.

This perch on a wide limb of the cypress stands well above the leafy canopy, and commands a panoramic view.  The thick forest rolls upslope to the higher ground to the east and descends steeply to a swamp in the south.  In the west, a steep spur of rock hides the river from view.  A supple vine close at hand trails over to a silvery cypress.

Through some odd effect of the tangle of vines or the lay of the land, the whisper of the wind is louder here, and every sparrow's chirp and mosquito's buzz is ten times magnified.  Through the maze of creepers and moss, the outline of a huge cypress can be seen to the west, and some of the vines close at hand disappear into its upper branches.

Someone has built a shelter from the elements against the trunk of the cypress.  Leafy branches have been skillfully woven into the limbs of the tree to make walls and a roof, as snug a room as one might wish.

The cypress stands regally among its fellows, its girth and height showing its victories in the slow, unceasing forest battles with weather and rivals.  Here a storm has broken a branch, there a vine has strangled a limb, but the cypress has overcome them all, and stretches its crown above the knoll it rules.

Broad branches in many directions make a firm floor underfoot.  Light filtering down through the leaves lends a color of enchantment, annihilating all that's made into a green thought in a green shade.  Sheets of silvery moss billow and ripple, like tent walls pierced with windows of curious shapes.  A dwarf seems to be peering through one of those windows to the northeast.

Nature's mischievous hand has left its mark at the joint of two big branches: the wrinkles in the bark bear a striking resemblance to a Dwarven face.  No sculptor could have bettered the swellings that form the beetling brows and the bulbous nose, complete with wart.  A fold supplies a broad smile, and the greenish moss provides a luxuriant beard.

The two trunks of the oak are so close together that from a distance they appear to be one.  Their branches are flourishing, and several of the larger limbs seem almost trunk-like themselves.  They fork into something very close to a natural lair for the small -- and the larger -- predators of the forest.

The tree has been lavish with its seed, and acorns and acorn caps litter the boughs.  Its resident red squirrels are especially sleek and sassy, springing from branch to branch in a world where food is abundant, shelter is free, and life is easy.

This limb of the oak hangs high above a little stream that winds its way down the hillside.  The splash of the water is pleasant, and a dip might be refreshing, but the stream is obviously shallow, and no convenient vines allow an easy or safe descent.

Here and there on the bark of the limb are little tufts of grey fur, the kind that a cat might leave behind if it was lying on its back scratching an itch.  The main difference is that the hairs are twice as long as any cat's, and the tufts cover a wide surface.  The trunk also shows deep scores, as if it had been used as a scratching post by impressive claws.

Not many elms populate the forest.  This one must have been a volunteer sprung from a seed carried by a far-flying bird.  It hasn't thrived in its setting, short on water and sunlight, and the vines trailing from the taller trees add yet another obstacle.

A ledge hardly the width of a loaded camel ascends the west side of the rock outcropping.  The fall to the river is abrupt, down a steep cliff with exposed strata of red and brown rock.  On the other side of the ledge, the shoulder of the rock rises high overhead, hiding the view to the north, but to the south a marshy swamp lies in the mists.
The narrow ledge, barely wide enough for two people to stand side-by-side, works its way along the cliff side.  Steps cut from the rock help the traveller surmount the steeper parts of the trail.

The trail runs through a narrow valley cut in the outcrop like a gash in its rocky skin.  A grudging concession by the rugged outcropping, the trail winds its narrow route deep-set among boulders that limit sight to a few feet.  A passage branches off to the northeast.

Over the millennia, the outcropping has bowed to its only master, nature: the wind has filled cracks in the rock with bits of silt and mulch from the bogs.  The result is a mottled harmony of bare granite and scrub brush determined to seize life on the barren rocks.  The only flaw in this example of nature's irrestible will is a patch of rusty soil at the base of one boulder, as if over the ages the elements, angry at the affront, had ground something metal under vengeful feet.

Water trickles down the face of the rocky slope from above, a soothing balm on the dry outcrop.  A small lip of rock leans out over the lower elevation to the east, allowing a sheltered view of the lower outcropping and bogs below.  Bits of rotting leather and pockmarked stones half-buried in the thin soil show that others have done a fair amount of watching here as well.

Midway up the face of the outcropping, a cleft in the stone provides shelter from the wind howling unchecked across the face of the mountain.  Water from a small spring bubbles into a pool at the back of the cleft and trickles down the slope.  Next to the pool is a crude firepit whose ashes suggest recent use.  Charred bones lie strewn about the outer edge of the cleft, away from some flattened indentations in the rough ground circling the firepit.

The trail levels out slightly, as if gathering energy before rising toward the pinnacle of the outcropping to the northwest.  Empty roosts are scattered among the crags, many of them with broken eggshells.

The main outcropping divides spectacularly as the land rises to a peak like a huge spike driven into the earth between the rugged outcrop to the southeast and the cliff edge to the southwest.  A small ledge to the north seems almost an afterthought compared to this rocky finger pointing defiantly at the heavens.

A small ledge clings desperately to the main outcropping, overlooking a dangerously entrancing vista hundreds of feet below.  A step onto the ledge dislodges bits of scree that skid across and down to fall in silence into the roiling waters of the river -- the ledge is fighting a losing battle against weather and time.  Beyond the churning waters lies the far side of the river: a vast, barren expanse empty of signs of habitation.

The narrow path skirts the edge of the rocky outcropping, ending in a sharp peak to the northeast.  The trail blends into the face of the rock like a scar from a long forgotten wound.  Along the western edge of the trail, a patchwork of lichens and stubborn mosses drinks in the moisture rising from the river far below.

The broader expanse of rock to the southwest tilts and sharpens to the north, as if the outcropping itself resisted further efforts to scale its imposing face.  It must have taken persevering labor to forge the narrow path that struggles the north and south route.  A roughly carved niche in the eastern face of the rocky wall offers more evidence that the path was the work of hands, not nature.

Part of the edge of the path has fallen away, and a broken slope leads down to the west.  On what remains of the ledge, massive boulders define a trail that rises to the north and east.  Far to the north is the summit of the outcropping, a sharp peak dominating the rugged landscape.

The slope ends sharply, jutting out at a dizzying height above the river.  The debris from the rockslide clutters the area except where it has fallen down a narrow channel, carved into the face of the rock, that allows a switchbacked route toward the river below.

The view north looks like nature's chaotic side was inspired to rend the bedrock itself, heaving the land up, gradually at first but culminating in a towering height hundreds of feet in the air.  Like a serpent attacking the feet of a giant, the river to the west rages over rapids, pounding against the rock in an angry competition between the two elements.  Along the rapids, shadows collect in hollows that mark the river's slow victory in the struggle between water and earth.

Halfway up the ancient oak, its enormous limbs form highways in the sky for the creatures of the canopy.  The weathered walkways cast dark shadows over the marsh below.  A leaf drifts down, taking a long time to fall, slowed in its descent by the rising bog gasses that clog and taint the air.

Deep claw marks, signs of nature red in tooth and claw, scar the wide branch near a broken arrow lodged in the wood.  The archer must have missed his target, because bloodstains streak the limb and the leaves below.  A large vine twists down from a vine-covered cypress to the south.

The limb groans under the unaccustomed weight of visitors.  Something has stripped the branch of its bark, maybe the insect larvae of a wood-boring beetle that now infest the creaking limb, making every step both distasteful and dangerous.  A plump, white grub inches its way to a richer feeding spot, and disappears into the limb.
Sunlight breaks through the canopy above, painting the branch with patches of light and shadow.  Only the rising stench from the bog below spoils the temptation to lie back and enjoy the sight.

The top of the oak provides a wide view of the surrounding lands.  To the north Forlorn Hope springs from the rocky ridge into the sky.  To the far south a shining line on the horizon may be the ocean, Altanen's destination, glistening in the sunlight.  The splash of Altanen's rapids rises over the sounds of the bog.

The branch takes a sharp, sudden bend, possibly in a direction set when the tree was young, and the limb grew toward a patch of sunlight.  The obscuring moss partly masks the turn, and an unwary traveller risks a dangerous fall.

The pleasant scent of living cypress wood is overlaid by a heavier, spicy aroma, possibly the silver-shaded moss that covers this tree alone of those that stand on the slope.  Vines weave in and out of the moss, connecting the branches of neighboring trees in a complicated network.  Judging from scuff marks on the boughs, some of the vines are routes as well marked as the paths on the ground below.

The water level in the Altanen has dropped, exposing a nearly flat strip of muddy bank.  To the west, a long streak of green is visible in the middle of the river, and there seems to be movement on it.

The mudbank ends, closed off by a shoulder of the cliff.  The view across the arm of the river shows that the island, although low, is fairly long, extending a good half-league downstream.  Low vegetation covers it, some kind of grey-green scrub or grass.

Toward the south across this arm of the river, a low scrub-covered island rises, dividing the river's flow.  The swift current sends up feathers of spray where it hits the island, but the water in this back-channel is slower and smoother.  To the east, a muddy strip of land lies at the foot of Galduta Isharon.

To the east looms the cliff of Galduta Isharon, a narrow river bank at its base.  An island lies further west, an easy swim through the flowing water.  To the southeast, the trees of the Bog Wallows rise above the edge of the swamp.

To the north looms the cliff of Galduta Isharon; to the east beyond the river bank, treetops rise above the mist.  A low island lies further west across the channel, an easy swim through the flowing water.

The water in the back channel flows southeast here, lapping at the shore of the low island, but smoother to the east toward the cliffs of Galduta Isharon.  Except for a covering of waist-high grasses, the island looks barren.

Swirling leaves and muddy streaks in the water show that a strong current pushes away from the swamp, apparently the outflow from the streams that feed it.  Easier water lies to the west toward the island.
The shore of the island to the west lies close by, its bank receding to the southwest.  Its appearance is much like that of the swamp across the river to the east, except for an absence of trees.
The shore of the island to the west lies close by, its bank receding to the northwest.  Exposed by the falling river level, it's covered with grass that looks to be waist-high on a Gor'Tog.

The water in the back channel flows southeast here, lapping at the shore of the low island, but smoother to the east toward the cliffs of Galduta Isharon.  Except for a covering of waist-high grasses, the island looks barren.

The animal runs in the grass, if that's what they are, cross and mingle with a bewildering complexity.  An occasional waving of the grass in a purposeful direction hints that something else inhabits the island.  Across the channel to east, the tops of trees rise above the mist from the river.

The animal runs in the grass, if that's what they are, cross and mingle with a bewildering complexity.  An occasional waving of the grass in a purposeful direction hints that something else inhabits the island.  Across the channel to east, the tops of trees rise above the mist from the river.

A long, low island stretches to the south, dividing the river in two.  The eastern channel must be deeper, for its water is relatively smooth and unruffled, but in the western arm the lowering of the river has uncovered jagged rocks, and the water foams and races between them with a loud roar.

To the north, the island narrows to a point, but to the south it broadens until it almost looks like a meadow covered with waving grasses.  The grass is beaten down in a few places, possibly animal trails.  The rapids to the west cloud the air with spray, making it hard to see what lies beyond them.

The animal runs in the grass, if that's what they are, cross and mingle with a bewildering complexity.  Taller patches here and there confuse the view as they wave in the wind and the drifting, blurring spray from the rapids to the west.

Suffused in muted pink light, a vibrant undersea mosaic spans the inner wall of the terrace and provides a colorful backdrop for a small meditating statue of Eluned.  The white coral goddess is seated in contemplative repose, gazing past a vine-draped sandstone colonnade and into the world beyond.  A spring warmth fills the air.

Some thoughtful soul has dragged driftwood into a crude shelter and stuffed the larger holes with weeds.  How well it keeps out the rain is anyone's guess, but it offers more protection than anywhere else on the island.

Grass extends in all directions.  From here, it's easy to forget that this is an island in the middle of a great river.  It looks like one could walk across this wild meadow to the trees distant in the east.

A narrow neck of the island curves north to southwest, covered with high grass.  The rapids must be close, judging by their noise, but the quieter channel to the east shows through breaks in the grass, with places where it would be possible to get into the river.

To the south from this spit of land, the Altanen has a strange appearance: a band of muddy water along the western shore, a clearer blue one along the eastern side, slowly blending as the river winds into parts unknown.  Its two arms join here, holding the low, grassy island that stretches to the north.  From here it could almost be a meadow or a pasture.

To the north, the island expands into a field of waving grasses, but to the south it shrinks to a narrow spit of land, barely above the surface of the water.  A bowshot to east or west would reach the river, but the roaring rapids to the west show there's no escape in that direction.

The animal runs in the grass, if that's what they are, cross and mingle with a bewildering complexity.  An occasional waving of the grass in a purposeful direction hints that something else inhabits the island.  Across the channel to east, the tops of trees rise above the mist from the river.
The shore of the island to the west lies close by, its low bank presenting no obstacle.  A bird circles overhead now and then, too high up to identify, but it might be a vulture.

The shore of the island to the west lies close by, but its bank looks undercut and higher than it is to the north.  The view to the east is obscured, with only the tops of the taller trees rising above the mist.

The shore of the island to the west lies close by, but its steep, high bank makes reaching it impossible.  The view to the east is obscured, with only the tops of the taller trees rising above the mist.

The two arms of the river join where it broadens at the south end of the island.  To the northwest, the turbulent rapids spill their water into the confluence, slowing dramatically in a cloud of spray.

The water surges first in one direction then in another, bouncing around, between, and sometimes over the rocks that were once below the surface of the river.  The current races along, sweeping past the banks on either side.

The water surges first in one direction then in another, bouncing around, between, and sometimes over the rocks that were once below the surface of the river.  The current races along, sweeping past the banks on either side.

As the flow of the broad river parts around the island, this western arm forces its way between and over clusters of rocks, barely above the surface.  The water races through the narrow channels, its speed and power increasing at every constriction.

The water surges first in one direction then in another, bouncing around, between, and sometimes over the rocks that were once below the surface of the river.  The current races along, sweeping past the banks on either side.

A portable sorting table with compartments full of sparkling gems seems out of place in this musty room, with its walls and ceiling that look held together by cobwebs and wasp nests.  Oiled paper tacked over one window frame creates a makeshift covering that blocks not only the elements, but also most of the light.  Two barrels offer seating near the counter where the gem dealer does business, and a ceiling lantern casts a glow whereby he is able to judge the character of his customers.

A massive oak counter topped with a fence of steel bars dominates the Mer'Kresh Office of Debts and Fees.  A smiling clerk behind the counter does his cheerful best to help Rissans who have problems with debts or with the city bureaucracy.

Wooden filing cabinets line the cypress planked walls of this tiny office, giving it a rustic scent.  Piles of neatly stacked papers cover the top of a driftwood desk that has been positioned to immediately catch the attention of anyone entering the room.  A velvet rope divides the small waiting area in an attempt to direct Rissans, impatient to get back to the hunt, into forming a line to wait their turn.

The path gradually rises to the northeast, sloping upward as it winds around a flat-topped hill.  Smooth waves of hardened lava lash out amongst shadowy remains, the basalt shining glassily against the backdrop of night.

A desolate scape of scorched shadows and piles of wreckage rolls out around you.  Flattened by forces at present unseen, everything is lit by an eerie, demonic red light the color of blood.  Remains of houses lie in restless piles amongst pools of frozen lava, skeletons of the former village of Crook.

A wide verandah with a canopy of honeysuckle and grape vines runs the full length of the building.  Colorful mosaics celebrating the healing arts cover the walls.  Above the doorway leading into the building, the greeting "Welcome to the Empath Guild of Ratha" is formed in blue and gold-colored tiles.

The long corridor serves as little more than a passageway to get from room to room and front to back of the guild hall.  Except for occasional scuff and gouge marks from careless visitors, the plaster walls are undecorated.

Rows of mostly barren wooden shelves fill the room, the few that are full contain empty jars and glass bottles.  Rounds of hard cheese, several braids of onions, and a string of sausages hang from ceiling hooks.

The crest of the Empaths' Guild has been skillfully recreated in broken tiles to pave the patio at the back of the Guild.  Carved limestone benches interspersed with young potted palms line the rim of the circular patio.  Behind them, crimson and orange daylilies dance happily in the breeze.  To the west beyond a wrought iron gate lies the Guild Leader's herb garden.

Sketches and drawings of herbs, flowers, and arcane alchemical equipment cover the walls of the guild office.  Bundles of jadice, rosemary, and lavender hang from overhead drying racks.  Pots of yelith and miniature roses sit on a bench in front of a window overlooking the garden.

At first glance the clearing appears to be covered with short grass, but each footstep releases citrus and pineapple scents.  Lemon thyme and low-growing chamomile have been planted along with the grass to form a slightly springy herbal carpet.  Their small yellow and white flowers are strewn among the deep green grass like stars across the sky.

Although the framework is complete, only part of the slats for the patio cover have been installed.  At the far end of the patio, workmen have carelessly left bundles of the slats and several stacks of tiles uncovered.  A young grapevine has been staked and tied to climb one of the outer support posts.  In a few years, it may cover the patio and provide shade and shelter, but for now it looks abandoned in a forgotten corner of the guild.

Small paths trace through the naturalized herb garden giving limited access to all the plants.  The sweet, heady perfume of moonflowers fills the air.  Practically invisible during the day, at night they bloom a pale silvery-white on the vine-covered wrought iron fence that surrounds the garden.  In the glow from the patio and the guild house windows, only the vague shapes of the other plants can be seen.

Lush vines laden with grapes block the sights and sounds of the street outside the guild.  Padded benches, tucked into the corners at this end of the verandah, provide comfortable seating for guild visitors.  A candle-lit chandelier illuminates the room.

The sweet scent of flowers fills the eastern end of the verandah.  A candle-lit brass chandelier casts a warm glow illuminating the mosaic on the inner wall.  Mounds of colorful canvas cushions have been set out as seating.

In a velvet robe punctuated with beetle-wing spangles, Menevia the Blind Seeress holds forth, seated at a round table.  She does not rise to greet you.  Querents huddle around her, awaiting answers on what the future holds.  Several cowled figures stand by a trelium display case, pointing at talismans, orbs and other trinkets, debating their virtues and price.

This pleasant gazebo is a surprising annex to Menevia's stuffy chambers below.  Light from the astral bodies envelops you through enchanted glass, a kind that permits the full spectrum to penetrate.  Stained glass lightcatchers of unicorns, chimeras and griffins cast tiny rainbows on everything in the room, including you.  Menevia seems totally aware of the state of the heavens, sensing rather than seeing.

The smell of rotting food swirls around the various-sized tables that fill the room.  Dented plates litter the ground amid broken chairs.  Long bars of steel run parallel to either side of each table and are anchored at both ends.
This side of the prison was reserved for those that misbehaved.  Damp air carries a biological odor that is not mitigated by the aromas of rotting food that emanate from the south.
Everything, from the walls to the doors is dark grey, shrouding the area in the dreary appearance of a rainy day.  Shreds of cloth litter the ground, although what they once were is unclear.

The dim light from the passages above casts a faint glow into the area.  This dark cell has been filled about halfway up the walls with an unusual black goo that smells worse than a paladin who hasn't washed his armor in many years.  Skulls, internal organs and half eaten animals float upon the surface.

A small, reinforced portcullis dangles from the ceiling, its operating chain broken in pieces on the floor.  Lanterns hang on the walls, providing light through the grime that coats them.  Dirtier still, the floor is caked with dirt and mud.

Black and grey stone forms the floor and walls of the prison hallway, punctuated by gaping openings that were once barred by doors.  Flickering shadows from torches filter upward from the stairs that lead below.

Black and grey stone forms the floor and walls of the prison hallway, punctuated by gaping holes where doors once stood.  The heavy material muffles sounds coming from inside the cells so that only the sound of footsteps against the ground are audible.  A musty odor envelops the entire area.

Dark stone walls enclose a large dirty cell used for holding prisoners.  A small pile of rotting hay covers the corner of the floor, the only form of bed in the cell.  Cracks in the walls and brickwork show how little care the guards had for the prisoners well-being.

Trapped between the foreboding stone walls to the west and the spiked fence to the east, the work yard stretches out to the north.  Countless years of mining the marble of the quarry have left the area sunken well below the ring road to the east, adding to the oppressive sense of confinement.

The ground here is uneven, rising and falling with no seeming pattern.  Gaping pits where blocks of marble have been cut free lie hidden behind high ground, unintentional traps for the unwary.  A spiked fence separates the work yard from the surrounding ring road above.  Near the compound wall is a deep pit covered with rough timbers, a staircase leading down into the darkness.

The flickering light of torches sends shadows scurrying across this expansive underground chamber.  A series of long ironwood worktables with accompanying benches dominates the center of the room.  Along one wall is a series of racks containing all the tools needed to work in the quarry above as well as prepare the garnets here in the Pit.  Stacks of unworked marble blocks glistening with crude garnets line another wall.  A staircase leads to the work yard above.

Flickering torches cast eerie shadows within the room, creating a foreboding dance of light within the dank pit.  Worktables and benches are pushed against the wall, each holding an assortment of tools for use.  Worked marble blocks stacked upon wooden slats within the center of the room await further preparations.

Dim light flickers upon a large sign fastened to the wall, baring a loud proclamation of moral intent.  Neatly piled upon wooden slats are roughly shaped marble blocks, each awaiting further work.  Workbenches line the center of the room, each holding the necessary tools to further the process of the material.

Well placed torches upon the wall create ample lighting over the workbenches.  Shaped marble blocks rest upon wooden slats, awaiting final shaping before moving onto the last of their processing.  Thick layers of debris line the floor, though a broom stands at the ready in a corner next to a waste bin.

Crates of garnets and slats of marble blocks rest to one side of the room.  Directly across, well lit workbenches loaded with supplies stand at the ready.  A sign carved with a stern warning is fastened upon the wall above the workspace as a deterrent to those with thieving fingers.

A massive desk dominates the western wall, flanked on either side by large racks spilling parchments and scrolls onto the ground.  Overhead, a gaethzen orb glows steadily in the gloom, chasing away the encroaching shadows.  Cabinets fill the remaining wall space, their open drawers gaping and empty.

Grey tendrils of light creep from a dingy lantern hung from the ceiling, barely illuminating even such a tiny space.  Nothing remains of the furnishings but splinters and mattress stuffing strewn about.

Flickering torchlight reveals deep gouges and scratches on the walls, mostly obscuring older images on the walls.  A shallow pool of water stands in one corner where guards used to scrub the newly arrived prisoners but now the water is fouled with refuse and debris.

Trees have been hacked down and dragged leaving nothing to hide behind, making escape through the front gate nearly impossible.  Anyone on the tower has a clear view of the entire area, able to shoot both inside and outside the compound.  Lizards lie sunning themselves on a rock that was too large to be moved.

Three roads meet in the center of this clearing.  Two branches lead into the jungle, and the last towards the compound.  All of them are level, creating a smooth path for animals to travel over.  Grass and other little green shrubs litter the area around the road, leaving the road looking empty but colorful.

The largest of the towers that surround the prison stands here on a small knoll, like a lighthouse overlooking its rocky shore.  Looking down over the southwest you can see the tiny boathouse that brings guards and prisoners alike to the island and the sheer cliff that keeps the prisoners from escaping.

Part of the road has been eroded by heavy rains, creating deep groves as the water runs down to find equilibrium.  Green areca palms have started to grow here and get thicker to the west, creating a tropical jungle.

Skirting the road that winds between the tropical trees and the walls of the prison is a single pendas plant.  Its broad red leaves stand out among the brown, sandy dirt of the path.  The hard walls of the prison have crumbled a bit.

Surrounding fishtail palms and bamboo threaten to overgrow the road, which gets narrower here.  Some of the cane has been cut short from past attempts to keep them from reaching the road.  To the east is a ladder leading up to a guard tower.

The upkeep on this guard tower is long overdue and much needed.  The floor has started to come apart, causing cracks and large gaps to appear in the surface of the bamboo.  Discarded knives and rusting shackles have been scattered about the decaying floor.

Deep within a dense planting of bamboo, a spiked iron fence struggles to remain upright.  The road cuts wide around the stand, moving perilously close to the dark tree trunks of the ever-present jungle.  High-voiced monkey calls echo through the foliage.

The road bends slightly around an enormous tree that rises up out of sight among the canopy.  Its shade has crowded out most of the normal undergrowth, leaving a clearer area for the road to pass through.

Wataba trees line the road, crowding close and blocking almost all sight of the spiked fence.  Looped over the limb of a bush close to the road is a green vine snake, its long tongue flicking in and out as it watches the rare traveler.  A thin path leads to the east, almost overgrown in the thick stand of foliage.

Philodendrons bloom in lush profusion along the spiked fence to the west.  A low rock outcrop helps keep the trees away from the road, which winds along between the fence and the rocks.  Maidenhair ferns cluster close to the roadbed, taking advantage of the increased sunlight.

Cattleya orchids give way to thick clumps of unidentifiable vines and bushes, dense and impenetrable.  Foliage swarms over the spiked fence enclosing the work yard, obscuring all views of the interior.

Purple cattleya has grown in thick patches to complement the rainbow-colored birds that can be seen flapping from tree to tree and squawking at one another.  To the east is a ladder leading up to the guard tower that oversees the prison work yard.

The view from the tower offers contrasting worlds to see.  Northeastward, the lush greens of the forest set within the deep blues of the surrounding ocean look surreal, as if painted by the gods.  However, in the opposite direction, the shabby work yard with its canvas of browns and greys looms behind the dangerously sharp fences below.

Bright pinks and reds of the vireya plants that have amassed here give varied color to the otherwise dark green.  A fortress of winding vines and other plants make any travel except along the road impossible.  The jungle canopy high in the air shakes from time to time.

Royal palms rise in shapely curves and turns, beside other large tropical trees, sometimes providing cool shade along the road.  The wind, rustling the palm leaves, grabs clothing as if in attempts to hold or push people around.  The start of the prison fence that encloses the work yard can be seen here.
Sand and shells give way to rich tropical foliage.  Sago palm and green bihai lend a rich emerald color to the vegetation against a background of bamboo and lush verdant grasses.
Gravel fills the roadside, lined with wispy grasses and weeds.  Guard towers rise above the white-painted prison wall which stretches endlessly beside the pathway.

Little flanks the road except sand and a field of creeping crabgrass.  The crashing sounds of waves echoes from beyond the headland.  A stone guard tower looms high above, a ladder leading inside its cold walls.

Though remaining sturdily in place against the wind, the old, lashed-together bamboo still creaks and groans with each step taken upon it.  A driftwood rail surrounds the edges of the platform, giving little to no protection against a plummet off the edge.  Above, palm leaves have been secured to the bamboo frame, creating a small bungalow to relax under.

Below the road, nestled in the curve of the cliff is a small beach.  Seabirds mill in the air, looking for washed up food or soaring aimlessly.  The sea breeze is strong here, wafting up from the distant ocean.

Running close to the drop of the cliff, the road is bare and easily manageable, comprised of layers of seashells intermixed with sand.  A few large rocks break up the flatness of the island, although it still gives the appearance of a flat-topped seamount rising above sea level.  A small shrine hugs the cliffside, clinging to the narrow space between the track and the sheer drop to the waters below.

One of the guard towers stands here overlooking the entrance to the prison, with walkways for the guards to observe.  The road is worn from many years of prison guards walking along the perimeter while patrolling or on the way to their posts.

Crafted of sturdy bamboo lashed together with rough vine, the guard tower seems sturdy enough to support a good amount of weight.  The view from this perch is perfect to assess the surrounding landscape.  A makeshift ladder leads back down to the ground.

At the top of the ladder, thick jungle surrounds a rocky, dirt road.  Far below, the crushed and broken skeletons of unfortunate souls who failed to find their freedom litter the jagged rocks, left there by the guards as a warning to others who might entertain thoughts of escape.  The road twists and turns through the jungle as far as the eye can see.

A narrow, rocky trail weaves back and forth up the mountain from the boathouse, hugging the sheer cliff.  The only way to continue from there is a very tall ladder.  The ladder stretches over three hundred feet straight up and is six feet wide, leaving plenty of room for even the largest prisoner or guard.
Darkness pervades this room, pierced only by a single bright light focused on a table and a soft glow emanating from an archway to the north.
Covered with tiny footprints, this small alley runs behind Noot's Teahouse.  Unused and hidden from the main street, this site is a perfect locale for a youth's first smoke or to sleep off a drunk.

rooms.desc: A large seven-tiered crystal chandelier is poised high above and casts warm light throughout the room.  The dining tables are draped with pure white tablecloths and adorned with centerpieces of freshly cut flowers.  Carved mahogany chairs are pulled to the tables, an elegant place setting before each one.  Plush gold-flecked deep green carpeting borders the inlaid wood floor that bears the image of a gilded yak and looks well-suited to dancing.

An air of formality can be felt throughout this stately room where conclaves are welcome to gather and collaborate on various guild matters.  The Crossing Traders' Guild crest is proudly displayed on the rear wall and next to it, in the corner, is a superbly stitched flag bearing the emblem of the Traders' Guild.  A large oval mahogany conference table dominates the room and is surrounded on all sides by finely crafted leather wingback chairs.

The smoke in this room is thicker and more cloying than any encountered at Catrox's Forge, but its source is entirely different.  The finest cigars, the most expensive pipeweed, and imported maugwort weed are being puffed on by the prosperous merchants gathered in this inner sanctum of commerce.  Rotund Halflings in fancy vests, grey-bearded Humans in elegant, fur-trimmed jerkins, Elves in shimmering raiment, all are among the land's elite traders who form the heart of the Guild.

Immaculate partitions with carefully hung works of art are interspersed throughout the stark gallery.  Crushed velvet roping imposes several feet of distance from these treasured pieces.  Hand-carved sconces are discreetly positioned to cast soft ambient light to accentuate each masterpiece.

The sheen of polished mahogany floors vanishes into dimness at the far end of the long hall.  As your eyes follow the length of the flooring, you notice a series of niches set into the walls.  Nearby, a delicate rope of fine silk stretches across the hallway.

The suite is reserved for the elite of the Traders' Guild governing hierarchy, particularly those outlanders visiting the Guild headquarters on business.  The walls are paneled with rich, dark huljik wood, oiled to a fine sheen.  A mahogany writing table, decked with a silver inkwell and eagle quill stands before a tall bay window which affords a panoramic view of the town's commercial district.  A high, carved sleigh bed faces the window, flanked by nightstands holding books on trade and travel.

Plain fittings display luxury goods from the farthest corners of the realms, but this wholesaler makes no attempt to puff up the goods or cajole the buyers.  This is a place where professionals do business with other professionals, all of whom know and disdain the weaseling tricks commonly played on customers.  Displays are sturdy and pleasant, but not fancy, and everything is brightly lit.  Rugs are a plain brown, walls are an unpanelled beige, and the atmosphere is one of business.

This seldom used corridor has become a favorite temporary storage room for excessive stock.  Stacks of various wares make quick passage through here difficult.  You notice a thick, steel door just peeking out from behind some wooden pallets.  A Gor'Tog guard leans against it, nonchalant and vigilant at the same time.

This seldom used corridor has become a favorite temporary storage room for excessive stock.  Stacks of various wares make quick passage through here difficult.  You notice a thick, steel door just peeking out from behind some wooden pallets.  A Gor'Tog guard leans against it, nonchalant and vigilant at the same time.

This room is in the process of being finished.  The polished mahogany walls and ceiling are angled in such a way that would project the Auctioneer's voice clearly to the rear of the hall as well as to those listening in the front.  In the emptiness of the room one can imagine the many items and Kronars that will one day exchange hands here.

The vault walls are clad in thick steel plates, one of which has been engraved "commissioned from Catrox the Smith".  Locked chests of various sizes, with members' names on them, are neatly stacked in metal racks.  You are being watched by the Gor'Tog guard through a narrow, almost imperceptible gap between two of the plates.

This cramped office, a former broom closet, is a close definition of chaos.  An old desk, cluttered with orders awaiting delivery to other provinces, occupies most of this room.  A mottled carpet covers the floor except in the few spots it is burned through from carelessly dropped cigars butts.  What wall space is available is covered with hastily drawn charts tracking the movement of goods between provinces.

The scent of grains and cut grass permeates the room.  A broad straw broom and long-handled dustpan are propped against sacks of grain that have been neatly arranged along the back wall.  The worn mahogany floors show signs of frequent use.  A faint chirping emanates from somewhere inside the grass bin.

Giant bins, huge wooden barrels and piles of overstuffed hogsheads all await distribution to their final retail destination or to warehouses and shippers around town for export to far corners of Elanthia.

This newly constructed room is devoid of any furnishing.  The breadth of the room is easily large enough to accommodate many potential buyers, while allowing them to converse freely without disrupting any auctions that may be underway.

The lavishly furnished guild continues its traditions with rich oak furnishings and dark, oil-stained mahogany walls.  The foyer provides a place for visitors to listen in on events held in the Moot Room, without disturbing the participants.

Here the Guild holds meetings and lectures for the townsfolk and interested guests.  There is always some informative, cultural or public relations event scheduled to transpire in this chamber.  Often, high-profile ceremonies where merchants contribute to the community fund, the Mayor's Charity Ball and other worthy causes are conducted here as well.

Leaning walls inlaid with panes of polished black onyx enclose this sunken, icy vestibule that is lit by sparkles of dark gold winking fleetingly like teasing ghosts.  Odd sounds echo back and forth, reminiscent of a choir bustling through rehearsal.
Dark grey stone walls and cold basalt floors stretch far beyond sight through the dimly lit corridors that branch from this central nexus.  Two dilapidated pine doors flank the southern passage.

The dark stone floor is uncluttered and swept clean of dust and debris, leaving the impression that something has been here recently.  In spite of the lack of rubble, the air smells dank, with a hint of decay.

The four hallways converge here, centered around a massive grid of wrought iron that stretches out over a shadow-draped pit sunk deep into the ground.  A thick noxious order of decay curls up from the depths of this repugnant cage.
The uneven dark stone walls bear strange, ancient etchings that depict gruesome scenes of war.  Dark colors outlining some of the carvings have permanently leached into the porous stone.
Vaulting high to the ceiling, a black crystalline archway opens a narrow corridor to the north.  A discordant choral chant echoes against the dark stone enclosure, carrying from far away.

The exquisite white marble floors are veined with swirls of verdant green forming the shape of a triple-tined claw pointing northward to the worship halls.  A great black crystal archway leads south, back to the clergy's quarters.
This great hall features vaulted walls of dark crystal and an inlaid floor of green-veined marble.  A faint, spiritual chanting converges from every which direction, buoyed by frigid air.
High onyx walls line a featureless passageway along whose mirror-like surfaces a shock of light occasionally crackles to show travelers the way.

A rusted iron lamp swings precariously from the vaulted onyx ceiling, disturbed by a strong breeze.  The erratic flicker cast from above draws ever-shifting apparitions of shadow on the smooth onyx walls, leaving one to wonder what is real and what is illusion.

The smooth onyx of the walls is disrupted here, with each wall carved in its own intricate, raised pattern.  The shallow illumination flowing from the southeast casts soft shadows from the raised features.
Diffused light from the northwest casts a dull glow against the smooth surface of the onyx walls.  The walls feel cold to the touch and no seams mar their perfect symmetry.

The smooth onyx floor has been shattered by thick, muscular roots pushing upward.  The roots intertwine into a contorted mass in the center of the hall.  The stench of burning flesh rises from the strange altar, yet no fire is visible.

Muted light from the southwest casts dark wavering images on the unblemished onyx wall and bounces to the neighboring wall.  Further shadows shimmer eerily on the polished floor, resembling writhing bodies caught in the throes of a painful death.

A wavering torch secured in a solid stone funnel is solidly fused into the glossy onyx wall near the high ceiling.  Occasional wafts of air cause the flame to twist slowly, an imitation of an ominous dance of the macabre.
The smooth, glossy finish of the onyx walls is unbroken.  The passage seems brighter to the southwest, where filtered light seeps into the room, reflecting eerie shadows on the polished surface.

Surrounded on all sides by smooth lustrous onyx walls, the enclosed environment lends the impression of being entombed in a box of solid rock.  Occasionally a glimmer of light will reflect dully across the unblemished surfaces, causing a brief moment of vertigo.

Sinister frescoes adorn the northern wall of this cavernous hall, where the dichotomy of the silver and onyx hallways merges into one.  The ceiling is a sweeping arch of black crystal, supported by pillars of darkly veined jade.  A twisting hallway with verdant malachite walls winds to the south.

Irregular formations of malachite create a treacherous cavern that winds in an erratic serpentine pattern to the south.  The air is crisp, cold, and fresh, with no hint of the musty pall draped over the rest of the ancient temple.
The icy air carries the faint tinkling of off-key wind chimes that echoes eerily through the dark malachite tunnel.  As one travels southerly down the hall, the temperature seems to drop rapidly.

A thin layer of frost coats the malachite formations, while slender icicles jab downward into the hall.  Vapor crystallizes with every breath, each a wraith of former life captured forever by the cruel clutches of the temple's heart.

The ice-laden floor suddenly gives way to an enormous chasm to the south.  Tendrils of intricate silver writhe out from the dusky malachite walls, intertwining to form a strange altar just before the lip of the gaping chasm.  Far in the distance to the south, a glimmering crystalline dais hovers inexplicably over the great pit.
Smooth and deathly cold to the touch, the silver walls are free of any markings.  A pale luminance from the northwest seems to beckon the unwary traveler.

Silver walls, their smooth surface polished to a glossy finish, refract the dim light invading menacingly from the southeast.  Odd reflections bounce between the polished surfaces, causing a moment of dizziness that quickly passes.
