Inky blackness shrouds this strange abyss, drowning the feeble light of silver stars beyond.  A cascading waterfall of light descends from the nothingness above, pooling into what you can comprehend only as a radiant lake of molten starfire.

A sensation of warmth and security enfolds your spirit as you drift upon the boiling tide of molten starfire.  A benevolent sense of peace and serenity pervades you, as if Life and Death meld into a singular emotion here.

Rough earthen walls crawl with lichen, mushrooms, and other slimy things that do not bear investigation.  The ground at the base of the ladder is a layer of mud and dead pine needles, with a few small bones near the walls.  The room seems more like an oubliette than a tunnel.

Markings on the tunnel walls are so smeared from running water that they are illegible, but some stone chips pressed into the walls under the marks form an arrow pointing east.  The floor here is a runnel of mud squishing underfoot.

A small pile of bones is cluttered by the southeast wall of the earth tunnel, perhaps washed there by a spring flood at some time.  Although tumbled and gnawed, the bones retain enough remains that the stench is eye-watering.  The mold beginning to consume the skeleton of the unfortunate creature detracts not at all from the scent.

Tepid, murky water trickles down the walls of the rough tunnel, making the passage clammy.  The chill comes as much from within as without, for here more than in the bog above can you feel the death in the air.

The smell of musty things rotting somewhere is strong in the air in this underground antechamber.  The floor is of stones, pressed into the earth and covered in mold.  The walls crawl with dampness, water seeping through the earthen ceiling and moving silently to the floor, disappearing under the slippery rocks.

Tattered clothing lies mostly buried in the muck of the floor, wedged against the rough walls.  A few forlorn bells chime when water drips from the ceiling onto the befouled heap, and a mocking laugh echoes through the tunnels in response.
The twisting tunnels are disorienting, spiraling through the dark like a demented seashell.  Air stirs sullenly as you pass, bringing the fresh reek of decay to brush against your face.

A curtain of water sheathes the walls and puddles on the floor, the liquid slowly oozing into the walls but making the ground underfoot a squelching pool of mud.  The earth walls here are a little smoother from the work of the murky water.
The twisting tunnels are disorienting, spiraling through the dark like a demented seashell.  Air stirs sullenly as you pass, bringing the fresh reek of decay to brush against your face.

A stone dam blocks the north part of the tunnel, keeping the bogwater collected on the muddy floor from seeping any farther.  At one time the dam might have covered the entire opening, but stones have fallen inward so that although the lower section is blocked, a hefty gap has opened at the top.  Chill air wafts over the stones, a bit more fresh than what the rest of the tunnels offer.

Stone surrounds you, grey and dank and unforgiving.  These tunnels were not carved from the stone, but built with stone blocks, roofed with slate, floored with stone chips.  The labor involved is hard to imagine, but the evidence stretches before you.

Large rocks lie tumbled on the stone floor, which is covered in a fine layer of grit.  The walls have gouges where the rocks have been torn out, whether by natural settling of the earth or by a conscious effort is hard to tell.  The sound of trickling water echoes from the northeast.

Lichen and moss grow on the walls, the latter close to the floor where, perhaps, the water sometimes seeps.  The lichen is grey and barely noticeable against the grey stone until a fat black spider crawls across it and out of sight.  Looking up, you see the ceiling is rough here and draped with cobwebs.
A trickle of fresh water seeps through the piled rubble of a long-ago rockfall.  Hints of fresh air drift through the stones, but the way east is decidedly blocked.

Water drips somewhere nearby, but the floor in this part of the tunnels is even and dry.  The thick stone walls with their rough surfaces make sound move strangely, and a scream would carry its own weight through the corridors.  From the northwest comes a low hum, more felt than heard.
Running water echoes from somewhere in the tunnels, along with strange scraping noises.  The grey stone walls divulge nothing, lowering flat and rough over the uneven floor.

A rough chunk of stone rises from the floor as though it grew from the mountains themselves.  Closer inspection reveals careful chiseling and subtle carving to create a flat-topped altar.  This part of the tunnel is hushed, the stone floor clean, the walls spotless, but thrums with power.  Someone -- or something -- keeps the altar in good repair.  Small bits of bone and feathers are arranged behind the altar, holding meaning known only to those who laid them there.

A pair of thick iron chains suspended from the ceiling are bracketed to the west wall, and from there hang to the floor, ending in an empty pair of manacles.  Small rodents scurrying over the metal into cracks in the walls cause the chains to rub the stone in a distinctive, teeth-clenching scrape.  Hints of gold in the wall, knee-high to a Dwarf, catch the eye.  From the northeast comes a low vibration through the stone.

Stones, piled one atop the other in a sort of pyramid, inscribe a circle on the ground, which is more dirt than water in this area.  Within the circle is a set of stone stairs that leads down into the darkness of what might be a tunnel.  The muck is kept at bay here with more stones set as though pressed against the sides of a well.  Beside the stairs is a flat granite marker.

An odd group of plants, their green stems topped by bright yellow pitcher-shaped flowers, grows in a circle around a rotting stump that rises through the brown and red moss.  A sickly-sweet smell from the plants overtakes the underlying scent of rot.  The sluggish water of the rill trickles to the south, while a buzzing of flying insects sounds much closer.

Like a sodden rag, the taste of the foul air lashes at you as you pass alongside the murky pool.  A small overflow meanders out of sight to the west, carrying indescribable bits of black with it.  The rill is hardly a hand wide but cuts deep through the moss and muck, which tremble under each footstep.

The sky can be glimpsed through the tangled, dead branches of the sodden trees standing sentinel in the boggy ground.  To the north, the mountains rise like sithannik backs, while close by the path northwards lies a pool of murky water.  The reek of decaying things belches from the pool when its contents settle and air bubbles burst on the surface.

The ground quakes with every carefully placed step over the soft peat.  Moss lies in a thin layer over earth and water, making it hard to discern where solid ground stands.  The moss squelches underfoot, sodden with the water and decaying plants -- and other decaying things -- of the bog.

Grey shapes flit among the standing, blighted tree trunks, moving with a steady purpose.  They dig at the ground with rhythmic thuds, then pick something up and vanish into the mist with it.  The figures seem not to notice the folk treading in the bog as they continue blankly doing their tasks.

A wall of brambles guards the top of a steep bank that drops westerly and sinks into the bog.  The colors in the bog are brilliant -- red, yellow, orange, and green moss, small red flowers, bright yellow plants -- but something sickly lies underneath.  From here nothing more definite can be seen, yet the sense of wrongness rises from the fecund ground like a mist.

Blighted pine trees, drowned in the bog, rise as pickets through the moss.  Clusters of sundew flowers, their sticky petals ready to trap unwary insects, gather at the bases of the trees and spread across the moss like pools of blood.  An unmoving sparrow perches on a dead pine branch, staring at the amber sap oozing across its claws.

The hint of path that you follow edges around a slime-covered pool only distinguished from the muck underfoot by a crop of water lilies struggling to stay afloat.  Intermingled with the sickly green leaves are strange fish, shadows under the shadowed water.

Exquisitely crafted maple shelves are set above tall marble topped counters.  A deep marble sink, surmounted by a solid brass water pump, shares one wall with a white porcelain stove.  A stone gargoyle, wings furled and its gaping jaws ready to serve as a waste disposal, sits conveniently near an unlonchai bucket.  The clever use of mirrors brings sunlight to a Wayerd pyramid tucked into a niche in the wall.

The open bazaar of the Undershard is a panorama of odd sights and smells, grey-blanketed stalls and rickety carts selling everything under the sun.  The merchants speak in a rapid-fire patois, their catcalls ringing out over the noise of people shouting in seven languages or more.

Citizens of the Undershard mingle all around, merchants and travelers haggling loudly over cheap wares or vanishing into the seclusion of blanket-draped stalls to negotiate for more private services.  The Market itself is a maze, the crowds making their own paths from vendor to vendor.

The shanty is little more than an open roofed partition, constructed of unmatched bits of wood, paper, and metal, with one side butting up against the cavern wall.  Soot stains the walls in one shadowed corner near the back where a ring of stones holds a small fire.  Roughly scrawled graffiti in several languages covers every clean spot on the walls and one symbol in particular, a bloody dagger, seems to predominate.  It probably belongs to the local gang of thugs whose home this seems to be.

Vibrant purple blankets are stretched over a wooden tent-frame, slits cut in the fabric to provide several views of the surrounding marketplace.  This is the office of the bazaar's master and warden, Ani'haan, and judging from the bloodstained axe hanging on a stand behind his desk, the place where rough justice is often dispensed.

A winding stair of polished stone has been cut from the face of the rock, spiraling up some thirty feet to great doors of ornate ironwood and flanked by two broad ramps.  An Elothean inscription chiseled into the stone at the foot of the stair denotes this as 'The Royal Way'.  The stair itself, once an informal gathering-place for the locals, is now blocked off with lengths of rusty chain.

Constantly buffeted by swarms of people, it is hard to get one's bearings or even keep safe footing in this labyrinth of makeshift stalls and grey-blanketed booths.  Openings seem to appear and vanish in the blink of an eye, as the crowds flow like the tides.

This broad corridor, its stone walls cracked and stained dark with moisture, runs between two large vaulted chambers.  The relatively dark and quiet vault to the south is overcome by sounds of parading and shouting to the north, where some sort of bazaar or festival is being held.

A low ring of crumbling stones encircles the lip of a great well just to the south, and a tunnel leads north to connect this open vault with another one up the passage.  Sounds of enthusiastic shouting in many languages drift down the corridor, as if some sort of festival is taking place.

The room looks like Budd is more interested in keeping shop than in chopping locks.  It's filled with odds and ends of merchandise: a crate of tincture jars sits next to a box of candle molds beside a wicker case of clippers and crocks.  And that's not counting the stuff on the counter or in the cabinet behind it.  At least it has the traditional mirror and barber chair.

No merry-go-round at a circus could be cheerier than the decor of this shop: bright calliope music plays from somewhere behind gilded and painted screens.  In place of counters, the merchandise rests on the tray-like backs of carousel animals suspended on shining brass poles: a snarling lion, a black stallion, a polar bear, and a woolly ram parade their wares.  A carriage drawn by unicorns is provided for patrons who need a rest from their shopping.

At the center of the showroom is a miniature festival wagon, its big wheels and high-backed seats gilded and brightly painted.  On it sit dolls of the eleven races for sale in the shop.  The dolls' clothes and accessories surround the display on a rainbow of colorful counters -- violet, blue, green, yellow, orange, and red.

Neat hedges trim the path, leading up to a nondescript home heavy with the scent of fresh tobacco.  A large CLOSED sign marks the shop's front door, although a cheery light still shines from the window and smoke puffs from the chimney.

Piles of fabric and cloth lie in cluttered heaps about the room, all but hiding the small store's owner.  Curled like a frightened kitten on a stool and working diligently at her mending, Meek appears to either not notice or not care who enters and who exits.  Shirts, skirts, jackets, and articles of clothing of all types hang behind her on a rack.

Rows of shelves, crammed with books on alchemy, tools of the trade, and a hodgepodge of herbs and components, line the room.  High on one wall, the lone window is covered over with heavy fabric, keeping the room in perpetual twilight to protect sensitive components.  The herbalist Idizieq stands behind the counter, happily working on his experiments at a low table in between helping customers.

A crystal chandelier, hanging in the center of the room, tinkles softly in the breeze from the open door.  Built to scale, a panorama of the city of Shard is encased in a glass display in the center of the room.  Trinkets are strategically located to show them at their best on each tower.  A heavily burdened table and stand huddle in opposite corners of the room.

All around are the trappings of opulence, from the crystal chandelier overhead to the plush black carpet that softens the floor.  The proprietor of this shop seems to be most interested in providing comfort for the clientele, while at the same time displaying the wares for sale in a most pleasant surrounding.  Resting in a semi-circle around the room are several divans, waiting to offer relaxation to weary shoppers.

rooms.t: [House of the Floating Reed, East Garden]
rooms.desc: Along the east side of the garden is a well-mulched bed of earth, edged with carved silverwood.  Planted with dragon's mouth orchids and firefall vines, a heady scent comes from the blooming plants.  Dim twilight filters through a large skylight, and underneath it is a small fountain made of shaped kokona reeds.  Twin jade lions frame a narrow winding bridge to the west, while a bamboo door to the north leads into a small shop.

Walls of split, polished bamboo enclose the low-ceilinged room, a low shelf hung on the western wall.  Wares for sale are spread out on a long silverwood table, and a wide rack has been hung with an array of brightly colored skirts.  A small sign has been posted on the wall of the shop, and a bamboo door leads back out to the garden.

Sanded black deobar planks line the floor to form a procession that leads to a single flint slab in the center of the room.  The walls are made from a dark grey wood, the material also used to craft the spare benches set along the sides.  A thick arch leads further into the building.

rooms.t: [House of the Floating Reed, Winding Bridge]
rooms.desc: Painted in a pure white, the narrow bridge goes neatly over the large square-shaped pool.  Two sharp bends in the middle of the bridge house a low mistwood bench between them.  Schools of fish swim about lazily in the water below, perhaps waiting for food from overhead.  The air is filled with a rather tranquil mist, dampening the open sky above.

Painted onto the wooden floor of the balcony is the image of a black water serpent, its long body seamlessly merging into a stone statue that coils around one of the balcony's wooden posts.  Set in the corner of the room is a small glass case displayed underneath a small lantern.  The balcony ends here, and to the north is a small, well-tended garden.

rooms.t: [House of the Floating Reed, Banquet Hall]
rooms.desc: Square pots have been set at either side of a break in the balcony railing, both carved from a pale jade.  Each is planted with a line of bamboo shoots in standing water, the thin stalks blooming into leaves in various shades of green.  Laid out with a spread of elegant dishes, a carved silverwood table sits opposite a set of narrow steps leading into a wide pool.

Airy and echoing, the entrance to the Museum is an open and welcoming space ringed with tall gilded columns soaring up to the high domed ceiling.  Atop a low marble pedestal, the massive fossilized skeleton of a war mammoth dominates the room.  Tall palm trees in carved stone planters raise their fringed leaves, vivid against the pale stone, as light spills in through curving crystal panes to splash across the softly gleaming marble of the walls and other surfaces.

Long and narrow, this room is paneled in rich, dark mahogany.  Plush, patterned rugs cover the cream-and-russet marble floor, and ornate brass lamps support softly glowing gaethzen spheres which shed a warm light on the polished counter.

Polished to a warm glow, mahogany paneling and plush floor rugs lend this room an intimate, hushed atmosphere.  Oversized armchairs provide a comfortable place to sit and chat, or to attend to visiting lecturers.  A carved stone fireplace with a wide mahogany mantel sits opposite floor to ceiling windows that afford a fine view of the tower at the heart of the city.  Spaced about the edges of the room are display pedestals and plinths bearing examples of some of the museum's rare and exotic finds.

Paintings and tapestries line the walls of this spacious room, interspersed with bronze gaethzen wall lamps.  Spaced along the lengthy tessellated corridor are display cases and pedestals holding more of the museum's treasures and oddities.  High arched windows between columns of creamy veined marble allow light to stream in from the opposite wall while offering a good view of the streetscape outside.

The snow at the top of this treacherous cliff is crusty and unstable, frequently giving way and making passage incredibly difficult.  Splintered shards of ice lie haphazardly about, crystalline missiles dropped from the overhanging cliffs when their weight becomes too much to bear.  Fine, powdery snow piles in sparkling drifts that hug the mountain's cliffs, filling in the shatter lines that spiderweb through the ice sheet's surface.

A pile of boulders rests uneasily at the top of the mountain's cap, feathered in elaborate ice crystal patterns growing over their surfaces.  Gritty snow crusted over with frozen melt forms a thick layer over the granite rock below, making the few bare spots seem dark by comparison.  Shifting ice from the massive glacier occasionally gives off a sharp crack that pierces the air, breaking the lonely silence of the frozen mountaintop.

Alberdeen the Provisioner is a rather rustic-looking Elf, more used to hunting and foraging than dealing with customers, but helpful nonetheless.  Salted and cured game, jerked meats, pickled eggs, and hard Elven waybread sit on simple shelves behind the counter, along with necessities like rope, sacks and simple tools.  The prices are reasonable, and one could equip a good-sized caravan or hunting party for a relatively modest outlay.

Bags of produce and carcasses wrapped in burlap hang from cool recesses between tangled roots and rafters shored up with earth.  Kegs of salt, hogsheads of flour, crocks of honey and cheese, are all piled high in niches dug into the cool floor of the cellar.  Crates of ropes, candles, sacks, and other general merchandise lie open, ready to be restocked upstairs as needed.

De'ali, a grandmotherly elf and the proprietor of this popular sweet shop, is somewhat plump for her kind, but pleasingly so.  In her starched white apron, she meticulously arranges bonbons on trays atop a spotless display counter.  A sweet, heady almost cloying aroma wafts up from the back.  You can hear laughter and conversation from below and from outside the door.

In a hollow just below ground, behind the shop's salesroom, is De'ali's Cooking Room, where wooden vats of simmering syrups and succulent fruits, herbs, nuts and other delights of the woods are transformed into scrumptious, sumptuous treats, almost magically.  Her young apprentices carefully monitor the process, gathered around the vats with long spoons and mixing paddles.  Despite their obvious dedication, they manage to laugh and gossip in the midst of their hot toil.

A tasteful, pale blue carpet and matching silk walls give this tent an open, airy feel.  Lighting is provided by a set of silver filigree lamps set most securely on the tent poles.  Fire is, understandably, a serious concern here.

Twisted and woven works of basketry art hang from hooks and line shelves in the cramped interior of this wattle-and-daub hut.  Blanca, renowned throughout Elanthia, is a master at basketweaving and the art of turning wicker and willow into marvelous and useful creations.  Whimsical containers shaped like animals, trees and flowers, as well as more practical baskets for carrying and storage, can all be had here.

Wood shavings cover the floor, causing a slightly musty odor to permeate throughout the workshop.  Scattered all around are examples of Yerui's knowledge of woods and his skill with tools, displaying a fine talent in design in the various statues, toys and sundry items set out for sale.

Several lean mannequins, obviously based on Elven aesthetics, are set up inside the showroom, sporting the latest outfits for the well dressed urban ranger.  The polished oak walls glow softly, with full-sized mirrors inset at intervals.  Perched on a chair standing like a crane is the famous Elven clothier Ongadine.  Barely attempting to mask a sigh, he pauses long enough to peer down his nose at you.

This rather claustrophobic room has a low ceiling and sharply curving walls.  It is barely large enough for someone to shed an old outfit and try on some smart new creation.  Straight pins and needles, wisps of thread and snippets of fabric are scattered all over the oak floor.

A profusion of loaves, rolls, biscuits and pastries greets you in this cheery hut, filled with the aroma of baking bread and rising sweetdough.  Mithin the baker stands smiling and ready to serve you.  A cool marble counter holds assorted fresh merchandise.

Wan illumination gently glistens where it touches the many silver wares perched upon shelves inside this shop, leaving dark shadows to pool in the lee of the stone counter that divides the room near the far wall.  A single, brightly lit lamp sits upon the counter, revealing that the merchant has not yet sought rest from the day's labors.  A roughly-hewn stone door leads back outside.

Casement windows, now closed against the coming of night, let in a faint shower of moonlight to spill over the carpet and furnishings of this room.  Shadows dance as the pale luminescence competes with the warm glow of a pair of brass lanterns situated atop costly birch cabinets lining the walls, forming an entrancing display if one were to stay and watch it for long.

Blue and white canopied stalls displaying bountiful baskets of produce nestle between quaint shops with flower-filled window boxes.  The square is crowded with people and filled with the noise of conversation and the shouts of merchants hawking their wares.  Hearthwives ladened with mesh shopping bags push aggressively forward as they vie with each other for the best produce.

Granite cobblestones line the lane, making travel easy for shoppers strolling by as well as traders delivering their wares.  Merchants display their specialties in the windows of small shops, painted in an array of candy-like pastel colors, hoping to attract customers as they engage in the daily battle for business in the competitive market.  Songbirds flit about the branches of a large cherry tree, entertaining the local children, as they remain safely hidden by its abundant leaves.

A tall cherry tree shades the lane on summer days, its trunk scarred from the shoes of local children who've climbed it just to see if they can.  Mixing with the everyday scents of the busy marketplace, a lingering aroma of freshly baked goods drifts through the air, drawing customers further along the lane.

Long rods suspended from the low ceiling display a mind-boggling variety of clothing.  Capes lined with silk, fine ceremonial tunics, and elegant frock coates nudge up against leather jerkins and other more protective garments, all awaiting the touch of a master tailor to define them more perfectly for their new owners. Bolts of fabric, march like small sentinels along sturdy shelves along the edges of the room, protecting the modesty of some of the more bashful patrons.

Though quiet elegance may be the watchword in the salesroom, mayhem comes closer to describing these surroundings. Clerks, their arms piled high with exquisite garments, hats, canes, and scarves, scurry back and forth, whistling happily over their work. Near a large window in the back of the room, a new shipment is arriving, the burly delivery men looking coarse and rough compared to the smaller, softer appearance of the salespeople.

After several feet of growth, the thick limb splits off into two main branches leaving plenty of room for friends to sit and contemplate their lives.  Scars left from years of pruning mar the tree's trunk, doing little to assist in the difficult climb back down.

A leaf from a nearby willow spirals through the air in front of you and settles upon the water, sending out soft circular ripples.  With an overwhelming sense of lethargy, you begin to watch the outermost ripple advance across the width of the lake, until some deeply-rooted instinct tells you what you're seeing is impossible.  When you blink, you find the lake is perfectly still, and there is no sign of the fallen leaf.

Traveling along this bank of the lake, you notice the water is so clear you can see the shallow, pebble-strewn lake bed.  Though the lake appears still, the pebbles seem to undulate slowly, redefining their shape, merging and separating.  Your sense of balance skews, and you find yourself leaning forward over the water.  It takes all of your strength to pull yourself upright and shake off the desire to sleep.

A mound of dirt covered by emerald grasses is all that separates two vastly different lakes.  As you travel the mound, you notice a marked difference between the shimmering light upon the surface of one lake, and the inky blackness of the other.  Just northwest you can see a delightful little meadow and several graceful willows, while southward, you notice that even the grass refuses to grow along the dark lake's banks.

Dead and dying willow trees surround you.  Grass grows in intermittent clumps along the muddy ground, looking frail and glasslike.  The sole of a boot, a knapsack and a tin cup lie half-buried in the path, sinking slowly into the mire.  You begin to take extra care to step lightly through the area.

You quickly step aside to avoid being impaled upon a sharp stump sticking out of the mud.  The trees and boulders in this place are haphazardly positioned, as if the ground were incredibly jostled then settled back down.  The mighty roots of a giant willow point skyward, while its gnarled branches sink into the muck.  A steamy heat rises from the south, blanketing the grove in a dense mist.

Deep pockets of mud trace their way along exposed rock which inclines to the south.  A thicket of thorn bushes spreads up the incline and disappears into a dense bank of fog.  Now and then, you hear a loud gurgling followed by a fantastic hiss, but the heavy mists surrounding you prevent you from seeing much of anything.

A small body of water lies to the west, swathed in a dense white mist.  You can hear a constant bubbling coming from its direction, but decide it is unwise to try to get a closer look.  The heat of the mist makes you perspire freely, and you are uncomfortably stuck to your clothes.  Breathing is difficult due to the moisture in the air.  Every step upon the exposed rock is treacherous.

Cascades of once-liquefied rock act like steps from a short stone rise to the east.  Plumes of steam from that direction drift into the area and make it difficult to see.  The only vegetation to be found is a simple black moss which hugs the rim of some seething steam vents.  Scalding water occasionally bursts from these vents and releases a noxious, gaseous odor.

Dense fog obscures everything around you, leaving little idea of what may sit in wait of your arrival.  The ground beneath you feels as solid as rock, and every now and again you hear a fantastic rumbling in the vicinity.  Moving slowly, you carefully check the area directly in front of you, searching out any hidden obstacles.

The veil of fog lifts momentarily, and to your surprise you find yourself surrounded by rock.  You are walking an incline pocked with many holes through which heat seems forced by underground bellows.  The ground is almost too warm to walk on, and you are dripping with perspiration.

The incline levels out, and the dense fog pitches and rolls like a swift-moving cloud upon the ground.  Just as you are about to step forward, the fog clears and you stop yourself in a heart-pounding rush of adrenalin.  Before you lies a massive yawning cavity in the earth, spewing forth a heavy column of steam.  The earth trembles, and there is a deep rumbling from far below.  Though your knees grow weak, you manage to steady yourself, knowing that one false move will plummet you to your death.

With a landscape more suitable to an uninhabitable moon, the geyser field is void of color in its endless grey march.  Solid rock beneath your feet takes on the appearance of sludge, though they are most certainly solid.  The humidity in the area is staggering.
Dull grey rock, melted by tremendous heat and then cooled to its solid form, undulates over the landscape.  Simple mosses and lichen are the only life form visible in this desolate area.

Thick forest and steaming field of rock meet along a marshy stretch of ground punctuated by mineral deposits and shallows of salt.  A few brave trees struggle to grow upon the flat, rocky area, and beyond them rises something dense and cloudlike.  The forested slope is dense and dark, giving no indication of its penetrability.

Stunted, misshapen trees struggle to grow near the edge of a seeming lake of rock, their leaves discolored to a sickly rust.  Heat rises from the ground in undulating waves within a thick, acrid moisture.

Two large geysers stand close together, creating a narrow passageway to the opposite end of the field.  The rock is slippery and coated with a slimy black moss.  A noxious, sulfuric odor hangs in the air, making it difficult to take a full breath.

Very little light penetrates the overlapping boughs which weave a perpetual shadow into the forest fringe.  A heavy heated mist hangs in the air, unmoving, somewhat seductive as it wraps around roots, branches, boots and ankles.

Rough-edged rock cuts through the spongy ground, creating an obstacle course beneath the low-hanging tree branches.  The flora seems bent on obliterating every inch of open space, which if not taken up by some shrub or sapling, is criss-crossed by thick garlands of moss.

Tiny pools of water bubble quietly on either side of a boggy path.  Springy and tentative, the path provides no security as it dips and sways beneath even the most inconsequential weight.  Cascading moss drapes in almost calculated symmetry, appearing and disappearing in the thickening fog.

The tops of trees appear alarmingly close to the ground, a sure sign of the bog's covetous nature.  With little light penetrating the inescapable haze, there is no way to accurately assess the terrain.  Each step is an adventure in balance, carrying the possibility of oblivion.

Creeping, crawling things march along rotting logs and across moss-covered rocks.  The fog settles in a thick blanket along the ground, obscuring the path but revealing a landscape in the throes of a slow, torturous death.  Gnarled branches reach hopelessly upward, seeking the sun.
A dead tree trunk snakes out of the misty bog like a ramp leading nowhere.  Odd, unfamiliar hoots and yelps ricochet in the distance, and mysterious pinging noises drift up from the mud.

Off to one side of the shifting path is a rotted, crooked wall of woven thatch.  Blackened holes where fungus has eaten through pock the thing from top to bottom, in patterns that often suggest faces in the eerie half-light of the shadowy bog.

A great tree with massive branches dominates the area, like an opened hand reaching defiantly from the greedy sod.  Though the fog eddies and swirls to incredible heights, it cannot obscure this stunning landmark.

A moderate slope in the ground provides some stable footing for a change.  A thick, thorny bramble snuggles up to a particularly dense fall of moss, looking like the silhouette of a young child leaning against its mother.

Brackish water filled with debris covers the ground, smelling like death.  Blurps and gurgles occasionally break the unsettling silence, sounding and smelling like a sluagh with stomach troubles.  A hapless victim of the bog is partially imbedded in the muck, nearly indistinguishable from the surrounding sludge.

A small stream flows from east to west, carrying the dregs of the bog's destructive feast.  Blackened leaves, dried twigs and rotted rodent carcasses are passed into the moving water like offerings, to be transported elsewhere and stacked upon a massive funeral pyre.

A sudden cold bristles the fog-laden air, wending around the dying trees.  There are tiny, glinting ice shards on a carpet of moss, and icicles forming on boughs and branches.  The chill is so all-encompassing, it's as if it is searching for the warm, beating heart of these barely-living things.

A fallen tree provides a roadway over the increasing sludge of the bog.  A series of hopelessly-tangled roots are exposed above the water, while the tree crowns are lost within the swirling mist.  An occasional slithering sound announces the presence of an otherwise undetected creature.
Part of the marshy floor dips toward a large depression at the base of a blackened oak.  Debris sloshes toward the tree, washing the rim of the depression before disappearing into it.

Every tree in the area has been uprooted and knocked on its side, so that a great circle has been devised.  The trees lay root to crown, forming a twisted, gnarled garland filled with swampy, murky water.

In the midst of the stinking quagmire of this forsaken bog grows a single bush, covered in bright pink flowers.  Like a blessing in the midst of damnation, it stands proudly, as if by sheer force of will it can overcome the death around it.

Criss-crossed branches make a shifting catwalk above the pungent, slimy ground.  A rich, loamy odor hangs heavily in the air, hinting of cinnamon.  In the froth of the churning fog, nearby shrubs take on the appearance of monsters frozen in mid-attack.

A long-forgotten wind chime defies humidity and time to produce a faint tinkle as a warm breeze passes by.  Broken furniture is sunken into the floor of the bog -- a chair here, a desk there, a chest of drawers further on.  The faint outline of a building foundation juts out of the mire, but is nothing more than a mess of rotting planks which suggest a living area, bedroom and what might have been a kitchen.

Muffled voices echo from the unseen boundaries of this painfully cramped void.  There is little room to maneuver, and at varying intervals there is a gush of water which spills in from above.  Hardly fit for any inhabitant, it is nonetheless populated by at least one furry skittering thing, which wraps itself around your ankles as it maneuvers through the darkness.

Cascading sludge pours from above, pooling in a fetid hollow within the roots which dangle from above.  The walls of this tiny cavern glisten with accumulated slime, and are populated by caterpillars, roaches and sightless beetles.  The incredible stench is enough to overpower even the most seasoned warrior.

Thick, searing mist shrouds the ghosts of several thatched-roof houses which stand to either side of a crumpled bridge.  Bits and pieces of the cobblestone road peek from the bog which is desperate to claim these man-made structures.  A lone tree, long dead, stands in the midst of what must have been the village green.

A marble statue, overgrown with lichen and sinking at an odd angle, stares into the mist as if searching for light.  Around its base is some cracked, circular stonework which was once the foundation of a large fountain.  There is also a rotting wooden gate standing before a flat area which, at one time, was the village cemetery.

An old tavern, its sign still creaking softly, stands with open doors as if ready for customers.  On a second-story balcony just above it, great garlands of moss drape in pretty patterns like scarves hung out to dry.

Polished brass still shines along the bar rails, and several stools remain intact.  A group of tables and chairs provide a place to sit and rest, though the sofas and footrests made of upholstery have been claimed by the rot of the bog.  At the far end of the room, upon one of the tables, sits a lovely pewter vase occupied by a dead rose.

Shrubs dead of rot line either side of the main road through this forgotten village.  Occasionally, the mist lifts enough to reveal colorful paint on the wretched buildings which stand in various stages of disrepair.

A three-story building stands at the end of a cul-de-sac just off the main road.  Flanked by withered junipers and graced with a lichen-covered porte-cochere, it was probably the residence of some wealthy former inhabitant.

A soggy carpet sends up the strong smell of decay, and the wallpaper is splashed with mud.  The furniture in this grand foyer is smashed to pieces, covered with moss and lichen, and turning a sickly black.  The bottom portion of a grand stairway has fallen apart, eliminating any possibility of exploration among the upper rooms.

A once-grand dining room sits in silent ruin.  The wreckage of a deobar table which seated at least twenty is lying in the center of the room, while its accompanying chairs are smashed and piled near the walls.  Only the crystal chandelier remains intact, though it is generously coated with decades of dust.

This conservatory is packed with broken instruments, including an ornate harp, and speaks of a love of the bardic arts.  Heavy tapestries hang on the wall, depicting a handful of musical themes, including a lyre concert, a singing minstrel and muses dancing to the tune of a flutist.

A damp, musty scent wafts upward from barrels spread around the room's perimeter and drifts from the back room of the shed.  Shelves running around the shop hold containers of powdered and liquid dyes.  A glass cabinet displays information about several types of paper made on the premises.  Amidst the clutter, a clean marble counter holds today's selection of fine handmade paper.

Thick bramble bushes surround you on every side but to the south, fencing you into this small thicket.  An arch of withered wood overhead keeps the vegetation from devouring this small space.  Errant thorny vines wreathed around the wooden arch create a dark canopy that seals this small cove off from the light.

The bramble passage widens here, creating a hollow in this thorny thicket.  Black drapes of silk and velvet have been strung from the wooden archway overhead that supports the wild vegetation, marking some sort of dark celebration.  At the southern edge of the bramble thicket, a glassy obsidian altar rises from the surrounding moss-carpeted byre.  Various statues of hideous-looking beasts line the living walls to the east and west, glowering malevolently at any who may enter.

Smooth walnut boards underfoot and rich blue velvet curtains along the walls make this an elegant nook where minstrels and performers can share their music with those in the ballroom.  Wooden chairs sit in neat rows facing the north, each with a silver stand set in front shaped like a lyre.  A cleared space made in front of them is framed by multicolored silk streamers that flutter onto the stage.

Dark dripping branches hang down from the low earth ceiling like knotted, grasping fingers reaching towards you.  Tiny rivulets of dirty water run in narrow branching grooves, pooling in strangely distorted tracks in the hard packed mud.

The flat bottom of a wooden coffin hangs down from the ceiling overhead, glistening darkly in the torchlight, with a dark ragged hole ripped in its side.  The floor is damp and slimy with mud and deeply rutted, as if someone or something has been dragged through it.

A gaping hole branches off from the main tunnel to the north, an inky blackness against the dark walls.  The black earth is scattered with tiny pale flecks, like stars on a cloudy night.  An ivory shard juts from the wall, standing out in the flickering light.

Tiny trickles of mud drip down from overhead as if disturbed by your passage.  This section of tunnel seems more freshly excavated, and the earth less packed down.  The dirt roof overhead is uneven and pitted with holes.

This branch of the tunnel dead-ends in a nightmare tableau revealed in the tenuous light.  Someone or something has piled stacks of polished bones into neat sorted piles, along with bits of stained rotting cloth.

The musty cavern air clings to the ground like a thick blanket of decay and old death.  Black glistening insects hang from the walls, grown fat and complacent living off the rich bounty buried overhead.

A line of ants climbs along the tunnel walls, passing busily in and out of a dark hole dug into the dirt.  Several other pits have been dug into the moist ground, but seem to have been picked clean of anything they might once have contained.

A hollow thump echoes as you travel down the tunnel, sounding strangely muffled against the dry earthen walls.  Looking down, you realize you are standing on a coffin lid, half buried in the dirt beneath your feet.

The narrow tunnel walls change abruptly here, as smooth ancient limestone to the east gives way to packed earth.  Jagged shards fallen from the wall litter the floor, forcing visitors to step carefully.  A blazing fire to the east casts a faint reddish light over the whole area.

A faint scratching sound out of sight sets your teeth on edge, as if tiny claws were scrabbling across a wooden table.  Staring yellow eyes flicker by the firelight and vanish quickly as half-seen shadows darting across the tunnel.

A natural cavern in the surrounding limestone forms a great bowl overhead, lit by a huge bonfire towards the eastern side.  The firelight glows red off an onyx slab piled high with unmentionable offerings set before a carved niche in the stone.  Piles of old gnawed bones are stacked in haphazard fashion along the northern wall, ending in a rounded opening heading west.

A broad round slab of polished marble dominates this tiny niche, covered in strange runic inscriptions.  The walls are made of chiseled granite blocks, clashing with the natural limestone of the cavern outside.  The floor around the slab is scratched and gouged, as if some burrowing animal has been digging at it.

An old wooden coffin sticks part way out of the southern wall, its side ripped open and its contents gone.  Bits of wood and less identifiable things lie strewn about, sticking up like thorns from the muddy cave floor.

Matted branches tangled together like worms form a living roof overhead, seeming almost to wiggle in the flickering light.  Pale patches in the dark walls reveal the location of ancient graves, so old that nothing remains but a faint ivory taint to the soil.

The tunnel branches off in three directions, bent and forked like a lightning stroke through the damp dark earth.  The constant wet dripping from the walls forms tiny rivulets which flow down the sloped branch to the east.

Glistening pearly snail tracks paint luminescent stripes along the underside of a stone slab forming part of the ceiling.  Although the slab is still unbroken, deep gashes along its surface reveal the labors of some clawed would-be intruder.

A sickening stench of decay rises from a noxious pool formed in a dip in the tunnel.  Bits of unidentifiable something float over the oily surface of the water, and somewhere in the darkness something makes a splashing sound.  The muddy tunnel floor rises to the west and southwest.

The tunnel makes a sharp bend, skirting the edges of a huge limestone boulder which looms over the passage to the west.  The stone's face is slick with sickly growths of dank moss.  To the north, the tunnel narrows quickly and dead-ends in solid rock.  A narrow crack in the stone looks passable.

Towering walls of greenish stone rise to either side and seem to press inward as you make your way through a natural crack in the stone.  Misshapen muddy tracks on the stone floor look almost like rat tracks, but are far too large.  Some of the tracks are smeared as if something had been dragged over them.

Scorched walls span the tower, and faint reflections of emerald green onyx are visible beneath the ash.  A long steep staircase has been cut into the walls, spiraling its way up the tapering interior.  A soot-blackened door, hanging precariously from one hinge, leads out.

Very little is recognizable from the workshop's original contents.  The walls are broken off at half their intended height and the area lies open to the elements.  The only obvious sign of the room's prior function, odd glowing stains marking the floor, are most likely the result of past experiments gone awry.

The whitewashed walls of this small room are cracking, as plaster pulls away from the lathes beneath and crumbles to the floor.  Once a cozy kitchen, the hearth is now cold and dirty, the pot within it blackened and burned.  The worn wooden table is still set for diners who will never arrive, while its chairs lie broken amidst the plaster dust.  A narrow wooden door leads out to the yard, while an archway leads north to another room.

The farmwife must have taken pride in her parlor, however time and rodents have taken over, leaving the room a shambles.  Tattered fragments of faded velvet draperies shift in the draft from a broken window.  The elegant brocade which once covered the tilting sofa has been shredded by the claws of rodents who gnawed the legs.  Dust blankets the room, blurring the details in a gentle fog.  An archway to the south leads to the kitchen, while a doorway to the east leads into a hallway.

The front door remains closed, the dirty glass panes allowing little light to penetrate the dim hallway.  The newel post has broken, allowing the bannister to sag away from the wooden stairs.  The stairs themselves seem sturdy enough, though covered in spiderwebs and dust.  An oddly-shaped door under the stairs leads to some kind of cupboard, while a doorway to the west leads back to the parlor.

Small tracks crisscross the dust blanketing this upstairs hallway, while pale, watery light filters through the filthy panes of a window at the top of the stairs, bathing the hall in a dim glow.  The doors which once guarded the rooms on this floor have been gnawed by rodents til they lie precariously askew.

The trappings of childhood cast off, this room evidently belonged to the young lady of the house.  A single doll lies on the narrow bed, and a carved wooden box perches upon the dresser.  A cupboard in the corner is open, revealing the remains of a white muslin gown, as well as more prosaic working dresses.

Goose feathers are everywhere in this room, evidently liberated from the feather mattress which lies on the ancient four poster bed.  Generation after generation of mice have found it a comfortable nesting spot, from the looks of things.  A wooden hatbox perches atop a dusty cupboard which stands in one corner of the room, its paint faded and scratched.

Shadows gather in the corner of this tiny room under the stairs.  The wood which lines the walls has warped slightly in the damp air which wafts from a small hole in the floor.  A rickety ladder leads through the hole to the darkness below.  The dim light from an oddly shaped door is the only source of illumination.

Row after row of wine racks line the natural cave that forms the cellar of the house.  The bottles have been shattered, the glass shards littering the room.  Tools used to cork the wine lie scattered about the floor.  A rickety wooden ladder leads up to a hole in the ceiling.

Great oaken casks line the walls of the cave, piled one atop the other.  Wine has seeped from the casks, forming dark stains on the floor.  A table along one wall contains glasses, as well as wooden mallets and devices to tap the casks.

A shallow ramp leads up toward the entrance of the cave, dimly visible in the distance.  Care has been taken to widen the ramp, and a wooden railing has been attached, making it easy for barrels to be rolled into the caves from the pressing vats.  A broken barrel lies at the bottom of the ramp, its slats stove in.

A dark grey carpet decorated with a pattern of crossing black lightning bolts covers the floor, matching the decoration on the grey-painted walls.  A constant, low thrum hangs just inside the range of hearing, its source nearby but not readily apparent.  Doors spaced in an even circle around the perimeter lead to initiates' private cells.

Bare, dark soil forms the floor underfoot.  The stony walls surrounding this circular room are similarly devoid of decoration, keeping instead the plain, natural look preferred by those mages who favor the element of Earth.  Doors leading to the initiates' private cells line the walls.

Deep blue carpeting covers the floor, its surface cut in a manner that suggests the rippling of waves upon the surface of a lake.  Bright blue spirals, representing the element of water, fill the walls between a series of doors leading to initiates' private cells.  The air here is moist and cool upon the skin.

Lush, red carpeting covers the floor, muffling any ambient noise into oblivion.  Images of bloated red suns, representing the element of fire, fill the walls between a series of doors leading to initiates' private cells.  The air here is significantly warmer than on the tower's other floors, although the reason is not readily apparent.

rooms.desc: Carpeting the color of a death shroud covers the floor, devouring the light as hungrily as Aldauth consumes souls.  The walls are devoid of decoration, instead painted a uniform black to match the floor.  Only the doors leading to initiates' cells betray any hint of color in this otherwise cold, bleak room.

Spotlessly clean, the small room contains only a table and four rickety chairs, a long cabinet with a washbasin perched on it, and a small fireplace built of rough-edged rock.  The walls have been carefully patched in several places, and covered with a fresh coat of whitewash.  Roughly sewn but bright and cheerful curtains hang at the window, and a teapot whistles softly from its hook in the hearth.

A simple bed is pushed into the corner, covered with a faded but freshly washed comforter.  A large window on the northern wall gives a view of the church steeple rising from behind a ridge of tumbled rock not far off.  From this distance, the devastation of the village is invisible, and one could believe it was still filled with friends and neighbors.

Painted in a now faded light blue, the walls provide a sense of serenity, accentuated by the mural of Hodierna and Damaris on the eastern wall.  A small bed with a sleek panther carved on the deobar headboard sits beneath the window.

Like a shell-laden beach, the ground here is laden with a myriad of items from bones, broken beads, twine, and metal shavings.  A large anvil rests next to a large forge that appears to double as a kiln.  Several Prydaen nearby appear to be stripping carcasses or working away at various crafts.

Built upon sturdy sets of stilts, several hammocks with thick pallets are suspended, waiting to hold the weary.  A simple dirt floor is covered by thin hides, with a small rock encircled firepit set into the center of the room.  A hide flap provides both entrance and exit to the room.

Soft robin's egg blue paper covers the walls of this large room, patterned with delicate arabesques in an even lighter shade of powder blue.  Several gaily-colored painted landscapes complement the rich hue of the paper, their heavy gilt frames resembling windows into perfect summer days.  The vibrant golden oak of the floor is muffled by a sumptuous woolen ivory rug with a deep, luxurious pile.  Several cheerful golden sconces provide bright -- but not harsh -- light, the oil they burn perfuming the air with a fresh citrus scent.

A group of wooden benches sits at the edge of the pond beneath a swaying willow that dabbles its long fingers in the shallow waters.  Broad lilypads cover the surface of the pond, their white and purple flowers smiling up at the sky.  Fat fish swim lazily among the trailing mass of roots and reeds under a rickety jetty, taunting local anglers with the intermittent flash of light on silver scales.

Jutting out from a marshy section of the pond shore, an elderly jetty hovers over the water.  The wobbly, uneven surface of the walkway, and the occasional gap where one plank has fallen away completely, conspire to make an unplanned trip into the dark waters a distinct likelihood.  Bits of old bait and scraps of fishing line have attached themselves determinedly to splinters in the ancient wood.

A front desk manned by a young Elven woman is all that composes this corridor-like room.  She smiles gently up at you from where she is working on embroidering a linen tunic with simple but bright flowers.  A sign behind her states the inn's fees for lodging, and stairs to her right lead up to the inn's bedrooms.

Spacious and open, the tavern allows for plenty of breathing room.  Axes, swords, and shields decorate the walls, all scratched with the wear of battle and all safely nailed in place that a patron might not grab one in a fit of drunken rage.  Situated behind the bar is a tall, muscular Elven woman with long red braids.  Judging from her demeanor and the way she handles the people who work and eat here, this can only be the owner, Savrin Kaerna.

This booth has been set aside from the rest of the tavern for those who wish more intimate conversation.  There is a clean table with a vase here, and padded seats for the weary.  Someone has gone to the trouble to make sure that there are real candles to light the otherwise darkened corner, and every now and then a server comes over to check the wicks and replenish the ones that are beginning to gutter.
Small but comfortable, a cheery fireside takes up a good part of the eastern wall.  The floor is covered with fur throws and a few overstuffed chairs complement the feeling of security and warmth.
This room is so tidy it is militant.  A small iron stove provides warmth, and a few cots in a corner are set up for sleeping purposes.  Someone has carelessly left a doll lying on the floor.

rooms.t: [The Gilded Unicorn, Top of the Stairs]
rooms.desc: Plain instead of fancy, this corridor of rooms is spotless, the wood solid and slightly gray from the wear and tear of time.  You can just make out the sounds of the tavern proper below you, the noise creeping through the scuffed floorboards and faded red carpeting.

This wooden house has been constructed in the upper branches of the old oak tree as a play area for any of the village children daring enough to venture up to this height.  A colorful rug braided from strips of yellow, blue and green cloth covers the floor, and several plump pillows are scattered around it.  One wall opens out to a narrow ramp that extends along a heavy branch.

The narrow wooden ramp extends out from the tree along one of its branches.  Oak leaves rustle softly around you, and through them the lights from Arthe Dale's homes twinkle like bright fireflies.  From somewhere off in the distance, the sweet melody of a lone flute hovers in the air.  Suspended high above the swimming hole, the branch is a good place for making an impressive dive into the water directly below.  An open doorway behind you leads back into the treehouse.

The fresh smell of hay and the sounds of snorts and whinnies fill the immaculately-tended stable.  The ponies belonging to the guests and the Burdock family are diligently looked after here by young Nubbin Burdock.  The young Halfling boy pauses in his grooming chores to pull a sicle fruit from his pocket and feed it to one of the ponies.

The mouth-watering aroma of baking dough and cinnamon makes your stomach rumble as you examine the tempting treats displayed in the glass case.  A Halfling lass adds a tray of freshly baked crullers to the tantalizing array.

The walls of this one-room cottage are painted a dappled pale blue and white.  Woven blue-green fabric shot with pale peach covers the bed and adjacent loveseat.  The white curtains on the window rise and fall gently with the breeze.  A carved walking stick rests on a workbench surrounded by tiny curls of wood.

Bright shapes of circles, crosses, crescents and stars glow mysteriously, floating in the darkness in front of you like a row of jack-o-lanterns.  You notice the dim silhouette of an oddly shaped building behind them, and you realize that the glowing shapes are brightly lit windows.  A sign has been mounted on the door of the house.

The glow from the burning fireplace fills the room with a warm light.  An incredible collection of souvenirs, knickknacks, toys and various odds and ends fills every nook and cranny of the room, casting peculiarly-shaped shadows on the walls.

This austere room belongs to the head of the Tanglefoot family.  A narrow bed covered with a brown flannel blanket and a plain wooden table and chair are the only furnishings here.  An old worn duffel bag sits in the corner, unused for years, but never forgotten.  A small sword is mounted on the wall above a wooden rack holding several hand-carved pipes.

This is the room that houses the youngest of the Tanglefoot clan.  There are several short beds here, each neatly covered with a colorful quilt, and each quilt covering the form of a small sleeping child.  A large wooden cupboard takes up most of one wall.

A huge oaken table dominates this large room.  This is the gathering place for the entire Tanglefoot clan.  A large assortment of straight-backed wooden chairs surround the long table, and a white runner edged with embroidered yellow butterflies and blue morning glories spans the length.  White ceramic candle sconces with the same butterflies and flowers are spaced regularly around the walls at a convenient height.

The kitchen is quiet and dark at this time of the night, but there are signs of someone's late snack left next to an old ice box.  The windows are open, and an evening breeze ruffles the curtains.  Ingredients for tomorrow morning's bread have been neatly arranged on the trestle table.

The bright moonlight reveals row after row of leafy plants in this orderly little garden.  A large snail leaves a wet iridescent trail across the back door stoop.  In the corner of the yard you can see the vague outline of a squat shed.

Neatly arranged hoes, rakes, spades and other garden tools line the walls.  Woven gathering baskets, some empty, some filled with bags of seeds, occupy one corner of the shed.  A wooden wheelbarrow has been left next to the door.  Bunches of drying herbs and flowers hang from the low ceiling.

The men's and women's dressing rooms to the southeast and southwest and the prop storage room directly south are all accessed from this central hub of behind-the-scenes activity, resulting in a hectic atmosphere during rehearsals or performances.  All traffic seems to flow to the northeast, where the stage wing awaits performers, musicians, and on occasion, nervous financiers.

Shelves are available for costumes used in the current production, or for storing actors' own clothes during performances.  Padded benches and plush carpets provide comfort for those changing, and mirrors above a long shared vanity allow performers to apply stage makeup or check their appearance before going to the wings.

Shelves and racks line every available portion of wall space, providing ample storage for props and costumes when not in use for the current show.  Gaethzen globes brightly light the room, so that needed items can be quickly located.

Shelves are available for costumes used in the current production, or for storing actors' own clothes during performances.  Padded benches and plush carpets provide comfort for those changing, and mirrors above a long narrow table allow performers to apply stage makeup or check their appearance before going to the wings.

In contrast to the main backstage area, which is alive with activity when the theater is in use, this stage wing is quiet.  Performers and stage hands wait here for their cues to pass through the curtain and onto the stage.

Stools and music stands wait in rows for use during performances.  Facing the stage, the conductor's stand is strategically located to allow for the direction of musicians and vocalists alike.  Off to the side, a box holds a bizarre collection of objects to be used for sound effects for productions.

The dark earth walls of this round chamber are lined with fine green mosses and delicate white starflowers.  Her black eyes sparkling above rosy apple cheeks, a bustling Halfling woman beams brightly at her customers as she combines the latest gossip with an expert patter about the quality knoll landscapes she purveys.

Thick branches stretch outward from the trunk of the tree, the crazy quilt of colorful grass and flowers below barely visible between the leaves.  The wide, knobby trunk provides an easy climb down to the safety of the ground.

At the top of the mound, a large open field emerges.  Speckled with occasional gooseberry, thimbleberry, and mintberry bushes, it provides a perfect area for picnics or fairs.  Pink clover and sweet woodruff cover the ground profusely, marred only by several tamped down patches indicating where tents and wagons have previously rested.

Water trickling down from the fountain provides a constant musical backdrop.  Tiny fish swim among the floating water lilies, darting up to the surface occasionally to search for their next meal.  The water, coming from wells far below the surface, remains cool to the touch in every season.

The reek of dead fish permeates your nostrils making you feel ill.  Besides the stench, you notice piles and piles of old crates almost entirely filling this rotting deobar-paneled warehouse.  One of the crates in the corner has been smashed open, straw and broken glass spilling across the floor from it.

You find yourself on a slimy cobblestone floor in a dark, dank and smelly chamber.  Noxious trickles of effluent seep through tiny cracks in the tortured walls, which appear to be on the verge of collapse.  The hole in the rotted timber high above is hardly convenient for escape, and you realize with a chill that you must find another way out.

The walls of this narrow corridor are closer than is comfortable.  Bits and pieces of once-glorious tapestries still cling to their surfaces, caked with crud and sagging from the weight of the water they have absorbed.  Certain stones in the wall threaten to fall at any moment, and the floor is smattered with debris.

Broken stones litter this part of the corridor.  The cobblestone floor is suddenly uneven, buckled by some ancient cataclysm.  A great boulder has punched its way through one wall, almost completely obstructing any northward progression.  Fine stress fractures trace the western wall, ending in a narrow crevice high above your head.

Tattered pieces of cloth are hung from rusted bars along each wall of this corridor.  While most of the fabric has disintegrated over time, a few remain somewhat complete, though dark splotches of mildew make it difficult to discern their patterns.  By the regularity of their placement, you gather that these are the remains of a series of heraldic banners.

Here you find a nearly intact raised mosaic floor.  Tiny tiles of many colors form patterns unlike any you've ever seen, its beauty still apparent despite the wreckage strewn about.  Touching one of the tiles, you are surprised to find it soft and pliable like cork, which might explain why this part of the corridor has endured the upheaval.  At the southern end, a great boulder has nearly blocked all passage in that direction.

Scant light filters in from a narrow section of grating in the ceiling far above.  Looking about, you find yourself hemmed in by walls on three sides.  On the floor, you see a series of battered and broken tiles, remnants of some ancient artisan's work.  After careful study, you believe they depict a wizened old mage holding forth a pulsating crystal.
Cascading nitre hangs thick along the walls of this passageway, which wends into utter darkness.  The fetid remains of a dead rat invite a host of vermin to keep you sorry company.
A collapsed hallway twists and turns in the darkness, filled with great piles of stone and rotted timber.

Rotting deobar planks clotted with reeking sewage comprise the floor of this narrow corridor.  Thin streamers of decayed silk hang from rusting iron sconces, while soggy, mottled tapestries of indeterminate design lie clumped along the baseboards.  Nitre is thick and cloying, and a steamy heat envelopes you.  What is left of the floor slopes like a ramp, leading into darkness.
Stone walls and floors echo each footstep as you cautiously make your way along the slippery incline.  A soft scuffling and distant chitter cut through the darkness, assaulting your imagination.
Cobblestone strewn with sludge and debris stretches out in this cavernous hold, set with a large iron gate at one end.  Rubble from the broken foundations of the Close lies in piles in each corner.
Putrid water filters through cracks in the stone walls and cuts moist paths through the clinging nitre.  A large desk lies on its side, swollen and rotting from the surrounding puddles of muck.

Fetid puddles combined with the absence of fresh air give rise to a suffocating humidity.  Your mind's eye envisions all manner of vermin scaling the moist stone walls or crunching beneath your feet.  There is a scraping sound which echoes from either side of this corridor.

The constant drip of water seeping through the walls becomes immediately irritating as you make your way through this large, dark room.  In some areas, the mire is ankle deep, threatening to slip you into its embrace.  A strong smell of decaying flesh permeates the dank air, but without adequate light, its source remains unknown.

The walls of this corridor are agonizingly close.  Nitre and foul-smelling slime streak your clothing and skin as you move slowly on the pitted stone floor.  A massive pile of rubble at the southern end makes it impossible to continue in that direction.

The walls of this corridor are agonizingly close.  Nitre and foul-smelling slime streak your clothing and skin as you move slowly on the pitted stone floor.  A massive pile of rubble at the southern end makes it impossible to continue in that direction.

In odd contrast to the sparsity of its surrounding rooms, this chamber houses the rotting remnants of someone's sleeping quarters.  A soggy bed snuggles up against one wall, flanked by a broken chair and a sloping nightstand.  A reed torch lies in a puddle of sludge, and a cracked mirror hangs on a slimy wall.  Though its current state is less than inviting, it would appear it was never outfitted for comfort.

Passing through this corridor, you are greeted by the overwhelming stench of the mushy, decaying rug beneath your feet.  Bedraggled and torn asunder, only the intricate thick binding along its edges is more or less intact.  A stark-white lizard appears out of a crack in the oozing walls and scurries for the other end of the corridor.
Iron brackets in the walls suggest that weapons once hung here, but nothing else remains in this spartan hallway.

A mass of crumbled wall and jagged rock fill the northern end of this corridor, making any further progress impossible.  Mixed in the rubble are shards of broken pottery and the bent remains of an iron torch ring.  Frozen in mid-crawl within a pool of mire, the mottled torso of a skeleton seems to be clawing its way from the ruins.

You find yourself in a narrow passageway where the stone walls have been overlain with wood slats.  Whatever purpose this room may have served at one time, it is now nothing more than a reeking mess of rotting boards and pooling ooze.  Every sloshing footfall stirs up a horrid odor as you make your way through.
A collapsing wall spans the width of the eastern end of this corridor.  Crumbling bricks lie strewn across the cobblestones, and a thin layer of mortar dust coats tiny puddles of effluent.

Something about this room causes you to give pause.  The air seems charged with some fantastic energy, and eventually you realize there is no destruction here.  Not a single stone is out of place, nothing putrid festers or fouls.  Though the hall bears no visible sign of an egress, something stirs you to press forward with extreme caution.  You give hefty consideration to the pristine floor, which is made of twelve massive tiles deeply etched with the icons of various items.
