rooms.desc: To your utter astonishment, you find yourself engulfed in a breathtaking array of vivid, sparkling colors.  Constantly shifting in their prismic dance, they seem to make up the very air in the room, for as you move the hues and tones retreat and reconverge like liquid.  You feel as though you are standing at the very source of rainbows.  A pleasant, resonant hum reaches your ears.

A fork in the burned tree's trunk provides precarious footing for those who venture here.  Slender, nearly-straight branches reach upward from the blackened wrack of the tree, like a multitude of fingers yearning toward the sky.  The higher canopy of the forest all around looms in every direction like walls of a living castle.

The murky waters of the river eddy here, making it a pleasant place to simply sit and relax.  A large piece of driftwood found its way here in some distant time, and is now covered nearly halfway with silt and mud, leaving it stuck firmly in place.  Along with a few tangled roots that jut out of the river bank, they provide relatively dry resting spots.  The long branches of willows bend toward the water, giving you the distinct impression of widows weeping for a lost love.

A breathtaking view of the tiered waterfall splashing over white rocky ledges can be seen from this garden pavilion.  A large, plump chaise lounge placed next to a wrought iron table spread with rich delicacies make it appear that this spot is ideal for a secret lovers' tryst.

On top of this unsteady perch you have a view of the surrounding area.  Most directions are blocked by the heavy growth of trees, but the ruined chimneys of the manor poke above the treeline like broken teeth in a decaying mouth.  Not too far away, you catch a glimpse of the river that flows by the preserve.

A minor clearing sits here, surrounded by thick-set willows in a strangely circular clearing.  The stump of a long-dead and decayed tree rises high in the center of the clearing.  A grandfather of willow trees to judge from the thickness of the stump that remains.  A strange mold covers the ground here and every step sends small puffs of spores into the air.  Only the damp air keeps them from swirling high enough to be a threat to eyes or nose.

Willow trees grow thick on all sides of you.  Long green fronds trail to the ground, still and lifeless in the heavy air.  Massive, gnarled tree trunks covered with dangling beards of moss look like old men hunched together in ragged cloaks.  To the south, the trees grow even taller, their heavy foliage casting a deep gloom over the fern-shrouded, damp ground.

Thick fungi grow at odd angles from the gnarled brown trunks of the numerous willows growing all about.  A damp musty smell catches at your throat and stings your eyes.  A curious object, shaped like a dog-sized insect, lies tangled in thick fibrous strands of fungal material at the base of one tree.  A trail of large black ants troops up to the corpse in an unending line as nature quietly reclaims its dead.

Great clumps of horsetail ferns sprout among the willows here.  The trees are thinner and more widely spaced, though they still grow close enough and thick enough to block your view after only a few feet.  Somewhere nearby, frogs croak in an irregular chorus.  Among the ferns, a lone bird calls, the sound echoing dully in the wet air.

Heavy mud grabs at your feet and every movement results in loud squelching noises.  To the north, a thick line of willows stands a silent watch over this seeping marshland.  Clumps of ferns grow on small outcrops of drier land.  The rest is a sea of heavy mud and thick swamp-grass.  Southward, the land rises a bit and willows return to overgrow the marshes.

A large patch of relatively dry ground sticks out from a grove of willows to the north.  Here and there, shallow pools of water glisten darkly through a heavy covering of marshflowers that cover their surface.  Hordes of bloodsucking insects throng around you, climbing into your eyes and nose and flying about your ears, their thin, high whining sound grating on your nerves.  To the south, the land continues its slow decline into the marshy bottomlands.

Scattered willow trees cover this rise in the damp landscape.  Marshland flows both north and south like a heavy sea around a low island and even here, the earth is damp enough to squish as you move.  Frogs in all directions sing a raucous chorus in a curious harmony of high and low voices and somewhere a bird calls out in a long, lonely cry.

A giant among willows has collapsed here, its foundation undermined by the seeping marsh as it spreads across the once-dry land.  Roots pulled free as the tree toppled now stand naked in the air as the dead giant slowly melts into the mud and decay.  A thick lacing of moss and less identifiable growths have sprung up along the trunk and branches where half a hundred spider webs gleam with collected dew among the still-green leaves.

Stagnant water splashes about your feet as you tread carefully on the slippery mud.  A rough path wanders along a marshy strand between a line of willows and the sluggish river that blocks any progress southward.  Slime-worms ooze their gelid way through the thick ooze at your feet as something with a shiny carapace and numerous legs springs out of the ooze to grab one of them and drag it, struggling weakly, back beneath the thin film of water on the mud.

A thin margin of fen runs down to a muddy riverbank.  South of that, a small river flows sluggishly, the current checked by tremendous growths of a drab-green water-weed that has formed thick mats across the stream.  An occasional fish breaks the soupy water to snatch at the unending clouds of midges and water-dancers that swarm above the stream.

A thin clump of willows grows on a relatively dry patch of higher ground surrounded by marshland.  Heavy clumps of rushes grow around the edge of the dry land and somewhere among them something is moving carefully.  A wading bird perhaps, in search of the numerous frogs who continually sound their varied notes on all sides.

The land rises to the north where a line of massive willows sweeps the ground with their deep green fronds.  As the land drops to the south, it becomes damp and marshy.  Thick hummocks of drier ground hold clumps of tiny wild-flowers, giving a curiously lovely splash of color to the drab grey and brown of the scum-covered pools between them.  A sea of mud to the south fades indistinctly into a sluggish brown river.

Rows of leather-bound books and pigeonholed racks of scrolls indicate the private library of the manor.  Time has been kind here and the place is surprisingly intact.  Whatever horror occured here long-ago, those involved could not bring themselves to burn or harm these ranked volumes.  Your eye is caught by something bizarre in this almost normal scene: in one large chair, a shrivelled corpse grins out at you eerily.  A blood-stained book still clutched in its gnarled hands.

A huge canopied bed dominates this large room.  Obviously the sleeping chambers for the Lord of this place, the decor reflects the hunting themes so common throughout the building.  To one side, a massive desk made of polished bones surfaced with ivory holds a jumble of papers.

This was a sitting room once.  Outfitted in an antique and elaborate style, the walls are hung with intricate tapestries and decorative moldings that still retain their heavy gilding.  Little furniture remains now and the fireplace shows where much of it ended up, to judge from the bits of gilded brass that were once handles and knobs and such among the ashes.

rooms.t: [Hunting Preserve, Manor House Upper Hall East]
rooms.desc: This would appear to lead to the master suite of the lord of this house.  A huge door, solid and well made, still stands in silent guard over this ruined domain.  An elaborate coat of arms has been woven into the carpeting here and the colors remain fairly bright and unsullied.

Near a set of grand stairs, the hallway seems in good shape.  Several doors remain in place, closing off unknown upper rooms.  The preserved head of a huge wild boar has broken loose from its wall hanging and dangles over the railing like an over-indulgent party-goer being ill.

This room is fitted out as a guest bedroom for overnight visitors.  The bedding has long since rotted away leaving only the iron frame and some leather scraps that once formed the supports for the mattress.  Scraps of cloth and bits of discolored ribbon show that perhaps a lady once dwelt here.  A patch of blood-stained plaster on one wall shows you she did not enjoy her stay.

A wide balustraded corridor runs around three sides of the upper hall.  Faded carpet still depicts a scene of dozens of fantastic animals being hunted in various ways.  Widely spaced doors hint at the luxurious size of the rooms on this level.

The hallway here is still relatively intact.  The walls retain a hint of the once-bright colors with which they were decorated.  A leak in the roof overhead has created numerous water-spots in the carpeting and allowed a unique collection of molds to spring up.  One or two of them look almost worthy of attention by the hunters depicted in the undamaged portions of the carpet.

rooms.t: [Hunting Preserve, Manor House Upper Hall West]
rooms.desc: This end of the hallway is a ruin of collapsed plaster and stonework.  Anything left here has been buried under piles of rubble and dust that have been turned into a form of cement by rain and frost.
One of a number of rooms set aside for guests, this one has been thoroughly ransacked and looted.  A cracked stone basin and part of the iron bedstead are all that remain in here.

A small storage area and workroom, this once held the supplies of linen such as sheets, blankets, towels and so on needed to keep people clean and rested.  A hole in the roof has let in years of rain and snow and dirt.  What is left of once crisp white sheets and warm woolen blankets is now an unspeakable mass of corruption and rot.  There seems something in the very air of this place that causes decay far beyond what one might normally expect.

Dark polished wood gleams dully in the subdued light of the entry hall of the manor.  Black and white tiles form a diamond pattern on the floor, reflecting the elegant taste of a bygone time.  Giant racks of antlers and mounted heads of snarling beasts line both walls.  A moth-eaten and ruined rug that was once the skin of some massive beast is crumpled up in one corner.

This was once the library of the house.  Long ago stripped of any valuables either by the owner or by later thieves, the room is bare and cold.  The tall windows are smashed and broken and choked with crawling vines that have snaked their way in along the frames.  The wooden shelves have been used for firewood as evidenced by the ash on the floor and the soot on the ceiling.  The desiccated corpse of some forest dweller is sprawled across a blood-stained and burnt rug in the middle of the room.

This small and intimate room was reserved for the lord of the manor and his close friends.  Rotting leather furniture and cobwebbed souvenirs of the hunt line the walls and focus on a large fireplace with a carved stone mantel.  Faded tapestries depicting people riding to hounds and pursuing stags and other scenes of blood-sport hang on the blotched and mildewed plaster walls.  Something once made a nest out of the stuffing in one of the couches and bits of fluff drift all over the room.

The remains of a large billiard table are scattered about this spacious chamber.  Tatters of green felt litter the floor and several cue sticks lie splintered here and there.  One wall still holds a dart board though the darts imbedded have become rusty and useless.  A silver and crystal chandelier that once hung above the table seems to have survived the disaster, looking almost incongruous now in its dusty splendor.

This huge room was the banqueting and festive hall for the manor in happier days.  Long trestle tables, now ruined and wrecked, once lined the great hall facing a raised dais for the lord and his noble guests at the far end.  Broken windows have let in rain and wind and the room is fetid with mold and rotfungus.  Once elegant wallpaper now dangles in forlorn tatters from the high walls.  A curious mound squats in one dark corner and from it there seems a trail worn in the muck on the floor.

This room once boasted a fine collection of mementoes of the hunt.  A few mounted heads yet remain on the walls.  Fierce creatures, some of which you have never beheld or even heard of, can still be seen here.  A massive cabinet that once held many curious and unusual weapons is now broken and empty.  One item still stands out, a small table, topped with a single gigantic scale.  You have no idea what it once adorned, but your respect for whoever hunted it rises.

This room was once used for weapon storage and maintenance.  Partly a museum and partly a workshop, racks and hooks for swords and spears line the walls and a small forge and anvil command the room's middle.  A broken boar-spear still lies in one corner, with dried blood on the blade.

Here is where feasts were prepared and the trophies of the hunt were cleaned and dressed for cooking.  Marble-topped tables still stand but most of the wooden fittings are gone leaving only bits and splinters.  A huge fireplace takes up the far end of the room.  Hung alongside it are a few corroded pots, skewers and less-identifiable artifacts.  To the north is the pantry and buttery.

This room has been almost completely gutted.  Only some brass fittings and hinges that once adorned the wooden cupboards remain.  Bits of wood, half-chewed and splintered, litter the floor.  Several stone tables and benches yet remain as well as some deep sinks used for food preparation.  Dried trails of slime criss-cross the floor and some even climb the walls.

A narrow landing sits at the top of a rotted wooden staircase.  Above you is a trapdoor and below you is only darkness and musty smells.  You can make out a row of massive objects below but little else.

Dark and shadowed, the room extends a good ways under this part of the building.  Huge casks stand in a row along the brick wall.  One or two evidence some attack as they seem to have been gnawed on.  But by and large, the casks seem intact.  Thick cobwebs stretch between them and all along the walls.  Dust and mold are heavy in the air as is the stink of rotting wine dregs.  A shadowy arch leads deeper into the gloom.

This room has a surprising chill to it.  Used once for cold storage, it lies abandoned to rot and waste.  You nearly trip over a moldering mess that was once a carcass of meat.  Iron hooks hang from the roof and threaten to impale you if you are not careful.  Once used to hang meat, they are rusty and many are coated with dried blood.  Rotting sacks of root vegetables and grain lie about, apparently left behind and forgotten.  They are ruined by the damp and time.

The space here is somewhat larger than a tunnel but only by a fraction.  To the northwest, deeper blackness shows a path.  Overhead, the roof seems to be startlingly regular and not made of the congealed slime and mud that can be faintly seen upon the walls.  Several large, square stones have fallen to the floor from overhead leaving a gaping dark hole.

From far to the northwest, a faint and ominous clicking sound can be heard.  The walls here are slimy and sticky, making them unpleasant to touch.  Tiny lumps of glowing toadstools along the floor keep you from totally losing your sense of perspective and direction.

The tunnel walls are covered with a sticky, drying, mass of slime.  Small, scabrous-looking mushrooms encrust the rocks here and there and gleam with a faint light.  You can barely make out the deeper blackness ahead and behind you.  The air stings your throat with a smell composed of rotting matter and refuse that makes the worst of the slums you have walked seem like gardens of roses in your memory.

Curving tunnel walls here are thick with a mucous-like substance that sticks to your hands and feet and equipment.  Heavy odors of rot and corruption invade your nostrils and make you gag.  Loud rustling sounds fill your ears.  Among the stinks and foulness, a tiny hint of fresher air drifts from the southeast.

This wedge-shaped chamber narrows down to a tunnel that passes to the southeast.  The air here is heavy with a foul stench of rotting matter and heavy ropes of thick mucous-like slime cover every surface.  An enormous toadstool, thick and tall as a Dwarf, glimmers with an evil yellow glow casting strange shadows all about.
