The shattered remains of the building above litter the ground of this low crawlspace.  A Gor'Tog skeleton lies crushed across the middle by a wide beam, its two large hands resting below the wood as evidence of its last futile effort to free itself.  A much smaller skeleton lies curled atop the first, its arms wrapped around the large ribcage.

Someone has recently died a messy death here.  The walls and even the ceiling are festooned with thick streamers of drying blood.  One cot is soaked with the crimson spew and everyone else awaiting treatment edges away from it as if it were a leper at a wedding feast.  A harried looking drudge is mopping ineffectually at a coagulating puddle of gore in the middle of the room.  You also see the dispensary.

rooms.t: [The Raven's Mask and Leatherworks, Embosser's Workshop]
rooms.desc: Hanging from a beam in the ceiling, a menu board sways gently in the breeze.  At the back of the alcove, a workbench cluttered with brushes, paints and other tools stands beside a mannequin.  The mannequin is currently adorned with a leather gambeson which is being decorated with the crest of the Pantel family.

The shrine room is shaped like a burrow, all corners rounded and smooth.  Mown grasses and meadowsweet stems cover the floor in a fragrant strewing, but the main focus of the shrine remains the statue honoring the god Glythtide.

The back room of the Rialto caters to the fashion tastes of all who have money to spend.  Knick-knacks and other inexpensive items are sold here, as well as some highly fashionable vestments.  Mannequins neatly line the back wall and are adorned with fashions available for immediate purchase.
The small hut smells overwhelmingly of fish.  Stinks might even be a better description.  A young lean S'Kra Mur fellow leans against a large barrel full of water and small silvery fish.
Murky darkness stretches in all directions.

The opulent beauty of Z'hutoya Way lies spread out below.  The northern guard tower is manned by a S'Kra sentry who never takes her eyes off of the street's occupants.  A curved snrhhti horn hangs from a nail in the tower's roof, its surface engraved with ancient sigils.

Rows of large, lush trees sway gently in the ocean's breeze, creaking as though they were old and tired.  The parade of foliage is but a brief line however, and ends abruptly, stopped by the massive walls of a large columnar building on one side and the ornate fencing surrounding the property on the other.  A sizeable oaken door in the front breaks the monotony of the marble structure.

Large loops of grey stone break up the floor's speckled surface into segments of polished marble and swaths of textured border.  The walls continue with this motif, broken by dark lines of mahogany trim and pale shades of white wood.  A lone mahogany door centered in the western wall mirrors a glass door on the eastern side of the room.  Two ornate stairways, one to the east and one to the west, curve gracefully over the doors.

Dreamlike shadows dancing between neatly arranged rows of leafy plants mimic the motions of a flock of yellow and gold butterflies cavorting within the glass confines of the room.  The frosted panes of etched glass, though not transparent, are glossy enough to double the constant shifting and fluttering of delicate wings such that any circling swirl of the flock makes the room explode in showers of flickering color.

Rising to this summit, a set of ornate stairs curves up from the foyer akin to the way a path might wind up a lonely and barren mountain.  It is the decorative banister that also speaks of such a pilgrimage, with its wooden figurines frozen in their upward journey for clerical transcendence.  If the gods look fondly upon the figures' destination, it is not seen in the architecture, as the upper hall is no different in design -- and perhaps no more holy but in the mind's eye -- than the lower floor.

The upper hall is crescent-shaped, beginning at the base of the eastern stairs and sweeping up to this point and around to the west before descending once more to the foyer.  It would take no witty Moon Mage to draw insightful comparisons to Katamba or one of the other moons, but in the end, this basic curve is not a tribute to some lunar orb, nor is it some lofty aspiration to recreate one of their forms, but simply an aesthetically pleasing quirk of the home's design.

Sheer white linens drape a four poster bed in the center of the room, their forms so light that even the gentlest of motion sets them drifting like lost souls, clinging desperately to the posts as if the bed were the only thing that keeps them from the void.  Profoundly silent, the linen's immaterial suffering can be shut out with but a closed eye or a turned head, their resemblance to the unliving ignored.

Dark as the color of fresh blood, a deep red carpet turns the light from a pair of braziers a ruddy shade.  A red-mahogany dinner table, barren of features but for the flickering of maroon shadows, rests directly in the middle of the carpet.  A distinct coppery smell lingers in the air, perhaps from the heating of the brazier's metal trim.

Thick, exposed beams of dark wood officially divide the kitchen from the dining room, but since there are no walls or doors blocking sight to the stove and utensils, the kitchen has been dealt the same opulent treatment as the rest of the home.  Still, a mahogany screen sits in the corner, folded up and ready to be used when dinner guests simply must be spared the sight of food being prepared.

Sectioning off the room is a long counter, creating a secure space for the elderly clerk whose slow movements have been known to anger citizens in a hurry to get on their way.  Mixing with the smell of old parchment is a lingering scent of stale tobacco coming from the direction of a cluttered, heavy desk tucked safely behind the barrier.  Hung above a wooden bench in the waiting area is a painted sign, lending low budget decoration to the plastered walls.

Not much bigger than a closet, this stark white office is dominated by a government issued desk that is covered in neatly stacked papers.  Secure filing cabinets line the back wall, leaving just enough room for the clerk on duty to move between them.  The cramped waiting area intentionally lacks furniture, encouraging citizens to take care of business as quickly as possible and be on their way.

Away from the elegance of the bank's public areas, two burly guards with a no-nonsense air about them protect the iron-lined exchange vault.  Liveried tellers glide in and out, handing leather pouches to the guards, who in turn pass the coins through a flickering moongate at the far end of the room.  On one side, a languid S'Kra Mur Moon Mage reclines upon a plush quilted silk divan as she concentrates upon maintaining her part of the network of gates used by the bank.

The incessant droning of the crowds outside is hardly dulled by the rickety structure.  Attempts to mend the numerous rotted holes in the wood are evident, and many of the attempted fixes display signs of being patched as well.  From time to time, an errant beggar will peek through the door, only to have Thuyza hurl the nearest empty ink bottle in his or her face.
This sparsely decorated room leads into the interior of the inn. Lamps hung on the walls illuminate a dirty carpet.

Crystal lamps hang from the ceiling of the bar, illuminating the room with rainbow sparkles of light.  The walls are paneled with varnished oak.  Soft music can be heard coming from the other rooms of the inn.  A long counter is set up in the middle of the room, with an elegantly lettered menu hanging behind it.

The high ceiling has a crystal chandelier hanging from its center.  Tables circle the hall's wood-tiled floor, leaving a large area open for couples to dance.  Soft music is being pumped into the room from some unseen place.  The walls are covered with festive tapestries.
This room is dominated by a large stage.  The only illumination for the area are the lights set up along the foot of the stage.  A few chairs are lined up on the floor for the audience's comfort.
The room is painted a soft indigo and hung with shaded lamps.  A comfortable looking couch rests against one wall.  Thick carpeting, woven with a intricate design, covers the floor.

The brightly lit hallway ends in a staircase that leads to the second floor.  A beautifully painted portrait hangs on the wood-paneled wall.  Music from other parts of the inn can be heard as soft background noise.  The air smells of freshly cut flowers.

Crystal lamps hung from the ceiling illuminate the hallway.  A staircase on one end of the hall leads back down to the main floor of the inn.  An intricately woven tapestry hangs the length of one wall while four doors are spaced evenly along the other.

The walls are painted a soft gold and hung with silky drapes.  A great oak bed, varnished a golden brown, takes up the greater portion of the room.  Large vases, veneered with gold leaf, are filled with beautiful yellow tulips that fill the air with a sweet scent.

The sweet smell of roses fills this room, coming from a number of vases full of freshly cut flowers.  A huge four-poster bed, draped with silken veils, fills up most of the chamber.  The walls are painted a soft pink with a rose-motif design.  All of the room's wood molding is beautifully carved with roses and leafy vines.

This room smells of unwashed clothes and bedding in need of a good airing out.  A number of pallets are thrown about on the floor, leaving little room to move about.  Shaded lamps provide a small bit of illumination for the chamber.  The walls, once white, have faded to a dingy grey.

A black lacquered bed, carved with gold dragons, sits in the center of the room.  The walls, one of which is completely covered by a large tapestry, are painted a dark blue.  Dragon statues stand in every corner of the room with small lamps held in their mouths to illuminate the chamber.

A single bronze sconce is mounted on the wall rendering a warm glow upon the redwood burl table.  A stuffed grendel is mounted on the wall high above the table and bench.  Hushed voices can be heard from nearby tables and booths.

The heat radiating from the stone fireplace warms this section of the tap room nicely.  The light from the brass lantern on this rough-hewn redwood trestle table competes with the amber glow from the fire.  Barrels chairs line either side of the table to provide seating for many friends.

The walls of this simple pavilion are pale beige translucent parchment panes framed with lacquered bamboo.  Brightly-colored floor cushions lie upon woven split-reed mats to add comfort to the weary around a low standing glossy teak wood table.

Tall ferns and weeping willows provide a sheltered nook for this single stone bench from the outside world.  Small bunches of pure white lilies nestle beneath the ferns, releasing their light fragrance upon the breeze.  The walled garden can be seen through the branches of the willows as their graceful limbs sway in the gentle breezes.

Protected from the other patrons behind tall ferns, the dining table is adorned with a crisp blue linen tablecloth.  Blue silk cushioned chairs sit before each perfectly arranged place setting at the lime-washed table. The soft fragrance of roses drifts from the small porcelain vase at the center of the table.

Pale mint-green walls greet a cream-colored ceiling with a molding of carved willow.  The bent willow furniture throughout the room is accented with celadon green and grey cotton cushions.  An unfinished willow canopy bed is draped with cream gauze across the top of the frame then secured at each post with a raffia tie.

Sparse in conventional furnishings, the room is dominated by a single piece.  A glossy teak platform sits in the center of the room, surrounded by deep red floor pillows.  A thick mattress, covered with a gold satin comforter, rests atop the black lacquered frame.  The walls are covered with a velvet-embossed crimson wallpaper and bordered at the crown with lacquered teak molding carved in intricate designs.

Soft apple green painted walls provide a fresh bright background for a mix of rose reds, strawberry pinks and milky whites.  The red and white floral print drapes match the panels and duvet on the simple pine canopy bed.  White wicker chairs with their pink rose patterned chintz cushions create a cozy nook for conversations.

White beaded board walls and floors are accented in pale blues and lavenders with just a whisper of grey.  Two short stout columns, parallel the floor-to-ceiling window, hold securely in their grasp a pale blue canvas hammock.  Two deck chairs made of driftwood sit to one side of the room.

A plush deep forest green rug embroidered with wisteria blossom covers the mahogany parquet floor.  An ivory satin comforter lays beneath matching pillows stitched with a fern design which, in turn, lean elegantly upon the elaborately carved headboard of a large feather bed.  A royal purple velvet divan sits at the foot of the bed.

An oval-framed painting hangs upon the butternut colored walls above the simple oak mantled fireplace.  Smoothly sanded unfinished oak floors are covered with a scattering of soft pastel rugs.  Large splashes of bright pink peonies are embroidered across a cream colored coverlet upon an oak sleigh bed.  A crochet throw drapes casually across one of the small over-stuffed chairs that snuggle close to the fireplace.

Long, tiered rows of cushioned benches cascade down to surround the stage in a semicircle, designed so that patrons from all walks of life will have a good view.  Softly glowing lamps are positioned low on the walls, allowing them to be easily shaded into total darkness during a performance so that sounds from the brightly lit stage seem to magnify outward like magic.  One aisle, surrounded by a red velvet rope, leads to a staircase accentuated by an arch that is decorated with a large, golden lyre.

Littered with a few discarded playbills, the long, darkened hallway continues towards the rear of the theater.  Yards of heavy fabric do little to muffle the jumble of melodies periodically drifting from a curtained arch, drawing the attention of performers as they pass by it on their way to the brightly lit backstage door.  Hung low on one wall is a nondescript service vent used by in-house staff during their daily routine of caring for the building.

Heavily quilted pads strategically blanket each wall, aiding the area's overall acoustics and muting from the rest of the theater any disruptive off-key notes created by practicing musicians.  Donated by the Rathan High Council of Nine to encourage fledgling talents, a walnut harpsichord facing a padded bench, an ebonwood cello leaning against a straight-backed chair and some tall island drums hiding a bamboo stool are situated in front of shelves stacked with replacement tools needed to play them.

Always being prepared for the next rehearsal or performance, this room constantly bustles with activity as performers, stagehands, scenery designers, prop handlers, costumers, wig and make-up artists rush to and fro, each with their own agenda.  Benches await those times when directors call everything to a halt for a meeting to track their production's progress.  Hung near the backstage door, a shelf is provided for those wishing to donate props to less fortunate entertainers in the chorus.

On each side of the room, wooden partitions form individual cubicles complete with privacy curtains, allowing featured male and female performers to be attended to by their own assistants while collecting their thoughts before curtain call.  Bit players are relegated to the far wall where a mirror stands ready above the long counter cluttered with makeup cases and various other accessories that may be needed.  Tall chairs await entertainers to take a seat as dressers and hairdressers work their magic.

Dark curtains obscure the performer's view of the audience while still allowing them a clear-cut view of the stage as they practice their lines or wait for cues during rehearsals and performances.  Carpenters, painters, builders and designers work off to one side making sure that scenery, set decor, tableaus and backdrops are maintained.  A metal door keeps out those who would disrupt productions by climbing a flimsy ladder leading up to the catwalk or running down the stairs to the orchestra pit.

Dark crimson curtains frame the long opening that looks out into the performance hall.  Oak plank flooring has been polished to a mirror like finish, reflecting the bright candlelight from a row of copper lanterns edging the semi-circular stage.

Arranged at the base of the raised stage, rows of straight-backed chairs form a half moon around a tall stool, allowing the conductor to make eye contact with each artiste during rehearsals and performances.  Thin metal stands, neatly placed in front of each seat, stand patiently awaiting the collected pages of sheet music used regularly by the theater's in-house musicians.  A narrow set of stairs leads discreetly to the wings while also making it easy for staff to access a small vent under the stage.

The stage above forms a wood ceiling for this cramped space.  Old furniture in need of repair and props from past performances are carelessly shoved towards the bare walls, becoming a forgotten document to the theater's history.  Sitting on a chipped table, placed conveniently near a worn-out divan, is a single oil lamp indicating that the space is still used for more than storage.

Hung high above the stage this catwalk consists of intersecting metal girders, allowing set designers, production crews and theater staff behind the scenes access to several props and lighting setups.  Not for the faint of heart, a flimsy ladder leads down to the wings so as not to disturb any rehearsals or performances that may be going on.  Due to the number of accidents that have occurred in the past, signs have been hung to remind the over confident of the dangers involved in working at this height.

The granite of the cliff thrusts out over the water, projecting far enough to give a clear view of the bluegreen water and jagged rocks directly below.  The young men and women here on the rock are all very wet, which is odd considering the only source of water is a truly appalling distance away, straight down.

Sheltered by the mass of the wall surrounding the city of Ratha, inside the stable the sound of the sea wind that is so constant outside sinks to a low murmur.  Soft straw covers the ground, muffling footsteps and the soft "whump" of hooves.  Unused bales are stacked ready, next to an open doorway leading into a supply room.  A small corral contains the horses currently for sale.

Stretching off into dimness, rows of individual stalls line either side of a broad passageway.  Since this is the main stable for the city, a large number of horses are always present, along with workers scurrying about their duties of caring for them.

Barely more than a large closet, the supply room is crammed with baskets, boxes, trunks, and other containers, all holding everything required for the basic care and feeding of horses.  An open doorway leads back to the main stable area.

Verdant sea vines crawl up the arching walls, finding welcome purchase in the crevices carved by rivulets of green-tinged water.  Thick and sinuous, the vines have wedged into small cracks and pried flakes of stone loose, littering the floor with shards of rock that crunch underfoot.
The great slab of granite forming the wall is adorned with a series of fluidly twining designs and has a sense of permanence amid the dissolving limestone.

Broken curls of flowstone, shards of stalactites and shattered gypsum crystals litter the floor of the small stone shelf.  The piles occasionally shift with the currents, sending some pieces sliding off of the shelf into the black deep.

Shellfish line the inside of a thin crease in the stone like pearly white peas in a deep grey pod.  They glow softly in the thin film of light in the water and seem to flicker when shadows pass overhead.

A granite precipice looms overhead, but the umbrageous ceiling is paled by darker shadows stirring below.  Without a clear path to the surface, the grip of the water's depth seems stronger and closer.
The quiet blackness seems to voice itself in the patient shushing of the currents.
The tenebrous deep reveals little but the vague outlines of rusting armor and bits of their former owners scattered across the cavern floor.
Shadows move with you in the darkness, accompanied by muffled barks and wails that bounce and warble through the depths.

Lying broken and slightly askew like a large cracked egg, a pale white Gor'Tog skull gleams through the darkness.  The former braincase has become home to a group of eyeless black fish that weave placidly in and out of the jagged-edged hollow.
Chilling currents pull and push, stealing body heat and making navigating the litter-strewn cavern floor more difficult.
The swirling currents of cold water bear down on interlopers in their realm, seeking to impose their will.
Visible through the thick darkness are the outlines of pale bones strewn across the floor below.
The somber darkness swallows all light and color.  Everything, even one's own form, becomes one with the swirling black.
Something reflective glints weakly through the darkness of the water below.
Muffled echoes bounce along the stone walls from every direction, ebbing and flowing with the gently whirling currents near the center of the cavern.
Shadows tint the waters in deepening shades of blue and violet, like veils of twilight lowered over evening.

Dusky water swirls against the stone, patiently wearing it away over the eons.  A thin vein of softer stone in the wall has all but dissolved, leaving a deep crevice that looks like a black scar in ebon skin.
Iridescent shells and yellowed splinters of bone collect in a small crevice in the stone, safe from the whirling current.

A thin layer of sand shifts across an ebon-veined basalt shelf below that refused to be dissolved by the relentless water.  Strong currents pull across the sliver of stone, carrying loose debris off into the inky deep.

Deep shadows hugging the periphery consume the walls and shroud the edges of the dark water, making the cavern feel infinitely larger.  Even the stout of heart would be moved to a startling feeling of insignificance in the center of the great mountain hollow.

What light permeates the deepening shadow catches on flecks of mica and metallic debris caught up in the current to the south.  Through the clear water, it looks like a dust storm whirling through the nighttime desert.

Silt deposited on the stone floor by the dancing currents lays in concentric ripples pointing in the direction of the water's flow.  The striated sand looks much like the gills of a giant sea creature.
Only forty hands from the surface, the water cools considerably and descends another shade into darkness.

A pile of rusting swords and armor sends a small tempest of ruddy flakes up into the whirling current.  Diminutive black fish dart voraciously through the maze of iron and steel, looking for smaller or slower kin to feed on.

Deep shadows hugging the periphery consume the walls and shroud the edges of the dark water, making the cavern feel infinitely larger.  Even the stout of heart would be moved to a startling feeling of insignificance in the center of the great mountain hollow.

The sound of water sloshing against the stone walls echoes through the cavern, occasionally punctuated by loud plops of moisture dripping into the pool.  Other, muffled sounds linger just beyond the reach of recognition before drowning in the steady rhythm of the water.

Pale streams of light shift across the darkness from an aperture in the rock overhead, settling on no particular outline but glinting from the wet stone.  The dank salty-sour tang of wet stone and decaying algae permeates the cool air of the cave.
Thin light permeates the threadbare cloak of darkness near the water's surface and alights on crystalline pool spar growing on the cave bottom.

A massive weapons rack lies pushed up against the north wall, piled high with pole-arm weapons.  A great iron bell hangs from the ceiling, an alarm in times of need.  A spare stick cot has been erected off in the corner.
Shelves full of swords, maces, and other small weapons cover the dark stone walls.  A spare stick cot lies in an out-of-the way corner, surrounded by racks of plate and chain armor.

Amidst the clamor of competition, this spacious tent provides a place to rest and recoup between bouts.  Several field chairs await the champions whose souvenirs of competition need delicate tending, while refreshments for keeping up one's strength and spirits are provided on a cloth-covered sideboard.  Near the entrance flap, a small collapsible table stands on rickety legs, bearing the Field Marshall's thick book of cheques.

rooms.t: [Winter Spice and Everything Nice, Main Floor]
rooms.desc: The cozy cabin features white cedar log walls and large windows framed by frostspun flannel curtains.  A towering riverstone fireplace dominates the space, its chimney stretching upward to the open beam ceiling.  Gaethzen lanterns shaped like icicles cast a warm glow, while the air carries a rich, inviting scent of cinnamon.

rooms.t: [Winter Spice and Everything Nice, Cozy Loft]
rooms.desc: The loft's slanted ceilings create a snug retreat, with an overstuffed chair tucked into one corner, draped with a blue and white plaid blanket.  A small side table teeters with stacks of well-loved books and a plethora of gaethzen lanterns provide ample illumination.

A lush meadow is covered in a veritable explosion of wildflowers with a path that winds its way past a thriving garden and a hot springs pool partially hidden by a wall of vines before ending near a large riverstone fire pit.  Tucked between the sprawling branches of several huge mimosa trees, an elaborate treehouse is raised on black ivy-covered pillars with a hand-hewn set of stairs meandering through branches to an arched door.  Beneath the house, an archway of braided roots rises from the ground to contain a spiraling portal patterned with endlessly shifting fractals in variegated viridescent hues.

Verdant vines heavy with sweetly scented white jasmine blooms cling to a large trellis to provide privacy within the pool tucked into the hillside.  Along one side of the steam-filled hot spring is a sturdy ironwood table stacked with fluffy cotton towels and an assortment of scented soaps.  Beyond the shelf, a sparkling waterfall cascades over a tall stone ledge and onto a bed of polished river rocks ringed with a lush carpet of moss.

Smoothly curved walls follow the bends and boughs of the trees surrounding the simple structure, with tall windows providing panoramic views of the canopy and an abundance of natural light.  Most of the space is taken up by a large kitchen, its shelves lined with glass bottles containing all manner of cooking ingredients.  In a corner nook, next to the large burnished copper brazier, is an oversized squashy armchair with sage green upholstery surrounded by uneven stacks of books and an eclectic collection of brightly patterned tea cups with sassy sayings painted in cheerful colors.  Beyond the kitchen is a beautifully curved spiral staircase leading upwards, while an arched door leads back outside.

Workbenches of various heights ring the edge of the room, polished ribbon-stripe tops fitted seamlessly into the irregularly curving walls lined with windows.  In the center of the room, directly below a large solarium dome, is a large lifesculpted lirisan desk inlaid with a stunning hex lily wrought of magenta glaes.  A chair of matching viridescent wood is carved to resemble a throne of tangled vines, the back dotted with deep pink flowers carved from druzy quartz.  A spiraling staircase with an intricate cast iron railing leads downward through the leaf-patterned ghostspine floor.

Just to the southwest the road is rutted, with an obvious track passing crosswise over it.  This is where the farmers usually cross with wagons of refuse, and take their pigs to feed on the daaknuts, often in depressingly large herds.  Depressing for any travellers caught on the wrong side of the stream of porcine livestock, that is.  The farmers are doubtless quite happy with the fertility of their pigs.

Brambly bushes create a close thicket criss-crossed by paths littered with fallen blueberries.  The smell of over-ripe fruit lingers in the air like drying honey.  Scraps of loosely woven netting -- an attempt to foil birds -- cling to the shrubs.

Dark green moss dapples the high stone wall skirting one side of the path, and fronds from the bushes overhang the narrow trail in places.  Tiny black ants have built several mounds near the base of one bush.  One struggles with a plump blueberry, straining to haul it back to the nest.

Ruined stalks of corn lie crushed in the dirt, the ears torn from the stem and cast haphazardly about.  The furrow of stricken plants continues to the east and west.  From within the drainage ditch edging the field can be heard the sounds of insects buzzing and something rustling in the vegetation.

Several forlorn stalks of corn still stand, seemingly huddled together for protection against whatever creatures roam the fields.  A fetid smell of stale water rises from the drainage ditch that skirts one side of the field.  Some blueberry bushes are visible to the northeast, just beyond a dirt path.

Water pools at the bottom of the ditch, just deep enough to soak feet and breed mosquitos.  Weeds sprout from the mud, and tufts of grass cling to the ditch walls.  An unseen frog croaks in the vegetation.  Small, almost invisible insects buzz near your ears.

Thick brick walls give way to a whitewashed plaster foyer.  Little effort was spent on furnishing the building, which contains only a platinum arch guarded by a Dwarven attendant and a small office off to one side.

Standing in the plain whitewashed room is a low stone counter made from cut stone blocks.  Vast, countless rows of differently sized shelves are behind the counter, and complex Dwarven mechanisms can be heard as they rearrange the package-covered storage.  Clerks shuffle endlessly back and forth between the counters and shelving as they assist patrons with their packaging and mailing needs.

A dingy iron-barred window allows little light from outside to filter into the cramped office -- in fact, it's difficult to tell whether it's day or night through the grime.  The space is dominated by a large desk behind which sits a surly Dwarven woman busily scratching at her ledger.

The long wooden structure is a single open room with bunks lining the walls and shuttered windows spaced every six paces.  The beds are not much more than planks covered with thin straw mattresses and a green wool blanket, but the barracks are dry and airy.  Colorful silk pennants hang from the rafters above, each marking a victorious battle in tarnished gilt thread and vibrant hues.

The scents of drying herbs mingle with the sharp tinge of camphor and the heavy, coppery smell of gore that underlies it all.  Three labeled willow baskets sit at the base of the tent's center pole, within easy reach of several smooth deobar pallets.  The wooden floor is still damp in places from its most recent scrubbing.

Small rocks and stones have settled in between the larger slabs and boulders, making the talus a treacherous climb.  Underfoot, loose rocks slide free and often mask voids in the pile that can easily swallow and crush a limb.

Flecks of mica in the granite catch the dim light and glisten like silver stars amid a stony grey-black sky.  In this stark terrain, beauty walks softly like cats' steps in the night and those who rush past might easily miss it.

The narrow route littered with scree and broken rock threads its way between boulders and great slabs of stone.  Howling like hounds in winter, the wind calls across the canyon and is answered by mournful echoes.

Cooking smells and a low hum of activity fill the large single room.  A bench-lined table and hearth dominate the eastern wall opposite an ironwood cupboard and tall stacks of woven grass baskets filled with drying herbs.  In the back, several children sit on a ring of pelts stripping yew branches, while others gather near a window for a lesson taught by an older boy with a drawing slate.

The low-ceilinged loft is lined with beds ranging in size from small bassinets and cribs near the fireplace to tall bunks near the stair, each bedpost hung with a small nightcap.  Mosaics of colorful drawings that narrate scenes from fables and folk tales adorn the plaster walls.

Thick walls struggle to contain the blistering heat of the workshop where the fires blaze endlessly night and day.  The flickering flames give a reddish glow to the racks and shelves of tools and equipment, all neatly placed and ready for use.  Workers enter in their protective gear from time to time, checking the equipment and reporting back to a sentry at the entry.

The sweltering heat from the nearby forges is a constant -- the walls absorb and radiate the heat at all hours of the day and night, never cooling as smiths keep the flames stoked.  Most of the stone walls are still rough and the ceiling high, but a counter with a bored clerk behind it takes up space along a tapestry-draped wall tucked away in the back corner.  The pathway along the floor from the north leading to the desk has been worn smooth from the traffic.

This room is set up with the intent of making one person comfortable and two people snug.  The floor is wooden but freshly swept, and a set of faded yellow curtains have been drawn back from the window.  A dresser with a water-filled basin set on top of it and a bed are the only pieces of furniture here, but you get the feeling that any more would have left the room cramped and cluttered.

Tucked up against the stone block wall is an low stone counter showing many dings and chips.  Fretwork screens carved from dark woods surround the counter, sectioning it off from the rest of the square.  Vast, countless rows of differently sized shelves are behind the counter, and complex Dwarven mechanisms can be heard as they rearrange the package-covered storage.  Clerks shuffle endlessly back and forth between the counters and shelving as they assist patrons with their packaging and mailing needs.

Exotic tapestries of every possible description drape the wall ringing the Carousel's core.  A circular roof supports a vast framework of iron and timbers rising to the building's apex.  Countless gears, pulleys and weights within the structure form the strikingly complex and beautiful mechanism which drives the Carousel.

A series of guarded arches line the southern wall.  The complicated framework of iron and timbers spans across the ceiling.  Countless gears, pulleys and weights form the strikingly complex mechanism which drives the Carousel.

Pristine white marble flows from the outer office into the room.  It appears as if the small white marble desk and cabinets are the same piece of marble that covers the floors.  A brass lantern sits on top of a cabinet, burning brightly, causing the area to be overly lit.

This cramped space is reasonably well enclosed, although the rough planks do little to hold back the dampness which seems to ooze out of the walls.  One end of this corridor ends at a small opening, giving access to the hovel outside.  The opposite corner is too deeply cloaked in shadows to judge what it contains.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

The chill dirt floor is criss-crossed by slender lines of light as they pass through gaps in the wooden plank walls.  The 'door' is little more than a heavy piece of cloth with a few loose boards leaning against it to keep it from being blown inward by the occasional stiff breeze.  Deep shadows cloak the far corners of the hovel, undisturbed by light or wind in spite of nature's best efforts.

rooms.t: [Thieves' Guild Bolthole, Beneath a Chicken Coop]
rooms.desc: An occasional feather and the rank smell of the chicken coop drift through the air of the bolthole.  Overhead, footsteps slap against the cobblestoned streets as the residents of the Halfling quarter make their way about their business.  Gaps between the floorboards allow a bit of light to filter in from outside.

rooms.t: [Thieves' Guild Bolthole, Beneath a Chicken Coop]
rooms.desc: Crates are piled one atop the other along each wall, some marked with the seal of the Trader's guild, others conspicuous in their lack of any markings whatsoever.  Boards laid across the crates serve to shore up the ceiling, though bits of dirt still trickle down as wagons roll over the cobblestoned street above.  A shielded lantern provides illumination for those who seek to practice their skills, secure from prying eyes.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

This cramped space runs in a straight line for the length of a moderately sized building.  The lighting provided by a pair of hanging lanterns is little better than complete darkness and the space is restrictive enough to make even the bravest of Gor'Togs feel a twinge of claustrophobia.  Though the space has received enough care to remain reasonably clean, long scratches on the floor reveal a history of somewhat less than gentle treatment.

Shipping crates are stacked throughout the area in a manner that indicates either a very complex method of organization or total chaos.  Each crate is stamped with the names of several locations that were probably intended to indicate their origin, destination, and various outposts through which they passed.  Curiously, however, not a single crate is marked in such a way that indicates that it ought to have ended up here.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

A group of men and women hunker down around a crate in one corner of this small shed, their attention focused on the cards in their hands.  The shack seems at first glance to be a flimsy affair, but despite the splintered boards, no drafts chill the interior of the structure.  Bales of straw piled around the door in the brick wall muffle the noise of the street outside and shield the glow of the lantern hanging from the ceiling.  Rickety wooden stairs lead down into darkness.

Musty straw squelches unpleasantly underfoot, absorbing the water that trickles down the walls of the cavern.  Empty crates serve as tables to hold muslin-wrapped bolts of jewel-toned velvet, pale silk and white lace, rapidly tarnishing silver or small boxes filled with assorted jewelry.  Other crates are piled one atop the other, their contents hidden from view, with narrow aisles running between them.

The floor slopes down to the west and south from this, the highest (and dryest) point in the cavern.  Smoked hams and sausages, bags of salt and spices, all hang from hooks in the ceiling.  Other perishable goods such as fabric are stacked in open crates which line the walls.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

A workbench at the back of the cavern contains an array of jeweler's tools -- a small vice, a brazier, a hammer and some pliers, and other less readily recognizable pieces of equipment for removing precious gems and melting down metals into unidentifiable lumps.  The lamp above the bench is unlit, and the jeweler nowhere in sight.  Wooden crates stacked one atop the other line the center of the cavern, forming small passages through the cave.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

The tunnel widens into a small cavern supported by an ingenious octagon arrangement of interlocking wooden beams along the walls and ceiling.  Mud forms an irregular moat spanned by wooden boards anchored to a rocky island piled high with barrels at the center of the cavern.  Fires burn around the perimeter of the space, helping to dry out the mud and keep the area warm.

Water trickles through the dirt ceiling, falling with a loud *plop* against the floor.  Someone has laid down rushes and wooden boards to reduce the chance of muddy footprints that could lead the guards to the guild's lair.  The passage is narrow enough to require well-fed Gor'Togs to sidle through sideways if they want to avoid knocking against the beams that support the walls and ceiling.

rooms.t: [Thieves' Guild Bolthole, Basement of Noot's Teahouse]
rooms.desc: Boxes and crates have been carefully piled to leave this part of the basement hidden from view.  The low ceiling provides a definite hazard to the heads of taller races as they make their way over to a low door in the back corner.

From this vantage point on top of the tallest warehouse, the Riverhaven Docks can be viewed without obstruction through a narrow gap between two rooftops.  To the west, the Town Hall and the Temple rise grandly above other edifices around the Square, while to the east the roof of the Mausoleum peeks above its vanguard of trees.  In the far distance, a glimpse of Lake Gwenalion glitters against the rustic blue-grey shoreline of Langenfirth.

Someone has thoughtfully placed a few old benches in a tight semi-circle at the foot of the tallest warehouse in the area.  This is the one spot in the Rookery which receives any direct sunlight, and for those residents who are out and about during the day, it makes a reasonable place to sit and discuss clandestine transactions or quietly make arrangements for the next night's activities.

Despite the efforts of some residents to brighten their surroundings with a splash of paint or a scrap of colored fabric hanging in a window, the area's silent and perilous nightly business overpowers the atmosphere with breathless suspense and no small measure of prickling fear.  Upon closer inspection, even the most meager dwelling has a sturdy lock on its door.

Heaped in a corner, a tangled fishing net buzzes with flies and festers with the nauseating stench of rotting fish.  When it was first dumped here, a steady trickle of brackish water dripped off it and pooled into what is now a sticky brown stain in the dirt.  At least, the circumstances suggest it's a pool of water, but in the Rookery any stain on the ground could just as easily be blood.

Stacked in a corner, a selection of rusty handcarts and rickety wheelbarrows leans up against a wall, surrounded by old tobacco ashes and a few scattered food wrappers.  A coil of heavy jute rope hangs on an iron hook nailed to the side wall of a locked wooden shack.  Beneath it, a pile of neatly-folded but grimy hessian tarps awaits usage during the night.

The impacted dirt pathway is treacherously pot-holed and as hard as stone underfoot.  Over the years, heavy rains and hot sun have petrified the deep ruts formed by heavily-laden handcarts passing this way under cover of darkness, their burdens of contraband moving silently through the side streets leading up from the docks, onward bound to unknown destinations in Riverhaven and beyond.

This corner of the Rookery is particularly dank and unwelcoming.  The buildings crowd together in such a way as to prevent any breeze from blowing through and clearing out the moist mustiness from the air.  Various mosses and lichens thrive in a spreading green belt at the base of every wall here, using the rising damp to their best advantage.

The lane closes in a dead end of tawdry tradesmen's entrances.  Several large trash containers lean against one wall, strewing sodden bags and empty food wrappers all over the beginnings of a deeply rutted dirt path which leads off to the west.  The town's refuse collectors are clearly among those people who avoid the area as much as possible.

A ragged lean-to teeters against the back wall of Natron's Workyard, a yellowing ivy creeping around the ill-fitting door of the abode and poking inquisitive tendrils into the cracks in its roof.  A large clump of weeds has sprung up at the side of the lane, thriving in an open gutter which draws away the used washing-water and other refuse thrown from the upper windows of the taller buildings.

The alley widens into a narrow lane lined with coarse structures which crouch up against the backs of the larger streetfront buildings.  Many of the squat huts and shacks appear fairly well-established and even passably maintained, but most ordinary folk are ill-at-ease here and move on as soon as their circumstances permit.  A restless sense of impermanence prevails.

Barely a scrap of sky can be seen above what appears to be a tottering pile of randomly arranged building parts, so cramped and crowded is the Rookery.  Uglier still than the unkempt facades they present to Crescent Way and neighboring thoroughfares, the back ends of Riverhaven's buildings in this quarter are graceless and functional, much like the many workaday dwellings which have sprung up in their shadows.

If this narrow passageway and its equally slender opening onto the alley were originally intended to provide an escape route in the event of fire, Damaris help those caught off guard in the servants' quarters and wayfarers' shanties which form the cluttered and cramped area nicknamed the Rookery.  Only rats can run through here more than two abreast.

rooms.desc: A towering stack of tea chests and wooden pallets sprawls outward from a recess between two storehouses, creaking quietly with every slight settling of one box against another.  Innumerable sets of footprints and wheelmarks criss-cross the alley, etching the signs of frequent business into the dead end's flint and grit surface.  Overhead, a faded wooden sign screeches a protest at every scrap of breeze which sets it swinging on its rusty iron chains.

Enclosed almost completely by the backs of tall structures, the alley is shrouded in long shadows even during the day.  Underfoot, indiscernible discarded items make the footing treacherous and slippery, forcing passers-by to thrust their arms outward, as if sightless, in hopes of grabbing some handhold to keep from stumbling to the filthy floor.

A short step away from the bustle of Blackmoon Road, this sunless alley slips into the shadows like an asp.  A thick silence hangs heavily in the hot breath of the buildings it serves, muffling footsteps and muting the busy hum of the outside world.  The ever-present stench of salt and drying fish crowds in, clinging to clothing and chiding remembrance of the industrious warehouses which dominate this part of town.

Built out of scraps from wooden crates and boxes, the bolthole is little more than a rough shelter from the wind.  An arch at the back of the shelter leads into a brick building in somewhat better repair than most around the neighborhood.  The smell of cooking onions and cabbages permeates the air, almost masking the sour stench of dirt and worse.

No more than five paces from end to end, this tiny room on the first floor of the building is full of worn-out furniture.  Tufts of padding poke out of comfortable chairs, a sofa has a small chest propping up a missing leg, and the low table in the center of the room is marred by water rings.  A clear path has been left between the arch on the outer wall and the cellar stairs.  Curiously enough, there doesn't seem to be any entrance from this apartment into the main part of the tenement.

A lantern hangs by the base of the stairs, casting a soft circle of light about ten paces across, but since the cellar is closer to twenty paces in width, much of the area is in shadows.  More lanterns would pose a risk of fire or the chance of outside notice, always something to be avoided by those who do business here.  The single lamp provides just enough light to see the piles of boxes, crates and barrels that fill the dank, dirt-floored basement.

Dampness coats the walls and floors of the boltholes used by the Thieves' Guild, barely noticeable as a faint, musty odor overlain by the earthy fragrance of wine and spices.  A thick rush mat covers the floor in this shadowed corner, though it's hard to see through the piles of boxes and crates, barrels and bundles, all heaped atop each other.

A tiny sitting area, an overstuffed chair and table, just barely qualifies this room for its designation as a suite yet it still manages to be comfortable and inviting.  Lace curtains flutter softly at the window, tapestries cover the walls adding splashes of color and a featherbed, easily large enough for three, occupies the remainder of the room.

Placed where the sloping roof meets an outside wall, the low oak-beamed ceiling is a rather tricky hazard to the tavern's taller guests.  Insuring that bare feet won't grow cold, an oversized hooked rug covers the floor and a carved ash rocker sits near a pot-bellied stove.  Pushed against the far wall, a brass frame daybed, covered with fat pillows, sits awaiting a tired body.
Convoluted limbs shaped like skeletal arms extend into the narrowing canyon, grasping at passersby.  The path twists and turns until it reaches a dead end.
Convoluted limbs shaped like skeletal arms extend into the narrowing canyon, grasping at passersby.  The path twists and turns until it reaches a dead end.
The rocky slope of the escarpment ends at an immense spire towering asymmetrically overhead.  At the base of the spire, some old bones document the untimely demise of unfortunate climbers.

The escarpment narrows into a rocky slope leading to a crooked spire that thrusts eerily toward the sky.  A singular collection of stones at the base of a stunted tree looks deliberate and purposeful in an otherwise disorganized landscape of broken rocks and rubble.
Towering over the surrounding bluffs and grasslands, this windswept spire provides a breathtaking view for any adventurers brave and agile enough to surmount it.
The escarpment narrows into a rocky slope leading to a crooked spire that thrusts eerily toward the night sky.  A stunted oak tree grows amidst the broken rocks and rubble.
The rocky slope of the escarpment ends at an immense spire blocking out an irregular swatch of the nighttime sky.
The spire twists and turns perversely, while the darkness and the incessant wind make the laborious climb even more formidable.
Towering over the surrounding bluffs and grasslands, this windswept spire is the highest point around for many miles.
Blandly anonymous, as all such places are, the weathered boards of the pier creak underfoot.  Heavy pilings on either side are lashed together by layers of tarred rope.

Darkness can be seen through a small window on the side of the simple room, which is cozy without being cramped.  Large wooden shelves built into the walls hold numerous books, and the area is tastefully decorated, with simple couches that are arranged in front of low tables.  A small returns desk stands near the door, and a few books are piled onto it.

To the south, a shallow pool sprawls beneath the forest canopy.  Its calm surface looks like a sheet of black glass until a falling leaf or skittering insect disturbs the illusion and sends concentric circles rippling outward from their movement.

Grease-clotted sticky black mud lies thickly on the stony ground and a dark mist hangs from the trees.  Moisture drips sluggishly from unseen sources and everything feels cold and clammy to the touch.

Filled with the ever-constant stench of rot, the unmoving air is humid and stifling.  Every surface close to the ground is coated with heavy moss or fuzzy mold that releases nose-tickling spores.  Iridescent slicks of slime reveal the paths of slugs across the smooth bark of a recently fallen ironwood limb.

Long knotted tendrils of grey-green maiden's tress moss hang from the unseen boughs above and fall gently to the ground where the dampness colors them a muddy brown.  A circle of spindly white mushrooms pushes through the spongy mat of rotting leaves and seems too bright and clean to belong in the understory.

The ancient forest seems to resonate with secrets gleaned from having witnessed many ages of men passing beneath.  Shadows cling to everything, making the darkness blacker and further shrouding the understory in mystery.

Sathmoor moss smothers the ground, feeding on the decaying mat of leaves and dead wood.  To the south, a large mound covered with the moss' invasive tendrils resembles a flattened ball of twine the color of dried blood.

Undulating rust-colored tendrils of sathmoor moss twist and tangle through tree roots and a copse of unfortunate mountain laurel that is being strangled by the parasitic vines.  Clusters of the moss' grape-like seeds occasionally drop from the canopy far above, landing with a series of thudding sounds that could easily be mistaken for footfalls.

In the soggy landscape surrounding the forest pool, many species of frogs croak their gravelly songs from the darkness.  There is a great range in their varied voices.  Some have a deep, guttural tone and hold their note for a roisan or more, while others have a higher-pitched allegro song and still others carry the mid-range with a halting staccato.
The smell of death and decay undiluted by even the slightest breeze is chokingly strong.  Each squishy step releases a fresh plume of miasma that hangs low in the air and attracts a cloud of insects.

Gossamer strands of an immense spider web stretch between the gnarled black branches of a dead sourwood tree half-buried in the mud.  The fine lines of the perfectly formed web catch the faintest light and glisten with moisture rising from the wet ground.  Now and again, the web twitches with the movements of its architect, a black orb weaver hidden by the darkness.

The oppressive pall of darkness in the understory weighs as heavily on one's soul as does the muck on one's feet.  Travel is further slowed by tangles of sathmoor tendrils, fallen limbs and mud-clad stones that ambush the unwary.  But the towering trees forming the forest canopy soar above it all and selfishly keep the sunlight all to themselves.

Though too dark to see, a plentitude of insects is evidenced by the constant humming and buzzing that underlies the croaking of frogs.  Other less recognizable sounds occasionally pierce the gloomy silence and echo through the wood.

A fallen tree covered in tufted pillows of green and brown moss lays partially submerged in the dark waters of the shallow pond nearby.  Nearly as tall as two Gor'Togs, its gangly root ball has been pulled out of the soft mud and cleaned of soil by years of rainfall.

The ground slopes down toward a swampy pool to the east and the spongy carpet of decaying mulch covering the forest floor is so soggy here that each step is a struggle.  The towering trees nearby seem rooted in the black muck out of sheer unwillingness to fight against its sticky stubbornness.
Thick clumps of grass cling to the rocky ground, interspersed with a multitude of boulders and rubble littering the terrain.  Surrounding the narrow valley are steep hills, their sides bare of trees.

Spreading out between the bare hills surrounding it, the valley remains rocky and windswept, but a few shrubs cluster along a trickling stream that burbles between some boulders.  Insects dance above the water while overhead bats dart and flit.
Grey hills empty of all but rocks curve around the valley floor.  Shrubs and grasses rise amongst the rocks and boulders of the valley bottom, clinging to whatever purchase they can find.

Hidden by a screen of reeds, the meager stream empties into a modest pool.  A few rocks break the surface while more reeds emerge from the muddy banks.  Barren hills rise above the valley but do nothing to block the ever-present wind.
The cell is completely barren except for a pair of manacles hanging from one wall.  An oak door with a small barred window looks to be the only means of escape.

There's an ever present chill here that's more atmosphere than temperature.  Devices of torture lie scattered about the room, ranging from an iron maiden to thumbscrews.  Several branding irons sit idle in a cold fire pit.  Three identical oak doors, with small barred windows, overlook the room.  You also see a rusted iron door.

rooms.desc: Light bleeds in from the northern passage providing just enough illumination to make out a rusted iron door in the southern wall.  To one side of the door, which has been frozen open by the passage of time, lies a broken stool.

The light is blinding in contrast to the gloom of the other passages as the excavations pass through an exposed vein of quartz crystals.  Phosphorescent fungi, in a rainbow of hues, join the profusion of lichens.  Their light reflects off the gleaming crystals in kaleidoscopic patterns.  The effect is both awe-inspiring and nightmarish.

The tunnel sinks ever deeper into the bowels of the world to the southeast.  Glowing lichens festoon the walls and ceilings of the passage, bathing everything in a sickly greenish light, making the area surprisingly bright.
There's a marked downward slope to this tunnel as it delves further into the cliffs.  Phosphorescent lichens emit a wan green light, minimal and rather ghastly, but barely adequate for exploration.

The high-ceilinged chamber is the collection point for a series of tunnels wandering yet deeper into the cliffs.  Ensconced torches flicker dimly, providing just enough light to reveal some dark markings along one wall.  A slow-moving stream of water meanders out of the southwestern tunnel.

The passage dead-ends at a rockfall.  Part of the ceiling has collapsed blocking any further exploration eastward.  Two heavy doors, one of oak and one of mahogany, are solidly embedded in the walls to either side of the passage.

A rusting iron stove sits in one corner of the room with an exhaust pipe leading up through a rift in the ceiling.  The stovepipe has split along one side and a soft moaning echoes through the tear as sea breezes wind their way down from the surface.  Bits of broken crockery lie scattered about, draped with veils of thick dust.  You also see an oak door.

A half dozen trestle tables stretch the length of the room.  Some wooden bowls and platters covered with petrified remains of an ancient meal are all that remain of interest.  At the northern end of the room, a smaller table has been raised upon a slight platform to oversee the forgotten banquet.  You also see a mahogany door.

A finely carved mahogany table oversees the rest of the dining hall and a skeleton occupies the captain's chair behind it.  The remains are pinned upright by a longsword jammed into its rib cage and through the rotting red velvet upholstery.  Moldering flags from various ships hang along the wall behind the table, the victims' identities long forgotten.

A wall of coarse stone blocks is built across the passage.  Water trickles through the crumbling mortar of the wall in several spots, pooling at the base and wandering off as a small brackish stream.  The sounds of running water echo from behind the wall.  You also see a large granite arch.

Rotten wooden cots covered in moldering canvas fill the room with the scent of decay.  A wooden locker handcrafted from pine stands to one side of the room and a stained sea chest lies at the foot of one cot.  You also see a large granite arch.
The ground here is much drier and covered with fine sand.  Small flecks of granite from the unfinished walls pepper the white sands.  A slight draft carries the tang of salt air.

Cobwebs are draped across the roof of the tunnel in a thick canopy.  The webs are occupied although the source of their builder's sustenance isn't obvious.  Hundreds of tiny black weavers scramble through the curtain of webbing alerted to the passage of potential prey.

Any further passage is halted by a vein of smooth alabaster stone cutting across the tunnel.  A slight breeze, redirected by the rough construction of the passage, comes from no particular direction.  A dwarven skeleton lies on the floor before the wall, a broken dagger still stuck between its ribs.

A short passageway, smoothly crafted of fine alabaster stone, opens onto a shadowed room to the west.  The eastern wall is covered with an intricate set of gear and pulley mechanisms set within the faint outline of a door.  You also see a stone lever set into the floor and a circular stone door.

rooms.desc: The passage ends at a stone staircase leading dimly up to the gloom of the ceiling.  The muted sounds of trickling water come from somewhere above.  To the east, the passage runs off into darkness.

The sounds of the shore fade away as the dank walls close in and the passage wanders farther into the cliffside.  The dampness, darkness and close quarters combine for an atmosphere indistinguishable from a crypt.

A faint trickle of water can be heard through the gloom.  The walls of the tunnel are slick with moisture and small puddles collect to the sides of the passage.  The rushing tides whisper occasional warnings from a narrow gap in the stone.
x: ;e move('go gap'); move('northwest'); move('northwest'); move('climb handholds')

rooms.desc: A cliff wall rises into the fog at the southern end of the fog-shrouded beach.  Every so the fog thins a bit, revealing shadowy outlines of uncertain origin.  Muffled sounds of surf, sea gulls, and tolling buoys sneak through the fog, echoing off the walls.
x: [Deadman Confide's Maze Room] - SCOUT AREA reveals room exits. Can lose sense of direction. A BESCORT is needed.

rooms.desc: A faint trail winds its way up the hillside, barely discernible through the dense undergrowth of shrubs and low grasses.  Weathered roots from nearby trees cross the path, creating uneven steps.  Scattered tufts of wildflowers cling to the slope, their petals trembling with every breeze.  Small stones displaced by passing feet dot the trail, rolling toward the forest's shadowy edge.

The trail opens into a wide clearing surrounded by towering oaks and slender birches.  Clusters of ferns line the edges, their delicate fronds brushing against moss-covered stones.  The ground here is packed dirt, interrupted by patches of hardy grass.  Scattered animal tracks mark the earth, while a hollowed log lies to one side, its interior home to small claw marks and broken twigs.

At the heart of the forest, slender saplings intertwine to form a graceful living arch.  Their braided trunks rise in perfect harmony, bark patterns blending where they meet.  Fresh green shoots sprout from the weave, forming delicate fronds that dangle like ornaments.  The ground beneath is clear of debris, marked only by soft mosses that thrive in the embrace of the arch's shelter.

The forest climbs a gentle slope, where large boulders protrude from the soil like ancient sentinels.  Their surfaces are mottled with patches of pale lichen and streaked with weathered cracks.  Between the stones, small saplings push upward, their leaves trembling in a faint breeze.  Evidence of burrowing animals shows in the loose dirt around the roots.

A narrow path snakes through dense thickets of brambles, their thorn-laden vines twisting in a chaotic weave.  The air is faintly sweet with the scent of crushed berries underfoot.  Stripped bark on the lower trunks of nearby trees hints at the passage of foraging animals.  In places, the trail is barely visible, partially obscured by clusters of creeping ivy.

A shallow stream cuts through the forest, its pebbled banks lined with water-smoothed stones.  Narrow reeds and patches of cattails grow in the calmer pools.  Fallen leaves float lazily downstream, brushing against the occasional piece of driftwood lodged in the current.  Small pawprints in the muddy bank suggest a recent visit from thirsty creatures.

At the base of the mountainside, a grove of silver-barked trees stands in quiet contrast to the rugged stone backdrop.  The trunks curve gracefully upward, their branches tangled with wispy vines.  A faint trail skirts the rocky incline, marked by scattered flakes of stone from above.  The low sound of rustling leaves accompanies the occasional movements of unseen woodland creatures.

Wisps of fog drift above the rock-strewn ground, while denser banks of mist roil overhead, obscuring the sky and the upper walls of the canyon.  Scrubby bushes and clumps of grass cling desperately to the loose scree at the foot of the cliffs, their stunted size and pale leaves testimony to the barren nature of the area.

Large boulders cover the ground, having fallen from the steep cliffs lining the ravine.  One has crashed into a tree, splintering it and scattering limbs and branches across the ground.  A few clumps of grass grow near a few small puddles formed in some of the craters created when rocks from above hit the ground.

Some long-forgotten catastrophe has brought down one cliff, creating a rockslide that blocks further progress.  A small start has been made at clearing the rockfall, but the small piles that have been removed only serve to show how much more remains in clearing the blockade.  What is unclear is who or what would be working to clear the impediment and why they would want to.

Granite walls loom out of the ever-present mist, towering high above the stony canyon floor.  Mist and fog flow across the ground and ooze amongst the occasional bush that grows in the scanty soil.  An occasional crash echoes through the ravine, but the source remains unknown.

A wide arbor of bent oak marks a curious corridor, moss dripping from branches and thick vines curling up trunks lending a near total wash of green.  A rustling can be heard all around, and faint snickers echo from the trees.

At the center of the clearing, a dense copse of poplar grows intertwined, forming a massive spiral of foliage that seems to shake with constant movement.  The forest is otherwise somewhat sparse here, the grass curiously picked clean of bristle or burr.
At the center of the clearing, a dense copse of poplar grows intertwined, covering a large boulder at the base.  The trees appear to have grown around the stone, nearly entirely engulfing it.

The dense copse at the center of the clearing bears several gaps in the foliage, allowing a view of the inside of the twisted trees.  Curiously, there is a total lack of any nests in the trees branches.

A quiet passage lined with plush gold-edged maroon carpeting and polished rosewood paneling runs along the back of the inn.  Trophies from hunting expeditions hang upon the walls -- a snarling snowbeast captured in a lifelike pose, and a buffalo head looming over those who pass through the corridor.  Unlike the upstairs rooms, these apartments are owned by their residents, local citizens who prefer the convenience of life at the inn.

rooms.desc: Carved mahogany moldings run the length of the hallway, the dark wood contrasting with the polished rosewood paneling on the walls.  The head and claws of a black leucro are mounted upon a wooden shield on the wall, the green glass eyes balefully surveying all who pass beneath its stretch of hall.  On the opposite wall, a hunting scene is mounted in a gilded frame.

The corridor bends to the northeast past the majestic figure of a desumos.  A triumph of the taxidermist's art, the golden mane and tawny pelt maintain their original sheen, while the glittering blue glass eyes and ivory fangs add to the realism.  Residents have donated crested wooden shields which hang upon rich silk banners along the walls.

A golden sunburst is inlaid into the rosewood paneling at the end of the hallway.  Carved within the sunburst is the image of a phoenix rising from the flames, its wings outstretched toward the sky.  The soft gleam of the gold is reflected in the rosewood walls.  In the corner, a brass pot holds an oversized fern.  The feathery fronds tumble over the sides of the pot to gently brush the deep maroon carpet.

Sunlight spills down into the room from the domed skylight far overhead, bathing the impressive collection of rare blooms that occupy the periphery of the foyer.  The vines of climbing plants have been allowed to entwine the elegant columns that buttress the high roof, lifting the greenery high above the marble floors.  A small artful waterfall and pond fills the space between a split marble staircase leading to the balcony above.

The taproom is smoky, dimly lit by lanterns hung upon the walls, and the heavy beams that support the floor above are low enough to make a Gor'Tog duck when entering.  Still, the room is kept clean, right down to the scarred but patiently cared for hardwood floor.  Opposite the bar, a cozy fire crackles merrily in the soapstone fireplace beneath an old oil painting.

Thick red woolen rugs with interweaving patterns of blue and green cover the marble floor of the balcony all the way from the intricately wrought iron railings to the tapestries that hang against the back wall.  Busts of several notable citizens of years past perch atop alabaster pedestals along the length of the wall, flanking both sides of a wide arch.

A gorgeous parquet dance floor stretches the entire width of the building, flanked on either side by tall windows letting in the daylight that gives the wood floor a honey-colored glow.  At the far end of the room, a long buffet table stands ready to refresh the guests of the house beneath a large gold framed painting of the great tower.  Hanging above the dance floor is a crystal and silver chandelier, dazzling the eye even though it remains unlit during the day.

Dominating the room is a heavy mahogany table surrounded by several high-backed chairs, placed here for smaller semi-formal gatherings.  Panels of dark wood cover the walls on one side of the room while a set of leaded glass windows framed by heavy draperies fronts the street on the other.  A large rough-cut granite fireplace next to a suit of armor at one end of the room contains a low fire to keep any chills out of the room.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, South of the Fountain]
rooms.desc: Dim twilight shrouds the fountain to the north, and the sound and smell of rushing water fills the air.  Small gaethzen orbs are set around the room, illuminating the edge while keeping the center shrouded in shadow.  An arched walnut door leads back into the foyer, while northwest and northeast lead around the fountain.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, East of the Fountain]
rooms.desc: Dim twilight shrouds the center of the large room in shadow, though the sound of rushing water can be easily heard from a nearby fountain.  To the east, twin oil lanterns hang from the mirrored underside of a low balcony, lighting a prominent display case in front of a row of small statues.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, North of the Fountain]
rooms.desc: The balcony's overhang in this area recedes somewhat, giving a good view of the dome above.  The sound of rushing water from a cascading waterfall comes from the back of an ornately carved fountain in the center of the room.  A large arch leads northward into a low hallway, while southeast and southwest lead around the fountain.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, West of the Fountain]
rooms.desc: Obsidian tiling running along the wall's lower border depicts many different phases of Xibar, Katamba, and Yavash, ranging from new to full.  Small gaethzen orbs set near the base of the wall illuminate the black marble floor.  In the exact center of the room, an intricate mosaic set in the floor forms a large image of a waxen conjunction of all three moons eclipsing the sun.  A double set of pillars leads into a well-lit hallway west of the large round room, opposite a large fountain shrouded in shadow.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, West Hall]
rooms.desc: A faint scent of cedar fills the air of a narrow hallway lit by dim torchlight.  Pushed against the west wall is a small table, which has an elegant vase sitting upon it, but the room has little decoration otherwise.  Rich mahogany carpeting continues southward down the hallway, while a narrow door leading into the library is at the north end of this narrow hall.

The hallway ends abruptly in a simple dead end, with no doors leading into other rooms.  The rich carpeting changes from dark red to a deep Katamba-black shade, but no curtains or other decorations distinguish this space.  Standing alone, a small table has been set up in this area, and a small tray sits on a shelf.  Elegant robes and other clothing have been hung on a rack bolted to the wall, while a stand holds a variety of hooded cloaks.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, Hall of Portraits]
rooms.desc: Gracing the walls of this narrow hallway is a long row of portraits, which depict the faces of several stern-looking Elothean nobles.  Despite the lack of windows, the room is well lit by several torches on either side of the walls.  The air has an overly clean, somber feeling, and the hall appears to be freshly dusted.  To the west is an elegant set of double doors and to the east the hallway narrows somewhat.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, Spiral Staircase]
rooms.desc: The torchlight is somewhat dimmer at this end of the hallway, where a row of portraits continues from the west.  A thin slash cuts diagonally through the canvas of the two portraits furthest east, both of which have been set behind thin panes of glass.  A large stylized image of the House crest hangs at the end of the hallway, and a spiral staircase of cast iron leads upward.

rooms.t: [House of the Waxen Moons, Observatory Entrance]
rooms.desc: The expanse of glass overhead is very dark, very little of the outside world visible through the large dome.  Small gaethzen orbs illuminate the path, periodically set into posts on the burnished hand railings.  Standing watch over a cast-iron spiral staircase is a pair of potted mistwood saplings, each decorated with an array of small crystals which refract the light from a small lamp behind each tree, illuminating the leaves like a swarm of fireflies.

Subtle scents mix together from pale-colored flowers in a narrow garden bed, which is well tended.  Planted near the wall, pruned bushes of blueberries and white bleeding heart are backed by a thin trellis covered in white moonflower ivy.  Save for the twilight from the glass dome overhead, the path is lit only by a few paper lanterns, making the delicate blooms stand out.

Paper lanterns on poles line a large garden with ferns surrounding mock orange flowers on this side of the balcony.  Water runs through the garden, passing beneath a trellis hung with thick silver lace vines that stand out in the dim light.  At the edge of the balcony, below the opening in the dome, is a low marble bench next to a small telescope.

Set into the shale tiling on the floor is a wide stream, which has been closed in with a single sheet of thick glass.  Red-stained gaethzen orbs are set periodically in the water, making the rushing stream glow like liquid fire.  A burnished railing glimmers faintly in the light from the stream, leading around an open area in the center of the room.

Soft, even light bathes the foyer, given off by a shimmering portal in the center of the north wall.  A large tapestry hangs beside a tall statue of a S'Kra Mur Bard, her mouth open in song and one arm reaching out toward the colorful fabric.  To the east, an ornate door stands open.

A large curved desk is positioned to face visitors entering the office of the Guildleader.  Several worn benches and chairs line the walls for students to wait or assemble for an impromptu class.  Just inside the doorway, a glass display rests on a scorched iron tripod.

The rough-hewn wooden walls of the lean-to tilt at uneven angles, the packed dirt floor worn smooth in places and scuffed in others.  A rusted lantern flickers weakly on a crooked, scratched table, casting uneven light that dances across the area.  Stale air carries the tang of salt and the ubiquitous stench of rotting rubbish.

Windows high up in the stone walls provide just a hint of fresh air over the stench of burning coal and molten metal.  Supported by chains from a wooden beam, a heavy ceramic crucible swings over the fire or over to the molds lined against the wall.  Shovels protrude from a pile of fuel nearby, the blackened coal waiting to be added to the fire.

A massive iron anvil mounted on a granite pedestal stands in the center of the tiled floor.  Against the wall, a iron forge awaits things to heat, casting a reddish glow over the room.  Small windows high in the wall and open stacks overhead draw some of the heat outside to mingle with the dusty air.

Sparsely furnished, the space was designed to serve its function with little fanfare.  A wide counter staffed by a rotating crew of clerks sits along one wall.  As one clerk disappears to fetch the wares their patron has requested, another swiftly takes the space to maintain a steady, efficient flow of wares and customers.

Neatly pressed, the colorful folds of the pavilion drape in precise lines, forming an octagonal floorplan over a tightly woven rush mat dyed with heraldic patterns.  The air hums with quiet chatter as discerning shoppers drift between displays, appraising the neatly arranged wares.

Neatly pressed, the muted folds of the pavilion fall in orderly pleats, forming an octagonal floorplan atop a rush mat dyed in soft greys and pale gold.  The hush of reverent voices threads through the air as robed patrons move with care among low tables and raised pedestals.  Each display bears tokens of solemn devotion.

Bits and pieces of lumber have been haphazardly nailed into a makeshift stall that creaks anytime a moderate breeze passes.  Most patrons observe the merchandise on display from just outside the perforated ceiling before stepping forward to rapidly make their purchases.  Luckily, the staff is quick to help shoppers and only a few dozen nails erupting from the walls pose any other danger.

The mowed field has piles of hay stacked all over.  Poles hung with colorful paper lanterns line the edge of the range.  Chalk lines have been put down and marked with numbered flags from one end of the clearing to the other.
